name: Mississippi Today
title: Mississippi reelects all four of its US House members
description: Voters fill out their ballots at Briarwood Presbyterian Church in Jackson during the midterm elections on Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026.
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
Mississippi’s four U.S. House incumbents easily won new two-year terms Tuesday. 
Democrats are attempting to reclaim a majority in the lower chamber of Congress, and they looked poised to do so as early results from around the country began pouring in. But Mississippi’s House incumbents, three of whom are Republicans, were all re-elected. 
1st Congressional District
In the 1st District in northern Mississippi, Republican Rep. Trent Kelly won a seventh term, defeating attorney Cliff Johnson, director of the MacArthur Justice Center and a professor at the University of Mississippi School of Law. 
The Associated Press declared Kelly as the winner, leading with 64% of the vote in incomplete and unofficial totals, and Johnson receiving 34.6%. Johnny Baucom, a Libertarian candidate from Columbus, trailed both with 1.4%. 
The historically conservative district stretches from northeast Mississippi to the populous DeSoto County on the northwestern side of the state.

Kelly serves on the House Armed Services Committee and chairs the Seapower and Projection Forces Subcommittee. He is the vice chair of Intelligence and a member of the Agriculture Committee. He has been a staunch defender of President Donald Trump, particularly the president’s defense and national security decisions.
Before becoming a law school professor, Johnson worked for five years as an assistant U.S. attorney during the Clinton administration. He had been hoping to become the first Democrat to represent Mississippi’s 1st District in Congress since Travis Childers won in 2008.  
Kelly first won a special election in 2015 to fill the seat after the death of former Rep. Alan Nunnelee. He has since been reelected to a full term six times.
2nd Congressional District
In the 2nd District in central and western Mississippi, longtime Rep. Democrat Bennie Thompson defeated Republican challenger Ron Eller, a cardiac physician’s assistant from Jackson.  
The Associated Press declared Thompson as the winner with incomplete and unofficial results, leading with 65.5% and Eller receiving 32%. Bennie Foster, an independent candidate from Jackson, trailed both with a little over 2%.
A native of Bolton, Thompson has represented the 2nd District covering Jackson and the Delta since 1993. He is the current ranking member and former chairman of the Homeland Security Committee.
A civil rights leader and former chair of the House Select Committee investigating the Jan. 6 Capitol attack, Thompson is a towering figure in state and national politics. That status has made him the prime target of Republican state leaders, who are poised to redraw his seat through redistricting after the U.S. Supreme Court’s Callais decision that gutted the Voting Rights Act earlier this year.
Thompson, the lone Democrat and lone Black member of Mississippi’s congressional delegation, has dominated his reelection contests ever since first entering Congress. 
3rd Congressional District 
In the 3rd District in central Mississippi, four-term Rep. Republican Michael Guest defeated Democratic challenger Michael Chiaradio, a farmer and entrepreneur from Shubuta.
The district covers central portions of the state, such as the GOP stronghold of Rankin County, and stretches from the Louisiana border in the west to rural Alabama border towns in the east.
Guest serves as chair of the House Ethics Committee, and also serves on the Homeland Security and Appropriations committees. He ran a steady, low-profile campaign, appearing at local events hosted by the Mississippi Federation of Republican Women and with U.S. Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith.
Chiaradio, a first-time candidate for Congress originally from New Jersey, is a former baseball player turned farmer living in rural Mississippi. He told Mississippi Today that he believed a localized message built around economic frustration could unite both disaffected conservatives and a fractured Democratic Party. 
4th Congressional District
In the 4th District in southern Mississippi, Republican Rep. Mike Ezell won a third term, defeating Democratic state lawmaker Jeffrey Hulum. 
The Associated Press declared Ezell as the winner, leading with 57.7% and Hulum receiving 39.5% with. Carl Boyanton, an independent candidate from Diamondhead, trailed both with 2.8%.
A native of Pascagoula, Ezell was formerly sheriff of Jackson County. He entered Congress after defeating former Republican U.S. Rep. Steven Palazzo in 2022. Before that, Ezell was the Jackson County sheriff. He serves on the Natural Resources Committee and the Transportation and Infrastructure Committee. 
Ezell has said he wants to introduce legislation that rolls back unnecessary federal regulations at the Federal Emergency Management Agency to make it easier for state and local governments to receive relief after natural disasters damage Mississippi communities. 
Hulum had been attempting to become the first Democrat to win the southern district since 2008. He currently represents Gulfport in the Mississippi House of Representatives, and he served in the U.S. Army for 22 years, retiring as a sergeant major. If elected, Hulum would have been be the first Black person to represent the 4th Congressional District.

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: Alan Wilson declares victory in SC governor’s race; Johnson concedes
description: COLUMBIA — South Carolina’s four-term GOP attorney general is moving to the Governor’s Mansion. Voters elected Republican Alan Wilson as South Carolina’s next governor and state Sen. Mike Reichenbach as lieutenant governor.  When Democratic state Rep. Jermaine Johnson conceded at 10:31 p.m., Wilson was leading with 52% of the vote, with 90% of votes counted,[...]
text:
South Carolina Republican Party Chairman Drew McKissick addresses the crowd at the GOP election night watch party on Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026, at the Moore Building on the South Carolina State Fairgrounds in Columbia. (Photo by John A. Carlos II/Special to the SC Daily Gazette)COLUMBIA — South Carolina’s four-term GOP attorney general is moving to the Governor’s Mansion. 
Voters elected Republican Alan Wilson as South Carolina’s next governor and state Sen. Mike Reichenbach as lieutenant governor. 
When Democratic state Rep. Jermaine Johnson conceded at 10:31 p.m., Wilson was leading with 52% of the vote, with 90% of votes counted, according to unofficial results. 
Johnson said he spoke to Wilson, who said he needed Johnson’s help to unite South Carolina. When he gets home, he’ll pray for Wilson, Johnson said.
“I believe that when we wish our leaders to fail, we are wishing our own selves to fail,” Johnson said at his election night party at Brookland Baptist Church in West Columbia “So, I don’t want him to fail. I want him to be the best governor this state has ever seen.”
The results were much closer than expected. The Associated Press had yet to call the race when Johnson conceded.
Wilson will take the helm from his former boss, Gov. Henry McMaster, South Carolina’s oldest and longest-serving governor in state history. Wilson was an assistant attorney general when McMaster was the state’s chief prosecutor.
Wilson, whose 31 years in the Army National Guard includes a combat tour in Iraq, campaigned as a career prosecutor and career soldier who will “continue to fight for the state of South Carolina.”
His platform included familiar GOP pledges to push for lowering taxes, expanding school choice, and continuing to “back the blue.”
He’s touted working with local, state and federal law enforcement officers in a tenure that spanned two Democrats and one Republican in the White House.
“I earned the respect of a large majority of the sheriffs and law enforcement in this state because they trust me to fight for you,” Wilson said last Thursday during a GOP rally in Rock Hill ahead of President Donald Trump taking the stage. 
“I’m honored that they have my back, and I’m going to have their back because they’ve got your back. And I’ve also got Donald Trump’s back because he has your back.” 
He’s gone to court repeatedly to combat the Obama and Biden administrations and support the Trump administration. Last year alone, Wilson’s office announced joining other Republicans or declared victory on more than 60 multi-state lawsuits.
Inside Alan Wilson’s historic GOP primary victory over Pamela Evette

Yet, he didn’t initially have Trump’s endorsement.
The president instead backed Lt. Gov. Pamela Evette ahead of a contentious, five-way GOP primary in June, propelling her into a first-place finish heading into the runoff, though by less than 3 percentage points. With Wilson showing momentum and picking up endorsements from their former competitors, Trump endorsed Wilson too — saying voters couldn’t go wrong with either candidate.
Wilson then trounced Evette by 37 percentage points, a historic margin, to become the GOP nominee.
Wilson, a native of Lexington County, noted during the runoff debate that Evette, the lieutenant governor since 2018, moved to South Carolina from Ohio 20 years ago.
He was the first gubernatorial candidate of either party to pick a running mate. He chose a Pee Dee legislator with a common bond: Like Wilson, the adopted son of U.S. Rep. Joe Wilson, Reichenbach was adopted as a child.
The Florence Republican, first elected to the state Senate in a 2022 special election, becomes the first Black lieutenant governor since Reconstruction.
His role is largely up to Wilson. The job of lieutenant governor has no official duties in state law, other than stepping up if something happens to the governor.
When Wilson announced his pick in January, Reichenbach said he hopes to use the job as a metaphorical megaphone to advocate for issues that are deeply personal for him, such as making adoptions easier and more affordable.
Johnson campaigned on a “New SC,” arguing that the Republican dominance over state politics hasn’t delivered for residents. 
South Carolina hasn’t elected a Democrat to the governor’s office since 1998, when state-Rep. Jim Hodges ousted David Beasley. It’s been 20 years since a Democrat won any statewide office.
It was the first open gubernatorial race since 2010, when state Rep. Nikki Haley became the state’s first female and first minority governor. Mid-way through her second term, Haley became Trump’s first United Nations ambassador, allowing then-Lt. Gov. McMaster to ascend to the job in January 2017.
In South Carolina, governors can’t be elected to more than two consecutive terms. But McMaster was in office for nearly two years before voters first elected him, giving him 10 total years.

The U.S. Capitol building in Washington, D.C., on June 29, 2025. (Photo by Jennifer Shutt/States Newsroom)U.S. Rep. Scott Fitzgerald (Official Facebook page profile picture)
Voters returned U.S. Rep. Scott Fitzgerald in the 5th District to his seat in the U.S. House of Representatives Tuesday.
With 77% of the ballots counted, the AP called the 5th District race for Fitzgerald (R-Juneau) at 9:14 p.m. Fitzgerald defeated Democrat Andy Beck of West Bend, winning a fourth term in office.
The 5th District covers all of Jefferson and Washington counties, most of Waukesha County and a portion of Dodge County.
Beck, who has worked in healthcare sales, marketing and customer service for a variety of firms, ran a grass-roots campaign. He raised a little less than $15,000 as of June 30, according to Federal Election Commission filings.  
Fitzgerald, a former state senator who was first elected to Congress in 2020, raised more than 10 times that amount, $1.7 million in the 2025-26 cycle, spending more than $1.3 million in the same period, Open Secrets reports.

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Hoosiers reject a possible casino in northeast Indiana
description: A new casino won’t be coming to northeast Indiana after voters in those counties rejected a referendum to add gaming Tuesday. Public Question No. 3 in Allen, DeKalb and Steuben counties asked, “Shall inland casino gambling be permitted in (your) county?” According to the Fort Wayne Journal Gazette, more than 58% — or 6,234 votes […]
text:
Gaming operators from around the nation can now bid to build a new casino in XXXX. (Getty Images)A new casino won’t be coming to northeast Indiana after voters in those counties rejected a referendum to add gaming Tuesday.
Public Question No. 3 in Allen, DeKalb and Steuben counties asked, “Shall inland casino gambling be permitted in (your) county?”
According to the Fort Wayne Journal Gazette, more than 58% — or 6,234 votes – voted no in Steuben County, according to unofficial final results. Nearly 65% – or 7,374 voters – opposed the casino in DeKalb County.
Allen County results were still coming in, but 59% of the votes were opposed with 98% reporting.
Business groups in Allen County backed the project as an economic development tool while opponents criticized gambling as a predatory enterprise that would be bad for Hoosiers.
An Indiana Gaming Commission study projected that an Allen County casino could generate $204 million in revenue and $61 million in annual state taxes. Steuben County Economic Development Corp. released a feasibility study in April with its own case for a casino there.
Lawmakers left Indianapolis off the list because it would take away business from two existing casinos in Shelbyville and Anderson. Some also preferred the unserved northeast Indiana corner because it would draw patrons from Ohio and Michigan.
House Enrolled Act 1038, approved earlier this year, authorizes a new license for an inland casino in one of the three northeast counties and knocks off one unused “racino” license for horse-racing wagering with slot machines.
Casino developers were to submit applications to the Indiana Gaming Commission by Dec. 1. If they reject the casino idea, the law provides, “a second public question under this section may not be held in that county.”
Whichever developer is selected would be required to invest at least $500 million across the prospective casino and non-gambling amenities, with at least 60% spent within two years of the license authorization.  The rest must be invested — and the development completed — within five years of when operations begin.
They’d also pay a fee to the state: $100 million for the license and $50 million to support former host communities hurt by casino closures. Additional payments to the host community or state could be part of the deal, too.

text:
Jon Echols, Oklahoma's next attorney general, speaks during the GOP Election Night Watch Party, Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026, at Skirvin Hotel in Oklahoma City. (Photo by Kyle Phillips/For Oklahoma Voice)OKLAHOMA CITY — Republican Jon Echols is set to be Oklahoma’s next attorney general.
Echols will succeed Attorney General Gentner Drummond who launched an unsuccessful bid for governor rather than seek a second term. 
He won the election over Democrat Nick Coffey. Echols said Coffey is a “good man” who ran a “valiant race.”
“This is just the end of our race, but this is the start of our mission,” Echols said during his victory speech at the Skirvin Hotel in Oklahoma City. “We campaigned on a simple platform, and that is that we are going to create: a safer, freer, stronger Oklahoma.”
He said as the next attorney general, he will ensure the law applies equally to all regardless of party affiliation.  
Echols, 46, served in the Oklahoma House for 12 years and was the majority floor leader for eight of them. He holds a law degree from Oklahoma City University.  
Echols lives in Oklahoma City where he practices law in civil litigation, regulatory compliance and consumer protection. 
He’s also owned healthcare and construction companies.
As attorney general, Echols has said he wants to protect the freedoms of Oklahomans and uphold Judeo Christian values, protect landowners from foreign interests and stand with President Donald Trump.
Echols will be sworn in as attorney general Jan. 11.

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Democrat J.D. Ford declares victory over Victoria Spartz in major upset for Indiana’s 5th District
description: Hoosier Democrat J.D. Ford declared victory in a major political upset Tuesday night, unseating three-term Republican U.S. Rep. Victoria Spartz in Indiana’s 5th Congressional District and flipping a seat the GOP had held for years. Ford, a two-term state senator from Indianapolis, defeated Spartz in a closely watched contest that became one of Indiana’s most[...]
text:
Republican U.S. Rep Victoria Spartz, left, speaks with Democratic state Sen. J.D. Ford following a news conference about flooding damage in Carmel, Indiana, on Aug. 31, 2026. (Photo by Tom Davies/Indiana Capital Chronicle)Hoosier Democrat J.D. Ford declared victory in a major political upset Tuesday night, unseating three-term Republican U.S. Rep. Victoria Spartz in Indiana’s 5th Congressional District and flipping a seat the GOP had held for years.
Ford, a two-term state senator from Indianapolis, defeated Spartz in a closely watched contest that became one of Indiana’s most competitive congressional races as Democrats sought to gain ground in the U.S. House.
With 93% of votes counted as of 10:15 p.m., Ford had received 51.6% of the vote to Spartz’s 48.4%, according to the Associated Press. Nearly 255,000 votes had been tallied at that point.
The victory marks a notable political shift in a district that stretches from Indianapolis’ northern suburbs into north-central Indiana, including Carmel, Fishers, Noblesville, Anderson, Muncie and Marion.
It also ends Spartz’s six-year tenure in Congress and sends Ford, Indiana’s first openly gay state legislator, to Washington after eight years in the Indiana Senate.
“Tonight, Hoosiers made history, and they sent a message that will be heard far beyond Indiana’s 5th District,” Ford said in a statement. “This victory belongs to every person who has felt ignored by Washington, every family struggling to make ends meet and every voter who refused to believe that change was impossible. Hoosiers are demanding leaders who put people ahead of powerful interests and deliver results that make their lives better. I’m truly honored that Hoosiers have trusted me to be the person who fights for that change, and that’s exactly what I intend to do.”
Spartz won reelection two years ago by more than 18 percentage points, and she carried the district by an even wider margin in her race before that. Her first congressional victory, in 2020, was much narrower, before Republican lawmakers redrew Indiana’s congressional boundaries the following year.
Ford’s win gives Democrats a pickup in Indiana as both parties compete for control of the U.S. House.
A competitive race in Republican territory
Ford’s challenge to Spartz drew growing attention from national Democrats in the months leading up to Election Day.
The Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee added Indiana’s 5th District to its list of competitive races in August, targeting a seat that had become more reliably Republican after the 2021 redistricting process.
An internal poll commissioned by Ford’s campaign over the summer showed Spartz leading 48% to 46%, within the survey’s margin of error. A separate poll released in October by House Majority PAC, a Democratic-aligned super PAC, put a generic Republican candidate at 48% and a Democrat at 47%.
The race also drew increased scrutiny from national election analysts.



Quotation







Hoosiers are demanding leaders who put people ahead of powerful interests and deliver results that make their lives better.


– Democrat congressional candidate J.D. Ford


Just days before the election, the Cook Political Report moved the contest from “Likely Republican” to “Leans Republican,” as the race grew more competitive.
Spartz acknowledged the political challenges ahead of the election.
In an October interview with State Affairs, the congresswoman described an “extremely difficult political environment,” pointing to economic concerns, population changes in the district and the possibility of lower Republican turnout in a midterm election.
“So the political environment is challenging, and we are not taking this election for granted,” Spartz said.
Ford’s victory adds to recent Democratic gains in Hamilton County and the surrounding Indianapolis suburbs, where Republicans have traditionally been dominant.
Competing messages on costs and accountability
Ford, who was first elected to the Indiana Senate in 2018 after defeating Republican incumbent Mike Delph, built his congressional campaign around household affordability, healthcare and government accountability.
He criticized President Donald Trump’s tariffs and their effects on Indiana families, farmers and businesses, while promising to challenge federal policies he said were driving up everyday expenses.
“All across the 5th district, I hear families talk about the high cost of groceries, utilities and gas,” Ford said in a statement to State Affairs before the election. “I will always listen to what matters to the people of the 5th district, and I will always fight to make life more affordable.”
His campaign also called for protecting Medicaid funding, preserving rural hospitals and lowering prescription drug costs.
On housing, Ford proposed restricting purchases by large corporations and international investors. He also supported requiring data centers to cover their own utility and water costs rather than shifting those expenses onto existing customers.
Sen. J.D. Ford, D-Indianapolis, questions Sen. Scott Alexander, R-Muncie, about his bill, which would regulate paid political influencers as lobbyists. (Photo by Leslie Bonilla Muñiz/Indiana Capital Chronicle)
The Democratic challenger pledged to hold regular town halls and strengthen congressional oversight of federal agencies.
Spartz, meanwhile, campaigned on her record of seeking federal spending reductions, healthcare changes and a more accountable federal government.
The Ukrainian-born congresswoman, a certified public accountant and former Indiana state senator, argued that another term would allow her to continue work on federal budget reforms and reducing the national debt.
“I want to finish major reforms I have started, particularly fixing healthcare, addressing our unsustainable national debt and overhauling Congress’s broken budget process,” Spartz said in October.
She also advocated stronger border enforcement, changes to legal immigration and expanded healthcare price transparency.
The campaign grew increasingly contentious in its final weeks, with the candidates trading accusations over Spartz’s family stock transactions, campaign advertising and their respective records.
Ford questioned Spartz’s financial disclosures and transactions involving her famil. Spartz disputed the allegations and accused her opponent of misleading voters.
The candidates also clashed over the terms of a potential debate. Ford called for a public event before constituents and Spartz proposed a televised discussion focused on policy.
From the Indiana Senate to Congress
Ford’s victory follows two terms in the Indiana Senate, where he has represented District 29 since 2018.
His first election was itself a notable upset. Ford defeated longtime Republican state Sen. Mike Delph, becoming the first openly gay member of the Indiana General Assembly.
He won reelection in 2022 with 51.7% of the vote.
In the legislature, Ford has been a prominent Democratic voice on LGBTQ+ rights, education, healthcare and government accountability.
Republican Rep. Victoria Spartz takes questions from a hostile crowd during a town hall on Friday, March 28, 2025, in Westfield. (Casey Smith/Indiana Capital Chronicle)
His election to Congress will also create an opening in his Indiana Senate district, which includes portions of Marion and Hamilton counties.
Spartz, who previously served in the Indiana Senate, first won election to Congress in 2020 after Republican Susan Brooks opted against seeking another term.
Her time in Washington included a shifting relationship with Trump, repeated calls for federal spending restraint and a high-profile reversal of her initial decision not to seek reelection in 2024.
She ultimately ran again that year, surviving a contested Republican primary before winning another term in November.
Ford will take office in January for a two-year term.
“Tonight, voters proved that no seat belongs to a political party. It belongs to the people,” Ford said. “Whether you voted for me or not, I will fight for you. I will listen, show up and never forget who sent me to Washington. To every voter, volunteer and supporter who made this historic victory possible, thank you. Tonight, we celebrate what Hoosiers made possible. Tomorrow, we begin the work of delivering the change they voted for.”

name: National
title: In historic night, voters elect first Black woman, first Black Republican as governors
description: Georgia voters elected the nation’s first Black woman governor on Tuesday while neighbors to the south in Florida became the first to elect a Black Republican governor. Former Atlanta Mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms will be the first Democrat to occupy Georgia’s top office in more than two decades. In Florida, Republican U.S. Rep. Byron Donalds […]
text:
Byron Donalds speaks at a rally in Tallahassee a week before Tuesday’s midterm election. Donalds made history becoming the nation’s first Black Republican elected to governor and the first Black candidate to win statewide office in Florida. (Photo by Jay Waagmeester/Florida Phoenix)Georgia voters elected the nation’s first Black woman governor on Tuesday while neighbors to the south in Florida became the first to elect a Black Republican governor.
Former Atlanta Mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms will be the first Democrat to occupy Georgia’s top office in more than two decades. In Florida, Republican U.S. Rep. Byron Donalds became the first Black person ever elected to statewide office there and the nation’s first elected Black Republican governor.
Those historic victories were called early during Tuesday’s high-stakes midterm elections, when Democrats hoped to claw back state power from Republicans, who have controlled a majority of governorships and state legislatures for the last 16 years.
A total of 36 gubernatorial elections were held Tuesday. As of 10:45 p.m. Eastern time, Democrats had won ten of those contested races and Republicans had secured three, according to The Associated Press.  
For the first time ever, at least three Black governors will serve simultaneously in the United States, according to Tuesday’s unofficial results. Lance Bottoms and Donalds will join Maryland Gov. Wes Moore, a Democrat, who easily won reelection Tuesday.
Before Moore, only two other Black governors had ever been elected: Deval Patrick in Massachusetts and L. Douglas Wilder in Virginia, both Democrats.
The only Black Republican ever to serve as governor was Pinckney Benton Stewart Pinchback, appointed to lead Louisiana during Reconstruction beginning in 1872.
Of the 36 gubernatorial elections on the ballot Tuesday, only a dozen were identified as competitive by the nonpartisan Cook Political Report with Amy Walter, which ranks the competitiveness of state and national races. Those included Alaska, Georgia, Florida, Iowa, Kansas, Michigan, Nebraska, Nevada, Ohio, Oregon, Texas and Wisconsin.
Currently, Republicans boast a 26-24 gubernatorial advantage over Democrats nationally. Aided by mounting disapproval of Republican President Donald Trump, Democrats hope to gain a national advantage for the first time since 2010.
Democrats are also aiming to flip hundreds of state legislative seats this cycle. Republicans currently boast control of 28 state legislatures and Democrats control 18, while three states have divided control of chambers, according to the National Conference of State Legislatures.
Democrat Deb Haaland will become the nation’s first Native American woman to serve as governor after the former Interior Secretary won election in New Mexico. Haaland is an enrolled member of the Pueblo of Laguna.
New Mexico will be the second state to be led by a Native American governor following Oklahoma, where current Republican Gov. Kevin Stitt is an enrolled member of the Cherokee Nation and former Gov. Johnston Murray was a member of the Chickasaw Nation.
In Texas, state Rep. Gina Hinojosa could become the nation’s third Latina governor. The Democrat leads the Republican Gov. Greg Abbott by a significant margin with 56% of the state’s votes counted, according to The Associated Press.
Only two other Latino women have ever served as governor, both in New Mexico: Current Democratic Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham and former Republican Gov. Susana Martinez.

name: Virginia Mercury
title: Virginians protect gay marriage, voting rights and reproductive rights in state Constitution
description: On Election Day, Virginians approved three amendments to enshrine reproductive, marriage and voting rights for former felons into the state’s constitution, the culmination of a multi-year journey through the state legislature galvanized by lawmakers, advocates and major federal shifts.  Over sixty-one percent of voters answered yes to Ballot Question 1 as of[...]
text:
Virginians For Reproductive Freedom campaign director Han Jones gives a victory speech and cheers on supporters after Virginia voter opted to enshrine reproductive rights into the state Constitution on Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo by Charlotte Rene Woods/Virginia Mercury)On Election Day, Virginians approved three amendments to enshrine reproductive, marriage and voting rights for former felons into the state’s constitution, the culmination of a multi-year journey through the state legislature galvanized by lawmakers, advocates and major federal shifts. 
Over sixty-one percent of voters answered yes to Ballot Question 1 as of 10 p.m. Tuesday, according to unofficial results from the Virginia Department of Elections. It asked if access to contraception, fertility treatment and abortions access should be protected. 
On Ballot Question 2, which asked if a defunct ban on same-sex marriage should be removed from the constitution, 56% of voters replied affirmatively.
The third ballot question asked whether the voting rights restoration process for formerly incarcerated people should become automatic or remain petition-based. 55% of voters said yes. 
The mood was optimistic and festive throughout the night at a watch party in Richmond hosted by Virginians For Reproductive Freedom, the coalition of advocacy groups that spearheaded outreach about the first of the three amendments. By the time results were called just past 9 p.m. for the referendum, glasses were raised, excited screams were had, and then dancing continued. 
 Reproductive rights amendment  

The first amendment  drew the most debate from lawmakers, healthcare professionals, advocates and the public — with tears, shouting, and a call of “out of order” on the day it first cleared the legislature in 2025 and increasingly intense campaigns for and against it this year. 
“Never again will our reproductive rights be a political football in Virginia,” said Han Jones, campaign manager for Virginians For Reproductive Freedom said Tuesday shortly after victory was declared. “It takes multi-year concerted work, but as you can see in Virginia, it’s paying off.” 
Constitutional amendments have to pass the General Assembly two years in a row before making it to ballots. The reproductive rights amendment received pushback each step of the way and opposition from every Republican member of the General Assembly while the two other amendments saw slim bipartisanship.
Proponents had sought the measure because Virginia is the only southern state without deep restrictions or bans on abortion. 
After federal protections were overturned by the U.S. Supreme Court in 2022, Justice Clarence Thomas suggested reviewing contraception next. 
That, paired with state-level cases challenging in vitro fertilization, prompted Virginia lawmakers’ holistic approach to protecting reproductive rights. 
It is now Virginians’ right to obtain birth control medication or devices as well as fertility treatments. 
People can also get abortions for any reason through their second trimester and a single physician — instead of three, as in previous years — will need to approve late-term abortions. 
 Same-sex marriages protected

The second amendment voters approved will lift a technical ban on gay marriage and affirm “that two adults may marry regardless of sex, gender, or race.” These unions must receive equal protection under the law. 
Since 2006, Virginia has technically banned gay marriage. 
The prohibition has been rendered moot since the Supreme Court ruled on Obergefell v. Hodges, which has upheld such unions nationally since 2015. 
But after federal abortion protections were removed by the Supreme Court, Virginia lawmakers set to work enshrining state-level protections moving forward. 
“Tonight’s victory belongs to generations of Virginians who organized, advocated and fought for equality, often without knowing whether they would live to see this day,” said Narissa Rahaman, Executive Director at Equality Virginia. 
 Voting rights will be restored to former felons

Virginians also approved the amendment granting automatic voter rights restorations to people with felony convictions who have completed their sentences. 
Historically, the state has disenfranchised people convicted of felony crimes unless they are pardoned by a governor or successfully petition one for restoration. 
The subjective process has not always been clear and restorations have ebbed and flowed across gubernatorial administrations. 
Numbers of grantees dropped under former Gov. Glenn Youngkin’s administration and applicants noted lack of clarity or guidance on the process.
Gov. Abigail Spanberger has restored more than 60,000 people this year.
Proponents of the measure argued that taking it out of the hands of governors will ensure clarity and that people who want to participate in democracy can do so. 
Though a largely Democrat-led initiative, Del. Mike Cherry, R-Colonial Heights, had carried a past version of the bill and voted with his Democratic colleagues to get it to ballots. 
“If a judge didn’t give you a life sentence, we shouldn’t give you a life sentence as a society,” he said in a recent call with The Mercury. “Once you’ve been adjudicated for your crime and you’ve served your time, then your right should be restored.” 
 Reproductive, marriage amendments face legal challenges

A circuit court judge has set a hearing date for Nov. 13 in a case that seeks to strike the reproductive rights amendment down. 
Filed by the Founding Freedoms Law Center, the legal arm of conservative advocacy group the Family Foundation, the case argues the ballot language was “misleading” and that proper procedure for amending the constitution was not followed. 
Founding Freedoms Law Center also recently filed a case on behalf of a pastor in Prince William County challenging the marriage amendment.  
“This fight is not over. It moves today to the courtroom and the Capitol,” Family Foundation president Victoria Cobb said in a statement. “When the blue wave that swept up these amendments recede, voters will see what’s been left in our Constitution.”

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: Democrats, in push for blue wave, continue domination in Massachusetts as they look to take back power in Washington
description: In a national political environment favoring Democrats, Bay State voters chose to stick with Healey and Markey at the top of the ticket for another term in this Democratic stronghold.
text:
GOV. MAURA HEALEY and US Sen. Ed Markey beat back long-shot Republican challengers as Democrats maintain control in Massachusetts, the AP called minutes after polls closed Tuesday, and the party looks poised to win key races around the country in the 2026 midterm elections.  
In a national political environment favoring Democrats, Bay State voters chose to stick with Healey and Markey at the top of the ticket for another term in this Democratic stronghold. The party is set to preserve control of Beacon Hill with supermajorities and send an all-Democratic delegation to Congress yet again in an election defined by voters’ dissatisfaction with President Trump and cost-of-living issues. 
Healey won a second term in the corner office by beating Republican nominee Mike Minogue. And Markey, after defeating US Rep. Seth Moulton in the Democratic primary, secured victory over Republican challenger John Deaton, granting the 80-year-old incumbent progressive senator from Malden another term to stack onto his five-decade career in Congress.  
Both officials consistently tied their opponents to Trump, who had only a 25 percent approval rating among likely Massachusetts voters in September, according to a MassINC/CommonWealth Beacon poll. Registered Democrats outnumber Republicans in Massachusetts by a 3-to-1 margin. 
Healey and Markey both had been leading their respective races by 20-plus points in polling prior to the election. Minogue and Deaton had tried to cast their opponents as failed politicians who ushered in an affordability crisis now hammering Bay Staters who are burdened by soaring housing, energy, health care, and child care costs — forcing some of them to leave Massachusetts altogether. 
In her victory speech Tuesday night, Healey hit on those affordability challenges that aren’t likely to quickly go away in her second term. 
“I promise you this: I’m going to work my hardest every single day for the things that matter in your lives, to show up, to deliver, and to stand up when you need it most,” she said. “Now, that starts with lowering your costs.” 
Minogue, a wealthy former biotech executive, spent nearly $20 million of his own money to power his bid to unseat Healey. No sitting Massachusetts governor has lost in a general election since 1974. 
“It’s our responsibility now to respect the will of the people,” Minogue told supporters gathered in Burlington. “An election determines who holds the office. It does not determine what we believe in.” 
GOP gubernatorial nominee Mike Minogue addresses the crowd at his election night event. (Laura Colarusso/CommonWealth Beacon)
Ultimately, the messages from Minogue and Deaton failed to resonate with voters and could not overcome larger political and economic trends favoring Democrats, even as residents remain concerned with the direction of the state. 
That includes in places like Bristol County, an area where the GOP had been on the rise in recent years and where both Healey and Minogue had spent considerable time over the course of the campaign. President Biden won the county by 12 percentage points in 2020, but Democrats only eked out a 1-point win in the 2024 presidential election and narrowly lost Fall River to Trump. 
But Democrats aimed to channel a nationwide blue wave to reverse GOP gains there and defend a number of vulnerable legislative seats after losing one to Republicans two years ago.  
In addition to Trump’s deep unpopularity, war with Iran and sweeping tariffs have caused gas prices to urge and contributed to a stunted economy. Healey and Markey also pounced on the Trump administration’s aggressive immigration enforcement actions — which have led to raids and arrests in places like New Bedford and Lawrence — and Republicans’ efforts to undo access to abortion.   
This year, elections in Massachusetts also featured a record-tying nine ballot questions on issues ranging from tax and housing policy to marijuana legalization to how elections themselves should be run.  
All told, roughly $25 million was spent supporting or opposing those nine questions as of the latest financial data. Results are still pending, but these measures will shape the policy trajectory on a range of issues and make clear the will of the voting public — prompting consternation from leaders on Beacon Hill about the ballot process, the money tied to it, and the ability of voters to take lawmaking powers into their own hands. 
The outcomes of the ballot questions will also be closely watched. Lawmakers have already teed up their own bills around public records, which would impose less stringent requirements on Beacon Hill than the version before voters, and tax refunds for residents.  
Elsewhere, Democrats across the country are eyeing gains to break up Republicans’ grip on Washington since the GOP secured the White House, Senate, and House in the 2024 election that returned Trump to power for a second term.  
Pollsters in recent weeks moved a slew of close races in Iowa, Pennsylvania, New York, and elsewhere in Democrats’ direction during a midterm election that traditionally heavily favors the party that’s out of power in Washington. But it’s still unclear what exactly the margins will be in Congress.  
In Massachusetts, Reps. Richard Neal, James McGovern, Katherine Clark, and Ayanna Presley cruised to reelection Tuesday, all but Neal running unopposed. As of 10 p.m., Massachusetts’ five other congressional districts had not yet been called by the Associated Press.
In New England, New Hampshire elected Democrat Chris Pappas to the Senate in a battleground race, the AP projected, and Democrats flipped a North Carolina seat by sending Roy Cooper to victory.
Republicans are also defending Senate seats in states like Alaska, South Carolina, and Texas and governor’s offices in Ohio and Iowa — races that had been tightening in polls leading up to Election Day, serving as a test for just how deep into red territory Democratic wins might stretch. 
“Voters have spoken, and Democrats will continue to lead Massachusetts,” said Steve Kerrigan, chair of the state Democratic Party. “Every generation of Massachusetts residents have faced the same choice: Wait for the future to arrive, or go out and build it. And every time, every time we’re faced with that choice, our commonwealth has picked up the tools and gotten to work.”

name: Maryland Matters
title: Months of congressional redistricting fights end with apparent Question 3 win
description: Question 3, the proposed constitutional amendment that would change the way Maryland congressional districts, appeared headed to passage Tuesday, with 60% of voters supporting it in early returns, capping months of fighting on the issue.
text:
Supporters of ballot Question 3, a proposed constitutional amendment that would ease restrictions on congressional redistricting, frame it as a vote against President Donald Trump. (Photo by William J. Ford/Maryland Matters)A Democrat-backed proposal in a Democratic state that was framed as a rebuke to President Donald Trump should have been a slam-dunk, but the fate of Question 3 was still up in the air when polls opened Tuesday.
But as returns started rolling in, it appeared that Question 3 was headed to passage. With 21% of precincts reporting at 9:42 p.m., 60% had voted for the constitutional amendment that could open the door to new congressional maps as early as next year, and roughly 40% had voted against it.
It was the most contested and most high-profile of three ballot questions — all three were winning in early returns — put before voters Tuesday, and one that Gov. Wes Moore had a large stake in.
“For more than a year, I’ve been clear: If other states were going to redraw their congressional maps in the middle of the decade, Maryland should be part of that conversation,” Moore said Tuesday night. “My position has not changed. Donald Trump does not get to rewrite the rules for his allies and then tell Maryland to sit on its hands.
“I am proud that the people of Maryland used their power to push back by approving Question 3,” he said.
Passage of Question 3 establishes that there are no criteria in the state constitution or Declaration of Rights for congressional redistricting. The change would all but eliminate the ability of voters to challenge future maps at the state level.
The ballot question was passed during a two-day special session of the General Assembly in August. It was immediately the subject of separate court challenges in two counties.
Judges in Anne Arundel and Dorchester found the question as written by the Democratic legislative super-majority was vague and insufficient.
The Maryland Supreme Court largely agreed with those findings but opted to overturn orders striking the question from the ballot and instead re-wrote the question — though it did little to make the effects of a vote on the issue clear, as polls showed voters were confused by the ballot language.
Passage of the amendment has been a priority for Gov. Wes Moore, who has called for new congressional maps for more than a year. Moore and others in his party see the amendment as a response to hyperpartisan redistricting in other states. They’ve branded passage as a way to stand up to Republican President Donald Trump.
Republican leaders have said supporting the question on congressional redistricting would take away their voice in the state.
Currently, Democrats hold seven of the eight congressional races. Democrats would like to redraw the districts to make it harder for Rep. Andy Harris, the lone Republican, to remain in Congress. Harris represents the 1st District, which covers the Eastern Shore and reaches into eastern Baltimore County.
Even if the amendment passes, new districts would not be in place before the 2028 election at the same time Trump is finishing his second and final term.
Rashena Draughn, 44,  who cast her ballot Tuesday morning at Maya Angelou French Immersion School in Prince George’s County, voted yes on Question 3.
“We have to fight fire with fire, said Draughn, a ninth-grade English teacher who moved to Prince George’s about three years ago from nearby Fairfax, Virginia. “The Republicans are not afraid to toe that line…. I think that the Democrats, for what it’s worth, should be able to respond in kind.”
In Baltimore, resident Kenneth Allen, 39, said he voted for Democrats, but opted to vote against Question 3. He said he has fears about unintended consequences that could harm Democrats if the maps are redrawn with the intent of unseating Harris.
Allen cited analysis showing that the GOP’s attempt to redraw districts in Texas and Florida could backfire, and voters could unseat Republicans in altered districts.
“They made these maps based off of the 2024 election, and they made some assumptions that they shouldn’t have made. And I don’t want us to go down that same [path],” Allen said.
And if Democrats take control of Congress, as many national polls suggest, that could “put a check on the current administration,” meaning redrawing Maryland’s maps could be moot.
“I don’t think there’s a reason to take away anybody’s representation,” Allen said. “Western Maryland and the Eastern Shore — give them their representatives, you know?”
Voters also appeared to give big wind to the two other questions on the ballot:
Question 1 asks voters to approve a change to the state constitution that would require binding arbitration between state government and unions that represent state employees. It was leading with 75% of voters supporting it to 24% opposing.
Question 2 would amend the state constitution to allow the governor to make temporary appointments to the 11-member Commission on Judicial Disabilities in the event of a recusal, disqualification or vacancy because of an expired term. It was leading by a 67-33% margin in early returns.
Jack Hughes, the president of the American Federation of State, County and Municipal Employees Council 3, called the apparent passage of Question 1 “a win not only for state employees but for Marylanders  who count on the services AFSCME members provide.”
“AFSCME members have worked tirelessly to pass this legislation,” he said. “Now, regardless of the administration, state employees will get the respect and resources they deserve.”
— Maryland Matters reporters William J. Ford and Christine Condon contributed to this story. This story will be updated.

text:
Oklahoma's next Commissioner of Insurance Bob Sullivan speaks during the GOP Election Night Watch Party, Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026, at Skirvin Hotel in Oklahoma City. (Photo by Kyle Phillips/For Oklahoma Voice)OKLAHOMA CITY — In a race that saw both candidates vowing to tackle the state’s soaring insurance rates, voters selected a Republican to lead the state’s Insurance Department.
Republican Bob Sullivan defeated Democrat Craig MacIntyre to become the state’s next insurance commissioner. Oklahoma’s current insurance commissioner, Republican Glen Mulready, could not run again due to term limits.
Sullivan, an independent agent and broker, will inherit a department that’s plagued by a lack of consumer confidence and questions about why the state’s insurance rates are now the highest in the nation.
He said Tuesday that he’s honored and grateful to be selected as the state’s next insurance commissioner.
“My 20-year career in this industry has taught me that we have problems in our state that require a specific skill set, and we bring that skill set to the Oklahoma insurance department,” Sullivan said. “And we’re going to bring insurance companies into a more realistic frame, bring back affordability to our marketplace, make sure your claims are paid, and make Oklahoma insurance great again. Make insurance fair again for the state of Oklahoma.”
The Insurance Department has two constitutionally mandated responsibilities — implement and enforce the state’s insurance laws and advocate for consumers.
Sullivan has vowed to wield a new state law that gives the commissioner increased oversight over insurance companies seeking to increase rates before they happen. He wants to use that law, which takes effect next year, to ensure Oklahoma’s rates are increasing at reasonable rates and not continuing to outpace neighboring states with similar weather patterns or natural disaster-prone areas such as Florida or California.
He also said he will improve the consumer advocacy division, which is designed to help Oklahomans navigate issues with claims denials, adjuster delays and poor communication from an insurer.

text:
State superintendent candidate Robert Franklin speaks at a campaign event in Edmond on Aug. 3. Franklin, a Republican, defeated Democrat Jennettie Marshall to win Tuesday's general election. (Photo by Nuria Martinez-Keel/Oklahoma Voice)OKLAHOMA CITY — A former teacher, school district leader and CareerTech center administrator who ran on his decades of experience in education has been elected Oklahoma’s state superintendent of public schools.
Robert Franklin, a Republican from Sand Springs, defeated Democrat Jennettie Marshall, of Tulsa, in Tuesday’s general election.
Franklin, 67, will govern the state’s public schools system as the leader of the Oklahoma State Department of Education and the state Board of Education. He ran a campaign focused on unifying Oklahomans to tackle the state’s teacher shortage and poor academic results. 
He also decried the political partisanship of former Superintendent Ryan Walters, a far-right wing firebrand who resigned last year.
Once sworn into office in January, Franklin will succeed state Superintendent Lindel Fields, who chose not to run for reelection. Gov. Kevin Stitt appointed Fields in October 2025 after Walters resigned to lead a nonprofit.
Democratic state superintendent candidate Jennettie Marshall, left, speaks with state Superintendent Lindel Fields after an Oklahoma State Board of Education meeting Sept. 24 in Oklahoma City. (Photo by Nuria Martinez-Keel/Oklahoma Voice)
Franklin began his career in 1981 with Sand Springs Public Schools as a special education teacher and later became a principal and assistant superintendent in the district. He joined Tulsa Technology Center in 2010 as an associate superintendent and remained until his retirement in 2024. 
An inductee in the Oklahoma Educators Hall of Fame, he then began teaching courses in educational leadership at the University of Oklahoma’s Tulsa campus.
Franklin also served on the Statewide Virtual Charter School Board from 2018 to 2024, including four years as the chair. He was one of two board members in 2023 to vote against a proposed publicly funded Catholic charter school. The Oklahoma Supreme Court later decided a publicly funded Catholic school was unconstitutional, and the U.S. Supreme Court upheld that ruling.
On the campaign trail — while another proposed religious charter school emerged — Franklin reinforced his stance against bringing faith-based teaching into public education, calling it unconstitutional and too heavy a burden to place on teachers.
His campaign focused on hiring more behavioral health specialists and counselors in public schools to help address disruptive student behaviors. He proposed expanding vocational education at the middle school level and changing Oklahoma’s model for state testing.
State superintendent candidate Robert Franklin speaks with news reporters at a campaign event Aug. 3 in Edmond. (Photo by Nuria Martinez-Keel/Oklahoma Voice)
After jumping into the race shortly before candidate filing, Franklin emerged in the lead of a seven-candidate Republican primary election in June. With significant support from Oklahoma educators, he defeated James Taylor in an August GOP runoff election.
Franklin said his 45 years of experience in education set him apart from his general election opponent. 
Marshall, 68, served eight years on the board governing Tulsa Public Schools, the state’s largest district. She spent her career as a pastor and in law enforcement, including 17 years as a parole officer and case manager for the state Department of Corrections.

Julie Fedorchak a second term in Congress.
Fedorchak was projected to win Tuesday night in a political rematch against Democratic-NPL U.S. House candidate Trygve Hammer, according to The Associated Press.
The Associated Press called North Dakota’s U.S. House race at 8:56 p.m. with Fedorchak leading 60% to Hammer’s 34% in early results.
In 2024, Fedorchak became the first woman elected to represent North Dakota in the U.S. House of Representatives.
After voting in Mandan on Election Day, Fedorchak said she would continue to push for conservative solutions to the nation’s problems even if Democrats take control of the U.S. House.
“I will be doing that in a bipartisan way, which is not all that different than what I have been doing the entire time I’ve been there,” Fedorchak said. “I have no trouble reaching across the aisle.”
Republican U.S. Rep. Julie Fedorchak inserts her ballot into a tabulation machine at Engage Church in Mandan, North Dakota, on Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo by Michael Achterling/North Dakota Monitor)
On the campaign trail, Fedorchak and Hammer differed on their support for the Iran war, how to address the $40 trillion national debt and their stances on new Medicaid work requirements that will be implemented next year. 
Fedorchak campaigned on supporting President Donald Trump, including promoting energy development, backing the war with Iran and securing the border. 
Hammer campaigned on holding the Trump administration accountable for its actions, asserting Congress’ power over tariffs, making healthcare more affordable and fixing Social Security insolvency. He also promoted tax policies that would ensure wealthy individuals and companies pay their fair share.
“We did everything we could. You win some and you lose some, and we’re just trying to make progress each time,” Hammer told the North Dakota Monitor Tuesday night.
Hammer said Fedorchak’s second term will be different with Democrats likely in the majority in Congress.
“Congresswoman Fedorchak can go there and continue to be a rubber stamp for Donald Trump, and it won’t make any difference because she’ll be in a vast minority,” Hammer said.
Fedorchak touted the success of the 2025 budget reconciliation bill, also known as the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, for delivering no taxes on tips or overtime and providing a new tax deduction aimed at seniors. 
Fedorchak co-sponsored the Stop Insider Trading Act during her first term, which would ban members of Congress from purchasing stocks while in office. She also co-sponsored and voted in support of the SAVE America Act, a bill that alters how Americans register to vote.
She did not participate in an in-person, public town hall during her first term in office but held a series of virtual tele-town hall events that featured constituents asking her questions. Fedorchak said the online events provided a larger forum for North Dakotans across the state to participate.
While Congress was on an August break, Fedorchak organized roundtable discussions in North Dakota with ag industry leaders on ethanol and trade policies.
She took issue with Trump’s strategy to import foreign beef as a way to combat inflation but also emphasized getting better trade deals to benefit ag producers. 
The House in mid-September went on a seven-week campaign break. It spent less than two weeks in session during August and September. 
Fedorchak did not pursue the North Dakota Republican Party endorsement at its state convention in Minot for her reelection bid this year and instead gained primary ballot access through petition signatures. She defeated NDGOP-endorsed candidate Alex Balazs in the June primary with 73% voter support. President Trump endorsed her reelection bid.
Prior to her time in Congress, Fedorchak served on the North Dakota Public Service Commission beginning in 2013 after being appointed to the position by Gov. Jack Dalrymple. 
Democratic-NPL U.S. House candidate Trygve Hammer speaks during a town hall event in Bismarck, North Dakota, on Oct. 29, 2026. (Photo by Michael Achterling/North Dakota Monitor)
Hammer received the Dem-NPL endorsement over Vern Thompson and Helene Neville. 
Hammer graduated from the Naval Academy and became a Marine helicopter pilot. He deployed to Iraq in 2003 as a platoon commander. After his service ended, he held a series of jobs that included rig work in the Bakken oil field, a freight train conductor and science teacher in Granville.     
Hammer lost a bid to join the North Dakota Public Service Commission in 2022 and a race for a state House seat in 2020.
Independent candidates Helene Neville and Republican-aligned independent candidate Charles Tuttle also ran for U.S. House. Neville had about 2% and Tuttle had about 4% of votes in early results.
This story was updated with reaction from Trygve Hammer and early results for independent candidates.

name: Michigan Advance
title: ‘Money Out of Politics’ ballot measure passes, constitutional convention fails
description: Proposal 2 on Michigan ballots, the “Michiganders for Money Out of Politics” initiative, has passed. The initiative will alter state campaign finance law to ban campaign spending from “regulated electric and gas utilities, contractors with over $250,000 annually in government contracts, and people and organizations with substantial connections to those utili[...]
text:
Michiganders for Money Out of Politics submitted its signatures in Lansing to make the November 2026 ballot. May 27, 2026. | Photo by Katherine Dailey/Michigan Advance. Proposal 2 on Michigan ballots, the “Michiganders for Money Out of Politics” initiative, has passed. The initiative will alter state campaign finance law to ban campaign spending from “regulated electric and gas utilities, contractors with over $250,000 annually in government contracts, and people and organizations with substantial connections to those utilities or contractors.”
Meanwhile, Proposal 1, a ballot measure asking Michigan voters if they want to call a constitutional convention, has failed, with the measure having garnered significant opposition from a wide range of groups.
Proposal 2 succeeded by a 62-point margin, with unofficial results showing “yes” votes taking 81.2% of the vote as of 9:38 p.m., when the race was called by the Associated Press, with less than 10% of the vote in.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“Tonight, David beat Goliath,” said Ken Whittaker of Michigan United, when Michiganders for Money Out of Politics claimed victory just after 9 p.m.
Christy McGillivray, executive director of Voters Not Politicians and a co-chair of the ballot effort, said the results show that there are limits to corporate power.
“We’re the ones that make change. Our representatives failed to deliver on holding corrupt pay to play politics accountable, so we said enough. And tonight Michiganders delivered,” McGillivray.
Christy McGillivray, executive director of Voters Not Politicians and a co-chair of the ballot effort, speaks to supporters in Detroit on Nov. 3, 2026 after The Associated Press called the race for the “yes” vote. (Screenshot)
The ballot proposal had broad support in polling leading up to Election Day and throughout the election cycle.  
Republican leadership in the state House had sought to keep the measure off the ballot by passing a version of it into statute in the Legislature, a move that Democrats said could have made it easier to amend or overturn later. However, Senate Majority Leader Winnie Brinks — also the Democratic lieutenant governor nominee — declined to take it up in the Senate, leaving the decision to the voters. 
An opposition group to the measure, Protect MI Free Speech, had filed a lawsuit against the Board of State Canvassers alleging that the ballot petition did not meet the threshold of valid signatures required to put it on the ballot. The Michigan Supreme Court declined to hear the lawsuit in early September. 
The constitutional convention proposal failed by a 50-point margin, with unofficial results showing “no” votes taking 75.5% of the vote as of 9:40 p.m., when the race was called by the Associated Press, with 15% of votes counted.
The measure is constitutionally mandated to appear on the ballot every 16 years, but has not passed since 1961, when Michigan’s current state constitution was crafted. The last three times the question was on the ballot — 1978, 1994 and 2010 — the measure failed by wide margins, similar to Tuesday’s early returns.
The measure faced an ideologically broad opposition movement, with groups ranging from Planned Parenthood of Michigan to Right to Life of Michigan coming out in opposition. Much of the opposition to the prospect of a convention came from concerns that it would have allowed special interest groups to exert their influence over the convention process and put in place new constitutional measures that would be beneficial to them.

name: Rhode Island Current
title: Matos beats Loughlin to win another term as Rhode Island lieutenant governor
description: Democratic Lt. Gov. Sabina Matos defeated Republican challenger John Loughlin to win reelection Tuesday, securing another four years in Rhode Island’s second-highest general office. Matos, 52, received 185,483 votes, or 59.21%, compared with 185,483 votes, or just under 41%, for Loughlin, 67, according to unofficial preliminary results from the Rhode Island [...]
text:
Lt. Gov. Sabina Matos speaks to supporters at the Rhode Island Democratic Party's Election Night watch party at The Graduate by Hilton Providence on Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo by Nancy Lavin/Rhode Island Current)Democratic Lt. Gov. Sabina Matos defeated Republican challenger John Loughlin to win reelection Tuesday, securing another four years in Rhode Island’s second-highest general office.
Matos, 52, received 185,483 votes, or 59.21%, compared with 185,483 votes, or just under 41%, for Loughlin, 67, according to unofficial preliminary results from the Rhode Island Board of Elections as of 9:09 p.m.
The victory lengthens Matos’ tenure in an office she has held since 2021, when appointed by Gov. Dan McKee after he exited the office himself to succeed then Gov. Gina Raimondo who departed to become U.S. Secretary of Commerce in President Joe Biden’s administration.
Matos was later elected to her first full term in 2022. She bested four other candidates in a competitive five-way Democratic primary in September before facing former Republican state representative Loughlin, a military veteran and talk radio host.
A standing room-only crowd at The Graduate in Providence erupted in cheers as Matos took the stage shortly after 9:30 p.m., flanked by family and supporters.
“Thank you Rhode Island,” she declared, addressing the crowd in Spanish. “This campaign was powered by labor and people. We knew all along this campaign was going to be an uphill battle but tonight we learned that hard work and all of those late nights really pay off.”
“It doesn’t matter how long you spend in elected office, or you spend in public office, you always feel like an outsider. But that’s OK. My campaign was built on the outsiders.”
Matos denounced federal immigration enforcement authorities for “terrorizing” people, while blasting Trump for federal policy overhauls restricting access to food assistance and healthcare for people in need.
“Gracias, gracias gracias,” she concluded.
She also thanked Loughlin for his service.
Loughlin gave his concession speech during a watch party at the Loom Hotel shortly before 9 p.m. 
“We did our best,” Loughlin said, noting some parental wisdom and his youthful years as an Eagle Scout growing up in Lincoln. “The outcome is not what we expected, but we did our best…We got a lot of serious problems to solve here in Rhode Island, and we wish [Matos] well.”
The race was close for most of its duration, with polls throughout the fall showing the candidates separated by narrow margins.
But two days before Election Day, a University of New Hampshire poll showed Matos leading Loughlin 56% to 41% among 753 likely voters surveyed from Oct. 27 to 31. The margin of error was 3.5 percentage points.
An October poll by Salve Regina University’s Pell Center had Loughlin and Matos statistically tied, with Loughlin at 44% and Matos at 43%.
The new poll also lent insight into why people said they would vote for Matos. Of the survey respondents who said they were voting primarily for Matos — rather than against Loughlin — 68% claimed their support was based more on her party affiliation than Matos as a particular candidate.
Voters in the newest UNH poll were more familiar with Matos than Loughlin. But Matos’ Republican challenger had a positive net favorability rating while Matos had a negative net favorability rating.
On the campaign trail, the two candidates sparred over what the lieutenant governor should do with the limited powers afforded the office under the state Constitution. The lieutenant governor in Rhode Island holds less official powers than in other states, and their chief duty is taking over for the governor in case the governor is incapacitated.
Republican candidate for lieutenant governor John Loughlin is shown at an Election Day campaign stop at Toll Gate High School in Warwick on Tuesday morning, Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo by Michael Salerno/Rhode Island Current)
A dispute over Loughlin’s financial disclosures also emerged in the final week of the election cycle. 
Matos’ campaign filed a complaint with the Rhode Island Board of Elections on Oct. 29, alleging that Loughlin’s campaign manager had improperly benefited from publicly financed television advertising purchases, by “skimming” some of the commission costs attached to those purchases.
Loughlin denied the accusations and explained that advertising commissions had been reinvested in additional airtime and TV spots, rather than diverted to his campaign manager’s ad firm. 
The complaint followed multiple amendments to Loughlin’s final final campaign finance report before election day, which ultimately listed $58,651 in expenditures for the reporting period ending Oct. 26.
Matos’ own campaign finance report from the period from Oct. 6 through Oct. 26 showed her outraising and outspending Loughline. Matos raised $48,202 in private contributions and spent $206,306, compared with $22,072 raised and $58,651 spent by Loughlin.
During this same period, Matos received $163,300 in public matching funds, compared with approximately $83,100 for Loughlin.
Senior Reporter Nancy Lavin contributed to this story.

name: West Virginia Watch
title: Riley Moore wins another term in U.S. House of Representatives
description: Rep. Riley Moore, R-W.Va., has won another two-year term in the U.S. House of Representatives.
text:
Rep. Riley Moore, R-W.Va., speaks at Blueridge Community and Technical College on Oct. 2, 2026. (Photo courtesy of Congressman RIley M. Moore's Facebook page)Rep. Riley Moore, R-W.Va., has won another two-year term in the U.S. House of Representatives. 
The Associated Press called the race for Moore at 9:22 p.m. Tuesday night. Moore pulled in 58.6% of votes, over Democrat challenger Ace Parsi, who had 41.4% of votes, according to unofficial results with 83% of votes counted.
“It’s been an honor of my life to represent West Virginia’s Second Congressional District,” Moore wrote Tuesday night in a post on the social media platform X. “I’m proud of the work I’ve done to advance critical infrastructure investments, strengthen our aerospace and defense industries, and bring new economic opportunities and good-paying jobs to West Virginia.
“I’ll never stop fighting for West Virginians!” he wrote.
Moore is the former West Virginia state treasurer. He was first elected to the House of Representatives in 2024.
Parsi is a former Morgantown community organizer who immigrated to the United States from Iran as a child. He won the Democratic primary over Democrats Stephanie Spears Tomana, a Fairmont teacher, and Steve Wendelin, who retired from the U.S. Navy. 
In a statement late Tuesday, Parsi said he had called Moore and conceded the race. He said he hopes Moore “will show up for every West Virginian in this district, because they deserve nothing less.
“I have had literally thousands of one-on-one conversations at this point,” Parsi said. “I carry these stories with deep gratitude and they fuel a mission to serve these people with everything I have. West Virginians saw something special in me, lifted it up, and added their own talents to the pot: designs, videos, music, conversations and jokes. Together, we built a campaign I never could have dreamed of creating on my own. To every volunteer, donor, and voter who was part of it: thank you.”

title: Democrat Rebecca Bennett topples GOP Rep. Tom Kean Jr.
description: Rebecca Bennett has flipped the 7th Congressional District to Democratic control four years after Rep. Tom Kean Jr. captured it for the GOP.
text:
Rebecca Bennett has flipped the 7th Congressional District to Democratic control four years after Rep. Tom Kean Jr. captured it for the GOP. (Photo by Dana DiFilippo/New Jersey Monitor)Former U.S. Navy helicopter pilot Rebecca Bennett (D) will oust GOP Rep. Tom Kean Jr., reclaiming a seat Democrats lost four years ago, the Associated Press projected Tuesday.
The contest in the 7th Congressional District between Bennett and Kean, a former state senator and son of a popular ex-governor, was the most closely watched House race in the state.
Democrats flipped the seat from GOP control in 2018 during President Donald Trump’s first term, and Kean won it back for the GOP in 2022.
This year, Kean not only faced an unfavorable national environment, but his reelection bid was complicated by a prolonged absence from Congress that the congressman later said was due to depression.

name: Florida Phoenix
title: Property tax slash crosses approval threshold on election night
description: A far-reaching homestead property tax reduction proposed by the Legislature garnered the approval of more than 62% of the unofficial vote, besting the 60% approval required to be enshrined in the Florida Constitution.  At full implementation, state economists estimated Amendment 3 would reduce local revenues by as much as $12 billion annually. For well over [...]
text:
A banner advertising voting hangs outside the Leon County Courthouse on Aug. 12, 2024. (Photo by Jay Waagmeester/Florida Phoenix)A far-reaching homestead property tax reduction proposed by the Legislature garnered the approval of more than 62% of the unofficial vote, besting the 60% approval required to be enshrined in the Florida Constitution. 
At full implementation, state economists estimated Amendment 3 would reduce local revenues by as much as $12 billion annually.
For well over a year, Gov. Ron DeSantis has been advocating for eliminating property taxes, although he took about as long to propose a statutory language to do so. The Legislature amended his plan to protect property taxes collected for schools.
“Big win on Amendment 3 for Florida homeowners!” DeSantis posted Tuesday night, replying to a Republican Party of Florida post that categorized the amendment’s passage as “an incredible VICTORY for Florida homeowners!”
Amendment 3 had the support of the state GOP and Florida Realtors. In the days leading up to the election, DeSantis hosted events throughout the state advocating for the amendment. 
The Florida Democratic Party opposed the amendment, as did public safety and law enforcement groups, such as the Florida Sheriff’s Association, as well as outgoing Senate President Ben Albritton, a Republican from central Florida. 
Former state lawmaker Jeff Brandes campaigned against the amendment, and even led a lawsuit challenging its language.
“Florida passed Amendment 3. The governor and the Legislature own what comes next. They have the responsibility to manage the fallout,” he posted to social media Tuesday, going on to list cities and counties he says will struggle with passage of the amendment.
“Floridians voted for lower taxes, and they count on their communities for the basics,” Brandes wrote. “Both are reasonable expectations. The governor and the Legislature can honor that vote by giving cities and counties a clear plan before they write their next budgets, so every community can decide how best to keep the services its residents depend on.”
Amendment 1
Voters rejected an increase in the capacity of the state’s budget stabilization fund, the rainy-day account tapped in case of emergencies or revenue shortfalls. 
The proposal, Amendment 1, received just more than 40% support. 
That means the state will continue to maintain up to 10% of the previous year’s net revenue in the budget stabilization fund, instead of the 25% proposed by the amendment. 
DeSantis railed against the amendment, but the Republican Party of Florida endorsed it. 
“Amendment 1 — a testament to our failed former speaker of the House — is deservedly going down in flames. Good riddance,” DeSantis posted to X Tuesday evening. He referred to Speaker Daniel Perez, with whom he has feuded for two years.
Amendment 2
The other measure on the statewide ballot was Amendment 2, Exemption of Tangible Personal Property on Agricultural Land from Taxation. 
That amendment would have excluded farming equipment like tractors from assessed taxes, but as of Tuesday night had 58.25%. According to a state estimate, the amendment would’ve reduced local government revenue by about $31 million starting in 2027.
The Florida Farm Bureau supported the amendment.

title: Providence voters overwhelmingly approve divestment measure
description: Providence voters overwhelmingly approved a citizen-led proposal Tuesday night that aims to restrict municipal investments connected to severe human rights violations abroad. Question 7 received over 76% support, or 20,925 votes overall, as of 8:53 p.m., with 76 of 82 precincts reporting. Question 7 was placed on the ballot through a citizen petition effort [...]
text:
Providence City Hall. Mayor-elect David Morales supported the measure to restrict city investments in locations tied to severe human rights violations abroad. (Photo by Alexander Castro/Rhode Island Current)Providence voters overwhelmingly approved a citizen-led proposal Tuesday night that aims to restrict municipal investments connected to severe human rights violations abroad.
Question 7 received over 76% support, or 20,925 votes overall, as of 8:53 p.m., with 76 of 82 precincts reporting. 
Question 7 was placed on the ballot through a citizen petition effort spearheaded by Providence for Palestine, a coalition of progressive organizations that collected more than 6,000 verified signatures after the City Council declined to enact the proposed ordinance.
Thousands of signatures put a question on Providence’s November ballot. One country is the target.

The proposal did not name Israel directly, but both opponents and proponents ​​have identified the country’s military actions in Gaza as the impetus for the measure.
Mayor-elect David Morales supports the measure, while his Republican opponent in the general election, Dave Talan, opposed it.
Outgoing Mayor Brett Smiley’s administration has had concerns about the legality of the measure. WPRI reported on Oct. 29 that the city had commissioned retired federal judge William Smith to review the proposal. The retired judge concluded in an Oct. 23 memo that the ordinance was likely unenforceable and could lead to litigation over the city’s pension investments. 
Supporters argue the measure was written to accommodate concerns about the city’s fiduciary obligations, including to its pensioners.
