name: Colorado Newsline
title: Melat Kiros, 29-year-old Democrat, wins election to Congress
description: Denver voters on Tuesday elected Melat Kiros, 29-year-old former attorney and democratic socialist, as the congressional representative from Colorado’s 1st District. The Associated Press called the race at about 7:30 p.m. Kiros led with 78% of the vote, ahead of Republican Christy Peterson with 14% and unaffiliated candidate Shimon Blau with 6%. Kiros is the[...]
text:
Melat Kiros, seen speaking at a demonstration in September, won election to Congress. (Photo by Lindsey Toomer/Colorado Newsline)Denver voters on Tuesday elected Melat Kiros, 29-year-old former attorney and democratic socialist, as the congressional representative from Colorado’s 1st District.
The Associated Press called the race at about 7:30 p.m. Kiros led with 78% of the vote, ahead of Republican Christy Peterson with 14% and unaffiliated candidate Shimon Blau with 6%.
Kiros is the first self-identified socialist and the first Black woman to be elected to Congress in Colorado history, and the second-youngest woman, after Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez in 2018, to be elected to Congress from any state. Born in Ethiopia, she was raised in Denver after immigrating to the U.S. from Ethiopia with her parents at 11 months old.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Her victory in the 1st District, Colorado’s most heavily Democratic congressional district, was all but assured with her shock primary victory in June over longtime U.S. Rep. Diana DeGette, who took office in 1997 four months before Kiros was born. Kiros joins a nationwide wave this year of other left-wing insurgents with the backing of groups like Justice Democrats and the Democratic Socialists of America.
How democratic socialist Melat Kiros stunned Colorado politics with congressional primary win

Her election to Congress from Denver — where two-thirds of Democrats and two-thirds of all residents under age 35 hold a favorable view of socialism, a 2025 poll found — is by far the biggest win to date for local left-wing groups like the Denver chapter of the DSA, which has risen in stature over the last decade and elected a handful of other candidates to Denver City Council and the state Legislature.
Kiros has faced criticism from some fellow Democrats for her views on Israel, most notably when she declined to characterize the June 2025 firebombing attack in Boulder, which targeted a group aiming to raise awareness of hostages held by Hamas in Gaza, as an act of antisemitism.
Shortly after her primary win, Shimon Blau, a Denver doctor, launched a campaign for the 1st District as an unaffiliated candidate, a decision motivated by what he called her “antisemitic rhetoric.” Blau qualified for the ballot after collecting the required 1,500 valid petition signatures.
After being fired from her job as a corporate attorney for writing an open letter supportive of student protests against Israel’s war in Gaza in late 2023, Kiros enrolled in a Ph.D. program in Denver and took a job as a barista before launching her long-shot challenge against DeGette in July 2025.
Galvanized by her opposition to U.S. aid to Israel and support for progressive priorities like Medicare for All, Kiros’ small army of staff and volunteers powered a grassroots campaign that handed DeGette her first-ever defeat at the Denver Democratic assembly in March, nearly knocking the incumbent off the ballot before the primary had begun.
Kiros and her supporters railed against the pernicious influence of campaign spending by corporations and the rich, faulting DeGette, long considered the most left-leaning member of Colorado’s congressional delegation, for accepting corporate PAC money while failing to deliver progressive reforms.
This is a developing story and will be updated.

name: West Virginia Watch
title: Carol Miller will continue to serve in US House
description: Rep. Carol Miller, R-W.Va., will be returning to the U.S. House of Representatives.
text:
Rep. Carol Miller was first elected to Congress in 2018. (Photo courtesy of Carol Miller for Congress)Rep. Carol Miller, R-W.Va., will be returning to the U.S. House of Representatives. 
The Associated Press called the race at 9:20 p.m. showing Miller beating Democratic challenger Vince George 56% to 40%. Belinda Fox-Spencer, a Constitution Party candidate, pulled around 3% of the vote. 
“It has absolutely been my honor to serve the people of West Virginia for the last eight years and I will continue to fight to improve access to rural healthcare and make life more affordable for West Virginians,” Miller said. 
Miller was first elected to office in the 2018 midterm, after then Rep. Evan Jenkins, R-W.Va., declined to run again to pursue a seat on the state Supreme Court. In that election, she beat state Sen. Richard Ojeda, D-Logan, who coincidentally was showing as ahead in a race for the U.S. House in North Carolina Tuesday. 
Miller, the daughter of Rep. Samuel Devine, R-Ohio, married into the Dutch Miller Auto Group family. 
Miller’s campaign ran off the cachet of President Donald Trump, who while underwater in polls nationally is still enjoying support in the Mountain State. 
This election is the first Vince George has run for federal office. He previously ran for Kanawha County magistrate decades ago. Over the years, he has worked as a social worker, teacher, legislative staffer and a lobbyist for environmental groups. 
Throughout the campaign, George accused Miller of not being there for constituents, taking to calling her “Cardboard Carol.” 
George said even though he didn’t win, he counted the campaign as a victory. 
“We’ve already changed the political landscape here in West Virginia and we will continue from here,” he said. “Maybe I didn’t win, but we put forward an argument and fight.”

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Kansas incumbents on track to hold onto U.S. House seats
description: TOPEKA — The four incumbents in Kansas’s congressional delegation were on track to hold onto their U.S. House seats, according to unofficial vote totals from the Secretary of State’s Office. In the Kansas City-area 3rd District, Democratic U.S. Rep. Sharice Davids gave a victory speech, and the Republican incumbents led in each of the other […]
text:
U.S. Rep. Sharice Davids speaks to supporters Nov. 3, 2026, in Overland Park after winning reelection to the 3rd District seat for a fifth time. (Photo by Clay Wirestone/Kansas Reflector)TOPEKA — The four incumbents in Kansas’s congressional delegation were on track to hold onto their U.S. House seats, according to unofficial vote totals from the Secretary of State’s Office.
In the Kansas City-area 3rd District, Democratic U.S. Rep. Sharice Davids gave a victory speech, and the Republican incumbents led in each of the other three districts. About 960,000 votes, or 82%, had been counted statewide as of 9:45 p.m.
Davids, speaking in front of a cheering, sign-waving audience at the Overland Park Convention Center, said Kansas has been in the spotlight leading up to Election Day.
“And frankly, good,” she said. “I think it’s about time. I think it is about time that people started paying attention to what’s going on in Kansas. I can tell you, there’s some stuff that Washington and the rest of the country could learn from Kansas.
“Kansans know how to break through this partisan noise that so many of us are tired of. How to focus on common sense solutions and how to get things done. Because not only are we pragmatic, but we work really hard out here.”
The Associated Press called the race for Davids just after 9 p.m.
The three Republican incumbents have benefitted this year from high-profile campaign visits from national Republicans, including the president and vice president, who came to the state to stump for U.S. Sen. Roger Marshall. The three Republicans are also favored to win, per the Cook Political Report.
U.S. Rep. Tracey Mann was leading by 17 percentage points in the 1st District, U.S. Rep. Derek Schmidt was up 1,000 votes in the 2nd District, and U.S. Rep. Ron Esters held an 8-point lead.
 
1st District
In the 1st District, Mann, a Salina Republican took the lead over Democrat Lauren Reinhold, an attorney from Lawrence who formerly worked for the federal government. Mann has served in Congress since 2021. The district he is seeking to hold onto covers most of western and central Kansas, and encompasses Manhattan and Lawrence, both of which have gone to Democrats in recent years. Libertarian Steven Jacob, a retired city of Lawrence employee, was also on the ballot and had around 2% of votes, per early totals.
Mann won the district by 39 percentage points just two years ago. He talked about the significance of this election when he took the stage Sunday in Salina before the president arrived for his final rally before Election Day. He said he wasn’t sure if it was the most important election of his lifetime, but “every election these days is really important.”
“It wasn’t long ago, you know, the lines in politics is you were right or you were left, right?” Mann said. “You were a conservative or you were liberal, you were Republican or Democrat. Now it feels to me like you’re normal or you’re crazy, right?”
Reinhold wrapped up her campaign by outlining her priorities for voters.
“My core priorities are Kansans, rewarding the hard work you all do every day with a government that supports you,” she said. “My priorities are making healthcare accessible. Reforming immigration to make our system work for the people in it. Restoring integrity to our government.”
 
2nd District
President Donald Trump carried the eastern Kansas 2nd District by 20 points in 2024, when Schmidt won the district by 19 points, but this year’s race between Schmidt and Democrat Don Coover has been close. Coover, a vet and veterinarian, led Schmidt, the state’s former attorney general, with 50% of votes compared to Schmidt’s 46%, per unofficial results. Schmidt was absent from Sunday’s rally with Trump, however.
In a final email appeal to supporters, Schmidt touted his record of “fighting for Kansas healthcare, higher education, small businesses, and citizens” across the 2nd District.
“And in the next two years,” Schmidt said, “I want to keep up that fight — pursuing policies that reflect our values, strengthen our communities, and help solve problems in communities big and small.”
Coover’s closing message: “More cattle, less bull.”
He predicted an election that has more to do with solutions to problems than party identity.
“It’s definitely going to be a change election because there’s a lot of people, I think, that haven’t been really engaged in the past, and they’re getting engaged now because they see the future and they don’t like the looks of it the way it’s going now,” Coover said Tuesday at the Shawnee County Democratic Party’s headquarters. “This is going to be a change election. I’m confident.”
“Our growing coalition of everyday Kansans — Republicans, Democrats and independents alike — is ready to ditch Derek and send a working rancher to Congress,” Coover said. “We need common sense leadership focused on real kitchen table solutions: lowering grocery bills, and clearing out the political bull in D.C.”
Libertarian John Hauer, an Army veteran from Topeka, had around 3% votes, as of 8:30 p.m.
 
3rd District
In the 3rd District, Davids, the Democrat, defeated Republican Eric Jenkins, a retired U.S. Army colonel and former member of the Shawnee City Council, and Libertarian Steve Hohe, a U.S. Air Force veteran from Shawnee who has thrice run and lost campaigns for the U.S. House.
Davids, who has held her seat since 2019, toured her district this weekend with a pitch to lower costs for Kansans.
“From young people casting their first ballots to small business owners, local farmers, and working parents across the Kansas Third, the message I heard everywhere was clear: Kansans are tired of partisan noise and corruption,” Davids said in a news release. “They just want practical, common sense solutions that lower everyday costs like groceries and gas.”
Jenkins, a retired Army colonel and Green Beret, reminded voters of his 34 years of military service.
“Those experiences taught me the importance of service, responsibility, and working alongside people from different backgrounds toward a common goal,” he said. “I’m grateful for the opportunities this country has given me and for the people I’ve had the honor of serving alongside.”
 
4th District
In the south-central 4th District, Estes was beating Democrat Katy Tyndell. Estes has served in the U.S. House for almost a decade, previously working in Wichita as a consultant and in local and state government. Tyndell is an attorney, nonprofit cofounder and works for her family’s oil and gas company in Wichita. 
Libertarian Drew Cranmer, a data engineer from Wichita, held about 5,800 votes.
Estes won the district by 20 points in 2024.
Speaking ahead of Trump at Sunday’s rally in Salina, Estes told the crowd the country was safer now than it was two years ago thanks to Trump’s crackdown on immigration. He warned the Democrats of today “aren’t your grandmother’s Democrat Party.”
“If you look at the socialist Democrat agenda that they have out there, you know, they want to close all the jails, they want an open border, they want to eliminate the president, and they want to defund the Department of War,” Estes said.
Tyndell, whose platform doesn’t match Estes’ description, made a closing pitch to voters Monday by praising the “skill, dedication, and hard work of Wichita’s aviation workforce.”
“These are the people who build the planes, support their families, and help power our local economy,” she said. “They deserve more than a thank you. They deserve a representative who will stand up for their jobs, their healthcare, their benefits, and the dignity of their work.”
Sherman Smith and Morgan Chilson contributed to this report.

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: Rep. Andy Barr wins race to replace Sen. Mitch McConnell
description: LEXINGTON — Kentucky voters have decided to give Republican U.S. Rep. Andy Barr a promotion to the U.S. Senate.  Barr, who has represented Central Kentucky since 2012, defeated Democrat Charles Booker, a former state representative from Louisville with 54.1% to 43.9%. The Associated Press called the race at about 9:15 p.m. “Let me tell you, […]
text:
Andy Barr speaks during his election night watch party on Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026, in Lexington, Kentucky. (Photo by Arden Barnes for Kentucky Lantern)LEXINGTON — Kentucky voters have decided to give Republican U.S. Rep. Andy Barr a promotion to the U.S. Senate. 
Barr, who has represented Central Kentucky since 2012, defeated Democrat Charles Booker, a former state representative from Louisville with 54.1% to 43.9%. The Associated Press called the race at about 9:15 p.m.











“Let me tell you, I have a vision for Kentucky,” Barr said in his acceptance speech in Lexington.  “My vision is optimistic. It’s a future defined by prosperity, opportunity, and growth. From Pikeville to Paducah, from Covington to Corbin, and everywhere in between, it’s time for Kentucky to become even stronger. It’s time for paychecks to go up and prices to come down. It’s time for more jobs, more opportunity, and more wealth for everyone, everywhere.




















“To achieve our vision for America, to fight for freedom over socialism, it will take work. But I promise you tonight, I will not shrink from it. I will dedicate myself to it. And protecting our Constitution and our way of life is central to everything I will do. I will protect and defend it. I will guard against those who would expand the Supreme Court, weaken our military, raise our taxes, and impeach our presidents.”








Leading up to November, the congressman was long seen as the favorite to win the race. He succeeds U.S. Sen. Mitch McConnell, who has held the seat since 1984. The longtime Republican said in 2025 that he would not seek reelection to another term. 
Barr was endorsed by President Donald Trump in a fiery primary battle against former Attorney General Daniel Cameron and businessman Nate Morris, who dropped out of the race as Trump appointed him to become ambassador to Colombia. 
Trump rallied in Northern Kentucky a couple weeks ahead of the election, partly speaking in support of Barr while also focusing on other races as the GOP braced for what was predicted to be a difficult midterm election for them. 
“You don’t mind if I talk about other people,” Trump said to Barr during the rally. “Andy is doing so well, I think we can talk about other people.” 
Ahead of the primary, Barr told the Kentucky Lantern he viewed his endorsement from Trump as a sign that he can “be a more effective senator because I have a close relationship with this president and this administration.” Because of his Washington connections, Barr felt best suited to take constituents’ requests from Kentucky and find solutions at the federal level. 
Barr also repeatedly tried to frame Booker as a “crazy socialist” throughout the election, frequently calling him “the Mamdani of Kentucky,” referring to New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, who won election in 2025, has since become a democratic socialist boogeyman for Republicans. In what was the only televised debate between the candidates, Booker said he believed in capitalism, but “we simply need to make sure that it works for the people.” 
Booker previously ran for U.S. Senate twice before. In 2020, Booker lost the Democratic nomination to former Marine fighter pilot Amy McGrath, who later failed to unseat longtime Republican U.S. Sen. Mitch McConnell. Booker then ran against Republican U.S. Sen. Rand Paul in 2022 and lost.
Booker won his party’s nomination this year in a field of candidates that included McGrath and Dale Romans, a Louisville horse trainer who attempted to carve a lane as an “independent Democrat.
Ahead of the general election, Booker told the Lantern he believed this race felt “like the perfect storm,” as he had a chance to build support across the state in his previous campaigns and the world had changed politically. 
“The bottom has fallen out for so many people in ways they can’t unsee: the rising gas prices, rising grocery prices, this devastation with Iran, this trade war with Canada,” Booker said.  “They’re seeing the swamp get bigger and bigger and deeper, and then they’re seeing people like Mitch McConnell and Andy Barr essentially give them the middle finger, and they’re tired of it.”
U.S. senators serve six-year terms.

text:
Stefany Shaheen speaks to supporters at a primary election results watch party in Portsmouth on Sept. 9, 2026. (Photo by William Skipworth/New Hampshire Bulletin)Stefany Shaheen spent years working up to Tuesday — and now her victory over Republican Anthony DiLorenzo in the 1st Congressional District will keep the seat blue. 
With 48% of the vote in, Shaheen led DiLorenzo 58.7% to 41.3%. The race was called by the Associated Press at 9:21 p.m.
Shaheen, 52, will replace longtime 1st District Rep. Chris Pappas, who vacated the seat to run for U.S. Senate. Shaheen, daughter of retiring U.S. Sen. Jeanne Shaheen, will continue the family’s legacy in Congress. 
Shaheen’s campaign aligned with popular Democratic policy issues for the midterm elections: affordability and the economy, healthcare, and government accountability for the Trump administration. 
Before running for House of Representatives, Shaheen served as a Portsmouth city councilor and member of the city’s police commission. In the private sector, Shaheen worked for ARMI, a company founded by Dean Kamen, where she was a biotech consultant. She has also sat on the board of multiple diabetes and health organizations. 
DiLorenzo, an automobile and real estate executive, owns over two dozen car dealerships and collision centers, as well as other businesses in the Seacoast area. The first-time candidate for elected office campaigned on reducing federal spending and inflation, maintaining President Donald Trump’s Immigration Customs and Enforcement efforts, and maintaining private healthcare, as well as lowering housing costs and addressing New Hampshire’s workforce demands.

title: Donalds defeats Jolly, becoming Florida’s first Black governor
description: Byron Donalds made history Tuesday by defeating Democrat David Jolly to become the nation’s first Black Republican governor, as well as the first Black person ever elected statewide in Florida.  The race was extremely close, with Donalds winning 50.1% of the vote over Jolly’s 48.6%, with about 99% of votes counted, according to the Associated […]
text:
Candidate for governor Byron Donalds speaks at a rally in Tallahassee one week before the election, Oct. 27, 2026. (Photo by Jay Waagmeester/Florida Phoenix)Byron Donalds made history Tuesday by defeating Democrat David Jolly to become the nation’s first Black Republican governor, as well as the first Black person ever elected statewide in Florida. 
The race was extremely close, with Donalds winning 50.1% of the vote over Jolly’s 48.6%, with about 99% of votes counted, according to the Associated Press.
“This might be the shortest speech I’ve given on the campaign trail but it doesn’t need to be long. Tonight we celebrate, tomorrow we work, and over the next four years we’re going to take Florida to a whole new level,” Donalds told a crowd  that celebrated his victory at the Seminole Hollywood Hard Rock Hotel in Davie.
President Donald Trump was the second person to congratulate him after the final results.The first call came from Jolly.
“Mr. President, I want you to hear from Florida that we are still red,” Donalds said recalling his conversation with Trump.
Headed into Election Day, Democrats were optimistic about a Blue wave, thinking they could recapture the governor’s mansion after a three-decade absence and also defeat Republican Florida Cabinet members who’d been appointed by Gov. Ron DeSantis to fill vacant positions. 
That did not happen.
Cabinet races
Along with the governor Florida’s Cabinet includes the state attorney general, chief financial officer, and the commissioner of agriculture. DeSantis appointed AG Ashley Moody to Congress to fill the seat vacated by Maro Rubio. He appointed his former chief of staff, James Uthmeir, to fill the post.
And when CFO Jimmy Patronis ran for congressional District 1 it left another vacancy on the Cabinet that DeSantis got to fill. For that position he appointed former state Sen. Blaise Ingoglia.
On Tuesday night Uthmeier and Ingoglia were both re-elected. Uthmeier defeated Democratic hopeful José Javier Rodríguez taking 51.01% of the vote. Also capturing 51.01% of the vote Ingoglia defeated Democrat opponent Annette Taddeo.
This is a developing story and will be updated.

Voters rebuffed the state question put on the ballot by lawmakers that would have made changes to the Judicial Nominating Commission. The 15-member panel vets judicial candidates and[...]
text:
The Oklahoma Judicial Center is the headquarters of the Oklahoma Supreme Court and Court of Criminal Appeals. (Photo by Carmen Forman/Oklahoma Voice)OKLAHOMA CITY – Oklahoma voters on Tuesday soundly rejected a proposed constitutional amendment that would give Republicans more influence over a panel that helps select judges.
Voters rebuffed the state question put on the ballot by lawmakers that would have made changes to the Judicial Nominating Commission.
The 15-member panel vets judicial candidates and forwards three names to the governor, who makes the selection from those. 
The panel has been a target for Republican lawmakers for years after a number of GOP-backed bills were deemed unconstitutional by courts.
State Question 845 sought to remove party affiliation restrictions and the prohibition that certain members not be attorneys or have family members who practice law. It also would change the length of time commissioners can serve and realign the district boundaries for where they can reside.
Supporters said it was necessary to better represent the Republican super majorities in the Legislature and reflect their control of all statewide elective offices.
Critics said the Legislature is attempting to make the panel overly partisan. 
The commission was established in 1967 by a voter-approved constitutional amendment following a judicial scandal where justices took bribes.

name: West Virginia Watch
title: West Virginia voters approve noncitizen voting constitutional amendment
description: West Virginia voters have approved an amendment to the state constitution prohibiting non-citizens from voting in state elections.
text:
Voting tables with "I Voted" dividers at the Historic Arkansas Museum in Little Rock, Arkansas on Tuesday, November 3, 2026. (Photo by Katie Adkins/Arkansas Advocate)West Virginia voters have approved an amendment to the state constitution prohibiting non-citizens from voting in state elections.
The Associated Press called the race for Amendment 1 at 8:43 p.m. Tuesday. At the time, 78.8% of voters supported the measure and 21.2% rejected it, according to unofficial election results from 73% of precincts counted.  
West Virginia state code already requires that only United States citizens cast votes in elections. Proponents of Amendment 1 said the state’s constitution is less clear: it requires voters to be citizens of the state, but does not specify that they be U.S. citizens. 
West Virginia Sen. Patricia Rucker, R-Jefferson, one of the sponsors of Senate Joint Resolution 9, which proposed the amendment, during the 2026 legislative session, told reporters in September that the legal prohibition isn’t enough because “laws can change.” 
“This proposed amendment would ensure that no future Legislature could just simply change the election law with only a bill,” she said. “It also gives us greater authority to enforce the law we currently have in place.”
In a written statement Tuesday, Rucker said she was “proud that West Virginia’s voters chose to protect the integrity of our elections tonight with their yes vote on Amendment 1. 
“The right to vote, especially as (a) naturalized United States citizen, is something I hold close to my heart,” Rucker said in the statement. “Tonight’s result ensures that all West Virginians can be confident that only United States citizens are participating in our elections, and that can’t be changed by any future Legislature or city deciding otherwise. This amendment strengthens our elections and helps preserve the freedoms we all hold dear.”
Besides Rucker, Senate Joint Resolution 9 was also sponsored by Sens. Chris Rose, R-Monongalia; Darren Thorne, R-Hampshire; Amy Grady, R-Mason; Craig Hart, R-Mingo; Laura Chapman, R-Ohio; Senate President Randy Smith, R-Preston; Rollan Roberts, R-Raleigh, Eric Tarr, R-Putnam; Jay Taylor, R-Taylor; Charles Clements, R-Wetzel; Trenton Barnhart, R-Pleasants; and Mark Maynard, R-Wayne. 
With the amendment passed, the West Virginia constitution will read as follows: 
“Only citizens of the United States who are citizens of this state shall be entitled to vote at all elections held within the counties in which they respectively reside; but a person who is a minor, or who has been declared mentally incompetent by a court of competent jurisdiction, or who is under conviction of treason, felony or bribery in an election, or who has not been a resident of the state and of the county in which he or she offers to vote, for 30 days next preceding such offer, shall not be permitted to vote while such disability continues; and, a person in the military, naval, or marine service of the United States shall not be deemed a resident of this state by reason of being stationed therein.”
According to Americans for Citizen Voting, an organization that works to pass citizen-only amendments around the country, 15 states have amended their constitutions to prohibit non-citizens from voting in local, state and federal elections.
The amendment was opposed by, among others, the West Virginia Citizen Action Group, who said it was unnecessary and “perpetuates long-debunked conspiracy theories and scapegoats our immigrant neighbors to sow mistrust in our election results.”

name: Georgia Recorder
title: Keisha Lance Bottoms will be Georgia’s next governor in historic win
description: Keisha Lance Bottoms, the former mayor of Atlanta, will be the first Democrat to occupy Georgia’s top office in more than two decades and the first Black woman governor anywhere in the country. Bottoms defeated her Republican opponent, healthcare executive Rick Jackson, who was endorsed by both outgoing Gov. Brian Kemp and President Donald Trump […]
text:
Democratic candidate for governor Keisha Lance Bottoms, the former mayor of Atlanta, speaks at a rally with former President Barack Obama and Sen. Jon Ossoff in south Atlanta on Oct. 28, 2026. Alander Rocha/Georgia RecorderKeisha Lance Bottoms, the former mayor of Atlanta, will be the first Democrat to occupy Georgia’s top office in more than two decades and the first Black woman governor anywhere in the country.
Bottoms defeated her Republican opponent, healthcare executive Rick Jackson, who was endorsed by both outgoing Gov. Brian Kemp and President Donald Trump and who spent $200 million of his own money on the race. 
The Associated Press called the race just before 9:30 p.m. Tuesday. 
Bottoms will be the state’s first Democratic governor since former Gov. Roy Barnes lost his bid for reelection in 2002. Republicans have had a grip on state government since Sonny Perdue won that election. Kemp has strong approval ratings but is term-limited and can’t run again. 
Bottoms, who served in the Biden administration after leaving city hall, ran a centrist campaign focused on pocketbook issues. In response to concerns over the massive growth of data centers and their impact on Georgians’ power bills, Bottoms proposed a pause on their construction. She proposed a mechanism for local governments to cut taxes on groceries and basic household goods.
Medicaid expansion was central to her campaign, just as it had been for the Democratic nominees who preceded her. Bottoms framed it as a way for the state to fund more healthcare services and prevent further hospital closures.
With her win, Bottoms was able to accomplish what Democrat Stacey Abrams narrowly missed doing nearly a decade ago. Abrams was about 55,000 votes short of beating Kemp in 2018, and Georgia’s statewide elections have been closely watched ever since. 
But Bottoms’ victory this year was far from certain. She and Jackson were neck and neck throughout the campaign, with Bottoms appearing to gain momentum as Election Day neared.
Both candidates attracted high-profile national figures to Georgia, including former President Barack Obama and former Vice President Kamala Harris who made appearances here during early voting to energize voters. On the Republican side, President Donald Trump visited the state twice during early voting, and other national Republicans like Sens. Rick Scott and Ted Cruz dropped in too in hopes of turning out conservative voters even as their chances of flipping Georgia’s U.S. Senate seat seemed to slip away.
Bottoms’ run for the governor’s seat has been a bruising one. She faced an uphill battle against the millions of dollars Jackson spent flooding the airwaves with ads depicting her record as mayor as catastrophic for Atlanta. Scenes from 2020 flashed repeatedly on screens across the state, reminding voters of the Wendy’s fast food restaurant and police cars that were set ablaze during protests in the wake of George Floyd’s murder in Minnesota. 
Jackson’s campaign attempted to make Secoriea Turner, an 8-year-old Atlanta girl who was killed during those protests, an icon of Bottoms’ alleged failures as mayor in spite of Turner’s family’s wishes.
Jackson’s campaign also framed Bottoms’ decision not to seek a second term in 2022 as her abandoning Atlanta at a difficult time, often repeating the line “bad mayors don’t make good governors” on the campaign trail. 
But in the last few weeks leading up to Election Day, Democrats in and outside of Georgia came to Bottoms’ rescue. She raised about five times as much during the final reporting period as she did during the rest of her entire campaign, and in the last few days of the race, she received a $5 million boost from the Democratic Governors Association and another $2.5 million from former New York City mayor and Democratic presidential candidate Mike Bloomberg. 
Kemp initially backed Jackson’s rival in the GOP primary, but he has campaigned vigorously with Jackson in the general election, with the two men frequently seen together at rallies and campaign stops across the state. Kemp, who has maintained high approval ratings, has touted the state’s economic strength and his administration’s focus on tax cuts on the campaign trail, pitching Jackson as the best person to succeed him and continue moving Georgia on a similar path. 
But the state’s economy and population grew, so did concerns over the cost of living, which gave Bottoms and other down-ballot Democrats an opportunity to campaign on what consistently polled as voters’ prevailing concern this year both nationally and here in Georgia.
This is a developing story. Check back for updates.

title: Rep. Chris Smith wins 24th term in the House

text:

Mark Baisley and self-funded third-party candidate Bob Chew.
The Associated Press called the race minutes after polls closed in Colorado at 7 p.m.
Hickenlooper, a fixture in Colorado politics for more than 20 years, will return to Washington for a second six-year Senate term that he has said will be his last. He previously served two terms as mayor of Denver and two terms as Colorado governor.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
He campaigned on restoring cuts to Medicaid, SNAP and other programs enacted by Republicans in their 2025 tax and spending law, accusing the Trump administration of “dismantling” the country’s healthcare system. He has also championed bipartisan efforts to address housing affordability, improve price transparency among healthcare providers, accelerate wildfire mitigation projects and more.
“What we’re going to do now — because the voters’ will is clear — we’re going to rebuild what he took apart,” Hickenlooper said during a speech at Colorado Democrats’ election night watch party in Denver. “We’re going to rewrite our health care system — not just the way it was, but better than it was. We’re going to expand coverage, have a better system.”
A onetime petroleum engineer turned restauranteur and real estate investor, Hickenlooper first became involved in Denver politics as a donor and downtown redevelopment booster in the 1990s, before launching a successful campaign for mayor in 2003. His first mayoral chief of staff was his friend and fellow Wesleyan University graduate, Michael Bennet, who later became superintendent of Denver Public Schools and was appointed to the U.S. Senate in 2009, a year before Hickenlooper was elected governor.
When the 120th Congress convenes in January, Hickenlooper and Bennet — who lost a Democratic primary for governor to Attorney General Phil Weiser earlier this year — will become the first pair of Democratic senators in Colorado history to serve for more than six years alongside one another.
Baisley, a former aerospace engineer, has represented Senate District 4, which includes six rural counties west of Colorado Springs as well as parts of Jefferson and Douglas counties, since 2023. He previously served two terms in the state House of Representatives.
Chew, a Navy veteran and businessman from Boulder, secured the ballot line of the Forward Party and described himself as an independent. He spent at least $3.4 million of his own money on TV and digital advertising, consultant fees and other campaign expenses, centering his message on plans to address the national debt.
Hickenlooper’s Senate record
Hickenlooper ran for president after leaving the Colorado governor’s mansion in 2019, but struggled to gain traction with voters and eventually dropped out at the urging of Senate Democratic leadership, who recruited him to challenge Republican U.S. Sen. Cory Gardner in a key Senate race instead.
After winning his seat, he was among a group of 22 Democrats and Republicans who crafted the 2021 Bipartisan Infrastructure Law, championing provisions to expand broadband access and boost investment in electric vehicle charging stations. The following year, he was credited by activists with keeping alive the negotiations that ultimately led to Democrats’ passage of billions in spending to fight climate change in the Inflation Reduction Act, though much of that spending was subsequently repealed by Republicans’ 2025 budget bill.
The moderate Hickenlooper faced criticism from many within his party for his votes in early 2025 to confirm many of Trump’s Cabinet nominees. His comfortable general-election win over Baisley and Chew comes after an unexpectedly strong primary challenge in June from progressive state Sen. Julie Gonzales, who came within 6 percentage points of unseating the incumbent despite a massive financial disadvantage.
Hickenlooper, who declined to debate Gonzales and largely absented himself from the campaign trail during the primary, later attributed the close result to “a lot of unhappiness and frustration” among Democratic and unaffiliated voters. He also said he regrets the confirmation of “every single one” of Trump’s Cabinet picks.
Hickenlooper, who will be 80 when the term he was elected to Tuesday expires in 2033, has long touted his breadth of experience in business and government as an asset in policymaking. In an October debate, he was asked why he wouldn’t wish to continue serving in a body where members have routinely served into their eighties and beyond.
“I have a lot of friends who’ve said that same thing,” Hickenlooper said, but added that he wanted to spend more time with his family in the future.

Oklahoma State Treasurer winner  Cindy Byrd, left, with husband Steve Byrd, right, speaks during the GOP Election Night Watch Party, Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026, at Skirvin Hotel in Oklahoma City. (Photo by Kyle Phillips/For Oklahoma Voice)OKLAHOMA CITY – Voters selected Republican State Auditor and Inspector Cindy Byrd on Tuesday to become Oklahoma’s next state treasurer. 
Byrd, of Coalgate, easily defeated Libertarian Kiefer Perry.
Byrd said her victory Tuesday shows that voters are willing to trust her.
“They know that I have worked hard for them to show them where their money is really going as the state auditor,” she said. “That’s important because you have to do that to make sure that there’s transparency and accountability in government. This next role is going to be more about collaboration and helping to fix those things that I reported as going wrong, and I’m really looking forward to that challenge.”
Byrd, 53, is term limited as state auditor and inspector after serving eight years. 
She defeated incumbent Republican State Treasurer Todd Russ in the June primary to earn the nomination with 62% of the vote.
Byrd initially announced she intended to run for lieutenant governor, but when President Donald Trump endorsed Republican T.W. Shannon, she made a last-minute decision to run for state treasurer.
Trump endorsed Byrd and a host of other Republicans on a campaign stop in Durant.
As state auditor, she oversaw several high profile audits, including that of Epic Charter school, Tulsa Public Schools, the Oklahoma Turnpike Authority and the State Department of Education.
Perry, 37, of Broken Arrow, acknowledged he didn’t think he would win and said he filed to maintain ballot access for Libertarians.
In order for Libertarians to continue to be recognized on the ballot, at least one candidate for statewide office must receive 2.5% of the total votes in either of the two preceding general elections.

text:
Voters elected Rhode Island General Treasurer James Diossa to a second term in Tuesday's general election. (Photo by Michael Salerno/Rhode Island Current)Democratic General Treasurer James Diossa secured another four years in office Tuesday, easily defeating Republican challenger Micholas Credle.
Diossa received 65% while Credle had 35%, according to unofficial results from the Rhode Island Board of Elections as of 9:13 p.m., with 39 cities and towns reporting
Diossa, 41, a former Central Falls mayor, was first elected general treasurer in 2022. His office oversees Rhode Island’s pension investments and other financial programs, including the state’s unclaimed property system.
During his reelection campaign, Diossa highlighted the growth of the state’s pension fund, expanded efforts to return unclaimed property and a mortgage assistance program for first-time homebuyers.
Credle, 45, a retired U.S. Army captain and first-time political candidate, campaigned on increasing transparency and accountability in the management of state pension investments. He drew support from many retired state employees angered by a 2011 pension overhaul that eliminated their 3% annual cost-of-living increases and tied future adjustments to the pension fund’s funding level, investment returns and inflation.
But Credle faced questions over the handling of his own finances. The Providence Journal reported the political newcomer admitted in court he had not paid child support since February.
A financial disclosure form filed with the Rhode Island Ethics Commission showed Credle reported receiving between $50,001 and $100,000 in VA disability benefits in 2025, along with $25,001 to $50,000 in Social Security disability payments and $10,001 to $25,000 in combat-related special compensation from the Army. The filing also listed Credle as a partner in three businesses, but did not report income from them.

title: Zach Dembo returns 6th District to Democratic hands after victory over Alvarado
description: LEXINGTON — Kentucky Democrats have regained control of a central U.S. House District with former federal prosecutor and Navy veteran Zach Dembo.  Gaining support from top Kentucky Democrats, like Gov. text:
Zach Dembo and his wife, Lindsey, celebrate his win in the 6th District Congressional race on Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo by Brian Simms for Kentucky Lantern)LEXINGTON — Kentucky Democrats have regained control of a central U.S. House District with former federal prosecutor and Navy veteran Zach Dembo. 
Gaining support from top Kentucky Democrats, like Gov. Andy Beshear, and national figures, Dembo was elected in Kentucky’s 6th Congressional District Tuesday evening. The unofficial results were 52.3% to 43.7%. Alvarado conceded shortly after 9 p.m., although the Associated Press had not called the win at 9:20. 
“Central Kentucky, tonight is your night,” he said to cheers from the crowd. I know we did this together, there are so many people in this room who believed in this race … thank you and hard work pays off.”
Republican U.S. Rep. Andy Barr, who represented the district since 2012, ran for U.S. Senate, opening the seat this year. Republican Ralph Alvarado, a former state senator and Tennessee Department of Health commissioner, attempted to keep the seat in GOP hands. He was backed by President Donald Trump in the primary, but tried to distance himself from the president in the general election. 
Dembo and Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear were greeted on stage by a round of cheers and applause at Lexington watch party. Beshear, who is also the chair of the Democratic Governors Association and had his eyes on races around the country, said Dembo’s win in Central Kentucky shows that “Democrats can win anywhere, and we should be fighting everywhere.” The governor said Democrats’ wins Tuesday sends a message against President Donald Trump’s policies.
“We’re sending a message of no more tariffs. We’re sending a message of no more of Trump’s war in Iran. We’re sending a strong message of ‘Enjoy the ballroom because your party only has two years left,'” Beshear said. “We are saying enough — enough of the toxicity, enough of the division, enough of the cruelty and enough of the meanness.”
Democratic-sponsored polls publicly released before November showed Dembo had an edge with voters over Alvarado. Race raters like The Cook Political Report and Sabato’s Crystal Ball moved the district from a safe Republican seat to a toss-up days before the election. 
Kentucky Democrats quickly fell in line after Dembo won the primary election to support him in the district. Beshear joined Dembo for a rally in Lexington on the first night of early voting last week. Before that, the governor appeared in an ad with Dembo poking fun at a cardboard cutout of former Gov. Matt Bevin, who Beshear defeated in 2019. Alvarado was Bevin’s running mate in that election. 
Speaking to reporters Tuesday night, Dembo said he hopes Trump is open to working on things to benefit Central Kentucky. During his October rally, Trump had promised the U.S. Department of Defense would invest in a pharmaceutical company in Winchester if Republicans contained control of Congress during midterms.
“If he doesn’t, then I’m going to oppose him,” Dembo said. “All that matters is what he’s doing for the Kentucky 6.”
Dembo previously worked in the Beshear administration. After Trump returned to office in January 2025, Dembo left his role as a federal prosecutor. Dembo previously told the Kentucky Lantern he did so because he “couldn’t stand by while the administration was playing politics with the justice system to carry out a personal political agenda instead of protecting the Constitution.” 
Zach Dembo supporters watched election returns at his watch party on election night. (Kentucky Lantern photo by Brian Simms)
Dembo carved out a lane as a moderate Democrat in the race, and referred to himself as such in his first televised debate with Alvarado on Fox56 in late October. From that encounter, Democrats also pushed a clip of Alvarado saying his wife “does a lot of the (grocery) shopping for us” to go viral from that debate in response to a question about how his family has been affected by rising grocery prices. The Alvarado team later defended the answer, telling WHAS: “By making an issue out of who does the grocery shopping, Zach Dembo proved he doesn’t understand how normal families divide responsibilities.”
Groups on both sides of the aisle spent heavily in the race, with PACs spending more than $6 million leading up to the general election. Those groups included PACS allied with Trump and Beshear. The Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee also had its eyes on flipping the seat, naming the seat as a district in play and putting the race on its Red to Blue program. 
Democrats last controlled the 6th Congressional District before the 2012 election, when former U.S. Rep. Ben Chandler was defeated by Barr. 
Rocky Adkins, who is a Democrat running for governor, spoke to reporters at Dembo’s watch party early Tuesday evening and was optimistic about how the night would go for Kentucky Democrats.
“I expect a really good night tonight for Zach Dembo. I think, without question, Zach is a hard worker,” Adkins said. “He’s done the ground work that you had to do as well as raising the money, getting his message out.”
Adkins added that no matter the outcome, Dembo had “left it all on the court” and ran a campaign focusing on concerns from Kentuckians about policies coming out of Washington, D.C.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Gov. Ned Lamont defeats Ryan Fazio, winning 3rd term
description: Gov. Ned Lamont, a Democrat buoyed by Connecticut’s extraordinary string of budget surpluses, won a third term over Republican Ryan Fazio.
text:
Gov. Ned Lamont, a Democrat buoyed by Connecticut’s extraordinary string of budget surpluses after a lost decade of chronic fiscal crisis, won a third term Tuesday over Republican Ryan Fazio in a midterm election dominated by the policies and unpopularity of President Donald Trump.
The Associated Press called the race for Lamont shortly after 9:15 p.m. on a night when the only drama in Connecticut was expected to turn on the degree to which Democrats would increase their General Assembly majorities the day after the 10th anniversary of Trump’s first election, the beginning of a difficult era for the state’s GOP.
Early results suggested a Democratic sweep by the six statewide constitutional officers: the ticket of Lamont and Lt. Gov. Susan Bysiewicz, and Secretary of the State Stephanie Thomas, Comptroller Sean Scanlon, Treasurer Erick Russell and Attorney General William Tong.
The victory positions Lamont, 72, a Greenwich businessman who came to national prominence 20 years ago as a left-wing U.S. Senate candidate opposed to the war in Iraq, to become Connecticut’s longest-serving governor since statehood. It the leaves 36-year-old Fazio to contemplate a second run in 2030.
“I think we’ve made real progress in the state in the last eight years. We still have our work to do,” Lamont said before the polls closed. 
Lamont never trailed in any public poll, even nearly every survey found voters rattled by the high cost of living and many uncertain about their own economic security. With high gas prices driven by the war on Iran and the president’s on-again, off-again trade tariffs, voter animus was directed at Trump.
Their race was run under the shadow of the intense national fight over control of the U.S. Senate and U.S. House, and the insistence by the president that voters treat him as being on the ballot — an invitation embraced by Democrats and ignored by Republican candidates in Connecticut.
“I think some people are paying attention to that,” a relaxed Lamont said. “I’m paying particular attention to Connecticut, everything we can do to make life a little more affordable for all our people.”
Lamont’s third term begins on Jan. 6, three days after his 73rd birthday. He has all but ruled out seeking a fourth term in 2030, smiling and saying, “Time marches on.”
Democrats were expecting another overwhelmingly victory in the suburbs that lined up behind the governor in 2022, giving him 56% to 43% win after a nail biter for the open seat in 2018.
Fazio was aiming to become Connecticut’s youngest governor, running on a relatively thin resume of five years representing Greenwich in the state Senate. 
Three of the state’s last four governors, Lamont included, failed in their first runs for the office. The exception was Gov. M. Jodi Rell, whose first and only run came after she succeeded John G. Rowland after his resignation. She won with 63% of the vote in 2006, then did not seek another term in 2010.

Republican gubernatorial candidate Ryan Fazio speaks to the media outside McKinley Elementary School in Fairfield on Thursday, Nov. 3, 2026. Credit: john moritz / ct mirror

Polling showed Fazio struggled to make impression on voters. His campaign was tightly focused on the high cost of taxes, electricity and housing in Connecticut, and he never leaned into telling a story about his own biography.
“It’s never my instinct to talk about myself, my background,” Fazio said as he campaigned Tuesday. “It’s just not who I am. I’m running to do the job, and I’m running to accomplish goals to improve the state economy, to deliver opportunity to people. So it’s just not my instinct.
“That said, I tried to make an effort towards the closing weeks of the campaign to talk a little bit more from the heart about why I chose to run, what motivates me,” Fazio said.
Fazio was an assured candidate in his two televised debates with the governor, both of which most likely served as audition for 2030. 
He avoided publicly complaining about having to run against a headwind generated by Trump, but he acknowledged a difficult day was coming.
“It’ll be a challenging Election Day, I think, for Republicans across the country,” Fazio said.
“But I also hear, ‘I’m voting for you, even though I’m a Democrat,’” Fazio said on a stop outside a polling place in Fairfield. “So I think there is going to be split ticketing, and I think you’ll see our campaign perform very well.”
Zachary Rairan, a first-time voter who emerged from the polling site a short while later, was not among those ticket splitters. 
The 19-year-old from Fairfield said his support for Lamont was driven by issues such as abortion as well as the governor’s support for a 2019 law that introduced regular minimum wage increases. But, he said, the national mood around the Trump administration was also a factor in his vote. 
“You can’t really disregard what’s happening at the national level,” Rairan said. “I don’t want to support a party that, at a higher level, takes advantage of people.” 
Another Fairfield voter, 67-year-old Matthew Benjamin, a Republican, was less enthusiastic about the prospect of four more years of Democratic leadership in Connecticut.

Matthew Benjamin, 67 of Fairfield, cast his ballot and purchased a few boxes of Thin Mints and Samoas from a Girl Scout troop outside the polling place on Nov. 3, 2026.  Credit: John Moritz / CT Mirror

“I came for the cookies,” he joked, holding up a boxes of Thin Mints and Somoas purchased from a local Girl Scout troop. 
For the first time in his life, Benjamin said, he voted a straight GOP ticket. His chief concern, he said, was “fraud” and candidates lot living up their promises. 
“I’m just tired of all the B.S.,” Benjamin said.

title: Democrat Phil Weiser elected Colorado governor
description: Colorado Attorney General Phil Weiser was elected the state’s 44th governor, defeating Republican Victor Marx and independent candidate Greg Lopez. The Associated Press called the race minutes after polls closed at 7 p.m. Weiser will be inaugurated on Jan. 12, 2027, succeeding Democratic Gov. Jared Polis, who is term-limited. A former dean of the University [...]
text:
Attorney General Phil Weiser, a Democratic candidate for Colorado governor, rallies Democratic voters at the Boulder Theater on Oct. 28, 2026 ahead of the midterm elections. (Photo by Chase Woodruff/Colorado Newsline)Colorado Attorney General Phil Weiser was elected the state’s 44th governor, defeating Republican Victor Marx and independent candidate Greg Lopez.
The Associated Press called the race minutes after polls closed at 7 p.m.
Weiser will be inaugurated on Jan. 12, 2027, succeeding Democratic Gov. Jared Polis, who is term-limited. A former dean of the University of Colorado School of Law and Justice Department antitrust attorney under two Democratic presidents, Weiser was elected attorney general in 2018 and reelected in 2022.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Though heavily favored in the general election, Weiser entered 2026 as the underdog in a head-to-head gubernatorial primary with U.S. Sen. Michael Bennet. Touting the dozens of lawsuits he has filed against the Trump administration as Colorado’s attorney general, Weiser billed himself as a “fighter” who would stand up to Trump’s attacks on immigrants, social spending programs and the rule of law.
That message resonated in a state where Trump remains deeply unpopular, and Weiser overcame Bennet’s financial advantage and widespread establishment support to win the June primary by a comfortable 14 percentage points.
Marx, a first-time candidate and self-described “high-risk missionary,” became a target of national ridicule when he struggled in interviews and debates to answer for sensational claims he has made about his personal background and work overseas. During the general election, he continued to face scrutiny over multiple alleged campaign finance violations, his views on abortion and past comments in which he recalled “grabbing (his wife) and slamming her into our front door.”
Victor Marx, the Republican nominee for Colorado governor, speaks at the 2026 summer conference of the Colorado Water Congress in Steamboat Springs on Aug. 19, 2026. (Photo by Chase Woodruff/Colorado Newsline)
Marx declined to debate Weiser and appeared on stage with him just once, at a Colorado Chamber of Commerce event during which Marx appeared to read prewritten responses to questions he had been provided in advance. Marx’s two GOP primary opponents, who labeled him a “con man” and “grifter,” declined to endorse him, while Weiser won the backing of prominent Republicans including former U.S. Rep. Ken Buck.
Lopez, who served a six-month stint as a GOP member of Congress in 2024, had unsuccessfully sought the party’s nomination for governor in both 2018 and 2022. He initially tried a third time before announcing in January that he would instead run as an unaffiliated candidate, and secured his spot on the ballot through petition signatures.
Lesley Dahlkemper, a Jefferson County commissioner, will serve as Weiser’s lieutenant governor, succeeding Lt. Gov. Dianne Primavera, who has served under Polis in the post for two terms.
Democratic tensions
As governor, Weiser will preside over a Democratic coalition that, even as it has cemented its grip on Colorado politics, has strained under the weight of internal conflicts and ideological divides.
Polis has clashed throughout his tenure with fellow Democrats in the Legislature and angered many in the party’s progressive wing with his moderate, business-friendly views on fiscal and regulatory issues. Those tensions have boiled over more frequently during his second term, as lawmakers largely rebuffed a sweeping package of housing reforms championed by the governor, and Polis issued record numbers of vetoes — including of the Worker Protection Act, a bill to ease union formation that has been a top priority of Colorado labor groups.
Polis’ standing within his party collapsed further in May, when he commuted the remainder of the prison sentence handed to Tina Peters, the Trump ally and former Mesa County clerk convicted for her role in a 2021 breach of her office’s secure election equipment in a failed attempt to uncover evidence of fraud in the 2020 election.
The decision earned Polis a formal censure from the Colorado Democratic Party, which barred him from participation in party events. The two-term governor, reelected four years ago by a nearly 20-point margin, was almost entirely absent from the 2026 campaign trail, aside from a handful of media appearances in which he urged Colorado voters to reject Amendment 87, a progressive income tax measure. He wasn’t present at Colorado Democrats’ election-night watch party in Denver.
Though he harshly criticized Polis’ grant of clemency to Peters, Weiser has otherwise been circumspect about how his administration might differ from the current one on specific policy matters.
During the primary, he declined to endorse the Worker Protection Act, preferring an unspecified compromise instead. And he has suggested state government should be more, not less, responsive to the concerns of the business lobby than it has been under Polis — a view starkly at odds with the one held by many liberal and progressive activists, who for years have seen their policy goals blocked by Polis’ veto pen or inaction by his regulatory appointees.
Late Friday, Weiser announced that he, too, opposed Amendment 87, an unwelcome surprise for some progressives who had backed him during the primary. He had previously declined to take a position on the measure, first because it had not been formally certified for the ballot and then because it was the subject of ongoing litigation. Bennet endorsed the amendment shortly before Weiser’s announcement.
Weiser said during an event last month that amid looming conflicts among state policymakers over the Worker Protection Act and other issues, he will aim to ensure all Coloradans are “at the table” and feel “listened to.”
“There are going to be a lot of decisions that I make, that people are like, ‘I’m really disappointed in that decision,'” Weiser said. “To which I’ll say, ‘I understand. I’ve listened to you. I’ll keep listening to you. You’re not going to like all of my decisions, but you’re going to know that I care about you. I listen to you. I’m going to be transparent.'”

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: Amendment to curtail KY governor’s pardon power wins by large margin
description: Kentucky voters have approved a constitutional amendment to curb governors’ pardon powers around elections.  The amendment won at the ballot box Tuesday by a vote of almost 40 percentage points. The change limits Kentucky governors’ power to grant pardons and sentence commutations around elections by blocking them 60 days before their election through the in[...]
text:
The Kentucky Capitol in Frankfort (Photo courtesy Legislative Research Commission)Kentucky voters have approved a constitutional amendment to curb governors’ pardon powers around elections. 
The amendment won at the ballot box Tuesday by a vote of almost 40 percentage points. The change limits Kentucky governors’ power to grant pardons and sentence commutations around elections by blocking them 60 days before their election through the inauguration in December. 
Sen. Chris McDaniel, R-Ryland Heights, had repeatedly proposed legislation for the amendment in the General Assembly for several years after former Republican Gov. Matt Bevin issued a flurry of controversial pardons after he lost the 2019 election to Democratic Gov. Andy Beshear.
Sen. Chris McDaniel, R-Ryland Heights. (LRC Public Information)
The campaign for the amendment was a quieter affair than others have been in recent years. No issue committees filed to support or oppose the issue. McDaniel sponsored some materials himself and traveled across the state leading up to Election Day to speak in support of the measure. 
“There is no check on the power to pardon, and so we’ve got to get ourselves to the point where there is a check,” McDaniel previously said in an October interview with the Kentucky Lantern. 
Bevin’s pardons were widely criticized. He issued pardons to people convicted of crimes including rape, murder and child abuse. One was for a Northern Kentucky man who had been convicted of raping a nine-year-old the year before. Another was for a convicted killer whose family raised money for Bevin’s campaign.
However, some were wary of changing the Kentucky Constitution because of one person. Scottie Ellis, a spokesperson for Beshear, told the Lantern in June that while Bevin had “abused the pardon authority and let violent criminals out of prison, … the solution should not be to limit a governor’s pardon powers but to ensure we elect good governors.”

name: Florida Phoenix
title: Moody wins U.S. Senate race, edging Nixon
description: U.S. Sen. Ashley Moody won her third statewide election Tuesday as Republicans kept hold of the Florida seat to which Moody was appointed after President Donald Trump nominated Marco Rubio as secretary of state. Moody defeated state Rep. Angie Nixon in a special election called to fill the remaining two years of Rubio’s term. The […]
text:
Florida Republican U.S. Sen. Ashley Moody campaigns in Lakeland on Nov. 2, 2026 (Photo by Mitch Perry/Florida Phoenix)U.S. Sen. Ashley Moody won her third statewide election Tuesday as Republicans kept hold of the Florida seat to which Moody was appointed after President Donald Trump nominated Marco Rubio as secretary of state.
Moody defeated state Rep. Angie Nixon in a special election called to fill the remaining two years of Rubio’s term. The Associated Press called the race just after 8:30 eastern time, with more than 90% of the votes counted. She led Nixon by about 2 percentage points, earning 50.9% of the vote compared to Nixon’s 48%.
Moody had previously won two statewide elections for Florida attorney general before Gov. Ron DeSantis appointed her to fill Rubio’s spot.
Moody spent much of her campaign calling Nixon a “socialist” due to Nixon’s decision to join the Democratic Socialists of America earlier this year. The DSA did not endorse Nixon but Nixon highlighted her progressive record as she campaigned throughout Florida, a state that had swung steadily to Republicans in the past several elections.
While Nixon pointed out that she did not agree with all of the DSA positions, the affiliation still became the focus of Moody’s criticism. It was a theme Moody revisited in her victory speech Tuesday night in Tampa.
“What a night, what a win,” Moody began. “You know, throughout this campaign, I said that this election would come down to freedom versus socialism. Well Florida chose freedom,” Moody said.
Moody also gave thanks to President Donald Trump, as well as DeSantis.
“I want everyone to know, whether you voted for me or whether you didn’t vote for me, I am your senator, I am here to serve you,” Moody said. “And if you ever need me, if I can ever help you in your pursuit of the American dream, please call my office. It would be my great honor to serve you.”
Nixon, who upset the Democratic establishment favorite Alexander Vindman in the August primary, got backing from notable progressive voices in the run-up to the November election, including independent U.S. Sen. Bernie Sanders of Vermont and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, a New York Democrat. 
While Moody painted Nixon as a socialist and radical, Nixon—in turn— kept reminding voters at campaign rallies and on social media of the Hope Florida scandal, and Moody’s role in the transfer of $10 million in Medicaid funding from a settlement with managed care plan Centene away from the state and into the Hope Florida Foundation, championed by First Lady Casey DeSantis.
Nixon didn’t mention Hope Florida in her concession speech, though.
“So I want y’all to hear me when I say this: We may not have won this election, but that outcome will not stop us from giving up, from getting up tomorrow to continue the fight to deliver what everyday hardworking Floridians need and deserve,” Nixon told an enthusiastic crowd of supporters that started changing Angie, Angie, Angie. “I’m going to wake up tomorrow and keep fighting against the against the corruption that’s keeping our wages stagnant and driving up our costs.” 
At the end of her remarks Nixon hinted that this may not be her last race.
“And I promise ya’ll that we may have lost this battle, but the war is not over. But I need ya’ll to stay in this fight. The war is not over. 2028 is around the corner. Ashley Moody, you better get it right because we’re coming for you.”
The crowd road with enthusiasm.
 This is a breaking news story and will be updated.

name: West Virginia Watch
title: Shelley Moore Capito secures third term as US Senator
description: Sen. Shelley Moore Capito, R-W.Va., will continue serving in the U.S. Senate after the election was called by the Associated Press in her favor about an hour after polls closed.
text:
Sen. Shelley Moore Capito, R-W.Va., delivers remarks at the Leatherwood Water Extension groundbreaking ceremony in Clendenin, West Virginia on Tuesday, Oct. 13, 2026. (Photo courtesy of U.S. Sen. Shelley Moore Capito’s office)Sen. Shelley Moore Capito, R-W.Va., will continue serving in the U.S. Senate after the election was called by the Associated Press in her favor about an hour after polls closed. 
Capito secured 57% of the votes counted, according to the Association Press around 9 p.m.. Polls closed at 7:30 p.m. She has won every general election for a federal position. 
“It is wonderful to be here to be declared a winner on such a night,” Capito said at her watch party in Charleston, West Virginia. “From the bottom of my heart, I want to say a great, great thank you. … I will continue to always serve you as I have for the last several years.”
Democratic challenger Rachel Fetty Anderson, a Morgantown-based attorney, received around 39% of the votes counted.
Capito, who is fourth in the Senate Republican majority leadership, stressed that her win means West Virginia will have a strong voice “at the table” in Washington, D.C.
“We are mighty in spirit and always have been,” she said. 
Capito, 72, has been in the U.S. Senate since 2015 and is the first woman from West Virginia to hold that position. She won elections by wide margins in 2014 and 2020.
She easily won a May primary challenge from six challengers, including current state Sen. Tom Willis, R-Berkeley. 
Capito has been re-elected to a six-year term in the U.S. Senate, beginning her third term in 2027.
She serves as chairwoman of the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee.
President Donald Trump endorsed Capito in her re-election campaign. 
Before serving in the U.S. Senate, Capito was elected to the U.S. House of Representatives and the West Virginia House of Delegates.
Fetty Anderson won a crowded and competitive Democratic primary race in May to challenge Capito in the general election.

name: WyoFile
title: Hageman wins Wyoming’s Senate race
description:
Democrat James Byrd is counted out early in the country’s reddest state.
The post Hageman wins Wyoming’s Senate race appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
Republican U.S. Rep. Harriet Hageman will become Wyoming’s next U.S. Senator after defeating Democrat James Byrd in Tuesday’s election. 
The Associated Press called the election for Hageman at 7 p.m. with 0% of the votes counted. AP calls an election “the moment the trailing candidates no longer have a path to victory,” according to the news organization’s policy.
Hageman, 64 and a two-term representative, will succeed Sen. Cynthia Lummis, another Republican who decided last year not to seek a second term. Byrd, 72, is a former state representative who served from 2009-2019.
Hageman won the election in the country’s reddest state, where President Donald Trump in 2024 won with more than 71% of the vote. She was Trump’s pick to defeat one of his biggest political enemies, Rep. Liz Cheney, in 2022 and earned his endorsement for Senate late last year.



Hageman aligned with Trump on most issues. An attorney, she has fought federal regulations on public land use, regulations she says hold back Wyoming’s economy. Fully 48% of Wyoming is owned by the federal government, public land on which miners, drillers and ranchers depend, land that’s also cherished by hunters and recreationists.
The U.S. Forest Service Roadless Rule that protected about 3.2 million acres in Wyoming from development or exploitation was just one issue that divided her and Byrd.
Hageman backed elimination of the roadless rule, calling instead for development of land that many value for its wildlife habitat. “The Roadless Rule has devastated America’s forests, watersheds, and rural communities,” she posted on Facebook. She characterized roadless areas as poorly managed forests that spawn devastating wildfires.
Byrd said the opposite was true, citing a Forest Service official’s testimony and agency statistics. Hageman “has no problem standing up there and flat out being dishonest and lying,” he said.
Hageman also sided with the state of Utah, which in 2024 sought to take over 18.5 million acres of federal property, an effort critics said would ultimately turn Western public lands private. The U.S. Supreme Court would not hear the case.
A fervent supporter of the president, she’s criticized the “far-left’s scarcity agenda” and boosted Wyoming’s fossil fuels in the face of rising global temperatures. Hageman sits on the House Natural Resources and Judiciary committees and Select Subcommittee on the Weaponization of the Federal Government, along with several other subcommittees.
She’s been a constant presence in the state, despite some rocky town hall meetings. “I have now completed 89 town halls in just 3.5 years,” she said in social posts.
She has touted work for constituents, claiming to have returned more than $18 million to constituents while in office.
Hageman took the debate stage in the primary, but ducked a debate with Byrd in the general election.
“We have one word for that in Wyoming: b—shit,” Byrd said after PBS cancelled the event. “If Harriet Hageman wants to hide behind silent non-responses, that’s her choice.”
Byrd said Hageman and the rest of the state’s federal delegation does not represent Wyoming but instead “the Beltway interests, the corporate boardrooms and the silicon bros.”
A Cheyenne resident, Byrd has worked in the fields of computer networking, geophysical exploration and software management.
He criticized the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, saying it cost the poorest Americans $1,200 on average while boosting income for the richest by $13,600. He laid high fuel prices and inflation on the sitting administration, saying it was responsible for beef imports, reliance on Russian fuel and threats to federal grazing leases.
“Wyomingites are being squeezed at every turn — at the grocery check-out, at the doctor’s office, and at the fuel pump,” he said. “Nobody gets a Republican or Democrat discount at the pump. We are paying way too much, and Washington did it to us.”

title: Kim Ahern elected Rhode Island’s first Democratic female Attorney General
description: Democrat Kim Ahern easily defeated Republican Alan Gordon in Tuesday’s general election to become Rhode Island’s next attorney general, succeeding term-limited incumbent Peter Neronha. The Associated Press called the race at 9:04 p.m. with an estimated 84% of the vote counted. Ahern received 66% of the vote to Gordon’s 34%, according to unofficial results fr[...]
text:
Kim Ahern is Rhode Island's next attorney general after besting Republican Alan Gordon in Tuesday's general election. (Photo by Michael Salerno/Rhode Island Current)Democrat Kim Ahern easily defeated Republican Alan Gordon in Tuesday’s general election to become Rhode Island’s next attorney general, succeeding term-limited incumbent Peter Neronha.
The Associated Press called the race at 9:04 p.m. with an estimated 84% of the vote counted.
Ahern received 66% of the vote to Gordon’s 34%, according to unofficial results from the Rhode Island Board of Elections.
Ahern, 43, is the second woman to be elected as the state’s top lawyer. Republican Arlene Violet was the first, serving from 1985 to 1987.
A former state prosecutor, Ahern served as deputy counsel for former Gov. Gina Raimondo and deputy chief of staff for Gov. Dan McKee. She most recently served as the head of the three-member Cannabis Control Commission, a position she held since the panel’s inception by the state in 2023.
Ahern won September’s four-way Democratic primary with 36.3% of the vote, defeating Keith Hoffmann, Neronha’s endorsed successor, who received 33%.
During her campaign, Ahern emphasized consumer protection, health care oversight and challenging federal policies she considers unlawful. A centerpiece of her platform is a proposal to create a Reproductive Justice unit within the attorney general’s office to defend abortion access, which she says is threatened by the Trump-Vance administration.
Gordon, 57, is a canon lawyer from West Greenwich for the Healing Church, a Christian sect that uses cannabis in its services. He campaigned on constitutional rights and government accountability, along with proposing criminally charging men for unwanted pregnancies.
Gordon ran unsuccessfully for attorney general as a member of the Compassion Party in 2018. He was unopposed in the 2026 Republican primary, but did not receive the party’s endorsement.

Morales’ victory over Republican Dave Talan furthers the political shift which began with the 28-year-old Democratic candidate’s victory over incumbent Mayor Brett Smiley in September’s primary.

Morales is scheduled to announce the co-chairs of his mayoral transition team at a press conference Wednesday at 2 p.m.
Talan, 77, a retired computer systems analyst and engineer, opposed rent stabilization and argued the city’s housing issues could be better soothed through more housing stock.
