name: WyoFile
title: Republican Eric Barlow wins Wyoming governor’s race
description:
The Campbell County rancher and state senator defeated two opponents and overcame criticism he wasn’t conservative enough.
The post Republican Eric Barlow wins Wyoming governor’s race appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
CASPER—Republican Sen. Eric Barlow, a Gillette rancher and former speaker of the House, will likely be Wyoming’s 34th governor following Tuesday’s general election. 
The Associated Press called the race at 7 p.m. with 0% of the votes counted. 
“We’re so thankful for all those who did participate and vote, and we look forward to working together to make Wyoming stronger, more prosperous and more independent,” Barlow told WyoFile shortly after the race was called Tuesday.
Barlow defeated Democrat Ken Casner and Constitution Party candidate Rebecca Bextel, who entered the race to directly challenge Barlow. 
His victory runs parallel to the last two times the governor’s seat was open in Wyoming, when the Republican nominee handily won the general election after succeeding in the primary election. 



In August, Barlow triumphed over Superintendent of Public Instruction Megan Degenfelder, who was backed by President Donald Trump, for the Republican nomination. Wyoming voters overwhelmingly supported the president in 2024, but have indicated more recently a considerable disapproval of the way he is handling the job. That’s according to the Wyoming Survey and Analysis Center’s 2026 election survey released last week. 
Barlow also succeeded in the primary election despite the Wyoming GOP endorsing another candidate, Brent Bien, and steady criticism from the right wing of the party that he was too moderate. 
When asked Tuesday night what he would tell voters who didn’t support him, Barlow said, “We’ll be working on their behalf, too.” 
“That’s the role of an elected official. It’s not to just represent those who may have voted for them or they like, but to actually represent the entirety of that constituency as governor,” he said.
Candidates for governor Eric Barlow, Kenneth Casner and Rebecca Bextel take the stage during the Wyoming PBS gubernatorial debate on Wednesday, Oct. 14, 2026, in Riverton. (Carl Cote/County 10)
Barlow’s win Tuesday puts Wyoming on track to welcome another traditional Republican governor with ranching roots. Current Gov. Mark Gordon and former Gov. Matt Mead also won office despite skepticism from their party’s flank. 
Gordon did not run for reelection and was technically prevented from seeking a third term, though he could have challenged that, as the Wyoming Supreme Court has ruled that term limits on the other top elected positions in the state are unconstitutional.
Born in Gillette and raised on the family ranch southwest of town, Barlow served as a U.S. Marine and worked as a large-animal veterinarian and a rancher before voters elected him to House District 3 in 2013. Voters then elected him to Senate District 23 in 2022. 
As a lawmaker, Barlow led the House as speaker in 2021 and 2022 and now chairs the Senate Labor, Health and Social Services Committee as well as the Mental Health and Vulnerable Adult Task Force. 
He kicked off his gubernatorial bid more than year ago, and focused his campaign on protecting public lands, funding education and solving Wyoming’s healthcare access and affordability issues. 
“I am a leader who stands firmly on sound, conservative principles and who will fiercely defend your rights, including the Second Amendment and the sanctity of life,” Barlow said in his campaign announcement in August 2025. “I will protect your private property rights, safeguard our public lands, and keep Washington, D.C., out of Wyoming’s business.” 
When it came to fundraising, Barlow also pulled ahead of his opponents, raising more than $2 million since he announced in 2025, and setting a new fundraising record for a statewide race in Wyoming. 
Most of Barlow’s raising and spending occurred before the primary election, but not all. Since winning the nomination, he raised about $335,000 and spent around $195,000. 
Wyoming’s election results are considered unofficial until they are certified by the state canvassing board next week. 
Elected officials, including Wyoming’s new governor, will be sworn into office on Jan. 4, 2027.

name: Daily Montanan
title: Montanans head to the polls with affordability top of mind
authors: Keila Szpaller, Micah Drew, Jordan Hansen
description: Astoria Beckstrom estimated she’d wait roughly an hour to register to vote at the Missoula County Elections Center. To Beckstrom, a University of Montana student who uses Montana Medicaid, the wait was worth it. Beckstrom said she’d been fighting to prove she really did still qualify for Medicaid, and remained a low-income Montanan after working […]
text:
Astoria Beckstrom, second on the right at the Missoula County Elections Center, is registering to vote for the first time. She expected to wait for roughly an hour. (Keila Szpaller/Daily Montanan)Astoria Beckstrom estimated she’d wait roughly an hour to register to vote at the Missoula County Elections Center.
To Beckstrom, a University of Montana student who uses Montana Medicaid, the wait was worth it.
Beckstrom said she’d been fighting to prove she really did still qualify for Medicaid, and remained a low-income Montanan after working a two-day event, earning $500.
Her student loan payment also had been delayed, and Beckstrom said many of her family members have lower incomes and face similar difficulties.
Affordability is a top priority for voters in the midterms this year, and on Election Day in 2026, Beckstrom, 22, was registering to vote for the first time.
“I need something to change,” Beckstrom said.
Montanans were heading to the polls to choose state and federal candidates in a midterm that has many Americans concerned with the direction of the Trump administration.
Many people also are worried about costs — of groceries, gasoline and utility bills.
Luke Scannell, a 25-year old in Helena, said he was thinking about government corruption and cost of living after he filled out his ballot on Tuesday evening.
Before Election Day, the Montana Secretary of State’s Office sent 533,647 absentee ballots, and as of 2 p.m. Tuesday, 66% had been received.
Some election judges said there were initial fears of voter intimidation, but those dissipated and security around ballot boxes was normal. Few lengthy lines were reported around the city, as many had already cast absentee ballots.
Longtime election judges in Helena, including city commissioner Julia Gustafson, reported the polls were busy in the morning and tapered off into the afternoon. Tuesday afternoon saw a slow but steady trickle of voters into the polls at the city’s library, Civic Center and the Lewis and Clark County Fairgrounds.
“Everything has been really smooth, especially from our perspective,” Gustafson said on Tuesday around noon.
  ‘Lesser of two evils’ 

For some college students, election day meant classwork in the field. Kate Wilkins and Thomas Derden, both students at Carroll College in Helena, were doing voter data analysis for a class. Wilkins is a political science major, while Derden is writing about the impacts of social media on partisanship and politics.
Kate Wilkins, left, and Thomas Derden pose outside the Lewis and Clark County Fairgrounds o Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026. (Jordan Hansen / Daily Montanan)
Mostly, it’s learning more about voters and voter habits. Wilkins described politics as “the air we breathe” and said it impacts everyone’s daily lives.
“It affects how you get up, the kind of job you can go do, the kind of education your kids can get, how easy or hard it is for you to put food on the table. All of that is dictated by the political climate in which we live,” Wilkins said.
She added it was important for people to educate themselves, and those around them on how politics impacted their daily lives.
“The first step is recognizing that politics is the mechanism by which we change,” Wilkins said.
In Whitefish, a reliably blue spot in deep red Flathead County — both the state senator and current state representative are Democrats — a lone figure stood at a main downtown intersection waving a “Vote Republican” flag.
Randy Simpson, a lifelong conservative, said he had stood on the same corner Monday as well as Election Day morning, and received a good amount of interaction from passing drivers — about a 10-to-1 ratio of thumbs up to middle fingers — which he said made it fun.
Whitefish resident Randy Simpson says he wants people to vote for Republicans despite not feeling enthusiastic about any on the 2026 midterm ballot. (Micah Drew/Daily Montanan)
Despite holding a clear sign that he wants his neighbors to vote for Republicans, he said he wasn’t actually excited about any of the Republicans on the ballot this year. Instead, he said he thinks the Democratic party is corrupt and while the Republicans might be too, he still leaned more conservative.
“It’s the lesser of two evils, right?” Simpson said.
 Candidates hit home stretch 

Several local candidates spent their election days holding signs and waving at voters near polling places.
In Kalispell, Jim Riley, a first-time Republican candidate running for House District 6, turned out with his whole family at the Flathead County Fairgrounds, where a majority of the area’s precincts vote.
Further south in Polson, another first-time candidate, 21-year-old Finley Warden, hit the streets at 5 a.m. with supporters, covering parked cars with signs for several blocks surrounding the city’s polling location.
“I feel really good about today,” Warden, running for House District 13, told the Daily Montanan.
He said if he ends up in Helena, he is looking forward to working on legislation that will fix that affordability crisis he says his generation is facing — he saw his own rent hike $150 recently — and being a reliably conservative voice for the community.
Despite the pre-dawn start to his last day of campaigning, Warden said he plans to stay out until polls close at 8 p.m.
Jim Riley, a first-time candidate for the legislature, holds signs with his family outside the Flathead County Fairgrounds on Nov. 3, 2026. (Micah Drew/Daily Montanan)
  DOJ monitors in Montana 

A news release from the U.S. Department of Justice said federal election monitors would be in Yellowstone County on Election Day. The DOJ was dispatching monitors to all 50 states.
The monitors would be checking for compliance with voting laws, including the Voting Rights Act and the Civil Rights Act.
“Today, the DOJ will further this mission by engaging in its largest monitoring effort in history — with approximately 1,000 election monitors and observers deployed, and, for the first time, in all 50 states,” the news release said.
No monitors had reported to Missoula County elections officials, but a longtime pollwatcher said the scene at the elections center was exciting.
Susan Campbell Reneau, going on 75, said she’s been watching polls in Montana since 1992 when she moved to the Treasure State.
Reneau said she gets emotional seeing the excitement and even the people coming to the elections center with their dogs.
“Everybody is in good spirits,” Reneau said.
Mary Giuliani, who dropped off a ballot at the elections center, said she always votes, but this election was crucial.
“This election and our next federal upcoming election are going to be really critical to upholding democracy,” Giuliani said.

title: Democrat Jamie Ager flips western North Carolina US House seat
description: Democrat Jamie Ager appears to have won North Carolina’s 11th Congressional District, flipping the seat.  Ager, the owner of Hickory Nut Gap Farm in Fairview, defeated state Rep. Jennifer Balkcom, a Republican from Hendersonville. The Associated Press called the race at 8:55 p.m.  “Instead of trying to move the mountains here in Western North Carolina, […]
text:
Jamie Ager and Jennifer Balkcom. (Photos: Campaign websites)Democrat Jamie Ager appears to have won North Carolina’s 11th Congressional District, flipping the seat. 
Ager, the owner of Hickory Nut Gap Farm in Fairview, defeated state Rep. Jennifer Balkcom, a Republican from Hendersonville. The Associated Press called the race at 8:55 p.m. 
“Instead of trying to move the mountains here in Western North Carolina, we decided to go right into them and meet people,” Ager said during his victory speech. “We got curious about what makes Western North Carolina such a special place to be.”
The district has been reliably red for most of the past 35 years. President Donald Trump won it three times, and it’s only elected one Democrat, Heath Shuler, to Congress since 1991. 
Democrats saw an opening with Ager, a homegrown farmer who’s well known in the community and comes from a political family with decades of history in Western North Carolina. He initially faced an uphill climb. 
But after disgraced GOP incumbent U.S. Rep. Chuck Edwards dropped his reelection bid in August, the tables turned. The North Carolina Republican Party picked Balkcom as Edwards’ replacement on Aug. 10, leaving her with less than three months to run a congressional campaign. 
Both candidates competed to appeal to Western North Carolina’s mountain values. In the end, Balkcom just couldn’t catch up. 
A tale of two farmers: Ager, Balkcom compete for NC-11 seat

Election forecaster Cook Political Report shifted the district from “toss up” to “lean Democratic” on Oct. 23. 
At the moment, Republicans hold a 218-214 majority in the House, with three vacancies. Democrats need a net gain of three seats to flip the chamber. 
Ager’s grandfather Jamie Clark represented the 11th Congressional District from 1983 to 1985 and 1987 to 1991. His brother Eric serves in the state House, as did their father John. 
This story is developing and will be updated.

name: New Hampshire Bulletin
title: Pappas defeats Sununu in pivotal U.S. Senate race
description: In an election that attracted attention across the country, Democrat Chris Pappas defeated Republican John Sununu to become New Hampshire’s next U.S. senator. He’ll be the first openly gay man elected to the Senate, and his win helps Democrats’ chances to take control of the upper chamber. The four-term U.S. representative from Manchester won 60% […]
text:
Chris Pappas meets with voters outside a New London polling location on Nov. 3. Pappas, an eight-year member of the House, battled John Sununu for a promotion to the U.S. Senate. (Photo by William Skipworth/New Hampshire Bulletin)In an election that attracted attention across the country, Democrat Chris Pappas defeated Republican John Sununu to become New Hampshire’s next U.S. senator.
He’ll be the first openly gay man elected to the Senate, and his win helps Democrats’ chances to take control of the upper chamber.
The four-term U.S. representative from Manchester won 60% of the vote as of 8:30 p.m., according to The Associated Press. AP called the race at 8:20 p.m.
Both Pappas and Sununu tried to define the race by affordability issues, which have been a driving force across the country this election cycle. Pappas put the blame on President Donald Trump for rising inflation amid a war in Iran that has spiked fuel prices and a tariff campaign that hit New Hampshire companies doing business with Canadian partners particularly hard. Sununu, on the other hand, pitched a series of old-school Republican free-market solutions to economic challenges, such as energy infrastructure deregulation and reining in federal spending.
Pappas also made campaign finance reform a key part of his campaign with proposals aimed at stemming dark money in politics. During the campaign he brought a parade of national Democratic figures to the state — particularly those rumored to be considering a run for president in New Hampshire’s influential primary election — including Kamala Harris, Pete Buttigieg and Gavin Newsom.
Pappas worked hard to tie Sununu to Trump, who has lost New Hampshire in three consecutive presidential elections and is suffering from low approval ratings. While Trump endorsed Sununu in the GOP primary, the Republican tried to distance himself from the president, going so far as to say in one campaign ad, “I’ve never even met the man.”
Sununu sought to frame this race about the future, specifically the post-Trump future. The candidate, who once penned an op-ed in the New Hampshire Union Leader under the headline “Donald Trump is a loser,” said during a WMUR debate last month, “In two years, the president will leave office, and my question is, where do we go next?” 
Sununu’s defeat is also a blow for one of New Hampshire’s most politically connected families. John E. Sununu is the brother of former Gov. Chris Sununu and the son of former governor and White House Chief of Staff John H. Sununu. John E. Sununu was himself a U.S. representative and held this same Senate seat from 2003 to 2009.
Pappas has been a reliably centrist vote in the House since 2018. His most notable votes were ones in which he crossed the aisle. That includes his vote for the Laken Riley Act in early 2025, an immigration and law enforcement bill pushed by Republicans in the wake of a Georgia woman’s death at the hands of an immigrant. The legislation was criticized by progressives and immigration advocates who argued it disregarded immigrants’ due process rights, gave too much power to state attorneys general and empowered ICE ahead of a series of aggressive enforcement surges. He was also one of six Democrats opposing the Marijuana Opportunity Reinvestment and Expungement Act — which unsuccessfully attempted to legalize marijuana federally — in 2020 over concerns about a provision to expunge federal convictions. In 2023, the Lugar Center ranked him the most bipartisan Democrat in Congress.
Pappas enters a Senate that’s in many ways defined by the Trump presidency. In the two years before Trump is term-limited out of office, Democrats will likely bicker over how to rebuke the president. Asked about the prospects of more impeachment proceedings or a potential removal — something some Democrats have suggested if they take control of Congress — during a WMUR debate last month, Pappas said “oversight and focused hearings” rather than impeachment would bring “the accountability that the American people deserve.” 
Pappas, whose family owns the Puritan restaurant in Manchester, has now won five straight congressional races.

name: Rhode Island Current
title: Foulkes defeats Block and Guckian to win governor’s race
description: Democrat Helena Buonanno Foulkes triumphed over her general election opponents Tuesday night to become Rhode Island’s next governor. Foulkes drew more than 57% of the vote, defeating independent Ken Block by 30 points, according to preliminary unofficial results as of 8:30 p.m. GOP nominee Aaron Guckian came in third with 14%, with 41% of ballots […]
text:
Democratic gubernatorial candidate Helena Bounanno Foulkes, backed by supporters, is interviewed by a WPRI 12 reporter outside the Salvation Army poling site on Pitman Street in Providence Tuesday morning, Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo by Michael Salerno/Rhode Island Current)Democrat Helena Buonanno Foulkes triumphed over her general election opponents Tuesday night to become Rhode Island’s next governor.
Foulkes drew more than 57% of the vote, defeating independent Ken Block by 30 points, according to preliminary unofficial results as of 8:30 p.m. GOP nominee Aaron Guckian came in third with 14%, with 41% of ballots counted.
The Associated Press called the race for Foulkes at 8:30 p.m., 30 minutes after polls closed at 8 p.m.
Cheers erupted from the crowd of supporters and party officials that packed the top floor of The Graduate Providence as results came in. Foulkes had yet to appear as of 8:40 p.m.
After handily defeating Gov. Dan McKee in the Sept. 9 primary, Foulkes remained the front-runner throughout the leadup to the general election. Foulkes, 62, of Providence  leaned on a massive fundraising haul, amplified by state party support, to blanket airwaves, social media and mailboxes with her campaign message around effective government and affordability solutions. 
A former CVS executive whose role as head of the retail pharmacy during the height of the opioid crisis drew sharp criticism from McKee during the 2026 primary battle, Foulkes’ professional record remained relatively unscathed during the general election. 
Independent gubernatorial candidate Ken Block inserts his ballot into the voting machine at Barrington Middle School. His wife Jen is next to him. (Photo by Michael Salerno/Rhode Island Current)
Block, 61, of Barrington instead criticized Foulkes for her ties to the state party and powerful labor unions, alleging that even as a new face in the State House, she represented “more of the same” in problematic government leadership. Foulkes in turn reminds voters repeatedly Block’s 2014 gubernatorial campaign, in which he ran as a Republican.
The founder and first statewide candidate for the Moderate Party in 2010, Block’s third gubernatorial run proved his most successful. 
Block also gained significant name recognition and support in the eight weeks leading up to Election Day, though his self-funded campaign never surpassed Foulkes in public polling.
Guckian, meanwhile, faced public pressure to drop out, especially after his GOP primary rival Elaine Pelino endorsed Block. But Guckian, 50, of East Greenwich, disregarded public opinions, even as his poll ratings and campaign funds dwindled.
Foulkes also ran for governor in 2022, losing to McKee in the Democratic primary by 3 percentage points. 
Foulkes will be sworn in in early January, starting a four-year term with a $163,295 annual salary.
Two other independent candidates also ran for governor. Jasjit “Jay” Gotra” and C.D. Reynolds each received less than 1%.
More than 355,000 voters had cast ballots through 7:45 p.m. on Election Day, representing 44.6% of registered voters. Results are preliminary, and unofficial, with mail ballots left in dropboxes on Election Day and those cast by military and overseas voters expected to be tallied and available by Nov. 10.
The Rhode Island Board of Elections will certify election results before Thanksgiving, following consideration of recount requests and an audit of ballot tabulating machines.

name: North Dakota Monitor
title: Election error caused some Bismarck voters to receive wrong ballot
description: An error resulted in some Bismarck-area District 7 voters receiving a ballot that omitted the district’s legislative races early Tuesday.  The error was caught and corrected by approximately 9:30 a.m. at the Liberty Elementary polling location, which opened at 7 a.m. Some District 7 voters had been erroneously handed a ballot for District 8, which […]
text:
Four stacks of ballots, one for each precinct served by the polling location, are stacked on a table for election workers at Liberty Elementary in Bismarck, North Dakota, on Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo by Jacob Orledge/North Dakota Monitor)An error resulted in some Bismarck-area District 7 voters receiving a ballot that omitted the district’s legislative races early Tuesday. 
The error was caught and corrected by approximately 9:30 a.m. at the Liberty Elementary polling location, which opened at 7 a.m. Some District 7 voters had been erroneously handed a ballot for District 8, which does not have any legislative races on the ballot this year. 
“Some of them who got the wrong ballot, they came back and noticed they got the wrong ballot, and that was corrected. But there might have been some people who didn’t realize they had the wrong ballot,” said Aaron Birst, the election inspector on site. 
Birst estimated around 120 people had voted before the error was corrected. About half used touch-screen voting machines, which were not affected. He said the error may have affected a maximum of 30 to 60 paper ballots. 
A dozen of those voters noticed they were handed a ballot for the incorrect district, alerted election workers, and were provided the correct version for where they lived. 
The error was ultimately traced to a mistake in how the paper ballots were organized before they were handed to voters. The polling location serves four precincts, two in District 7 and two in District 8, and each precinct has its own ballot version. Each version is kept in a separate stack of blank ballots, and election workers hand the appropriate version to a voter based on where they live.
Birst said two of those ballot versions became intermingled because the identifier number was very similar, resulting in some voters being handed a ballot for District 8 even though they live in District 7.  
Statewide races, including two ballot measures, were unaffected by the mistake. The only difference between the two ballot versions is whether District 7 House and Senate contests were included. 
There is no remedy for voters who put the wrong ballot into a tabulator, North Dakota Secretary of State Michael Howe said. 
“You’ve already cast a ballot,” Howe said. 
North Dakota’s top election official said he is incredibly frustrated and feels for voters who were unaware and for the candidates. Election officials sprang into action as soon as they could, he said.
“One error is too many,” said Howe, who added he wasn’t aware of similar errors elsewhere in the state. 
The ballot error is why election officials emphasize that voters view their sample ballot online so they know what races to expect, Howe said.
Sen. Michelle Axtman, R-Bismarck, and Democratic challenger Kevin Horneman are competing in the Bismarck Senate race. Republicans Steve Sauter and Greg Vetter are running for the two District 7 House seats, as are Democrats Jason Thoms and Tiffany Williams-Rice. 
Thoms said he’s thankful the error was caught early on Election Day. The Democratic candidate said the biggest issue is some voters may not have had the opportunity to vote for their next legislators. 
“It’s disappointing to hear a mistake was made,” Thoms said.
Axtman cast her ballot at Liberty Elementary Tuesday morning. She said she received several calls from voters who had received ballots without her name on it. The senator is confident the Secretary of State’s Office and county auditor will be able to determine the extent of the error. 
“Thankfully, I got a ballot with my name on it,” Axtman said. 
U.S. Department of Justice election monitors, who declined to provide their full names, visit with an election official at El Zagal Shrine Hall in Fargo, North Dakota, during the midterm election on Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo by Dan Koeck/For the North Dakota Monitor)
Department of Justice monitors
Howe said no issues were brought to his office’s attention regarding the U.S. Department of Justice election monitors in Cass County.
The election monitors were part of a nationwide effort coordinated by the department’s Civil Rights Division. It was the first time the Department of Justice has had Election Day monitors in all 50 states, the department said in a Tuesday statement.
The monitors planned to watch for compliance with federal voting rights statutes that protect the right to vote, according to the DOJ’s statement.
Three members of the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the District of North Dakota volunteered for the program, said U.S. Attorney Nick Chase.
The League of Women Voters of North Dakota, which had 30 to 35 Election Day observers in Cass County, did not identify any concerns with the federal election monitors, said treasurer Carol Sawicki. The federal monitors visited multiple voting sites in Cass County.
“They didn’t get in the way. They didn’t disturb things. They were only there an hour, and they didn’t seem to question any of the voters that we knew about,” Sawicki said.
The Native American Rights Fund sent 18 election observers to nine locations in North Dakota to monitor areas with significant Native American populations.
Jacqueline De León, senior staff attorney, said in an interview around 5 p.m. that the organization was alerted to a couple of minor issues in North Dakota, but those were resolved and the voters were able to cast their ballots.
North Dakota Monitor journalists Amy Dalrymple and Michael Achterling contributed to this report.

title: Magaziner wins reelection to US House
description: Democratic U.S. Rep. Seth Magaziner held onto his seat in Tuesday’s election, defeating Republican Vic Mellor in the race for Rhode Island’s 2nd Congressional District. Magaziner, 43, of Providence, won his third term representing a district he technically does not live in with 61.3% of the vote. Mellor, 56, a Warwick businessman and Marine veteran, […]
text:
Democratic U.S. Rep. Seth Magaziner waves to supporters outside the Narragansett Pier School on Election Day, Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo by Laura Paton/Rhode Island Current)Democratic U.S. Rep. Seth Magaziner held onto his seat in Tuesday’s election, defeating Republican Vic Mellor in the race for Rhode Island’s 2nd Congressional District.
Magaziner, 43, of Providence, won his third term representing a district he technically does not live in with 61.3% of the vote.
 Mellor, 56, a Warwick businessman and Marine veteran, captured 38.5% of the vote. He had defeated East Greenwich oral surgeon Dr. Stephen Skoly in September’s Republican primary. 
Polls in Rhode Island closed at 8 p.m. The Associated Press called the race at 8:36 p.m. with 42% of the vote counted.
While Republicans control both the House and Senate by a slim margin, Democrats need only pick up a net four seats in each chamber to take over Congress. All 435 House seats are up for election while a third of the Senate seats are.
There was never much doubt that both Magaziner and U.S. Rep. Gabe Amo, who represents Rhode Island’s 1st District, would prevail. The Cook Political Report’s House Race Ratings predicted both seats would remain solidly Democrat.
The day after Mellor won his primary, Magaziner seized on Mellor’s participation in the Jan. 6, 2021, march on the U.S. Capitol as one of the talking points against his Republican contender, and held a press conference outside the State House to denounce Mellor, who showed up to listen. 
Mellor, largely self-financed his campaign with nearly $3 million in loans, plus another $765,000 in contributions, and spending about $3.8 million, according to Federal Election Commission filings as of Oct. 14. 
Magaziner’s campaign reported spending around $909,000 during the election cycle. He entered the final weeks of the campaign season with a reported $1.58 million cash on hand, compared to Mellor, who had about $44,000 remaining in his account and approximately $2.96 million still owed in outstanding loans.
Magaziner won his 2024 contest with 58.2% of the vote.
He will begin his next two-year term in January 2027.

Gabe Amo handily defeated two opponents in Tuesday’s election to win a second full term representing Rhode Island’s 1st Congressional District, a race widely considered to have a solidly blue outcome.

Amo, 38, Rhode Island’s first Black member of Congress, entered the final weeks of the race with a big financial advantage over his two opponents. The congressman reported nearly $2 million in cash on hand as of Oct. 14, according to Federal Election Commission filings. 
First-time candidate Keenan, 33, a Providence small business owner and health care operations consultant made her first run for office, reported $1,832 on hand at the end of September.  
DeSouza works in a data career, according to his campaign website. DeSouza’s campaign account had $112 in it as of Oct. 14.
While Republicans control both the House and Senate by a slim margin, Democrats need only pick up a net four seats in each chamber to take over Congress. All 435 House seats are up for election while a third of the Senate seats are.
Amo was first elected in a 2023 special election, beating out a horde of Democratic opponents in an unusually crowded primary. He won his first full term in the 2024 General Election. Amo worked as a special assistant to the president and deputy director of the White House Office of Intergovernmental Affairs during the Biden administration.

text:
Rhode Island Secretary of State Gregg Amore, a Democrat, was unopposed in Tuesday's general election. (Photo by Michael Salerno/Rhode Island Current)Democratic Secretary of State Gregg Amore secured a second four-year term Tuesday. He ran unopposed in Rhode Island’s general election.
Amore, 60, received nearly 117,000 votes while another 5,700 votes went to write-in candidates, according to preliminary, unofficial results from the Rhode Island Board of Elections. The results reflect all 39 of the states municipalities reporting as of 8:29 p.m.
The former state representative and high school history teacher was first elected secretary of state in 2022 after serving a decade in the General Assembly representing a portion of East Providence.
During his first term, Amore advocated for election accessibility, government transparency and a new state history center to showcase Rhode Island’s most treasured documents.
Amore also spent much of the last two years pushing back against the Trump administration’s efforts to obtain Rhode Island voters’ confidential registration data. He refused to turn over an unredacted voter file to the U.S. Department of Justice in 2025, prompting a federal lawsuit that a judge dismissed in April. 
The administration appealed that decision, which is scheduled for oral arguments in Boston on Dec. 10.

title: Cooper becomes first Democrat to win US Senate race in NC since 2008
description: Former Gov. Roy Cooper has secured North Carolina’s U.S. Senate seat, becoming the first Democrat to win a Senate election in the Tar Heel State since 2008. He appears to have defeated Republican Michael Whatley by about 2-1 in early unofficial returns. The Associated Press called the race for Cooper around 8:25 p.m., just 10 […]
text:
Former N.C. Democratic Gov. Roy Cooper, left, and Republican Michael Whatley, right. (Photos by NC Newsline)Former Gov. Roy Cooper has secured North Carolina’s U.S. Senate seat, becoming the first Democrat to win a Senate election in the Tar Heel State since 2008. He appears to have defeated Republican Michael Whatley by about 2-1 in early unofficial returns.
The Associated Press called the race for Cooper around 8:25 p.m., just 10 minutes after the first vote totals were reported.  Whatley conceded about 10 minutes later. 
“I want to thank the people from across this great state who have entrusted me with their vote. While the results today are not what we’ve been working for, my commitment to you and this great state remains as strong as ever,” Whatley said in his concession speech at his election event in Gastonia.
Cooper is no stranger to winning statewide elections: He won two terms as governor and four as attorney general. Now, that success is translating to the federal level.
The race could play a role in control of the U.S. Senate. With a 53-47 split, Democrats need a net gain of four seats to flip the chamber. 
Cooper consistently polled ahead of Whatley, often by double digits, in a state President Donald Trump won three times. The former governor campaigned under his “Make Stuff Cost Less” slogan, holding events all over North Carolina.
Whatley is a former chair of the Republican National Committee and North Carolina Republican Party. He closely aligned himself with President Donald Trump, who endorsed him in the GOP primary. But he had never run for public office before, and struggled with name recognition. 
Election forecaster Cook Political Report moved the race from “lean Democratic” to “likely Democratic” on Oct. 6. 
Over the past two months, Republicans deployed Trump twice and Vice President JD Vance three times to the state. They aimed to shore up support for Whatley and GOP candidates down the ballot, but it wasn’t enough. 
Cooper will succeed retiring GOP U.S. Sen. Thom Tillis. That makes Cooper North Carolina’s junior senator, where he will serve alongside Republican U.S. Sen. Ted Budd beginning in January.

name: Maryland Matters
title: Gov. Wes Moore projected to win reelection in rematch with Republican Dan Cox
description: Maryland Gov. Wes Moore (D) was headed toward an easy reelection Tuesday, once again nothing a resounding win over Republican challenger Dan Cox in a rematch of their 2022 race.
text:
Gov. Wes Moore (D) makes a point during his Oct. 6 debate with Republican challenger Dan Cox. Moore appeared headed to an easy victory Tuesday. (Photo by Larry Canner Photography/Courtesy of MPT)Maryland Gov. Wes Moore (D) was projected to win reelection Tuesday, according to the Associated Press, which would mark his second win over Republican challenger Dan Cox in a rematch of their 2022 race.
No vote totals had been released, but the AP called the race just minutes after the polls closed. Moore, the  state’s first Black governor, also beat Green Party nominee Andy Ellis and Working Class Party nominee Cathy White.
The two other top Democrats in statewide office, Attorney General Anthony Brown (D) and Comptroller Brooke Lierman (D) were expected to win reelection over Republican challengers who were unable to gain traction against the incumbents. But the AP had not yet called those races.
Moore’s repeat race against Cox was not a given: Nine Republicans tossed their hats in the ring for the primary, including Baltimore Blast owner and businessman Ed Hale, a lifelong Democrat who switched parties for the race, and John Myrick, a federal consultant and previous Harford County sheriff’s deputy.
Republican gubernatorial nominee Dan Cox speaks to reporters after his debate with Gov. Wes Moore (D) on Oct. 6, 2026, at Maryland Public Television. (Photo by Bryan P. Sears/Maryland Matters)
In the end, Hale proved the only real challenge to Cox and his running mate, gun shop owner Rob Krop, who won the June primary with 43% of the vote to Hale’s 36%. Republican voters again selected Cox, a former state delegate, despite his 2022 loss to Moore by a margin of 64.5% to 32.1%.
Back then, Moore was a first-time candidate, brandishing his record as a former nonprofit executive and author. This time around, Cox repeatedly sought to make the election a referendum on Moore’s first term, citing snags in the effort to rebuild the Francis Scott Key Bridge, repeated state budget deficits and rising costs for consumers.
Cox also tried to take a stand against data centers, calling for a statewide moratorium and trying to paint Moore as pro-data centers. Both men have supported data centers in the past and both have shifted their positions, with Moore signing an executive order in September calling for greater state oversight.
But in Maryland, where registered Democrats outnumber Republicans more than 2 to 1, Cox’s message failed to gain any true momentum. And he was running with just a fraction of the funds that Moore had at his disposal: Cox reported raising $371,822 in his campaign finance report last month with the Maryland State Board of Elections, to just under $17 million reported by Moore.
During his campaign, the governor tried to paint Cox as a MAGA adherent. Cox took chartered buses to the Jan. 6, 2021, U.S. Capitol insurrection and tweeted at the time the Vice President Mike Pence was a “traitor” for not rejecting the 2020 election results that cost President Donald Trump the presidency.
But Cox took care to put distance between himself and Trump on the campaign trail, claiming he was focused on state issues instead, and said he regretted the Pence tweet.
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
Moore largely focused his campaign on his efforts to combat cost-of-living woes and to fight Trump’s agenda.
“I do want to level with you: I do know the past year and a half has been hard,” Moore said during a debate with Cox last month. “I do know that while we have had many successes together as a state, that we are still fighting against Donald Trump’s illegal tariffs, still fighting against these endless foreign wars, and still fighting against these cuts to health care. … This is the agenda that Dan Cox says he supports 100%.”
Still, Moore has seen his approval ratings decline gradually during his first four years in office. In an April poll from the University of Maryland, Baltimore County, Moore’s job approval fell below 50% for the first time, and 6 in 10 respondents indicated that they believed the state was heading in the wrong direction.
Between October 2024 and April 2026, Moore’s approval rating fell from 54% to 48%.
“For Wes Moore, the individual, there’s been a downward trend. It’s also a downward trend in the way people think about the economic conditions in Maryland. All these things are trending in the wrong direction if you’re the person in charge of the government,” said Mileah Kromer, the poll’s director, at the time of its release.

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Kansas voters to decide battleground U.S. Senate race
description: OVERLAND PARK — Democratic pastor Adam Hamilton led the Republican incumbent U.S. Sen. Roger Marshall in early vote counts that included one of Kansas’ most populous counties. With more than 125,000 votes counted as of 7:17 p.m. in eight counties, Hamilton led with more than 73,000 votes compared with Marshall’s 50,000 votes, according to unofficial […]
text:
Adam Hamilton, a pastor and the Democratic candidate for U.S. Senate, speaks at an Oct. 12, 2026, event in Lawrence, Kansas. (Photo by Sherman Smith/Kansas Reflector)OVERLAND PARK — Democratic pastor Adam Hamilton led the Republican incumbent U.S. Sen. Roger Marshall in early vote counts that included one of Kansas’ most populous counties.
With more than 125,000 votes counted as of 7:17 p.m. in eight counties, Hamilton led with more than 73,000 votes compared with Marshall’s 50,000 votes, according to unofficial results from the Kansas Secretary of State’s Office. The Libertarian candidate, David Graham, trailed around 2,000 votes.
Marshall, a former OB-GYN in central Kansas and first-term U.S. senator, has faced a tough reelection bid against Hamilton, a Johnson County pastor and the co-founder of one of the largest United Methodist congregations in the country. He’s attempting to become the first Democrat elected to the U.S. Senate in Kansas since 1932. 
In a race that has become the most expensive in Kansas history, Marshall and Hamilton have held nothing back, relentlessly attaching each other’s pasts and affiliations, perceived or otherwise, while trying to convince voters of which future they ought to choose.
Polls closed at 7 p.m. Central Time in most of Kansas, but four western Kansas counties are in Mountain Time. Hamilton is expected to digest the night’s results at a watch party in Overland Park, while Marshall will watch results roll in among other Republican candidates at a party in Wichita. 
Voter turnout was strong Tuesday in Kansas’ three largest counties, said Brian Caskey, the state elections director, during a virtual press conference Tuesday afternoon. As of 3:30 p.m., 55% of registered voters in Johnson County had turned out to vote, along with 44% of voters in Sedgwick County and 35% of voters in Wyandotte County. The first returns released included Sedgwick County. 
After his final rally Monday night in Overland Park, Hamilton said he would be proud of his campaign regardless of the results.
“Kansans are tired of the chaos, corruption and indecency in Washington that’s making life harder and more expensive,” Hamilton said. “No matter what the results are tomorrow night, I’m proud of the campaign we’ve run, and I’m proud of how we’ve stood up for the issues that matter.”
Hamilton has campaigned on affordability, health care and ending the war in Iran. He beat out 10 other primary candidates to become the party’s nominee in April, and Marshall’s lone primary opponent endorsed Hamilton. 
In the months since, national attention has flocked to Kansas. The Center for Politics at the University of Virginia changed its rating Monday in the Kansas U.S. Senate race to “leans D,” a remarkable shift from the “safe R” rating the race had back in July.
Outgoing Kansas Gov. Laura Kelly, a Democrat, said Hamilton has run a campaign that shows “what he says is what he means” in a time when voters nationwide have grown accustomed to broken promises.
“I don’t think he comes across as a Democrat or a Republican, and I think he just is sort of party-free,” Kelly told Kansas Reflector on Thursday. “I think that he’s been able to get Kansans to trust him.”
Polls ahead of Election Day put Marshall and Hamilton neck-and-neck, while Marshall has been supported by two visits each from fellow Republicans President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance. Marshall has accused Hamilton of being controlled by U.S. Sen. Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-New York, while Hamilton has criticized Marshall for failing to break with Trump when his administration’s policies hurt Kansans. 
Marshall has relied on his record in the Senate and loyalty to the Trump administration to resonate with voters, often touting efforts to advocate for year-round E15, a gasoline-ethanol blend, and introducing legislation that targets large financial institutions’ partnerships with major credit card networks such as Mastercard and Visa.
Marshall, at a Trump rally in Salina on Sunday, made a final pitch that every vote matters, and that a vote sends a message in Kansas. He said every time he would see former U.S. Sen. Bob Dole, R-Kansas, he would tell Marshall: “Roger, remember where you’re from.”
“I think that’s so important,” Marshall said. “And I want to make sure that everybody — whether you’re from Salina or, like I was, raised in El Dorado and lived in Great Bend now for 25 years — let’s let Washington know where we’re from.”
Trump said Tuesday on X that Marshall “is one of the Best Senators in the United States of America.”
“He loves Kansas more than anyone, with the possible exception of me!” Trump said.
In the same post, he called Hamilton a “Radical Left LUNATIC Dumocrat, whose Values are not those of the People of Kansas!”
In a video message before Election Day, Kansas GOP Chair Danedri Herbert said this election is critical for Republicans.
“In Kansas, there are 900,000 registered Republicans and only about 500,000 registered Democrats,” she said. “We know that if we vote, we win. But we need you to do your part.”
Graham, the Libertarian candidate in the race, was barred from participating in the candidates’ two debates ahead of Election Day. He encouraged voters in a statement to Kansas Reflector to avoid voting for the lesser of two evils. 
“Vote for freedom,” he said.
He said he’ll be watching Tuesday night to see how many people cast votes for libertarian candidates, who he said are gaining ground across the country.
“Regardless of the results, I shall continue working to provide a pro-freedom alternative to voters,” Graham said. “We need to end the two-party stranglehold on our country! I am optimistic about America!”
Tim Carpenter contributed to this report.

title: Jack Reed wins sixth term in US Senate
description: Democratic U.S. Sen. Jack Reed has secured a sixth term after easily beating Republican Ray McKay and independent first-time candidate Michael Bahry, the Associated Press reported Tuesday night. Polls in Rhode Island closed at 8 p.m. The AP called the race at 8:01 p.m., even with zero percent votes counted. But ten minutes later, with […]
text:
U.S. Sen. Jack Reed speaks to Head Start advocates and workers inside the Park Square Children’s Center in  Woonsocket on Aug. 19, 2026. (Photo by Christopher Shea/Rhode Island Current)Democratic U.S. Sen. Jack Reed has secured a sixth term after easily beating Republican Ray McKay and independent first-time candidate Michael Bahry, the Associated Press reported Tuesday night.
Polls in Rhode Island closed at 8 p.m. The AP called the race at 8:01 p.m., even with zero percent votes counted.
But ten minutes later, with less than 1% votes counted, the AP had Reed at 58% of the vote with McKay at 38% and Bahry at 4%
The Cook Political Report’s Senate Race Ratings predicted the outcome for Rhode Island’s Senate seat in Tuesday’s election as “solid Democrat.”
Reed will turn 77 on Nov. 12. U.S. senators serve six-year terms.

He is the senior Democrat on the Senate Armed Services Committee and served as its chairman between 2021 and 2025. He also serves on the Appropriations committee, the Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs committee and the Intelligence committee. 
Reed, a West Point graduate and Army veteran first elected to the Senate in 1996, went into Tuesday’s election with a sizable lead. A University of New Hampshire (UNH) poll published Sunday found his support had grown to 63% while Republican McKay had been stuck at 32%.
Only 3% of voters in the UNH poll said they supported Bahry, of East Providence, a former visiting lecturer at Salve Regina University.
McKay, 65, of Warwick, a former city administrator and network and telecommunications manager,  lost the 2024 Republican primary to Patricia Morgan who was then defeated by U.S. Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse in the November general election. A Warwick city ordinance prohibiting municipal employees from running for office derailed his plan for a 2014 run against Reed.
Reed will begin his next term in January 2027.

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: Rep. Rob Menendez wins reelection to third term
description: Rep. Rob Menendez faced no GOP challenger in the Hudson County-based 8th Congressional District. He starts his third term in January.
text:
Rep. Rob Menendez faced no GOP challenger in the Hudson County-based 8th Congressional District. (Photo by Dana DiFilippo/New Jersey Monitor)Rep. Rob Menendez (D) cruised to reelection over a trio of third-party challengers to win a third term in Congress, the Associated Press projected Tuesday.
Menendez was always heavily favored to win the Hudson County-based 8th Congressional District. The area is overwhelmingly Democratic, and Democrats there boast one of the state’s most robust get-out-the-vote machines. Republicans have won the district only once in the last half century.
Menendez, the son of former U.S. Sen. Bob Menendez, faced three minor party challengers: independent Aristotle Eliopoulous, Craig Honts of the Socialist Workers Party, and Da’Shone Hughey of the We the People Party. None was considered a serious electoral threat.

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Kansas voters to decide governor’s race: Democrat Cindy Holscher or GOP’s Ty Masterson
description: In the final poll of the Kansas gubernatorial campaign, voters decide whether to elect Democrat Cindy Holscher and Republican Ty Masterson.
text:
Democrat Cindy Holscher debates Republican Ty Masterson on Sept. 12, 2026, at the Kansas State Fair in Hutchinson. The two state senators were locked in a tight race heading into Election Day. (Photo by Anna Kaminski/Kansas Reflector)WICHITA — Kansas voters will resolve Tuesday the political fates of gubernatorial candidates Ty Masterson and Cindy Holscher in a campaign fueled by affordability concerns and conflict over surging property taxes, emergence of data centers and state budget priorities.
The contest developed into a tightrope as President Donald Trump twice campaigned in Kansas on behalf of Masterson, who presides as president of the Kansas Senate. Trump was dismissive of consumers’ complaints about high costs. Holscher, one of Masterson’s colleagues in the Senate, won support from Democratic Gov. Laura Kelly and fought to bring the race into toss-up territory. She pushed a narrative that emphasized bitter inflation rates.
Holscher, who grew up in Missouri as the granddaughter of tenant farmers, said she acquired a tough work ethic and relied on that instinct when fighting for working families, public schools, reproductive freedom and healthcare access. She blamed Masterson for failure to take the bite out of property taxes and called for a moratorium on new data center projects.
“Property taxes are too high,” said Holscher, the Overland Park Democrat. “Health care is too expensive. Why are all the hospitals closing?”
In a Johnson County rally Monday, she claimed Masterson fumbled his role as Senate president and missed opportunities to make life more affordable for average Kansans.
“He’s been busy cutting favors for himself, billionaires and special-interest donors instead of delivering results for everyday Kansans,” Holscher said. “Ty has failed to lower property taxes. He has refused to expand Medicaid and he has done nothing to make life more affordable.”
Masterson, a lifelong Kansan who directs a Koch-funded business laboratory at Wichita State University, said the 2026 gubernatorial election offered voters a stark choice between a proven GOP conservative and a Democrat with socialist instincts.
“I’ve never seen it more clearly,” Masterson told Johnson County voters on eve of Election Day. “The direction she wants to go, it’s in the voting record, she wants boys in girls sports, in women’s bathrooms, trans surgery for children.”
Masterson, who championed devastating 2012 state income tax cuts signed into law by GOP Gov. Sam Brownback, said Holscher was all wrong on tax policy.
“She voted against taking tax off Social Security, taking tax off food,” Masterson said. “She voted against every effort we made to try to constrain property taxes. Her answer to everything is to try to legalize marijuana and expand Medicaid.”
Masterson blamed high fuel prices on environmental radicals who stood in the way of refinery expansion in the United States. Attempts to blame Trump for gasoline and diesel price spikes due to his war with Iran was simply wrong, he said.
On Monday, the latest New York Times poll gave Holscher a slim 1 percentage point edge over Masterson.
Trump dove into the governor’s race at a Park Hill rally, which was the first of two presidential rallies in Kansas leading up to Election Day. He urged MAGA adherents to vote against Holscher.
“We must also defeat crazy Cindy Holscher,” the president said. “Cindy Holscher is the most radical candidate to ever run for Kansas governor. I would call her a radical lunatic.”
Kelly, who didn’t endorse Holscher until after the Democratic senator convincingly won the August primary, said she wanted the next governor to care about all Kansans.
“I want somebody who will protect our schools. I want somebody who understands and will work for and always pay attention to our rural communities,” Kelly said. “And, as I’m sure you’ve heard me say before, I want somebody who doesn’t look like a mob boss.”

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: While the votes are counted, the stitches go in
description: The gallery's Election Day Sewing Project creates a meditative space on a day that can feel stressful and chaotic for some.
text:
At a long, cloth-clad table inside the Yale University Art Gallery (YUAG), close to two dozen people focused their Election Day jitters on the needles and thread before them, sewing bright fabric triangles, whimsical flowers, button-sized circles and neat letter cutouts onto pre-cut felt squares. 
The activity marks the gallery’s third annual Election Day Sewing Project, designed to create a meditative space on a day that can feel stressful and chaotic for some. 
“The act of sewing, it’s a communal project,” said Molleen Theodore, curator of programs at YUAG. “And in many ways, that’s how our governments works … just being open to having your design next to somebody else’s, and having them live next to one another.”
The program began four years ago, after YUAG hosted a community sewing project with Indigenous artist Marie Watt, as part of its exhibition “Place, Nations, Generations, Beings.” That project expanded into the gallery’s “Sidewalk Studio,” a series of outdoor events that ran through the summer. 
Theodore, who has held the position since 2011, remembered how excited she was to call the organization’s facilities team multiple times, to ask them to bring more tables out onto the sidewalk, to seat the waves of people who kept coming out. 
“It was magic,” she said. She credited colleagues who have a sewing or quilting practice, including YUAG’s Bradley Associate Curator of Academic Affairs Sydney Simon and Documentation Photographer Jessica Smolinski, and quilter Jackie Gleisner, who worked at the Yale Center for British Art across the street.  

Nine-year-old Leon Delossantos at the third annual Election Day Community Sewing Project at the Yale University Art Gallery in New Haven on Nov. 3, 2026. He came out with his mom, poet and educator Rohanna Ssanyu Delossantos, and his grandmother, Rita Wagener.  Credit: Lucy Gellman / CT Mirror

When the 2024 election cycle came around, she proposed the same program to the gallery as a kind of nonpartisan pop-up that could stitch the community together no matter how folks voted — and provide a free, family-friendly activity when schools were closed on Election Day. The first one, in the midst of a divisive national election cycle, was such a success that she has kept them going each election day since. 
Tuesday, three generations of sewers lined both sides of the table, hunched over their needles and thread as they worked through designs that ranged from blocky, geometric Christmas trees to half-rotated triangles spinning through two-dimensional space. At one end of the table, writer Rohanna Ssanyu Delossantos and her 9-year-old son, Leon, puzzled through their first designs together. Beside them, her mom, Rita Wagener, spaced out the “c” and “e” in a bright quilting square already set with the first three letters of the word “peace.”  
Delossantos, a social studies teacher at New Haven Adult & Continuing Education who this year completed her first book of poetry, “The Maribou Who Crossed The Sea,” said she was grateful for the opportunity to tap into a free, kid-friendly public program on a day dedicated to civic engagement that can feel stressful. 
As she spoke, new, neat lines of purple thread appeared through the felt, the needle poking its head up as if to announce itself and then disappearing again.  
“I guess when looking at an election that can feel divisive, it’s a beautiful thing to be reminded that we all can sit together,” she said. To Delossantos, sewing feels like a necessary act as much as a meditative one: she will reliably mend an item of clothing before throwing it away. She’s not a seamstress, she said — that honor goes to her mom, who has been sewing for over three decades —  but she can get the job done.

Bethel resident Rita Wagener at the third annual Election Day Community Sewing Project at the Yale University Art Gallery in New Haven on Nov. 3, 2026.  Credit: Lucy Gellman / CT Mirror

Next to her, Wagener celebrated the significance of Election Day with a stitched prayer for peace. An immigrant from Uganda, where she survived the brutal regime of dictator Idi Amin in the 1970s, Wagener said she thinks of voting as both liberatory and a chance to “express your feelings by putting them on paper.” 
“It’s a freedom to find someone who believes what you believe,” she said. 
Across the table, friends Mitali Temurnikar and Amrita Sridhur echoed that sense of gratitude for a calm moment. Sridhur, who was visiting from Boston, said the event gave her a chance to create a miniature, felted rangoli for the upcoming festival of Diwali, which they both celebrate. “I’m thinking about leaving it with her [Temurnikar],” she said of her friend with an encouraging smile. 
On his way out, former New Haven Mayor John DeStefano and his granddaughters, Eleanor and Josephine, paused to soak in the moment. DeStefano, who has participated in many elections as both a candidate and a voter during his time in New Haven, smiled before helping the girls gather their belongings.
“Look,” he said, gesturing to where gallery staff had started asking attendees to clean up. “People are still around, talking to each other.”

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Kansas considers wording change on citizen voting, something already included in state Constitution
description: TOPEKA — Kansas voters are deciding whether to pass a proposed constitutional amendment that changes wording on voting laws allowing only U.S. citizens to vote – even though the state Constitution already says that – but that opponents worry can lead to more significant changes in the future.  Proponents of the amendment say the proposal […]
text:
Kansans are voting on a constitutional amendment in the November 3 general election that would require anyone who votes to be a U.S. citizen, even though the state's constitution already says that. (Photo by Tim Carpenter/Kansas Reflector)TOPEKA — Kansas voters are deciding whether to pass a proposed constitutional amendment that changes wording on voting laws allowing only U.S. citizens to vote – even though the state Constitution already says that – but that opponents worry can lead to more significant changes in the future. 
Proponents of the amendment say the proposal clarifies the language about citizens voting. 
But opponents worry the proposed change will allow the Legislature to require proof of citizenship in the future, making legal access to voting harder. 
“This amendment is hard to explain to folks because first off, it doesn’t sound like that big of a change going from every person who is a citizen can vote to no person can vote unless they are a citizen,” said Amii Castle, a law professor at the University of Kansas.
She said there is a difference between “every person who is a citizen” and “only citizens” that could lead to a requirement that people prove their citizenship. 
“The supermajority in our Legislature has a documented history of attempting to restrict voting in various ways,” Castle said. “My concern is that they’re going to use that to justify or as a pretext to say, ‘Well, wait a minute. We amended our constitution. Now it says only citizens can vote, therefore, prove your citizenship. Bring your documents.’”
Efforts have been made at the state and federal level to require proof of citizenship before voting, and some would require that people show documents that track any name changes they have had. For instance, a birth certificate would show citizenship but if you’ve married and changed your name, you would have to also show a marriage certificate.  
Brennan Center of Justice said about 9% of American citizens of voting age don’t have proof of citizenship documents “readily available.” 
“We also uncovered evidence of racial disparities in these numbers: while just over 8% of self-identified white American citizens don’t have citizenship documents readily available, that number is nearly 11% among Americans of color,” the organization said. 
Rep. Pat Proctor, who is running for secretary of state and who led the charge to put the  amendment on the ballot as head of the House Elections Committee, framed it at political rallies as a way to ensure only citizens can vote. 
He also said the state already tried to pass a proof of citizenship law and it was shot down by the Kansas Supreme Court because it was in opposition to federal laws. 
While that is true, Castle said, a change on the federal level could open the state to try again. 
“There is the SAVE Act in Congress that was passed by the House and not by the Senate, but they ain’t done,” Castle said. “The Save Act explicitly would require documentary proof of citizenship to vote in a federal election.”

name: Pennsylvania Capital Star
title: Gov. Josh Shapiro cruises to a second term in Pennsylvania
description: Gov. Josh Shapiro and Lt. Gov. Austin Davis handily defeated their Republican challengers in Pennsylvania’s gubernatorial election, securing a second term.
text:
Gov. Josh Shapiro speaks after state lawmakers approved a $50.8 billion state budget Sunday, July 12, 2026. (Photo by Ian Karbal/Pennsylvania Capital-Star)This story will updated throughout the night. 
Gov. Josh Shapiro and Lt. Gov. Austin Davis handily defeated their Republican challengers in Pennsylvania’s gubernatorial election, securing a second term. 
The Associated Press called the race within two minutes of the polls closing. With only 3% of the vote counted, Shapiro had 85% of the vote compared to Garrity’s 14%. Libertarian candidate  Ken Krawchuk had less than one percent of the vote with many more ballots to be counted.
It was an outcome long-expected by most pundits and political analysts in the commonwealth, based on polls, as well as campaign fundraising and spending.
Shapiro, a national figure in the Democratic Party who was briefly considered as a running mate for former Vice President Kamala Harris in 2024, has maintained a strong approval rating among Pennsylvania voters, even as Republicans won statewide elections while he was in office.
Throughout the campaign, Shapiro held a substantial fundraising advantage over Garrity, who easily earned the GOP nomination in the spring primary.
Democrats are attempting to win the coveted “trifecta” in Harrisburg. Along with retaining control of the governor’s residence, the party hopes to win a majority in the state House and Senate, allowing Shapiro to more easily enact a number of long-promised policies.
Shapiro campaigned with embattled Democrats around the state and made the pitch to give his party control of the three branches of state government a key part of his campaign. Currently, Democrats have a narrow majority in the state House. Republicans have controlled the Senate, where they hold a 27-23 majority, since 1994.
If given a trifecta, Shapiro has said he first plans to raise the state’s minimum wage to $15 an hour from $7.25. He has also advocated for legalizing recreational cannabis since his first year in office, though Republicans in the Senate have halted any efforts to follow through with a plan.
House Democrats have also pushed for a paid family leave policy, which would require employers to give workers time off to take care of sick family or when they become new parents. They have also pushed for election reform. In the past, they’ve passed legislation that would establish early voting as it exists in other states, allow what’s called pre-canvassing of mail-in ballots before election day,
How the race unfolded
In 2024, Garrity won the race for state treasurer, breaking Shapiro’s previous record for most votes received in a statewide election in Pennsylvania.
That made her a frontrunner to challenge Shapiro in 2026 before the campaign had even begun in earnest. She ran unopposed in May’s Republican primary, earning the endorsement of a number of prominent Republicans before any other candidates had even announced.
But her selection was not without controversy. Supporters of state Sen. Doug Mastriano, who was defeated by Shapiro by nearly 15% in 2022, accused party leaders of putting their thumb on the scale. While Mastriano declined to run after mulling the option, some of his supporters mounted a write-in campaign.
And Shapiro quickly went on the offensive.
Shapiro tried to tie Garrity to her support for President Donald Trump, whose approval rating has cratered throughout his second term. In 2020, Garrity supported Trump’s efforts to overturn the results of the election that he lost to Democrat Joe Biden, though she later tried to distance herself from the “Stop the Steal” movement.
In the final hours of the campaign, Trump endorsed Garrity in a social media post.
He and Democrats also painted her as extreme, pointing to her previous stances on abortion. In the past, Garrity called herself “100% pro-life” and after Roe v. Wade was overturned, she sold anti-abortion merchandise.
Garrity, meanwhile, attempted to tie Shapiro to previous controversies. In a series of unconventional campaign videos designed in the style of an episodic thriller, Garrity’s campaign highlighted a taxpayer-funded settlement over a sexual harassment complaint against one of Shapiro’s top advisors in 2023 and invoked allegations that he was involved in an alleged cover up of the murder of a Philadelphia teacher as Attorney General.
She also ran an ad made with artificial intelligence featuring a computer-generated Shapiro bragging about supporting data centers. Deepfake ads are currently permitted under Pennsylvania law, though some state lawmakers have said they want to ban or regulate them.
And she accused Shapiro of being more focused on his rumored 2028 presidential ambitions than the state of Pennsylvania.
One of the first major flashpoints to emerge in the campaign was over data centers.
Garrity accused Shapiro of hypocrisy on the subject, having previously supported the development of hyperscale data centers in the state. But Garrity herself had supported the same projects and had called for deregulation, so the Shapiro campaign threw the accusation back at her.
In August, Shapiro signed an executive order creating requirements for local approval of new data center projects, clean energy standards and local job creation.
Garrity went on a listening tour, meeting local officials around the state, and called for an indefinite pause on the development of new data centers.
