With a second convincing election win under his belt in a swing state, Shapiro is hoping his coattails can deliver the Democratic “trifecta” in state government and a Democratic majority in the Pennsylvania U.S. House delegation. If one or both occur, he would be positioned as a potential candidate in his party in 2028.

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: Sen. Cory Booker handily wins reelection
description: Sen. Cory Booker, a former Newark mayor, first joined the U.S. Senate in 2013. He will begin his third full term in January after winning reelection Tuesday.
text:
Sen. Cory Booker, a former Newark mayor, first joined the U.S. Senate in 2013. He will begin his third full term in January after winning reelection Tuesday. (Photo by Dana DiFilippo/New Jersey Monitor)New Jersey reelected U.S. Sen. Cory Booker (D) to a third full term over a challenge from former Tabernacle Deputy Mayor Justin Murphy, the Associated Press projected.
Booker, a former Newark mayor and one-time presidential candidate, was the heavy favorite to win another six-year term in the Senate. Republicans have not won an election for U.S. Senate in New Jersey since 1972.
Booker entered the Senate in 2013 after winning a special election prompted by the death of Sen. Frank Lautenberg. Booker won his first full term the following year.
Murphy, an attorney and U.S. Navy veteran, acknowledged the long odds he faced during the campaign, including by joking about his lackluster fundraising.

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Kansas voters to settle rematch in attorney general’s race, pick others to run statewide offices
description: TOPEKA — Kansas voters are poised to choose a new secretary of state and insurance commissioner while deciding whether to send incumbents back to the treasurer and attorney general’s offices. Among the contests for statewide office, the attorney general’s race –  a rematch of2022 between Republican incumbent Kris Kobach and Democrat Chris Mann – was […]
text:
Republican Kris Kobach, left, and Democrat Chris Mann tangled in a Topeka television debate on Oct. 6, 2026, and voters will decide which will represent the state as attorney general in the November 3 election. (Photo by Tim Carpenter/Kansas Reflector)TOPEKA — Kansas voters are poised to choose a new secretary of state and insurance commissioner while deciding whether to send incumbents back to the treasurer and attorney general’s offices.
Among the contests for statewide office, the attorney general’s race –  a rematch of2022 between Republican incumbent Kris Kobach and Democrat Chris Mann – was the most closely watched. Four years ago,  Kobach narrowly defeated Mann by just 15,892 votes, or 50.8% to Mann’s 49.2%. 
Kobach and Mann sit on the opposite sides of most issues.
In an October debate, Mann, who was a police officer until a drunk driver hit him during a traffic stop, believes the attorney general should enforce the law rather than get involved in partisan politics. 
“My opponent has never worn a badge,” Mann said. “He’s never stood toe-to-toe with violent criminals on the street or in a courtroom. Instead, that man has run for almost every office in the state of Kansas, and he’s done it because he wanted to push his political agenda.”
Kobach, who was secretary of state from 2011 to 2019, focused on immigration and what he called his “extremely effective” crackdown on fentanyl abuse.
 
Secretary of state
The race for the state’s top election official brought together three candidates with different views on election administration: Republican Pat Proctor, Democrat Jennifer Day and Scott Morgan, a candidate with Kansas United, a new alternative party in the state.
Proctor, who has represented a Leavenworth district in the Kansas House since 2021, refuses to answer questions from Kansas Reflector but is on the record speaking against an imaginary and undefined “axis of ballot harvesting.” He chaired the House Elections Committee and led the effort to put the constitutional amendment on the general election ballot to ensure only citizens can vote in Kansas, which is already in the constitution.
Day, who served in the Kansas House for one session before resigning because she moved out of district, and Morgan both said Kansas elections are secure and called the amendment redundant. 
Day told Kansas Reflector she decided to run because of Proctor’s initiatives to restrict voting rights. 
The Secretary of State’s Office should be “quiet and boring,” she said.
“The majority of Kansans really appreciate leaders that are not looking to make headlines and are really just wanting to do the job,” she said.
Morgan, a former Republican, said he believes Kansas voters want new options outside of the Republican and Democratic parties. 
“It’s just providing a choice is all it really is,” Morgan said. “We are an alternative. We’re trying to be the center-left and center-right, forming a coalition, instead of with the extremes.”
 
Insurance commissioner
Republican Dan Hawkins, Democrat Dinah Sykes and Libertarian Ric Koehn are vying for state insurance commissioner. 
Hawkins and Sykes are both experienced politicians. Hawkins has served in the Kansas House since 2013, and as House speaker for the past four years.
Sykes has been a Kansas senator since 2017 and served as Senate minority leader since 2021. 
“The cost of health insurance in Kansas is simply out of control,” Sykes said in announcing her campaign. “Families and consumers can’t afford to keep up with the rise in premiums — on health care, auto, property or any other kind of insurance for that matter.”
Sykes also said she wouldn’t take money from the insurance industry. 
In his campaign announcement, Hawkins, a strong supporter of President Donald Trump, said he would strive to create a “competitive insurance environment.” He believes deregulation would increase consumers’ options, lower costs and make insurance issues easier to navigate.
“No Kansan should be denied coverage,” he said. “Just like President Trump has made it his mission to make life miserable for foreign cartels, it will be my job as insurance commissioner to do the same for any insurance company that does not follow the law.”
Koehn, on the Libertarian website, said his focus would be to return “the insurance industry to the free market.” He opposes taxes, subsidies like the one Kansas offered to the Kansas City Chiefs, foreign wars and public education, the website said. 
 
State treasurer
Republican incumbent Steven Johnson, Democrat Juan Luengo and Libertarian Eric Lund are candidates to run the state treasurer’s office. 
Johnson has been the treasurer since 2023 and formerly served in the Kansas House from 2011 to 2023. Johnson has campaigned on the work he has done in the office, including reducing investment fees, creating efficiencies that saved tax dollars and increasing financial education opportunities. 
He partnered with businesses statewide to offer financial literacy opportunities, which he said will strengthen individuals and communities economically.  
Luengo, who has a business background and is CEO of Engage Insurance Group, has focused on his leadership skills and the ability of the office to support small businesses by expanding programs that are already offered. 
“Small business powers America. They’re the largest employer, yet they don’t have a seat at the table,” Luengo said. “If we can help them grow, scale, innovate and provide job creation — looking at what Texas and Florida are doing, we can do it better.” 
Lund, who has a degree in accounting and worked in finance as an auditor throughout his career, said on the Libertarian website that the treasurer position is an administrative one and not a legislative one. 
Lund said he would work with the Legislature and governor to cut government spending and taxation. He would look at reforming the Kansas Public Employees Retirement System and to eliminate all sales taxes.

name: Maryland Matters
title: Heavy Election Day turnout follows heavy early voting; no major problems reported
description: More than 1 million Maryland voters had cast ballots before the sun came up Tuesday, but election officials said they were still expecting a “robust turnout” for Election Day. For Maryland State Election Administrator Jared DeMarinis, that means everything from staffing to supplies, lines and weather can become a pressure point on the smooth operation […]
text:
Voters patiently wait in line to cast their ballots Tuesday at Maya Angelou French Immersion School in Prince George's County. (Photo by William J. Ford/Maryland Matters)More than 1 million Maryland voters had cast ballots before the sun came up Tuesday, but election officials said they were still expecting a “robust turnout” for Election Day.
For Maryland State Election Administrator Jared DeMarinis, that means everything from staffing to supplies, lines and weather can become a pressure point on the smooth operation of elections.
“Everything’s a pressure point. I got nearly 2,000 precincts,” he said. “It is a massive operation to think about logistically, and you have this one-day, finite number of hours to do it.”
Despite scattered reports of problems, however, officials said the day was generally smooth, under clear and warm skies.
“There’s always you know outliers, but nothing of major you know significance, and the local directors were able to resolve those things. No no issues for voters or impacting voting,” DeMarinis told reporters outside the Burtonsville Elementary School precinct in Montgomery County.
Early voting, mail-in ballots in Maryland likely to top 1 million before Election Day

Voters said they turned out to take a stand on Question 3, the constitutional amendment on congressional redistricting, to push for change on the cost of living and to express their anger at President Donald Trump. Some came out because they feel it’s an obligation to vote.
Ella Gericke, a longtime southeast Baltimore resident, said she voted in favor of Question 3 because it was backed by top Democrats. But she said it was her frustration with high prices drove her to the polls Tuesday — and she blames Trump.
“You take a $20 bill in the store, and I got a jar of mayonnaise and a couple bananas,” said Gericke, who lives in Brewers Hill. “That’s it.”
Aaron Tracey of Baltimore said he went to the polls to vote for Democrats, and hopes that the party is able to take control of Congress.
“Between ICE, the war in Iran and just all these major changes that haven’t been stopped by anyone —  I hope if the Democrats do get a majority, they can at least push back and try to revert some of these changes,” Tracey said.
For Tracey, there weren’t any particularly competitive congressional races on the ballot, with all seven incumbent Democrats in the Maryland delegation to the U.S. House expected to be reelected. But Tracey said he wanted to vote anyway, to ensure he’d done his part.
“I want to make sure that, at the very least, if something doesn’t change, I at least know that I voted to try and make a change,” Tracey said.
Eric Leath, 57, is a registered Democrat an auto parts salesman living in Kent Island, said he voted in favor of Question 3 because he believes the federal courts will push back against any unfair maps drawn in the future.
“The Supreme Court actually has final say,” he said. “It won’t be like the governor saying ‘I’m drawing the lines and here you go.’ At least there’s someone actually reviewing whatever he’s doing, whoever they may be … At least there’s checks and balances.”
Kent Island High School is one of the polling locations for Queen Anne’s County for the 2026 general elections. (Photo by Danielle J. Brown/Maryland Matters)
Until recently, Kent Island resident Kim Wheatley, 63, was a registered Democrat, but she switched parties this year and voted for Dan Cox for governor Tuesday evening at Kent Island High School.
“I really wanted Dan Cox to win this year,” she said. “I was really tired of what we’ve been dealing with.”
She said that she was no longer aligning issues that the Democrats were focused on, including the Question 3, which would let Democratic lawmakers redraw congressional District 1, the only seat held by a Republican.
“I said no to it,” she said. “I think things are fine the way they are.”
Although Dorthea Taylor of Prince George’s County walked with a slight limp to vote Tuesday morning, she said it’s important for “people to do their civic duty.”
When it came to Question 3, Taylor said one person helped convince her to vote “yes” for it: former President Barack Obama (D), who appeared in a series of last-minute ads urging Marylanders to vote for Question 3.
“He doesn’t speak arbitrarily, and he doesn’t just put his name on anything. He doesn’t just endorse every Democratic idea, or candidate, or whatever,” Taylor said. “He’s my forever president.”
At the Robert J. DiPietro Community Center in Laurel, voters were told late afternoon they could be in line for hours before casting their ballots. Jazmynn Wilson, a Laurel resident and elementary school teacher, said the long wait was “ridiculous,” considering how long officials had to prepare for a smooth election.
“That shouldn’t be the case. It’s a way to discourage people, because the line is three hours long right now,” Wilson said. “I’m sad that [voters] have to wait in those long lines to do something that should be simple, especially with technology and AI and all the things we can do.”
Voters line up outside of the polling place at the Southeast Anchor Library in Baltimore’s Highlandtown, where a small line persisted during the early afternoon. (Photo by Christine Condon/Maryland Matters)
While many were frustrated with the wait time, others viewed it as a potential positive. Laurel resident Ian Coles, who works at a local Chick-Fil-A, said the long wait time wouldn’t deter him as he headed into the poll. To Coles, longer lines could mean that more people are eager to vote.
Economic concerns and personal freedoms, he said, were at the forefront of his mind in his mission to vote on Tuesday. He also feels citizens have gotten too relaxed with the federal administration’s actions, especially because they don’t believe their “voices carry power.”
“We’ve kind of become aimless as a country,” Coles said. “I think [elections], while on a smaller scale, can hopefully make larger ripples as we go.”
Justice Department monitors
One area of potential friction this election, besides the occasional long wait, was the presence of Justice Department monitors to Prince George’s County polling places for compliance with federal law requiring language assistance be provided to voters who need it.
It’s not unusual for federal officials to monitor local elections, but the monitoring this year comes at a fraught time between state elections officials and the Trump administration. Maryland is one of more than two dozen states that have fought attempts by Justice to access highly sensitive voter data.
DeMarinis said statements made by federal officials coupled with the monitoring have created some apprehension with voters. He said the presence of the monitors should have no effect.
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
“They’ve come in the past,” DeMarinis said, adding that election officials have made an effort to alert the public to the presence of federal monitors this year.
“They are limited in their scope. They can’t interfere, harass, threaten, or talk to voters in the process. They’re just going to be observers,” he said.
Fast response to problems is the order of the day, he said.
“Today is the Election Day. There is no more tomorrow,” DeMarinis said. “If a voter walks away, I get upset because that means that that voter basically was disenfranchised, didn’t make their voice heard. I’ll move heaven and earth to make sure that we rapidly respond, and that nobody is going to be turned away, walk away because of any sort of one of our issues.”
— Maryland Matters reporters Danielle J. Brown, Christine Condon and William J. Ford contributed to this report.

name: Georgia Recorder
title: U.S. Sen. Jon Ossoff wins reelection in Georgia and coasts to a second term
description: Six more years. That’s what Georgia voters gave Democratic U.S. Sen. Jon Ossoff on Tuesday, handing him a win over Republican Congressman Mike Collins and sending him back to Washington for a second term. The race was called by the Associated Press around just before 8 p.m. Tuesday.  Ossoff was the only Democratic senator up […]
text:
Sen. Jon Ossoff speaks at a rally with former President Barack Obama and Democratic candidate for governor Keisha Lance Bottoms, the former mayor of Atlanta, in south Atlanta on Oct. 28, 2026. Alander Rocha/Georgia RecorderSix more years.
That’s what Georgia voters gave Democratic U.S. Sen. Jon Ossoff on Tuesday, handing him a win over Republican Congressman Mike Collins and sending him back to Washington for a second term.
The race was called by the Associated Press around just before 8 p.m. Tuesday. 
Ossoff was the only Democratic senator up for reelection in a state won by President Donald Trump in 2024, and heading into 2026, his Georgia seat was seen as a top target for Republicans.
But Ossoff maintained a lead in the polls and a fundraising advantage over the Trump-endorsed Collins throughout the race, boosted by his strengths and by Collins’ weaknesses.
Congressman Mike Collins, who is the the GOP nominee for Georgia’s U.S. Senate seat, speaks on stage with President Donald Trump at a rally in Dalton on Friday, Oct. 16, 2026. Ross Williams/Georgia Recorder
Ossoff’s prospects seemed to improve early on when outgoing Gov. Brian Kemp announced last summer that he would not run for the Senate seat, leaving the GOP with no clear contender. Kemp then backed former football coach Derek Dooley in the race, but Dooley emerged from a three-way contest for the nomination only to fall to Collins in a runoff. 
Collins was peppered by a series of scandals throughout his campaign. He is under investigation by the House Ethics Committee over allegations that he used government funds to pay an intern who was dating his chief of staff but who was not performing any duties. His son-in-law is a far-right social media influencer who promotes antisemitic content, and another former staffer has posted Nazi and Ku Klux Klan imagery on social media. 
Collins was also likely dragged down by his close association with President Donald Trump, whose approval rating is at a low point in Georgia as voters struggle with high gas prices and inflation.
Ossoff’s campaign touted support from several high-profile Republicans, including former U.S. Sen. Jeff Flake of Arizona and Republican mayors from cities including Valdosta and Tifton. GOP supporters largely touted Ossoff’s constituent services and particularly his efforts to advocate for Georgia farmers in the wake of Hurricane Helene in 2024.
Ossoff, 39, won his seat after defeating Republican Sen. David Perdue in a tight 2021 runoff in which he and fellow Democratic Sen. Raphael Warnock flipped both of Georgia’s Senate seats and helped their party win the majority in that chamber.
Previously, Ossoff worked as an intern for the late civil rights leader and Congressman John Lewis and was the CEO of a company making investigative documentaries. In 2017, he ran unsuccessfully for a U.S. House seat in what became a nationally watched election. 
He is seen as a rising star in the Democratic Party, thanks in part to viral clips of him aggressively questioning federal nominees in confirmation hearings and sharply critiquing Trump and Republicans on the campaign trail.
Ossoff’s name often appears on lists of potential Democratic presidential candidates, but he has consistently claimed that he intends to serve his six-year term and will not run for president in 2028. 
This is a developing story. Check back for updates.

name: Alaska Beacon
title: US Department of Justice sends election monitors to urban and rural Alaska
description: The U.S. Department of Justice said federal election monitors will be deployed to Anchorage and the Dillingham and Kusilvak census areas on Election Day, according to an agency announcement on Tuesday morning. The DOJ monitoring initiative, announced last week, is larger this year than previous years, with approximately 1,000 monitors posted across all 50 st[...]
text:
A polling site opened at the Loussac Library in Anchorage on Election Day on Nov. 3, 2026. There was no evidence of federal monitors at the polling location, but officials with the U.S. Department of Justice announced that Anchorage was one of three regions, along with Dillingham and Kusilvak census areas, where federal election monitoring would take place on Election Day. (Photo by Corinne Smith/Alaska Beacon)The U.S. Department of Justice said federal election monitors will be deployed to Anchorage and the Dillingham and Kusilvak census areas on Election Day, according to an agency announcement on Tuesday morning.
The DOJ monitoring initiative, announced last week, is larger this year than previous years, with approximately 1,000 monitors posted across all 50 states. 
Assistant Attorney General Harmeet K. Dhillon with the Civil Rights Division at the Department of Justice, said that election integrity is among the Trump administration’s top priorities. 
“I am very proud we are deploying the largest monitoring effort in DOJ history, and pursuing transparency for elections in an assertive and nondiscriminatory manner,” Dhillon said in a statement.
The Department provided no details about specific precincts in the three regions where federal monitoring would take place.    
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX. 

DOJ election monitors were deployed to the Dillingham and Kusilvak census areas in the 2024, 2023 and 2022 elections, as well as other regions.  
The effort is coordinated by the DOJ’s Civil Rights Division, officials said. Officials said the election monitors will include personnel from multiple DOJ divisions, the  U.S. Attorney’s Offices and federal observers from the Office of Personnel Management.
The agency said DOJ monitors will be observing polling places for compliance with federal voting laws, including the Voting Rights Act, National Voter Registration Act, Help America Vote Act, Uniformed and Overseas Citizens Absentee Voting Act and Civil Rights Acts. Monitors will also watch to ensure people with disabilities have access to vote under the Americans with Disabilities Act. 
“The Division’s Criminal Section enforces federal criminal statutes that prohibit voter intimidation and voter suppression based on race, color, national origin, or religion,” the announcement said.
Federal elections monitoring has taken place for decades, but there is heightened scrutiny and concern around election interference this midterm election as President Donald Trump has pressured election officials and said without evidence that Democrats will try to manipulate the results. The Trump administration’s DOJ has also focused on noncitizen voting, including demanding states’ voter lists, a slew of lawsuits and attempts to suspend ballot counting in California and Washington. A federal judge threw out the California case, and the U.S. Supreme Court declined to hear an appeal on Monday. A federal judge in Alaska rejected another case filed by the DOJ on Sunday that was intended to pause the U.S. Senate election result if Republican incumbent Dan. S. Sullivan lost by a narrow margin. 
In Alaska, the DOJ announced plans to deploy federal monitors in the 2024 election, including for compliance with federal law on language assistance, the Bethel, Dillingham, Kusilvak, and Nome census areas and the North Slope and Northwest Arctic boroughs. 
In 2023, federal monitoring of local elections took place in the North Slope Borough, and the Dillingham and Kusilvak census areas. In the 2022 midterm election, federal monitors also deployed to Dillingham, Kusilvak and Bethel census areas as well as Sitka. 
The DOJ’s Civil Rights Division has an online form for voters to report complaints of federal law violations. 
The Alaska Division of Elections has a voter complaint form for violations of the Help America Vote Act on its website, and a complaint hotline at 1-888-465-5857. It also has resources for accessibility assistance, including language assistance, on its website or by phone at (907) 465-4611.
The ACLU of Alaska, a civil rights non-profit, is part of a nationwide coalition running the nonpartisan Election Protection Hotline at 866-OUR-VOTE. Voters can call for information about voting rights, legal assistance or to report voter intimidation.

name: WyoFile
title: Wyoming Supreme Court allows major wind turbine project to advance
description:
State’s high court disagrees with lower court ruling that the proposed clean energy project near Glenrock must connect to the power grid.
The post Wyoming Supreme Court allows major wind turbine project to advance appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
The Wyoming Supreme Court ruled Tuesday to allow the Pronghorn H2 wind project on state trust land near Glenrock to move forward.
The court ruled that the Wyoming State Board of Land Commissioners’ approval of the Pronghorn H2 wind lease south of Glenrock could advance to the Industrial Siting Council, even though the court also found that neighboring landowner Michael Stephens and Stephens Land and Livestock have standing to sue.
The Wyoming Supreme Court, with no judges dissenting, reversed Douglas District Court Judge F. Scott Peasley’s decision to toss the deal. Peasley threw out the lease because the project did not connect to the power grid, interpreting the “wind energy leasing” rule as requiring a grid connection. The supreme court disagreed.
At the same time, the state’s high court also found that the petitioners have standing to sue because of their proximity to the project, calling the harms to views and property values “substantial, immediate and pecuniary.”
The justices rejected the other challenges to the project, regarding how much money it would raise for the state, future mineral interests and impacts to wildlife. The court found that the land board is allowed to set rates on a case-by-case basis, and that companies could still lease the minerals on the state land, provided they cannot unreasonably get in the way of the wind farm. 
The Pronghorn H2 project still has to go through the Industrial Siting Council permitting process, which can take several years and may address other concerns the plaintiffs have.
“These decisions were never political, they were made to ensure the highest and best value for our state lands, buttressed by the legal and contractual obligations made by the state,” Gov. Mark Gordon said in a statement. “Today’s Supreme Court decision affirms the original vote made by the State Board of Land Commissioners granting this lease.”
The plaintiffs can file within the next 15 days for a rehearing, although these requests are rarely granted.
There are about 1,500 wind turbines spinning in Wyoming with a generating capacity of approximately 3,700 megawatts — that’s about 25% of the state’s total electrical generation capacity, according to multiple sources compiled in April by WyoFile.

name: Source New Mexico
title: New Mexico voters (mostly) ready to make history in governor’s race
authors: Joshua Bowling, Patrick Lohmann, Matt Mondschein, Leah Romero
description: Source New Mexico headed to the polls in Albuquerque, Española, Las Cruces, Rio Rancho, Santa Fe and Santo Domingo Pueblo to talk with voters about the issues and candidates that brought them to the polls on Nov. 3, 2026.
text:
Voters cast ballots on Election Day, Nov. 3, 2026, at Mesilla Town Hall. (Photo by Leah Romero for Source NM)By 5 p.m. in New Mexico, 672,450 registered voters had cast ballots — approximately 48% of the state’s 1.4 million voters had cast ballots, according to the Secretary of State’s Office, which will next report voter turnout after the polls close.
In 2022, New Mexico had a 52.3% voter turnout in the November midterm.
Nearly 49% of the voter casting ballots so far are registered Democrats, followed by Republicans at 32.4% and unaffiliated voters at just under 18%.
Overall, Democrats make up 39.6% of the state’s voters, followed by Republicans at 30.4% and unaffiliated or Decline to State voters at 28.1%.
New Mexico’s high Democratic turnout echoed the national trend of record turnout and expectations that Democrats might win back control of Congress and curtail the Trump administration’s policy agendas.
Across the Albuquerque and Rio Rancho areas Tuesday morning, voters said they were backing the candidates and ballot measures they believed would push back against the Trump administration’s policies.
Voters in the area overwhelmingly told Source NM they hoped their votes would counter federal efforts to implement cuts to services such as Medicaid and SNAP. 
As news regarding the federal government’s efforts to monitor polling places nationwide spread ahead of Election Day and as immigration advocates prepared for the possibility of federal interference, Albuquerque resident Jessica Queen said she felt like voting in Albuquerque was a calm spot in an otherwise turbulent national political landscape.
“I’m grateful to be in blue New Mexico,” she said.
Polling spot Carlos Gilbert Elementary in Santa Fe on Election Day, Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo by Matt Mondschein/Source NM)New Mexico voters fill out ballots at Carlos Gilbert Elementary in Santa Fe on Election Day, Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo by Matt Mondschein/Source NM)New Mexico voters fill out ballots at Carlos Gilbert Elementary in Santa Fe on Election Day, Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo by Matt Mondschein/Source NM)Voters cast ballots on Election Day, Nov. 3, 2026, at Mesilla Town Hall. (Photo by Leah Romero for Source NM)The line to vote at the Sandoval County Administration Building on Nov. 3, 2026, wound around the lobby and stretched to the entrance during the noon lunch hour. (Photo by Joshua Bowling/Source NM)Philip Dodge, a 73-year-old Rio Rancho resident, said he discussed the issues on Tuesday’s general election ballot with his family before coming to the Sandoval County Administration Building to vote. (Photo by Joshua Bowling/Source NM)Jane Fleenor of Rio Rancho told Source NM the governor’s race was the most important issue on her ballot Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo by Joshua Bowling/Source NM)Mark Rodriguez and Aramea Atencio, left and right, made a date out of voting together at Carlos Gilbert Elementary in Santa Fe on Election Day, Nov. 3, 2026. The couple said they were most excited to vote for Democratic gubernatorial candidate Deb Haaland and added that Trump administration immigration policy motivated them to vote. (Photo by Matt Mondschein/Source NM)New Mexico U.S. Rep. Teresa Leger Fernández (D-N.M.), alongside state Rep. Tara Lujan (D-Santa Fe), wave to cars outside the Rodeo de Santa Fe Fairgrounds on Election Day, Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo by Matt Mondschein/Source NM)
Jim Libbin voted at the Las Cruces Village Independent Living Social Center. (Photo by Leah Romero for Source NM)Zane James of Albuquerque cast his ballot Tuesday morning, Nov. 3, 2026, at Eldorado High School. (Photo by Joshua Bowling/Source NM)Michael Quintana, a Santo Domingo Pueblo member and gas station general manager, said Nov. 3, 2026, that Democratic gubernatorial nominee Deb Haaland, if elected as the state's first Indigenous governor, would finally give pueblos "a voice." (Photo by Patrick Lohmann/Source NM)Matthew Thomas, left, voted Tuesday morning, Nov. 3, 2026, at the Doña Ana County government building. (Photo by Leah Romero for Source NM)Juan Velasquez of Albuquerque said he got a ride to the nearest polling place on Nov. 3, 2026, vote “MAGA all the way.” (Photo by Joshua Bowling/Source NM)New Mexico supporters of Republican gubernatorial candidate Gregg Hull outside the Rodeo de Santa Fe Fairgrounds on Election Day, Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo by Matt Mondschein/Source NM)Jolyne Marshall of Albuquerque said her top priority was “stopping the descent into fascism.” (Photo by Joshua Bowling/Source NM)Joseph Calabaza, 70, said rising gasoline prices were at the top of his mind Tuesday when he walked into the Santo Domingo Pueblo to vote for Democrats up and down the ballot. (Photo by Patrick Lohmann/Source NM)Joann Crespin, Santo Domingo Pueblo member and retired special education teacher, said she wanted to vote for Democrat Deb Haaland in the governor's race and in support of school bonds on Election Day, Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo by Patrick Lohmann/Source NM) New Mexico Democratic gubernatorial nominee Deb Haaland, second from left, joined Santo Domingo Pueblo Gov. Raymond Aguilar, Jr., second from right, in the pueblo during her first Election Day stop on Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo by Patrick Lohmann/Source NM)
Further north, at the Sandoval County Administration Building, Rio Rancho residents told Source NM they were similarly excited to vote for Haaland.
Philip Dodge, a 73-year-old Rio Rancho resident, said he discussed the issues on Tuesday’s general election ballot with his family before coming to the Sandoval County Administration Building to vote. (Photo by Joshua Bowling/Source NM)
Philip Dodge, a 73-year-old U.S. Navy veteran, said he voted for “anything non-Republican.” He took exception with federal cuts to programs such as Medicaid, which he said his son depends on. And he said he was outraged at the way U.S. Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth is “disrespecting the military.”
When asked if he voted for Hull, who was the longest-serving mayor in Rio Rancho’s history, Dodge shook his head to say “no.”
“I see the way the roads are around here,” he said.
Regardless of political parties, every Albuquerque and Rio Rancho voter who spoke with Source NM after leaving the polls Tuesday said they voted in favor of Constitutional Amendment 4, which would let state lawmakers collect an annual salary for their work for the first time.
Juan Velasquez, an Albuquerque Republican who said he voted “MAGA all the way” Tuesday, said he backed the proposal to pay lawmakers.
He said he voted for Republicans all down the ballot because he believes their policies are better for the economy, particularly in a state like New Mexico that routinely ranks among the poorest in the nation.
To him, paying lawmakers is another way to address that problem.
“This is a poor state to begin with, then you go into politics and you’re still poor,” he said. “I think they should all get paid. Why shouldn’t they?”
Nearly every voter Source NM spoke with in Albuquerque and Rio Rancho also said they wanted to see Deb Haaland, the former U.S. Interior Secretary running as New Mexico’s Democratic gubernatorial nominee, make history Tuesday evening by becoming the nation’s first woman Native American governor.
“I’m pulling for Auntie Deb,” Albuquerque resident Queen said after casting her ballot at the Bernalillo County Clerk’s Office.
Haaland starts day on Santo Domingo Pueblo
New Mexico Democratic gubernatorial nominee Deb Haaland, second from left, joined Santo Domingo Pueblo Gov. Raymond Aguilar, Jr., second from right, in the pueblo during her first Election Day stop on Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo by Patrick Lohmann/Source NM)
Haaland, an enrolled Laguna Pueblo member, began Election Day on Tuesday morning visiting the Santo Domingo Pueblo, which has around 2,300 enrolled members and sits between Albuquerque and Santa Fe.
The Pueblo is one of four that has endorsed her campaign for governor and also endorsed her for her first congressional campaign in 2017, when she became one of the first Native Americans elected to the U.S. House.
Haaland, who also made history as the first Indigenous cabinet secretary under President Joe Biden, told Source NM she hadn’t dwelled too much on the historic nature of her candidacy before Election Day, but she did say representation matters in politics. 
“It mattered when I became one of the first Native women in Congress. It mattered when President Biden nominated me, and it’ll matter here,” she said. “Lots of Native people all across the country [are] running. So, I feel grateful that, perhaps in some small way, I might have inspired them to believe that they could run for office, too.”
Source NM spoke to 10 voters outside the Pueblo’s community center, all of whom said they had voted for Haaland. Most of them said Haaland being Indigenous at least partially influenced their decision to vote for her, though others said her success as a former Interior Department Secretary and their former congressional representative heavily factored in, as well. 
“She’s a strong lady, and we can always depend on her,” said Sammy Garcia, a tribal council member. “We’re proud of her, what she has done for us, and now we’re depending on Deb Haaland to see if we can help our tribe.”
Eliana Bailon, a 22-year-old Santo Domingo Pueblo member, said she hopes Haaland’s candidacy counteracts stereotypes on tribal land and shows that women can be strong leaders in what are often “patriarchal” societies.
“Her being a woman, it gives us women more power,” she said. “As you may know, most pueblos don’t really have women leaders, so I think it’s really important that she could be at a higher position.”
Bailon arrived at the polls Tuesday afternoon with her partner, Derek Masawiestewa, a 23-year-old, Santa Ana Pueblo member who had never voted before. She urged him to cast a ballot, including for Haaland.
“She was like, it’s very important,” Masawiestewa told Source NM. So he put in an application Tuesday for same-day registration. “I’m just hoping I can make a difference.”
Governor’s race, Trump policies resonate at Santa Fe, Española polls
The governor’s race between Democrat Haaland and Republican Hull also dominated discussion at various polling spots in Santa Fe.
Mark Rodriguez and Aramea Atencio, left and right, made a date out of voting together at Carlos Gilbert Elementary in Santa Fe on Election Day, Nov. 3, 2026. The couple said they were most excited to vote for Democratic gubernatorial candidate Deb Haaland and added that Trump administration immigration policy motivated them to vote. (Photo by Matt Mondschein/Source NM)
For Aramea Atencio and Mark Rodriguez, a couple who voted at Carlos Gilbert Elementary, the prospect of electing the first Native American woman governor brought them out to vote. 
“That was my main motive — to support women, support indigenous peoples,” Atencio said. “This is their land and everything else follows after that.”
Arthur Montoya, voting at the Rodeo de Santa Fe Fairgrounds, also prioritized the governor’s race and said he was casting a ballot for Hull. 
He told Source NM that the most important issue for him this election was voting for candidates that “show up for every New Mexican” and are not “influenced by outside forces.” 
He added that federal policies set by the Trump administration did not affect his ballot, saying that he’s focused on New Mexico and that he’s “not really concerned about Washington. It’s about us.”
The opposite held true for Steve Montoya, a Navy veteran who voted down the ballot for Democrats at the Dan Roybal Community Center in Española. When asked what the top issue was for him when he cast his ballot, he told Source NM, “The Republicans got everything so screwed up right now that we need to get back on track.” 
He added that the Trump administration’s foreign policy in particular was a cause of concern because “what they have done to our reputation around the world. That is the biggest thing.”
On the eve of the U.S. elections, the Trump administration again launched military strikes against Iran after starting the war in February. Since then, gas and oil prices have increased, which U.S. Rep. Teresa Leger Fernández told Source NM motivated the high voter turnout this midterm election. 
“I think the key issues that New Mexicans are voting on is they are tired of the division. They’re tired of the corruption. They’re tired of the cost,” Leger Fernández said outside the Rodeo de Santa Fe Fairgrounds. When asked about concerns about possible election interference, she added that when voters show up in “overwhelming force,” then “Trump and Republicans who want to overturn our elections, who want to suppress our vote, they have a very hard time doing it. We’re not going to let them do it.”
Rodriguez echoed the sentiment after voting at Carlos Gilbert Elementary in Santa Fe, telling Source NM he cast his vote today to be “a thorn in [Trump’s] side, trying to vote against him at all costs.” 
Ready for change in Las Cruces
More than 60 people stood in line at Corbett Center Student Union on New Mexico State University’s main campus in Las Cruces Tuesday morning. (Photo by Leah Romero/Source NM)
Polling locations also were busy in Las Cruces the morning of Election Day, with several voters telling Source NM that they voted Democrat down the ballot because they were tired of Republican corruption, particularly at the federal level.
“The past few years of every time I opened my phone it’s just, from the top down from our government, it’s just pedophilia, and racism and fascism and it’s a lot of doom scrolling everywhere you go,” Las Crucen Matthew Thomas told Source NM. “So I thought I needed to do something to combat that.”
He added that he voted against state constitutional amendment 4 that proposed paying state legislators because he feels that lawmakers already receive money from outside sources. “I thought, why do they need our money when they’re already getting paid under the table from who knows how many sources,” Thomas said.
Jim Libbin told Source that he also voted against the constitutional amendment this time because he would like to see legislators convene in Santa Fe more often. 
“It just seems like a pretty good salary for a 30-day session every other year,” Libbin said. “I know they work all year long, but if they’re going to increase salaries then it seems to me they ought to have a longer session and do their work there.”
Libbin, however, said he voted Republican on the “major issues” on the ballot this election because he believes it is time for change in Democratic-led state, in which the majority party has control of both legislative chambers and the governor’s office. 
“We’ve been dominated by the Democratic Party for so long and we end up at the bottom of the heap in everything,” he said.
Mesilla Park resident and educator Roberta Madrid told Source that while she has voted for candidates on both sides of the aisle in the past, she supported Democratic candidates Tuesday because the Republican Party is “kind of cuckoo right now and we can’t let our country die.”
Madrid previously lived in Arizona for 20 years, a Republican-leaning state, and believes they’ve passed policies harmful to public education. “New Mexico has its issues, but they truly support public education,” Madrid said. She added that New Mexico’s gubernatorial race was particularly important to her and she voted for Deb Haaland, hoping to see a Native American woman elected to the office.
Manuel Jimenez, a third-year New Mexico State University student studying secondary education, told Source that Tuesday was his first time voting in an election. Immigrant rights were what motivated him to cast his ballot. 
He said he hasn’t seen his mother and other family for a long time because they live in Mexico and fear their visas will be taken away if they try crossing into the U.S. from Ciudad Juárez.
“Seperation is a big problem, not only for me, but I’m sure for a lot more people that come from Mexico and other places around the world,” Jimenez said, adding that he wants to see policies past that would help immigrants feel safer across the entire country.
“I just thought it would be important to vote right now, knowing that I can do it and have an impact in the smallest way,” he said. “Knowing that my vote also will help not only me, but a lot more people, one way or another.”

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: Incumbents Rogers, McGarvey cruise to easy victories in Congressional races
description: Two incumbents, one Republican, one Democrat, crushed their opponents early on election night with plus 40 point victory margins. Incumbent 5th District Congressman Hal Rogers crushed his Democratic opponent Ned Pillersdorf  with a 44 point margin when the Associated Press called the race at 7 p.m. Rogers, the longest serving House member at 88 who […]
text:
U.S. Rep. Hal Rogers talk to reporters at the 2026 SOAR Summit in Corbin. (Kentucky Lantern photo by McKenna Horsley)Two incumbents, one Republican, one Democrat, crushed their opponents early on election night with plus 40 point victory margins.
Incumbent 5th District Congressman Hal Rogers crushed his Democratic opponent Ned Pillersdorf  with a 44 point margin when the Associated Press called the race at 7 p.m.
Rogers, the longest serving House member at 88 who is also known as the Dean of the House, has served Eastern and South Kentucky since 1981. He is known for bringing projects and funding to one of the poorest regions of Appalachia.
“It is a tremendous honor to earn the continued confidence of the people of Southern and Eastern Kentucky. I will continue to listen to my constituents and fight for the conservative values that make this nation so great,” Rogers said in a statement. “Our work together has never slowed down. In fact, we are working hard every single day to create a brighter future in Kentucky’s Appalachian region. Southern and Eastern Kentucky is a special place to call home and I’ll continue to give my all for the people I serve whether I’m here or echoing their voice in Washington.”
Democrat Ned Pillersdorf of Prestonsburg, hoped to make issues out of a lack of affordability and changes to Medicaid and SNAP that will hurt many families in Eastern Kentucky. But name recognition and incumbency apparently won out.
U.S Rep. Morgan McGarvey of the 3rd District in Jefferson County beat Republican Maria Teresa Rodriguez by a 52 point margin.
U.S. Rep. Morgan McGarvey of the 3rd District, gives a victory speech at the Galt House on Tuesday night. (Kentucky Lantern photo by Sarah Ladd)
In his victory speech, delivered before a crowd of some 200 gathered at the Galt House in downtown Louisville, Democratic U.S. Rep Morgan McGarvey said the results are the result of failed policies out of Washington D.C. 
“I want to be really clear-eyed for a second about what this means,” he said. “This is a big night, but this is not about party. This is certainly not about me. This is about us. This is about decency over division. This is about compassion over cruelty. It’s about cohesion over corruption.” 
He said “this election is about not looking back to those times” when the country was segregated and other “hard times” in the United States’ history. 
“This is about gas being over $4 a gallon and diesel being over $6.50 a gallon right here in Kentucky because our president chose to go to an unjust war with Iran, putting our troops at risk and our country less safe,” McGarvey said. “And of course, he’s driving our costs up while he and his friends do nothing but get richer. This is about stopping the corruption we see coming right out of the White House. But I will tell you, as dark as it seems today, we have been through hard times in this country before. We’ve been through worse.”

name: New Hampshire Bulletin
title: Affordability takes center stage as New Hampshire voters head to the polls
authors: Ethan DeWitt, Molly Rains, William Skipworth, Maya Mitchell
description: There was a common refrain at the New Hampshire polls on Tuesday: frustration with high prices.  The issue of affordability dominated a contentious midterm election cycle marked by clashes over candidates’ relationships to President Donald Trump, the Iran war, and concern over rising costs for childcare, healthcare, groceries and more.  Amid record turnout p[...]
text:
A voter emerges from a voting booth in New London during the November 2026 midterm elections. (Photo by William Skipworth/New Hampshire Bulletin)There was a common refrain at the New Hampshire polls on Tuesday: frustration with high prices. 
The issue of affordability dominated a contentious midterm election cycle marked by clashes over candidates’ relationships to President Donald Trump, the Iran war, and concern over rising costs for childcare, healthcare, groceries and more. 
Amid record turnout predicted by Secretary of State David Scanlan last week, voters formed snaking lines in front of schools and city halls. At stake are control of the New Hampshire governor’s office, a U.S. Senate seat, two U.S. House of Representatives seats, and control of the New Hampshire House and Senate. 
Also to be determined are two ballot measures: One to eliminate a defunct state official position and another that would cap school districts’ property taxes.
As they filed into the polls earlier today, voters from across the state outlined the concerns and goals shaping their decisions at the ballot box.
At Winnacunnet High School in Hampton, many voters said they were bringing affordability worries to the polls. (Photo by Molly Rains/New Hampshire Bulletin)
Focus on affordability
At Winnacunnet High School in Hampton on Tuesday morning, multiple voters identified affordability as the central concern driving them to the polls.
David Burns, a Democrat who said he had lived in Hampton for 25 years, said the rising prices of groceries, healthcare, insurance and gas were among his main concerns. He said he voted for all Democrats in hopes they would lower costs. 
“My line of thinking is, the mansions should pay more, and you’ve got to support your schools,” he said. 
Also at the polls Tuesday was Robert Gagalis, who said the economy, high taxes and housing costs were his main motivators.
“It’s always an issue,” he said. 
John and Jane Romps of Manchester said that in the current economy, they were “OK.” The two retirees said they “couldn’t take any more politics” but were thinking about inflation when they were voting. 
Others recognized rising prices but said it did not win them over to Democrats.
In Hooksett, Chris Babelcastro called affordability “a big concern.” But speaking of Democrats, he added: “My belief is they kind of got us into this to begin with.”
Nearby, Mike Weinman also said high prices were a problem, but he did not attribute them to a particular party. He was voting Republican to support Trump’s actions and policies against “diversity, equity and inclusion” efforts. “I think some things over this president’s tenure have changed for the positive,” he said. 
Affordability was a motivator for Al Bertocci, of Tilton, who also voted Republican.
“When’s the last time any one of these clowns on either side have gone in a grocery store?” he asked.
“I Voted” stickers, designed by New Hampshire fourth and fifth graders, line the railings outside the Webster Elementary School in Manchester. (Photo by Maya Mitchell/New Hampshire Bulletin)
Corruption concerns
Bertocci voted straight-ticket Republican because he believes Democrats are taking corrupt kickbacks feeding into an affordability crisis. Still, he said he was frustrated with both parties.
“I just don’t like both parties fighting constantly and getting nothing done,” he said. “They don’t do anything.”
Bertocci, 73, thinks Pappas epitomizes that.
“He hasn’t done jack s—t,” he said of the Democratic Senate candidate. He said Pappas’ husband has been a lobbyist for Uber, Amazon and other companies, but Pappas still voted on bills affecting those companies
Bertocci, a retiree who moved from Massachusetts to Danbury seven years ago and then to Tilton a year ago, said he was a Democrat “for many, many years” but said he believes the party leaders are only in it for themselves these days.
“It’s not our parents’ or grandparents’ Democratic Party anymore,” he said.
Zoe Hill (right), a candidate for state representative and the child of Executive Councilor Karen Liot Hill, holds signs in support of Democrats alongside a fellow support at the Lebanon City Hall polling location during Election Day, Nov. 3. (Photo by William Skipworth/New Hampshire Bulletin)
Health costs
Two years ago, Scott Stafford split his ticket the New Hampshire way: by voting for Democrats up and down the ballot but choosing Republican Kelly Ayotte for governor.
On Tuesday outside Londonderry High School, Stafford’s ballot was completely marked for Democrats, including Democrat Cinde Warmington for governor. He voted for candidates he said would support older people. Specifically: Medicare.
A Kaiser Family Foundation study found that the average Medicare Advantage beneficiary in the U.S. had a choice of 35 plans for 2027 compared to 39 plans on 2026, ahead of open enrollment in October, as insurers retreat from certain markets amid rising costs. Stafford said he had heard worries about reduced choice from many older friends this year.
“I spoke with the woman that set mine up and — pretty slim pickings here in Rockingham County,” he said. “There’s only very few choices out there this year. Last year was great.”
He added: “This year, I got to get all new doctors.”
Stafford said he isn’t precisely sure how that situation might be improved, but he expects Democrats will have a better plan than Republicans. “I had to make sure I voted all the right people,” he said. 
Driven by the tax cap
Voters statewide were also asked a hyperlocal budget question. Question 2 asked voters whether they wanted a two-year tax cap on their school district that would bar school boards from proposing budgets that raise constituents’ school property taxes more than the value of inflation and any new construction in town. If adopted, the cap could be overridden by a 60% vote at the district’s annual meeting. 
Should 60% or more of voters approve in any school district, the measure will pass.  
Some voters said the tax cap question was an animating reason to vote Tuesday. 
Dan Hebert poses for a photo after voting in the Concord Heights neighborhood. Hebert voted for a tax cap because he was upset with the Concord School District’s recent fiscal decisions. He’s also concerned about how property taxes affect people on a fixed income like himself. (Photo by William Skipworth/New Hampshire Bulletin)
In the Concord Heights, Dan Hebert voted for a tax cap, and he said his vote was motivated by whats going on locally.
“I think every town is different,” he said.
He stressed that he respects the teachers and the work they do. However, he wants Concord School District and the state to seek other forms of revenue because of how hard property taxes hit people on fixed incomes, like himself. (Hebert receives benefits for his disability.)
“I also think that the property tax, being the only tax, is benefiting a certain group of people, ” he said. “And it’s not my people.”
Hebert usually votes absentee because his disability, which requires him to use a power wheelchair to move around, prevents him from getting into a standard voting booth. However, this year, he came in person because he saw a lot of politicians disparaging mail-in voting and was concerned his vote wouldn’t be counted. 
Randy Stevens, 36, of Manchester, voted against a tax cap, even if it may impact his taxes.
Stevens has children in Manchester schools, and said that he does not “mind paying more taxes to take care of my community.” 
Supporters hold signs for Republican candidates outside of Webster Elementary School in Manchester. (Photo by Maya Mitchell/New Hampshire Bulletin)
“I think it’s really important, and I also recognize that cost of living is going up for me and for everyone else, and that we have to continuously adjust and provide the level of education that our children need to be successful when they grow up and they’re adults into our community,” he said. “I really don’t know the minutia and the details. But if it means investing into my community and my educational system, I’m going to do that.”
Stevens said he always votes for candidates who “care about the people” he serves as executive director of Hope Recovery New Hampshire. He said human service problems are always top of mind when entering the voting booth. 
Candidate quality
For some voters, it was more about the candidates than the issues.
Linda and Gene Rosenthall pose for a photo after voting in New London during the November 2026 midterm elections. Each split their ballot between Republican Gov. Kelly Ayotte and Democratic congressional candidates Chris Pappas and Maggie Goodlander. (Photo by William Skipworth/New Hampshire Bulletin)
Husband and wife duo Gene, 60, and Linda Rosenthall, 63, of New London, said they both voted for Republican Gov. Kelly Ayotte to be reelected but chose Democrats Chris Pappas and Maggie Goodlander in the two congressional races.
Ayotte is counting on split-ticket voters like the Rosenthalls to bring her her first reelection victory. It’s a formula set by previous governors in the historically purple state that prides itself on independence. Her predecessor, Chris Sununu, also a Republican, swept through four consecutive elections while Democrats won in every single congressional race during that time. A September St. Anselm College poll found that 13% of voters planned to split their ballot between the two parties.
The Rosenthalls said the biggest motivators for them was putting a check on the Trump administration, which they vehemently oppose. Gene, a retired airline pilot, called the president an “embarrassment” to the country on the global stage.
Kirk Ballard, 55, voted at Lebanon City Hall Tuesday. He said he was sad to see Jeanne Shaheen retiring instead of running for reelection, but thought that Pappas “looks like a good guy.” He voted for Warmington, he said, because “I’m never going to vote for a Republican governor.”
He had a unique motivation behind some of his local votes. For county sheriff, Ballard wrote in his own name as a protest vote.
“Because I was arrested on, what I would call, in my opinion, from my perspective, an illegitimate domestic dispute charge, and I was sent to the Grafton County jail for two months without bail,” Ballard said. “… I don’t agree with the way the Corrections Department works. I don’t believe in the way that the police department, here at least, responded.”
Other voters brought personal experience into the Pappas-Sununu contests. 
Andy Desrosiers was a teacher at Salem High School when John E. Sununu and his siblings attended. “Comes from a great family,” Desrosiers said outside the polls in Windham. 
When Gov. Chris Sununu was on the ballot for eight years, Desrosiers voted for him. 
But that goodwill didn’t earn John Sununu Desrosiers’ vote Tuesday. Frustrated by a litany of decisions by President Donald Trump, from attacking Iran to imposing military-style crackdowns on undocumented people, Desrosiers is voting for change, and John Sununu was not the candidate to bring it, he said.
John Sununu’s opposition to abortion — he voted for multiple federal abortion restriction bills from 2002 to 2008 and earned a 100% rating from the National Right to Life Committee in 2006 — was also a dealbreaker for Desrosiers.
As he talked, Denise Dolloff came up beside Desrosiers. “My former student!” Desrosiers said.
Dolloff knows John Sununu too; she was his classmate at Salem High. And on Tuesday, she voted for him. 
“Christine was my sister’s closest friend in high school. And I think Peter worked for my parents for their business when he was a teenager,” Dolloff said, naming two other Sununu siblings. “There was a Sununu for almost every grade at one point in time,” she added. 
While she and John Sununu live in different towns today, he gives her a hug every time she sees him, Dolloff says. “He never forgot his roots,” she said. “He came to an event last St. Patrick’s Day in Salem and he went around shaking hands and remembering so many people’s names.”
And while he differs from his brother Chris — such as not being as comfortable on camera — there’s a hardworking, earnest side to John that might not translate in an interview, she said. Dolloff, a Trump supporter, argued it would allow him to separate himself from the president when needed. 
Desrosiers was less sure.
“Right now, his association with anything Trump would give me a reason to not vote for him,” he said. 
Poll workers at the Concord Ward 8 polling location help people register to vote on Election Day. (Photo by William Skipworth/New Hampshire Bulletin)
