text:
The U.S. Courthouse stands in downtown Wichita in 2024. (Photo by Max McCoy/Kansas Reflector)TOPEKA — A Kansas postal worker was indicted on Election Day for stealing thousands of pieces of mail, including hundreds of Republican political mailers.
Investigators for the U.S. Postal Service found more than 4,400 pieces of mail in Kelly Cram’s Baxter Springs garage. Nearly 400 of them were political mailers from Republican candidates or Republican-affiliated groups, according to a federal indictment filed Tuesday.
“The agents found no political mail related to candidates of any other political party or any political action committees affiliated with another political party at Cram’s residence,” the indictment said.
Cram, 59, had a rural mail delivery route out of Pittsburg. She had worked for the postal service since 2009 until she was put on administrative leave in early October, when investigators searched her garage, according to the indictment by a federal grand jury in Wichita. 
The grand jury indicted Cram of one count of unlawful secretion, destruction and delay of mail. The USPS’s Office of Inspector General is investigating the case, according to court documents.

name: Alaska Beacon
title: Alaska elections officials say most rural early voting sites flagged by lawsuits opened Monday
description: Alaska elections officials told a state Superior court judge on Sunday that 13 of the 18 rural early and absentee-in-person voting locations that were flagged in lawsuits filed late last week for failing to open as scheduled would be open on Monday — one day before Election Day. The remaining five communities were not able […]
text:
Voters cast their ballots at a polling site in the school library of Tanaina Elementary School in Wasilla on primary Election Day on Aug. 18, 2026. (Photo by Corinne Smith/Alaska Beacon)Alaska elections officials told a state Superior court judge on Sunday that 13 of the 18 rural early and absentee-in-person voting locations that were flagged in lawsuits filed late last week for failing to open as scheduled would be open on Monday — one day before Election Day.
The remaining five communities were not able to confirm early voting sites, officials said. And at least three more early voting locations were not open in Western Alaska’s House District 38 on Monday, according to state Rep. Nellie Jimmie, D-Toksook Bay, who joined one of the lawsuits. 
Jimmie is among several state legislators and the Alaska Democratic Party who filed a lawsuit against the Alaska Division of Elections on Friday over rural early voting sites failing to open early. Sites in 18 rural communities from St. Lawrence Island to the Copper River basin did not open as scheduled and failed to notify voters, according to the filing.     
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX. 

The 18 communities named in the lawsuit are Alakanuk, Chignik Bay, Chistochina, Ekwok, Gambell, Goodnews Bay, Holy Cross, Huslia, Kongiganak, Manokotak, Mountain Village, Nanwalek, Napaskiak, Newhalen, Pedro Bay, Pilot Station, Quinhagak and Toksook Bay.
On Sunday, attorneys for the state responded in court filings confirming 13 of those were “equipped, prepared and planning to open as scheduled” for voting on Monday, Nov. 2.
Those they said would be open include Chistochina, Ekwok, Gambell, Huslia, Manokotak, Mountain Village, Nanwalek, Pedro Bay, Pilot Station, Quinhagak and Toksook Bay.
Officials said they contacted the remaining five locations — in Alakanuk, Chignik Bay, Goodnews Bay, Holy Cross and Kongiganak — and were not able to confirm staffing for early voting at those locations as of Sunday. 
Attorneys for the division argued in court filings the state has done “everything practical” to ensure early and absentee-in-person voting is available in the affected communities. They said residents still had the opportunity to vote on Election Day. They said absentee-in-person voting is not required by law, and “the division nor the court can force a location to open.”
A court hearing on the lawsuit was canceled Monday, as the parties had negotiated and “had found solutions for the remaining sites,” according to an order by Superior Court Judge Thomas Matthews.
Staff with Jimmie’s office reported that early and absentee-in-person voting did not open in Akiak, Napaskiak and Kwigillingok on Monday, even though the state’s elections website said they were open. Additionally, Tuluksak was open by appointment, despite being listed as closed, Jimmie said.     

Rep. Nellie Unangiq Jimmie, D-Toksook Bay, speaks Tuesday, May 13, 2025, on the House floor. (Photo by James Brooks/Alaska Beacon)
 

The Alaska Beacon was not able to independently verify the open voting locations or where polling places remained closed on Monday. 
A spokesperson for the division did not respond to questions about the discrepancies in the division’s listed polling locations and hours on Monday. 
As of 5 p.m. Monday, the division’s website lists two open voting sites in Chignik. The site did not list a voting location in Alakanuk, and voting sites at Goodnews Bay and Kongiginak were listed under temporary closure. A Holy Cross site was listed as open for just two hours. 
Early and absentee in-person voting in Mertarvik, Tuluksak, Tuntuntuliak and Tununak were listed as temporarily closed on the website on Monday. 
Alaska Democratic Party Chair Jenny-Marie Stryker confirmed Monday the party had agreed to cancel the court hearing as they were “working with the division” ahead of Election Day.  
When asked about the discrepancies in early voting locations hours on Monday afternoon, Stryker acknowledged both parties were struggling to verify where absentee-in-person voting was available. 
“We’re confident the Division of Elections is working hard to address these challenges — but the fact that the parties in this litigation are scrambling at the 11th hour to recruit and certify absentee voting officials speaks to how far the Division still has to go,” she said. 
“When voters are receiving conflicting or inaccurate information about which locations are open and accessible, it’s clear we have reason to remain concerned,” she said. “We are far from satisfied and will continue working to ensure rural Alaskans have the access to vote that they deserve.”
Progressive groups challenge state over early voting location closures
The lawsuit filed by the Alaska Democratic Party and lawmakers names Lt. Governor Nancy Dahlstrom and division director Carol Beecher in their capacity as administrators of the state’s elections as defendants.     

Lt. Gov. Nancy Dahlstrom and Division of Elections Director Carol Beecher listen to testimony at a July 27, 2026, in Anchorage hearing on Ballot Measure 2. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)
 

The 18 affected communities named are predominantly Alaska Native, and all but one are only accessible by boat or plane. Early voting began Oct. 19, and in the days following the early or absentee-in-person voting sites did not open — some voters who traveled far distances including by boat and plane, were turned away, according to the lawsuit.
Attorneys for the plaintiffs asked the court to require that the division restore and maintain absentee-in-person voting in those communities, provide a site-by-site report and publish accurate information for voters to cast their ballots in the affected communities. They asked the court to expedite a decision as voting is underway and continues through Election Day at 8 p.m. Tuesday, Nov. 3.
The lawsuit cites similar problems in 2022, 2024 and this year’s August primary elections, where several early voting sites opened late or not at all due to staffing shortages. In August, Nunapitchuk voters reportedly had only three hours to vote on election day. Additionally, 75 absentee-in-person ballots were disqualified because they failed to reach the division’s regional office in time to be counted in time. 
Rural state representatives are joining the lawsuit including Jimmie, House Speaker Rep. Bryce Edgmon, I-Dillingham and  Rep. Robyn Frier, D-Utgiavik. All are running for election. 
“Year after year, the Division has failed to open polling places in rural Alaska, making it harder to vote here than anywhere else in the state,” Jimmie said, in a joint email statement ahead of filing the lawsuit on Thursday. 
“If I was home in Toksook currently and not in Bethel, I would not be able to vote early,” she said. “The right to vote must be meaningful in practice, and recurring disruptions require more than assurances that individual problems will be addressed.”
In the affected communities, the lawsuit cites some local officials running the absentee-in-person polling places who reported not receiving the necessary ballot materials from the division. Some said they were not given proper training on how to administer the voting locations. 
The lawsuit also cites the Alaska Democratic Party conducting its own calls to independently verify the status of early and absentee-in-person voting locations. From Oct. 26 to Oct. 29, callers conducted over 600 status checks, an average of 160 sites per day. The party said callers were not able to reach anyone in over 150 calls, and in over 80 instances sites were closed, temporarily closed or operating on changed hours. In over 60 instances, a site’s reported closing time did not match the hours listed on the division’s website. 
The lawsuit argues elections officials are violating their legal duties to administer elections — and maybe further violating requirements for language assistance under a federal consent decree. The parties argue that failing to open early and absentee-in-person sites may deprive voters of in-person language assistance they are entitled to in Yup’ik speaking regions, such as the Dillingham and Kusilvak census areas. 
Another lawsuit filed against the division on Thursday by a Washington D.C. based political non-profit, Midnight Sun Independence Fund, argues the failure to open early voting sites is a violation of Alaskans’ constitutional rights. It also asks for the court to require the division to open and operate all early and absentee-in-person voting locations as scheduled. On Monday, the parties reached a resolution and the case was dropped, according to court filings.
Division of Elections mounts defense in court
Attorneys for the division said in court filings that the state strives to administer as many absentee-in-person sites as possible. They said the division signs agreements with absentee voting officials, and “they tell the Division what times and locations they will be available for voting.”
They argue the division’s website states that “information is subject to change,” and said the division makes updates when notified. 
They argued against a court intervention, saying the division had taken all practical steps to open absentee-in-person voting sites, and “extreme and practically impossible steps” like flying division employees and supplies out to villages would not reach those locations before the end of the day Monday. They said diverting division staff and resources to five communities would “irreparably harm” the division.
Attorneys for the division argue election officials have fulfilled their duties under the law, and there is no requirement to “supply an official” at an absentee-in-person voting site. They said there is no constitutional right to vote absentee-in-person, and voters have other opportunities to cast a ballot, either by-mail or in-person on Election Day. 
Lawmakers called for immediate corrective action as early voting began
Both lawsuits cite a letter from Anchorage Democrat Bill Wielechowski sent on Oct. 23, four days after early voting began, to the Division of Elections notifying officials that the 18 rural absentee-in-person voting locations were not open as advertised, which was likely a violation of state and federal election law. 
On Oct. 26, Beecher responded to Wielechowski, saying that those communities were among 109 absentee-in-person voting sites that confirmed with the division in April, and the division had sent out ballot materials in early October. Beecher said the division had followed up with the 18 communities but did not say which had opened and which remained closed. 
“Of the eighteen sites listed in your letter, three have now declined to open, twelve have confirmed they are open, and we are working to hear from the remaining three locations,” she said. “Locations are free to change or extend their hours, up to the closing of the polls, to provide additional opportunities to vote.”
On Oct. 28, Jimmie also sent a letter to Beecher and Dahlstrom calling for answers for the early and absentee voting site closures and an “immediate statewide corrective action plan.” 
She asked the division for information on what is being done to restore voting services, how it will notify voters and what options will be made available whose access to voting has been disrupted or delayed. 
Currently, state law allows only ballots cast before 8 p.m. Nov. 3 to be counted. 
Jimmie reported that on Oct 27, more than a week after early voting began, at least 17 communities did not have open polling sites, including at least seven communities in her district — Mertarvik, Kongiganak, Tununak, Tuluksak, Toksook Bay, Nunapitchuk and Akiak. 
The next day, October 28, she reported at least 14 statewide were not open, including six or more in her district — Napaskiak, Tuntutuliak, Toksook Bay, Tuluksak, Tununak and Chevak. “Several more communities could not be reached,” she wrote. 
“Voters in my district are showing up to vote at the time and place the state told them to, and finding a locked door,” Jimmie said in a statement announcing the letter. “In communities like mine, where the next option is a plane, boat, or snow machine ride away, this tells voters that their voice is not valued.”
Jimmie also said she raised similar problems with the division after the August primary election, around polling sites opening late and ballots from Nunapatchuk not reaching Bethel in time to be counted. “My questions about voter recourse, documentation of affected turnout, and corrective measures were not adequately answered,” she wrote.
Part of the response she did receive was election officials asking Jimmie to help recruit poll workers in her district, a request she said was inappropriate because she is running for re-election.
House Speaker Rep. Bryce Edgmon noted in a joint statement Thursday that the Legislature passed a bipartisan elections reform package that aimed to address some of the ongoing issues for rural voters. That included creating a rural liaison in the division to help with staffing and opening rural polling sites. Gov. Mike Dunleavy vetoed the bill, and the Legislature declined to override the veto by two votes. 
“Making voting accessible in a state as vast, rural and remote as Alaska is the state’s responsibility,” Edgmon said. “The Legislature upheld our end of the deal in passing a bipartisan bill that would have improved access, strengthened transparency, and maintained the integrity of our elections. Governor Dunleavy vetoed that bill.”

name: Alaska Beacon
title: Alaska’s U.S. Senate race draws significant donations from AI company employees
description: Alaska’s U.S. Senate race has drawn more money to campaigns from employees of AI companies than any other 2026 Senate race, an analysis of Federal Election Commission records shows.  The actual numbers of donors are small, but at least 19 employees contributed approximately $119,000 to the campaigns of Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan and his Democratic […]
text:
Sen. Dan Sullivan, R-Alaska, and former U.S. Rep. Mary Peltola, D-Alaska, listen to a question at a candidate forum held Aug. 27, 2026, by the Alaska Oil and Gas Association. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)Alaska’s U.S. Senate race has drawn more money to campaigns from employees of AI companies than any other 2026 Senate race, an analysis of Federal Election Commission records shows. 
The actual numbers of donors are small, but at least 19 employees contributed approximately $119,000 to the campaigns of Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan and his Democratic challenger, Mary Peltola, with most people giving close to the maximum legal contribution limit. A donor can give $3,500 per election, or $7,000 for the primary and general together, and $5,000 a year to a leadership Political Action Committee or PAC.
Many of the donations to both candidates came from employees of Anthropic, one of the country’s leading AI companies. None of the AI-company donors list an Alaska address, with most living in California.
Sullivan is seeking reelection against Peltola in a tight contest that could help determine control of the Senate. Neither campaign responded to requests for comment. The race also includes Republican Gerald Heikes and Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. Heikes does not have a campaign, which makes it impossible for him to get donations. Sullivan Jr. has not  received any contributions from the AI-company employees examined.
The already close race has become even more contentious following a report in the New York Times that Peltola recruited Daniel J. Sullivan as a spoiler for the race. Peltola’s campaign has denied any involvement in the effort to the Times.
The Alaska race is only first when counting money flowing from AI company employees to both candidates’ campaigns. Once donations to PACs are included, South Dakota Senate campaigns pulled in the most in contributions. Other individual Senate candidates received more money, but the donations going to both Sullivan and Peltola pushed Alaska to the top. For example, in Florida, the Republican candidate for Senate received $68,000 from AI company employees and $113,000 when including donations to PACs, but the Democratic candidate, Angela Nixon, received just $250.
Sullivan alone was fifth out of other candidates for Senate races around the country in terms of donations received from AI company employees and Peltola was 14th. The top individual candidate is Republican Mike Rounds of South Dakota with $165,100 to his campaign and PACs from AI company employees.
In the Alaska races, Peltola received at least $56,000—nearly all of it from Anthropic employees.  Sullivan received approximately $63,000 from AI-company employees for his campaign. Another $35,000 came through his leadership PAC, True North, bringing his combined total to about $98,000. Of the 10 Senate candidates receiving the most from AI-company employees, Sullivan had the fewest donors, but he received the most per donor.
For the analysis, Anthropic, OpenAI, and xAI were counted as AI companies, while the larger universe of big tech counted employee contributions from Google, Microsoft, Meta, Nvidia, Amazon and Apple.
Big Tech and AI-company donors reveal different patterns
When including contributions from employees at Google, Microsoft, Meta and other Big Tech firms, Peltola’s campaign ranks fifth among Senate candidates nationwide, compared with Sullivan’s 16th-place ranking. Peltola has received support from close to 150 Big Tech employees when compared with four for Sullivan. Most of Peltola’s big-tech money came through online fundraising platforms such as ActBlue.
Most of the money to both candidates came through joint fundraising committees rather than direct donations. Joint fundraising committees raise money from large donors and split the funds across campaigns. Sullivan’s contributions mainly came from One Team Senate Majority, which splits contributions among the National Republican Senatorial Committee and other Republicans’ campaigns, and his joint fundraising committee, Sullivan Victory. More than half of Peltola’s contributions came from the Fish Family Freedom Fund, which she formed in January with the Alaska Democratic Party and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee. 
Large contributions from a small number of employees in the same industry can suggest that donors see a candidate as favorable to their interests, said Brendan Fischer, Director of Strategic Investigations at Campaign Legal Center. However, he cautioned against using employer data as proof of coordinated giving. 
Political money often flows toward races where donors believe their contributions can have an impact, Fischer said. Donors wanting to influence the chamber’s balance of power may be attracted to Alaska’s race since it could determine control in the Senate.
The issue of data centers and AI has become contentious, recent polling shows. Data centers contain the IT infrastructure needed to train and implement artificial intelligence. Some people are concerned about the environmental impacts of data centers through their electricity and water use, according to an AP-NORC poll from September. The poll concludes that in America, 67% of Democrats and 49% of Republicans are worried that data centers will impact water supply. The poll also establishes that 57% of Democrats and 50% of Republicans believe that AI will harm society more than help it in the next 10 years. Additionally, Republicans have expressed greater support for data centers than Democrats, USA TODAY reported. 
Alaska’s data center debate
The AI-employee money comes as Alaska candidates debate over AI infrastructure investment in the state. Sullivan has advocated expanding data center development in the state, and has pushed for the federal government to locate advanced AI data centers on Alaska’s military bases. In April, the Air Force sought developers for potential AI data centers on about 4,700 acres across three Alaska installations. Peltola has focused less on data centers and more on “affordability and energy costs,” according to a Newsweek report.
Sullivan also has a personal financial connection to the data center industry. According to The Alaska Current, Sullivan holds approximately $5 million in stock in his family’s chemical company, RPM International, whose subsidiaries supply specialized coatings used in data centers.
The issue of  AI infrastructure also has drawn scrutiny from groups within the state.
Krystal Lapp, the Interim Executive Director of Alaskans for Data Center Accountability — one of the most vocal groups expressing their dissatisfaction with large-scale data centers — says this election will have significant impacts on the Alaskan land and the allocation of resources. 
“With the boom of AI, we’re definitely seeing politicians and everybody else inviting people up here because we’re Alaska. Everyone has thought of us as a place that they could take from,” Lapp said, referring to land grabs for building data centers. “We look like a cash cow, but they’re not going to benefit us.” 
In September, the Alaska Beacon reported that the Alaska Department of Natural Resources decided to transfer 30 square miles of land to the state-owned economic development agency AIDEA for a “multi-use industrial and energy development district.” The Matanuska-Susitna Borough uses natural gas energy. Data centers in this area could increase demand for insufficient natural gas resources. AIDEA officials have said that there aren’t existing plans for data centers, but that they could potentially be built.   
“I am against the executive orders that were put through and I am against the gutting of the public process,” Lapp said. “By taking away that public process, they take away that responsibility piece.”
Stanford student journalists Arshya Gaur and Bridget Stuebner reported this story with the DataTalk campaign finance AI agent developed by Big Local News and the Stanford Open Virtual Assistant Lab as part of a journalism class at Stanford. The FEC data was independently fact-checked and verified by Gerald Rich of Big Local News at Stanford.

name: Alabama Reflector
title: Alabama voters go to polls with affordability and national issues on their minds
authors: Anna Barrett, Ralph Chapoco, Ben Sessoms, Forrest Terrell, Andrea Tinker
description: Alabamians cast ballots throughout the morning in what could be one of the more critical midterms in recent memory.  In more than 30 separate interviews in Jefferson, Montgomery, Autauga, DeKalb and Lee counties, voters choosing most frequently cited the economy as their number one concern, but national issues were also on many people’s minds. “I […]
text:
A sign saying "Vote here" is seen outside the Frank Brown Recreation Center in Auburn, Alabama on Nov. 3, 2026. Voters in more than 30 interviews around Alabama Tuesday cited affordability issues as a major concern, though several also brought up national concerns. (Anna Barrett/Alabama Reflector)Alabamians cast ballots throughout the morning in what could be one of the more critical midterms in recent memory. 
In more than 30 separate interviews in Jefferson, Montgomery, Autauga, DeKalb and Lee counties, voters choosing most frequently cited the economy as their number one concern, but national issues were also on many people’s minds.
“I think making things like bare necessities accessible—diapers, formula, obviously the cost of groceries—when it comes to talking to outside of the world of babies,” said Sara Tameze-Rivas of Homewood, who voted for Democratic gubernatorial nominee Doug Jones. “But I mean, so many people are having to make decisions like ‘what am I foregoing this week? You know, what do I have to do to get by with things?'”
Jack Stanley, a retired U.S. Air Force instructor who voted for Republican gubernatorial nominee Tommy Tuberville, said his chief concerns were “things like Social Security, solvency and health insurance, pharmacy prices, things like that.” 
Voter Guide: 2026 Alabama general election

The votes came as the U.S. Department of Justice Tuesday morning announced it planned to “monitor or observe” elections in Jefferson, Montgomery and Mobile counties. As of midday, no problems had been immediately reported.
“I heard earlier there were places with long lines, but no significant problems,” said Kim Bailey, president of the League of Women Voters of Alabama, in an interview Tuesday morning. 
Polls will remain open until 7 p.m. tonight. 
The cost of living was a major theme for voters around the state. Anna Parker, a sewing machine operator from Fort Payne who voted for Tuberville, said she hoped the next governor would work to improve healthcare costs and said she struggled to pay for necessities.
“I can’t afford to drive back and forth to work, and I’m only 15 minutes away from where I work,” she said. “It’s sad the way the country is now.”
Emily Broome, a graduate student at Auburn University who voted for Jones, said it was “disappointing” to see politicians promise to address affordability and then fall short.
“That’s definitely something that’s been on my mind, especially as a student who lives off of a grad school stipend,” she said. “It’s really, really hard. I feel like it’s me paying my rent or gas. It should not be the most important part of my week.”
Voters also cited national issues in casting ballots. Immigration was on the minds of some voters, including Krista Parker, a retired educator from Valley Head who voted for Tuberville. 
“I love closed borders,” she said. “You want to become a part of our country? Welcome, but do it the right way. They’re taking away all the help that was there for us, our citizens, our veterans, and they’re putting it toward someone who just crossed the border illegally, and I don’t like that.”
Eva Marroquin, an assembly worker from Fort Payne who voted for Jones, said she did not like the tactics used by Immigration and Customs Enforcement, “especially toward breaking families apart.”
“I get it toward criminals, but toward innocent people that are here trying to work and get something for their families, I feel like that’s the part where it’s messed up,” she said.
Bart Barrontine, a retired state worker who voted straight-ticket Republican in Prattville, said he wanted “democracy, I don’t want communism.”
“The national election, the Democratic Party was pretty much socialist communism,” he said. “That is what their platform is. They want to take away law enforcement, take away our right to bear arms. It is socialism.”
Michael Melancon, a retiree who lives in Auburn who voted for Jones, said the war in Iran was a factor for him. 
“I was in the army during Vietnam,” he said. “I know what war is. In my opinion, the current Republican Party is totally out of bounds on all issues.”
James Stewart, another Auburn retiree who voted for Jones, said he was also concerned about data centers. 
“I think the state’s environment has been compromised enough, and I think that people don’t they don’t realize that they don’t employ very many people, and they cause a tremendous amount of environmental damage as well as quality of life with the sound and everything else,” he said. “We can do something better than just dump them all in Alabama, in Mississippi.”
But concerns over the cost of living cut across both parties. Shineka Maye, a Montgomery business owner who voted for Jones, said she wanted to see “lower taxes, specifically the grocery tax.”
“It’s ridiculous that other states have lower taxes on groceries and Alabama is still stuck,” she said.
Amber Whitting, a small business owner in Prattville who voted for Jones, said she had pocketbook and national issues in mind.
“Everything is too expensive,” she said. “Nothing is affordable anymore. I would rather have someone go for the issues instead of what the president says. I want someone with a backbone.”
This story was reported by Anna Barrett, Ralph Chapoco, Ben Sessoms, Forrest Terrell and Andrea Tinker. It was written by Editor Brian Lyman.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Man charged with mailing letters containing powder to officials ahead of elections
description: Federal authorities charged an Oklahoma City man with sending hundreds of letters containing nonhazardous powder to public officials.
text:
Federal authorities charged an Oklahoma City man with sending hundreds of letters containing nonhazardous white powder to public officials ahead of the 2024 and 2026 elections.
The powders turned out to be yeast or flour, though not all letters have been fully tested, the FBI said in a court filing made public Tuesday.
Robin Martin is charged with conveying a hoax and mailing threatening communications. Martin was arrested Monday and was expected to make an appearance Tuesday in U.S. District Court in Oklahoma City.
Online records do not list an attorney who could comment on his behalf, and several relatives didn’t immediately respond to social media messages seeking comment.
Federal authorities announced last month that they were investigating letters with “suspicious substances” that had been mailed to congressional and election offices nationwide and urged recipients to treat the mailings as “potentially hazardous.”
The packages led to the evacuation in October of election offices in Louisiana and Oklahoma. Numerous states, from Idaho to Florida, said their election offices either received letters or had them intercepted by the Postal Service.
Investigators believe more than 700 mailings appeared to be associated with the same sender. They were addressed to election officials, members of Congress, pollsters, news media and federal law enforcement, FBI agent David Cole said in an affidavit.
The investigation stretched back to 2024 when multiple election officials in every state reported mail with a white substance and a three-page letter declaring war, the FBI said. Some bore ominous messages that could only be read under ultraviolet light.
The sender wrote a return address as “U.S.T.E.A., United States Traitor Elimination Army, Takoma Park, MD.”
A common message in the 2024 and 2026 mailings was a warning to recipients about upcoming arrests for treason “or worse!!”
The FBI said it has video evidence of Martin’s car stopping in October at mailboxes at Postal Service sites in Oklahoma City, Dallas and San Antonio. Investigators also gleaned his fingerprints from a letter addressed to FBI Director Kash Patel, whose first name was written as “Kashyap.”
The Democratic Socialists of America apparently assisted the FBI in the investigation. The FBI said it believes Martin, posing as someone using the name George Livingston, posted a message to a DSA email list in October, warning that members were traitors and eligible for arrest for treason if they vote in the Nov. 3 election.

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: KY economic incentive board creates new requirements for data centers tax breaks
description: Hyperscale data center developers are eyeing a potentially massive, controversial sales tax break passed by Kentucky state lawmakers, but they might have to meet a number of requirements recently outlined by a state board to get it. The Kentucky Cabinet for Economic Development published new policy documents Monday afternoon detailing these new hoops for dat[...]
text:
Many of the attendees at the Mercer County Fiscal Court meeting brought signs expressing opposition to data centers. (Kentucky Lantern photo by Liam Niemeyer)Hyperscale data center developers are eyeing a potentially massive, controversial sales tax break passed by Kentucky state lawmakers, but they might have to meet a number of requirements recently outlined by a state board to get it.
The Kentucky Cabinet for Economic Development published new policy documents Monday afternoon detailing these new hoops for data center developers to jump through before receiving a sales and use tax break on data center equipment that can last, depending on the investment by the data center developer, for up to 50 years. 
Those requirements include data center developers providing the state with an independent economic impact study, getting community buy-in through providing letters of support from local elected officials and having the data center developer say how much taxes it would have to pay without any tax breaks. 
The policy documents — one an overview and another detailing the approval process — cite Democratic Gov. Andy Beshear’s executive order seeking to implement data center impact protections as the reasoning for providing the “additional policy recommendations”.
The documents also appear to leave open the possibility of state officials reducing the size and timespan of the tax breaks. That depends on if the data center developer meets economic development goals including job creation commitments, or if the developer is already receiving local tax breaks, such as through industrial revenue bonds issued by a county. 
To get the sales tax break, data center developers have to receive approval from the Kentucky Economic Development Finance Authority, which meets regularly every month to approve state tax breaks and other business incentives. A Cabinet for Economic Development spokesperson did not immediately provide a response to emailed questions by the Lantern about the new policy documents. 
During an Oct. 29 press conference, Beshear told reporters the state’s latest policy on the tax break would “evaluate whether it’s fair, how much of a tax break it’s giving, and to potentially reduce the state incentive by a certain amount based on that.” 
“We want each of these to be fair. We do believe we’re going to have to look at them individually,” Beshear said, mentioning each project proposal can be different. “This is entirely new to us, so we’re trying to go about it in a very rational way, but one that again empowers communities.” 
Beshear said data centers are “an intensely local decision” and that communities should be able to decide whether to deny them or accept them. He has previously said he doesn’t believe data centers should receive any incentive. 
Earlier this year, the progressive think tank Kentucky Center for Economic Policy estimated Kentucky could miss out on billions of dollars of tax revenue from the sales tax break if applied to just a few large data centers. 
Jason Bailey, the executive director of that think tank, told the Lantern the policy documents appear to put into action Beshear’s executive order, along with the possibility of scaling back the size of the tax breaks. But he still sees a need for the Kentucky legislature to act on the issue when they meet again next year. 
“This would not excuse the need for the General Assembly to come in and pass legislation that actually creates mandates for local participation, for taxes being paid, for employment being created and that scales back what is a really enormous tax break,” Bailey said. “All the cabinet can do is try to negotiate the terms, but their powers here are ultimately limited.” 
Bailey said the policy documents would provide helpful information to the cabinet, but he also believes such information should be made available to the public, subject to the state’s open records law, as well. 
In 2025, the GOP-controlled state legislature passed a law expanding the tax break opportunity, known as the Qualified Data Center Program, to apply to hyperscale data centers developers looking to build across the state as a potential economic development boon. 
Since then, the statewide tax break has garnered strong pushback and criticism from residents in Kentucky communities where hyperscale data centers are being proposed, those residents having concerns about environmental impacts and rising utility bills. 
Amid the criticism over the state sales tax break, some Republican state lawmakers have suggested rolling back the sales tax break for data centers. The primary sponsor of the bill that expanded the sales tax break statewide, House Majority Whip Jason Nemes, R-Middletown, in a campaign ad said he would continue pushing for electricity ratepayer protections against data center impacts. 
A spokesperson for the GOP caucus in the Kentucky House of Representatives did not immediately provide commentary on the policy documents. A spokesperson for the GOP caucus in the Kentucky Senate declined to comment. 
The Kentucky Economic Development Finance Authority discussed updates to the sales tax break program during its Oct. 29 meeting. 
Some Kentuckians with data center concerns attended that meeting including Max Moran, the executive director of the group We Are Mason County. That group is suing the county over the local planning and zoning process that’s made way for a planned hyperscale data center campus being built in the county by the technology company Meta. 
Moran said he was glad to see the policy documents included various protections, saying members of his group had productive conversations with the cabinet at the meeting. 
Community Benefit Agreements negotiated between data center developers and county fiscal courts for Mason County and Carroll County also indicate that developers plan to seek the state sales tax break, such agreements requiring that the county governments support those efforts by developers.  
“If they go through and they don’t live up to what they promise and everything, then that board, with the state’s backing, would revoke their tax break exemptions for sales and use tax,” Moran said. “Which I agree with completely.”

title: Election workers, volunteers work to protect and promote the right to vote in NC on Election Day
description: For Ren Pridgeon, 72, working on Election Day is a five-decade tradition. “I have never missed an election,” said Pridgeon with a broad smile. “I worked my first election when I was 22 years old.” Pridgeon was serving as a poll worker Tuesday outside of John Chavis Community Center in southeast Raleigh. Pridgeon can recall […]
text:
Ren Pridgeon has been working and volunteering in various capacities with elections in Raleigh, North Carolina for 50 years. (Photo: Clayton Henkel/NC Newsline) For Ren Pridgeon, 72, working on Election Day is a five-decade tradition.
“I have never missed an election,” said Pridgeon with a broad smile. “I worked my first election when I was 22 years old.”
Pridgeon was serving as a poll worker Tuesday outside of John Chavis Community Center in southeast Raleigh.
Pridgeon can recall voting for Jimmy Carter in the 1976 presidential electon, but is now more concerned with voter education.
“I see the importance of it — making people aware of what they’re voting for,” said Pridgeon. “Of course, I don’t tell anyone who to vote for.”
Pridgeon tells those disinterested in politics that the failure to cast a ballot is the same as giving your vote to a candidate or a policy you dislike.
“A lot of people complain, ‘My child has lost her free lunch or they may reduce social security or cut this and that,’” said Pridgeon. “My first question is ‘Did you vote? No?’ The conversation is over.”
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
Pridgeon said he also wants younger voters to understand that it’s not just the candidates at the top of the ticket they need to pay attention to. Judicial contests may not garner much attention, but may have a larger impact on an individual’s life.
“Hopefully, you won’t get tied up in the legal system,” Pridgeon said. “But if you do, you want a judge who is at least going to listen, and perhaps feel what you’re feeling before they make their decision.”
As the 2026 midterms wind down, Pridgeon said he thinks a lot about his children and grandchildren and the future that he hopes they will have.
“When I go into the booth, I vote my heart because I do my homework and check out platforms not only from Democrats but from Republicans,” he said. “That’s the thing I like about Election Day itself. In the primaries, you have to vote [what’s best] for your party, but on Election Day, you vote your heart.”
After five decades of working the polls, Pridgeon isn’t quite ready to give it up. He plans to volunteer again for 2028.
Having faith in democracy
Rev. Suzanne Parker Miller spent Election Day serving as a poll chaplain for Faith United to Save Democracy. (Photo: Clayton Henkel/NC Newsline)
At Pullen Park Community Center, the Rev. Suzanne Parker Miller was spending Election Day serving as a poll chaplain for Faith United to Save Democracy. The nonpartisan, multi-faith organization is focused on voter protection campaigns in North Carolina, Arizona, Georgia, Michigan, Ohio, Pennsylvania, Texas, Virginia, and Wisconsin.
“I’m here as a peacekeeper, as a poll observer, a clergy person, to be able to just make sure that people are having the chance to vote,” said Parker Miller.
The Moravian minister who lives in Raleigh had heard that the U.S. Justice Department was dispatching federal monitors to polls, which could possibly discourage some voters from casting a ballot.
US Justice Department to send election monitors to these NC counties

“We were told that there would be some type of federal presence in Wake County today,” said Parker Miller. “I didn’t know what to expect today, which is just always a little unnerving. But I’ve done this in the past and what I came in expecting today was to also have a very peaceful and fair and free election.”
Parker Miller said a successful Election Day would be an uneventful one.
“Everyone should have the right to vote if they are a registered voter and they have had their citizenship. So we want to make sure that they don’t have any hindrance to physically get into the polling place,” she said.
Regardless of the outcome of the midterms, Parker Miller said she hopes the political parties can find a way to set the rhetoric and rancor aside after Tuesday.
“Government, when it works, we don’t notice it,” said Parker Miller. “I’m really hoping that we can get back to things working for the common good.”
Polls close this evening at 7:30 pm. Eligible voters can find their Election Day polling location on the state Board of Elections’ Voter Search page.
North Carolina voters will decide on a number of important races on Nov. 3, 2026 as well as a flurry of bond issues and constitutional amendments. (Photo: Clayton Henkel/NC Newsline)

title: US Supreme Court justices doubtful of Colorado rule in Catholic preschool case
description: Conservative U.S. Supreme Court justices appeared doubtful Tuesday of yet another Colorado policy involving the balance of state anti-discrimination protections for LGBTQ+ people and religious exemptions. The Archdiocese of Denver and two Catholic preschools say in a lawsuit that they were unable to participate in Colorado’s universal preschool program, know[...]
text:
The U.S. Supreme Court heard arguments Tuesday in a Colorado case over the balance of protections for LGBTQ+ people and religion. (Photo by Jane Norman/States Newsroom)Conservative U.S. Supreme Court justices appeared doubtful Tuesday of yet another Colorado policy involving the balance of state anti-discrimination protections for LGBTQ+ people and religious exemptions.
The Archdiocese of Denver and two Catholic preschools say in a lawsuit that they were unable to participate in Colorado’s universal preschool program, known as UPK Colorado, because the state will not allow the religious educational institutions to exclude LGBTQ+ children and parents. 
Attorneys for the schools and the state Tuesday argued before the Supreme Court about whether Colorado’s anti-discrimination policies improperly target Catholic schools for their sincerely held beliefs, violating the free exercise clause of the First Amendment, or if Colorado applied the requirement universally with no intention to exclude the schools. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Justice Brett Kavanaugh said that with 2,000 preschools and only 34 of them Catholic in Colorado, there are plentiful opportunities for families to find a preschool that suits their needs, so the state can respect both religious beliefs and the rights of LGBTQ+ parents. 
“It seems like this is a … would-be solution in search of a problem that is unnecessary to create this clash,” Kavanaugh said. “Why has this been provoked when there’s an ability for everyone to go to the school, a good school that’s a fit for them, and respect religious rights?”



Quotation







Your Catholic schools will reject the child merely because their parents are homosexual.


– Justice Sonia Sotomayor


Nicholas Reaves, attorney with the Becket Fund for Religious Liberty, who represents the plaintiffs in the case, said he does not think the state has presented a “really good reason” to prevent religious schools from receiving the public benefit of UPK funding, as is required by the legal standard of strict scrutiny. Sarah Harris, principal deputy solicitor general for the U.S. Justice Department, also argued before the court in support of the plaintiffs in the case.  
Liberal justices said the Catholic schools are looking for a specific accommodation and exemption to a universally applied principle, while in previous cases, religious schools were just asking to be treated the same as other schools, Justice Elena Kagan said. Laws shut down by previous rulings explicitly discriminated against religious schools, while Colorado’s UPK rules do not. 
Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson said that many other religious schools, including Catholic schools, agreed to Colorado’s anti-discrimination provisions. Justice Sonia Sotomayor said the Catholic schools involved in the case chose not to participate in the program because they will not receive a special exemption allowing them to exclude children from a specific protected class.
“Your Catholic schools will reject the child merely because their parents are homosexual,” Sotomayor said. “If it’s a sincere religious exercise to exclude Blacks, this principle would permit the exclusion of those Black children.”
Religious preschools welcome
Helen Norton, deputy solicitor general for Colorado, argued that the state holds all preschools to the same standards, including teacher training, student-teacher ratios and equal opportunity. Religious schools are welcome to teach their beliefs on sex, gender and marriage. All of those standards are generally applicable to all participants. 
“Colorado welcomes religious preschools to UPK,” Norton said. “The only thing Colorado asks is that they comply with the same conditions that every publicly funded preschool must meet, religious and secular alike.”
The St. Mary Catholic Parish in Littleton and the St. Bernadette Catholic Parish in Lakewood both operate preschool programs that were not part of UPK since the state requires providers to accept applicants without regard to the family’s religion, sexual orientation or gender identity. 
The schools applied for public funding through the universal preschool program and were denied when they requested religious exemptions from the state’s equal-opportunity rule. They claimed their rights under the free exercise clause of the First Amendment were violated by their exclusion. 
A U.S. District Court of Colorado judge ruled in June 2024 that the UPK requirement that prohibits discrimination against LGBTQ+ families is valid. The Denver-based 10th Circuit Court of Appeals upheld the district court’s decision in October 2025, and the Supreme Court accepted the case in April. The church and schools filed the lawsuit against Lisa Roy, executive director of the Colorado Department of Early Childhood. 
The Supreme Court will weigh in on aspects of a 1990 ruling in another case that raised the question of religious exemptions to state laws. The court held in Employment Division v. Smith that a person’s religious beliefs are not an automatic exemption from compliance with a law against conduct the state is free to regulate. Attorneys for the state heavily relied on this ruling.
The initial lawsuit made several references to past cases related to LGBTQ+ discrimination in Colorado that made their way to the nation’s highest court. That includes a case in which the Supreme Court said a Colorado web designer does not have to make websites for same-sex couples, and another in which the court said a cake shop owner could deny a same-sex couple a wedding cake based on religious beliefs. 
Most recently, the court sided with a Christian counselor against Colorado’s law that bans licensed providers from conducting “conversion therapy,” a discredited practice of trying to change a person’s sexual orientation, such as to eliminate same-sex attraction, or gender identity.
Conservative justices wondered how Colorado did not predict a conflict such as the one posed in the preschool case, given the state’s history of court challenges to LGBTQ+ protections. 
Six of the justices on the Supreme Court are Catholic — five in the conservative majority, and one, Sotomayor, in the liberal minority. Justice Neil Gorsuch, who is Episcopalian, was raised Catholic.
The court is expected to announce a decision in the case by June.

name: Alaska Beacon
title: Alaska election shenanigans date back to territorial days
description: The 1910s were a momentous period in Alaska history, marked by major expansions in education, self-governance, and infrastructure development, including the creation of what is now the University of Alaska system, the Alaska Legislature and the Alaska Railroad. They also show that tumultuous elections are nothing new in Alaska.
text:
Historical front page.The 1910s were a momentous period in Alaska history, marked by major expansions in education, self-governance, and infrastructure development, including the creation of what is now the University of Alaska system, the Alaska Legislature and the Alaska Railroad. They also show that tumultuous elections are nothing new in Alaska. 
James Wickersham (1857-1939) was the territory’s longtime delegate to Congress and he used his pulpit to advocate for those lasting institutions. Yet, some of his later elections were mired in controversy, and in one case he contested an outcome until after his opponent’s death. Amid the turmoil and death, there was an epidemic, socialist challengers, anti-immigrant sentiments, a fraudulent governor, non-secret ballots, partisan antics, electioneering and racism. In other words, it was the usual election shenanigans up north, back in those pioneering days.  
Wickersham served throughout the decade, except after the two elections he lost. On both occasions he was reconsidered as the winner. There was the candidate who won but died before he was later announced as the actual loser. There was another election in which Wickersham did not participate. On that occasion, the results were voided in his favor. 
On September 30, 1918, Wickersham held his first public meeting in Anchorage, the territory’s still-new railroad hub. Around 800 voters packed the Empress Theatre for his two-hour campaign speech. Like politicians before and since, he pandered to area interests, noting his strenuous support for the Alaska Railroad. Indeed, his five-hour speech in the House of Representatives on January 14, 1914 was a key moment in the passage of the Alaska Railroad Act. At that time, it was also the longest speech in House history. 
Like politicians before and since, he maligned his rivals, whom he described as being in the pockets of corporate interests, the Guggenheim Syndicate specifically. And he praised his allies, including J.F.A. Strong, the disgraced governor who was ousted earlier that year after revelations about a falsified background. Rather than a Kentucky veteran of multiple wars, Strong was a Canadian bigamist with no military experience. Wickersham declared, “It is much better to be a Canadian than a German.” World War I was nearing its conclusion, with Germany as the central opponent, and Wickersham’s campaign opposite just happened to be the son of German immigrants. 
As he had in five previous elections, Wickersham strove to become Alaska’s delegate to the House of Representatives, the territory’s only Congressional representative from 1906 to statehood in 1959. While the position was accorded no vote, it was a powerful platform from which to argue on behalf of Alaska interests. Alaskans first voted for senators and a voting representative in 1958, and for president in 1960. 
With relatively little trouble, Wickersham successfully won campaigns in 1908, 1910, 1912 and 1914. The issues truly began with the 1916 election, which was also notable for the participation of socialist candidate Lena Morrow Lewis, the first woman to run for an Alaska-wide position. 
Socialism was then a popular cause among Alaskan laborers, miners and fishermen. The election was moved from August to November as of 1914, and poll taxes on male workers were established in 1913. By coincidence perhaps, both actions undercut the socialist vote. Many laborers had left the territory for the season by November, and the $4 poll tax was a heavy burden for the average worker. Lewis tallied 1,340 votes, more than 9% of the turnout, and finished third. 
The leading candidates were Wickersham and Charles A. Sulzer (1879-1919), that son of German immigrants. The latter managed a copper mine at Sulzer, a long-since abandoned community on Prince of Wales Island. The town was apparently named for Sulzer’s brother William, who founded the mining company and was a notable New York politician with his own skeletons. William served less than ten months as Governor of New York in 1913 before he was impeached and convicted for campaign finance fraud. These charges, however true they may have been, could more accurately be read as punishment for publicly breaking from the Tammany Hall political machine. 
Before airplanes, snowmachines and even a limited road system, Alaska was a difficult, time-consuming territory to traverse in winter. The election results took months to gather. It was a narrow race, and newspapers alternated stances, declaring one or the other winner as a dozen votes here, a dozen votes there, were added to the totals. A supposedly final tally in early March found Wickersham the winner by a mere 31 votes. More surprising for modern Alaskans, residents also voted by a two-to-one margin to ban alcohol in the territory.
However, immediate concerns arose over the returns from six districts. Secret ballots, that is, voting as people today would understand the process, was still such a sufficiently new and foreign concept then that it was widely referred to as the “Australian ballot.” And in those six districts, there were no official, secret ballots. Instead, there were partisan ballots listing only one candidate. On March 20, 1917, Judge Robert W. Jennings ruled that those districts should be disregarded, flipping the outcome to a 19-vote win for Sulzer, who was duly seated.
With the onset of the 1918 election cycle, Wickersham was still officially contesting the 1916 results. A House investigation sided with him, and he was formally seated on January 7, 1919, even as votes were being counted in the sequel. He served the final two months of the term. 
The 1918 election was more of the same, only faster and more intense. The worldwide influenza pandemic, often referred to as the Spanish Flu, peaked in Alaska right around the election. Public gatherings were banned in several towns, meaning a surcease of sorrow from overabundant campaign speeches and rallies. Police shut down one illicit Wickersham rally during a quarantine. In some places, voters took their turns while wearing masks. 
And the result was a seeming 33-vote Sulzer win, then reduced to a 31-vote margin, which Wickersham naturally contested. Once again, allegations swarmed, a mass of accusations all tinged with mud and flying in all directions. Both sides accused the other of illegally convincing Alaska Natives to vote, of distributing paper or cardboard cutouts that allowed illiterate voters to identify the desired candidate on the ballot. Opponents later charged pioneering Tlingit lawyer and politician William Paul of similar tactics. 
In public, Wickersham vehemently opposed Alaska Native suffrage except as allowed by the stringent requirements of the 1915 Alaska Native Citizenship Act, the 15th Constitutional Amendment notwithstanding. Under the act, only Alaska Natives who “severed all tribal relationships,” “adopted the habits of a civilized life,” and passed “an examination by a majority of the teachers” from a presumably “civilized” school could legally vote. The Alaska Native right to vote was subsequently clarified by the 1924 Indian Citizenship Act and the 1965 Voting Rights Act, though inconsistently enforced.
Stakeholders, witnesses and members of Congress repeatedly debated the meaning of the law, of the words in the law, to the point of literal distraction. As Representative Carl R. Chindbloom of Illinois later wearily concluded: “Take this record, and you will find the evidence is so inconclusive, so hazy, so misty, that it is impossible for anybody to reach any definite conclusion in respect to the Indian vote.”
Wickersham also accused Sulzer and his allies of stacking election officials with fellow Democrats, “that in each precinct the said Democratic commissioner appointed two Democrats and either a Republican opponent of contestant or a Socialist as the three election judges and clears of said election in said precincts, and thereby the whole election machinery.”
Among his more specific and colorful anecdotes, Wickersham charged William Mahoney, the Democratic commissioner for the Ketchikan recording district, with personally rounding up the sex workers in town—”sporting gals” in the parlance of the day—and escorting them to the polls. The ladies had presumably been financially coerced into gracing the polls with their presence and political preferences. And there were plenty of such women to influence. Ketchikan then possessed an earned reputation as the “Wickedest Town in the West.”
Given the position in dispute, the detailed accusations and accompanying testimonies are preserved within the Congressional Record and other government documents. This includes Wickersham’s complaint of Mahoney “himself hauling a big, fat [Black] prostitute to the polls in his carriage,” words spoken aloud in Congress and separately published in 1920.
The most consequential argument revolved around where voters were required to vote. Alaskan law required voters to vote in their town of residence, where they were registered essentially. For example, Sulzer should have voted in Sulzer. In reality, many settler towns of the era were ephemeral, and quite a few more remotely situated Alaskans voted within their division but not their precise precinct, as frequently permitted by election officials. Sulzer voted in Ketchikan and, therefore, his vote should technically have been disqualified.
By this point, Sulzer and Wickersham had dominated Alaska political news for years, and many observers were tired of the repetition. From the Seattle Post-Intelligencer: “It might be better for Alaska if both Mr. Sulzer and Mr. Wickersham should withdraw from politics and give their supporters a chance to start anew. There must be other men in Alaska as competent as they are, without their personal following and personal enemies.”
Sulzer had little opportunity to speak on the allegations. On April 15, 1919, he died while traveling on a steamship from Sulzer to Ketchikan. Because Wickersham had not yet proven his case, Sulzer was considered the official incumbent, and a special election was held on June 5 to choose his replacement. Wickersham refused to participate. As he saw it, the legitimate winner was still alive, and no successor was needed. Attorney General George Grigsby (1874-1962) instead carried the day and was formally seated that July. 
In his lengthy legal career, Grigsby earned his own crooked reputation, from his choice of defendants to his shady methods. As Alaska legal historian Pamela Cravez noted, “It wasn’t unusual for evidence to magically appear or disappear at one of Grigsby’s trials. Witness stories changed, and his final arguments were always entertaining if not always accurate.” 
The House of Representatives collectively dragged its feet on the issue, finally addressing the issue more than two years after the election. The Republican-slanted House then favored the Republican Wickersham. Returns from several isolated precincts, including Chicken and Cache Creek, each favoring Sulzer, were thrown out. Meanwhile, other questionable returns that favored Wickersham, such as soldiers voting in Fairbanks, were allowed to remain. These choices gave Wickersham a 37-vote win.
On March 1, 1921, the House voted 182 to 162 in favor of removing Grigsby and 177 to 162 in favor of seating Wickersham in his stead. The former judge surely enjoyed the rest of his term, the following two days. 
Grigsby believed Wickersham was primarily concerned about the paycheck. “This is nothing but an attempt to grab off salary and allowances of $21,000 for Wickersham on a technicality,” Grigsby told the Alaska Daily Empire. Wickersham indeed received all due payments for the entirety of the two-year term, not just his three days actually in office. After accounting for inflation, $21,000 in March 1921 is roughly $390,000 in 2026 dollars. This was politics as the pioneers played the game.

name: California
title: Californians are choosing 8 statewide leaders today. Only 1 of them gets Gavin Newsom’s office
description: Besides picking a new governor, California voters are electing an insurance commissioner, attorney general, superintendent, treasurer and controller.
text:
In summary
Besides picking a new governor, California voters are electing an insurance commissioner, attorney general, superintendent, treasurer and controller. 


With all the attention on who will succeed Gavin Newsom in the governor’s office — not to mention that little thing called Congress — it’s possible to forget that a lot of other people are vying for key statewide roles. 
But they’re important jobs that keep the state running: Who will serve as California’s top cop and prosecutor? Who will regulate the state’s struggling insurance market? Who will oversee elections, and make sure your vote gets counted?
We’re staying tuned. You should, too.
Attorney general
Rob Bonta, the current attorney general and a Democrat, is running against Republican Michael Gates for the role of the state’s top law enforcement officer. Bonta has held the job since 2021, during which time he has filed or joined dozens of lawsuits against the Trump administration. Gates, a former trial attorney, worked for the city of Huntington Beach for more than a decade. 
Superintendent of public instruction
Two school board presidents are going head to head in the race for state superintendent – a role with limited authority that nonetheless offers a big platform to reach millions of children in the state’s public schools. Sonja Shaw, a Republican who served on the Chino Valley Unified school board and has been an outspoken critic of protections for transgender students, is up against Richard Barrera, a Democrat who served on the San Diego Unified school board. Barrera is backed by the state’s largest teachers union, the California Teachers Association, and the California Charter Schools Association. 
Lieutenant governor
Two longtime public leaders are facing off for the role of lieutenant governor, a largely ceremonial job which acts as a stand-in when the governor is absent and can serve as a tiebreaker in the state Senate. Fiona Ma, a Democrat and the state’s treasurer since 2019, is facing Gloria Romero, a Republican who served nearly a dozen years in the state Legislature as a Democrat.
State controller
Malia Cohen, a Democrat who promises “transparency, efficiency and fairness,” is up for reelection as the state’s chief accountant. She faces a challenge from Herb Morgan, a Republican who founded an investment firm in San Diego and promises to expose waste and fraud in state government. 
Secretary of state
Election day is a good time to reflect on the importance of the secretary of state, whose office is responsible for ensuring votes are counted correctly, issues voter guides and certifies candidates and statewide ballot initiatives. The office also handles corporate business filings, maintains state archives and collects data about lobbying and campaign finances. The incumbent, Democrat Shirley Weber, has served since 2021. She faces Republican Donald Wagner, an Orange County supervisor, former mayor of Irvine and state assemblymember. 
Treasurer
A surprising duo is squaring off for the role of the state’s top banker: Eleni Kounalakis, a Democrat who has served two terms as the state’s lieutenant governor, is running against Jennifer Hawks, a Republican Silicon Valley retiree who has not served in elected office. The treasurer manages unspent taxpayer dollars and handles state borrowing and debts.
Insurance commissioner
In one of the state’s most heavily contested races, voters are choosing between two Democrats to regulate the state’s struggling insurance market as wildfire risks grow and insurers pull away. Former San Francisco supervisor and consumer advocate Jane Kim is facing off against Ben Allen, a state senator from Los Angeles for this important role. 
Board of Equalization
Four districts are up for election in this five-member group, the nation’s only elected tax board. Among its jobs: hearing taxpayer appeals, advising county assessors and setting the taxable value of property owned by utilities and railroads.
For District 1, which covers much of inland California, Nelson Esparza, a Democratic Fresno city councilmember, is up against Shannon Grove, a Republican state senator and businesswoman.
For District 2, covering coastal California north of Los Angeles, incumbent Democrat Sally Lieber is facing a challenge from John Pimentel, a Democrat and member of the San Mateo County Community College District Board of Trustees. 
For District 3, representing the Los Angeles area, Democratic state Assemblymember Mike Gipson is running against Samuel Sukaton, a Democratic labor union organizer.
For District 4, representing the San Diego area, Republican Denis Bilodeau, a taxpayer association president and Orange city councilmember, is facing off with Tom Umberg, a Democratic state senator.

name: California
title: 14 propositions are on the California ballot. Voters are deciding on taxes, healthcare and more
description: California's 14 s ballot measures include a billionaire tax, voter ID, changes to recall elections, and a bid to speed up building by limiting environmental reviews.
text:
In summary
California’s 14 s ballot measures include a billionaire tax, voter ID, changes to recall elections, and a bid to speed up building by limiting environmental reviews.


Voters are deciding the fate of 14 statewide propositions, including the contentious billionaire tax. The campaigns for and against these propositions have spent a total of nearly $1 billion — the most in history on state ballot measures. 
Beyond the billionaire tax, Californians are facing decisions on a wide range of topics, including how recall elections are conducted, speeding development by capping environmental reviews, and whether the state should put more money toward housing and medical research.
This story will be updated as election results come in.
Prop. 1: This measure would authorize the state to borrow up to $11.25 billion toward housing construction and renovations, mostly for rental units. Many developers and local governments that receive the money would have to reserve a portion of it for affordable housing for low-income renters or for specialized housing that serves the homeless. 
Prop. 2: Voters are deciding whether to allow the state to deposit more money into its reserves, otherwise known as the rainy day fund. California has a fairly volatile tax system that rises and falls with the incomes of its highest earners, but 1970s-era state rules limit how much money the state can save in surplus years.
Prop. 3: This income tax for high earners would send more money to K-12 education. First passed in 2012 as a temporary measure, this tax, which affects individuals making over $360,000 a year, would become permanent if voters approve Prop. 3. 
Prop. 4: This measure would allow the state and local governments to create public financing for political campaigns, which proponents say could help cap political spending. In order to accept public money for campaigns, candidates usually have to accept certain spending limits.
Prop. 5: California’s recall elections ask voters whether they want to oust the officeholder and who they want instead. This measure would make it so that recall elections only ask whether voters want to remove the elected official from office. A second election would determine who should replace the officeholder. 
Prop. 37: The state would create a new fund that gives out loans to middle-class homebuyers if Prop. 37 passes. Homebuyers who benefit from the fund would slowly pay back the state. 
Prop. 38: This measure would pump $8.4 billion in state funding to immunology research — with a catch: About half the money would go to one, three-person nonprofit organization, the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy. Gary K. Michelson, the institute’s co-founder, put this proposition on the ballot.
Prop. 39: This ballot proposition would increase identification requirements for California voters. This campaign, funded in large part by Illinois billionaire Richard Uihlein, would require state voters to provide proof of citizenship at the polls or write their Social Security number or other government-issued ID number on mail-in ballots. 
Prop. 40: The contentious billionaire tax would enact a one-time 5% tax on billionaires’ net worth. The healthcare workers union that put the measure on the ballot says it would raise roughly $100 billion over five years and help struggling healthcare programs. Opponents point out that billionaires pay a large share of state taxes already and worry it could cause them to flee the state.
Prop. 41: Created by the opponents to the billionaire tax, this measure would invalidate Prop. 40 by creating stricter rules about new California taxes. If both Prop. 40 and Prop. 41 pass, whichever gets more votes will prevail.
Prop. 42: Also created by the opponents to the billionaire tax, Prop. 42 would make it harder for the state to levy a new tax on wealth, such as investment accounts or personal property, and effectively invalidate the billionaire tax. If voters approve both Prop. 40 and Prop. 42, the measure with the most votes will win. 
Prop. 43: This measure would make it harder for local citizen-driven tax measures to pass. These local tax measures only need a majority to win, but if Prop. 43 passes, they would need two-thirds of the vote. 
Prop. 44: Health clinics would need to spend at least 90% of their annual revenue on patient care if Prop. 44 passes. The measure is backed by the same union that proposed the billionaire tax, Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West. 
Prop. 45: Voters will decide whether to pare down California’s landmark environmental review law, known as CEQA. The 1970 law requires agencies to consider environmental harm before building, but developers say the law is often a tool to delay much-needed affordable housing and infrastructure projects.

title: What voters are saying at the polls on Election Day 2026
authors: J. Patrick Coolican, Atra Mohamed, Max Nesterak

text:
People vote inside a polling place at the 40th Street Park Recreation Center in Minneapolis, Minnesota on Election Day, Tuesday, November 03, 2026. (Photo by Steven Garcia/Minnesota Reformer)This article will be updated throughout the day with additional voter interviews.
A lot has happened these past two years.
This is the first election since the start of President Donald Trump’s war in Iran and the inflation that it’s fueled.
Every week seems to bring a new story about the defrauding of the state’s social safety net programs.
The Trump administration sent 3,000 masked agents here for Operation Metro Surge, which left two American citizens dead and thousands more cowering in their homes.
And state Rep. Melissa Hortman was murdered in a politically motivated assassination.
Now, after one of the most expensive and negative campaign cycles in state history, the voters get to have their say. We sent reporters out across the metro and beyond to talk to them on Election Day.
After Trump targeted them, Minneapolis voters fight back
Faduma Abdi, 40, a mother of three who lives in the Cedar-Riverside neighborhood and works at a nursing home, said she previously voted to fulfill her civic duty, but today she voted to fight back against Trump by voting for every Democratic candidate on the ballot.
“Trump targeted us, and now we have the opportunity to fight back. He called us ‘garbage.’ And that’s not acceptable,” Abdi said.
She liked some of his promises in 2024 to improve the economy, create jobs and promote family values (though she didn’t vote for him). But that was all a lie, Abdi said. 
Naima Jama, a 35-year-old mother of three who recently started working in home care, said she voted for every Democratic candidate on the ballot, including Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan for U.S. Senate, U.S. Rep. Ilhan Omar and Attorney General Keith Ellison.
Jama, who lives in the Cedar-Riverside neighborhood, also cited Trump’s repeated attacks on the Somali community — including sending ICE agents to terrorize the community — as her rationale for voting for Democrats. 
She said the president promised to improve the economy and go after the criminals, but U.S. citizens were detained and immigrant businesses shut down.
She also pointed to the economy as a reason for her straight-ticket protest vote against Trump. She said she lost her job seven months ago and couldn’t find a new one until a few weeks ago. 
“I have never been without a job, even during the Great Recession, but under Trump, who promised the American people economic prosperity, my children went to bed hungry.”
Republican voters in Cottage Grove cite fraud, crime
Retired federal employee and Air Force veteran Larry Dean, 64, voted against the incumbents on his ballot. 
“Because this place is a mess,” Dean said outside his voting place in Cottage Grove. “Everything from world-class fraud that’s never been seen before to immigration stuff that should have never been allowed to happen, and crime. The whole state is wrecked.” 
On the national level, he said America is a “work in progress.” He said the DOGE cuts that decimated the federal workforce worked out well for him, calling it “a gift.” He was put on administrative leave when he already planned to retire. 
“So I got paid for what I was going to do anyways,” Dean said. 
His pension checks also came in without delay, though he built up savings in case they didn’t start arriving for several months. 
Dean said he is worried about the integrity of this election, even though he trusts his own precinct. His concern is over the widespread availability of absentee ballots, which he believes should only be available for people who aren’t able to vote in person. 
“It’s cheatable and that cheating happens in the city,” Dean said. 
People bring their “I voted” stickers to the memorial for Alex Pretti during the midterm election in south Minneapolis Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026. Pretti was shot and killed by federal agents in January.(Photo by Nicole Neri/Minnesota Reformer)
Anna Kessler, 37, voted for all Republicans, saying Democrats have gone too far left on social issues such as abortion, immigration and LGBT topics. 
“We’re doing a lot of LGBT and things that have nothing to do with education,” Kessler said. “In our schools, we’re all about safe spaces rather than this should be a safe space for everybody to learn and grow as individuals. But we’re nitpicking certain things.” 
She voted for Republican Senate candidate Michele Tafoya even though she calls herself a “pro-choice Republican” and supports abortion rights up to 12 weeks in certain circumstances. 
“It certainly seems much more humane to be in that stance rather than say, ‘Hey, the baby’s born. Do not intervene. Do not engage.’ — is what we have been doing in this state.” 
Lance Dawson, 68, split his ticket at his precinct in Cottage Grove. For attorney general, he voted for Republican Ron Schutz over Attorney General Keith Ellison, whom he doesn’t believe did enough to combat fraud in state social service programs. 
On the other big races, he broke for Democrats and voted for Sen. Amy Klobuchar for governor, Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan for Senate and Matt Little for U.S. House. He said he wants Flanagan and Little in Congress to serve as a check on Trump. 
“(Trump) is full of pride and views everything through his own lens. He doesn’t feel the pain of the people,” said Dawson, a retired retail manager. 
He pointed to Trump’s news conference on Monday in which he fixated on the reflecting pool in Washington while his party braces for significant midterm losses from voters outraged over inflation. 
“The criticism of (former President Joe) Biden was he was old. Are we not going through that again?” Dawson said. “There needs to be an age limit or a psychological examination before running for president.”
