name: Michigan Advance
title: National and state labor leaders rally in Detroit for Democratic candidates
description: DETROIT — National AFL-CIO President Liz Shuler joined state labor leaders at a Detroit union hall Tuesday morning to rally for Democrats in the final stretch of a midterm election that has drawn national and international scrutiny. Schuler spoke alongside Democratic Attorney General nominee Eli Savit, renowned civil rights activist Charles Mauldin and other[...]
text:
AFL-CIO President Liz Shuler addresses supporters at the UNITE HERE Local 24’s Detroit office on Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo by Minnah Arshad/Michigan Advance)DETROIT — National AFL-CIO President Liz Shuler joined state labor leaders at a Detroit union hall Tuesday morning to rally for Democrats in the final stretch of a midterm election that has drawn national and international scrutiny.
Schuler spoke alongside Democratic Attorney General nominee Eli Savit, renowned civil rights activist Charles Mauldin and others at a canvass launch at UNITE HERE Local 24’s office, a hospitality workers’ union that is a part of AFL-CIO, the largest federation of labor unions in the nation.
“I don’t know about y’all, but I’m sick of the TV ads. Every state I’ve been to, it’s nothing but division. It’s nothing but toxicity and attacks, and you know why they’re doing that,” Shuler said to a packed room of mostly Black supporters donning Unite Here! shirts. “They know if the working class comes together and unites around these issues, that they’re toast.”
Schuler said the labor community has a unique ability to cut through the noise of the political ads that have inundated Michigan’s airwaves.
“We open people’s ears in a way that no one else does,” she said.
Democratic attorney general nominee Eli Savit addresses supporters at the UNITE HERE Local 24’s Detroit office on Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo by Minnah Arshad/Michigan Advance)
Shuler’s presence in Detroit reflects the high stakes of the election, and of turnout in the Black-majority city. In the U.S. Senate election, Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed and Republican nominee Mike Rogers have battled to win over the city’s residents. Black voters, a strong Democratic voting bloc, make up about 14% of the state’s population, and the party will likely need strong turnout among people of color to win.
Antonio George, the Michigan political director of Unite Here Local 24, told Michigan Advance that the surprise endorsement by Democratic U.S. Rep. Haley Stevens’ of Rogers on Sunday was a “real big hit in the gut, especially for working people, especially for this union specifically.” 
Unite Here Local 24 had endorsed Stevens in the primary, then rallied behind El-Sayed in the general election.
“For [Stevens] to cross lines like that, you tell the unions, you’re telling the Detroit residents, we don’t matter,” George said. 
He said union members were angry and surprised by her announcement on Sunday, and her appearance with the Trump-endorsed candidate at a predominantly Black church in Detroit was especially offensive. 
Civil rights leader Charles Mauldin addresses supporters at the UNITE HERE Local 24’s Detroit office on Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo by Minnah Arshad/Michigan Advance)
For the general election, George said Unite Here has knocked 150,000 doors for El-Sayed and he plans to continue canvassing before the polls close Tuesday.
Mauldin, who was a student leader in the Selma, Alabama, civil rights protests in the 1960s, began his address at the canvas launch by leading a rendition of Woke Up this Morning With My Mind Stayed on Jesus. 
In a “Black Voters for Abdul” t-shirt, Mauldin said he’s spent the last 10 days traveling across the state to rally for Democrats.
“I don’t have an office to run for but I’m here to run for you. I’m a foot soldier,” he said. “A foot soldier is a person who does a lot of work, but doesn’t need a lot of credit.”
AFL-CIO President Liz Shuler and Democratic attorney General nominee Eli Savit talk with supporters at the UNITE HERE Local 24’s Detroit office on Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo by Minnah Arshad/Michigan Advance)
Savit said in one of his final addresses since launching his campaign in May 2025 that the last few months have been marked by a “divisive, cynical attempt funded by Elon Musk and his allies” to pit communities against one another and to prove that people of different races, religions and backgrounds can’t stand together. 
“Well we’re gonna send them a goddamn message tonight,” Savit said.
Savit told the Advance after the event that he’s optimistic and excited about the Democratic Party’s chances Tuesday night.
“Labor and working people built the state, so there’s no better way to end our campaign to spend Election Day than with our friends in labor.”

text:
Duke Energy Florida's office located in St. Petersburg. (Photo via Duke Energy's website)The Florida Public Service Commission (PSC) on Tuesday rejected Duke Energy Florida’s proposal to pay data center costs, 5-0.
The agency found that the proposal did not demonstrate compliance with legislation passed earlier this year that requires large load customers to bear their full costs of service without shifting them to the taxpayers.
The announcement is not a surprise, as PSC staff recommended late last month that the panel deny Duke’s proposal for a large data center tariff.
“Today’s decision reinforces our commitment to upholding those protections as Florida’s energy needs continues to grow,” said PSC Chair Gabriella Passidomo Smith in a written statement. “We appreciate Duke Energy’s efforts to address the unique challenges associated with serving these large load customers and are confident the company can build on those efforts to develop a tariff that meets the Legislature’s requirements while supporting Florida’s continued growth.”
The Florida Legislature passed and Gov. Ron DeSantis signed legislation earlier this year (SB 484) establishing requirements for electric public service utilities serving large load customers, such as hyperscale data centers. Utilities must “reasonably ensure” large load customers bear the full cost of their electric service and that neither those costs, nor risk of nonpayment, are shifted to the general body of ratepayers.
Duke’s proposal, originally filed in a petition to the PSC, was the first test of whether the law protects ratepayers. In hearings before the PSC in September, Duke declined to make public the full costs for residential and small business ratepayers.
“Duke Energy Florida appreciates the Florida Public Service Commission’s careful review,” said Duke spokesperson Ana Gibbs. “We remain focused on getting this right for Florida by supporting economic growth and new jobs while protecting costs for customers and ensuring that data centers pay their full cost of service.”
Consumer advocates cheered the outcome.
“The only reason that utility regulators denied Duke’s plans to pass data center costs to families and small businesses is because of legislation preventing them from doing so,” said Brooke Ward, Florida state director for Food & Water Watch. “Otherwise, Florida ratepayers would be on the hook to subsidize the billionaire tech class looking to build data centers in our communities, at our expense. Today’s vote is a victory for affordability and testament to the importance of laws that put people above corporations.”
Data centers have been emerged a huge issue on the campaign trail nationally and in Florida this year.
Republican gubernatorial candidate Byron Donalds has received more than $6 million in direct donations and advertising support from data center boosters, as reported by Seeking Rents’ Jason Garcia.
A year ago he voted for the U.S. House’s version of the One Big Beautiful Bill, which includes a 10-year moratorium on enforcement of state or local regulations for “artificial intelligence models, artificial intelligence systems, or automated decision systems.” He has since said he no longer supports that provision but does support the power of local governments to decide whether they want data centers in their communities.
Democratic gubernatorial candidate David Jolly has said that, if elected, he would impose a one-year moratorium on construction of data centers. After visiting a part of Northern Virginia with the highest density of data centers in the country in September, he said a complete ban on data centers “should be on the table.”

(Photo by Ephraim Rodenbach, MTSU Seigenthaler News Service)
Tennesseans will elect a new governor on Tuesday and for the first time in state history, it’s almost certain to be a woman.
U.S. Sen. Marsha Blackburn, a veteran of state politics, is the Republican nominee and first-term Memphis City Councilmember Jerri Green is the Democratic one.
Beyond that history-making election, the eyes of many political-watchers across the country will be on Congressional District 9, the Memphis-based district that was redrawn during a hastily-called special legislative session in May after the U.S. Supreme Court overturned key segments of the 1965 Voting Rights Act in Louisiana v. Callais. The race is a matchup between Democratic state Rep. Justin J. Pearson and Republican state Sen. Brent Taylor, both of Shelby County.
Republican lawmakers redrew the state’s congressional districts in an effort to ensure GOP representatives will be elected to all nine districts, but national Democrats have their sights set on holding the new District 9 and picking off Congressional District 5.
The Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee has invested in Democrat Chaz Molder’s race against Republican nominee Charlie Hatcher in District 5. Hatcher, a dairy farmer and former state agriculture commissioner, beat incumbent U.S. Rep. Andy Ogles in the August GOP primary. Molder is the two-term mayor of Columbia.
All congressional seats are on the ballot as well all 99 state House seats and 17 of Tennessee’s state Senate seats.

“His energy will be good:” Supporters of congressional candidate Chaz Molder volunteer in Spring Hill


By J. Holly McCall - Tuesday November 3, 2026 11:52 am





Betty Belle Nicks, a volunteer for 5th Congressional District candidate Chaz Molder, was holding a sign for the Democratic mayor of Columbia outside Spring Hill (Tennessee) Library on Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo by J. Holly McCall/Tennessee Lookout)
Outside the Spring Hill, Tennessee, library, Betty Belle Nicks held a sign touting Democratic Congressional candidate Chaz Molder, waving to drivers as they honked car horns. 
“His energy will be good for Congress,” said Nicks of Molder, a two-term Columbia mayor running in the recently-redrawn 5th District against former state agriculture commissioner Charlie Hatcher.
But supporting Molder is far from Nicks’s first political experience. 
Nicks hails from the Clement family, which has a decades long history of electoral politics and public service.
She’s named for her aunt, former state Sen. Anna Belle Clement O’Brien; her sister is state Sen. Sara Kyle of Memphis. 
Nicks’s uncle, Frank Clement, Sr., was a three-time Tennessee governor in the 1950s and 1960s. Her first cousin, Bob Clement, represented the 5th Congressional District from 1987 to 2002. 
Nicks shared a spot outside the library with other Molder supporters, Kim and Houston Jameson. 
Houston Jameson, a retired Maury County oncologist, said his family lived down the block from Molder’s family and he shared memories of the politician’s childhood. 
“He came to our son’s 3rd birthday party dressed as a Power Ranger,” Jameson said. 
Molder launched his campaign for the 5th District in September 2025, under a congressional map redrawn by the Republican legislature in 2022. That redistricting divided the district, which had included all of Davidson County, into three parts. 
The May redistricting came after a U.S. Supreme Court ruling in Louisiana v. Callais dealt a serious blow to the Voting Rights Act of 1965. Tennessee Republicans drew the new districts in an effort to give their party an advantage in the sole Democratic-held district, the Memphis-based 9th Congressional District. 
Hatcher defeated two-term incumbent U.S. Rep. Andy Ogles in the August Republican primary.









At a West Nashville poll, voters have concerns about affordability, healthcare, progressive agenda


By Anita Wadhwani -  11:41 am





Colette Moore, 86, said her vote this year was against a progressive agenda. “I don’t want the progressive party to take over this country,” said Moore, a Republican, as she stood  outside a polling place at Harpeth Valley Elementary School in Nashville. Moore said she hoped the president could finish out his term without hindrance from progressives in power. 
Voting inside the school, located in the Bellevue suburb, has been “pretty low key” with “steady turnout,” said Heidi Dixner, a poll supervisor. 
Among the voters streaming out of the schools was Rachel Talley. Talley said the issues she was most concerned about in Tuesday’s election were corruption, affordability and healthcare. Talley declined to specify her party or whom she voted for. 
Sanae Barber said she was “very concerned about homelessness, all the growth in Nashville and what it means for long term residents.”  Barber declined to say who she voted for.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Entergy argues data centers are net positive for Mississippi electric customers
description: Amazon data center facility in Canton, Thursday, Oct. 22, 2026.
text:
Mississippi Today Ideas is a platform for thoughtful ideas to be shared about our state’s past, present and future. Opinions expressed in guest essays are the author’s own and do not necessarily represent those of Mississippi Today. You can read more about the section here. 

In May 2025, we projected that data centers would drive residential electricity rates in Entergy Mississippi’s service territory 16% lower in 2030 than they would have been without data center growth. We are well on track to achieve that result.
This summer, the Mississippi Public Service Commission approved a rate plan that keeps Entergy Mississippi’s rates well below the national average and prevented what otherwise would have been a $4.87 per month increase per 1,000 kilowatt hours in July, compared to June rates. New revenues from Mississippi data centers, like Amazon’s, are a primary reason why rates didn’t go up. The Public Service Commission also approved a 41-cent rate decrease per 1,000 kilowatt hours that appeared on customer bills in October. Data center revenues also produced this decrease.
Gov. Tate Reeves signs an Amazon beam during an announcement about an Amazon data center planned for Ridgeland on Thursday, April 9, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
How did these benefits start coming to customers so quickly? It is because Mississippi took the right approach.
In 2024, the Mississippi Legislature came together in a special session and passed Senate Bill 2001 with near-unanimous support. Gov. Tate Reeves signed it, positioning the state to compete for large-scale technology investment. What made it work was the question legislators asked from the start: How do we protect existing utility customers while attracting investment? 
The answer was in the details. The contracts require data centers to pay their fair share, plus provide additional benefits for all customers. At Entergy Mississippi, each data center customer pays a minimum charge that covers the costs to serve it, and every service agreement is individually priced to reflect actual infrastructure needs, whether that’s $100 million or several billion dollars.
The results have come quickly. In two years, Amazon has announced four separate data center campuses and $25 billion in total Mississippi investment. Across most of Entergy’s service territory – including Mississippi, Arkansas and Louisiana where big tech companies are locating – data center agreements are projected to deliver $7 billion in savings to 2.3 million customers over 20 years thanks to our Fair Share Plus pledge.
Public service commissioners in all three states have validated those numbers. In Mississippi specifically, new data center revenues are funding $300 million in grid reliability investments through the Superpower Mississippi plan, with no additional cost to existing customers for those upgrades.
This growth is producing grid reliability improvements, construction jobs and long-term tax revenue. At the same time, electric rates will be lower than they otherwise would have been. 
Other states are still wrestling with how to bring data centers and their economic benefits without creating unintended consequences that have a negative impact on residents. Some have designed tariffs so restrictive they’ve driven data center customers away. Others haven’t designed adequate protections at all.
Mississippi found a path that welcomes data center benefits for Mississippians and protects existing customers. This path was created within the existing regulatory framework, in two years, with validated results, and has become the template for how all future Entergy contracts with data centers will be structured.
Mississippi’s data center story is different. That $5 monthly benefit is only the beginning of how data centers will help keep Entergy Mississippi’s rates low and protect customers.   
Mississippi got this right. The numbers are confirming it.

Jeremy Vanderloo serves as Entergy Mississippi’s vice president of business operations and strategy, leading the company’s overall strategy to drive growth and enhance operations. Prior to his current position, he led Entergy Mississippi’s regulatory affairs and interactions with the Mississippi Public Service Commission. A U.S. Naval Academy graduate and Marine Corp veteran, Vanderloo also earned a Juris Doctor and MBA from Mississippi College and practiced electric utility regulatory and employee benefits law before joining Entergy.

title: ‘Just be kind’: Kansas Gov. Laura Kelly offers job advice to potential successors
description: LAWRENCE — Outgoing Gov. Laura Kelly recommends her successor — Republican or Democrat — assemble a cabinet composed of subject matter experts rather than political ideologues and not forget to be kind in the heat of battle inside the Capitol. Kelly, who ends her two-term run as Kansas governor on Jan. 11, said it would […]
text:
Gov. Laura Kelly, on the cusp of completing her second term as Kansas governor, answers a question on her job advice to the next governor during the Oct. 29, 2026, Kansas Economic Policy Conference at the University of Kansas. (Photo by Tim Carpenter/Kansas Reflector)LAWRENCE — Outgoing Gov. Laura Kelly recommends her successor — Republican or Democrat — assemble a cabinet composed of subject matter experts rather than political ideologues and not forget to be kind in the heat of battle inside the Capitol.
Kelly, who ends her two-term run as Kansas governor on Jan. 11, said it would be a mistake to assume the job of governor was easy. She said the buck stopped at the governor’s desk for many issues before state government.
“I will give them no unsolicited advice. I think every outgoing governor ought to feel the same way,” Kelly said during the question-and-answer portion of the Kansas Economic Policy Conference last week at the University of Kansas. “But, if asked, I think the one thing I would tell governors is the most important thing you can do is build a qualified team. You need people in those positions who really know what they’re doing and know how to manage, but also who are visionary and have at least some political radar.”
She said day-to-day responsibilities of a governor and the broad sweep of complex challenges landing in that person’s lap required maintenance of a collaborative working environment.
“You can’t do it all yourself. Each agency is unique, and a lot of work. Most of them are very high maintenance,” Kelly said.
This Election Day, until polls close at 7 p.m. Tuesday, voters of Kansas can make themselves heard in terms of congressional races and contests for state executive branch offices, the Kansas Legislature and judicial positions. Ballots included a proposed amendment to the Kansas Constitution affirming only U.S. citizens had the right to vote. On the municipal front, ballots contained an array of local topics.
Kansas voters bring to close debate about whether the governorship should be entrusted to Republican Ty Masterson of Andover or Democrat Cindy Holscher of Overland Park. Both are members of the Kansas Senate, and previously served in the Kansas House. They have long public policy records touching on all sorts of subjects, which helped remove some of the guesswork for voters.
Masterson was endorsed by President Donald Trump and was a point of emphasis during two rallies headlined by Trump and two by Vice President JD Vance. Holscher wasn’t Kelly’s first choice among Democrats, but the governor endorsed and campaigned for Holscher after she won the party’s nomination in August.
Kelly, who served the Topeka area in the Kansas Senate for 15 years, was elected governor in 2018 and reelected in 2022. As governor-elect in December 2017, Kelly said she anticipated difficulty convincing experienced state workers to return after fleeing their jobs during the administration of Republican Gov. Sam Brownback. At that point, Kelly said, Kansas was struggling financially.
“I needed the very best,” she said. “I was pleasantly surprised, when I won, the number of really qualified people who came out of the woodwork. People came back into public service, left really high-paying jobs. It’s a calling in some ways. It’s an addiction in other ways.”
She said her process of filling positions in the executive branch wasn’t about what political party an applicant belonged to, how much money an individual donated to her campaign or whether that person was a friend or the ally of a friend.
“We didn’t take into consideration any of that,” the governor said. “We’ve gotten through … scandal-free. You think back to … where somebody’s in a position, not qualified for it, and they screw it up really badly. They do either wrong things or bad things, and that really reflects on the governor. The buck does stop here.”
Kelly said she would recommend the next Kansas governor not amplify political polarization that had become “so ugly and nasty.”
“I would just ask them as they’re working on the budget, as they’re negotiating with the Legislature on a bill, to be kind,” she said. “Whatever you’re doing is going to impact people in their real lives. Just be kind.”

name: Colorado Newsline
title: Commentary: The government must not be required to fund discrimination
description: The U.S. Supreme Court today heard a Colorado case that could walk back what legal precedent has established for years. In 2020, Colorado voters overwhelmingly approved a tax-funded universal preschool program. The Legislature passed a law to implement the program, including basic requirements such as a minimum number of instructional hours, maximum educator[...]
text:
Christ the King Chapel, at the Archdiocese of Denver campus, is pictured in 2021. (Photo by Faith Miller/Colorado Newsline)The U.S. Supreme Court today heard a Colorado case that could walk back what legal precedent has established for years.
In 2020, Colorado voters overwhelmingly approved a tax-funded universal preschool program. The Legislature passed a law to implement the program, including basic requirements such as a minimum number of instructional hours, maximum educator-to-child ratios, qualification standards for teachers and other best practices.
The statehouse also required preschool providers to give children an “equal opportunity to enroll and receive preschool services regardless of race, ethnicity, religious affiliation, sexual orientation, gender identity, lack of housing, income level, or disability” of both the child and their family. This seems perfectly in line with a universal program, as universal typically means all — without exception.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
However, some religious preschools, including St. Mary’s Catholic Parish, refused to agree to this nondiscrimination requirement and sued Colorado to be let into the program anyway, arguing that Colorado was discriminating against their religious beliefs by requiring them to admit LGBTQ+ children or children with LGBTQ+ families to get funding. Apparently, to them, “universal” should allow exceptions.
If it seems backward to suggest that states can’t condition funds on reasonable requirements, that’s because it is. In fact, most government-funded programs include conditions that must be met before funding is available. Nondiscrimination requirements have been mandated to receive funding for decades. For example, in 1981, the Maternal and Child Health Services Block Grant was amended to require funded programs to comply with the Age Discrimination Act, the Americans with Disabilities Act and the Civil Rights Act’s nondiscrimination requirements. Even school voucher programs typically require participating private schools to comply with nondiscrimination requirements.
Even more backward is the suggestion that states must fund private entities even when those entities openly state their intention to discriminate, just because the discrimination is based on a religious belief. Governments cannot be in the business of funding discrimination. To require Colorado taxpayers to fund preschools that openly intend to discriminate against LGBTQ+ people because of a religious belief opens the door to state funding for other types of discrimination based on claimed religious beliefs. Any attempt at defining what counts as a religious belief would require deciding that some beliefs don’t count as religious. Preventing the government from making that choice is exactly what the First Amendment was intended to do.
It was not so long ago that religious beliefs were used to justify slavery and later segregation. It was barely a generation ago, in 1983, that Bob Jones University argued that it was an unconstitutional limitation on its free exercise of religion to have its tax-exempt status revoked because of its religious beliefs prohibiting interracial dating and marriage. There, the Supreme Court decidedly declared that prohibiting discrimination was an overriding governmental interest that justified limitations on religious liberty. It said that racial discrimination in education violated a fundamental national public policy and that “not all burdens on religion are unconstitutional.”
Requiring preschools to admit students without regard to their identities or the identities of their parents to receive government funding — taxpayers’ money — should be a settled issue. Just as those at St. Mary’s can quote the Bible to justify discriminating against LGBTQ+ people today, so too did those at Bob Jones University quote the Bible to justify their racially discriminatory admission policy.
If schools want government benefits, they have to play by the government’s rules. Colorado says universal means all preschoolers. Colorado taxpayers voted to fund every preschooler. The Supreme Court must not reverse decades of law that has established where the line between religious liberty and illegal discrimination stands.

title: CommonWealth Beacon Election Day insights
description: 12:30 pm · Jennifer Smith, senior reporter Two efforts to roll back existing laws look like they are in serious trouble at the booth. Question 8 would dismantle the state’s […]
text:
12:30 pm · Jennifer Smith, senior reporter 
Two efforts to roll back existing laws look like they are in serious trouble at the booth. Question 8 would dismantle the state’s recreational cannabis industry and Question 9 would repeal a recently passed firearms law.  
The bid to undo the recreational cannabis law approved by ballot measure just 10 years ago is now the most expensive question of the cycle, with almost all of the money behind the effort coming from SAM Action Inc., a Virginia-based nonprofit that exists primarily to oppose the recreational marijuana industry. Polling heading into Election Day found residents deeply skeptical about the measure, with support stuck in the low 30s at best.  
Nor do they seem eager to toss the sweeping 2024 firearms law, which expanded restrictions on who can carry what firearms, and where. This is a repeal referendum, which means a “no” vote repeals the law, and polled support for the repeal has been hovering around the same level as undoing the recreational cannabis system: 31 percent or lower. 
11:45 am · Jennifer Smith, senior reporter
The ballot question that looks most likely to become law (with all the caveats that nothing is over until it’s over) is Question 1, which would make the Legislature and governor’s office subject to public records law. Polling throughout the fall found a healthy majority (between 63 and 84 percent depending on the poll) of respondents expected to vote yes. 
It is widely regarded as the heir to State Auditor Diana DiZoglio’s ballot measure last cycle that explicitly authorized her to audit the Legislature, and is one of two measures where lawmakers have potential legislation queued up that could undercut it if the question passes.
11:30 am · Jennifer Smith, senior reporter
With Election Day underway, it’s direct democracy pulling the most focus here in the Bay State. Voters are deciding the fate of nine ballot questions on policy areas ranging from an obscure tax cap law, to public records access, to zoning reform, to conservation funding. 
If you’re still cramming for the ballot box test, we have you covered with a guide to all nine questions.

title: Voters head to the polls across Kentucky
description: Polls at 6 a.m. opened to a beautiful fall day in Kentucky, as voters made their way to precincts around the state. Voters will decide who is going to replace U.S. Sen. Mitch McConnell, as well as all six Congressional districts. One of those, the heavily contested 6th District will be heavily watched by politicos […]
text:
The Hill polling place in Lexington combines several voting precincts. Workers there said there were no lines, but a steady stream of voters passed through all morning. (Kentucky Lantern photo by Linda Blackford)Polls at 6 a.m. opened to a beautiful fall day in Kentucky, as voters made their way to precincts around the state.
Voters will decide who is going to replace U.S. Sen. Mitch McConnell, as well as all six Congressional districts. One of those, the heavily contested 6th District will be heavily watched by politicos because Kentucky’s polls close at 6 p.m., which make it, along with Indiana, the earliest in the nation.
Voters will also be deciding on a constitutional amendment that would curb the governor’s pardon power before and after elections, an answer to the hugely controversial pardons made by former Gov. Matt Bevin shortly before he left office.
Also, every seat in the state House of Representatives is up, as well as several state Senate seats here.
Early voting was up about 30% from the last midterm election in 2022.
Political experts will also be watching to see what kind of night it will be for Gov. Andy Beshear, who is also head of the Democratic Governors Association. He put financial and personal campaign support behind Zach Dembo, the Democratic candidate in the 6th District, and a host of Democratic gubernatorial candidates. All those results will be parsed in light of Beshear’s gubernatorial ambitions.
A steady stream of voters entered Morton Middle School in Lexington, Ky. on Election Day. (Kentucky Lantern photo by Linda Blackford)
Attorney General Russell Coleman is monitoring the election from his Election Integrity Command Center; federal election monitors are also expected to be on hand in Lexington and Louisville.
Coleman said that just before 11 a.m. there had been 82 complaints to the election fraud hotline, ranging from legal questions to electioneering. Voters who suspect election law violations can call the Election Fraud Hotline at (800) 328-VOTE or make a report online.
Stay tuned at www.kentuckylantern.com for all the latest news and results.

name: Rhode Island Current
title: No drama, lots of voters as Election Day kicks off in Rhode Island
description: A brisk start to Election Day in Rhode Island puts the state on track to top turnout in the 2022 midterms, and potentially, 2018, too, said Miguel Nunez, executive director for the state Board of Elections. Nunez’ projection came during the elections panel’s mid-morning meeting Tuesday, which was scheduled to address potential Election Day problems. […]
text:
Helena Buonanno Foulkes, holding her granddaughter Georgia, 10 months, enters the Salvation Army polling site on Pitman Street in Providence to cast her ballot on Tuesday morning, Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo by Michael Salerno/Rhode Island Current)A brisk start to Election Day in Rhode Island puts the state on track to top turnout in the 2022 midterms, and potentially, 2018, too, said Miguel Nunez, executive director for the state Board of Elections.
Nunez’ projection came during the elections panel’s mid-morning meeting Tuesday, which was scheduled to address potential Election Day problems. But as of 10 a.m., voting across the 414 statewide polling locations had gone smoothly, Nunez told the elections board.
More than 39,000 voters had cast ballots in the first three hours since polls opened, which, combined with early and mail ballots brought the total to 168,711 — 21% turnout, Nunez said.
Orchard Farms Elementary School in Cranston was the busiest polling place Tuesday morning, while the East Providence Senior Center had the fewest voters: just three people showed up by 10 a.m., Nunez said.
In 2022, voter turnout topped 43%. Four years earlier, in 2018, 48% of registered voters cast ballots.
The state’s Sept. 9 primary also saw record turnout, driven by a surge in younger voters and high-profile races including for Providence mayor and Rhode Island governor. Fewer state and local races are considered competitive in the general election, with many primary victors now running unopposed.
The contest between Democratic Lt. Gov. Sabina Matos and her Republican challenger, John Loughlin, appears the closest based on public polling.
John Loughlin, Republican candidate for lieutenant governor, at an Election Day campaign stop at Toll Gate High School in Warwick on Tuesday morning, Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo by Michael Salerno/Rhode Island Current)
Persephone Allen, an educator, identified David Morales’ campaign for Providence mayor as one factor which drove her — and her child, in a baby carrier — to Parenti Villa in Providence’s Federal Hill neighborhood.
“I think that he’s thinking about the needs of people in Providence,” Allen said, “and I’m excited about how energized and present he is in the city, and also how he’s particularly thinking about the housing crisis.” 
Morales faces Republican challenger Dave Talan.
The titular governor’s race has garnered public attention, fueled in part by attack ads and campaign finance complaints related to the three main candidates. 
Independent gubernatorial candidate Ken Block has filed two complaints against  Democrat Helena Buonanno Foulkes, alleging that state party spending on digital ads and mailers for Foulkes exceeded the cap in state law. Meanwhile, Republican nominee Aaron Guckian faces a complaint from his primary opponent, Elaine Pelino, for failing to document the in-kind contributions from his private plane trip to Florida last month.
Matos has also submitted a complaint against Loughlin, contending that his campaign manager skimmed money off ad payments for his own benefit, a violation of the restrictions around the state matching funds program. Both Matos and Loughlin are participating in the matching funds program, which provides taxpayer-funded money to supplement private donations, as long as candidates agree to contribution and spending limits.
Chris Hunter, a spokesperson for the elections board, declined to comment on any of the campaign finance complaints, which remain private pending a potential investigation and evidence of wrongdoing. The elections panel also did not discuss the complaints during the morning meeting.
Hunter confirmed there were no staffing shortages at the polls Tuesday, a problem which led to seven polling sites in Providence opening late during the primary. Following the mass callouts and no-shows of 100 poll workers on Sept. 9, city and state election administrators put special emphasis on finding enough people to commit to the paid day job for Election Day.
Voters enter Parenti Villa at 25 Tobey St. in Providence to cast their ballots in the general election on Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo by Alexander Castro/Rhode Island Current)
At Parenti Villa, poll workers Fran Paranzino and Karen Hirsch described a robust but smooth start to the day. “Very busy,” Paranzino said of the morning’s turnout at the Tobey Street location. “I think we’ve gotten close to 300 folks already.”
“It’s just really great to see the community come out,” Paranzino added.
Hirsch said that roughly 700 people had voted at Parenti Villa during the primary.
The issues with poll workers calling out on Primary Day hadn’t transpired again, the two poll workers said, with Hirsch calling Tuesday’s operations “much smoother” so far.
“So far, we haven’t had any issues,” Paranzino said. “No one’s been reassigned. When the board of canvassers came around, they said everything looked great.” 
The number of poll workers across the state was not immediately available.
The elections board meets again at 6 p.m. to review Election Day voting, and address any new problems. Polls close at 8 p.m.

name: California
title: ¿Controlarán los demócratas el Congreso? Su camino pasa por California. No te pierdas estas contiendas
description: Estas son las elecciones más trascendentales a la Cámara de Representantes de Estados Unidos en el estado de California, que podrían determinar el control del Congreso, así como el futuro rumbo del Partido Demócrata.
text:
This article is also available in English. Read it here.
Los votantes de California desempeñarán un papel clave a la hora de determinar qué partido controlará la Cámara de Representantes de Estados Unidos, y por cuánto margen, al concluir el martes la votación para las elecciones de mitad de mandato de 2026.
 Los demócratas están a punto de arrebatar al menos tres escaños que actualmente ocupan los republicanos de California, después de que los votantes aprobaran la Proposición 50 el año pasado, que rediseñó cinco de los distritos de California para favorecer a los demócratas como contramedida a la manipulación electoral a favor de los republicanos en Texas.
 Los dos distritos restantes rediseñados —uno en el Valle Central y el otro en los condados de San Diego y Riverside— son más competitivos, a pesar de que los demócratas superan en número a los republicanos en el registro de votantes.
 En algunas contiendas electorales participan candidatos progresistas que buscan desbancar a los veteranos titulares, quienes, de tener éxito, podrían inclinar al partido hacia la izquierda.
 Se prevé que varias contiendas para el Congreso en California sean muy reñidas, ya que los condados están contabilizando las papeletas recibidas hasta siete días después del día de las elecciones.
 Esto es lo que CalMatters está observando: 
El Valle Central y el área de San Diego son lugares clave
 La contienda más reñida de California enfrenta al congresista republicano David Valadao, de Hanford, quien lleva 12 años en el cargo, es un ganadero lechero y blanco constante de los demócratas a nivel nacional, y al recién llegado a la política Randy Villegas, profesor de ciencias políticas.
 Los demócratas esperan que Villegas, quien cuenta con el respaldo del senador Bernie Sanders y la representante Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, pueda desafiar las convenciones políticas y ganar en el Valle Central, una región históricamente conservadora y con una fuerte presencia agrícola. Villegas apoya la cobertura médica universal y el cuidado infantil universal, aunque también ha propuesto suspender los impuestos federales sobre la gasolina y el diésel.
 Valadao, el único republicano que quedó de los que votaron a favor del juicio político contra el presidente Donald Trump tras los disturbios del 6 de enero de 2021, busca su séptimo mandato. Destaca la importancia del bipartidismo y el pensamiento independiente, pero ha enfrentado duros interrogatorios sobre su decisión de apoyar el megaproyecto de ley de Trump que, en última instancia, dejará sin cobertura médica a más de 2 millones de californianos en los próximos cuatro años.
 Más al sur, en los condados de San Diego y Riverside, dos funcionarios locales electos —Marni von Wilpert, concejala demócrata de la ciudad de San Diego, y Jim Desmond, supervisor republicano del condado de San Diego— compiten por ocupar el escaño del representante republicano Darrell Issa, quien optó por retirarse en lugar de buscar la reelección en un distrito rediseñado.
 Von Wilpert y Desmond están llevando a cabo campañas tradicionalmente centristas que recuerdan a la política anterior a Trump . Von Wilpert ha evitado a la izquierda progresista emergente y, en cambio, ha hecho campaña con la exvicepresidenta Kamala Harris. Desmond se ha esforzado por distanciarse de Trump y de la retórica MAGA del presidente, a pesar de haber recibido su respaldo.
 Las encuestas públicas han mostrado consistentemente una ligera ventaja de von Wilpert sobre Desmond, y el Cook Political Report, una publicación no partidista, cambió la calificación de la contienda de “indecisa” a “con tendencia demócrata” en marzo. Las encuestas internas de la campaña sugieren que la contienda está muy reñida. 
Los progresistas intentan reformar el Partido Demócrata
 En varias contiendas electorales de California participan dos demócratas debido al sistema de primarias del estado, en el que se eligen los dos candidatos más votados.
 Entre las contiendas más seguidas se encuentra la carrera para suceder a la expresidenta de la Cámara de Representantes, Nancy Pelosi , quien ha respaldado a Connie Chan, supervisora de San Francisco. Chan, inmigrante china de Taiwán, es conocida por oponerse al desarrollo urbano que podría desplazar a los inquilinos o alterar el carácter de un barrio. Se enfrenta al senador estatal Scott Wiener, un legislador prolífico que ha impulsado varias leyes para acelerar la construcción de viviendas y garantizar salarios competitivos en proyectos subsidiados por el estado.
 En el área de Sacramento, se libra una batalla intergeneracional entre la representante Doris Matsui, de 82 años, y la concejala de Sacramento, Mai Vang, de 41. Matsui cuenta con una enorme ventaja financiera y ha prestado a su campaña 4 millones de dólares desde las primarias. Vang, por su parte, goza de un gran impulso político como joven progresista emergente, con gran habilidad para desenvolverse en los medios y capaz de interactuar directamente con sus seguidores a través de TikTok e Instagram.
 En Los Ángeles, el congresista Jimmy Gomez, que busca la reelección, se enfrenta al desafío de la socialista demócrata Angela Gonzales-Torres. El congresista, que lleva cinco mandatos, ganó las primarias de junio por un amplio margen, pero ha perdido apoyo en medio de una investigación del Comité de Ética de la Cámara de Representantes sobre acusaciones de agresión sexual, las cuales él niega. Una encuesta reciente mostró a Gonzales-Torres con una ventaja del 51% frente al 45% de Gomez. 
Los resultados inesperados en los distritos que se rigen por la Propuesta 50 podrían poner en peligro a la mayoría
 Se prevé que tres legisladores republicanos en ejercicio o ex republicanos pierdan sus puestos a raíz de la Proposición 50.
 Tanto el representante Young Kim como el representante Ken Calvert, ambos contendientes por el distrito 40 de California, se quedarán sin trabajo. La manipulación de los distritos electorales transformó drásticamente el distrito 41 de Calvert, pero en lugar de retirarse, optó por desafiar a su colega Kim. Ambos se esforzaron por superar al otro en las primarias, pero Kim ha retomado desde entonces un enfoque más centrista y fiscalmente conservador.
 El representante James Gallagher, quien sucedió al fallecido representante Doug LaMalfa al frente del primer distrito congresional del norte rural del estado, está a punto de perder ante el expresidente pro tempore del Senado, Mike McGuire , demócrata. El distrito fue rediseñado para excluir varias zonas rurales y conservadoras cercanas a la frontera entre Oregón y California.
 El representante Kevin Kiley, quien abandonó el Partido Republicano a principios de este año, busca la reelección en el 6.º Distrito Congresional, en lugar de su antiguo 3.er Distrito, que fue modificado significativamente para favorecer a los demócratas. Se enfrenta al Dr. Richard Pan, médico y exsenador estatal que se postula como candidato contrario a la iniciativa “Make America Healthy Again” (Hagamos que Estados Unidos vuelva a estar sano). Kiley espera captar votos de republicanos, independientes y demócratas moderados.

Happy Election Day! If you’re looking for updates about voting and results, we’ve got you covered here all day and into this evening.
First up: In-person Election Day voting has begun. Amid worries of federal interference, Gov. Gavin Newsom has said 134 election law attorneys and 1,000 volunteer poll workers will be deployed to guard against voter intimidation and suppression. Another 54 people will be manning a hotline, run by the California Democratic Party, that voters can call to report suspicious activity at the polls: 1-877-321-VOTE.

Voter voices: Perry voters cite immigration, school vouchers as key issues


By Brooklyn Draisey - Tuesday November 3, 2026 10:15 am





The Mcreary Center serves as a voting location in Perry, Iowa on Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo by Brooklyn Draisey/Iowa Capital Dispatch)
Some Perry residents braved the rainy weather Tuesday morning to vote in the midterm state and federal elections before heading to work, including 62-year-old Paula Davidson.
Davidson, a Republican, said she didn’t want to share who specifically she voted for at First Christian Church as soon as the polling place opened “because it gets so ugly, how the Democrats are,” but confirmed she voted along party lines. Her peers also plan to vote, she said.
“We need to get the Republicans voted in here. The Republicans are quieter than the Democrats, so you don’t hear a lot of noise from the Republicans throughout the campaigns, but election day, the end of election day, it always proves it,” Davidson said. “So I’m hoping this is the same thing.”
Immigration was Davidson’s biggest concern heading into the voting booth, she said, as “Democrats don’t seem to care who’s here.” American citizens who commit crimes are monitored through parole and “we know the bad ones from the good ones,” Davidson said, but undocumented immigrants don’t have the same oversight.
“They could be doing anything, nobody knows who they are,” Davidson said. “It’s scary.”
Perry residents Rodney and Teresa Dowd voted in the midterm election on Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo by Brooklyn Draisey/Iowa Capital Dispatch)
Teresa and Rodney Dowd, who have lived in Perry for nearly 50 years, both identified themselves as independent voters who select whoever they believe is the best candidate, which Teresa said “is a mix” between political party affiliations.
The married couple voted Tuesday morning at the McCreary Center in Perry.
Rodney said he voted for Rob Sand in the gubernatorial race, as he supports the candidate’s stance on school voucher programs.
The pair are confident in the integrity of the voting system for the midterm elections, and that government agencies have “done their due diligence” in ensuring accurate voting counts,  Teresa said. Rodney said voting was how the U.S. — “the greatest country in the world” — was formed, and one where elections are free.
“If you don’t vote, you can’t complain,” Teresa Dowd said. “Maybe we like to complain.”

name: California
title: Prop. 38: This billionaire-backed measure would approve $8.4 billion for health research
description: Supporters say Prop. 38 is needed to ensure health research dollars keep flowing even as Trump tries to cut science. Opponents say the measure is poorly written, lacks transparency and seems to heavily benefit one particular nonprofit.
text:
In summary
Supporters say Prop. 38 is needed to ensure health research dollars keep flowing even as Trump tries to cut science. Opponents say the measure is poorly written, lacks transparency and seems to heavily benefit one particular nonprofit. 


Your November ballot includes billions of dollars in proposed bonds, including money for immunology research in an effort to find cures for Alzheimer’s, cancer, heart disease and other ailments.
Proposition 38 would provide $8.4 billion to California’s public and nonprofit health laboratories to find cures for the diseases affecting the immune system. Half the money would go to one unnamed research institute meeting specific requirements. 
Reporting by CalMatters found only one institute in California currently meets those criteria: the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy. The institute’s primary funder was billionaire Gary K. Michelson, who wrote Prop. 38 and was by far the largest donor to its political campaign.
The bond is expected to cost a total of $12 billion with interest — about $500 million to $600 million annually for some 20 years, according to the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office.
Like all bonds the state issues, borrowing over time means spending more on the project than paying for it upfront. But issuing bonds allows the state to continue spending on other services, from schools and student financial aid to consumer health subsidies and running prisons. 
Arguments for and against measure
The backers of Prop. 38 argue that as the Trump administration seeks to pull federal science funding from California and elsewhere, a California-only health research fund is essential.  
They say the bond spending would pay for itself, since Prop. 38 ensures that 10% of the revenue generated from research would go back to the state’s coffers. And cures funded with Prop. 38 money must be cheaper when sold to California residents — 20% less than the average national price.But opponents of Prop. 38 don’t believe drug companies or other firms could produce enough sales to actually make the measure neutral in cost to California. Revenue from research funded by the bond would need to exceed $120 billion after 20 years for California to recoup its investment.
“It is remarkably hard to do, and I don’t see any justification for the speculation that they’re going to bring in this much money to pay back the people of California,” said Jonathan Eisen, a biologist at UC Davis who has received several million dollars in ultra-competitive federal grants from the National Institutes of Health. He spoke at an October press conference hosted by the campaign opposing Prop. 38. 
California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy signed an affiliation agreement with UCLA in 2024, which promises UCLA 7.5% of the net revenue from any drugs or research created by the institute’s staff that go to market. Four senior UCLA officials sit on the institute’s board.
Additional reporting by CalMatters shows that the California institute had only three employees as of September — far fewer than the 51 staffers it planned to have hired by last year. It’s supposed to employ an additional 90 employees, including leading scientists, by next summer. The institute’s five-year business plan and budget show it was projected to spend more than $200 million on personnel and construction by mid-2026. A senior UCLA official in September said that the institute has spent closer to $20 million.
Opponents of Prop. 38 fault the measure for requiring half the money go to a single institute and limiting which other researchers can receive the other half. They say science research is best performed in a competitive environment that’s open to all of California’s nonprofit and public university scientists.Dr. Susan Bookheimer, a UCLA researcher on Alzheimer’s and autism who also spoke at the press conference, said other major science funding initiatives penalize applicants if they don’t possess the necessary staff and equipment when they submit applications. Bookheimer has secured more than $100 million in federal research grants from the National Institutes of Health. 
But Andrew Dale backs Prop. 38 for its emphasis on immunology research and cures. He is a cancer survivor whose lymphoma was treated with an immunotherapy about a decade ago.
“Patients right now are waiting on the same kind of breakthroughs that saved me, and any type of delays, it could cost them the time they just don’t have,” he said at a September press conference hosted by the Yes on 38 campaign.  
Gov. Gavin Newsom and the California Democratic Party endorsed Prop. 38. So has the state’s GOP as well as dozens of patient and research advocacy groups. The union of graduate students and post-doctoral researchers at the University of California, whose pay often relies on science research funding, has also endorsed the proposition. Backers of Prop. 38 outraised the no camp $72 million to $12,000 as of Oct. 26.
A poll last week indicated that 57% of likely voters backed Prop. 38, according to the Public Policy Institute of California. 
Voters will have an opportunity to decide on another large science bond measure in March 2028. That election is slated to include a proposition approved this summer by the Legislature and Newsom that would sell $7.5 billion in bonds for a far wider array of science research, such as biomedical research, wildfire prevention and water supply.

name: California
title: Billions on the line for schools as voters decide Prop. 3 high-income tax
description: Proposition 3 would make permanent an income tax on the wealthy to fund K-12 schools and other services.
text:
In summary
Proposition 3 would make permanent an income tax on the wealthy to fund K-12 schools and other services. 


California schools, already grappling with declining enrollment and tight budgets, will dodge a steep revenue cut if voters approve Proposition 3.
Prop. 3, put forth by the state’s largest teachers union, would make permanent an income tax on the wealthy to fund K-12 schools and other services. Originally passed in 2012, the tax was renewed in 2016 and is slated to expire in 2031.
Since it first passed, the tax has generated between $5 billion and $15 billion a year, up to 15% of schools’ overall revenue. If the tax isn’t renewed, schools would lose that money beginning in 2031 and likely have to make deep budget cuts.
The California Teachers Association has made an aggressive push to pass the measure, spending nearly $60 million on advertising and sending members to knock on more than 200,000 doors around the state. Union president David Goldberg called the measure “vital” to protect schools and teachers’ jobs.
The tax applies to individuals who earn more than $371,000 a year or couples who earn more than $743,000. If Prop. 3 passes, those earners would continue paying an income tax rate of  12.3%, one of the highest rates in the country.
A bait-and-switch?
The state can’t indefinitely pile taxes on wealthy residents, opponents of Prop. 3 have said. Those residents, about 200 of whom might also face a one-time 5% tax if Prop. 40 passes, would only relocate to lower-tax states, leaving a big dent in state tax revenues.
Opponents also argue that the tax was intended to be a Band-Aid to get schools through the Great Recession, and making it permanent amounts to a bait-and-switch. Opponents also questioned whether the tax is still necessary, considering declining enrollment and increased government spending on schools the past few years. 
Once the tax is collected, the money flows into the state’s complex Prop. 98 school funding formula, which guarantees 40% of state revenues go to schools. Of that money, 89% goes to K-12 schools and 11% goes to community colleges. Any extra money generated by the tax goes toward a rainy day fund.
Rising costs, declining enrollment
California funds schools based on how many students show up for class each day, a number that’s been declining for about a decade as families leave for less expensive states, immigration declines and families have fewer children. 
At the same time, schools have faced skyrocketing insurance costs and expensive repairs on aging buildings, among other expenses. Although the state has boosted school funding the past few years, school administrators say the money hasn’t kept up with rising expenses.

text:
Photo from Monday's National Weather Service Melbourne Florida Facebook page.Some voters are calling on Gov. Ron DeSantis to extend the time to vote past tonight’s 7 p.m. deadline due to the flash flooding over Florida over past couple of days, which in some cases is making it difficult for voters to leave their homes.
Voters in seven counties were being directed to temporary polling locations in the face of widespread flooding that prompted the governor to issue an emergency order Monday allowing election officials to move voting sites ahead of Election Day.
Amy Keith, executive director of Common Cause Florida, said in a remote conference call Tuesday morning that “we have voters who now can’t reach their polling locations because of flooding.”
“We are helping those voters to find their temporary polling locations to identify a voting solution that can work for them,” she said, adding, “And if it comes to it, then we’ll also push to expand voting hours if we have to.”
Flash flood warnings went into effect Monday in portions of Brevard, DeSoto, Hardee, Highlands, Indian River, Martin, and St. Lucie counties. Flood warnings remained in effect until 9:30 a.m. Wednesday in Brevard, Indian River, Martin, and St. Lucie counties, according to the National Weather Service.
The Florida Division of Elections has listed new polling locations in most of those counties as well as precincts in Palm Beach and Okeechobee counties. WPLG in Miami has reported a change in one voting precinct in Broward County due to flooding.
After Florida Secretary of State Cord Byrd wrote on social media Monday night that his agency had provided an updated list of polling locations in counties affected, several individuals responded by calling on DeSantis to extend the time to vote.
“If the process of counting can continue for many days after an election then counties’ polling locations affected should give a 24 hour extension to go out and vote even if they relocated the poll,” wrote an individual named Angie G on X. “No one wants to put themselves in danger when they can’t even leave their homes because of flood[s].”
Common Cause was working with voters who have encountered delays due to problems with voting check-in machines in Broward County, Keith said. “We’re following those issues very closely and will do whatever is needed to help ensure that every eligible voter can cast their ballot.”
Common Cause Florida runs the “Florida Command Center,” which serves as a “nerve center” for rapid response to voting problems across the state and has trained nearly 1,500 poll monitors and legal observers.

name: Delaware
title: New SNAP stocking rules take effect Wednesday, with small Delaware stores facing biggest adjustment
description: Federal standards require more staple-food choices at participating stores as Delaware has 734 SNAP-authorized locations statewide WILMINGTON, Del. — New federal food-stocking requirements take effect Wednesday for many retailers that accept Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program benefits, with convenience stores, corner markets and other small-format ret[...]
text:
Effective Nov. 4th, The U.S. Department of Agriculture rule requires affected SNAP retailers to carry at least seven varieties of food in each of four staple-food categories: fruits and vegetables; meat, poultry or fish; bread and cereals; and dairy products. Image created using AI on 11/3/26
Federal standards require more staple-food choices at participating stores as Delaware has 734 SNAP-authorized locations statewide
WILMINGTON, Del. — New federal food-stocking requirements take effect Wednesday for many retailers that accept Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program benefits, with convenience stores, corner markets and other small-format retailers expected to face a bigger adjustment than traditional supermarkets.
The U.S. Department of Agriculture rule, published May 8, requires affected SNAP retailers to carry at least seven varieties of food in each of four staple-food categories: fruits and vegetables; meat, poultry or fish; bread and cereals; and dairy products.
Stores qualifying under the stocking standard must carry at least three units of each qualifying variety. That amounts to at least 28 different staple-food varieties and 84 individual stocking units. At least one perishable variety also must be available in three of the four staple-food categories. The requirements must be implemented by Nov. 4.
The new standards do not apply in the same way to every business authorized to accept SNAP. Specialty food stores and some retailers qualifying under other federal criteria may be treated differently.
Delaware has 734 SNAP-authorized retail locations, according to a recent compilation of USDA retailer-locator data. The dataset includes 280 convenience stores, 77 supermarkets, 74 grocery stores, 46 superstores, 25 specialty stores and 23 farmers markets or similar outlets. New Castle County accounts for 416 locations, Sussex County for 189 and Kent County for 129.
Why small stores feel it most
Large supermarkets generally already stock far more than the federal minimum. For small neighborhood stores, however, the rules may require changes in inventory, refrigeration, suppliers and shelf space.
USDA itself identified convenience stores, small grocery stores and combination stores as the businesses most likely to be affected.
The department estimated that complying with the rule will cost currently authorized retailers nationwide about $77 million during the first year, followed by roughly $1 million to $2 million annually over the next four years.
During the federal rulemaking process, retailers and trade associations raised concerns that small stores could have particular difficulty meeting dairy and grain requirements because of limited refrigeration, shelf space, product demand and the potential for spoilage.
USDA acknowledged that some currently authorized stores could become ineligible for SNAP participation because of the higher standards. The agency nevertheless said the changes were intended to improve the range of nutritious foods available to SNAP households and strengthen program integrity.
That could make the impact particularly noticeable in neighborhoods and rural communities where a convenience store or small grocery may be one of the closest places accepting SNAP.
For shoppers, the change could mean more staple foods available at those stores. For owners, it could mean carrying products that previously were not part of their regular inventory.
What stores must carry
The four staple-food categories are fruits and vegetables; meat, poultry and fish; breads and cereals; and dairy.
Under the new federal standard, qualifying stores must have:

Seven distinct varieties in each category.
Three stocking units of each variety.
At least 28 qualifying varieties overall.
At least 84 qualifying stocking units overall.
At least one perishable variety in three different staple-food categories.

The USDA also revised how it decides whether foods count as separate varieties. Whole-grain bread and non-whole-grain bread, for example, can qualify as separate varieties, as can whole-grain and non-whole-grain pasta. Shredded cheese and non-shredded cheese also may count separately.
Butter, jerky and many snack or dessert foods do not count toward the staple-food stocking minimum.
Enforcement will not necessarily mean every existing store receives an inspection Wednesday.
USDA said newly applying retailers and stores seeking authorization for new locations will be evaluated under the new standards after the implementation date. Existing stores generally will be assessed when they go through SNAP reauthorization, although federal regulations allow USDA to review a retailer’s continued eligibility at other times.
Shopping options increasingly include online orders
The stocking change comes as SNAP participants increasingly have options beyond traditional in-store shopping.
Delaware Health and Social Services says SNAP benefits may be used to buy eligible groceries online from authorized retailers. SNAP benefits cannot be used to pay delivery, shipping, service or membership fees.
An older DHSS online-purchasing guide lists Aldi, Amazon, Food Lion, Giant, Sam’s Club, ShopRite, Walmart and Weis Markets, but that document is dated February 2022 and should not be considered a complete current list without confirmation from the state or USDA.
The expansion of online EBT purchasing gives some SNAP households additional options, particularly where transportation or nearby grocery choices are limited. But independent neighborhood stores continue to compete largely on convenience and proximity.
What happens next
USDA said it plans to notify authorized retailers about the requirements and provide information intended to help businesses comply.
Stores found short of required inventory during an inspection also may be able to demonstrate that qualifying products were ordered or received during the previous 21 days by producing invoices, receipts or similar records.
A retailer denied authorization or reauthorization because it fails to meet the stocking requirement generally must wait six months before applying again.
For Delaware shoppers, the practical effect will depend on how many small stores already meet the standards and how many need to change their inventories.
USDA has not published a Delaware-specific estimate showing how many of the state’s retailers will have to add products or how many might ultimately decide not to continue accepting SNAP.
TO GO BOX

What: New USDA SNAP retailer stocking standards
When: Nov. 4, 2026
Minimum stocking standard: Seven varieties in each of four staple-food categories, with at least three units of each variety
For shoppers: Use the USDA SNAP Retailer Locator to find authorized stores.
For retailers: The USDA SNAP Retailer Service Center can answer questions about authorization and compliance at 1-877-823-4369, 8 a.m. to 8 p.m. Eastern time, Monday through Friday.
More information: USDA Food and Nutrition Service and Delaware Division of Social Services SNAP program pages.

description: The U.S. Department of Justice shed some light Tuesday morning on where it will deploy observers for what it has called its largest ever Election Day monitoring effort. In Louisiana, its personnel will be at polling sites in East Baton Rouge, Lafayette and Orleans parishes, according to a statement from the agency.  No information was […]
text:
A man looks over a sample ballot outside a fire station that doubles as a polling place in New Orleans' Garden District on Election Day, Nov. 8, 2022. (Greg LaRose/Louisiana Illuminator)The U.S. Department of Justice shed some light Tuesday morning on where it will deploy observers for what it has called its largest ever Election Day monitoring effort. In Louisiana, its personnel will be at polling sites in East Baton Rouge, Lafayette and Orleans parishes, according to a statement from the agency. 
No information was provided on the specific precincts where monitors will be placed.
Justice officials say they have dispatched monitors for decades in federal election cycles to ensure voting laws are being followed, but they acknowledge this is the first time they are being sent to all 50 states. Approximately 1,000 election monitors and observers from the DOJ’s Civil Rights Division are part of the effort.
Election monitors typically look into whether polling places are in compliance with federal laws such as the Voting Rights Act and that measures have been taken to ensure access for the elderly and disabled. 
This year’s DOJ monitoring mission unfolds as it has led the Trump administration’s court actions to suspend vote counting in California and pause the U.S. Senate race in Alaska. President Donald Trump has claimed without evidence that Democrats will “cheat” to ensure their party prevails in the congressional midterm elections.
“Election integrity has been one of the top priorities for this Administration and this Division,” Assistant Attorney General Harmeet Dhillon said in the statement. “I am very proud we are deploying the largest monitoring effort in DOJ history, and pursuing transparency for elections in an assertive and nondiscriminatory manner.”
Louisiana Secretary of State Nancy Landry confirmed last week her office had been made aware Justice monitors were being sent to the state, but federal officials had not provided her with details on how many were coming or where they would be stationed.
Landry’s staff is monitoring a hotline, 1-800-883-2805, where voters can report concerns or ask questions.

title: Death row inmate’s attorneys press for execution pause until Indiana provides drug quality records
description: Jeffrey Weisheit’s attorneys are asking Gov. Mike Braun to stop Thursday’s execution until Indiana provides evidence that the drugs it plans to inject are potent, pure and properly stored. The lawyers submitted additional materials Tuesday, a day after Braun denied Weisheit’s request to commute his death sentence to life without parole. Their separate reques[...]
text:
Attorney Joseph Perkovich speaks outside the Indiana Government Center in Indianapolis on Oct. 19, 2026, after the morning session of death row inmate Jeffrey Weisheit’s clemency hearing. (Photo by Casey Smith/Indiana Capital Chronicle)Jeffrey Weisheit’s attorneys are asking Gov. Mike Braun to stop Thursday’s execution until Indiana provides evidence that the drugs it plans to inject are potent, pure and properly stored.
The lawyers submitted additional materials Tuesday, a day after Braun denied Weisheit’s request to commute his death sentence to life without parole. Their separate request for a temporary reprieve and an independent review of Indiana’s execution procedures is still pending.
Weisheit was sentenced to death for murdering 8-year-old Alyssa Lynch and her 5-year-old brother, Caleb, in a 2010 house fire near Evansville. His execution remains scheduled before sunrise Nov. 5 at Indiana State Prison in Michigan City.
The supplemental filing focuses on what the state has disclosed about the latest round of pentobarbital purchased for $275,000. The Department of Correction confirmed Monday that it has the drugs, and an inventory log released to the Indiana Capital Chronicle that afternoon records the receipt of six 50-milliliter vials on Oct. 29.
But the log does not include testing results, expiration dates or temperature readings. Weisheit’s attorneys emphasized that Indiana has not supplied documentation verifying the drugs’ potency, purity and stability, or records showing storage temperatures for the new supply.
The Capital Chronicle previously obtained DOC temperature logs through public records requests, showing readings outside the recommended storage range.
“Indiana is singular in its apparent failure to conduct any testing to ensure the potency, purity, and stability of its execution drugs. This willfully disregards rudimentary practices,” attorney Joe Perkovich said in a news release.
Story continues below.
Weisheit-2026.11.03-SUPPL.reprieve.app
 
DOC did not address the Capital Chronicle’s questions about whether any efficacy testing has been carried out.
Weisheit’s attorneys pointed to disclosures in other states. A 2017 Arizona settlement requires officials, upon request, to provide an analysis identifying execution chemicals and their concentrations within 10 days after seeking an execution warrant. A March 2025 affidavit from South Carolina’s corrections director described laboratory testing of pentobarbital before a scheduled execution.
Tuesday’s filing also raises questions about Pharmaneek Inc., the Indianapolis pharmacy identified as Indiana’s execution drug supplier. The pharmacy is on probation and faces a Nov. 9 hearing over alleged violations of compounding restrictions. The board has not ordered its suspension in that proceeding.
DOC and the Indiana attorney general’s office defended the state’s preparations Monday but declined to discuss supplier information, citing state confidentiality law.
A reprieve would postpone the execution without commuting his death sentence.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Tears and prayers at Jackson State vigil after nightclub shooting kills 2
description: Jackson State University President Denise Jones Gregory, center left, joins freinds of slain JSU student Jada Henderson after a campus vigil on Monday, Nov. 2, 2026.
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
Some bowed their heads in prayer, as candles glowed Monday evening at Jackson State University. Others wiped away tears. Many offered hugs as they remembered one of their own, one of two college students killed by gunfire the night before. 
University President Denise Jones Gregory, joined by about 200 others, tearfully gave her condolences to the family of Jada Henderson, a freshman from Atlanta studying psychology, who was killed in a weekend shooting at a Jackson nightclub 6 miles northeast of campus. 
“When one of our Tigers hurts, every single one of us bleeds,” Gregory told students, administrators and community members who gathered for the vigil. “To our students standing here tonight, I see your pain, I see your worry, I see your exhaustion and I see your grief.”
Jackson police say Henderson was killed after two men in ski masks entered the nightclub and began shooting. Police have not made any arrests or identified a motive. The investigation continues. 
The shooting also killed Lovdai Poindexter, 20, of Brandon, and injured six others, who were taken to a hospital for treatment. Poindexter was a student at Holmes Community College. 
Serenity Wilson, a JSU freshman studying marketing, was among Henderson’s friends. During the vigil, she asked the community to pray for her fallen friend.
“Our friend was here one minute, now she is gone,” Wilson said.
Ladorian “Gray” Shelton, a junior creative writing major from Jackson, said he was devastated by Henderson’s death, even if he did not know her. The shooting, he said, brought back memories of losing a high school classmate to gun violence.
“It hurts the spirit. This is another peer. I wanted to see them graduate and be happy. This didn’t have to happen,” Shelton said, as dozens of other students crowded near him, some holding electronic candles that lit up the gathering.
Jackson Mayor John Horhn, right, and Police Chief RaShall Brackney bow their heads during a vigil for a slain student on Monday,. Nov. 2, 2026, at Jackson State University. Credit: Candice Wilder/Mississippi Today
In response to the shooting, Jackson State officials canceled classes on Monday and Tuesday for undergraduates, while graduate courses were moved online, according to a social media statement from the university. 
Gregory said students’ safety and well-being remain the highest priority as university officials work with law enforcement and public safety officers. Campus officials encouraged students to use campus resources for support and counseling. 
Jackson Mayor John Horhn, who attended the vigil, had called for the nightclub to be shut down in a statement Sunday. 
As the vigil came to a close, Gregory joined Wilson and some of Henderson’s friends at a bench.
“So, what was Jada like?” Gregory asked. 
“Lovely,” one student responded. 
“Feisty,” Wilson interjected. Then laughter erupted.
