name: California
title: California decides on housing bonds with Prop. 1 and Prop. 37
description: The two borrowing measures — Propositions 1 and 37 — tackle the state’s affordable housing crisis in very different ways and by targeting very different constituencies.
text:
In summary
The two borrowing measures — Propositions 1 and 37 — tackle the state’s affordable housing crisis in very different ways and by targeting very different constituencies. 


California voters are weighing two unprecedented housing bonds, Propositions 1 and 37, that take aim at the state’s affordable housing crisis in very different ways.
Prop. 1 would give the state permission to borrow a record-breaking $11.25 billion, with the lion’s share going toward the construction of affordable housing for low-income renters and homeless Californians.
Prop. 37 is a first-of-its-kind revenue bond that would have the state borrow as much as $25 billion from private investors and lend that money to qualifying homebuyers to help cover the bulk of their down payments. Plenty of experts have questioned how this untested program would work, but most agree that it would not come at the expense of state taxpayers. 
Recent polling, campaign finance data and political history all suggest that both bonds are likely to win.
An estimated 60% of likely voters support Prop. 1, while a whopping 65% back Prop. 37, according to the most recent Public Policy Institute of California survey. No money has been spent to oppose either measure. Bonds also tend to outperform all other types of ballot measures. Voters have approved 23 of the 26 up for a vote since the turn of the century. 
A familiar borrowing proposal
Prop. 1 carries a historically large price tag, but is otherwise a conventional policy approach. California regularly puts affordable housing spending on the state credit card, especially after the Legislature and former Gov. Jerry Brown axed the state’s main funding source in the wake of the Great Recession. 
The most recent major bond in 2018 saw the state borrow $4 billion. Developers and affordable housing advocates have been lobbying the Legislature for a successor since then.
The tone of the “Yes” campaign took on a heightened degree of urgency this year. The money from that most recent bond is now all but depleted. A recent redesign of the state’s carbon emission market, one of California’s signature climate change programs, is also likely to nix one of California’s few other sources of money for affordable housing. 
If Prop. 1 passes, nearly two-thirds would be used to fund apartment buildings dedicated to cash-strapped Californians including those facing homelessness. The remaining haul would be split among different programs: Low-cost home loans for low-income and veteran buyers; support for farmworker, student and tribal housing; technical innovation grants and grants for cities planning new dense housing development.
Supporters say the new spigot of cash could unlock nearly 40,000 affordable units that are ready to break ground but lack state funding. That isn’t anything close to the 312,500 units that state regulators say the state needs to build every year to meet its housing goals. But affordable housing advocates say it would be a welcome boost for a state that has especially struggled to build for its neediest renters.
Something completely different
Prop. 37 is meant to help Californians a bit higher up the income spectrum, but who still can’t quite crack homeownership. The proposed borrowing program is principally backed by the California Association of Realtors and former Democratic Assembly Speaker Bob Hertzberg. 
Critics of the measure have questioned whether privately financed downpayment loans will be affordable for Californians who most need the help. Hertzberg has countered that wealthy philanthropists, foundations and other charitable spenders could be convinced to provide the funding to the state at below-market interest rates.

name: California
title: Prop. 4: Will California allow public campaign financing for state, local candidates?
description: Prop. 4 would allow the state and most local governments to set up public campaign financing if they choose to. Supporters say it would curb private money in politics and diversify the pool of candidates. Critics doubt its effectiveness and say taxpayers should not subsidize campaigns.
text:
In summary
Prop. 4 would allow the state and most local governments to set up public campaign financing if they choose to. Supporters say it would curb private money in politics and diversify the pool of candidates. Critics doubt its effectiveness and say taxpayers should not subsidize campaigns.


In 1988, California banned candidates in statewide and most local races from using public funds to run for office.
Voters are deciding whether to reverse it with Proposition 4, which would authorize state and local governments to set up public campaign finance systems.
Proponents include good government groups and Democratic leaders, who say that would make it easier for candidates without wealthy backers to run. They argue it would boost competition and counter the influence of major donors, especially as statewide elections in recent years have grown more and more expensive. 
“We need to change the way we finance election campaigns so candidates can run and win without having to raise big money, and they can spend their time listening to voters rather than their donors,” said Trent Lange, president of California Clean Money Campaign and co-chair of the Yes on Prop. 4 campaign.
Some critics of Prop. 4 say the public should not subsidize political campaigns, period. Others argue that fraudulent candidates could scam the system, and taxpayers could end up subsidizing candidates they don’t support. Some are also skeptical that public campaign financing could curb private spending in politics, saying there’s little evidence it works.
“The voters have been quite clear they don’t want taxpayer money being used for politics,” said Assemblymember Carl DeMaio, a San Diego Republican. “Unfortunately, politicians simply can’t take no for an answer.”
Seven charter cities in California, including San Francisco, Berkeley and Oakland, were spared from the 1988 ban and already have public campaign financing. Prop. 4 would give state and other local governments the option to set up similar systems if they choose to. 
The funds wouldn’t be available to just anybody: To qualify, candidates must meet criteria such as proving they have a certain number of small donors or agreeing to cap how much they raise and spend on their campaign. Eligible candidates could receive the funding as a grant, a matching fund indexed to their total donations, or a voucher voters can give to campaigns, depending on the design of the system.
Prop. 4 offers some instructions to state and local governments that want to establish such a system. 
Candidates would need to prove they have enough public support and to agree to certain spending limits to receive funding, but the measure doesn’t spell out how much. Candidates could not use the money to pay for legal defenses, fines or personal loans to their campaigns and public funds meant for education, public safety and transportation could not be used. 
Opponents say the rules aren’t specific enough to have teeth.

name: California
title: California voters could reshape the state’s landmark environmental law with Prop. 45
description: Backed by business groups and opposed by environmentalists, Prop. 45 would put deadlines on environmental reviews and lawsuits for housing, water, broadband and transit projects.
text:
In summary
Backed by business groups and opposed by environmentalists, Prop. 45 would put deadlines on environmental reviews and lawsuits for housing, water, broadband and transit projects.


Voters are deciding whether to amend the California Environmental Quality Act, the state’s landmark environmental review law, by setting deadlines for environmental reviews and related lawsuits on certain projects. Supporters say the changes would reduce building costs.
The California Chamber of Commerce sponsored Proposition 45, the Building an Affordable California Act. If voters approve, it would limit the length of environmental reviews for projects deemed “essential” to 365 business days and require courts to resolve litigation in 270 calendar days. Those projects include housing, water, broadband and transit developments.  
Proponents say the savings from building more quickly would pass to consumers. Supporters spent $41 million campaigning for the measure. The Building a Better California political action committee was the largest donor, giving $10 million to the campaign. The organization is funded partly by current and former Google executives Sergey Brin and Eric Schmidt. Two of the largest investor owned utilities, Pacific Gas & Electric Company and Southern California Edison, together donated $4.4 million.
Environmental groups argue the measure goes too far in weakening a law meant to protect people from environmental harms. Opponents, which include a coalition of environmental, health and union organizations, have spent $30 million trying to stop it. Wendy Schmidt, a Democratic philanthropist, was the largest donor, giving $10 million to the campaign. The political action committee Clean and Healthy California Sponsored by Environmental Organizations contributed $7 million. 
The California Democratic Party opposes the measure. The California Republican Party supports it, while county Republican groups are split. 
Deborah Sivas, environmental law professor at Stanford University, said Prop. 45 would radically change current law. It would shift power “away from local governments and to developers by giving them some new tools … and limiting what courts can do in terms of reviewing decisions that agencies and local governments make,” she said. 
CEQA and housing
California’s environmental review law, signed in 1970, requires agencies to assess the environmental impacts of developments and help mitigate them. 
Over decades, developers have raised concerns about the process, arguing litigation and bureaucracy slow down construction. 
State legislators have tried to fix the problem by passing laws that exempt or streamline certain projects from environmental review. In 2025, Gov. Gavin Newsom signed laws that exempt many urban housing projects from the full review process. 
But some supporters of Prop. 45, including the California Building Industry Association and the California Council for Affordable Housing, say those changes don’t go far enough. 
“It’s an important piece of the puzzle, but (that type of housing) does not produce quickly or at scale,” said Jennifer Hernandez, an attorney who helped write the measure. “We need quicker, at scale, affordable housing.” 
Supporters say Prop. 45 would help California redevelop large, unused sites like malls and parking lots into housing and make it easier to build away from urban areas. 
Pro-housing groups, public agencies divided 
Pro-housing and local government groups usually support CEQA reform, but Prop. 45 has divided many of them. 
Housing advocates in the Bay Area, including East Bay for Everyone and the Greenbelt Alliance, oppose the measure. Other Yes in My Backyard groups are neutral, including Abundant Housing Los Angeles and both California YIMBY and YIMBY Action — the movement’s two flagship advocacy groups. 
The split between pro-housing groups lies in whether California should keep building outward onto undeveloped land or promote construction in urban centers. Some supporters, including Oakland Democratic Assemblymember Buffy Wicks, have said the state needs all types of housing.
Others say building away from urban centers would make it harder to address climate change. 
“We believe we can (and must) solve the housing and climate crises simultaneously. That means building communities with denser housing and alternatives to automobile dependence,” wrote Max Dubler of California YIMBY in a blog post explaining the group’s neutral stance on Prop. 45.
Public agencies and local governments that could benefit from the building rules were also divided. 
The California Municipal Utilities Association opposes the measure. But most other groups representing local governments, including the League of California Cities and California State Association of Counties, remained neutral. 
Financial impacts for Prop. 45
Prop. 45 supporters argued that streamlining development would make life more affordable for Californians, but the long-term financial benefits are unclear.
An analysis by Blue Sky Consulting Group, commissioned by the California Chamber of Commerce, estimated the measure would produce $1.5 billion in savings and additional revenues for public agencies over 10 years that would reduce overall housing costs. 
But the measure would initially cost local governments and public agencies more as they adjust to the measure’s rules, according to the Legislative Analyst’s Office, a nonpartisan adviser to the Legislature.

name: California
title: Prop. 44: Voters decide on spending restrictions for healthcare clinics
description: Californians are deciding on a union-sponsored ballot measure that would force community clinics to spend more on patient care.  Proposition 44 would require community clinics to spend at least 90% of their annual revenue on patient care or pay fines to the state. While spending varies by clinic, on average, clinics today spend about 80% […]
text:
Californians are deciding on a union-sponsored ballot measure that would force community clinics to spend more on patient care. 
Proposition 44 would require community clinics to spend at least 90% of their annual revenue on patient care or pay fines to the state. While spending varies by clinic, on average, clinics today spend about 80% of revenue on providing services, according to a nonpartisan analysis by the Legislative Analyst’s Office. 
The labor union Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West placed Prop. 44 on the ballot. The union argues the measure will add a layer of accountability to how clinics spend taxpayer dollars. Clinics are the safety net for an estimated 7 million low-income Californians and are paid largely through reimbursements from public insurance programs and federal grants. 
Union spokespeople point to “excessive” executive salaries — some of which recently became the subject of a complaint filed with the Internal Revenue Service — as an inappropriate use of taxpayer dollars.
“Money should not be directed towards excessive executive compensation or other non-essentials that we have seen within … our clinic system,” Renée Saldaña, a union spokesperson, said.
The opposition, led by clinics, has raised $39 million to defeat the measure, more than double the $17 million supporters report contributing so far. Clinics say they’ve got a lot to lose, and so do their patients. An analysis commissioned by opponents estimates the measure could cost clinics about $1.7 billion in noncompliance penalties in the first year, forcing some of them to close or reduce services. 
“This puts our patients in danger, limiting our patients’ access to care,” Dr. Jerry Abraham of Kedren Health, a community clinic in South Los Angeles, said during a recent rally. “Unfortunately, that doesn’t mean patients’ need for care goes away. Guess where they are going to go? If they can’t come to clinics, they’re gonna go to the emergency department.” 
Clinic leaders add that their health centers are already heavily regulated by state and federal health authorities. 
A key question in this proposal is exactly what type of costs would qualify as appropriate healthcare spending.
Prop. 44 leaves the answer up to the state attorney general, directing that office to issue guidance and decide what’s appropriate healthcare spending. Depending on those guidelines, clinics argue they could be penalized for spending on critical items such as medical equipment upgrades, support staff and construction projects, or for keeping money in their budget reserves. 
Prop. 44 is the second attempt by the healthcare workers’ union to restrict clinic spending – a similar bill failed to advance last year. 
The California Primary Care Association, which represents about 2,000 community clinics, sued the union twice. First, it sued to keep the measure off the ballot, but a federal judge dismissed that case over the summer. In September, the clinics filed a separate case accusing the union and its president, Dave Regan, of exploiting the ballot process to coerce clinics into accepting the union’s bargaining demands. 
The union said the allegations were “categorically false.” This second lawsuit is still pending.
SEIU-UHW has gained a reputation for targeting health providers via the ballot box. The union sponsored proposals to regulate dialysis clinic operations in three consecutive election cycles; those measures failed all three times.
The union has also backed Proposition 40, the attention-grabbing initiative which would impose a one-time 5% tax on California residents worth $1 billion or more. 
Supported by the California Health Care Foundation (CHCF), which works to ensure that people have access to the care they need, when they need it, at a price they can afford. Visit www.chcf.org to learn more.

name: California
title: California chooses next insurance commissioner: Jane Kim or Ben Allen
description: Californians are choosing a new insurance commissioner after almost a decade of deadly wildfires that threw the state’s property insurance market into a crisis from which it is still trying to recover. Two Democrats are competing for the position for the first time. Jane Kim, the former San Francisco supervisor, wants to create a public […]
text:
Californians are choosing a new insurance commissioner after almost a decade of deadly wildfires that threw the state’s property insurance market into a crisis from which it is still trying to recover.
Two Democrats are competing for the position for the first time. Jane Kim, the former San Francisco supervisor, wants to create a public disaster insurance program. State Sen. Ben Allen says a comprehensive wildfire-mitigation plan is the way to fix what ails insurance in California: availability, especially in areas of high fire risk; and affordability, as insurers raise premiums, citing increasing disaster risk and rising replacement costs.
Almost half of the state’s residents report paying more for home or renters’ insurance than last year, according to a new poll by the Insurance Fairness Project, a national insurance information hub, and Data for Progress.
The commissioner also regulates auto, life, pet and some types of health insurance, as well as workers’ compensation. It’s a wide-ranging position that some experts say requires a “brutal” balancing act.
Allen, whose constituents include Palisades Fire survivors, would bring recent legislative experience in insurance and other related topics, such as utility liability for wildfires. 
Kim last held office in 2019, with experience that includes passing the state’s first $15 minimum wage and free community college for San Francisco residents.
An Allen victory would also be a win for the California Democratic Party, which endorsed him, and the varied labor and business advocacy groups that supported him. Business interests also spent millions of dollars supporting him and opposing Kim, including outside political action committees funded by investor-owned utility companies such as Pacific Gas & Electric and Southern California Edison, as well as tech companies and billionaires.
Kim said at a debate last month between the two candidates that she is running “against the status quo.”
A win by Kim would be the latest triumph in the progressive wave and proof of the enduring popularity of the populist message of Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders, her most famous endorser. Her top direct donors are labor unions. The California Labor Federation endorsed her, and the Working Families Party, the group she used to lead, provided the bulk of outside funding to her campaign.
Kim has acknowledged that launching public disaster insurance would be hard, and could take years. Her plan involves diverting insurance premiums homeowners pay to their insurance companies to a public program that guarantees wildfire coverage. The idea has many critics, including not only the insurance industry but also consumer groups with insurance expertise, which warn of tremendous risk to the state. 
Allen said at the debate that Kim’s public insurance plan would not work in California, calling it “unmoored and unresearched.” Kim called his plans more of the same.
Whoever voters choose to replace Commissioner Ricardo Lara will face plenty of challenges in dealing with past disasters as well as preparing for future ones. 
The new commissioner will have to hold insurers accountable for paying claims quickly and fairly, as survivors of last year’s Los Angeles County fires continue to deal with insurance delays and denials. Lara’s department has pending actions against State Farm, the biggest individual insurer in the state, and the last-resort FAIR Plan over their handling of claims from the Eaton and Palisades fires.
As California braces for El Niño, insurance will play an important role. The current commissioner, the insurance industry and other experts are urging the state’s residents to protect their properties against flooding and wind damage, and to consider flood insurance.

title: Live Election Coverage
description: Hoosiers go to the polls today in Indiana’s general election. We have five journalists out and about tracking the key races. Keep up with all the news throughout the day and evening right here.
text:
(Getty Images)Hoosiers go to the polls today in Indiana’s general election. We have five journalists out and about tracking the key races. Keep up with all the news throughout the day and evening right here.



Key Events


Nov. 3, 2026 9:53 am
Early voting shatters 2022 totals










Early voting shatters 2022 totals


By Niki Kelly - Tuesday November 3, 2026 9:53 am





More than 755,000 Hoosiers voted early in person statewide — an increase of 40% from four years ago. 
That’s according to an Indiana Election Division report run Monday afternoon. The number could still grow, as counties finish reporting. In the 2022 midterms, about 538,000 Hoosiers voted early in person. 
Indiana had nearly 4.8 million residents on the rolls after the Oct. 5 registration deadline. Early voting began the day after.
When combined with returned mail ballots, traveling board votes and email votes, almost 848,000 Hoosiers had voted as of Monday, which is far above the 689,000 absentee votes cast in 2022 — and represents about 45% of the roughly 1.9 million vote total that election.
The Marion County Clerk’s Office on Oct. 27, 2026. (Photo by Niki Kelly/Indiana Capital Chronicle)
Indiana law refers to both mail-in ballots and early in-person voting as “absentee” votes. 
While it’s too early to know if this year’s turnout will eclipse previous years, Indiana traditionally has one of the worst turnout rates in the country. The 2020 general election hit a recent high-water mark of 65%, buoyed by an unusual election year with additional absentee voting flexibility, but sank to 40% in 2022’s midterm contest. In 2024, a presidential year, turnout was 62%.
According to the Monday report, about 7,100 disabled or injured Hoosiers — or their caretakers — had already voted by traveling board. Bipartisan teams deliver ballots to such voters and help them complete ballots if they’re not physically able to so themselves.
About 2,700 Hoosiers had voted by email. No one voted by fax. 
More than 14,000 would-be voters still hadn’t returned their mail ballots to county clerks, which must be received by 6 p.m. today.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: U.S. Justice Dept. monitors arrive at voting sites in New Haven
description: The Trump administration informed state and local officials on Oct. 21 that it would send two teams of DOJ monitors to polls in New Haven.
text:
This story will be updated.
Zachary Denver showed up at Davis Street School at 6:30 a.m. Tuesday not to vote — but to ask voters questions.
That was the first reported sighting of a planned Trump administration operation in New Haven. It wasn’t the last.
The administration had informed state and local officials on Oct. 21 that it would send two teams of two Department of Justice monitors to the polls in the city on Election Day. No other city in Connecticut was set to receive such visits, according to the secretary of the state’s office.
Davis Street is the Ward 26 polling place in Upper Westville. Denver — an assistant U.S. attorney based in New Haven’s office — stood in the parking lot for an hour. He approached 10 voters and interviewed three, according to Ward 26 Alder Amy Marx and Democratic Ward Co-Chair Laura Cahn.

Federal election monitor, Zachary Denver, was at a New Haven polling place on Nov. 3, 2026. Credit: Contributed photo via New Haven Independent

There was also a report of a monitor at the Ward 27 polling place in Westville and at the Ward 13 and 17 polling places in the Annex and Fair Haven Heights.
“He was just skulking nearby my vehicle. I was voting, getting in my car,” said Rose Chadwell, who encountered Denver after casting her ballot at Davis Street. “He seemed reasonable.”
Chadwell said Denver identified himself as working in a “civil rights” office. He had on “no uniform. Just regular, laid back. “A white guy with a nice haircut.”
Marx and Cahn said they approached Denver. He at first would not identify himself, they said. Eventually he did and they took a photo of his badge.
“His presence was quiet and not obtrusive,” Marx said.
“Nonetheless,” she said, it sent “a chilling message that we’re being watched by the federal government. It is extremely disconcerting that he refused to tell us who he was and what he was doing” at first. The monitor did not enter the polling place, they said.
A second voter told the Independent that he asked about what “signage” was inside the polling area, and if “anything prevented you from voting.”
A third voter, Aly Fox, said she encountered Denver at the Mauro-Sheridan polling place Tuesday morning. (She said that Denver did not identify himself by name, but he did identify himself as working for the DOJ. She recognized him as Denver based on a photos the Independent published in this article above.)
“He was asking about accessibility, if there were stairs, any issues getting to the polling place, asking if there was adequate signage,” Fox said. He asked if there were signs “in multiple languages, then asked about physical accessibility” of the polls. He also asked if he could have Fox’s email address in case he had any follow-up questions.
“It was surprising,” Fox said about the encounter. She said she had been listening to NPR on her drive to the polls and had heard about how unlikely it would be for voters to encounter DOJ monitors today.
A DOJ email identified Denver as the “team lead” in Tuesday’s monitoring operation in New Haven. His LinkedIn page states he joined the New Haven office in May and graduated New York University law school in 2013.
New Haven Independent’s Paul Bass contributed reporting.
This story was first published Nov. 3, 2026 by New Haven Independent.

name: Alaska Beacon
title: First Alaska election results to come Tuesday evening, final unofficial results in 2 weeks
description: The Alaska Division of Elections expects to report the first results from the state’s general election between 8:45 p.m. and 9 p.m. Tuesday night, with updates through the early morning hours Wednesday. The state’s closest races may not have an unofficial winner for more than two weeks. Historically, between 75-90% of Election Day results are […]
text:
Alaska Division of Elections program manager Brian Jackson answers questions from reporters shortly after completing the state's ranked choice voting tabulation in 2024. (Photo by Andrew Kitchenman/Alaska Beacon)The Alaska Division of Elections expects to report the first results from the state’s general election between 8:45 p.m. and 9 p.m. Tuesday night, with updates through the early morning hours Wednesday.
The state’s closest races may not have an unofficial winner for more than two weeks.
Historically, between 75-90% of Election Day results are available by noon Wednesday, with results from rural precincts trickling in through the following days.
The final unofficial results will not be available until Nov. 18, and the division expects to publish an official result on Nov. 25. 
Because a disproportionate number of Democratic voters have cast ballots in advance of Election Day and some advance votes are counted after Election Day, initial results will be more right-leaning than the final result.    
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX. 

Under Alaska’s election system, general-election voters may rank each of the four candidates for an office in order of preference.
If one of the four receives at least 50% of the first-choice votes, they win.
If none of the four hit that mark, the person with the fewest first-choice votes is eliminated, and voters who picked them have their votes go to their second choice.
The eliminations and redistributions continue until only two candidates are left, and the person with the most votes wins.
Under a policy established in 2022, the Division of Elections performs the ranked choice tabulation on Nov. 18, the deadline for the last absentee ballots to be counted.
More than a third of likely voters have already cast ballots
Between 260,000 and 300,000 Alaska voters are expected to participate in this year’s general election, or about half of the state’s 604,771 registered voters, based on the turnout in the past two midterm elections. The state saw 267,047 voters in 2022 and 285,009 in 2018.
By the time Election Day polls open at 7 a.m., more than a third of the state’s likely voters will have already cast ballots. At 4 p.m. Monday, the Division of Elections reported that it had already received just under 100,000 early and absentee votes.
Early votes are done in person at 11 locations on the Railbelt, in Juneau and Nome. Voters’ ID is checked on site, before a person votes.
As of the end of the day on Oct. 31, more registered Republicans than registered Democrats had voted early, but the number of Democratic votes was disproportionately high: 14.6% of the state’s registered Democrats had cast early votes through Oct. 31, compared to 10.9% of the state’s registered Republicans. 
Alaska has more than twice as many registered Republicans as registered Democrats, but more than 65% of the state’s 604,771 registered voters are registered to neither of America’s two largest parties.
Countable absentee votes will trickle in until Nov. 18
Absentee ballots can be cast by mail, fax, or in person at dozens of locations across the state. Because a voter’s ID is reviewed after the ballot is cast, some absentee ballots will be rejected for procedural errors or because the voter wasn’t properly registered. Generally, the statewide rejection rate is less than 5%.
More than 14,000 absentee ballots had been sent out but not yet returned as of Sunday noon; past trends indicate most of those will eventually arrive and be counted.
Absentee ballots can arrive by mail as late as Nov. 18 and still be counted, but historical trends show all but a relative handful of absentee ballots arrive within one week of Election Day — this year, that’s by Nov. 10. The busiest day for absentee ballot returns is typically the day after Election Day.

name: Alaska Beacon
title: Polls open at 7 a.m. Tuesday in Alaska — and plenty is at stake on Election Day
description: On Tuesday, Alaska could elect its first Democratic governor since 2002, roll back the clock on the way it conducts elections, help decide control of the U.S. House and Senate for the final two years of President Donald Trump’s second term and possibly elect the first Indigenous woman to the Senate.  Here’s what to consider […]
text:
Campaign signs crowd a slope on Sept. 23, 2026, at the intersection of Muldoon Road and Northern Lights Boulevard in Anchorage. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)On Tuesday, Alaska could elect its first Democratic governor since 2002, roll back the clock on the way it conducts elections, help decide control of the U.S. House and Senate for the final two years of President Donald Trump’s second term and possibly elect the first Indigenous woman to the Senate. 
Here’s what to consider when voting and what to watch for as the results come in:
U.S. Senate
In a four-person race, incumbent Republican Dan S. Sullivan is being challenged by Democratic candidate Mary Peltola, independent Dan J. Sullivan and Republican Gerald Heikes.
Polling throughout the race has indicated Peltola has a small lead over Sen. Sullivan, but the difference has been consistently within the margin of error, indicating that either could win. Dan J. Sullivan and Heikes are each expected to get less than 3% of the vote.
As a result, Alaska’s Senate race is one of a relative handful of toss-up seats that could decide whether Republicans or Democrats control the Senate.[Voter Guide: 2026 General Election Voter Guide: The candidates, the ballot measures, and the tools you need to cast your vote.]
Sen. Sullivan has been a reliable supporter of President Donald Trump and the Senate’s Republicans; if Peltola were to win, it would increase the chances of a Democratic takeover. Peltola has campaigned on an anticorruption platform and appears likely to support Democratic efforts to investigate the Trump administration.
While both Peltola and Sullivan support oil and gas drilling on federal land in Alaska, other Senate Democrats oppose such drilling and could override Peltola.
In addition, Peltola has said she would support restrictions or a ban on deepwater trawling in federal waters near Alaska, but Democratic control of the Senate could put Sen. Patty Murray, D-Washington, in control of the Senate committee that handles fisheries, and Murray has supported the trawl industry.
During his latest term, Sullivan has successfully advocated for a vast expansion of the U.S. Coast Guard and military in Alaska, bringing hundreds of millions of dollars in construction projects to the state.
The Trump administration and other Republicans have indicated that they may seek to dispute the legitimacy of a Peltola victory, citing a New York Times article that reported Democratic campaigners recruited Dan J. Sullivan as a spoiler who could siphon votes away from Sen. Sullivan.
The chance of a successful challenge would fall if Peltola defeats Sen. Sullivan by a margin that is larger than the number of votes received by Dan J. Sullivan. 
In addition, if Sen. Sullivan is re-elected, there would be no challenge.
Governor
Democratic candidate Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins and three Republicans — Bernadette Wilson, Dave Bronson and Treg Taylor — are seeking to succeed Gov. Mike Dunleavy, a Republican who is term-limited and unable to run again this year.
While ranked choice voting could allow Republican votes to transfer from a lower-finishing Republican to a higher-finishing one, historical trends show many Republicans are unwilling to rank more than one or two candidates, and polling indicates Kreiss-Tomkins has high odds of becoming the first Democratic governor of Alaska since Tony Knowles left office in 2002.    
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX. 

Kreiss-Tomkins has campaigned on an ambitious series of policy goals, including the restoration of a pension plan for teachers and state employees, advance funding for public schools, a multimillion-dollar bond issue for electrical improvements across the state, a temporary ban on new large-scale computing data centers, changes to the way the state conducts elections and restrictions on trawl fisheries.
The election of a Democrat could cause ripple effects in the state’s relationship with the Trump administration, which has withheld federal payments to Democratic-led states, including disaster relief money.
Wilson, who President Donald Trump has endorsed and polls have indicated is the leading Republican candidate, has advocated a more aggressive push toward policies pursued by Dunleavy during his eight years in office, including more funding for the Permanent Fund dividend, even if it means breaking an eight-year-old limit on the size of transfers from the Alaska Permanent Fund. 
Taylor, attorney general under Dunleavy, has proposed policies mostly in line with Dunleavy, as has Bronson. Both men have advocated a harder limit on spending from the Alaska Permanent Fund, as has Kreiss-Tomkins. 
Ballot Measure 2
The general election ballot includes two ballot measures, but Ballot Measure 3 is a largely inconsequential revision to the state’s existing ban on noncitizen voting.
Ballot Measure 2, conversely, would have major impacts in the state. If passed, it would repeal the state’s current system of elections, in which all candidates for an office run together and the top four vote-getters advance from the primary to the general election, which uses ranked-choice voting.
In place of that system, Alaska would return to party-run primaries, where political parties set the rules for who may participate. One candidate from each party would advance to the general election, and ranked choice voting would not be used.
In addition, the state would no longer have a law requiring third-party political donors to disclose the source of their money; contributors would be able to give money anonymously.
Because of a conflict with Ballot Measure 1, passed during the August primary election, enacting Ballot Measure 2 likely also would eliminate a limit on direct financial donations to governor candidates, allowing donors to give unlimited amounts of money in governor races. A final ruling on that elimination would take place after the election.
U.S. House
Unlike in the Senate, Alaska’s U.S. House race is unlikely to be decisive in determining control of one half of Congress. National polling indicates Democrats are likely to take control of the chamber.
Incumbent Republican Rep. Nick Begich III is being challenged by independent candidate Bill Hill, federally-imprisoned Democratic candidate Eric Hafner and Libertarian Jim McDermott.
The Alaska Democratic Party opposes Hafner and is urging party members to back Hill instead. Nevertheless, pre-election polling indicates Hafner could get 5% or more of Alaskans’ first-choice votes, and analysts believe that helps Begich’s re-election chances.
Begich, first elected in 2024, has been a reliable vote for President Donald Trump and Republicans in the House. 
Hill has not said whether he would join Republicans or Democrats in the House but has said he would not serve under current Speaker of the House Mike Johnson, R-Louisiana. 
Alaska Legislature
Both the Alaska Senate and Alaska House are currently controlled by coalition majorities; the majority in the Senate includes Republicans and Democrats, while the one in the House includes Democrats, independents and Republicans.
Over the past two years, the coalitions have been in conflict with Dunleavy, who vetoed more than 25% of all legislation passed by the House and Senate, a record since statehood.
If the coalitions continue and Kreiss-Tomkins is elected governor, the state’s legislative and executive branches would be aligned on major issues including school pensions and funding.
If the coalitions continue but a Republican is elected governor, or if Kreiss-Tomkins is elected but enough Republicans are elected to the Legislature to form a majority, some kind of discord is likely to continue.

name: Ohio Capital Journal

text:
Getty Images.Good morning Ohio, it’s Election Day! Tell all your friends and family to vote.
Polls are open from 6:30 a.m. to 7:30 p.m.
You can check your voter registration, and find your voting precinct and polling location, by checking with the Ohio Secretary of State here.
If you are in line to vote by 7:30 p.m., stay in line, you can still vote.
Non-Military absentee ballots must be received by your board of elections by 7:30 p.m. If you have a non-military absentee ballot, it is too late to mail your ballot with the U.S. Postal Service and you must bring it to your local board of elections by 7:30 p.m.
Military and overseas absentee ballots must be received (by mail) by boards of elections by Nov. 7 to be counted.

It’s Election Day! Here’s what’s at stake in Ohio


By Ohio Capital Journal Staff - Tuesday November 3, 2026 9:05 am





[Voter Guide: 2026 Ohio General Election Voter Guide: Races, deadlines, and the tools you need to cast your vote.]
This is an extremely important election for the state of Ohio.
Voters will decide on statewide leadership of Ohio for the next four years, with impacts on nearly everything: Ohio laws, education, utility bills and energy, healthcare, elections, constitutional rights, roads and bridges, support for local police, firefighters, EMTs, and libraries.
Ohio voters will select a new governor, attorney general, auditor, secretary of state, and treasurer.
Ohio voters have another U.S. Senate election.
Ohio voters also have two Ohio Supreme Court races to decide.
Voters will also decide on a proposal from Ohio Republican lawmakers to amend the Ohio Constitution to include a voter photo ID requirement in elections, which is currently required under state law.

Polls have opened in Montana


By Micah Drew - Tuesday November 3, 2026 7:07 am





Most polls in Montana opened at 7 a.m. this morning and Montanans have until 8 p.m. to get to a polling location.
“Election Day is here, and there is nothing like the energy and pride across Big Sky Country as Montanans make their voices heard at the ballot box,” said Secretary of State Christi Jacobsen in a statement. “Our dedicated Montana Election Team is honored to serve our voters from Sidney to the Swan and everywhere in between.”
Jacobsen and election officials across the state remind Montana voters of important information for Tuesday’s General Election:
Polling place hours: Polls began opening at 7 a.m. on Tuesday and close at 8 p.m. (Note: Polling places with fewer than 400 registered in-person voters must open no later than noon.)
Find your polling location: Montanans can verify their polling place location and hours by visiting voterportal.mt.gov.
View sample ballots: Voters can view their official sample ballot at voterportal.mt.gov.
Photo ID requirements: Election workers will ask voters for photo identification at the polls. More information is available at votemt.gov/voter-identification.
Absentee ballot reminders: Absentee ballots must be received by election officials by 8 p.m. on Election Day. Ballots can be hand-delivered directly to county election offices or polling places.
Track your ballot: Absentee voters can track the status of their absentee ballot by visiting voterportal.mt.gov.









Montanans cast most votes ahead of election day


By Micah Drew - Monday November 2, 2026 10:37 am





With one day left until midterm Election Day polls close in Montana, more than 300,000 votes have already been cast. 
The Montana Secretary of State’s office reported that as of Sunday night, 56.6% of the more than 530,000 absentee ballots sent out had been returned, including around 45,000 from Yellowstone County, 41,000 from Missoula County, 34,000 from Gallatin County and more than 31,000 from Flathead County.

title: Alaska North Slope crude oil records fifth-highest monthly average price in history
description: The average price of a barrel of Alaska North Slope crude oil in October was $122.21, according to figures published Monday by the Alaska Department of Revenue. That figure is the fifth-highest nominal average on record, according to the department’s regular tracking, and foretells millions of dollars in extra revenue for the state in the […]
text:
Fireweed blooms on either side of the trans-Alaska pipeline near mile post 86, Dalton Highway in 2006, two years after the 2004 Dall City fire. (Photo by Craig McCaa/BLM Alaska)The average price of a barrel of Alaska North Slope crude oil in October was $122.21, according to figures published Monday by the Alaska Department of Revenue.
That figure is the fifth-highest nominal average on record, according to the department’s regular tracking, and foretells millions of dollars in extra revenue for the state in the current fiscal year.
Only three months in 2008 and March 2012 had higher average values. Adjusted for inflation, the October average ranks significantly lower. 
Oil revenue typically pays for about one-third of Alaska’s annual general-purpose spending, and higher prices likely mean more money for services and the Permanent Fund dividend when state legislators reconvene in January.
Higher prices also mean individual Alaskans pay more for heating fuel, gasoline and diesel.
This spring, the department forecast that ANS crude would average $75 per barrel in Fiscal Year 2027, which runs from July 1 of this year through June 30, 2027.

SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX. 
Instead, prices since July 1 have averaged $98.13 — almost 25% higher than expected. Oil production in FY27 has been almost 7% below the forecast, but that also appears to be changing. In October, the North Slope averaged 524,446 barrels of oil per day, the highest monthly average so far in FY27. 
While the Iran war has driven oil prices upward through most of 2026, shipments through the Strait of Hormuz have risen and were only about 25% below prewar levels in October.
Prices have stayed persistently high, the Economist reported on Oct. 29, because Chinese oil demand has rebounded and because market traders fear a new escalation of violence in the Middle East.
The Economist’s analysis was based on Brent crude, a global standard based on oil from the North Sea. 
Alaska North Slope crude is selling for even more than Brent, thanks to refiners who are currently willing to pay a premium.
In October, oil buyers were willing to pay an average of $13.91 more for a barrel of North Slope oil than a barrel of Brent, the largest premium since May and one of the largest in history.
“The premium reflects tightness in the Pacific basin, where ANS trades,” said Aimee Bushnell of the Department of Revenue on Oct. 22. “Shipping disruptions tied to the Iran war have limited Middle East crude deliveries to major importers such as China, Japan, India, and South Korea. Uncertainty over shipping and delivery has led refiners to place a premium on crude that avoids high-risk routes, and grades from the Americas are among the safest options.”

name: California
title: Prop. 5: Will California voters change the rules for recall elections?
description: Democrats want to make recalls simply about whether an official should be recalled, not about who should replace them. The contest looked to be a toss-up going into Election Day, with the no side holding a small edge.
text:
In summary
Democrats want to make recalls simply about whether an official should be recalled, not about who should replace them. The contest looked to be a toss-up going into Election Day, with the no side holding a small edge. 


California voters are weighing in on whether to change the state recall process that allows voters to remove elected officials from office before the end of their terms.
Proposition 5 would break the recall process into two parts: Voters would first decide in an election whether an official should be removed from office. If successful, they’d vote again in a follow-up election on who should replace the recalled official. Under the current system, voters are asked both questions at the same time. 
Democratic lawmakers placed the constitutional amendment on the ballot in 2024. It was endorsed by Gov. Gavin Newsom, who survived his own attempted recall in 2021. 
The outcome of Prop. 5 was far from certain going into Election Day: 45% of people polled in mid-October by the Public Policy Institute of California said they would vote for it, while 52% said they wouldn’t. The numbers were more even than voters’ response at first blush — a similar poll in early September found 59% of likely voters said they likely would vote no and just 35% said they would vote yes.
Where Prop. 5 came from
In the aftermath of the failed recall of Newsom in 2021, Democratic lawmakers and Secretary of State Shirley Weber began advocating for changes to the process. The Newsom recall effort cost taxpayers about $200 million, and another $100 was spent in the campaign to stop the recall by Newsom’s potential replacements to get their message out to voters. Newsom walked away unscathed, with 62% of voters electing to keep him in office. 
Weber and good governance groups argued the current system leads to unnecessary state expense, confuses voters, and can lead to ‘undemocratic’ outcomes, since the winner needs a plurality of the vote, not the majority, to win. 
They supported Senate Constitutional Amendment 1, authored by Democratic Sen. Josh Newman, who was recalled himself in 2018. The effort became Prop. 5 when Democratic lawmakers passed it in 2024. Republican lawmakers voted against it, arguing the reform was not needed, would dilute the power of voters and lead to additional special election costs because of the need to hold two elections. 
Unlike some of the tax measures on the ballot that have spurred multimillion-dollar spending sprees, no group has spent any money on the effort, according to CalMatters campaign finance tracker. 
Although recalls are often initiated, they rarely make it to voters. Only 11 recalls have made it to the ballot in California since 1913, and only six have been approved by voters. The current recall process is how Republican Gov. Arnold Schwarzenegger came into power, replacing Gray Davis in 2003.

name: California
title: Prop. 43: Should it be harder to raise local taxes for specific services?
description: California’s Prop. 43 would require two-thirds of votes to pass any local taxes that pay for specific services, such as wildfire prevention, education and healthcare.
text:
In summary
California’s Prop. 43 would require two-thirds of votes to pass any local taxes that pay for specific services, such as wildfire prevention, education and healthcare. 


Should California make it harder to pass local taxes designated for specific services?
That’s the question posed by Proposition 43, which would require a two-thirds vote to pass any local special taxes, such as those paying for wildfire prevention, education and healthcare.
Californians already approved a two-thirds vote requirement for special taxes in 1996. So why do we need to vote on it again?
That’s because for decades, it was widely assumed that the requirement applied to all special taxes — until 2017, when the state Supreme Court ruled that it applied specifically to taxes that local officials put on the ballot. 
But the justices did not say whether the same requirement applied to citizen-driven tax measures, when individuals or groups gather enough signatures to put them on the ballot. Since then, several high-profile tax measures, such as the hefty Los Angeles tax on mansion sales and a Sonoma County sales tax to fund emergency response, passed with a simple majority.
Prop. 43 would not scrap existing taxes, but would apply to future tax initiatives. 
The Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, an anti-tax group that sponsored Prop. 43, argues the measure would close the loophole the court created and clarify that the requirement applies to all local special taxes. The two-thirds requirement has existed since 1849, when the state Constitution required a two-thirds vote for the state to borrow money, said Jon Coupal, president of the association. 
“The power to tax is (the) government’s most draconian power,” he told CalMatters. “The people of the state of California have made it a policy that when you are going to exercise that power, it should require a higher degree of consensus.”
But local government officials, labor unions and affordable housing advocates opposed the measure, arguing it would allow “minority rule” because it would only take a third of voters to block special taxes, making it harder for locals to connect revenue for essential services.
Darrell Roberts, president of the California Professional Firefighters union, called Prop. 43 an insurmountable roadblock to raising local funding, stressing that Los Angeles voters are voting this November on a half-cent sales tax to hire more firefighters. 
“The motivation behind Prop. 43 is clear. It’s the same motivation that is behind efforts to restrict mail voting and otherwise rig the system to prevent everyday citizens from having a say in their own government,” Roberts wrote in an op-ed.
Prop. 43 was sparked by opposition to the Los Angeles mansion tax, which added a 4% tax on real estate sales of more than $5.3 million and 5.5% on sales more than $10.6 million. The tax, approved by 58% of voters in 2022, has generated $1.4 billion in revenue for the city. 
Anti-tax advocates and businesses fought the tax, arguing it impeded local development, including affordable housing. Earlier this year, Coupal championed an extensive ballot measure that would have retroactively canceled out the mansion tax, but reached a last-minute compromise with the Democratically-led Legislature to put Prop. 43 on the ballot instead. 
Democratic legislators voted for the deal but have urged voters to reject it. Assembly Appropriations Chair Buffy Wicks, an Oakland Democrat who wrote Prop. 43, said she wrote it merely to kill a worse proposal.
“The clock was running out, and we had a choice to make: Leave a retroactive measure on the ballot that threatened billions in local funding, or accept a much narrower constitutional amendment that I still believed was bad policy,” she said.

title: What we’re watching today: 14 props, Congress in the balance
description: Election Day is here and it’s an exciting one. Tonight we’ll start to learn which party controls Congress in the final two years of President Donald Trump’s term, whether Californians want to tax billionaires and if Democrats will continue a run that dates to 2010 of winning every statewide office. We have reporters all over […]
text:
Ballots are sorted at the Los Angeles County Ballot Processing Center in City of Industry on June 3, 2026. Photo by Jae C. Hong, AP Photo




Election Day is here and it’s an exciting one. Tonight we’ll start to learn which party controls Congress in the final two years of President Donald Trump’s term, whether Californians want to tax billionaires and if Democrats will continue a run that dates to 2010 of winning every statewide office.
We have reporters all over the state and we’ll be posting updates all day and night. Here are a few stories we’re watching: 

How is voting going? As of Monday, more than a quarter of all ballots, or 26.44%, have been returned, according to the voter data firm Political Data Inc. That’s 3 percentage points higher than the November 2022 midterm election, when 23.34% of ballots were returned a day before Election Day.


Will contested ballots count? The Trump administration for weeks has been trying to set aside about 20,000 California ballots, alleging that some of them went to noncitizens. The U.S. Supreme Court on Monday denied the administration’s request to sequester the ballots. That’s a win for California officials who found flaws in the administration’s data and argued the Constitution grants to states the power to oversee elections.


What are Newsom’s poll watchers up to? Gov. Gavin Newsom will deploy 134 election attorneys to five congressional districts to preempt what the Democrat describes as potential election interference by federal monitors. The attorneys will be in the Sacramento area, the Central Valley, Orange County and San Diego and will stay “as long as necessary,” reported The Sacramento Bee. “We’re not screwing around, nor is (Trump),” said Newsom last week on a late-night show when he announced the plan.


What’s going on in the East Coast and Midwest?: House Republicans’ narrow lead could flip this election, and it could happen before Californians are done voting. Eighteen races in Iowa, Michigan, Ohio, New York, Pennsylvania and other states are considered tossups, and Democrats would need to secure 218 seats to eke out a slim majority. Flipping the Senate would be a taller order, and the party would need to nab four more seats for a majority.


Will there be a ‘red mirage?’: For close races in almost every major election, early returns show Republicans winning or faring better than expected. Then as more votes are tabulated, Democrats pull ahead. It happens in California too, reports CalMatters’ Ryan Sabalow, like during the June Los Angeles mayoral race. But that so-called red mirage wasn’t because California Democrats were rigging the election, but rather Republicans were turning in their ballots earlier and the state, like usual, took a long time to tally votes. This election might be a little different though, as Democrats have been returning their ballots earlier both in California and in other states.

We’ll be posting live updates all day so come to CalMatters for the latest news.
One more thing, if you haven’t voted — or know someone who is still making up their mind — there’s still time to check out our voter guide. 



Thank the CalMatters team this Election Day, for all their hard work to bring you and millions of California voters trusted and nonpartisan information. Our 501(c)(3) nonprofit newsroom is powered by people like you. Please give.

Other Stories You Should Know


New law to help families figure out college costs


Jackie Cordero in front of McHenry Library at UC Santa Cruz on Oct. 27, 2026. Photo by Jessica Parga for CalMatters




A new state law will empower college students to advocate for more financial aid, report Mariam Farag and Max Guerra for CalMatters.
Generally, students cannot receive more financial aid than the college’s published full cost for tuition, housing, food, books and related expenses. But often those estimates understate the cost by thousands of dollars. 
Starting the fall of 2027, colleges must explain how students can adjust the total cost of attendance so they can receive more financial aid, such as from state, federal or private sources.
Jackie Cordero, a student at UC Santa Cruz, is currently going through the process of requesting an adjustment to her cost of attendance. But the process has not been easy, and she’s struggled to provide financial documentation the school requested.

Cordero: “I still am a little confused about the process and approaching (the financial aid office) can be a little difficult.”

Read more.



CalMatters journalism — Live!


Agnes Varnum joins CalMatters as the Director of Editorial Events.




Some of the best stories come from a room full of people, and we’re thrilled to have someone who knows how to build live journalism experiences. Today, we’re welcoming Agnes Varnum as CalMatters’ new director of editorial events. She’ll lead our live events, from legislative conversations in Sacramento to our statewide Ideas Festival, and more to come.
Agnes is no stranger to the team. A few years ago, she helped us map out what events could look like at CalMatters. Now she’s sticking around to build them. She joins us after more than 15 years of bringing journalism off the page and into the room, including eight years running events at The Texas Tribune, where she ran their annual event program and was the director of the Texas Tribune Festival.
One moment she’ll never forget: The first morning the festival launched a new outdoor street fair, it poured. Sen. Amy Klobuchar of Minnesota spoke to a tent packed with people huddled around the stage, straining to hear, while water streamed down the street. Nobody left. Luckily the skies cleared, and the day went on to great success. 
Want to host a CalMatters event, or have a great idea? Reach her at agnes@calmatters.org.






California Voices
CalMatters columnist Dan Walters: State water regulators last week revised its water flow plan, and while Newsom is portraying it as a truce, it will most likely be just another chapter in California’s ongoing water wars. 
Votes from people who register to vote on Election Day count the same as everyone else’s, so it’s a mistake to overlook the nearly 1 million young Californians who are eligible to vote but are unregistered, writes Laura Brill, CEO and founder of The Civics Center.

name: California
title: California’s legislative races put tech-backed Democrats and Republican gains to the test
description: California voters are deciding whether Republicans will hold onto seats they flipped in 2024 and whether business-backed groups can help elect more moderate Democrats.
text:
In summary
California voters are deciding whether Republicans will hold onto seats they flipped in 2024 and whether business-backed groups can help elect more moderate Democrats. 


The results of Tuesday’s election aren’t expected to topple the Democratic supermajority in either house of the state Legislature, but they will offer a window into two major questions: Can Republicans hold on to the legislative seats they flipped in 2024? And, will Big Tech and big business succeed in electing pragmatic moderates over more liberal Democrats?
Republicans are fighting to hold onto the modest gains they made in 2024, which party leaders attributed to their message resonating particularly with Latino voters. Republican-aligned independent expenditure committees are spending big to keep them.
It’s been a record year for outside spending by independent expenditure committees, led by Grow California, funded by billionaire investors Chris Larsen and Tim Draper, and California Leads, funded by Meta and Google. Both groups say they hope to be a counterforce to unions, which have responded with millions in election spending this year. 
Assembly
All 80 seats in the state Assembly are up for election to two-year terms this year. Sixty-seven assembly members are running for re-election, and there are 13 open seats.  
Here’s a look at some key races:
Assembly District 7
Republican incumbent Josh Hoover faces retired teacher and superintendent Amy Slavensky, a Democrat, for this seat representing areas of northeast Sacramento County, including Citrus Heights, Folsom and Rancho Cordova. Independent expenditure committees spent close to $3.5 million supporting Hoover and opposing Slavensky. Hoover’s supporters include business groups, cardrooms and the Legislative Action PAC, a business-backed committee formed by Republican strategists.
Registration: Democratic 37%, Republican 32%, no party preference 22%
Assembly District 12
 Marin County Supervisor Eric Lucan is going head-to-head with Rohnert Park City Councilmember Jackie Elward in this expensive Democratic showdown to represent all of Marin County and about two-thirds of Sonoma County. Grow California has spent more than $2.5 million supporting Lucan and has continued to spend heavily even after he asked them to stop at the beginning of October. 
Registration: Democratic 58%, Republican 15%, no party preference 19%
Assembly District 27
Former Merced mayor and attorney Mike Murphy, a Republican, is battling Democratic Fresno County Supervisor Brian Pacheco in this open seat vacated by a Democrat. Republicans are targeting the majority-Latino district encompassing parts of Merced, Madera and Fresno counties, which President Donald Trump carried in 2024 by 2.7%.
Registration: Democratic 40%, Republican 28%, no party preference 24%
Assembly District 36
Republican Incumbent Jeff Gonzalez is trying to hold on to the seat he flipped in 2024. His challenger is Democratic Imperial mayor Ida Obeso-Martinez, a nurse practitioner. The district covers Imperial County and a large part of Riverside County, as well as portions of the eastern Coachella Valley. It went for Trump in 2024 by 1.4%.
Registration: Democratic 41%, Republican 29%, no party preference 23%
Assembly District 47
Democrat Leila Namvar, a public arts analyst for the city of Indio, brings the financial backing of the Democratic Party to her challenge to Republican incumbent Greg Wallis. The purple district combines Republican-leaning areas near Redlands with the Democratic enclave of Palm Springs. Independent expenditure committees funded by Google, Meta and oil and gas companies have spent millions supporting Wallis and attacking Namvar.
Registration: Democratic 39%, Republican 33%, no party preference 20%
Assembly District 58
The most heated race so far this cycle is between Republican incumbent Leticia Castillo and Democratic challenger Clarissa Cervantes, a Riverside city councilmember. The two are back for a rematch after Castillo flipped the traditionally Democratic seat in 2024. The district includes parts of San Bernardino and Riverside counties. Attack ads have targeted Cervantes’ prior DUI arrests and claims about drug use, while a Democratic strategist’s X post about an old adult entertainment site run by Castillo rocked Sacramento politicos.   
Registration: Democratic 42%, Republican 27%, no party preference 23%
Assembly District 68
Perhaps the most expensive race this year is between two millennial Democrats on the Santa Ana City Council: David Penaloza and Jessie Lopez in a district that includes parts of Anaheim, Orange and Santa Ana. Penaloza, the more moderate candidate, is endorsed by the California Democratic Party and supported by the new tech-backed PACs, while Lopez is backed by Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders and the Working Families Party. Outside groups have spent $9.1 million since the primary, according to the California Target Book.  
Registration: Democratic 48%, Republican 22%, no party preference 24%
Senate
Half of the 40 Senate seats are up for election to four-year terms. Eleven senators are up for re-election, and several members of the Assembly are running in the nine contests without an incumbent.
Senate District 16
Democratic incumbent Melissa Hurtado is spending big from her campaign committee to fend off a challenge from Republican Guillermo Gonzalez, a small business owner and a former aide to Republican Rep. David Valadao. The Central Valley district includes portions of Fresno, Kings, Tulare and Kern counties and went for Trump in 2024 by 8.9%. Legislative Action California, funded by Google, AT&T and oil and gas companies, has spent millions supporting Gonzalez. 
Registration: Democratic: 39%, Republican: 29%, no party preference: 24%
Senate District 24
In the battle to succeed Sen. Ben Allen, Brian Goldsmith, an entrepreneur and former senior adviser for the pro-Israel advocacy group Democratic Majority for Israel, faces fellow Democrat John Erickson, a West Hollywood city councilmember and former vice president of Planned Parenthood Los Angeles. The coastal Los Angeles district includes Malibu and Santa Monica. This Senate race has seen the most outside spending — $8.5 million — since the primary, mostly for Goldsmith, according to the California Target Book. 
Registration: Democratic: 49%, Republican: 21%, no party preference: 23%
Senate District 26
Two Democrats are vying to replace departing progressive Sen. María Elena Durazo in this deep blue Los Angeles district. Community college trustee Sara Hernandez faces Sarah Rascón, a planning commissioner for East Los Angeles. Outside special interest groups spent nearly $7.4 million, almost all of it to support Hernandez; only $419,000 went toward Rascón.
Registration: Democratic: 60%, Republican: 11%, no party preference: 23%
Senate District 40
Democrat Mara Elliott, a former San Diego city attorney, is competing to replace termed out Senate GOP Leader Brian Jones in the San Diego-area district. She faces Republican challenger and former Assembly candidate Kriste Bruce-Lane. Elliott is overwhelmingly backed by Democratic power brokers and labor groups, who have spent more than $1 million to support her and oppose Bruce-Lane, who’s affiliated with conservative advocacy group Reform California. 
Registration: Democratic: 35%, Republican: 33%, no party preference: 24%

name: Mississippi Today
title: ‘Lost in the System’: What it’s like to be stuck for months in a Mississippi Jail
description: At the end of June 2026, Hinds County’s jails had 131 people waiting more than six months without a charging decision from a prosecutor, including 56 who had been held over a year, an analysis by The Marshall Project found.
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
Mississippi is one of only a handful of states that have no limit on how long someone accused of a felony can sit in jail while waiting for a prosecutor to formally charge them.
Cases can be delayed for many reasons. Judges have crowded dockets. Retrieving evidence from the police can take months. But before all that, a district attorney must decide whether to move forward with a case once an arrest has been made. In Hinds County, prosecutors routinely take months — or sometimes years — to do so.
Altogether, these conditions leave people waiting in jail, unsure what’s taking so long or when there will be an update in their case.
Public defenders say the people who end up stuck in jail typically fall into one of three categories: people who can’t afford their bail, people denied bail by the judge, and people with mental health challenges that need to be addressed before they can be released.
The Marshall Project spoke to three men who have waited for months at the Raymond Detention Center without formal charges — known as an indictment — after they were arrested for nonviolent offenses. During this period, their lives have been in limbo: losing jobs, time with family, and their health, all while sitting without answers inside a notoriously dangerous jail currently under the control of a federal court-appointed administrator.
Credit: Kayla Salisbury for The Marshall Project
When you can’t afford your freedom: Depaul Davis, 412 days
September 2026 marked one year that Depaul Davis has been waiting on an indictment. Davis, who has long struggled with homelessness, said he was working day labor jobs to try to scrape together enough money to secure permanent housing when he was arrested last year.
A judge set Davis’ bail at $75,000. Bail bondsmen typically take $7,500 upfront, but that was far beyond his ability to pay. Without any family to turn to for help, his only choice was to remain in jail, waiting to see if prosecutors would take his case to a grand jury. In Mississippi, the district attorney’s office cannot pursue felony charges without an indictment from a grand jury.
“I was staying on the streets, trying to keep labor jobs, waiting to get on a Section 8 housing program,” Davis said. “I couldn’t afford a lawyer, couldn’t afford anything.”
Davis said he only expected to be in jail for about two weeks after making his first court appearance last year. Twelve months later, what’s most frustrating isn’t the roaches, or the countless nights spent sleeping on the floor of an overcrowded cell — it’s that behind bars, his life is frozen, unable to pick up work or continue his search for a real home.
“I was looking at apartments on Highway 80, trying to get housed so I could get stable,” he said. “It can get old, staying at a hotel just one or two days until you run out of money.”
He knows the first step is finding a steady job, maybe something in the service industry. Then, he said, he wants to go back to school for business or hospitality management. He dreams of one day running the hotels he used to sleep at just to get one night of clean sheets and a shower.
More than anything, he said, he wants to get out so he can begin taking steps toward turning his life around. “Life can tear at you in so many different ways,” Davis said, and he’s tried his best to endure the wait gracefully. But at times, it can be hard to comprehend how a whole year has gone by without any movement on his case.
“I can get a little impatient, trying to understand. It’s just frustrating because I can’t make progress,” he said in September. “I’m 29 now, and I don’t want to be found in this same situation at 30 years old.”In October, Davis turned 30. Still in jail.
Credit: Kayla Salisbury for The Marshall Project
When the judge won’t set your bond: Malik Sterling, 254 days
On his 29th birthday, Malik Sterling found himself in jail and only able to see out of one eye.
Roughly two weeks earlier, Sterling was riding a dirt bike for the first time when he flew off the bike, severely injuring his left eye. He had surgery scheduled with an eye doctor to try to save it. But days before his appointment, he was arrested.
An arrest on a nonviolent charge would typically mean the possibility of release on bail, but a judge gets the final say. In Sterling’s case, the judge disqualified him from bail because of a prior felony charge. If the previous case was still open, it would make Sterling ineligible for bail in Mississippi. His lawyer, however, argued in a July motion that the court closed the old case months ago.
But Sterling was still denied bail and has been sitting in jail since February, waiting for prosecutors to decide what to do with his case.
Jail officials wouldn’t let Sterling go to his scheduled medical procedure, he said, delaying treatment another two months before he was finally allowed to see an outside doctor. By then, it was too late to save his eye.
“The only thing they said they could do for me was remove it,” said Sterling, whose left eyelid now droops over a milky surface. “I done lost everything, including the eye.”
Neither the county sheriff nor the court-appointed receiver responded to multiple requests for comment about Sterling’s access to medical care. The receiver, Wendell France, is barred by a federal judge from making public comments.
In addition to his vision, Sterling said he’s felt the loss of the past seven months in nearly every area of his life, from finances to family to his sense of stability.
“Everything I had going before I came here, I lost. All I’ll be coming home to is the pair of clothes [I came in with]. I can’t go to school, can’t go to work,” he said. “I ain’t got nothing to go back to. I just hope my loved ones are there for me when I get home.”
Sterling used to see his 5-year-old son and 4-year-old daughter — whose nickname is tattooed above his right eyebrow — every weekend. But without any way to load money into his account on the jail’s phone, Sterling rarely speaks to them anymore.
“I liked to buy them things, like if they do good on their report cards, but I can’t now because I can’t fend for myself financially,” he said. Last time they spoke, Sterling said, his son wanted a Paw Patrol truck, while his daughter hoped for a Barbie doll. “But I can’t do nothing for them,” he sighed. “I got nothing.”
Before his arrest, Sterling mainly worked odd jobs: cutting grass and landscaping or washing cars. He’d planned to start school online and pursue a business degree, but he can’t continue his education until he gets out of jail. In the meantime, he said, the connections and repeat customers he built up while working have fallen away.
“I’m basically just like a dead body to the world,” Sterling said, adding that the hardest part has been waiting without a clear end date. He asked his attorney for a timeline — any sense of when the district attorney’s office might decide whether to pursue his case — but he knew that nothing was certain in a court system rife with lag and delay.
“Most frustrating is not knowing: how long it’ll be, when I can go to court. I’m just sitting here,” he said. “I don’t got no court date, I don’t know nothing … As of now, I’m just lost in the system.”
Credit: Kayla Salisbury for The Marshall Project
When your mental health leaves you stuck in the system: Kahari Thicklen, indicted after 135 days
Kahari Thicklen didn’t know his symptoms — erratic behavior, mood swings — had a name when he entered jail in April 2026.
Thicklen now realizes he has a mental health condition and described the coping mechanisms he plans to rely on to rebuild his life once he’s out of jail: mainly, seeking quiet environments where he can better manage his thoughts and emotions. But even though his mood and behavior stabilized, 24-year-old Thicklen continued to sit in jail waiting on an indictment.
“Because of my mental health, it’s taken time to figure out a good solution,” Thicklen said in September, adding that he was nevertheless surprised to still be sitting in jail after nearly 5 months. “I did think it would take a little shorter time, maybe more like 2 months… but I know [in this legal system], anything can happen.”
While in jail, Thicklen missed his only child’s first birthday in August. He said he tries to call his sister, who has custody of the baby, daily to speak to his son — but it’s not the same as holding him or looking into his eyes, watching him develop from an infant to a toddler.
Equally challenging, Thicklen hasn’t been able to work while in jail; he spoke of the debts he imagines piling up while he sits in his cell, from medical bills to car insurance.
“It’ll take a toll on you,” he said. “Some days you might wake up depressed, some days you might wake up mad, and some days you’ll be okay.”
Before his arrest, Thicklen worked warehouse jobs and most recently drove forklifts for an auto manufacturer. Eventually, he plans to go back to school, ideally in a hands-on trade like culinary school or welding. But he said his first step will be getting a job in a familiar industry and trying to make enough money to clear the hundreds of dollars in debt that’s likely accumulated while he’s been stuck behind bars.
In August, the district attorney’s office indicted Thicklen on only one of the three charges he was initially arrested for, and declined to act on the remaining allegations. Because prosecutors are not legally required to dismiss them, those charges could linger on his record forever.
“In their minds, it’s not their problem to clean up his record,” Thicklen’s attorney said in September. “But a kid who had a mental health episode does not need to be here, sitting in one of the most dangerous jails in the state.”
Thicklen has since been moved to another facility, with a trial date scheduled for March 2027, according to his lawyer and court records.
When asked about the first thing he’ll do whenever he gets out, Thicklen said: “Call my job and try to get back on the schedule.” But he acknowledged there was no guarantee his old employer would take him back after so many months off the job.
“If I can’t go back there, I’ll go somewhere else,” he said resolutely, before pausing. “I just hope it doesn’t take too long.
This article was published in partnership with The Marshall Project, a nonprofit news organization covering the U.S. criminal justice system.
