title: Ohio Supreme Court layout could change with election results
description: With the results of Tuesday’s general election, the Ohio Supreme Court could become a 7-0 fully Republican bench, keep the status quo of one Democratic justice, or see a slight shift with a second Democrat. Two justices are attempting to defend their seats: Republican Justice Dan Hawkins and Democratic Justice Jennifer Brunner. Should Hawkins and […]
text:
The Gavel outside the Supreme Court of the State of Ohio. (Photo by Graham Stokes for Ohio Capital Journal. Republish photo only with original article.)With the results of Tuesday’s general election, the Ohio Supreme Court could become a 7-0 fully Republican bench, keep the status quo of one Democratic justice, or see a slight shift with a second Democrat.
Two justices are attempting to defend their seats: Republican Justice Dan Hawkins and Democratic Justice Jennifer Brunner.
Should Hawkins and Brunner defend their seats, the court would remain a 6-1 Republican majority. If Brunner loses to her Republican opponent, the court would then be a full Republican panel. If Hawkins is defeated, his Democratic opponent would make the bench a 5-2 Republican majority.
The Ohio Supreme Court races are listed under partisan labels on ballots due to a law passed in 2021 by the Republican majority Ohio General Assembly. Justices and judges who ran for the seats still spent significant time on the campaign trail promoting their impartiality and deference to state laws, along with judicial independence as a vital part of their branch of government.
Justices on the state’s highest court are the last arbiters for appeals from lower state courts, and they consider cases that contain questions about violations of the Ohio Constitution. The most recent panel of justices has seen topics ranging from redistricting, data centers, and education, to abortion, victim’s rights, and gender-affirming care.
Brunner is the only statewide elected Democrat currently in office. Her opponent on Tuesday is a former Franklin County Common Pleas judge, Republican Colleen O’Donnell.
O’Donnell is also a former immigration judge, who presided over asylum cases in Laredo, Texas. As part of her campaign, she touted the fact that she never granted asylum for anyone during her tenure.
The Republican won a tight primary election in a crowded field that included appeals court judges. She and her opponents in the primary support “originalism,” a judicial method that promotes seeing the U.S. Constitution and other founding documents as concrete ideas, and judging cases based on views the writers had on the documents when they were written.
“I do not take the view that the Constitution, for example, is a living, breathing document, and so I honor both substantive and procedural judicial restraint,” O’Donnell told the Capital Journal in May.
The former common pleas and immigration judge served in the Ohio Attorney General’s Office, clerked for a federal judge and worked in private practice before being appointed to serve as judge in the Franklin County Common Pleas Court. She became an immigration judge after she left the Franklin County court in 2023.
Brunner has been on the bench since 2021, and has been the sole Democrat since the 2024 defeat of former justices Michael Donnelly and Melody Stewart. Before coming to the supreme court, she was a judge on the 10th District Court of Appeals, and the Franklin County Common Pleas Court. She also served as Ohio Secretary of State.
The justice is currently suing the state to repeal the law that applied partisan labels to the supreme court races.
Brunner told the Capital Journal before the election that she sees it as a First Amendment issue which causes voters to assume she agrees wholesale with the Democratic platform.
“And I’m not in in a position to say, ‘well, it’s more nuanced here,’ or ‘no, it’s not the same here,’ or even ‘yes, it is the same,’ because I’ve got the code of judicial conduct,” Brunner said in August.
First District Court of Appeals Judge Marilyn Zayas decided to fight to the seat currently held by Hawkins. As her Democratic campaign moved past the primaries, she said she felt a different energy in the 2026 election.
“I’m seeing how we are losing faith in our court because of politics, and politics has no place in our Ohio Supreme Court,” Zayas said at the Ohio Democratic Party’s primary event in May.
Hawkins was elected in 2024, taking over for fellow Republican Justice Joe Deters. Deters chose not to run for re-election, but to run for the seat that was held by Justice Melody Stewart. He previously served on the Franklin County Court of Common Pleas.
On social media, he campaigned with the idea that there would be no special treatment or “gray areas” in his method of judging.
“The moment justice becomes selective it stops being justice,” a post on his Facebook page stated. “That is a line this court will never cross while I’m on the bench.”

name: California
title: Californians vote on nation’s first wealth tax on billionaires
description:
Some of the state’s wealthiest residents have spent hundreds of millions to defeat Prop. 40, the “billionaire tax.”
Supporters say billionaires should pay their “fair share” and help fund social services.
text:
In summary
Some of the state’s wealthiest residents have spent hundreds of millions to defeat Prop. 40, the “billionaire tax.”
Supporters say billionaires should pay their “fair share” and help fund social services. 



California voters are deciding whether the state will levy a first-of-its-kind tax on billionaires. 
If it passes, Proposition 40 would assess a one-time 5% tax on the net worth of the state’s roughly 200 billionaires, targeting their stocks, bonds, business holdings and other valuable personal property. 
Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West, the union pushing the measure, says it would generate an estimated $100 billion for healthcare and education to be spent over the next five years. The nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office estimates the tax would raise “tens of billions of dollars” over several years, well short of the union’s projection, and says billionaires leaving the state could cut income tax revenue by less than $1 billion a year.
The results could also be complicated by two competing ballot measures: Propositions 41 and 42. Proponents of those measures designed them to conflict with Prop. 40, which means if either countermeasure receives more votes than Prop. 40, it nullifies the billionaire tax.
The union and other supporters argue that billionaires should pay their fair share to support social services programs the Trump administration cut last year. 
From the outset, Prop. 40 revealed divisions in the Democratic Party and galvanized some of Silicon Valley’s wealthiest executives to spend hundreds of millions to defeat it.
Gov. Gavin Newsom became one of its earliest opponents, attempting through backroom negotiations to keep Prop. 40 off the ballot altogether. He endorsed Prop. 42, the billionaire-backed countermeasure designed to ban all wealth taxes in California and kill Prop. 40. Newsom, along with a cadre of Democratic allies such as Planned Parenthood of California and the California Teachers Association, argued a one-time tax would not solve the state’s fiscal woes and would drive wealthy residents out of state.
Despite party and labor divisions, the California Democratic Party and California Federation of Labor Unions supported the initiative and opposed its counter measures, arguing the state needs more revenue to shield workers and everyday Californians from the effects of dramatic federal healthcare cuts expected to kick 2 million residents off health insurance.
Billionaire opponents spend heavily
Billionaire opponents and business interests poured $316.7 million into the campaign to stop Prop. 40 — including support for Props. 41 and 42 — telling voters nearly the same message: Wealthy residents who contribute jobs to the economy and income tax to state coffers have already left, and more will follow if the initiative passes. They also made a largely misleading claim that lawmakers could lower the threshold of the wealth tax to include everyday Californians.
Google co-founder Sergey Brin led the opposition, publicly moving out of state and donating $102 million to Building a Better California, a political committee he founded to oppose the tax. The group has served as a passthrough for other billionaire donors to oppose Prop. 40. 
Billionaire tax opponents also placed Props. 41 and 42 on the ballot.
Prop. 41 prohibits the state from collecting taxes that circumvent the state spending limit set in 1979, which Prop. 40 is designed to do. It also requires the state to audit future tax proposals before they reach voters and identify potential spending cuts in the programs they’d fund.
Prop. 42 prohibits the state from taxing financial assets, private businesses, pensions and other forms of wealth. It also prohibits retroactive taxes. These provisions directly conflict with the billionaire tax.
The state constitution dictates that when there are multiple competing ballot measures on the same ballot, the one that receives the most votes wins, nullifying its competitors. 
Allegations against healthcare union’s leader
Prop. 40 is the brainchild of Dave Regan, president of Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West. He has been mired in scandal in recent months. Some members of SEIU California, the political umbrella organization representing the healthcare workers union, have accused him of threatening and intimidating women over the years and of attempting to “extort” support for the measure, according to an internal investigation commissioned by SEIU California and SEIU, the union’s national parent organization.
Separately, the California Primary Care Association, which represents clinics and opposes Prop. 44, another ballot measure run by Regan’s union, alleged in a recent lawsuit that the health workers union violated anti-racketeering laws in part by asking clinics to support the billionaire tax in exchange for killing the clinic initiative.
The union and Regan have called these allegations “categorically false” and characterized them as a “smear campaign” designed to derail the billionaire tax. 
If Prop. 40 survives, billionaires who lived in California on Jan. 1, 2026 would be assessed the tax based on their net worth as of Dec. 31, 2026. Payments would be due in one lump sum or in installments over five years.
Supported by the California Health Care Foundation (CHCF), which works to ensure that people have access to the care they need, when they need it, at a price they can afford. Visit www.chcf.org to learn more.

name: California
title: Know a young adult? Tell them in California you can register and vote on Election Day
description: An estimated 1.4 million young Californians who are eligible to vote are not registered. Many just need a little help or a push but don’t receive it.
text:
Guest Commentary written by

Laura Brill
Laura W. Brill is the CEO and founder of The Civics Center, a nonpartisan nonprofit promoting young voters. She is also an attorney and clerked for Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg.


My email inbox is full of news about poll results, and increasingly they’re about California. Likely voters, they say, are leaning this way or that on various ballot measures or in the race to be mayor of Los Angeles or our state’s next governor.
One thing the polls never discuss is the unregistered voter. I’m not talking about people who are ineligible or who have chosen not to participate. I’m talking about the roughly 1 million young people in California who are eligible to vote but no one has helped them to register. 
That means they aren’t in the voter files, so pollsters deem them “unlikely” to vote. 
For many that’s not because of an inherent lack of interest in politics. Candidates and campaigns often make no real effort to reach them and get them registered. Nor does anyone else.
It’s a vicious cycle. It’s also a big mistake. 
In California — as in at least 20 other states and Washington D.C. — eligible voters have a right to show up on Election Day, get registered and cast their ballots. Their votes count the same as yours, mine and everyone else the pollsters have deemed “likely” to vote.
A huge number of the missing voters are young. Let’s start with the youngest: Based on state voter files and American Community Survey data, there are nearly 300,000 18-year-old Californians who are eligible but not yet registered to vote. That’s 56% of California’s 18-year-olds.
But it’s not just 18-year-olds. The California Secretary of State reported recently that more than 4 million eligible adults of all ages were not registered to vote. But among California’s 4.2 million citizens who are almost 18 to 25 years old, 1.4 million are unregistered (California allows teens to pre-register as early as age 16).
Same-day and early registration voting means they still have a chance to make choices today. 
Why are the youngest voters routinely excluded in this way? It’s not as if there’s no money available to welcome them to our democracy and help them cast their first ballots. 
Ballotpedia reported last week that nearly $800 million had been spent on California’s ballot measures — and that doesn’t include money spent on candidate campaigns. Imagine if just a fraction of that went to educating the youngest voters about the issues on our ballot and to get them ready to weigh in.
The numbers tell us the opportunity for engagement is there. The Civics Center looked at the voter files for four states with same-day registration on Election Day, including California. All four experience a huge spike in 18-year-olds registering to vote on that final day versus any other day of the year.
And this probably won’t come as a surprise, but people who register to vote close to an election tend to turn out at high rates, our analysis found. That’s the reason they are getting registered in the first place — they want to vote.
The next time you read a poll, instead of worrying or seeking reassurance about our favored candidate or ballot measure, we should ask: Who is missing and what can we do to fix that? 
I’d also love to ask the pollsters: How do you know young unregistered Americans are unlikely to vote, when you don’t poll them in the first place?

name: California
title: In California governor’s race, voters choose between experienced liberal and upstart conservative
description: Polls have for months widely favored Democrat Xavier Becerra for governor in the most populous Democratic state in the country. Republican Steve Hilton is banking on dissatisfaction with the cost of living to get independents and even some liberals to consider him.
text:
In summary
Polls have for months widely favored Democrat Xavier Becerra for governor in the most populous Democratic state in the country. Republican Steve Hilton is banking on dissatisfaction with the cost of living to get independents and even some liberals to consider him.


Californians are choosing their next governor: a longtime liberal politician pitching his government experience or a Republican first-time candidate vowing to dramatically upend Democratic power structures. 
The race between Democrat Xavier Becerra and Republican Steve Hilton to succeed Gov. Gavin Newsom is one of the most consequential on the ballot. Polls for months have put Becerra ahead of Hilton by double digits, a predictable lead in a state with nearly twice as many registered Democrats as Republicans and where a Republican hasn’t won a statewide office in nearly two decades. 
Hilton, a former Fox News host who has urged voters to end “16 years of one-party rule,” is banking on frustration with the state’s high cost of living to drive undecided voters, independents and even some Democrats to support a Republican for a change. 
He represents the best hope in years for a GOP victory. He has raised more than $33 million to Becerra’s $38 million and is running hard on a series of ambitious promises to lower costs by slashing regulations and taxes. He portrayed Becerra as the embodiment of the California political status quo, someone who would make decisions that benefit influential special interest groups like organized labor. 
“It’s the people against the machine,” he said of his campaign in a virtual town hall last week. 
His message of change, promises to slash gas prices and frequent invocations of Californians moving out-of-state resonated with Brad Gerig, who voted in Roseville last week. It was the first time Gerig, 34, could recall voting for a Republican, he said. The EMT and firefighter said he wants to be able to afford to stay and raise a family in California, so he was willing to “try something different.”
“I think it’s worth a shot,” Gerig said. “I think for everybody living in this area there’s an inherent angst for a little bit better. There’s no reason it should be as expensive as it is.”
But Hilton has struggled to rid himself of the baggage from President Donald Trump’s endorsement in a state Trump lost by 20 percentage points in 2024.
Becerra has reminded voters of Hilton’s link to Trump at every turn, and cast himself as a fighter who would, like Newsom, challenge decisions in Washington such as Trump’s aggressive deportation campaign. 
He has dismissed Hilton as unserious and primarily campaigned on his longtime experience representing Los Angeles in Congress and serving as state attorney general and as U.S. health secretary. Those roles have earned him a wide swath of influential liberal allies.  
“Xavier Becerra has stood with us for more than 30 years,” said Tony Hoang, executive director of the LGBTQ+ rights organization Equality California, at an event in San Francisco last week. 
He highlighted Becerra’s role as one of the small minority of congressmembers who voted against the anti-gay marriage Defense of Marriage Act in 1996. 
At the same event, Becerra touted his opposition to Trump.
“Donald Trump is on this ballot,” he said, without naming his opponent once. “We see right through you, Donald Trump. And we see through all those MAGA friends and relatives who are trying to push that agenda on us.”
Becerra’s comfortable standing is reflected in the relatively muted nature of his campaign: Becerra agreed to meet for only one debate with Hilton this fall. He has spent much of his time campaigning not for himself but against a Republican-backed voter ID measure and on behalf of other California Democrats. 
The election comes at a particularly delicate time for California. 
Street homelessness rose for years and only began to decline again in 2025. Wildfires have made it harder to buy homeowners insurance. Inflation, much of it attributable to Trump’s warin Iran, tariffs and immigration crackdown, have added to the already-high cost of living.
The state budget, always subject to the boom and bust of the stock market, has become particularly dependent on the fortunes of the artificial intelligence industry. Under Newsom, the state has made aggressive regulatory moves to curb the use of climate-warming fossil fuels. But despite recent polling that shows a majority of Californians support the green transition, fewer are willing to pay higher prices for energy than were a decade ago.
And the state’s liberal politics have often put it in the crosshairs of the Trump administration, which has withheld federal funds, challenged California’s environmental policies and attempted to intervene in this election. 
Both candidates agree the state has become unaffordable for working families. That’s about all they agree on.
Becerra has proposed mostly incremental changes to existing state policies, such as continuing recent efforts by Newsom and lawmakers to reduce the bureaucratic hurdles to approving new housing construction. 
He wants to expand state mortgage assistance programs and said he’s committed to the clean energy transition, but open to delays or tweaks to trim costs. He has not endorsed any new taxes on residents, but wants the state to assess a fee on corporations whose employees make so little they qualify for public healthcare. 
Hilton, a British American who was once a close adviser to former British Prime Minister David Cameron, ran on a deregulatory agenda, promising to slash environmental rules and the gas tax and allow more home construction on exurban, undeveloped land. 
One of his signature campaign promises was to eliminate the income tax on residents’ first $150,000 in earnings and make the income tax flat above that — amounting to an expensive tax cut for the highest earners that he’s said he would pay for with spending cuts. It’s one of his many promises that would need legislative approval, and he has not said how he would get Democrats in the Capitol to support them.

name: California
title: Prop. 5: Will California voters change the rules for recall elections?
description: Democrats want to make recalls simply about whether an official should be recalled, not about who should replace them. The contest looked to be a toss-up going into Election Day, with the no side holding a small edge.
text:
In summary
Democrats want to make recalls simply about whether an official should be recalled, not about who should replace them. The contest looked to be a toss-up going into Election Day, with the no side holding a small edge. 


California voters are weighing in on whether to change the state recall process that allows voters to remove elected officials from office before the end of their terms.
Proposition 5 would break the recall process into two parts: Voters would first decide in an election whether an official should be removed from office. If successful, they’d vote again in a follow-up election on who should replace the recalled official. Under the current system, voters are asked both questions at the same time. 
Democratic lawmakers placed the constitutional amendment on the ballot in 2024. It was endorsed by Gov. Gavin Newsom, who survived his own attempted recall in 2021. 
The outcome of Prop. 5 was far from certain going into Election Day: 45% of people polled in mid-October by the Public Policy Institute of California said they would vote for it, while 52% said they wouldn’t. The numbers were more even than voters’ response at first blush — a similar poll in early September found 59% of likely voters said they likely would vote no and just 35% said they would vote yes.
Where Prop. 5 came from
In the aftermath of the failed recall of Newsom in 2021, Democratic lawmakers and Secretary of State Shirley Weber began advocating for changes to the process. The Newsom recall effort cost taxpayers about $200 million, and another $100 was spent in the campaign to stop the recall by Newsom’s potential replacements to get their message out to voters. Newsom walked away unscathed, with 62% of voters electing to keep him in office. 
Weber and good governance groups argued the current system leads to unnecessary state expense, confuses voters, and can lead to ‘undemocratic’ outcomes, since the winner needs a plurality of the vote, not the majority, to win. 
They supported Senate Constitutional Amendment 1, authored by Democratic Sen. Josh Newman, who was recalled himself in 2018. The effort became Prop. 5 when Democratic lawmakers passed it in 2024. Republican lawmakers voted against it, arguing the reform was not needed, would dilute the power of voters and lead to additional special election costs because of the need to hold two elections. 
Unlike some of the tax measures on the ballot that have spurred multimillion-dollar spending sprees, no group has spent any money on the effort, according to CalMatters campaign finance tracker. 
Although recalls are often initiated, they rarely make it to voters. Only 11 recalls have made it to the ballot in California since 1913, and only six have been approved by voters. The current recall process is how Republican Gov. Arnold Schwarzenegger came into power, replacing Gray Davis in 2003.

title: Should California voters be required to show their ID to cast a ballot?
description: California voters will decide if they should prove their citizenship in order to vote under Proposition 39.
text:
In summary
California voters will decide if they should prove their citizenship in order to vote under Proposition 39.


In the laundry list of measures on the November ballot, few have stood out more than a GOP-backed initiative to require government identification to vote. 
California voters are deciding on Proposition 39, which would require voters to show a government ID, such as a driver’s license, at polling places. For mail ballots, voters would need to write the last four digits of their Social Security or other government-issued number. Prop. 39 would also require county election officials to annually check their voter rolls for noncitizens, and the state would be required to provide a free voter ID card for voters upon request.
The measure has amassed $37 million in support from Republicans nationwide, and could be a bellwether for similar initiatives in other states.
There is widespread consensus among experts that voter fraud is rare in California, and election officials, including Secretary of State Shirley Weber, have said such claims are unfounded. 
What do supporters say?
Backers say requiring voter ID would be a small yet meaningful step to help deter voter fraud and guarantee California’s elections are secure. They also note that 36 other states require or recommend some form of identification to vote, according to the National Conference of State Legislatures, although only 10 states are considered strict about it.
Republican San Diego Assemblymember Carl DeMaio put the measure on the ballot in tandem with his right-wing political group Reform California after similar previous failed attempts in the state Legislature. He and others have emphasized national polling that shows bipartisan support for voter ID requirements.
“We’ve structured this initiative based on what voters across the political spectrum would want,” DeMaio told CalMatters in March.
The measure qualified in March after proponents collected more than the 875,000 signatures required to put the initiative on the November ballot.
The California Republican Party and Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association are major endorsers, and major donors include packaging magnate Richard Uihlein, who’s contributed $17 million, and Airbnb co-founder and White House official Joe Gebbia, who’s given $8 million. 
Southern California businessman Steven Bray and Reform California each contributed more than $3 million.
What do opponents say?
Prop. 39 detractors argue that showing voter ID is a needless hurdle that would prevent eligible voters from casting ballots. Critics include a coalition of civil rights, voting and good governance groups who say ID requirements are unnecessary because noncitizen voting and impersonation is rare. People who recently moved or changed their last name might not yet have an updated ID and would be unfairly kept from voting, groups such as Common Cause and the American Civil Liberties Union claim.
“There is no widespread noncitizen voting that would justify adding these strict requirements,” League of Women Voters of California Executive Director Jenny Farrell said.
Opponents also point to its potentially high expenses to the state. The measure could cost tens of millions to the low hundreds of millions of dollars to implement, according to the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office.
Democratic heavyweights have played a big role in putting a public face to the opposition. U.S. Gov. Gavin Newsom and Sen. Adam Schiff stumped at No campaign events across the state, as well as gubernatorial favorite Xavier Becerra who created a committee with Assembly Speaker Robert Rivas to raise money to oppose it.
The Democratic Party is the biggest donor at nearly $6.5 million of the opposition’s $35 million total. California labor and tribal groups have given more than $2 million each. Philanthropists Quinn Delaney and Patty Quillin combined have given $3 million.

name: California
title: Will Democrats control Congress? Their path runs through California. Watch these races
description: These are the most consequential U.S. House races in California, which could determine control of Congress as well as the future direction of the Democratic Party.
text:
In summary
These are the most consequential U.S. House races in California, which could determine control of Congress as well as the future direction of the Democratic Party.


California voters will play a key role in determining which party controls the U.S. House of Representatives, and by how much, as voting for the 2026 midterm election concludes Tuesday.
Democrats are poised to flip at least three seats currently held by California Republicans after voters approved Proposition 50 last year, which redrew five of California’s districts to favor Democrats as a countermeasure to pro-Republican gerrymandering in Texas. 
The remaining two redrawn districts — one in the Central Valley and the other in San Diego and Riverside counties — are more competitive, even though Democrats outnumber Republicans in voter registration.
A handful of races feature progressive challengers seeking to oust longtime incumbents who could push the party to the left if they are successful. 
Several California congressional races are expected to be close, as counties tabulate ballots received up to seven days after Election Day. 
Here’s what CalMatters is watching:
Central Valley, San Diego area seats pivotal
California’s most hotly contested race features 12-year Republican incumbent Rep. David Valadao of Hanford, a dairy farmer and perpetual target for national Democrats, and political newcomer Randy Villegas, a political science professor. 
Democrats hope Villegas, who is endorsed by Sen. Bernie Sanders and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, can defy conventional political wisdom and win in the historically conservative, agriculture-heavy Central Valley. Villegas supports Medicare for All and universal child care, although he has also called to suspend federal taxes on gas and diesel.
Valadao, the lone remaining Republican who voted to impeach President Donald Trump after the Jan. 6, 2021 riots, is seeking his seventh term. He touts the importance of bipartisanship and independent thinking, but has faced tough questioning over his decision to support Trump’s megabill that will ultimately strip health care coverage from more than 2 million Californians in the next four years.
Further south in San Diego and Riverside counties, two local elected officials — Marni von Wilpert, a Democratic San Diego City Council, and Republican San Diego County Supervisor Jim Desmond — are competing to fill the seat of Republican Rep. Darrell Issa, who chose to retire rather than seek reelection in a redrawn district. 
Von Wilpert and Desmond are running traditionally centrist campaigns that harken to pre-Trump politics. Von Wilpert has eschewed the insurgent progressive left and instead campaigned with former Vice President Kamala Harris. Desmond has worked overtime to distance himself from Trump and the president’s MAGA rhetoric, despite receiving Trump’s endorsement. 
Public polls have consistently shown von Wilpert with a slight lead over Desmond, and the nonpartisan Cook Political Report switched the race from “tossup” to “lean Democrat” back in March. Internal campaign polling suggests the race is close.
Progressives try to remake Democratic Party
Several California races feature two Democrats because of the state’s top-two primary election system. 
Among the most-watched is the race to succeed former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi, who has endorsed Connie Chan, a San Francisco supervisor. Chan, a Chinese immigrant from Taiwan, is known for opposing urban development that could displace tenants or disrupt a neighborhood’s character. She faces state Sen. Scott Wiener, a prolific legislator who has authored several laws to expedite housing production and secure competitive wages on state-subsidized projects. 
In the Sacramento area, an intergenerational “battle of the ages” is underway between Rep. Doris Matsui, 82, and Sacramento City Councilmember Mai Vang, 41. Matsui has a massive financial advantage and has loaned her campaign $4 million since the primary. Vang has political momentum as a young, insurgent progressive who is media savvy and able to directly engage with supporters via TikTok and Instagram.
And in Los Angeles, incumbent Rep. Jimmy Gomez faces a challenge from Democratic Socialist Angela Gonzales-Torres. The five-term congressmember won the June primary by double digits but has bled support amid a House ethics investigation into allegations of sexual assault, which he’s denied. A recent poll showed Gonzales-Torres leading 51% to Gomez’s 45%.
Upsets in Prop. 50 districts could endanger majority
Three incumbent Republican or former Republican lawmakers are expected to lose their jobs in the wake of Prop. 50.
Either Rep. Young Kim or Rep. Ken Calvert, who are both competing for California’s 40th District, will be left jobless. Gerrymandering drastically reshaped Calvert’s 41st District, but rather than retire, he chose to challenge his colleague Kim. Both scrambled to “out-Trump” the other in the primary election but Kim has since returned to a more centrist, fiscally conservative approach.
Rep. James Gallagher, who succeeded the late Rep. Doug LaMalfa in representing the rural north state in the 1st Congressional District, is poised to lose to former Senate President ProTem Mike McGuire, a Democrat. The district was redrawn to remove several conservative and rural areas near the Oregon-California border. 
Rep. Kevin Kiley, who left the Republican Party earlier this year, is seeking reelection in the 6th Congressional District rather than his former 3rd District, which was significantly reshaped to favor Democrats. He faces Dr. Richard Pan, a physician and former state senator running as an anti-Make America Healthy Again candidate. Kiley hopes to pull votes from Republicans, independents and moderate Democrats.

name: California
title: California adopted a new water plan. It’s unlikely to end the state’s water wars
description: The state's Water Resources Control Board passed a revised water flow plan, but both farmers and environmentalists dislike it. Newsom wants to portray it as a truce.
text:
Gray Davis became governor in 1999 and one of his first acts was to decree that there would be no major changes in water policy for eight years, which he assumed would be his two terms in office.
Davis, a veteran politician who had climbed the political ladder one rung at a time, was well aware of the decades-long stalemate on the fundamental issue of how water should be apportioned between farmers and flows to support fish and other wildlife. He was also notoriously averse to political conflict and didn’t want what had been dubbed “water wars” to be rekindled during his governorship.
Davis was recalled five years later and the conflict continued after his departure. During Jerry Brown’s second stint as governor, from 2011 to 2019, he embraced the concept of “voluntary agreements.” If farmers would reduce diversions from the Sacramento and San Joaquin rivers and their tributaries, they could avoid the mandatory cutbacks that environmental groups and their allies favored.
Gavin Newsom continued down that path after succeeding Brown. With just two months remaining in his reign and a likely presidential campaign to follow, Newsom wants to claim that he settled the perennial water conflict. It would pave the way for construction of a tunnel that would carry Sacramento River water under the Sacramento-San Joaquin Delta and into the California Aqueduct.
Last week, the state Water Resources Control Board passed a revised water flow plan, officially renamed the “Healthy Rivers and Landscapes Program,” but the agricultural stakeholders who had originally accepted the concept backed away, saying it contains too much regulation.
“It’s unrecognizable,” said Jennifer Pierre, general manager for the State Water Contractors, which represents public water agencies serving 750,000 acres of farmland and 27 million people. 
Meanwhile, environmentalists, who had never liked the voluntary agreements approach, renewed their call for more direct regulation of flows into the Sacramento-San Joaquin Delta.
“This plan fails the four million people living in the Delta, the 12 million more who live in the greater San Francisco Bay Area, and all Californians,” Barbara Barrigan-Parrilla of Restore the Delta, said. “Implementing the voluntary agreements will further diminish their economies, public health, and access to clean water.”
Thus, what Newsom would like to portray as a truce will most likely be just another chapter in an ongoing battle, probably shifting to the courts. A legal conflict would probably bring into play a question that both Brown and Newsom have wanted to avoid: whether the state’s regulation of water legally supersedes water rights, some of which date back to the 19th century.
The new policy’s already shaky viability also must contend with still another unknown — opposition from President Donald Trump’s administration. The state shares jurisdiction over water allocation with the federal Central Valley Project and the new policy is meant to cover federal water deliveries.
Through both of his stints in the White House, Trump has taken the side of farmers in their political and legal battles over water. The Feds control more water than any other player, and the U.S. Bureau of Reclamation has publicly echoed farmers’ criticism that the plan is regulatory overreach and possibly illegal.
Moreover, the plan assumes that its projects to improve water flows and wildlife habitat will be partially financed by the federal government.
That said, Trump’s presidency will end in two years and the chances of having a state-level plan finalized by then are nil, so the federal side of the water conflict will likely depend on which party wins the presidency in 2028. Thus, the success or failure of Newsom’s presidential quest — assuming there is one — could be the decisive factor in California’s water conflict.

name: California
title: Will Californians vote to save more tax revenue in rainy day fund?
description: Prop. 2 would allow California leaders to sock away up to 20% of the state’s general fund tax revenue, double the current cap of 10%. It would also require the state to save more when revenue is growing faster.
text:
In summary
Prop. 2 would allow California leaders to sock away up to 20% of the state’s general fund tax revenue, double the current cap of 10%. It would also require the state to save more when revenue is growing faster.


California’s booming stock market is bringing in billions of dollars in unexpected tax revenue.
Proposition 2, or the Save for California’s Future Act, aims to shore up the state’s rainy day fund by allowing state leaders to save up to 20% of the state’s general fund tax revenue, up from the current ceiling of 10%. 
The state would also be required to save more when revenue is growing faster, and allow state lawmakers to use some of it to pay down California’s $20 billion in federal unemployment insurance debt. 
Supporters say saving more now would help the state weather a future economic downturn. 
California has been stuck in a boom-or-bust state budget cycle because its tax revenue depends heavily on wealthy residents’ stock market earnings. Some economists have warned the current economic boom may not last, and the state could face deeper budget uncertainties due to federal budget cuts and potential tax filing delays triggered by natural disasters.
Gov. Gavin Newsom and Democratic legislators spearheaded Prop. 2, which is also endorsed by labor unions, chambers of commerce and a coalition of advocates for healthcare, housing and transit. 
“If you don’t have a rainy day fund, then what happens is you get forced to contemplate cuts to core essential services,” said Assembly Budget Chair Jesse Gabriel, an Encino Democrat.
But opponents, including most Republican lawmakers, say saving more would only embolden legislators to spend more. The state should refund taxpayers during a good year, not set the money aside, they argue.
“When they say we’re here for fiscal responsibility, it’s like the devil offering a Bible study. Don’t buy it,” said Assemblymember Carl DeMaio, a San Diego Republican.
California leaders and voters have historically established reserves several times, but always quickly withdrew all the funds during budget crises. In 2014, voters approved a law that required the state to save more aggressively and made it harder to withdraw money. 
The law requires the state to set aside 1.5% of its general fund revenue and any spikes in capital gains tax revenue each year for reserves and paying down debts. State lawmakers are allowed to withdraw up to half the balance from the reserves when the governor declares and the Legislature ratifies a budget emergency, unless they’ve already done that the previous year and the emergency remains. There are no limits on what lawmakers can spend the money on.
Prop. 2 would keep those rules and allow the state to save more. Critics say state leaders have too much leeway in spending the money. 
David Crane, a former economic adviser to former Republican Gov. Arnold Schwarzenegger, said the rules let “governors bake in spending based on optimistic forecasts, knowing they can always dip into reserves if revenue falls short.”

name: California
title: We went to court to check on California illegal voting cases. Here’s what we learned
authors: By Marek Warszawski of KVPR; Eli Chavez of KCRW of Tyche Hendricks, KQED and Noah Abrams, KRCB
description: Experts say the federal government must prove that noncitizens intentionally violated election law. Regardless, defendants may face dire immigration consequences.
text:
In summary
Experts say the federal government must prove that noncitizens intentionally violated election law. Regardless, defendants may face dire immigration consequences.


A 51-year-old business owner and father of seven was the first of more than three dozen California residents to appear in court to face allegations by the federal government that they violated voting laws because they are not U.S. citizens.
Camilo Giles Jimenez, a U.S. legal permanent resident from Mexico who, according to the criminal complaint, has lived outside Kerman, in Fresno County, since at least 2017, pleaded not guilty to three misdemeanor counts Wednesday afternoon in federal court in downtown Fresno. The government charges say he voted in three elections in violation of the law that bans noncitizens from voting for president or Congress. 
During the 10-minute hearing before Judge Stanley A. Boone, federal public defender Erin Snider said Jimenez, who was dressed in a peach polo shirt, faded jeans and white Nike sneakers, owns a paving company. Neither Jimenez nor Snider answered questions from reporters.
Justice Department officials announced the charges against Jimenez and 27 other California residents on Oct. 19 as part of a coordinated effort they said was designed “to root out fraud” in U.S. elections and protect electoral integrity. On Monday, the department announced charges against 12 more people in California. 
Many of the defendants are not charged with illegally voting, but with illegally registering to vote or lying on their naturalization applications. 
More court appearances are set for the coming days and weeks. 
Legal experts say that to gain convictions for illegal voting prosecutors must prove that these people willfully committed a crime, which could be difficult. Regardless of any criminal convictions, even legal residents could be deported whether or not they knew they were breaking the law.
The cases
Twenty-three of hose accused are from Southern California, six are from the Bay Area, four are from the Sacramento region and seven are from Fresno County and the Central Valley. 
One of those arrested in the mid-October sweep, 72-year-old Omar Muñoz of Commerce, told KCRW that six police vehicles, a helicopter and at least six reporters arrived at his home just after 5 a.m. on Oct. 19. 
“It’s a show,” Muñoz told the station. “I said, ‘Wow!’ I said, ‘I’m not a killer.’”
Omar Muñoz is one of over two dozen people in California charged with voter fraud. Photo by Eli Chavez, KCRW
Muñoz was still wearing pajamas when he was shackled around the waist and legs and transported to downtown Los Angeles. He was released that afternoon but would not speak to the specifics of the charges against him.
Justice department officials have said these indictments are the tip of the iceberg in what they allege is widespread voter fraud in California. 
“Every illegal vote cancels out the vote of a lawful American citizen,” Acting Deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter said in a news release. “Each of the 28 defendants charged today appears on the list of more than 20,000 likely noncitizen registrants we provided to California election officials last week. California refused to look at that list. Today’s charges show exactly what that refusal puts at risk.”
Wednesday, a federal judge sided with California by rejecting a bid by the Trump administration to separate out any ballots sent in from people on that list. The decision by U.S. District Judge David Carter is a setback for the federal government in its efforts to exert more control over state-run elections ahead of the Nov. 3 midterm. On Monday, the Supreme Court denied an appeal by the Department of Justice to wade into its fight with California over voter rolls.
“Never before in American history has the federal government, on the eve of an election, sought to coerce a state and local government to abandon their own Constitutional elections procedures and bend to the will of the Executive Branch,” Carter wrote in his 26-page decision. “In bringing this lawsuit, the Executive would have this Court believe that it reigns as a sole sovereign. But California and its people are sovereign, too.”
The California Newsroom tried to speak with many of the defendants, and their lawyers, but except for Muñoz, all inquiries were turned down or received no response.
In its case against Jimenez, the government alleges the Fresno County resident submitted a voter registration application to the Fresno County Registrar in 2022, and checked a box indicating he is a U.S. citizen. Jimenez is also accused of voting in recent elections.
The complaint says Jimenez subsequently told agents that he registered to vote after receiving his green card. Jimenez also said that he had been voting since 2023, according to the complaint, although he denied ever claiming he was a citizen.
Standard of proof
To prove its case against Jimenez and the other defendants, the government must show they deliberately broke federal law by voting as noncitizens, according to UCLA law professor Rick Hasen.
The federal statute prohibits anyone who isn’t a U.S. citizen from voting to elect the president or members of Congress. Doing so is punishable by up to one year in prison, a fine or a combination of both.
“In order to violate the statute, there has to be proof that the person did so intentionally,” Hasen said. “That is, they knew they were not eligible, and they did it anyway.”
For example, Hasen said it is not necessarily considered intentional if a government office, like the Department of Motor Vehicles, mistakenly offers someone who is not a citizen the chance to register to vote.
“Suppose you are told by a government official you can register to vote, even if you’re not a citizen, and the person registers, then they might be doing so knowing that they registered but not knowing that they were violating the law,” Hasen added.
Even a statement that a defendant makes acknowledging that he or she voted would not automatically prove the government’s case, Hasen said. Prosecutors must still show defendants were knowingly and willfully breaking the law.
He said successful prosecutions or guilty pleas by noncitizens accused of voter fraud are rare.
“It seems to be a very small problem relative to the number of voters in the country,” Hasen said, adding that it is more about, “trying to make an example of some people, rather than showing evidence that there’s a massive problem of election fraud in the United States.”
Potential immigration consequences
While intentionality is key to a criminal case, it may not matter when it comes to immigration consequences. Regardless of whether someone meant to break the law, unlawful voting and falsely claiming to be a citizen, including by signing a voter registration form, can be grounds for deportation and for denial of an application for U.S. citizenship. 
Many of the people charged have lived in the U.S. legally for years and are in the process of applying for citizenship, according to the federal complaints against them. That could now be denied to them, even if the government doesn’t move to deport them.
Stanford University Law Professor Jennifer Chacón says that one reason noncitizen voting is rare, is because the price to pay is so steep.
“The fact that these individuals can be criminally prosecuted, barred from naturalization, subject to deportation, all demonstrates why, as a general rule, noncitizen voting is not a problem,” she said, “because there are many, many consequences to it, and people are generally aware of that.”
Federal prosecutors said that the names they provided in California are only a small fraction of a wider problem. “We are investigating thousands of more similar cases throughout the nation,” Bill Essayli, U.S. Attorney for the Central District of California, told reporters. 
While the Department of Justice has emphasized that the number of noncitizens charged with voting and related offenses has grown to more than 150 in this Trump term from a total of 13 under Biden’s entire term, other analysts point out that it is small compared to the number of registered voters.
California has 23 million voters, Attorney General Bob Bonta noted, saying those who face charges in the state are “just a drop in the bucket numerically, and it makes the point that there is no widespread voter fraud.”
Speaking on KQED’s Forum program, Hasen cast doubt on the federal government’s statements. “What I think they’re actually trying to do,” he said, “is to project the image that there’s a widespread voter fraud problem in this country, and to kind of mimic the claims that President Trump has made, that noncitizens are voting in droves and affecting the outcome of elections.”
This story was reported by KVPR, KCRW and KQED with The California Newsroom, a collaboration of public media outlets that includes NPR, CalMatters, KQED (San Francisco), LAist and KCRW (Los Angeles), KPBS (San Diego) and other stations across the state.

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: Our polling shows strong support for statewide restrictions on cellphones in schools. Will the Legislature act?
authors: Tatishe Nteta, Jesse Rhodes, Jesse Usher-Barrett, and Sydney Brake
description: Local school districts, including the state’s largest district, are increasingly moving forward on their own, creating a patchwork of local policies in the absence of statewide action.
text:
IN RECENT YEARS, support for restricting cellphone use in the nation’s public schools has grown dramatically. According to the National Conference of State Legislatures, 42 states, Washington, DC, and Puerto Rico have passed legislation restricting cellphone use in K-12 public schools.
Proponents of these bans cite studies that find they improve classroom dynamics, with teachers in schools that have instituted stricter restrictions reporting greater satisfaction, less disruption, and more focused classrooms. 
However, opponents note that research on student outcomes, including test scores, attendance, and bullying, has found limited effects. They point to studies showing that, in the years after these bans were instituted, some schools saw increases in disciplinary actions such as suspensions, and argue that these bans adversely affect parents’ ability to communicate with their children, particularly during emergencies and for children with medical conditions or disabilities.   
In the Commonwealth, about 80 percent of the state’s school districts have adopted some form of cellphone policy or restriction, according to the Massachusetts Association of School Superintendents. Boston Public Schools, the state’s largest school district, recently announced plans for a “comprehensive bell-to-bell ban on all personal electronic devices,” which includes phones, laptops, tablets, smartwatches, and smartphones, beginning at the start of the 2027-28 school year. 
Are these policies popular among residents of the Bay State?  Since 2024, we have asked a representative sample of Massachusetts residents, “Do you support or oppose restricting the use of cellphones by public school students during official school hours, except for an emergency or a medical condition or disability?”  We find widespread support for these restrictions, with about 3 in 4 residents expressing support for the ban in four surveys since October 2024, as shown in the figure below

In our most recent poll, close to eight in 10 expressed support for these restrictions, and the policy is supported by majorities of all gender, generational, class, and racial groups. 



Restrictions on cell phones are overwhelmingly popular among Democrats (79 percent), Republicans (80 percent), independents (74 percent), liberals (83 percent), moderates (75 percent), conservatives (79 percent). Put in terms of the last presidential contest, restrictions are backed by identical shares of Harris (79 percent) and Trump (79 percent) voters. 



Notably, parents are especially supportive, with 86 percent of adults with children under 18 supporting restrictions, compared with 76 percent of those without children under 18. 
Our findings are largely consistent with a December 2025 EdTrust-Massachusetts poll conducted by the MassINC Polling Group, which also found broad majority support for a ban on cellphones and smartwatches.   
To date, the Legislature has debated the issue, but not passed legislation.  
Proposals to restrict cellphone use in schools have passed in different forms in the House and Senate. They must be reconciled by a conference committee of House and Senate members before the session ends on January 5 or the process will have to start over in the new two-year legislative session begins after that date.   
Meanwhile, local school districts, including the state’s largest school district, are increasingly moving forward on their own, creating a patchwork of local policies in the absence of statewide action. 
With the public strongly in support of restricting cellphone use in schools, state legislators on Beacon Hill can be confident that legislation creating a uniform, statewide policy on cellphone use would be well-received. 
Tatishe Nteta is Provost Professor of Political Science at the University of Massachusetts Amherst and director of the UMass Poll. Jesse Rhodes is a professor of political science at UMass Amherst and co-director of the UMass Poll. Jesse Usher Barrett is a PhD student in political science at the UMass Amherst and a graduate research fellow for the UMass Poll. Sydney Brake is a PhD student in political science at UMass Amherst and a graduate research fellow for the UMass Poll.
