name: Tennessee Lookout
title: From governor to Congress to Senate speaker, how the Lookout is following TN’s midterm election
description: Tennessee will elect a new governor in Tuesday’s election, but down-ballot races for the U.S. House and the state legislature could also affect congressional map redrawings and the election of the next state Senate speaker.  Polling suggests the Democratic Party nationwide is expected to have a strong night nationally, but how that translates to Tennessee, [[...]
text:
Democratic candidate Allie Phillips, pictured in Clarksville on the final day of the early voting period in Tennessee, is running for one of several state House districts Democrats hope to flip. (Photo by John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)Tennessee will elect a new governor in Tuesday’s election, but down-ballot races for the U.S. House and the state legislature could also affect congressional map redrawings and the election of the next state Senate speaker. 
Polling suggests the Democratic Party nationwide is expected to have a strong night nationally, but how that translates to Tennessee, a state that President Donald Trump won by nearly 30 percentage points in the 2024 election, is a major question. 
Any Democratic upsets of GOP incumbents in the Tennessee state Senate could decide who Republicans elect as the speaker to replace retiring Lt. Gov. Randy McNally. 
Tennessee’s Senate speaker automatically becomes the lieutenant governor and first to take over in case the governor is incapacitated. 
Tuesday’s election will also be the first time Republicans’ new gerrymandered U.S. Congressional map will face an electoral test, and Democrats in the state House are looking to gain seats for the first time in 30 years. 
Here’s what reporters at the Lookout will be watching Tuesday night.

SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX. 
Does Blackburn crack 50% in the governor’s race? Can independent Hatley hand a win to Democrat Jerri Green? 
Tennessee hasn’t elected a Democrat to a statewide office since 2006, when Gov. Phil Bredesen won reelection. As the GOP nominee, Blackburn is favored to beat Democratic nominee Memphis City Councilmember Jerri Green. 
But independent candidate David Hatley has spent almost $12 million of his own money to make it a three-way race. Hatley, a hot tub mogul from Washington County and self-described conservative, could play spoiler if he pulls votes from Blackburn. 
For Hatley to become a true spoiler, he will need more than 20% of the vote. But if he gets around 10%, he could force Blackburn to become the first person elected governor of Tennessee since 1938 to not receive 50% of the vote.
State Senate races in Knoxville, Murfreesboro, Memphis and Chattanooga could make or break Johnson’s speaker bid
Senate Majority Leader Jack Johnson, a Franklin Republican, has been spending heavily on a handful of colleagues this year as he faces Sen. Paul Bailey, a Sparta Republican, in a tight battle Nov. 10 for the Senate speaker’s seat.
Johnson’s PAC contributions this year dwarf Bailey’s by about $450,000 to $63,900, yet the two lawmakers are believed to be separated by only one vote in the speakership race, with two or three uncommitted senators as the caucus election draws near.
It will take 14 votes within the 27-member caucus to capture the Senate speaker’s post unless a Republican incumbent is upset on election night.
Spoilers or contenders? Two independent candidates for TN governor try to shake up the race

Tennessee’s Senate is skewed toward Republicans, who control 81% of the seats, despite Democrats receiving around 34% of the presidential vote in 2024. Only seven of the seats held by Republicans have a partisan lean of less than 60% toward the GOP.
Traditionally, seats with less than 60% GOP support have a higher chance of flipping in a wave election, and four of those are up for election this cycle. Sens. Richard Briggs, Brent Taylor, Bo Watson, and Dawn White hold those seats, but each is barely under the 60% threshold.
Johnson’s political action committee, JACK PAC, has spent money on campaign advertising or given direct contributions to all four members. During the general election, he has spent around $35,000 supporting White and more than $28,000 attacking Taylor’s Democratic opponent.  
Johnson said Monday he is not trying to shore up support in advance of the caucus election.
“My focus is on electing Republicans and protecting our Senate Republican supermajority so we can continue advancing conservative policies important to Tennesseans,” Johnson said in a statement to the Lookout.
Bailey’s PAC has donated to White’s PAC, but he hasn’t spent any money on advertisements to boost candidates or attack their Democratic opponents. His PAC also gave to Sens. Ferrell Haile, Bill Powers and Ed Jackson.
The PACs for Johnson and Bailey have given to former House member Jimmy Matlock, who is expected to win the seat being vacated by Lt. Gov. Randy McNally. 
The Cook Political Report described a recent gerrymander of Tennessee’s 9th Congressional District as “brutally effective.” Sen. Brent Taylor, left, a Shelby County Republican, will test that against Democratic state Rep. Justin Pearson, right. (Photo by John Partipili/Tennessee Lookout)
Will the May gerrymandering of Tennessee’s U.S. House map hold?
Republicans are trying to stretch their U.S. House majority in the state from 8-1 to 9-0, after redrawing the state’s map in May, following a ruling by the U.S. Supreme Court that states with a history of racial discrimination no longer had to create majority-minority congressional districts.
The new map created nine districts that Trump carried in 2024 by at least 60%. Cook Political Report, an independent news outlet that analyzes federal races, rated all of Tennessee’s districts as Solid Republican. 
But national Democrats are spending money to contest U.S. House Districts 5 and 9.
Taylor, an Eads Republican, faces Memphis Democratic Rep. Justin J. Pearson in the 9th District race.
Former Tennessee Agriculture Commissioner Charlie Hatcher, a Republican, faces Chaz Molder, Columbia’s Democratic mayor, in a race for U.S. House District 5. 
One sign of hope for Democrats is that in a statewide U.S. Senate race in 2018, the last midterm election when Trump was president, under the current district lines, Democrats narrowly lost both districts 5 and 9 by less than 0.5%.
Democrats are trying to flip three state House seats, GOP two
Democrats will not gain a majority in the state House, but the party is trying to flip seats in Clarksville, Knoxville and Memphis in several 2024 rematches.
The most flippable is a Memphis district held by GOP state Rep. John Gillespie. The District 97 seat is the only one a Republican holds in the state legislature that former Vice President Kamala Harris won in the 2024 presidential election. 
Gillespie is matched up against Democrat Jesse Huseth again this year after narrowly defeating him in 2024.
Republicans’ top pickup opportunity is a Clarksville seat held by Democratic state Rep. Ronnie Glynn. Trump carried the District 67 seat in 2024, but Glynn won a narrow 131-vote victory that same year. 
Other potential opportunities for Democrats include a district in Knoxville where Republican state Rep. Elaine Davis faces Democrat Bryan Goldberg, another 2024 rematch.
Democrats also plan to challenge a Clarksville seat, where Republican state Rep. Michael Lankford faces Democrat Allie Phillips. Phillips ran in 2024 against the late state Rep. Jeff Burkhart. Lankford was appointed in December to serve out the rest of Burkhart’s term after his death. 
Republicans also want to flip a seat in Nashville’s suburbs that Harris won with just over 50% of the vote. Democratic state Rep. Caleb Hemmer held the seat for the past four years, but he chose not to run this cycle. Democrat Mark Proctor faces Republican Bill Hancock.

name: Alabama Reflector
title: It’s time: Alabamians go to polls for critical midterm elections
description: Voters across Alabama go to the polls Tuesday to elect officials, legislators and judges in over 160 federal, state and local elections. Alabamians will choose their first new governor in nearly 10 years, with Republican nominee Tommy Tuberville, the state’s senior U.S. Senator, facing Democratic nominee Doug Jones, his predecessor on Capitol Hill.  All seve[...]
text:
A sign saying "Vote" is seen at Messiah Lutheran Church in Montgomery, Alabama on May 19, 2026. Voters in Democratic and Republican primaries on Tuesday selected nominees for over 160 federal and state offices. Alabamians go to the polls Tuesday to cast ballots in the 2026 midterm election, where more than 160 races are on the ballot across the state. (Anna Barrett/Alabama Reflector)Voters across Alabama go to the polls Tuesday to elect officials, legislators and judges in over 160 federal, state and local elections.
Alabamians will choose their first new governor in nearly 10 years, with Republican nominee Tommy Tuberville, the state’s senior U.S. Senator, facing Democratic nominee Doug Jones, his predecessor on Capitol Hill. 
All seven U.S. House districts are contested, and four of them have different boundaries than the 2024 election. The U.S. Senate seat is also contested. There are four statewide constitutional amendments on the ballot. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Sample ballots for all 67 counties can be found on the Secretary of State’s website. Voters can find which legislative district they reside in here. 
Alabama Reflector’s voter guide, breaking down each statewide, federal and legislative race, can be found here.
The ballot
Tuesday’s election is a rematch of Jones and Tuberville’s 2020 Senate race where Tuberville won by 20 points. Alabama is considered a solidly Republican state. But three recent polls showed Tuberville ahead of Jones by smaller margins than 2020. 
Two polls released on Oct. 20 were Republican leaning: The Alabama Poll, run by Michael Lowry, a former aide to U.S. Rep. Robert Aderholt, R-Haleyville, and a poll conducted by the right-leaning Cygnal for Alabama Daily News and Gray Television. Each found 51% of respondents said they would likely vote for Tuberville, and 39% for Jones, leaving about 9% undecided. The margin of error for each was 4% and 4.38%, respectively.
A poll released Wednesday by Democratic-leaning firm Blueprint Polling showed the race as a toss-up. It surveyed 695 likely Alabama voters, 48% of whom indicated support for Tuberville and 45% for Jones, with 7% undecided. The poll has a 3.72% margin of error. 
Of the seven U.S. House races, Alabama’s 2nd Congressional District in southeast Alabama has drawn the most national attention. After the U.S. Supreme Court this spring weakened the Voting Rights Act in a case known as Louisiana v. Callais, the Alabama Legislature reverted to a 2023 congressional map, previously struck down as racially discriminatory, for the 2026 election. The map change triggered a special primary election in August after a special session of the Legislature. 
The 2023 map reduced the Black voting-age population in the 2nd district from 48.7% to 39.9%. It was considered an opportunity district for Black Alabamians in 2024, leading to the election of U.S. Rep. Shomari Figures, D-Montgomery. His election marked the first time in the state’s history voters sent two Black Alabamians to Congress. 
Rep. Rhett Marques, R-Enterprise, who was a candidate in Alabama’s 1st Congressional District before the special primary, has been a state legislator for eight years. He won the Aug. 11 special primary election with more than 50% of votes in a field of six Republicans. 
The new district was rated R+7 and was expected to be a fairly easy Republican pick-up. But Figures outraised Marques, and the favorable national environment for Democrats prompted the non-partisan Center for Politics to rapidly shift the race in favor of the incumbent over the last week and a half. The center on Monday moved the race from “Toss up” to “Leans Democratic” in its final ratings. 
Each party hopes to pick up some seats in the state Legislature, focusing in Madison and Montgomery counties, and the Birmingham area. There are also 16 open seats in the Legislature due to retirements, lawmakers seeking other offices or incumbents losing primaries, but not all are contested. 
Across both chambers, six independent candidates qualified for five districts. All 140 legislative seats are on the ballot, but only 17 Senate and 36 House seats are contested with state-qualified candidates.
Each constitutional office and federal legislative race is also contested. 
Voters will also decide on four statewide constitutional amendments. There are additional amendments that only apply to specific counties, which can be found on respective sample ballots. 
Although Alabama does not have early in-person voting, voters can cast an absentee ballot through the mail. Absentee voting is up in some of the state’s larger counties. More than 3,000 voters applied for an absentee ballot in Baldwin County, and nearly 2,600 returned their ballot as of Monday morning, according to the Baldwin County Circuit Clerk’s office. In 2022, about 2,200 voters cast an absentee ballot in the coastal county, according to the Alabama Secretary of State’s Office. 
More than 4,100 voters applied for an absentee ballot in Montgomery County, and more than 3,500 returned their ballot as of Monday afternoon, according to the Montgomery County Circuit Clerk’s office. In 2022, about 2,500 voters cast an absentee ballot in the Capitol’s county, according to the Alabama Secretary of State’s Office. 
A message seeking comment with Secretary of State Wes Allen was left Monday morning. 
How to vote
When do polls open?
Polls will be open from 7 a.m. to 7 p.m. on Tuesday. 
Where do I find my polling place?
The Alabama Secretary of State’s website allows you to check voter registration and the location of your polling place. You can find it here.
What do I need to vote?
Voters must present a valid photo ID before voting. Valid forms of ID include: 

Alabama driver’s license (not expired or expired less than 60 days)
Alabama Law Enforcement Agency digital driver’s license
Alabama Non-Driver ID (not expired or expired less than 60 days)
Alabama Photo Voter ID card
State-issued ID (Alabama or any other state)
Federal-issued ID
U.S. Passport
Employee ID from the federal government; state of Alabama; county; municipality, board or other entity of Alabama
Student or employee ID from a public or private post-secondary educational institution in Alabama or other states (including colleges, universities, postgraduate technical and professional schools)
Digital student or employee ID from a public or private post-secondary educational institution in Alabama or other states (including colleges, universities, postgraduate technical and professional schools)
Military ID
Tribal ID

What happens after Tuesday?
The candidate with the most votes will be the officeholder for that office’s term. For state offices, that is four years. For candidates running for the U.S. House of Representatives, that is two years, and six years for the U.S. Senate.

name: Tennessee Lookout
title: Federal Election Day observers headed to Tennessee
description: Teams of federal election monitors will be present in Tennessee on Tuesday as part of the Trump administration plan to “oversee federal voting protections and investigate potential election fraud,” according to a Justice Department spokesperson. About 1,000 monitors will be deployed across the country, with a presence in each state, according to the spokespe[...]
text:
The Department of Justice is dispatching 1,000 election observers across the nation, with a presence in each state including Tennessee. Pictured: Voters line up in a Clarksville poll during the last day of the early voting, Oct. 29. 2026. (Photo by John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)Teams of federal election monitors will be present in Tennessee on Tuesday as part of the Trump administration plan to “oversee federal voting protections and investigate potential election fraud,” according to a Justice Department spokesperson.
About 1,000 monitors will be deployed across the country, with a presence in each state, according to the spokesperson, who declined to share how many will be present in Tennessee or in which counties. 
“We will not share the full list until Election Day,” the spokesperson said. “Every monitor will merely observe and report any potential violations of federal law to the Department, which will be reviewed after Election Day.”
Shelby County Election Commissioner Linda Phillips confirmed Monday that she had received notification federal monitors will be at Memphis polling locations.
“No reason has been shared regarding why our county was selected, but we are one of three Tennessee counties to receive the notice,” Phillips said in a statement. Phillips  noted the last time election monitors were present in Memphis and Shelby County was 2018. 
Phillips did not identify the other Tennessee counties. A spokesperson for Tennessee Elections Coordinator Mark Goins did not reply Monday to questions about other counties federal monitors are expected to visit.
DOJ observers not uncommon
The presence of DOJ monitors on Election Day is not uncommon, voting rights experts said. Yet the Trump administration decision to deploy 1,000 across the nation, and in each state, is a significant expansion of the federal presence, according to the Campaign Legal Center, a nonpartisan legal advocacy organization. During the 2026 primary, the DOJ dispatched monitors to 11 states. 
The monitors are DOJ employees. Because the Trump administration is deploying so many this year, it has tapped employees outside of the DOJ’s civil rights division and those with voting rights experience who have typically served as election monitors in the past, according to the Campaign Legal Center.
Federal poll workers are charged with observing polling places and documenting compliance with federal civil rights laws such as the Voting Rights Act. They are subject to the same state laws as private and volunteer election observers: they have no authority over poll workers or election officials, cannot interfere with a voter’s right to cast a ballot, attempt to influence votes or intimidate voters. 
“They’re not allowed to enforce state law,” said Adam Altendorf, organizing director of Organize Tennessee, a nonpartisan organization that trains volunteer election observers. They are also not allowed to enforce federal law, he said.
“They’re not allowed to really talk to voters until after they’re done voting,” he said. “They’re prohibited, of course, from engaging in any sort of political activity.”
Altendorf noted that Tennessee would also have many volunteer and bipartisan election monitors on hand to observe polling sites, including observing federal polling workers, too.
“This isn’t the first time DOJ has sent poll monitors to Tennessee,” he said. “They were here in 2018 and in 2016 as well, so it’s not new, but I think it’s a new DOJ for a lot of folks. That’s why we have poll monitors, especially everywhere in Shelby County, because in some cases we’ll be making sure everyone’s following the rules.”
Reporter Cassandra Stephenson contributed.

name: West Virginia Watch
title: Many WV SNAP recipients will have two sets of work requirements to keep food assistance, healthcare
description: Many low-income state residents will soon be required to meet two sets of work requirements — one to keep healthcare and another for food assistance — according to an analysis from the West Virginia Center on Budget and Policy.
text:
A sign advertises that SNAP benefits are accepted at a Hornbacher’s in north Fargo, North Dakota, on July 7, 2026. (Photo by Ceilidh Kern/For the North Dakota Monitor)Many low-income state residents will soon be required to meet two sets of work requirements — one to keep healthcare and another for food assistance — according to an analysis from the West Virginia Center on Budget and Policy. 
About 84% of state households that rely on the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program include a person who’s on Medicaid, according to the Center’s analysis of American Community Survey data from 2020 through 2024. 
In the years 2020 through 2024, an average of 127,400 West Virginia households received SNAP. Of those, about 107,300 households — or 84% — included someone with Medicaid coverage. The data does not indicate how many of the Medicaid recipients are part of the expanded program. 
About 49,000 West Virginia households with children received both Medicaid and SNAP. 
As of Jan. 1, 2027, both programs will have work requirements. Under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, people who are on expanded Medicaid through the Affordable Care Act will be required to work or volunteer for 80 hours per month in order to keep their benefits.
SNAP recipients are also required to do at least 80 hours per month of work, training or volunteering in order to keep receiving benefits. The One Big Beautiful Bill Act extended the upper age limit for the work requirements from 54 to 64. It also removed exceptions for being homeless, a veteran or a former foster care youth under age 25.
Sean O’Leary, senior policy analyst at the West Virginia Center on Budget and Policy, said if the two work requirement processes aren’t streamlined, it could mean that more eligible people lose their healthcare and food assistance. 
“(The concern is) basically since there’s so many households participating in both, they’re going to be responsible for managing two work requirement reporting eligibility renewals every month,” O’Leary said. “The documents that are requested, the deadlines — if that’s not streamlined, then you’ll likely see more eligible people lose their assistance, both of SNAP and Medicaid.”
The analysis says the reporting requirements are likely to result in eligible people losing their healthcare and food benefits due to missing a notice or encountering a technological problem.
According to the West Virginia Department of Human Services, anyone meeting the SNAP work requirements will automatically satisfy the Medicaid work requirements, but those meeting the Medicaid requirements do not automatically meet the SNAP requirements. 
“Our focus is on helping more West Virginians overcome barriers to employment and return to the workforce,” Angel Hightower, communications specialist for the state Department of Human Services, wrote in an email to West Virginia Watch. 
“We want people who are able to work to have the opportunity to do so, while making sure those who qualify for assistance continue to receive the support they need,” she said. “We recognize that many families are facing difficult circumstances, and we’re committed to making this transition as smooth as possible while helping people find a path toward greater financial stability and independence.”
So far under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, more than 22,000 West Virginia residents have lost their food stamps, according to the Center on Budget and Policy. 
An analysis by the state health department earlier this year estimated that about 33,000 West Virginia residents would be affected by the Medicaid work requirements.

name: North Dakota Monitor
title: Worker training, voter education called keys to smooth election
description: Election workers are primed for Election Day after nearly a year of training, working primary elections and guiding tens of thousands of North Dakotans through early voting. “The general public does not realize how many previous months and how many hours the staff puts into getting ready for Election Day,” said Linda Chadduck, a 47-year […]
text:
Paulette Neff, an election judge at the Morton Mandan Public Library, talks to a voter about their ballot during early voting on Oct. 28, 2026. (Photo by Michael Achterling/North Dakota Monitor)Election workers are primed for Election Day after nearly a year of training, working primary elections and guiding tens of thousands of North Dakotans through early voting.
“The general public does not realize how many previous months and how many hours the staff puts into getting ready for Election Day,” said Linda Chadduck, a 47-year election worker veteran in Stutsman County. 
North Dakota voters on Tuesday will elect their sole member of the U.S. House, choose several statewide office-holders and weigh in on statewide ballot measures related to amending the constitution and providing free school meals.
[Voter Guide: 2026 General Election Voter Guide: The info you need to cast your ballot.]
Chadduck worked Stutsman County’s elections for 37 years until retiring in 2016. Since then,  she has worked as a precinct inspector.
The state’s elections have been seamless because of the training provided to the county auditors by the Secretary of State’s Office, she said, who in turn pass that training onto county election officials and poll workers.
“It’s an ongoing thing from the beginning of the year until after the state canvassing board in November,” she said. 
Chadduck, who was honored by the secretary of state as the 2026 Election Hero, has at times had to correct false information about the election process.
Linda Chadduck, center, stands with Stutsman County Auditor Jessica Alonge, left, and North Dakota Secretary of State Michael Howe, right, after being awarded with the 2026 Election Hero Award on Oct. 20, 2026. (Photo courtesy of Secretary of State’s Office)
This year, a friend alerted her to a social media post that incorrectly warned voters not to allow election judges to initial the ballot they receive. Chadduck texted her friend the correct information, that election workers are supposed to initial the ballots.
“It has to have their initials on it,” Chadduck said. “Because if there is a recount, and it’s not initialed, then it does not count.”
Chadduck has also corrected people who incorrectly say that voting machines can be hacked or are connected to the internet.
“No, they are not. They do not even have a place to hook up to the internet in them,” she said.
Governor predicts good results for Republicans in North Dakota but maybe not everywhere else

Educating voters is also an important part of the job for Paulette Neff, an election judge in Morton County, who has worked elections for the past 15 years. 
Neff said she likes to go over the ballot with voters before placing it in their hands.
“A lot of people think they have to fill everything out on the ballot, and they don’t have to,” she said. “The big thing is not to have them over vote because then that will kick the ballot out, so I have to tell them that.”
In Richland County, many poll workers have multiple elections under their belts, but this year the county also has some first-time election workers, said Auditor Sandy Fossum.
Fossum, past president of the North Dakota Auditors and Treasurers Association, said she provides additional one-on-one training for poll workers if they have additional questions.
“I try to do whatever it is to make them have a better experience,” she said.
Polls open on Election Day between 7 a.m. and 9 a.m., depending on location. Polls will close at 7 p.m. local time. 
Peggy Hertz, center-left, an election clerk at the Morton Mandan Public Library, hands a check-in receipt to a voter next to election clerk Sharlene Grosgebauer, left, during early voting on Oct. 28, 2026. (Photo by Michael Achterling/North Dakota Monitor)
No registration is required in North Dakota. Acceptable forms of identification include a North Dakota driver’s license; a nondriver state-issued identification card; a tribal ID or a tribal letter; a certificate from a long-term care facility. 
Absentee ballots must be received by 7 p.m. Tuesday. Absentee ballots are not accepted at polling places, but can be dropped off with the county auditor or county dropbox.
Election results will be posted on the Secretary of State’s website beginning at 8 p.m. Central.
Fossum said North Dakotans should keep in mind that polls stay open to allow voters to cast ballots if they are in line by the time the poll closes, which can delay a county’s ability to verify vote totals to be posted on the Secretary of State’s website. She added that some precinct workers need to travel up to 50 minutes to deliver results to the county courthouses.
As of Monday evening, more than 101,000 North Dakotans had cast their ballots early during the 2026 election, according to the Secretary of State’s Office. 
More than 242,000 North Dakotans voted during the 2022 midterm election, a nearly 43% turnout.
North Dakota Monitor reporter Michael Achterling can be reached at machterling@northdakotamonitor.com.

name: Arkansas Advocate
title: Arkansas’ political history on display at Little Rock printing business
description: Elections may come and go in Arkansas, but the campaign bumper stickers, buttons and yard signs can live on even longer. Want proof? Just step inside Ad Craft of Arkansas. A visit to the downtown Little Rock business offers a glimpse at how the state’s campaign messages have changed over the years. For nearly seven […]
text:
Randi Evans, president of Ad Craft of Arkansas, poses with past campaign signs for Bill Clinton in her office on Friday, Oct. 30, 2026 in Little Rock, Arkansas. (Photo by Andrew DeMillo/Arkansas Advocate)
Elections may come and go in Arkansas, but the campaign bumper stickers, buttons and yard signs can live on even longer.
Want proof? Just step inside Ad Craft of Arkansas.
A visit to the downtown Little Rock business offers a glimpse at how the state’s campaign messages have changed over the years. For nearly seven decades, Ad Craft has been the go-to printer for campaign signs, stickers, shirts and other political swag.
The logo for Hallie Shoffner’s Senate campaign on a t-shirt press at the Ad Craft building in Little Rock, Arkansas on Friday, Oct, 30, 2026 (Photo by Andrew DeMillo/Arkansas Advocate)
“I love doing campaigns. They are so much fun,” said Randi Evans, the president of Ad Craft. “And I’m friendly to everybody. I do both sides. And when I’m doing spoof stickers, they attack both sides and they’re for both sides.”
A sign outside Ad Craft advertises the “Bumper Sticker Hall of Fame,” and the business lives up to that advertising indoors. Ad Craft’s walls are adorned with stickers, buttons and other campaign paraphernalia throughout the state’s history.
They include red-white-and-blue signs from Bill Clinton’s bids for governor and president, and a poster for the late David Pryor’s campaign for Congress. 
A 1982 bumper sticker proclaims, “Repeel Frank White” alongside the image of a banana peel, in opposition to the then-Republican governor’s campaign. Other familiar names throughout Arkansas politics, from Wilbur Mills to Mike Huckabee, can be seen throughout the offices.
Bumper stickers from past campaigns are affixed to the wall at Ad Craft of Arkansas (Photo by Andrew DeMillo/Arkansas Advocate)
Evans proudly displays one of her most popular signs, a parody of Democratic nominee Al Gore and running mate Joe Lieberman’s campaign sign that was made during the 2000 presidential recount. The campaign logo was transformed into “Sore Loserman.”
“We made yard signs and bumper stickers and t-shirts, and in that 31 days we made about $3,000,” Evans said. “Without even being online.”
Campaign buttons and bumper stickers may feel like a relic in an increasingly online political era of TikTok videos and dueling social media posts. But Evans said there’s still a demand for traditional campaign messages.
“This state really likes yard signs, especially along the Delta,” Evans said. “It’s a good visual thing. It tells you who’s out there. By the time you get in a voting booth, if you don’t pay any attention, basically you remember whose sign you saw.”
Ad Craft’s work stretches well beyond elections, and their work has included signage and printing for other businesses and events.
Evans, whose dad started Ad Craft in 1958, said she hopes to continue the business for another couple years to be able to work on printing materials for 2028 campaigns. But she said she is interested in talking with people who may want to buy the business at some point.
“I would like for them to be politically motivated, because that’s what my dad started doing,” she said.
Signs and buttons at Ad Craft of Arkansas, which has been printing political signs for nearly seven decades. (Photo by Andrew DeMillo/Arkansas Advocate)A collection of campaign buttons on display at Ad Craft of Arkansas, which has been printing political signs for decades.  (Photo by Andrew DeMillo/Arkansas Advocate)A sign from Dale Bumpers' Senate campaign is displayed inside Ad Craft of Arkansas. (Photo by Andrew DeMillo/Arkansas Advocate)A collection of campaign bumper stickers from over the years is displayed on the walls of Ad Craft of Arkansas. (Photo by Andrew DeMillo/Arkansas Advocate)A campaign sign for David Pryor's congressional campaign is on display in Randi Evans' office at Ad Craft of Arkansas. (Photo by Andrew DeMillo/Arkansas Advocate)Randi Evans shows a poster made during the 2000 presidential recount in her office at Ad Craft of Arkansas. (Photo by Andrew DeMillo/Arkansas Advocate)A sign outside Ad Craft of Arkansas about its political memorabilia collection. (Photo by Andrew DeMillo/Arkansas Advocate)

name: Arkansas Advocate
title: The biggest questions looming over Arkansas’ midterm election
description: Is Arkansas going to be part of a blue wave, or is the state going to be a red holdout? Tuesday’s midterm election comes as Democrats hope a favorable national environment could create upsets in a state that hasn’t elected a Democrat to statewide or federal office in 16 years.  Early voting has been underway […]
text:
A car speeds past a voting location at Second Presbyterian Church in Little Rock’s Pleasant Valley neighborhood on Tuesday, March 3, 2026 (Photo by John Sykes/Arkansas Advocate)Is Arkansas going to be part of a blue wave, or is the state going to be a red holdout?
Tuesday’s midterm election comes as Democrats hope a favorable national environment could create upsets in a state that hasn’t elected a Democrat to statewide or federal office in 16 years. 
Early voting has been underway for more than two weeks, but thousands of ballots are yet to be cast. Arkansas’ midterm election has several closely watched races for U.S. Senate, governor and Congress. It also features some heated races for the Legislature and four measures lawmakers placed on the ballot. You can find the Arkansas Advocate’s election coverage here.
Here are some of the top races to watch in Tuesday’s results:
Hallie Shoffner, Democratic candidate for the U.S. Senate, campaigns outside the Pulaski Heights United Methodist Church in Little Rock, Arkansas’ Hillcrest neighborhood on Tuesday, March 3, 2026. (Photo by Katie Adkins/Arkansas Advocate)
US Senate: Can Democrats pull off an upset?
Twelve years ago, Republican Sen. Tom Cotton was the insurgent Republican who unseated a two-term incumbent he tied to a president unpopular in the state.
This year, Democrats are hoping to do the same thing to Cotton with Hallie Shoffner as the party’s nominee. Shoffner and Libertarian Jeff Wadlin are challenging Cotton, who chairs the Senate Intelligence Committee.
Arkansas Sen. Tom Cotton addresses supporters at Republican Party headquarters in downtown Little Rock Tuesday evening after being declared winner of his party’s primary. (Photo by John Sykes/Arkansas Advocate)
Cotton and Republican allies have outspent Shoffner, and recent polling has moved the race in the Republican lawmaker’s favor.
But Democrats hope that President Donald Trump’s low approval numbers along with discontent over the Iran war and fuel prices could help the party in a solidly Republican state.
U.S. Congressional District 2 candidates Chris Jones (D) and incumbent Rep. French Hill (R) debate at the Arkansas TV studios in Conway, Arkansas on Thursday, Oct. 15, 2026. (Photo by Katie Adkins/Arkansas Advocate)
US House: Is central Arkansas capable of being flipped?
This isn’t the first time national Democrats have believed Republican U.S. Rep. French Hill’s 2nd District seat was within reach. 
The party focused heavily on efforts in 2018 and 2020 to unseat Hill in the central Arkansas district, but fell short. This time, they think they have another opening with Democrat Chris Jones’ challenge.
[Voter Guide: 2026 General Election Voter Guide: The candidates, the ballot measures, and the tools you need to cast your vote.]
The Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee has labeled the seat as one it believes can be flipped, and Jones has had the support of national Democrats like Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker.
Hill has also had support from outside groups, including cryptocurrency-focused political action committees, that are running ads backing his bid.
The state’s other three Republican U.S. House members also face challenges in Tuesday’s election, but Hill’s seat is expected to be the most competitive.
Arkansas Legislature: A crack in Republicans’ supermajority?
Tuesday night will test whether Republicans will maintain their grip on the state Legislature, with Democrats hoping to break the 75-vote supermajority needed to pass most budget bills in the House.
A key part of Democrats’ strategy is Washington County, where the party hopes to make gains and unseat Republican Rep. Steve Unger.
Other heated House races include the campaign for a Maumelle-area district between Republican Stephen Bright and Democrat Cassandra Mayes. 
In the Senate, Democrat Allison Grigsby Sweatman and Republican Rep. Brandon Achor are vying for outgoing Republican Sen. Jane English’s seat. 
Gubernatorial candidates for Arkansas, Colt Shelby (L), Sen. Fred Love (D), and Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders (R), take the stage at the Arkansas TV studios in Conway, Arkansas on Tuesday, Oct. 13, 2026. (Photo by Katie Adkins/Arkansas Advocate)
Governor’s race: What impact will Libertarian bid have?
Polling and fundraising numbers indicate Republican Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders is in a comfortable position, despite the national mood about the president for whom she worked as White House press secretary.
The biggest question surrounding the governor’s race results is how much of an impact Libertarian Colt Shelby could have.
Shelby and Democratic state Sen. Fred Love are challenging Sanders on similar themes, saying the governor’s priorities have been misplaced. Love has vowed to sign an executive order repealing the state’s school voucher program under Sanders’ signature education law if he’s elected.
The election comes as Sanders raises her national profile ahead of the 2028 presidential election, authoring a book scheduled to come out a week after the midterms. 
(Photo by Tess Vrbin/Arkansas Advocate)
Ballot measures: Will voters allow economic development districts?
There are four proposals going before voters that the majority-Republican Legislature put on the ballot. They include a measure aimed at strengthening the state constitution’s prohibition against noncitizen voting and another expanding the constitution’s right to bear arms.
But the proposal that could be the closest is Issue 3, a measure that would allow the creation of local economic development districts.
The proposed constitutional amendment has the backing of the state’s business lobby, the governor and a bipartisan coalition of lawmakers. 
But it’s also run into resistance from some conservatives and progressives who say the proposal leaves too many details up to the Legislature. Polling indicates a large number of voters are undecided on the issue.
A fourth proposal on the ballot would allow the state to issue up to $500 million in bonds for water and wastewater improvement projects.

text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
Mississippi voters will decide today who will fill a U.S. Senate seat, four U.S. House seats, two state House seats, numerous judgeships and several local races or referendums.
The federal midterm elections will determine control of both chambers of Congress, and Mississippi’s U.S. Senate race is being watched nationally as Republicans and Democrats battle across the country.
Mississippi voters have returned about 2.5 times as many absentee ballots as they had at this point in the 2022 midterms. But there was no Senate race on the ballot in 2022, and the numbers remain below the last presidential race.
As of Monday, circuit clerks’ offices had received 116,453 absentee ballots, according to the Secretary of State’s office. At the same point in 2022, the day before that election, they had received 46,120.
The absentee ballot count this year is still below the 2024 federal election cycle, but voter turnout usually increases in presidential election years. At this point in the 2024 election, 197,903 absentee ballots had been received.
In-person absentee voting ended at noon Saturday, Oct. 31. Mail-in absentee ballots must be postmarked by Election Day, Nov. 3, but they can be received within five business days, by Nov. 10. 
Mississippi Today readers can follow the races live as results come in. You can also read our election guide for more context on the elections and our FAQ for answers to frequently asked questions about voting.
READ MORE: Hyde-Smith and Colom make final pitches in Mississippi Senate midterm race
Polls in Mississippi will be open today from 7 a.m. to 7 p.m. Anyone in line by 7 p.m. can still vote after closing time. 

All Mississippi voters are required to present a photo ID. If you do not present an acceptable form of photo ID, you are entitled to cast an affidavit ballot, but must then present an ID at your local circuit clerk’s office within five business days. For voter ID information or help obtaining valid identification, call 1-800-829-6786.
To find your polling location, view sample ballots and see who your current officeholders are, go the the secretary of state’s My Election Day page.
You can check your voter registration status through this portal on the Secretary of State’s website. For your circuit clerk’s address and contact information, go to the secretary of state’s County Election Information page here.
Those who wish to report an issue with voting can call the Mississippi Secretary of State’s Elections hotline at 1-800-829-6786 or email ElectionsAnswers@sos.ms.gov.

title: Jones, Figures call on young voters in final Democratic rally before midterm elections
description: Amid chants encouraging voter turnout and sets of rap and R&B music, Alabama Democrats on Monday called on young voters at Alabama State University to turn out in Tuesday’s midterm elections in the final campaign rally for two campaigns. Speaking to more than 3,000 attendees, most of whom were ASU students, U.S. Rep. Shomari Figures, […]
text:
U.S. Reps. Shomari Figures, D-Montgomery and Terri Sewell, D-Birmingham, and Democratic gubernatorial nominee Doug Jones raising their hands on stage at one last rally before the 2026 midterm elections at the Oliver-Dunn Acadome at Alabama State University in Montgomery, Alabama, on Nov. 2, 2026. Alabama Democrats at the rally called on young voters to turn out in Tuesday's election. (Anna Barrett/Alabama Reflector)Amid chants encouraging voter turnout and sets of rap and R&B music, Alabama Democrats on Monday called on young voters at Alabama State University to turn out in Tuesday’s midterm elections in the final campaign rally for two campaigns.
Speaking to more than 3,000 attendees, most of whom were ASU students, U.S. Rep. Shomari Figures, D-Montgomery, said candidates should stop talking about young voters and start talking to them. 
“I say we can’t just keep blaming y’all for not voting. We gotta give you a reason to go vote,” said Figures, seeking re-election in Alabama’s 2nd Congressional District, which was altered the most of the state’s four affected districts by a U.S. Supreme Court order this spring. “I say we gotta give you a reason to believe in people and believe that government can actually work the way it’s supposed to work for you.”
Following a decision from the U.S. Supreme Court this spring in a case known as Louisiana v. Callais, the Alabama Legislature reverted to a 2023 congressional map, which was previously struck down as racially discriminatory, for the 2026 election. The map change triggered a special primary election in August after a special session of the Legislature. 
The new map reduced the Black voting age population by nearly 9 percentage points. The district was expected to be a relatively easy pick-up for Republican nominee Rhett Marques, a state representative from Enterprise. But Figures has outraised Marques during the campaign, and the nonpartisan Center for Politics Monday moved the race from “Toss up” to “Leans Democratic” in its final ratings. 
Turnout in Montgomery County, which generally leans Democratic, will be critical for Figures and the Democratic Party’s statewide campaigns. U.S. Rep. Terri Sewell, D-Birmingham, who is running for reelection in an altered 7th Congressional District, told attendees that Black voter participation is crucial in Tuesday’s election. 
“I want you all to know that we cannot do this without you, and they’re counting on you not voting. They want you to not vote,” she said. “When I was your age, they didn’t want me to vote, but we voted. We voted like our lives depend upon it because it does.”
Sewell introduced Democratic gubernatorial nominee Doug Jones, who walked on stage to “Teach Me How To Dougie.” Voters across the state have tried to get Jones to do the dance associated with the song, but he has mostly refused. He did not on Monday night. 
“Just for you, I embarrassed the hell out of myself,” he said. “As you have heard from this stage, tomorrow we have a historic opportunity to change the direction of this state.”
Jones faces Republican U.S. Sen. Tommy Tuberville in the governor’s race. Tuberville is largely considered the front runner, but recent polls have shown a smaller gap than in 2020, when Tuberville defeated Jones in the 2020 U.S. Senate campaign. 
Alabama House Minority Leader Rep. Anthony Daniels, D-Huntsville, focused on reaching the approximately 619,000 Black registered voters in Alabama that he said do not cast ballots in every election. According to the Alabama Secretary of State’s office, almost 872,000 Black Alabamians are registered to vote as of September. 
“We’re counting on you to turn out in record numbers to save our representation,” he said. “They attempted to take away our representation in Congress, and now it’s time for us to fight back.”
Polls open Tuesday at 7 a.m. and close at 7 p.m. Polling locations can be found here.

name: West Virginia Watch
title: Commentary: Why West Virginia is one of the few states still supporting Trump
description: A survey has come out which shows that Trump is underwater in almost every state. East of the Mississippi River, Trump is only above water in Alabama and West Virginia. In West Virginia, he has a positive favorability rating with 48% of state residents versus a negative rating with 41%.
text:
President Donald Trump speaks at a Nov. 1, 2026, rally in Salina, Kansas. (Photo by Sherman Smith/Kansas Reflector)A survey has come out which shows that Trump is underwater in almost every state. East of the Mississippi River, Trump is only above water in Alabama and West Virginia. In West Virginia, he has a positive favorability rating with 48% of state residents versus a negative rating with 41%.
My best friend passed away a few years ago. He had been my closest friend since we met when I was 21 and living in a single wide trailer. He was my next-door neighbor, and babysat my two sons on the very few occasions when my wife and I had had enough money to go out to eat. I loved him like a brother.
Son of a coal miner, Don was born on the West Virginia/Pennsylvania border and dropped out of high school to work in the West Virginia coal mines. He ended up in Georgia after he got out of the Army.
A truck driver, he supported Sen. Bernie Sanders for president way back when. But when the Democrats went the other direction in 2016, he became a big Trump supporter and stayed faithful until his death. We talked a lot about exactly why.
He viewed Sanders as for the common person. Although I disagree with Bernie on some issues, I generally do agree. Somehow, he decided early on that Trump was also for the people on the bottom of the rung. And he is not the only one. Per polling, Trump is very popular with white men without college degrees. In fact, it’s about the only group that still supports him and forms the MAGA base.
Here is why: some otherwise good people are brainwashed. But they just don’t understand that fact. It’s just an unfortunate part of human nature. 
Such brainwashing is especially easy to do in today’s climate of political alienation and mistrust, leading to the MAGA cult which believes Trump can do no wrong. One manifestation is the Evangelicals knowing that Trump has flawed person morality, but believing that he is still “God’s vessel.”
Trump’s supporters believe 100% of whatever crazy stuff Trump feeds them. Why?  Because they go to social media sites that reinforce their MAGA cult misperceptions, watch biased news channels Fox, OAN and Newsmax, and associate with people who have similar conspiratorial views. And that is exactly why we had a Trump promoted attempt by his MAGA cult to overthrow our government. These people beat up 140 law enforcement officers, but believed that they were “patriots” because their Supreme Leader told them so.
West Virginia is plagued with many ills. For example, it has some of the worst physical and mental health problems in the nation, coming in 46th on America’s Health Rankings. And the state faces economic problems due in large part to its reliance on a failing industry — coal mining. One study rated its economy as the worst of any state.
A segment of West Virginia’s population is looking for a savior to lead them out of the forest. But Donald Trump is a false prophet, moving in the opposite direction. Someday, I believe that will become obvious.

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: Commentary: Bull Nelson would have checked three of Hegseth’s four boxes
description: Holy Warrior Pete Hegseth has declared holy war on “fatties, trannies, beardos” and “weirdos” in the military. History, which I taught in a community college for two dozen years, instructs that in combat, corpulence and competence are not mutually exclusive. From William the Conqueror to Stormin’ Norman Schwarzkopf, more than a few famous battle captains […]
text:
The assassination of General Bull Nelson by General Jefferson C. Davis. (Cover of New York Illustrated News, Saturday, October 18, 1862 via Wikipedia)Holy Warrior Pete Hegseth has declared holy war on “fatties, trannies, beardos” and “weirdos” in the military.
History, which I taught in a community college for two dozen years, instructs that in combat, corpulence and competence are not mutually exclusive.
From William the Conqueror to Stormin’ Norman Schwarzkopf, more than a few famous battle captains have been on the stout side.
Famous at least in his native Kentucky, rotund Gen. William “Bull” Nelson was a brave soldier best known for playing an outsized role in keeping the commonwealth out of the Confederacy.
General William “Bull” Nelson (Library of Congress)
Bull would have checked three of the defense secretary’s four boxes. He was a bearded 6-4 (some sources say 6-2), 300-pounder (body mass index 37, obese).
The circumstances of his death were weird. Another Yankee general shot Nelson in a popular Louisville hotel.
Bull’s personality was weirder. The New York Herald found him “rough in manners, a stern disciplinarian, quick and decided in all of his actions, no respecter of persons, trampling upon even his dearest friends when they stood in the path of his duty; but kind at heart, tender to his men in suffering, a good scholar and a hard student.”
Born in Maysville in 1824, Nelson was a sailor before he was a soldier. He graduated from the Naval Academy, went to sea and fought in the Mexican- American War.
With the Civil War looming, he uniquely offered his services to President Lincoln. On March 6th, 1861, two days after Lincoln’s inauguration, the burly Bull went to the White House and supposedly told the president, “Here I am; if you don’t like me, that’s the worse, for you.”
In May, after America’s most lethal conflict started, Lincoln tapped Nelson for a secret mission to help keep their native state under the Stars and Stripes.
Kentucky, a border slave state where loyalties were divided, had declared itself neutral, a stance most citizens supported and the pro-Union party accepted for the time being.
The Unionists worried that the well-armed, equipped and trained State Guard, which leaned steeply Southern, might try to force Kentucky out of the Union at gunpoint. Pro-Union Home Guard companies were being organized statewide, but they needed firepower to check the State Guard.
Lincoln had Nelson oversee the secret shipment of 5,000 military rifles to the Home Guards. In the summer, most of the State Guards joined the rebel army, and possible civil war in the state was averted.
After the state forthrightly declared for the Union in September, Nelson became an Army brigadier general of volunteers. In the first half of 1862, he fought in the battles of Shiloh, Tenn., and Corinth, Miss. In late summer, he was wounded in action helping defend central Kentucky from invading Confederate armies.
With the enemy threatening Louisville, Nelson, who had been promoted to major general of volunteers, took command in the city and vigorously prepared its defenses. He ordered regular Army Brig. Gen. Jefferson C. Davis, a Hoosier, to organize the Home Guards. Davis disliked the assignment and detested his assigner, Robert Emmett McDowell wrote in “City of Conflict: Louisville in the Civil War 1861-1865.”
On Sept. 22, the generals clashed at the old Galt House, Nelson’s headquarters.
Nelson angrily rebuked Davis for not knowing the precise number of companies he had organized. He relieved Davis on the spot and banished him to Cincinnati.
Davis left but was back in the Falls City on Sept. 28 with Indiana Gov. Oliver Perry Morton in tow. The Republican Party bigwig also hated Nelson.
Davis confronted Nelson at the Galt House around 8 a.m. on the 29th. He charged Bull “with having insulted him at their last meeting and demanded satisfaction,” McDowell wrote. “Go away, you damned puppy; I don’t want anything to do with you!” Bull roared, according to McDowell.
The 5-9, 125 pound Davis wadded up a hotel registration card and threw it at Nelson, hitting him in the face. Nelson delivered a backhanded slap to the side of Davis’ head, glared at Morton and asked, “Did you come here to see me insulted?” The governor meekly replied in the negative.
Nelson then decamped for the stairs, evidently intent on seeing Maj. Gen. Don Carlos Buell, the Army of Ohio’s commander, in his second-floor headquarters, McDowell wrote.
Davis borrowed a pistol from Louisville lawyer Thomas W. Gibson, who had lived in Indiana, and shot Nelson in the chest at close range. Bull might be Hegeseth’s idea of a “fatty.” But Neldon mustered “the strength, the incredible vitality, to walk up the stairs and reach the upper hall before he toppled and fell,” wrote McDowell.
The general was borne to the closest room and laid on a mattress which had been placed on the floor. He entreated Silas F. Miller, the hotel proprietor, to summon a clergyman.” I wish to be baptized,” Bull pleaded. “I have been basely murdered.”
An Episcopal pastor apparently arrived in time to grant the general’s dying wish. His life ebbed away within the hour, McDowell wrote. Nelson was first buried in Louisville’s Cave Hill Cemetery, but his remains were reinterred in the Maysville Cemetery.
McDowell suggested that “in a way, though, the aftermath of the affair was more shocking than the assassination….nothing was done; no court was appointed. General Davis was never brought to trial.” Because the brass hats desperately needed veteran combat commanders like Davis, they found it easier to buy his questionable claim of self-defense. (Davis was indicted for manslaughter in Jefferson Circuit Court but was never tried.) He returned to duty, survived the war and died in 1879 at age 51.
Opened in 1863, Camp Nelson, now a national monument in Jessamine County, was named for Bull. The camp evolved into the largest recruiting station for Black troops in Kentucky and was also a refuge for the soldiers’ families who, too, were escaping enslavement.
There was yet another weird twist to Nelson’s demise. “A garbled version of the murder spread like wildfire, carrying consternation in its wake,” McDowell explained. “For a while it was actually thought that Jefferson Davis, President of Confederacy, had slipped into Louisville and murdered Nelson!”

name: Virginia Mercury
title: It’s Election Day in Virginia: Here’s what to know before heading to the polls
description: Virginians will vote Tuesday in the 2026 midterm elections, with control of Congress and three proposed constitutional amendments at stake after a record early voting turnout.  Polls are open statewide from 6 a.m. until 7 p.m., giving voters their final opportunity to weigh in on races for the U.S. Senate and all 11 of Virginia’s […]
text:
Voters cast ballots in a past election at a Henrico polling place in 2025. On Election Day 2026, Nov. 3, Virginians will elect a new slate of congressional representatives and approve or reject three constitutional amendments. (Photo by Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images)Virginians will vote Tuesday in the 2026 midterm elections, with control of Congress and three proposed constitutional amendments at stake after a record early voting turnout. 
Polls are open statewide from 6 a.m. until 7 p.m., giving voters their final opportunity to weigh in on races for the U.S. Senate and all 11 of Virginia’s U.S. House seats, along with proposed protections for reproductive rights, marriage equality and voting rights. 
More than 1.6 million Virginians voted early through Saturday, the final day of in-person early voting. The Call the Map tracker recorded 1,630,073 ballots, including 1,310,540 cast in person and 319,533 returned by mail. Additional mail ballots are still arriving. 
That total surpasses the 976,558 early ballots cast in the 2022 midterms. Stephen Farnsworth, professor emeritus of political science at the University of Mary Washington, said the growing participation reflects voters’ embrace of early voting.
“Virginians really like no-excuses early voting. That steadily increasing turnout speaks to how convenient it is as well as how comfortable voters feel with that approach,” he said.
Farnsworth said polling and early voting patterns give Democrats reason for optimism, particularly as they challenge Republicans in districts that previously drew less attention.
“It’s clear that Democratic efforts to expand the map to previously less competitive congressional districts have triggered a lot of enthusiasm among voters who are used to living in places where the contests were less uncertain.”
 What voters need to know

Anyone in line by 7 p.m. can vote. Virginians can find their assigned precinct through the Department of Elections’ voter information portal. Election Day polling places may differ from early voting locations. 
Voters should bring acceptable identification, although those without it may sign an ID confirmation statement. Eligible residents who missed the registration deadline can register at their precinct and cast a provisional ballot, subject to eligibility verification. 
Completed absentee ballots delivered in person must arrive by 7 p.m. Tuesday. Mailed ballots must be postmarked by Election Day and delivered no later than Friday, Nov. 6. 
Election night results will remain unofficial until local officials finish reviewing provisional ballots, counting eligible late-arriving absentee ballots and completing the canvas. 
State officials will then certify the results, a process that state law dictates must be carried out no later than the first Monday in December, which is Dec. 7 this year.
 Virginia’s congressional battlegrounds

Democratic U.S. Sen. Mark Warner is seeking a fourth term against Republican Bert Mizusawa, a retired U.S. Army major general. 
Warner has emphasized his legislative experience and opposition to President Donald Trump’s economic and healthcare policies. Mizusawa argues his military background and Republican connections would give Virginia greater influence with the administration. 
Democrats currently hold six of Virginia’s 11 House seats, compared with five for Republicans, and hope to expand that advantage as both parties compete for the national majority. 
In the 1st District, Henrico Commonwealth’s Attorney Shannon Taylor is challenging Republican U.S. Rep. Rob Wittman of Westmoreland, who has served since 2007. The district stretches from Richmond’s suburbs to the Northern Neck and Williamsburg area. Taylor has criticized Wittman’s healthcare votes, while he has defended Republican spending policies. 
The  2nd District features a rematch between Republican U.S. Rep. Jen Kiggans and Elaine Luria, whom Kiggans defeated in 2022. Both are U.S. Navy veterans competing in a Virginia Beach-centered district with a large military population. Independents Matt Baker and Bishop Staten are also running. 
Former Democratic U.S. Rep. Tom Perriello hopes to reclaim the 5th District from Republican U.S. Rep. John McGuire of Goochland. Trump carried the Charlottesville-to-Southside district by about 12 percentage points in 2024.
Perriello has focused on affordability and independence from party leadership, while McGuire has emphasized his support for Trump. Independent Cooke Harvey is also on the ballot. 
In the 6th District, journalist and “Dopesick” author Beth Macy is challenging Republican U.S. Rep. Ben Cline of Botetourt County. Macy has outraised the incumbent, although major election forecasters continue to rate the Shenandoah Valley-to-Roanoke district safely Republican. 
Democrats are defending the 7th District, where first-term U.S. Rep. Eugene Vindman of Woodbridge faces Republican Douglas Ollivant and four other candidates. Housing cost, federal jobs and data center development have figured prominently in the contest 
 Three constitutional amendments 

Virginia voters will also decide whether to amend the state Constitution on reproductive rights, marriage and voting eligibility. 
Question 1 would protect decisions involving abortion, contraception, fertility treatment and pregnancy-related care, along with patients and providers.
Third-trimester abortion restrictions would remain permissible, with exceptions when the patient’s health is at risk or the pregnancy cannot survive. One doctor instead of three would be required to sign off on the late-term abortions. 
Virginia’s constitutional ban on same-sex marriage would be removed under Question 2. The measure would guarantee the right of two adults to marry regardless of sex, gender or race and require equal treatment of legally valid marriages. 
Under Question 3, voting rights would be automatically restored upon release from incarceration following a felony conviction. The proposal would also establish a fundamental right to vote and revise the constitutional disqualification involving mental capacity. 
 Local races and school funding referendums 

Local offices are also on the ballot in several Virginia communities, including a contentious school board race in Chesterfield, along with referendums on school funding. 
Voters in 47 localities, including Richmond, Chesterfield County, Norfolk and Newport News, will decide whether to authorize an additional sales tax of up to 1% to pay for public school construction and major renovations. 
The tax would not apply to groceries or essential personal hygiene products, and voter approval would allow, but not require, local governments to impose it.

title: Virginia report reveals major gaps in access to career and technical education courses, credentials
description: Virginia’s career and technical education review found regional disparities in access to courses and credentials, according to a state report released Oct. 1. State agencies recommend expanding credentials in underserved areas, prioritizing high-demand fields, strengthening employer partnerships, and improving data transparency to better align student traini[...]
text:
State lawmakers authorized the Virginia Board of Education and the Board of Workforce Development to complete a statewide review of all CTE courses, pathways, and industry-recognized credentials offered in Virginia’s public schools earlier this year. (Photo courtesy of Creative Commons via Pixabay)Virginia’s career and technical education review found regional disparities in access to courses and credentials, according to a state report released Oct. 1. State agencies recommend expanding credentials in underserved areas, prioritizing high-demand fields, strengthening employer partnerships, and improving data transparency to better align student training with workforce needs.
During the last legislative session, the General Assembly authorized the Virginia Board of Education and the Board of Workforce Development to complete a statewide review of all CTE courses, pathways, and industry-recognized credentials offered in Virginia’s public schools. 
The work comes as the state seeks to align K-12 educational programming with current and emerging workforce needs. 
The Virginia Department of Education acknowledged in the report that the commonwealth’s 10 most frequently earned CTE credentials do not consistently meet expectations for industry recognition and alignment.
In response, the department said it is developing definitions and criteria for industry-recognized credentials to guide the evaluation of existing and future credential offerings. 
“The Virginia Department of Education is committed to strengthening this alignment, and we are actively engaged in the development of definition and criteria for industry-recognized credentials that will guide the evaluation of both existing and future credential offerings,” the agency stated. 
“School divisions will continue to have the flexibility to identify and offer any CTE course, pathway, or credential approved by the Virginia Board of Education, ensuring responsiveness to local workforce needs as we work toward a more rigorous and industry-aligned credential landscape.”
Virginia public schools offer 520 unique CTE courses, with 367 being industry-recognized credentials and 82 career pathways, according to data collected from 2024-2025.
Other findings showed that the strongest career clusters are agriculture, business management, health sciences, human services, and information technology.
However, the review found that course and credential availability varies considerably across regions, despite relatively consistent pathway access. It also found unequal credential access, with Region 2, or the Tidewater area, leading at 214 compared with Region 8, or Southside, at 54.
Stakeholder input identified cybersecurity, advanced health sciences and specialized skilled trades as opportunities for program expansion.

As schools and colleagues move forward with supporting CTE, Del. Terry Austin, R-Botetourt, emphasized the importance of tailoring programs to each region’s specific workforce needs.
“We need to look at regionally what that region needs, and we should cater our academics to that more so than let’s just offer everything,” Austin said in an Oct. 26 interview, echoing his call for a more focused approach to CTE offerings.
For example, an area with heavy industry might prioritize welding, while an IT-focused region might emphasize technology; cosmetology and horticulture should also reflect local demand. 
The boards recommended expanded credential access, prioritizing workforce alignment, strengthening regional collaboration and improving data transparency.
The boards also suggested stronger credential and pathway standards and improved tracking of long-term student outcomes.
Virginia allocated $20 million to expand CTE development programs across the Virginia Community College System. The funding will support additional capacity for 900 students in health-related programs, including nursing and medical assisting, and 1,000 students in workforce programs, including welding and HVAC.
Prince William County Public Schools offers a four-year aviation maintenance technology transfer program. (Photo courtesy of Prince William County Public Schools)
 Legislative solutions

State lawmakers have proposed bills to make workforce training more directly integrated into the education system.
Del. Wendell Walker, R-Lynchburg, is carrying House Bill 1023 that would bring industry professionals into classrooms.
In another proposal, HB 1383, being proposed by Del. Delores Oates, R-Warren, would make community college coursework more accessible to technical professionals seeking teaching licenses.
On credential quality and workforce alignment, Senate Bill 733, proposed by Sen. Danny Diggs, R-York, would establish standards for workforce training programs outside traditional degree pathways.
Del. Destiny LeVere Bolling, D-Henrico, is carrying HB 428, which would give students additional ways to demonstrate workforce readiness. 
Lawmakers will convene in Richmond starting on Jan. 13 to discuss CTE legislation and other issues.

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: SC Republicans, Democrats make final campaign push at Columbia-area breweries
description: COLUMBIA — Republicans and Democrats in South Carolina made their final get-out-the-vote pitch ahead of Election Day at breweries just a few miles apart. Alan Wilson’s two-week bus tour of the state concluded Monday night at Steel Hands Brewing in Cayce. Volunteers for the GOP gubernatorial nominee’s campaign added their signatures to the bus as […]
text:
Attorney General Alan Wilson, the GOP nominee for governor, ends his two-week bus tour at Steel Hands Brewing in Cayce, South Carolina, on Monday, November 2, 2026. Campaign volunteers signed the bus, which has a photo of Wilson and his running mate, state Sen. Mike Reichenbach. (Photo by Katharine Wilson/SC Daily Gazette)COLUMBIA — Republicans and Democrats in South Carolina made their final get-out-the-vote pitch ahead of Election Day at breweries just a few miles apart.
Alan Wilson’s two-week bus tour of the state concluded Monday night at Steel Hands Brewing in Cayce. Volunteers for the GOP gubernatorial nominee’s campaign added their signatures to the bus as supporters gathered for short speeches by Wilson and other Republicans for statewide office.
At the same time, Democrats drank steins of beer and ate bratwursts on the outdoor patio of Bierkeller Brewing Co. overlooking the Columbia Canal, sometimes chanting “New SC,” the theme of Rep. Jermaine Johnson’s gubernatorial campaign.

For more on our 2026 election coverage and information on voting in South Carolina, check out our Voter Guide.

Polls are open from 7 a.m. to 7 p.m. Tuesday statewide.
The election guarantees a change in state leadership, with no incumbent on the ballot this year for governor, attorney general, commissioner of agriculture, and comptroller general.
Voters will also choose who replaces the late U.S. Sen. Lindsey Graham for the next six-year term. All House seats in Congress and the Statehouse are also on the ballot.
Democrats’ ‘opportunity’
At Bierkeller Brewing, Democratic Party leaders told roughly 50 attendees that a “New SC” involves electing Democrats up and down the ballot. Candidates in attendance were introduced as soon-to-be officeholders.

U.S. Rep. Ro Khanna, gubernatorial candidate Rep. Jermaine Johnson, and lieutenant governor candidate Sam Skardon talk to reporters during a pre-election rally at Bierkeller Brewing Co. in Columbia, S.C., on Monday, Nov. 2, 2026. (Photo by Skylar Laird/SC Daily Gazette)

Each gave a message of hope, sometimes altering the state motto from “While I breathe, I hope,” to “While I breathe, I vote.”
“For far too long in this state, people have given up all sense of hope,” said Jaime Harrison, the former state Democratic Party chair who lost to Graham in 2020, then headed the Democratic National Committee.
It’s been 20 years since a Democrat won any statewide office in South Carolina. This year marks the first time in over 50 years that Democrats have a candidate on the ballot for every race, including all 124 state House seats. And they’re enthusiastic about flipping offices.
“We are on the brink of history, y’all,” said Vincent Coe, the nominee for state treasurer.
Other Democratic candidates at the event included Sylvia Wright, who’s running for superintendent of education. When Sam Skardon, Johnson’s pick for lieutenant governor, asked everyone who’d already voted to raise their hand, nearly every hand went up. Candidates pointed to early voting numbers as likely helping them.
