During the two-week window that concluded Saturday, more than 1 million people cast ballots, according to data from the state Election Commission.
It’s impossible to know how many of those were Democrats, since voters don’t register by party in South Carolina. But Democrats are traditionally more likely to vote early than Republicans.
Momentum is propelling Democrats in polls nationwide. This is the year for Democrats, Johnson said, adding there might not be a better chance to elect Democrats to statewide office in South Carolina.
“It will be a shame on us if we squander away this opportunity right here, right now,” said Johnson, of Hopkins, first elected to the state House in 2020. “We may not ever see this opportunity come up for us in our lifetime again.”
Not in attendance were two Democratic candidates with the biggest chance of creating an upset: Dr. Annie Andrews, a pediatrician running for the U.S. Senate; and retired Vice-Adm. Nancy Lacore, who’s running for the 1st Congressional District. Both live in Charleston County and campaigned together at The Refinery at the same time as the Columbia event.
GOP candidates
At Steel Hands Brewing, Wilson said the GOP gathering was about fun and fellowship but also a final call to action to the dozens of attendees to get themselves and friends to the polls Tuesday.
“As your next governor, I will always put you first. I won’t be a perfect governor, but I will be an accessible governor,” said Wilson, the state’s attorney general since 2010. “I will be an accountable governor, and I will be a governor who will always fight for you,’ Wilson said. 

U.S. Rep. Joe Wilson, U.S. Sens. Tim Scott and Darline Graham, Attorney General Alan Wilson, the GOP nominee for governor, and Cody Simpson, the GOP nominee for agriculture commissioner, rally at Steel Hands Brewing in Cayce, South Carolina, on Monday, Nov. 2, 2026. (Photo by Katharine Wilson/SC Daily Gazette)

U.S. Sen. Darline Graham, who faces Andrews to keep the seat she was appointed to after her brother died July 11, could barely talk. She seemed to have a case of laryngitis.
Wilson jokingly told the crowd that Graham was limited to two words to try to save whatever voice she had left.
Graham is in her first campaign ever at Trump’s encouragement. The president has visited South Carolina twice in the last two weeks to rally support for her as polls showed her in a statistical tie with Andrews.
“It has been a great campaign. This is the final stop, and I have enjoyed every minute of it,” Graham said. “I promise you, I will work so hard for this state every single day, and I am just so proud to serve South Carolina. So, I just humbly ask for your vote tomorrow. Sorry my voice is gone, but again, encourage you to get out and vote.”
Other candidates at the function in Lexington County, home to both Wilson and Graham, included Cody Simpson, the GOP nominee for agriculture commissioner; state Superintendent Ellen Weaver; and Wilson’s dad, U.S. Rep. Joe Wilson, who’s represented the 2nd District since 2001.
The congressman in Columbia
Campaigning with Johnson again was U.S. Rep. Ro Khanna of California, who’s among potential 2028 presidential contenders already visiting the state.
“I chose to be here because I truly believe that there is no election that will be more historic for the future of our country than putting Jermaine Johnson as governor in South Carolina,” said the congressman who represents Silicon Valley.
Absent from the Columbia event was U.S. Rep. Jim Clyburn, who’s so confident in his own re-election, he spent the weekend campaigning for U.S. Senate candidates in other states.
On Friday, he was in Mississippi with Scott Colom. On Sunday, he was in Detroit campaigning for Abdul El-Sayed, the Democrats’ nominee for U.S. Senate in Michigan’s tight race.
Clyburn is expected to easily win an 18th term representing South Carolina’s 6th District, the only U.S. House seat in South Carolina safely drawn for a Democrat.

name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: Trump targets Louisiana with election eve tele-rally: ‘I don’t see how Julia can possibly lose’
description: The 10-minute “tele-rally” on the eve of Election Day was the first occasion in which the president has actively campaigned for Letlow since she secured the Republic Party’s nomination in June.
text:
President Donald Trump encouraged Louisiana supporters who dialed into a tele-rally Monday night, Nov. 2, 2026, to vote on Election Day for Congresswoman Julia Letlow in the state's U.S. Senate race. (Photo by Alex Wong/Getty Images)President Donald Trump, winding down a monthlong string of in-person rallies ahead of Tuesday’s midterm elections, used technology Monday night to speak to his supporters in Louisiana, urging them to vote for Congresswoman Julia Letlow in the state’s U.S. Senate race. 
The 10-minute “tele-rally” on the eve of Election Day was the first occasion in which the president has actively campaigned for Letlow since she secured the Republic Party’s nomination in June. The call was planned late last week, just after early voting turnout data showed numbers favoring her opponent, Democrat Jamie Davis. 
Democrats accounted for more than 42% of all votes cast in the seven-day period, compared with 39% for Republicans. Black voters posted their highest turnout rate ever in a midterm election, accounting for 34% of the ballots cast.
Trump’s call was open only to invited supporters who were given access numbers to dial into the teleconference. A recording of his message was posted to YouTube soon afterwards. 
Trump called Davis “a loser” who he said “wants to destroy all of the tremendous success” Louisiana has seen during his presidency. 
“I don’t see how Julia can possibly lose to this person. I have no idea who that person is,” the president said.
Trump highlighted several industrial projects announced in Louisiana since Republican Gov. Jeff Landry took office in January 2024. He specifically mentioned the expansion of liquified natural gas terminals and the selection of Vermilion Parish for a new SpaceX launch facility, which Trump said he recommended to company founder Elon Musk. 
U.S. House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-Benton, introduced the president, who asked listeners to ensure that the speaker and Letlow are sent back to Congress. 
Trump’s pleas come as national election analysts predict Democrats will gain control of the U.S. House of Representatives and have a chance to gain a majority in the U.S. Senate.
“If they get their claws onto a win tomorrow, it would be the beginning of a very, very sad period for our nation,” Trump said to his Louisiana listeners, who he claimed numbered in the “hundreds of thousands.”
The Republican National Committee organized the call, one of nine the president took part in Monday, and couldn’t be reached immediately to confirm that count.

name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: Commentary: Before Louisiana bets on nuclear, we should look at offshore wind
description: If the goal is clean, dependable electricity, Louisiana should also evaluate offshore wind.
text:
A jack-up installation vessel works on RWE's Kaskasi wind farm in the North Sea near Germany. (Photo courtesy of RWE)Louisiana has nuclear fever. In March, Gov. Jeff Landry released the state’s first Nuclear Strategic Framework, and the U.S. Department of Energy named Louisiana one of five finalists to host a federal nuclear fuel campus in July.
Last month, the Louisiana Public Service Commission approved a program allowing utilities to spend up to $2 million of ratepayer funds studying new nuclear reactors.
The excitement around nuclear as a source of zero-emissions power is understandable. New data centers, natural gas terminals and other industries are driving demand for power and zero-carbon technologies faster than Louisiana has seen in decades.
However, if the goal is clean, dependable electricity, Louisiana should also evaluate offshore wind.
We can look at two of the largest power plants built in recent years — Georgia’s Plant Vogtle and Virginia’s Coastal Virginia Offshore Wind project — to compare the costs and benefits of offshore wind and nuclear.
Georgia’s Plant Vogtle Units 3 and 4 are the only new nuclear reactors finished in the U.S. in more than 30 years, with a combined capacity of approximately 2.1 gigawatts. Construction began in 2009, and the reactors came online in 2023 and 2024, taking 15 years to complete and costing more than $35 billion. Ultimately, the Vogtle plants came in seven years behind schedule and $21 billion over budget.
Now, compare this against Dominion Energy’s Coastal Virginia Offshore Wind project off Virginia Beach. Its construction began in November 2023, and all 176 wind turbines will be installed by the end of 2027. In total, CVOW will take four years to complete, compared with Vogtle’s 15 years. The project will cost about $11.7 billion, compared to Vogtle’s $35 billion, and CVOW has a 2.6 GW nameplate capacity, more than Vogtle’s two new reactors combined.
Offshore wind also comes out ahead when looking at the cost of construction per megawatt-hour of power production. Vogtle’s new units cost more than $35 billion and produce 17.2 million MWh per year. CVOW will cost about $11.65 billion and produce 9.5 million MWh. That makes offshore wind roughly 40% cheaper per megawatt-hour of annual production, and CVOW will be finished in less than half the time of the Vogtle reactors.
Wind skeptics will point out that a nuclear reactor runs around the clock while wind turbines depend on the wind. However, offshore wind provides the most consistent power during the winter, a season that is increasingly straining Louisiana’s grid.
In 2021, Winter Storm Uri forced rolling blackouts in MISO South and in 2025, Entergy Louisiana set a new winter peak record. These cold fronts bring strong winds that can be captured by offshore wind. During Winter Storm Fern this January, South Fork Wind and Vineyard Wind performed as well as gas plants and helped mitigate high power prices due to spikes in the cost of natural gas.
Finally, there is the question of who benefits. Offshore wind plays to strengths Louisiana already has. Louisiana companies with oil and gas roots helped build Block Island, the nation’s first offshore wind farm, and have worked on East Coast wind projects since.
A 2024 supply chain study found offshore wind could create 3,700 jobs in Louisiana and identified more than 450 Louisiana businesses ready to serve the industry. Offshore wind could be the next chapter of offshore energy production that helps keep our coastal communities and maritime industries working and prosperous as the offshore oil and gas industry continues to lose jobs.
Current politics favor nuclear and shun offshore wind. In August, RWE gave up the Gulf’s only federal offshore wind lease. Louisiana’s previous goal of 5 gigawatts of offshore wind by 2035, set by former Gov. John Bel Edwards, has been quietly shelved.
However, politics are constantly changing, and Louisiana should be ready when the window of opportunity for offshore wind opens again. Louisiana has spent a century proving it can be a leader in generating offshore energy. The engineers, shipbuilders, vessel crews, and fabricators who built the offshore oil and gas industry are already building wind projects for other states. I hope that one day we can leverage this expertise to build offshore wind off our own coast.

name: New Hampshire Bulletin
title: New Hampshire Democrats face an uphill battle to win control of state Senate
description: As voters fan out to polling places and newsrooms prepare all-night coverage, much of the attention today will focus on control of the U.S. House and Senate. But what about New Hampshire’s legislative chambers?  Recent state polls favoring Democrats and Democratic advantages in candidate recruitment this year suggest the New Hampshire House is in reach […]
text:
The sun sets behind the State House on Nov. 2, 2026, the eve of an election that will decide which party controls the New Hampshire House and Senate for the next two years. (Photo by Dana Wormald/New Hampshire Bulletin)As voters fan out to polling places and newsrooms prepare all-night coverage, much of the attention today will focus on control of the U.S. House and Senate.
But what about New Hampshire’s legislative chambers? 
Recent state polls favoring Democrats and Democratic advantages in candidate recruitment this year suggest the New Hampshire House is in reach for a Democratic flip.
The Senate might be a different story. 
While the New Hampshire House and Senate have stayed under single-party control for every election since 2012, Republicans have historically had a better chance of holding the Senate than the House. Since 2001, Republicans have won the House in nine of the 13 elections, but have won the Senate in 10. 
And the Republican-led redistricting in 2022 has resulted in a state Senate map that has helped Republicans win more seats than the statewide voting percentages would predict.
Republicans currently control 16 of 24 seats; to win back a 13-seat majority, Democrats, who currently have eight, would need to take back five of those seats. To win a tie, they will need four. 
But Democrats have a margin problem too: Of the five sitting Republican incumbent senators who won with the smallest margins in 2024 — and who are in theory the best targets for Democrats — only three of the five won with tight margins. In 2024, Democrats lost to Republican Sens. Tim McGough by 1.86%, Victoria Sullivan by 2.89% and Denise Ricciardi by 3.06%. But Democrats lost to the next two most-vulnerable Republicans — Sens. Daniel Innis and Kevin Avard — by more than 11%.
The takeaway, says Anna Brown, executive director of the Warren B. Rudman Center for Justice, Leadership & Public Service at the UNH Franklin Pierce School of Law, is that Democrats have an uphill battle. 
“Democrats don’t just need to get 51% statewide,” Brown said in an interview Monday. “They need to have an incredible performance. They need to have huge voter turnout in these Republican-heavy districts as well.”
Here are five races to watch tonight that could determine control of the state Senate.
Tim McGough vs. Shannon Chandley
In Senate District 11, which comprises Amherst, Merrimack, Milford and Wilton, McGough, of Merrimack, is facing a rematch. Former Democratic Sen. Shannon Chandley is trying again to retake her seat. Chandley, who served as a senator from 2018 to 2020 and from 2022 to 2024, lost to McGough two years ago by 673 votes. 
Aside from the potentially high name recognition in the race, the contest features another quirk: McGough was ousted from his committee by Republican Senate President Sharon Carson after allegations that he had been abusive to employees in the State House. 
Victoria Sullivan vs. Leonard Bell
Another hard-fought race to watch is in District 18, which covers Litchfield and Manchester Wards 5, 6, 7, 8 and 9.
Sullivan, a former state representative and current director of a nonprofit employment organization, who narrowly ousted former Democratic Senate President Donna Soucy in 2024, is now defending that win. Her challenger is Democrat Leonard Bell, an adjunct faculty instructor at Southern New Hampshire University.
The race has been anything but civil. “I live in that district, and it has been nasty,” Brown said. “The mailers for that district are nasty, nasty, nasty, nasty, and in a very expensive race as well.”
Denise Ricciardi vs. Matt McLaughlin
Also closely defending her seat is Ricciardi, a state senator since 2020 and a retired former owner of a Medicare insurance company, who has made education a central focus of her tenure. 
Ricciardi’s District 9, which comprises Bedford, Fitzwilliam, Greenfield, Hinsdale, Jaffrey, Lyndeborough, Mont Vernon, New Boston, Richmond, Sharon, Temple, Troy and Winchester, is one that was heavily changed in the last redistricting. But Ricciardi has not always toed the Republican line; for instance, in 2025, she voted against Senate Bill 101, an “open enrollment” public school bill, though she did support a subsequent bill, House Bill 751. 
Ricciardi is in another rematch. Her Democratic opponent, Matt McLaughlin, lost to her by 1,024 votes. McLaughlin, a retired commercial airline pilot and U.S. Navy pilot, is from Bedford, like Ricciardi. He has criticized Ricciardi for support of education freedom accounts and for voting absences the senator says were health-related; Ricciardi has argued McLaughlin would raise taxes.
Daniel Innis vs. Rebecca Harned
Sen. Dan Innis, who represents District 7, has a more comfortable 2024 margin to defend: 11.01%. As a farm owner and professor of marketing and hospitality management at the University of New Hampshire, Innis has represented a district that includes Alexandria, Andover, Boscawen, Bradford, Bridgewater, Bristol, Danbury, Franklin, Goshen, Grafton, Hebron, Henniker, Hill, Hillsborough, Newbury, Orange, Salisbury, Sutton, Tilton, Warner, Webster and Wilmot.
His Democratic challenger, Rebecca Harned, is a principal research scientist at UL Research Institutes, and previously served as the senior adviser to the U.S. Fire Administration. She has advocated for more state spending toward public schools, and for partially reversing state business tax cuts to help pay for that. Innis has criticized Harned for that tax position, and has argued she supports unsustainable increases to public school budgets that harm taxpayers.
Kevin Avard vs. Carryl Roy
Avard, the owner of a small cleaning business, won his 2024 election by 11.82%. But District 12, which comprises Brookline, Greenville, Hollis, Mason, New Ipswich, Rindge, and Nashua Wards 1, 2, and 5, has flipped in the past. 
Carryl Roy, the Democrat challenging Avard, is the owner of an event-DJ business and a Hollis School Board member. She has sought to argue that low state funding of public schools under Republicans has increased property taxes and has pushed for more clean energy in the state. Avard has said he stands for school choice and strong public school investment, but has criticized the increases to state education advocated by Roy. 
Structural problems for Democrats
To have any chance of winning back the state Senate Democrats must clear a structural barrier: The current state Senate districts favor Republicans.
In 2024, 51.33% of people voted for a Republican state Senate candidate across the state, compared to 48.6% for Democrats. Yet Republicans won 16 of the 24 seats of the chamber, or 66.66%. That overrepresentation occurred to a lesser degree in 2022, when 50.5% of New Hampshire voters picked a Republican state Senate candidate compared to 49.5% a Democrat, but Republicans took 54.16% of the seats (13 of 24).
Both of those elections came after the then-Gov. Chris Sununu signed into law a new state Senate district map passed by Republican lawmakers, in 2022, as part of the once-a-decade redistricting process mandated by the state constitution. 
An analysis of that 2022 map by New Hampshire Public Radio, produced as part of a partnership with the Bulletin, found that the distribution of voters in the map meant Democrats would need to win 54% of the statewide popular vote in order to win a majority of seats, 13. 
That 2022 NHPR analysis, which used an “efficiency gap analysis” deployed by political scientists, drew upon voter registration data from the 2020 presidential election.
“In many ways, it looks like a best-case scenario for Democrats would be even getting to a tie: 12 seats,” Brown said. “As opposed to flipping the Senate, which would require not only amazing Democratic turnout but also probably poor Republican turnout, and then a lot of independents swinging more left as well.”

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Indiana makes progress in cutting childcare voucher waitlist
description: The waitlist for a childcare voucher in Indiana declined from 41,175 children in May to just 9,006 children at the end of October — a 78% decline Gov. Mike Braun credits to a major investment by his administration following a year-and-a-half hiatus for new sign-ups. “Making life more affordable for Hoosiers is a top priority […]
text:
Toys are scattered along a shelf at Shepherd Community Center's Minnie Hartmann Neighborhood Childcare facility on Tuesday, July 21, 2026. (Photo by Leslie Bonilla Muñiz/Indiana Capital Chronicle)The waitlist for a childcare voucher in Indiana declined from 41,175 children in May to just 9,006 children at the end of October — a 78% decline Gov. Mike Braun credits to a major investment by his administration following a year-and-a-half hiatus for new sign-ups.
“Making life more affordable for Hoosiers is a top priority of mine,” the governor said in a news release Monday. “These results reflect focused efforts to deliver immediate relief to families and accelerate access to affordable child care.”
The Child Care Development Fund, or CCDF, is a state-administered federal program offering childcare vouchers to low-income families.
The state paused sign-ups for childcare vouchers in late 2024, pushing more families onto a waitlist for assistance.
Braun asked lawmakers on the State Budget Committee in April to redirect $200 million from the Financial Responsibility and Opportunity Growth Fund to the Child Care and Development Fund, with the goal of moving 14,000 children off the waitlist.
In a statement Monday, Braun said nearly 48,000 Hoosier children are now receiving CCDF vouchers. That’s up from 40,000 children in May, according to the state’s CCDF dashboard.
He described the voucher system as an economic engine for the state, granting families the flexibility to pursue better jobs and new skills.
“What we have is a crisis of affordability, and so to get more families access to these dollars and to reduce the waitlist is a very good thing,” said Sam Snideman, vice president of government and sector relations for the United Way of Central Indiana.
Still, Snideman said the investment came too late for childcare providers forced to close in the interim, and still exclude hundreds of families pinched by inflation who don’t meet the income threshold.
Childcare subsidies are typically restricted to families who are at or below 135% of federal poverty, or $44,000 for a family of four.
“The reality is that we probably have hundreds, if not thousands, of other kids and families who still need access to some sort of support in order to afford childcare,” he said.
Reimbursement rates remain low too, in some cases the equivalent of $1 a week, Snideman said.
“We still have some work to do as a state to ensure that a voucher has the value that it takes to provide the care for a child. We want to make sure that it doesn’t cost more to process a payment than the payment is worth.”
The latest round of funding prioritized enrollment of siblings of current voucher holders, as well as infants, toddlers and pre-school age children.
The state also created exemptions for children of foster and kinship families, children with special needs, homeless children, children of childcare workers and children of Ivy Tech students.

name: Maine Morning Star
title: With key races up and down the ballot, Maine voters turn out for Election Day
description: This Election Day, Maine residents are considering a lot on their ballots, from local initiatives to statewide elections, including several races with national stakes.  More than 290,000 Mainers have already cast a ballot, surpassing early voting numbers during the last midterm election in 2022 and approaching those from the 2024 presidential contest. It’s p[...]
text:
Voters wait in line on the last day of early, in-person voting at Portland City Hall on Oct. 29, 2026. (Photo by Emma Davis/ Maine Morning Star)This Election Day, Maine residents are considering a lot on their ballots, from local initiatives to statewide elections, including several races with national stakes. 
More than 290,000 Mainers have already cast a ballot, surpassing early voting numbers during the last midterm election in 2022 and approaching those from the 2024 presidential contest.
It’s possible that the outcome of some of the state’s most closely-watched races won’t be known for at least a week, according to Secretary of State Shenna Bellows, who said it’s likely some federal elections will be determined by a ranked-choice runoff.
Meanwhile, election officials across the country are bracing for possible federal interference, with the Trump administration already involved in lawsuits in California and Alaska, and preparing to persevere through any instability.
State courthouses in Portland, Bangor and Augusta will remain open until 9 p.m. Tuesday to accept emergency filings related to the election. 
Federal election monitors will be in Portland, South Portland and Lewiston Tuesday as part of the U.S. Department of Justice’s plan to send 1,000 monitors to locations in all 50 states. 
Have a question about a specific race? Want to know where a candidate stands on an issue, or how to find your polling place? Check out Maine Morning Star’s Voter Guide.
Federal races
The most high profile race in Maine this cycle is for the U.S. Senate, as Democrat Troy Jackson takes on incumbent Republican Susan Collins. 
It’s not the ticket voters expected to see even six months ago, after Graham Platner blew onto the political scene and overwhelmingly won the Democratic primary in June. But, following sexual assault allegations that he denies, Platner dropped out and Jackson quickly replaced him as the Democratic nominee. 
Voters are also reckoning with Collins’ alleged involvement in a pay-for-play scheme, first reported by ProPublican in September. 
It’s unclear how much the accusations will influence voters. Last month, several people said they were unsurprised and unmoved, with ​​most voters firmly aligned with their chosen party, while some swing voters said they are reconsidering their support of the senior senator — a key bloc in Collins’ 2020 win.
Across four debates last month, Jackson and Collins faced off over an extensive list of issues, ranging from energy prices to gun rights to the future of democracy. 
Both candidates made final appeals to voters this weekend. Collins emphasized her track record of bringing federal funds back to Maine for local projects, while Jackson highlighted Collins’ votes in support of President Donald Trump’s agenda. 
Democrats view Collins’ seat as a key pickup opportunity in their efforts to gain more control in the U.S. Senate, and they’re hoping time has run out on the senior senator’s staying power, given the Trump administration’s increasing unpopularity. 
Collins, Jackson make their closing appeals in Maine’s pivotal US Senate race

Polls have shown that race to be close, with the Cook Political Report deeming it one of seven toss-up Senate races. If that holds true, the results may not be known for days. With six declared write-in candidates, Maine Secretary of State Shenna Bellows said last month that the Senate election will likely go to a ranked-choice runoff. To avoid the runoff, Collins or Jackson must get more than 50% of total votes. 
It’s a similar situation in Maine’s 2nd Congressional District, where Republican Paul LePage and Democrat Matt Dunlap are fighting to replace Democratic Rep. Jared Golden in the U.S. House of Representatives. 
There is one declared write-in candidate in that race, so if Dunlap or LePage don’t get more than 50% of votes, the district will also see a ranked-choice runoff. 
It wouldn’t be an unprecedented situation for the 2nd District. In 2018, Golden defeated incumbent Republican U.S. Rep. Bruce Poliquin in the nation’s first congressional election to use ranked choice voting to determine the winner. Since then, Golden has repeatedly defended his seat through the runoff process, mostly recently in the 2024 election against Republican Austin Theriault, which went to a ranked-choice runoff and then a recount.
Golden announced last November that he would not seek reelection. LePage had already announced his campaign, and faced no Republican primary challengers. Dunlap had intended to challenge Golden, and went on to defeat three other candidates in a ranked-choice runoff in the June primary. 
The race is among those that will determine which party will hold a majority in the U.S. House of Representatives, and party leaders have watched the campaigns closely in the lead up to the election. In September, the Cook Political Report shifted its rating in Democrats favor, ultimately rating the district as leaning Republican.
Neither candidate seeking to replace Golden has tried to emulate his unique relationship with his party. Instead, the former governor has campaigned hard on the backing of national GOP leaders. And while Dunlap is more progressive than Golden on many issues, the national Democratic Party was slow to back him, and Dunlap hasn’t embraced their support on the campaign trail.
Not as contentious as the other congressional races is Maine’s 1st District, where Republican Ron Russell is again challenging incumbent Democratic U.S. Rep. Chellie Pingree. 
It’s a rematch for the two candidates, who faced off in 2024, when Pingree had a decisive victory over Russell. 
The pair met for one debate last week, and squared off over healthcare, Social Security and the Iran War. Although it’s been a quiet campaign trail for both candidates this year, they have made their primary disagreement clear: Russell’s support of and Pingree’s opposition to Trump’s agenda in Congress. 
The Cook Political Report had rated the district solidly Democratic in the lead-up to the election.
State races 
Mainers will also be voting on who will succeed Gov. Janet Mills in the Blaine House. With the two-term Democrat terming out, three candidates are vying to replace her: Democrat Hannah Pingree, Republican Bobby Charles and independent Rick Bennett. 
In the final days before the election, all three candidates made a final pitch to voter,in a manner that mirrored their individual campaign styles: Bennett focused on meeting voters where they’re at, Pingree highlighted her prominent endorsements, and Charles went on the offensive, challenging critics to debate him on stage at the Auburn Mall.
Pingree, considered the frontrunner in the race, has raised more money than both of her opponents combined. According to reports filed with the Maine Ethics Commission, the Democrat raised more than $4.9 million. Charles has raised just over $2 million, and Bennett has raised slightly below a million dollars.
The entire state Legislature is also up for election, and the results will determine the balance of the parties under the new governor. 
As a potential Democratic wave looms, Trump’s DOJ angles for last-minute power over midterms

Democrats currently hold narrow majorities in both chambers. The Maine Senate has 20 Democrats, 14 Republicans and one independent, Rick Bennett, who unenrolled from the Maine GOP in June 2025. In the Maine House of Representatives, Democrats hold 75 seats to Republicans’ 73, with one independent and two unenrolled members.
The nonpartisan newsletter Sabato’s Crystal Ball at the University of Virginia’s Center for Politics released its final analysis of state legislative races earlier this month. Senior columnist Louis Jacobson marked the Maine Senate as likely to remain in Democratic control while the Maine House is considered leaning Democratic, with Jacobson naming it one of the 15 most competitive legislative chambers in the country. 
And outside groups — that don’t have to disclose their donors — have spent big in legislative races. According to data from the Maine Ethics Commission as of Thursday, outside groups spent roughly $4.6 million in state elections.
The number of unenrolled candidates running in legislative races this year is higher than it’s been in at least a decade, with 19 vying for the Maine House and seven for Senate.
Several unenrolled candidates said they ran as independents because of increasing polarization, and voters’ desires to distance themselves from it. But despite the message they’re campaigning on, not all independents are truly unaffiliated, with some receiving the financial backing of partisan groups. 
There are also additional races for local and county positions — like the Cumberland County district attorney and the Hancock County sheriff — and ballot questions, which range from restrictions on syringe service programs to bans on data centers and Flock cameras. 
Maine Morning Star reporters Eesha Pendharkar and Emma Davis contributed to this report.

name: National
title: Party control could flip state leadership across the country
description: While much of the national attention on today’s midterm elections has focused on control of Congress, voters across the country will also choose which party controls the levers of state power.  Across the states, more than 6,000 legislative seats are up for grabs, leaving the partisan control of numerous chambers hanging in the balance.  And […]
text:
Republican Rick Jackson rallies supporters in Roswell, Georgia, last week as he campaigned for Georgia governor. This year, voters in 36 states will elect governors with at least a dozen races characterized by analysts as competitive. (Photo by Ross Williams/Georgia Recorder)While much of the national attention on today’s midterm elections has focused on control of Congress, voters across the country will also choose which party controls the levers of state power. 
Across the states, more than 6,000 legislative seats are up for grabs, leaving the partisan control of numerous chambers hanging in the balance. 
And voters will choose governors in 36 states. Only a dozen of those races are considered competitive by independent analysts, but Democrats have a shot at winning control of a majority of governorships for the first time in 16 years.
Midterm elections generally favor the party that doesn’t control the White House. Voters’ growing disapproval of President Donald Trump and frustration over high prices has given Democrats a shot at not only flipping control of Congress but also making major gains in state governments, where Republicans have held a majority of governors and legislative chambers since 2010.
“For the most part the Republicans are kind of playing defense more than offense,” Katy Owens Hubler, director of elections and redistricting at the National Conference of State Legislatures, told Stateline earlier this election cycle. 
Democrats could win majority of governor’s offices for first time in 16 years

Currently, Republicans boast a 26-24 gubernatorial advantage over Democrats. The math could change depending on the outcome of today’s elections, particularly as Democrats are competing closely in some reliably conservative states.
The nonpartisan Cook Political Report with Amy Walter, which ranks the competitiveness of state and national races, identified a dozen races for governor considered competitive this cycle. Those include: Alaska, Georgia, Florida, Iowa, Kansas, Michigan, Nebraska, Nevada, Ohio, Oregon, Texas and Wisconsin. 
In recent weeks, Cook moved its ratings of the Florida and Texas governor races from Likely Republican to Lean Republican. That means the GOP candidates are still favored in those states, but “given the grim political environment for the GOP,” the analysts could not rule out an upset in one or both states.  
Democrats’ improving prospects are evidence of the broader political challenges facing Republicans across the country, said Mark Jones, a political science professor at Rice University in Houston.
“It’s a rebuke of the Trump model, and especially the Republican Trump model,” he said. “But it’s also something that isn’t uncommon for midterms.”
In states such as Alaska, Georgia, Florida, Iowa, Nebraska, Ohio and Texas, a Democratic governor could reinvigorate the left, which has struggled to compete with the GOP’s grip on state power, providing a new check on Republican lawmakers. 
Experts say Democratic control of more governor’s offices could mean more bipartisan compromise — or gridlock — in state capitols, depending on which party controls the legislature. In Nevada, a Democratic governor could initiate a new era of policymaking: Republican Gov. Joe Lombardo has vetoed more than 160 bills approved by the Democratic-controlled legislature during his term.
Democrats are also aiming to flip hundreds of state legislative seats this cycle. Republicans currently boast control of 28 state legislatures and Democrats control 18, while three states have divided control of chambers, according to the National Conference of State Legislatures.
Democrats have a shot at flipping state legislatures across the country

Since President Donald Trump’s second term began, Democrats have flipped a dozen seats in special elections in Arkansas, Iowa, Florida, Georgia, Michigan, Minnesota, Mississippi, New Hampshire, Pennsylvania, Virginia and Texas, according to tracking by the Democratic Legislative Campaign Committee, which works to elect Democrats at the state level. They also flipped another 18 seats in last year’s general elections in New Jersey and Virginia. 
Heather Williams, president of that organization, has repeatedly characterized 2026 as “a once-in-a-generation opportunity” to transform state legislative power for the party.
The outcome of gubernatorial and legislative races will undoubtedly affect local policymaking in upcoming legislative sessions. But both parties have identified control of congressional redistricting as another prize up for grabs this cycle.
Set off by a White House push to give Republicans more seats in the U.S. House, 10 states have completed middecade redistricting — a phenomenon unseen since the 1800s.
“We know Democrats and their national allies will continue to pour millions into state legislative races because they understand what’s at stake: the legislators elected in 2026 will shape redistricting and the balance of power for years to come,” Republican State Leadership Committee President Edith Jorge-Tuñón, said in a July statement to Stateline. 
Stateline reporter Kevin Hardy can be reached at khardy@stateline.org.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Polls open today as CT decides on governor, General Assembly
description: Connecticut’s yearlong campaign for governor draws to a close today as voters go to the polls in all 169 cities and towns.
text:
Connecticut’s yearlong campaign for governor draws to a close today as voters go to the polls in all 169 cities and towns, with more than a half million of the 2.22 million eligible voters already having cast ballots.
Polls are open from 6 a.m. to 8 p.m., with all six statewide constitutional officers, five U.S. House members and 187 members of the General Assembly on the ballot in a year dominated by states where control of Congress will be resolved.
Neither of the state’s two senators are on the ballot, and the Cook Political Report rates all five U.S. House races in Connecticut as “solid Democratic” — an assessment shared by independent expenditure groups that have shunned the state.
Gov. Ned Lamont intends to vote Tuesday morning at Greenwich High School, then works his way north to an election night party at Dunkin Park in Hartford. His tentative stops include Stamford, Norwalk, Fairfield, Bridgeport, New Haven, Meriden, Newington, Hartford and West Hartford.
His Republican challenger, state Sen. Ryan Fazio of Greenwich, voted on Oct. 19, the first of 14 days of early voting. His Election Day schedule was unavailable Monday. Fazio’s election night party is at the Doubletree by Hilton hotel in Stamford.
The election is a laboratory of sorts: Will Connecticut’s second statewide election with early in-person voting and its first with no excuse absentee voting produce a higher voter turnout?
In the midterm election of 2022, when Lamont, a Democrat, won his second term and U.S. Sen. Richard Blumenthal his third, the turnout was 57.62% Before the first votes are cast Tuesday, the turnout was already about 23%. 
At the end of early voting Sunday night, 505,973 ballots had been cast: 455,169 during the two weeks of early voting and 50,804 by absentee ballot, the secretary of the state’s office reported Monday.
Another 20,854 absentee ballots had been issued and not yet returned. To be counted, absentee ballots must arrive at local clerk’s offices or be deposited in official drop boxes outside town halls by 8 p.m. Tuesday.
By nearly a 4-1 margin, more Democrats than Republicans voted in the first days of early voting, but the gap closed to a little more than a 2-1 Democratic advantage: 216,155 to 89,157, with 149,857 unaffiliated or minor-party voters.
As of late October, the state’s 934,070 unaffiliated voters were the largest bloc of voters in Connecticut, followed by 802,247 Democrats and 485,827 Republicans.
The gubernatorial race between Lamont, a Democrat, and Republican Ryan Fazio is the first since the General Assembly dramatically increased the public financing grant to $18 million.
Whatever Fazio’s challenges have been as a Republican trying to unseat a wealthy self-funded Democrat in a blue state, money has not been among them. Spending by the two candidates has been roughly equal through Oct. 27.
Lamont had spent $18.7 million of the $20 million he contributed to his own campaign account, including a $2.2 million loan; Fazio, $17 million, with $2 million left to spend. 
The money Lamont gave his campaign goes back to him if unspent. In 2022, Lamont spent $26.2 million.
From Oct. 21 to 27, the period covered by the last report, Fazio spent more than $2 million, nearly all of it on television advertising ($1.2 million) or direct mail ($848,306). Lamont spent $1.16 million, most of it on television.
Neither party expects a significant change in the balance of power at the General Assembly, where Democrats have won strong majorities in every election since the 2018 midterm.
Democrats now have majorities of 102-49 in the House and 25-11 in the Senate.
On Thursday, Democrats plan to endorse the reelection of House Speaker Matt Ritter, D-Hartford,  for an unprecedented fourth term as speaker and House Majority Leader Jason Rojas, D-East Hartford, as his second in command. The caucus will take place with a buzz about Ritter’s potential departure to become interim president of the University of Connecticut.
With the retirement of Senate President Pro Tem Martin M. Looney, Senate Democrats are set to endorse Senate Majority Leader Bob Duff of Norwalk as Looney’s successor and Sen. Gary Winfield of New Haven as Duff’s.
House Minority Leader Vincent J. Candelora, R-North Branford, and Senate Minority Leader Stephen Harding, R-Brookfield, are expected to continue as the GOP leaders.
The new legislative terms begin Jan. 6, the opening day of the annual legislative session. The winner of the gubernatorial will be sworn in and address a joint session of the General Assembly the same day.

title: Polls open in Wisconsin’s midterm elections
description: Polls open on Tuesday in Wisconsin’s midterm elections at 7 a.m. and will remain open until 8 p.m. Anyone still in line when polls closed should remain in line and will still be able to vote.  As of Monday afternoon, 857,764 absentee ballots had been requested and 777,739 of those had been returned. Voters still […]
text:
The polling place at Village on Park on Madison's South side in 2023. (Photo by Henry Redman/Wisconsin Examiner)Polls open on Tuesday in Wisconsin’s midterm elections at 7 a.m. and will remain open until 8 p.m. Anyone still in line when polls closed should remain in line and will still be able to vote. 
As of Monday afternoon, 857,764 absentee ballots had been requested and 777,739 of those had been returned. Voters still in possession of their absentee ballot shouldn’t drop it in the mail but should instead bring it in person to their polling place or their municipal clerk’s office. 
Voters who aren’t registered or need to update their registration can do so at the polls on Tuesday but will need a proof-of-residence document with their current address on it to do so. The state Department of Motor Vehicles announced it would extend its hours until 6 p.m. on Monday and Tuesday so voters can obtain a free photo ID if they need one. 
To get an ID, Wisconsin residents need a document such as a birth certificate to prove their identity and a document such as a bill or lease to prove their residency. 
The results in Tuesday’s elections will likely not be known for hours after the polls close — mostly because of the hundreds of thousands of absentee ballots, which clerks aren’t allowed to begin processing and counting until the polls open. 
In most municipalities, absentee ballots are opened and put through the voting machines at the same polling place that voters would have cast their ballot if doing so in person. But in a few dozen communities, including the state’s largest city of Milwaukee, absentee ballots are processed and counted at one central count location. 
This process means that reports of vote totals early in the evening Tuesday may not signify the eventual winner and that Milwaukee’s large amount of votes is unlikely to be reported until late. 
Information about what’s on the ballot and where to vote can be found at MyVote.WI.gov

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Opinion: Time falls backward. Kansas voters head to the polls for a midterm election. The cycle begins anew.
description: Overnight, between Saturday and Sunday, the hands of America’s clocks swept backward an hour. Groggy Halloween partiers slept an extra 60 minutes. Young and old alike dozed into the morning, waking refreshed and ready for a new month. Sure, most of us hate the spring time change, when a vanished hour pinches schedules and circadian […]
text:
Clocks dropped back an hour over the weekend, as part of the usual shift. Likewise, voters will head to the polls today for midterm elections. (Photo by Max McCoy/Kansas Reflector)Overnight, between Saturday and Sunday, the hands of America’s clocks swept backward an hour.
Groggy Halloween partiers slept an extra 60 minutes. Young and old alike dozed into the morning, waking refreshed and ready for a new month. Sure, most of us hate the spring time change, when a vanished hour pinches schedules and circadian rhythms alike. But the fall switch — that calm relaxation into the cool months — holds a special place in our sleep-deprived hearts.
The change this year came two days before the U.S. midterm elections, those down-ballot contests beloved by political journalists and dogged partisans alike. Everyone else, I suspect, grits his or her teeth and goes along for the ride.
Both our Sunday columnist, Max McCoy, and contributor Huascar Medina have written their musings on this particular, peculiar time, two years into the term of President Donald Trump and two years away from — well, something else.
McCoy focused on the global, existential implications. Medina wrote about western Kansas and worried about what comes next. Each one quotes Emporia Gazette editor William Allen White’s adage: “When anything is going to happen in this country, it happens first in Kansas.”
Each man has bared his soul. I have little to add in explicating the fraught nature of this moment.
But perhaps I have a small contribution to make from my experience as a journalist in swing states. I’ve covered 10 elections over the years, in Florida and New Hampshire and Kansas, and I can tell you this: As certain our clocks change twice a year, so do elections ebb and flow each two years.
Politicians overstep their mandates. Scandals mushroom. Democrats spend too much, while Republicans cut too much. Voters, who have witnessed all this before, throw the bums out time and again.
New bums appear, and the cycle begins afresh.
I can already hear the outraged splutters of those dedicated progressives who follow my work. They will mention, as they should, the unprecedented destruction of President Donald Trump and his administration. Yet the most precedented reaction of all time would be a midterm sweeping out incumbents. Polls and models suggest that’s what we’ll see tonight.
Like the time change, these shifts in the body politic suggest nothing so much as the shifts of seasons and the ages the man. The year, born in the chill of winter, blossoms into adolescent spring and mature summer. Sweet senescence follows in the fall, and then the old man makes way for the baby.
Each one of us, if so blessed, trace these shifts in our own lives. Time passes, and we pass with it, yet we know that others will follow us on similar journeys.
What we must resist — passionate advocates and Machiavellian operatives alike — is taking any season of the year or life of American politics as permanent. We may claim we will be teenagers forever. We may claim that the summer can’t possibly end. We may claim an everlasting majority for one party of another.
Those claims disintegrate as surely as knee cartilage. We will age. School starts again. The opposition party adapts and wins again.
None of this obviates the necessity of fighting for the causes in which we believe. Persistent, dedicated efforts for change can pay off over time, but they require a mindset that persists beyond single years, election seasons or even lives.
Let me send you out into the maelstrom of election madness today with these thoughts from the German sociologist Max Weber:
“Politics is a strong and slow boring of hard boards. It takes both passion and perspective. Certainly all historical experience confirms the truth – that man would not have attained the possible unless time and again he had reached out for the impossible. But to do that a man must be a leader, and not only a leader but a hero as well, in a very sober sense of the word. And even those who are neither leaders nor heroes must arm themselves with that steadfastness of heart which can brave even the crumbling of all hopes. This is necessary right now, or else men will not be able to attain even that which is possible today.”
Clay Wirestone is Kansas Reflector opinion editor. His first book, “Opinionated: Kansas Journalists Who Proved Why Commentary Matters — Then and Now,” was published in September 2026 by the University Press of Kansas. Through its opinion section, Kansas Reflector works to amplify the voices of people who are affected by public policies or excluded from public debate. Find information, including how to submit your own commentary, here.

name: Georgia Recorder
title: Here are five things to watch as Georgia voters head to the polls on Election Day
description: Who will be Georgia’s next governor? Will Republicans overcome the apparent Democratic lead built up during early voting? Which party will run state government starting next year?  And when can Georgians expect to learn the answer to these questions and others?  This year’s ballot is packed with a nationally watched U.S. Senate race and competitive […]
text:
Georgia's ballot marking devices display the candidates and ballot questions for the Nov. 3 midterm elections. Election workers in Bartow County, Georgia conducted their pre-election tests of the voting equipment on Oct. 6, 2026. Maya Homan/Georgia RecorderWho will be Georgia’s next governor? Will Republicans overcome the apparent Democratic lead built up during early voting? Which party will run state government starting next year? 
And when can Georgians expect to learn the answer to these questions and others? 
This year’s ballot is packed with a nationally watched U.S. Senate race and competitive statewide contests as both parties battle for control of four open seats, including the governor’s office. 
Here’s what some of Georgia’s political experts are watching, and what they say Tuesday’s election results could reveal about the state of Georgia politics.
Anticipating results
Expect voters and candidates alike to be eagerly awaiting results once the polls close Tuesday night.
For some initial results, Georgians likely won’t be kept waiting long. At a Monday press conference, Secretary of State Brad Raffensperger said that he expected the absentee and early voting results to be finalized within an hour of polls closing, as is required by Georgia law. 
Secretary of State Brad Raffensperger speaks with reporters during a pre-election press conference on Nov. 2, 2026. Maya Homan/Georgia Recorder
“I like to go to bed early, so I want to be done before midnight,” he said. “We did that in 2024. There’s no reason why we won’t do it here tomorrow.”
But while Raffensperger said he is hoping Georgians will be able to know the full results before bedtime, it may take longer to determine the winner in races where only a small margin separates the winner from the loser, which could happen with hotly contested state House races.
Early results can also be misleading, said Gbemende Johnson, an associate professor of political science at the University of Georgia. Johnson cautioned against what she called an election “mirage,” which can lead voters to think that a certain candidate is further ahead than they are before results are fully tallied.
“If the areas that are reporting initially and the quickest tend to favor one candidate or the other, it can give you the sense that oh, that candidate is going to take it home,” she said.
She said voters should stay mindful of which areas the results are coming in from and how many votes there are left to tally from elsewhere.
“There’s always the question of where are they coming from? Are they areas that are traditionally red, traditionally blue, or maybe there’s a hue of purple?” she said. “That is why you want to be careful about early assessments.”
Voter turnout
Jazzed by the prospect of registering their discontent with the Trump administration at the polls, Democrats appear to have built a solid lead during early voting. A key question going into Tuesday is whether Republicans can get enough voters to the ballot box on Election Day to overcome that lead.
What early voting can – and can’t – tell us about Georgia’s midterm election so far 

Unlike in some states, Georgia voters do not indicate their party affiliation when registering to vote, which makes predicting the outcome of a race based on early voting an inexact exercise. Pundits must instead rely on data like voters’ race and age and turnout levels in heavily Democratic or Republican areas.
Based on that limited information, Republicans have been sounding alarm bells about lower turnout in rural parts of the state fertile with conservative voters and higher turnout in metro areas thick with liberals.
“There’s no sugarcoating it, the Democrats have been working hard,” said outgoing Gov. Brian Kemp stumping for Republican candidate for governor Rick Jackson at a Cherokee County diner Monday morning. “They’ve been motivated. They outpaced us in early voting. But you know what? This situation is no different than it was in 2018. And if we have a big turnout tomorrow, we are going to win this race.”
In 2018, Kemp was narrowly elected governor during what was the first midterm election of the Trump era, although Georgia Democrats also made significant gains in the Legislature that year.  
An imbalance in early voting turnout inspired the University of Virginia-based election forecaster Sabato’s Crystal Ball to shift the race Monday from a toss-up to slightly favor Democrats. 
The polling prognosticators found that Black voters made up nearly 32% of Georgia’s early voters, up from 26% in 2024 and 29% in 2022. In Georgia, Black voters tend to favor Democratic candidates while white voters skew more toward Republicans.
A statewide temperature check on Trump
In visits to Georgia and other states, Trump has urged voters to “pretend” he’s on the ballot and campaigned with candidates in an effort to energize the president’s supporters to vote for Republican candidates. 
Voters in midterm elections identify a culprit for rising cost of living: Trump’s tariffs

But voters are increasingly blaming Trump policies for issues like the rising cost of living, and his approval rating has hit a record low of 33%. Polling from the Atlanta Journal-Constitution showed that both Keisha Lance Bottoms, the Democratic nominee for governor, and incumbent Democratic U.S. Sen. Jon Ossoff had an edge with likely independent voters. Given those factors, some experts question whether steadfast supporters of the president will be able to deliver Republican candidates a victory in a state like Georgia, which Trump narrowly lost in 2020 and won in 2024.
“The MAGA coalition is still pretty intact,” said Emory University political science professor Andra Gillespie. “But I think it becomes a question of, can you rely on the MAGA base alone to be able to win an election in a year that is going to be hard for Republicans?”
The role of split ticket voters
Independent and split-ticket voters played a crucial role in the 2022 midterms, when Georgians reelected Kemp, a Republican, and U.S. Sen. Raphael Warnock, a Democrat, during the same cycle.
Emory University political science professor Bernard Fraga said that although split-ticket voting used to be quite common in Georgia, the majority of voters these days tend to vote strictly along party lines.
Sen. Jon Ossoff speaks at a rally with former President Barack Obama on Oct. 28, 2026. Alander Rocha/Georgia Recorder
“I think this year the big question is how large the magnitude of that effect will be,” he said. “Because it looks like Ossoff’s lead is so large that you’d have to have historically super high levels of split-ticket voting for Bottoms to not get over the top.”
Fraga added that he will also be paying close attention to the results from precincts in Atlanta’s Buckhead neighborhood, where Bottoms was relatively unpopular during her time as mayor of Atlanta and where he says split-ticket voting is still somewhat common.
Rick Jackson speaks at a campaign rally in Canton Oct. 24, 2026. Ross Williams/Georgia Recorder
But he said there is a key difference between the 2022 midterms and this year’s election: Kemp was running as an incumbent candidate and was able to rely on his political record to entice Democratic-leaning voters. Jackson, in contrast, has never held political office.
“Rick Jackson is not a known quantity in the same way for people who would otherwise be drawn to vote for the Democrats,” Fraga said. “So I think that’s a big question.”
The next class of political leaders
Regardless of who ascends to Georgia’s top political offices this year, the state’s next slate of leaders will look different.
That’s because a number of statewide offices — including governor, lieutenant governor, secretary of state and attorney general — are wide open.
[Voter Guide: 2026 General Election Voter Guide: The candidates, the ballot measures, and the tools you need to cast your vote.]
All four seats are currently held by Republicans. Kemp, who is nearing the end of his second term as governor, is term-limited and prevented from running again. Lt. Gov. Burt Jones, Attorney General Chris Carr and Raffensperger, the secretary of state, all launched their own bids for governor but lost to Jackson.
A slew of candidates, including many who are currently members of the state Legislature, are competing to fill those seats. Candidates hoping to fill their vacant seats in the state House and Senate will also likely bring a new set of faces and names into the mix when the new session starts in January.
Alan Abramowitz, a professor emeritus of political science at Emory University, said that in addition to being crucial constitutional offices, downballot positions could offer a glimpse into the future of Georgia — and national — politics. Kemp spent eight years as secretary of state before running for governor. The late President Jimmy Carter also served as a state senator before he became governor of Georgia.
“Watch the secretary of state, lieutenant governor, attorney general,” Abramowitz said. “Those are the offices that tend to produce candidates for governor, candidates for U.S. Senate.”

name: Michigan Advance
title: It’s Election Day. Here’s what voters need to know
description: Election Day marks the culmination of months of campaigning in Michigan for races that will likely determine party control of crucial seats on both a state and federal level — including the U.S. Senate, governor’s office, a number of key U.S. House races and both chambers of the state Legislature. As of midafternoon Monday, the Michigan […]
text:
Signs informed attendees at Lansing's No Kings protest on Oct. 17, 2026 of a nonpartisan voter protection and information hotline. (Photo by Katherine Dailey/Michigan Advance)Election Day marks the culmination of months of campaigning in Michigan for races that will likely determine party control of crucial seats on both a state and federal level — including the U.S. Senate, governor’s office, a number of key U.S. House races and both chambers of the state Legislature.
As of midafternoon Monday, the Michigan Department of State reported that more than 2.3 million Michiganders had already cast ballots, including more than 743,000 who voted in person at early voting sites and more than 1.5 million who returned absentee ballots by mail. 
For those who still have to cast their ballots, polls are open from 7 a.m. to 8 p.m. local time in Michigan. While most of Michigan voters will be casting ballots in the Eastern Time Zone, four counties in the Upper Peninsula — Dickinson, Gogebic, Iron, and Menominee — use Central Time instead and won’t finish voting until 9 p.m. Eastern Time
Concerns about a federal presence at the polls have been voiced throughout the election cycle, and local clerks throughout Michigan have worked to ease fears from potential voters.
A test ballot is submitted to an early voting tabulator in the Lansing Elections Office prior to the August primary. July 20, 2026. | Photo by Katherine Dailey/Michigan Advance.
Advocates are also working to ensure voters know what to do if they do encounter election interference, law enforcement presence or any other problems while voting. The national, nonpartisan Election Protection Coalition has launched a hotline, 866-OUR-VOTE, for reporting voting problems and seeking assistance.
Hotlines are also available in Spanish at 888-VE-Y-VOTA, in Arabic at 844-YALLA-US, and in Asian languages at 888-API-VOTE.
Federal election monitors from the Department of Justice are expected in Detroit, East Lansing, Flint, Grand Rapids, Hamtramck, Lansing and Warren. Federal monitors are standard and have been present at elections around the country for years. They function as observers to ensure voters are able to freely cast their ballots, and in Michigan’s primary, were described by election officials as “polite and unobtrusive.” 


Andrew Walchuk, the policy director and counsel for Common Cause, did express concerns about a potential lack of proper training for DOJ poll watchers after the Civil Rights Division has been “decimated by this administration.”
The real concern, however, comes if federal troops or armed federal law enforcement, including ICE, are present at polling places, which is illegal. 
A “Know Your Rights” flyer from the National Police Accountability Project explains that local police can be present if election officials or members of the public call for assistance — though “sustained law enforcement presence at a polling location could constitute voter intimidation or interference under state criminal law.” 
In Grand Rapids, advocates with GR Rapid Response to ICE are maintaining a hotline of their own, 616-238-0081, to report any local ICE presence.
“If there are armed federal agents, whether they are from DHS or the FBI or any other federal entity, they’re not allowed to be there,” Walchuk said. “Federal law for 150 years has forbidden federal agents, armed agents, from being at the polls, and so that is something that, if anyone does see agents at the polls, they should call the hotline.”
Michigan State University voting in 2020. (Photo by Anna Liz Nichols/Michigan Advance)
Once polls close, results will not be immediately available, especially in elections that may come down to just a few percentage points.
Though many concerns about election interference are centered on Election Day itself, advocates, including Jessica Ayoub, the deputy political director of the ACLU of Michigan, are also preparing to combat any interference in the election certification process. 
“Michigan law is clear: boards of county canvassers in Michigan must certify the election results based solely on the record of votes cast. They tally the votes and certify the results,” Ayoub said in a press call with the Election Protection Coalition. “The role of boards of county canvassers is not discretionary. Canvassers double check the math. They do not police our elections.”
Ballotpedia’s summary of Michigan law states, “Automatic recounts are required if the vote differential between the two candidates is .1% or less for statewide elections, including ballot measures, 75 votes or less for state senate elections, and 25 votes or less for state house elections.”
A candidate can also request a recount if they meet certain requirements and file a request officially “not later than 5 p.m. of the second day after the day the board of state canvassers certifies the results of the election.” 
In Michigan, canvassers are required to certify results no later than the 14th day after the election.

name: Ohio Capital Journal
title: Election 2026: Competitive congressional races to watch in Ohio
description: Ohio’s competitive congressional races could play a role in determining which party holds power in the U.S. House.  There are currently 218 Republicans, 214 Democrats, one independent and two vacancies in the U.S. House. Midterm elections typically favor the party that is not currently in power.  “I think if the Democrats are on track to […]
text:
The U.S. Capitol. (Photo by Ashley Murray/States Newsroom)Ohio’s competitive congressional races could play a role in determining which party holds power in the U.S. House. 
There are currently 218 Republicans, 214 Democrats, one independent and two vacancies in the U.S. House. Midterm elections typically favor the party that is not currently in power. 
“I think if the Democrats are on track to win the House, they’re probably coming out of Ohio with five seats, maybe six seats,” said Kyle Kondik, managing editor of Sabato’s Crystal Ball. 
[Voter Guide: 2026 Ohio General Election Voter Guide: Races, deadlines, and the tools you need to cast your vote.]
Ohio’s 7th Congressional district has become a competitive race with the Cook Political Report labeling it as a “toss-up.” 
Incumbent Republican U.S. Rep. Max Miller is facing Democratic candidate Brian Poindexter.
Allegations of domestic violence against Miller caused several prominent Republicans to call for his resignation over the summer — a movement led by Miller’s ex-father-in-law, U.S. Sen. Bernie Moreno. Miller denies the allegations against him.
Miller, who has served in Congress since 2023, is under investigation by the House Ethics Committee for allegations he “may have engaged in domestic violence and abuse or illegal drug use.”
The Northeast Ohio district begins just outside Cleveland and covers Medina and Wooster. 
“My guess is that if we did not have this controversy with Miller, he would still be in a somewhat competitive race,” Kondik said.  “I think he’d be favored, whereas now I don’t think he’s favored.”
Republicans currently hold 10 out of 15 Ohio U.S. Congressional districts, but the Ohio Redistricting Commission unanimously passed a new congressional map last year, increasing the Republican advantage in the state 12-3. 
“You have to take it in the context of the cycle,” Kondik said. “If this was 2024, different story, you probably would say that the Republicans are in good shape to (go) the whole 12-15.” 
U.S. Reps. Marcy Kaptur, Greg Landsman, and Emilia Sykes all have districts that are generally considered more favorable to Republicans than it was during the last election. President Donald Trump won Ohio by 11 percentage points in 2024. 
Ohio’s 9th Congressional District is a rematch of the 2024 election between incumbent Democratic U.S. Rep. Marcy Kaptur and Republican Derek Merrin. 
The race was so close two years ago that the outcome was not declared until weeks after the election. Kaptur beat Merrin by 0.7 percentage points in 2024 despite President Donald Trump winning the district by seven percentage points.
The Northwest Ohio district covers a small section of the Lake Erie coastline, including Sandusky and Toledo, before moving inward to the Michigan and Indiana borders. 
Kaptur has represented the Northwest Ohio congressional district since 1983 — making her the longest-serving woman in congressional history. 
Former Ohio state Rep. Derek Merrin served four terms as an Ohio state representative for the Toledo district from 2016 to 2025.
The Cook Political Report labeled the district as “lean Democrat.” 
Incumbent Democratic U.S. Rep Landsman is facing Republican Eric Conroy in Ohio’s 1st Congressional district, which includes Cincinnati, Warren County and borders Kentucky. 
Landsman has served in Congress since 2023 and Conroy is a former CIA officer. 
The Cook Political Report labeled the district as “likely Democrat.” 
“I think (Landsman) would be the lowest hanging fruit for Democrats to win,” Kondik said. 
Republican Carey Coleman is challenging Ohio Democratic U.S. Rep. Emilia Sykes for Ohio’s 13th congressional district, which includes Summit County and parts of Stark and Portage counties. 
Sykes has served in Congress since 2023 and Coleman is a former radio host.

The Cook Political Report labeled the district as “likely Democrat.” 
Incumbent Ohio Republican U.S. Rep. Mike Carey is running against Democratic candidate Don Leonard for Ohio’s 15th Congressional district, which includes parts of Franklin County and extends out near Dayton.
Carey has been in Congress since 2021 and Leonard previously taught regional and city planning at Ohio State University.
Incumbent Ohio Republican U.S. Rep. Mike Turner is competing against Democratic candidate Kristina Knickerbocker for Ohio’s 10th Congressional district, which includes the Dayton area.
Turner has held office since 2003 and Knickerbocker is an U.S. Air Force Veteran and oncology nurse practitioner.
The Cook Political Report labeled both of those races as “Lean Republican.”
“If you see Carey or Turner lose, you know the (Democratic) wave is really on,” Kondik said. 
Election Day is Nov. 3 and polls will be open from 6:30 a.m. to 7:30 p.m.

 Catching Our Eye

• The Ohio governor and your life. Cleveland.com’s Jeremy Pelzer reports, “Why it matters who wins the Ohio’s governor’s race and how it will affect daily life.”
When Ohioans elect their next governor on Tuesday, they aren’t just picking a new name to put on “Welcome to Ohio” signs: they’re choosing someone who will have a tangible effect on their daily lives over the next four years and beyond.
Either Democrat Amy Acton or Republican Vivek Ramaswamy will play a big role in shaping how much state residents pay in taxes, the jobs they have, how good their schools are, their healthcare costs, and the condition of the roads they drive on, among a litany of other everyday concerns.
• Local school levies. The Statehouse News Bureau’s Jo Ingles reports, “More than 130 Ohio public school districts are asking voters for dollars Tuesday.”
There will be 133 local school levies on the ballot in Ohio Tuesday. The leader of a group that represents school boards throughout Ohio says it’s been difficult for school districts on the ballot because of uncertainty with local property taxes.
Ohio School Boards Association CEO Tom Hosler said schools on the ballot are dealing with uncertainty as they face rising costs, state funding that has lagged inflation, and growing concerns about property taxes. With questions about funding that could come about from property tax changes, Hosler said it’s been a challenge for districts to figure out what they can or cannot do if levies don’t pass.
• Data centers. WOSU’s Katie Geniusz reports, “From Trenton to Grove City, data centers are on Ohio ballots this election.”
Ohio leads the nation in data center-related ballot measures in the upcoming election, with 21 initiatives across 18 municipalities.
Voters in these areas — from Trenton in the state’s southwest to Defiance in the rural northwest — will have the opportunity to decide whether to adopt regulations that would limit the construction of hyper-scale data centers.
Ohio has more than 200 data center projects planned or under construction — the fifth highest in the nation.
