name: West Virginia Watch
title: Miners file case against West Virginia coal safety officials over silica dust
description: The United Mine Workers of America and 52 miners have filed a lawsuit against the state Board of Coal Mine Health and Safety, asking it pass a limit on the amount of silica dust being produced in coal mines.
text:
Exposure to mixed coal mine dust that contains silica — a carcinogen — can lead to the development of pneumoconiosis, commonly known as black lung disease. (Getty Images)The United Mine Workers of America and 52 miners have filed a lawsuit against the state Board of Coal Mine Health and Safety, asking it pass a limit on the amount of silica dust being produced in coal mines. 
The union and the miners filed an emergency petition with the West Virginia Supreme Court on Oct. 29 to mandate that the board pass regulations limiting the amount of silica dust in coal mines. 
The suit is the latest salvo in a decades-long fight to limit the dust, which has driven the number of cases of black lung to a high not seen since the 1970s. 
Attorney Sam Petsonk, representing the miners, said silica dust rules were supposed to be passed in the state back in the 1980s, but didn’t come to fruition.
“The industry found one way after another to prolong and delay and distract and dodge any trick in the book,” he said. “They have fought dust regulation with a fiery vengeance.” 
The petition describes miners, some as young as their 30s, developing pneumoconiosis, due to the mining of thin-seam coal, which requires more sandstone to be cut in order to be extracted. 
Pneumoconiosis is when dust — from coal and rock — are breathed in over a prolonged amount of time, slowly destroying the lungs. 
History buffs may recall cutting sandstone led to the Hawks Nest Tunnel Disaster, in which hundreds of men died from inhaling silica while cutting a tunnel in Fayette County back during the Great Depression. 
Compounding that, the suit states coal operators have a financial incentive to mine thin-seam coal due to a tax credit passed in the 1990s, which charged a reduced severance on the coal. 
In 2024, federal regulators with the Mine Safety and Health Administration passed a rule to limit the amount of silica dust in the air, with it set to take effect in 2025. But after President Donald Trump won a second-term, the agency reversed course and indefinitely delayed implementation. 
Petsonk said the lawsuit is a way to kick the process into gear, in light of federal inaction. He said past efforts have seen the state be pushed to adopt new safety standards, and in turn the MSHA followed suit. 
“That’s what, unfortunately, may have to happen at this time as well, given MSHA’s abandonment of the silica rule,” he said. 
Thomas Clark, the administrator of the Coal Health and Safety Board did not respond after being left a voicemail. John F. Willems, assistant state attorney general representing the agency, forwarded a request to comment to media liaison, noting that person would not be in the office until Friday. 
Jared Hunt, spokesman for the West Virginia Supreme Court, confirmed the case has been docketed, but said it would likely be heard next year.

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: A wastewaster manager faces 3 years in prison for hiding 3 years of E. coli contamination from SC
description: A South Carolina wastewater treatment plant manager pleaded guilty to federal Clean Water Act violations for concealing an E. coli contamination.
text:
Matthew J. Perry Jr. U.S. Courthouse in Columbia, where John Lorick, senior manager for the Saluda Commission of Public Works, pleaded guilty Thursday, Oct. 29, 2026, to federal Clean Water Act violations. (File photo by Abraham Kenmore/SC Daily Gazette)COLUMBIA — A South Carolina wastewater treatment plant manager pleaded guilty to federal Clean Water Act violations for concealing E. coli contamination.
John Lorick, senior manager for the Saluda Commission of Public Works, entered a guilty plea in federal court Thursday. He faces a maximum penalty of three years in federal prison and fines between $5,000 and $50,000 per violation.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Investigators found the 45-year-old from Ninety-Six diluted water samples to hide E. coli levels elevated due to an inoperative chlorination system.
On dozens of occasions over more than three years, the town of Saluda’s plant released raw, untreated sewage directly into the Little Saluda River, which flows into Lake Murray.
“The defendant not only completely failed to treat sewage many times but also falsified records and reports to hide these failures. EPA will ensure that those who endanger public health and lie to the government to evade detection of their wrongdoing are found out and held accountable,” Charles Carfagno, special agent in charge of EPA’s criminal enforcement program in South Carolina, said in a statement.
The town of Saluda has a permit allowing the plant to release of set levels of pollutants, but without a working chlorination system, the E. coli levels violated that permit.
Lorick knowingly allowed this to happen 10 to 12 times a year between 2022 and March 2025, federal prosecutors said. One such release, which occurred from July 27-28, 2025, killed approximately 1,529 fish about a mile downstream from the plant, leading to the investigation.
“South Carolina’s natural resources are one of the many gems of our state. Lorick’s actions were harmful to the environment, the wildlife that rely on the Little Saluda River and potentially anyone who recreated in the water,” U.S. Attorney Bryan Stirling for South Carolina said in a statement.
Lorick took no steps to repair the system or notify regulators of the issue.
“The intentional pollution of our state’s natural resources, especially our essential water resources, can never be tolerated,” Myra Reece, the director of the state Department of Environmental Services, said in a statement.
United States District Court Chief Judge Sherri Lydon accepted the guilty plea and will sentence Lorick at a later date.
Lorick’s plea came in the same week that York County officials reported a massive sewage spill into Lake Wylie. The spill happened Oct. 26, after a pump station overflowed, dumping 500,000 gallons of sewage into Little Allison Creek on the southwest end of the lake.
Unlike Lorick, however, county staff reported the issue to state environmental regulators.

name: VTDigger
title: Universal primary care will strain a shrinking doctor workforce
description:
Free care would drive up demand for appointments faster than Vermont can train or recruit clinicians.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Universal primary care will strain a shrinking doctor workforce.
text:
Dear Editor,
As someone who has worked in Vermont’s healthcare financial advisory sector over the past year, I think Olivia Gieger’s recent VTDigger report does a great service by highlighting universal primary care, a goal both gubernatorial candidates view as important for Vermont. However, turning this vision into reality requires overcoming substantial structural and financial challenges.
On the care side, our delivery system is under immense strain. With nearly a third of our primary care doctors over 60 and 16% planning to retire, leave Vermont or reduce hours soon, eliminating cost-sharing will spike demand before capacity exists. Expanding access will likely force greater reliance on nurse practitioners rather than doctors. While nurse practitioners are vital to our system, studies show that relying on them to fill physician shortages can inadvertently drive up downstream costs through higher diagnostic testing and specialist referral rates. 
Actual 2027 program costs will certainly exceed the outdated cost estimate of $281.9 million projected in 2015. Grown at the same rate as hospital budgets over the period — which have averaged over 3% annually, tracking medical inflation — the $281.9 million initially projected by state analysts for 2017 could be closer to $400 million by 2027, if the scope remains constant. However, if we look at total Vermont healthcare costs in 2024, which I calculate at $7.5 billion, and use Maine as a composition proxy for primary care at 10% of the total, Vermont’s program would be closer to $750 million. We will also have to pay a premium to induce new doctors to relocate and fill our current shortages, creating additional expenses.

READ MORE

On the financing side, the federal Employee Retirement Income Security Act barrier is our primary obstacle. Because federal ERISA preemption bars Vermont from mandating that self-insured employer health plans, which make up about three-quarters of employer plans, join a state-funded risk pool, taxpayers face an unfunded $80 million to $100 million gap based on my estimate of 135,000 to 145,000 self-insured lives at an annual conservative cost of $600 to $700 per person. 
Additionally, bypassing a Medicaid waiver would needlessly forfeit around $107 million in Medicaid funding, much of it federal. Induced demand will likely outpace provider access at all levels, and offering free primary care may incentivize some to drop comprehensive insurance altogether, potentially increasing uncompensated emergency care and eliminating any projected emergency department savings, at least in the short term.
Total program costs without physician relocation bonuses would be $400 million to $750 million per year, and indirect costs of ERISA preemption and the Medicaid waiver would bring the total to $587 million to $957 million per year. Attempting to fund this project with almost $1 billion of taxpayer liability and cost shift using a targeted high-earner surtax is risky. 
The tax relies on about 3,500 filers who already generate over 30% of state income tax revenue, according to the Vermont Department of Taxes, meaning the tipping point for cannibalization of our general fund from out-of-state migration is only a few hundred departures. One billion dollars of total cost for universal primary care spread over the high-earner cohort would result in an average tax increase of $285,714 per filer per year. 
The numbers above are order of magnitude only. These challenges are formidable, but they may be solved. I look forward to seeing how Vermont meets this new moment in healthcare.
Myers MermelManchester, Vt.

title: Greetings, readers: I’m the new editor of the Washington State Standard. Pleased to meet you.

I suspect it’s easy for people who work here every day to take its beauty for granted. I know the place. I’ve been there many times in the […]
text:
The Washington State Legislative Building in Olympia, as seen on Oct. 28, 2026. (Photo by Sean Robinson/Washington State Standard)A flood of memories drowned me a week ago as I climbed the steps to the entrance of Olympia’s Legislative Building, a grand structure built in 1928. I suspect it’s easy for people who work here every day to take its beauty for granted.
I know the place. I’ve been there many times in the course of my journalism career,  but it had been a while. This visit was different. 
I wasn’t walking in as a reporter. I was walking in as the new editor-in-chief of the Washington State Standard, a mere eight days before a big election.
The building, 287 feet high, towered like a mountain. I felt small. My nerves jangled, intimidated by the prospect of new responsibilities and duties.
Did we really build this? I asked myself. Could we even dream of building it now in this fractious age?  
Memories came again. In my mind’s eye, I saw the faces of statehouse reporters, young and old: co-workers, friends, and competitors. One way or another, all found their way to the marble floors of this civic cathedral, the church of the People’s Business.

How did I get here? How did this happen?
When I started in journalism, I wasn’t thinking about saving the world. I just wanted to tell good stories. My first naive effort for a weekly Seattle newspaper profiled a community activist who wanted to fix a neglected street in a seedy suburb. Did my story matter? I didn’t know – but I noticed the street got fixed.
I wrote many more stories after that for the Tacoma News Tribune, where I became an investigative reporter and later an editor. Some of those stories highlighted examples of state government failing its duty to serve people.
In the end, people are the point. You can find the idea in the Standard’s statement of purpose: “We help readers understand how Washington state government works and how decisions made by those in power affect people living and working here.”
I like that approach. I’ve never lost sight of it. I hope to amplify it at the Standard, where I’m working with a team of three reporters who know their business: Jerry Cornfield, Jake Goldstein-Street, and Aspen Ford. We’re about to cover a big election. The night will be long. We’ll be there, covering the results and their implications.
We live in changing times. Communities served by the journalism industry have lost sources of connection. Over the past decade, the decline of traditional statehouse coverage has become a cliche.
States Newsroom, the nonprofit parent of the Standard, with outlets and partners in all 50 states, is trying to change that. I know that sounds like mandatory cheerleading for my new employer, but let me be clear: Nobody told me to write this. Two months ago, I had no idea I would be here.
I was aware of the Standard in the competitive sense before I applied for the job, but that was all. I was working for The News Tribune. I wasn’t thinking about opportunities until circumstances beyond my control changed my fortunes. In real time, an old journalism friend flagged the job opening at the Standard. 
I rolled the dice and applied, but not before I did some research.
“Fair. Fearless. Free.” That’s the States Newsroom mantra.
Decent slogan, I thought. Are they serious? 
I delved deeper, and found plenty of news: good stories, straight reporting covering policy, power and politics. Fair? Yes. The stories sought perspective from all sides. Fearless? Yes. The stories pulled no punches. 
Free? Yes. That was clear too, and — this still floors me — you can actually READ the stories without the incessant bombardment of popups and ads.

Are you kidding me?
A few days after I started this gig, an old journalism friend met me for lunch. He spent years covering the Legislature, and he knows everything. As we walked across the vast Capitol campus to a sandwich shop, he ranted a little, pointing to parking spaces, and how hard it is for ordinary folk to find them anywhere nearby. How hard should it be to get to the place where people in power make big decisions?
I laughed, but I knew what he meant. Yes, power matters – but people matter more. I’m looking forward to this new journey. I hope you feel the same way. I’m happy to be here. I encourage you to subscribe to our free newsletter and donate to support our work. 
Once more unto the breach, dear friends.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: What do people think about America in its 250th year? CT residents weigh in
authors: Sarah Gordon, Julia Levine, and Rachel Molenda
description: The CT Mirror asked residents about their thoughts on America as it celebrates 250 years since the signing of the Declaration of Independence.
text:
Over the summer and fall, Connecticut Mirror photographers Sarah Gordon and Julia Levine traversed the state to ask residents what they think about the country as it celebrates 250 years since the signing of the Declaration of Independence. From community events and campaign rallies to parades and reenactments, they asked Connecticut residents about their thoughts on America today and in the future, what issues they care about and one thing they would want to change about the country.
Here’s what nine people shared:
Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror
Avon resident Margaret Bratton, 60, a registered Republican, has served 18 years on the town’s Board of Finance and two years on the Town Council. She stood on the corner of Country Club Road and West Avon Road on a sunny late October afternoon with Chris Shea, Republican nominee for the 5th congressional district, and other supporters waving at passing school buses and cars. 
What are your thoughts about America at this point in time?
Bratton: I think right now we’re going in the correct direction. It’s taking a little bit of work to clean up from the previous administration. If we were talking at the national level, and I hope people are patient, give a little extra time to get that all set up, and as they’re saying, they’re setting the table, they’re fixing things, setting the table, and then once that’s done, I think it’ll take off.
If you could change something about this country, what would it be?
Bratton:  I think we used to be much more pro-America in America. Now it seems like some people are saying sort of pro-America, but then they’re always having the word “but” after it. And I just think we were a little bit more patriotic, and we should get back to that.
Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror
Vice-chairwoman of the Mashantucket Pequot Tribal Council Latoya Cluff, a tribal resident and registered voter, recently became a grandmother for the first time and she said it’s been causing her to think differently about the future.  
It was the first Schemitzun for her grandson, Essence Brown Young, 9 months old, and he wore traditional moccasins and a leather apron around his diaper. In late August, the annual Feast of Green Corn and Dance celebrates resistance, culture and community. Cluff carried him through the arena for Grand Entry, dancing as intertribal drum groups took turns playing and hundreds of representatives of indigenous tribes danced. 
What are your thoughts about America at this point in time?
Cluff:  I really don’t believe that we’re in a good place in a lot of areas. But the fact that we are able to still celebrate who we are as Indigenous people is a win, but that also comes with some cost as well, I would say for sure.
If there was one thing you could change about the country today, what would it be?
Cluff: Oh man, there’s honestly, there’s many things. I’m not sure where I would begin, but again, I think equality, fairness, protection. I think it’s huge, and I don’t believe that everyone is receiving protection; they’re being treated equally; they’re getting quality of services, healthcare, education, housing. Those are just some issues that I think are paramount, and they’re not being serviced to the people that need them the most.
Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror
Emery Marrs, an unaffiliated voter from New London who identifies as a non-binary transgender woman, used silk vein fans in rich colors as it danced along the boardwalk at New London’s Pride Festival at Ocean Beach Park in August. It was the 13th annual daylong event hosted by OutCT, a nonprofit organization in southeastern Connecticut that creates educational, cultural, and social programs for the LGBTQIA+ community. 
What are your thoughts about America at this point in time?
Marrs: My thoughts about America at this time is that we’re doing what we can, but we could do a lot more to make everybody feel included and safe. A lot of people in America are more so concerned about themselves than other people and the safety of others. And a beautiful way to work on communities to start accepting people for who they are and embracing them for being different than you.
If there was one thing you could change about this country, what would it be?
Marrs: The one thing that I would change in America would be the separation culture. There’s a lot of separation culture in America where people are more concerned on making categories and having labels and keeping everything. You’re here, I’m here. When we should all be together because we’re just all one big thing.
Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror
Hartford resident William Nickeo took advantage of early voting in the primaries to submit his ballot on the first day at Hartford City Hall. 
What are your thoughts about America at this point in time? 
Nickeo: My thoughts are kind of mixed right now. I mean, there are things going on that we’re struggling to get right. Hopefully, with this new election, this new incoming committee, it will start to straighten out as much as it can.
When you think about the future for America, what would you love to see?
Nickeo: I would like to see a place where everyone is living, not above their needs, but to their needs or a little bit better. Again, I will keep touching on the healthcare. Make sure everyone has that. You have the means to provide for yourself and your family — purchase a house, invest in yourself, invest in your family, invest in companies and things like that.
Credit: Julia Levine / CT Mirror
Amanda Matava, an archivist at Trinity College, grew up in Newington and now lives in Burlington. The 34-year-old independent voter is also a lieutenant in the First Company Governor’s Horse Guards where she performed drills on horseback at Burlington’s 250th celebration in July.
What’s one thing that you would change about America if you could?
Matava: I would change the polarity. I would change the inability to have conversations. I would really like people to kind of cross bridges and not burn them on either side. It doesn’t matter what side you’re on, because the less we converse with each other, interface with each other, and the more we feel like we’re on opposite sides, trying to each destroy the country, the worse it is for everybody. 
What do you hope for the future of America?
Matava: I hope for America to be kind of the inspiration for other places. I do work in other countries as part of my job, and I’ve been able to interact with other places and see how things are there. One thing that we’re really good at is our institutional history here, and that’s kind of a gift. A lot of places don’t have that, or a way of preserving it. And so, to be able to look back and look at our history and use it to move forward is, is really, actually, I don’t want to say unique, but it’s something that is a gift and shouldn’t be taken for granted.
Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror
Francise Jean-Louis, a 39-year-old registered voter from Stamford, unfurled a giant Haitian flag as she stood on the steps of Bridgeport’s Government Center in July. The founder of the nonprofit Haitian American Collaborative, Inc., she helped organize a rally to call on Congress to protect Temporary Protected Status recipients from Haiti. 
What are your thoughts on America at this time and where we are at as a country?
Jean-Louis: I think how I view America today is kind of in a sad place, and I just hope with the next administration they’re able to kind of fix and help all the damage that’s happening now.
What is an issue in your life that you care a lot about? 
Jean-Louis: The lack of resource to our people. So, if you think about like, the other communities — I won’t single one out — they’re getting resources. They’re getting support. They may even also be immigrants, but it looks different for that group of immigrants or individuals. And for us, our history goes way back with America. And you would think the support would look different. The biggest issue for me is a lack of support for our people.

Credit: Julia Levine / CT Mirror

Burlington First Selectman Douglas Thompson, a Republican, gave a speech at the town’s reading of the Declaration of Independence in which he described the document as planting seeds that don’t always grow right away. “It’s always been a story of divisions at times, but you know in the end we all come together, and I’m and I’m very optimistic for us,” he said of the country.
How do you feel about America right now?
Thompson: The Constitution planted the seeds, and some of those seeds didn’t bear fruit for some time. So I think that I am very proud to be an American. Very proud we’re still going to have our challenges. It’s it’s always been a story of divisions at times, but you know in the end we all come together, and I’m very optimistic for us.
What’s one thing that you would change about America if you could?
Thompson: I like to see more dialogue, less division. It’s OK to disagree. It’s healthy to disagree, but we should respect each other even if we disagree. And when you have the conversations, you oftentimes move a little bit this way, a little bit that way, and that’s how we get consensus. That’s how we get. So I would say I wish that we had a lot more of that, a lot more dialogue.
Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror
Thirteen-year-old Copper Montanari, of Ellington, joined her father and two friends on the boardwalk of Ocean Beach Park for OutCT’s Pride event. They excitedly made beaded necklaces and bracelets with large pride flags draped around their shoulders as capes and smaller pride flags painted on their faces. 
What is an issue in your life that you care a lot about?
Montanari: An issue in my life right now is probably being bullied a lot in school because of who I am and expressing myself. Because, I understand people wanting to, seeing people different and thinking, “Oh, that’s not normal.” But it just takes it to a whole ‘nother level when it’s physical and really takes away my confidence, you know?
And you see that kind of going on around the country and on a bigger scale sometimes. Like when you look at some of the administration and how they’re treating people too. And I’ve seen people take their own lives over this. And it really hurts me seeing that happen because I’ve known close people who have taken their own lives because of bullies and people around them who don’t support them.


If you or someone you know is in mental health distress or is thinking of suicide, please call or text 988 for the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline, or chat www.988lifeline.org. In an emergency, call or text 911.


If there was one this you could change about this country, what would it be?
Montanari: Probably giving us more rights. And to be able to express ourselves more. Because that’s one thing that I don’t like that’s going on. Because I feel like everyone should be themselves, you know, and everyone should be able to believe in what they want to believe without being judged for it.
Credit: Julia Levine / CT Mirror
As president of the Burlington Historical Society, Stacey Glastris, a 48-year-old unaffiliated voter, believes in stewarding the town’s history, especially as there’s less focus on preservation efforts, she said at a public reading of the Declaration of Independence in July.
How do you feel about America right now?
Glastris: I feel like sometimes it’s in turmoil. We definitely have quite a few differing views from a political side, but my focus here, especially with this event, is to bring everybody together and celebrate the country. It, too, was in a lot of turmoil 250 years ago, so not unlike today. But we persevered, and I feel like this is something that we need to celebrate.
What do you hope for the future of America? 
Glastris: I hope we continue to be as strong as we have been. I mean, I’m sure there’s going to be other storms we’re going to have to weather, and I’m sure there’s going to be other conflicts and turmoil. But given the strength and the determination of the folks in this country, you know we were built on some strong folks, and we still have strong folks in this country. And I feel as though going forward, we’re just going to continue to grow and build as a nation.
Editor’s note: Excerpts edited for length and clarity.

name: Wisconsin Examiner
title: UW Regents choose next UW president
description: The University of Wisconsin Board of Regents unanimously chose Tonjanita Johnson, a senior vice chancellor in the University of Alabama System, to be the next president of the Universities of Wisconsin.  Johnson, 57, has served as the senior vice chancellor for academic and student affairs at the University of Alabama System since 2019.  “I am […]
text:
Tonjanita Johnson will serve as the next UW system president.  (Photo courtesy UW system) The University of Wisconsin Board of Regents unanimously chose Tonjanita Johnson, a senior vice chancellor in the University of Alabama System, to be the next president of the Universities of Wisconsin. 
Johnson, 57, has served as the senior vice chancellor for academic and student affairs at the University of Alabama System since 2019. 
“I am deeply honored by the confidence the Board of Regents has placed in me and excited about the opportunity to serve the people of Wisconsin,” Johnson said in a statement. “Public higher education has the power to improve lives, strengthen communities, and shape a state’s future.” 
Johnson’s appointment will begin on or about Jan. 1, 2027. She’ll be the first person of color to lead the UW system.
Renée Wachter has been serving as the interim president since May. She will return to serving as the chancellor of UW-Superior when Johnson takes up the president role.
Johnson will be the 10th system president and will succeed Jay Rothman, who was fired from the position in April after the Board said it had lost confidence in him. 
Johnson was chosen from a group of three finalists that included Steven Gareth Holley, executive vice chancellor and chief operating officer at the University of Mississippi, and Bernard  Savarese, vice president for academic affairs, research, and student success at the University of Tennessee System. 
“I look forward to working with our chancellors, faculty, staff, students, elected leaders, and partners across Wisconsin to ensure that our universities remain engines of opportunity, innovation, and economic vitality,” Johnson said. “My goal is to help our remarkable UW universities become even stronger, more connected, and more consequential to the future of Wisconsin.” 
In her position at the University of Alabama System, Johnson has overseen academic and student affairs, worked as the primary liaison to the Board of Trustees Academic Affairs and Student Affairs Committee and worked with campus and system leadership on institutional priorities and policy development. She has also represented Alabama’s public universities with government agencies, education partners and national organizations.
Regent Vice President Ashok Rai, who chaired the presidential search committee, said in a statement that the regents’ goal was to “identify an exceptional leader who understands both the enormous responsibility and the extraordinary potential of the Universities of Wisconsin, and who can chart a bold course for our future.” 
“Dr. Johnson brings the vision, experience, and leadership to do exactly that. She understands complex public university systems, she believes deeply in their ability to change lives and strengthen communities, and she has the ability to bring people together around a shared direction for the future,” Rai said.

name: Source New Mexico
title: New Mexico lawmakers still split on legislative compensation ballot question as Election Day nears
description: As Election Day nears, some New Mexico lawmakers remain split on a ballot measure that would let them collect an annual salary for their legislative work.
text:
New Mexico voters will decide the fate of Constitutional Amendment 4, which would give state lawmakers an annual salary for the first time, during the Nov. 3, 2026, general election. (Photo by Anna Padilla for Source NM)As Election Day nears, some New Mexico lawmakers remain split on a ballot measure that would let them collect an annual salary for their legislative work.
Constitutional Amendment 4, which appears on the Nov. 3 general election ballot, asks voters to approve or deny a measure that would let state lawmakers earn a salary equivalent to the state’s median household income, which is currently about $68,000. If approved, it would go into effect for lawmakers who are sworn into office beginning in 2029, according to the New Mexico Legislative Council Service.[Voter Guide: New Mexico General Election 2026 Voter Guide: The candidates, the ballot measures, and the tools you need to cast your vote.]
New Mexico is the only state in the nation to not pay its lawmakers, though they receive per diem allowances for traveling to legislative meetings and are eligible to collect pensions after leaving office.
The latter continues to be a sticking point for opponents of the measure within the Roundhouse. State Sen. Jay Block (R-Rio Rancho) told Source NM that he doesn’t completely dismiss the arguments in favor of the proposal. But, he said lawmakers already have access to generous benefits.
“I think it would allow small business owners some flexibility to serve their community and keep their small business viable…because it’s more than just 30 days or 60 days,” Block said. “I see that side of the argument. But I also see the side where these people ran for office knowing they weren’t getting paid. They get a pretty generous retirement, as well.”
Block added that he has already voted against the constitutional amendment.
Across the aisle, Sen. George Muñoz (D-Gallup) also voted against the constitutional amendment.
Muñoz, who chairs the powerful Senate Finance Committee, told Source NM that he believes the per diem and mileage reimbursements lawmakers receive should adequately reimburse them. He said he believes that offering a salary in line with the median household income will encourage advocacy groups across the state and region to bankroll candidates who can further their agendas during the legislative session.
“If I go to Santa Fe right now, a hotel room’s like $250 a night, so I think it shouldn’t cost you anything” to be a lawmaker, he said. “This will change the Legislature completely. You’ll get more nonprofits pushing candidates to push their agendas than ever before. It’s a way to recruit people.”
Lawmakers who support the measure say that it would “level the playing field” for future candidates. Currently, supporters often say, only the “three Rs” can easily run for office: the rich, retired and resourceful.
If approved, the amendment would go into effect for lawmakers who are sworn into office beginning in 2029, according to the New Mexico Legislative Council Service, meaning unpaid lawmakers would not suddenly start collecting paychecks after its passage.
Some supporters, such as state Rep. Marianna Anaya (D-Albuquerque), say voters have an opportunity to empower people who can’t take enough time off or otherwise afford to run for office.
Recently, she said her legislative office was denied state funding to buy simple office supplies such as stamps. A colleague of hers was denied funding to buy a color printer to get colored versions of the numerous charts and graphs legislative committee members review, she said.
“That money is coming out of our pockets,” Anaya said. “We are actively paying and losing money by serving as legislators.”
When asked if she thinks the salary level should be equal to the median individual income, rather than the median household income, Anaya said “there are a lot of us that are the head of the household.”
Some lawmakers who voted against it didn’t adhere to the usual arguments that it would overpay lawmakers who serve in 30- and 60-day sessions or that it would attract people seeking a paycheck. 
For state Sen. Shannon Pinto (D-Tohatchi), one of the few elected Democrats to oppose it during the legislative session, it was personal. Pinto, who was first appointed to hold her late grandfather’s seat in the state Senate, said she opposed it because she wants to “serve my time the way my grandfather did.”
When asked if she’d also oppose the measure on Election Day, she said she’ll “try to be consistent.”
The Legislature was divided when it voted in February to put the question on the ballot. It cleared the state House of Representatives on a 41-26 vote and the state Senate on a 23-19 vote.
New Mexico voters may also be similarly split.
A September Albuquerque Journal poll conducted by Research and Polling, Inc., found that 39% of likely voters surveyed supported the measure and 21% opposed it. However, it also found that 34% of likely voters were undecided or didn’t know, and 6% answered that it “depends.”

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Pharmacy linked to Indiana execution drug invoice faces possible suspension
description: Lawyers seeking a reprieve for Jeffrey Weisheit ahead of his execution this week say Indiana purchased pentobarbital, the lethal injection drug it plans to use, from Pharmaneek Inc., an Indianapolis pharmacy on probation and facing possible suspension of its license. Weisheit’s attorneys asked Gov. Mike Braun on Monday to halt the Nov. 5 execution and […]
text:
Gov. Mike Braun is being asked to halt Jeffrey Weisheit’s Nov. 5 execution while Indiana reviews its lethal injection procedures and drug procurement. (Getty Images)
Lawyers seeking a reprieve for Jeffrey Weisheit ahead of his execution this week say Indiana purchased pentobarbital, the lethal injection drug it plans to use, from Pharmaneek Inc., an Indianapolis pharmacy on probation and facing possible suspension of its license.

Weisheit’s attorneys asked Gov. Mike Braun on Monday to halt the Nov. 5 execution and order an independent review of Indiana’s lethal injection procedures and drug purchases. Their application cites pharmacy inspection problems, questions about execution team qualifications and gaps in planning for complications.
The Department of Correction confirmed Monday that it paid $275,000 for the drugs and has them in its possession for Weisheit’s execution. The agency has not released an updated inventory log, which tracks drug purchases, use and disposal, however.
DOC officials declined to discuss the supplier or other procurement details, citing Indiana’s execution secrecy law.
“The Department of Correction is in compliance with Indiana laws that govern the confidential procurement of drugs utilized to carry out a court-ordered execution,” the agency said in a statement. “We remain confident in our process and our ability to humanely carry out the lawfully imposed sentence for the murders of two innocent children.”
The Indiana attorney general’s office and Pharmaneek did not respond to requests for comment before publication.
Story continues below.
Invoice - September 2026
 
The reprieve application asks Braun to exercise his authority as governor rather than seeking a court order.
Indiana law shields the identity of the pharmacist, pharmacy, wholesale drug distributor or outsourcing facility that provides a lethal substance to the Department of Correction. It also makes information that could identify suppliers — including names, addresses, phone numbers and tax identification numbers — confidential, bars its disclosure through discovery and prohibits its introduction as evidence in civil or criminal proceedings.
Pharmaneek is scheduled to appear before the Indiana Board of Pharmacy on Nov. 9 — four days after Weisheit’s scheduled execution — over allegations that it violated restrictions on compounding, the preparation of customized medications.
The board’s Oct. 1 order alleges noncompliance with those restrictions and directs the pharmacy to explain why its license should not be suspended on an emergency basis or subjected to further sanctions.
The board has not ordered a suspension in that proceeding.
Text recoverable beneath a black redaction on DOC’s Sept. 25 invoice includes an address that matches Pharmaneek’s principal office in Indiana secretary of state records and its address in state licensing records.
Those licensing records, dated Oct. 26, list both Pharmaneek’s pharmacy license and its controlled substance registration as on probation.
The Indiana Capital Chronicle previously obtained the $275,000 invoice for the state’s execution drug purchase in October through a public records request. The document describes the purchase only as supplies and does not specify a drug or the number of vials or doses. Weisheit’s attorneys identify Pharmaneek as the state’s pentobarbital supplier.
The Board of Pharmacy placed Pharmaneek on indefinite probation under a settlement approved in March. The agreement documented failed inspections, including expired medications on active pharmacy shelves, inadequate temperature monitoring and deficiencies in handling returned medication.
The board’s final order barred compounding during probation until the pharmacy met specified environmental and inspection requirements. The settlement also imposed a $1,500 fine and required corrective action plans.
In the settlement, Pharmaneek attributed some inspection problems to areas undergoing remodeling and said it had implemented a corrective action plan.
Indiana parole board urges governor to reject death row inmate’s bid to avoid execution

The final settlement also states that the attorney general’s investigation found the allegations in the original consumer complaints lacked merit, although other apparent violations were discovered. The reprieve application repeats accusations from those earlier complaints without noting that finding in the settlement.
A separate U.S. Food and Drug Administration inspection of Pharmaneek between March 30 and April 8 identified inadequate precautions against cross-contamination, insufficient verification of water quality and a damaged ceiling tile above an area where medication was prepared.
“Your facility is not maintained in a good state of repair, creating insanitary conditions whereby drug products may be contaminated with filth,” the inspection report states.
The FDA document concerns nonsterile drug production and expressly says its observations do not represent a final agency determination of compliance. It does not establish that Indiana’s execution drugs were contaminated.
Temperature controls were among the violations documented in Pharmaneek’s March settlement with the state. The agreement recorded a compounding room temperature of 84 degrees, a failure to monitor temperatures in an area holding medications ready for delivery and inconsistent temperature logs for drug-storage areas.
Separate concerns have involved storage at the Indiana State Prison. The Capital Chronicle previously published DOC logs showing drug temperatures outside the recommended range of 68 to 77 degrees Fahrenheit on several consecutive days in January and February 2025, with readings as low as 62 degrees. Pentobarbital’s labeling permits temporary temperature excursions between 59 and 86 degrees.
Defense attorneys have questioned whether those conditions affected drugs used in Benjamin Ritchie’s execution. Indiana executed Ritchie on May 20, 2025, for murdering Beech Grove police officer William Toney. DOC has not released documents showing storage of the newly purchased supply for Weisheit.
The reprieve application also includes an Oct. 27 letter from anesthesiologist Dr. Mark Heath questioning the qualifications required of personnel who establish intravenous access.
Alyssa Lynch, 8, and her brother, Caleb, 5, were killed in a 2010 house fire set by Jeffrey Weisheit. Weisheit is seeking clemency ahead of his scheduled Nov. 5 execution. (Courtesy photo)
“The Indiana protocol does not require or specify that the personnel inserting the IVs have the requisite experience, credentials, or certifications,” Heath wrote.
Indiana’s written protocol does require execution team training at least quarterly, including practical IV instruction with regional emergency medical services oversight. It also provides for physician involvement, monitoring of IV lines and backup doses of pentobarbital.
The attorneys argue those provisions do not adequately address what happens if staff cannot establish IV access or an execution fails. They urge Indiana to review its procedures following Tennessee’s failed Sept. 30 attempt to execute Christa Pike and that state’s decision to order an independent investigation.
Weisheit was sentenced to death for murdering 8-year-old Alyssa Lynch and her 5-year-old brother, Caleb, in a 2010 house fire near Evansville. His execution is scheduled before sunrise Nov. 5 at Indiana State Prison in Michigan City.
His request for a temporary reprieve is separate from his petition to have his death sentence commuted. The Indiana Parole Board recommended against clemency Oct. 28. Braun makes the final decision.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: PODCAST: CT candidates make final push ahead of Election Day
description: WSHU’s Ebong Udoma spoke with CT Mirror’s Mark Pazniokas to talk about the final hours leading up to Election Day.
text:
Election Day is finally here. What has the final push looked like for candidates in Connecticut?
WSHU’s Ebong Udoma spoke with CT Mirror’s Mark Pazniokas to talk about the final hours leading up to Election Day as part of the collaborative podcast Long Story Short. Read Mark’s coverage here.
WSHU: Hello, Mark. Connecticut Democrats now have supermajorities in the state House, 102 to 49, and in the Senate, 25 to 11. Yet lawmakers broadly agree Democrats might hold even larger margins after this election. How much lower could Republicans fall?
MP: Well, the modern record for dubious achievement in a General Assembly majority is in the post-Watergate election of 1974, and you know, as is the case today, where the unpopularity of Donald Trump is driving down, or looks like it will drive down, numbers for Republicans. In 1974, it was a fellow named Richard Nixon and the scandal of Watergate, and that was the all-time low in the state senate. The Republicans only won seven seats.
WSHU: Wow!
MP: And in the House, it was 33. After the Barack Obama landslide of 2008, Republicans won 37 of the 151 seats in the House. But one of the things that was very, very different in 1974- I mean, that was truly an earthquake in the sense that we went from strong Republican majorities overnight to completely flipping to strong Democratic majorities. What we are looking at this year is simply a continued erosion of the Republican base in the General Assembly this year. It’s not going to be anything nearly as dramatic as in 1974, when Republicans lost 60 House seats in Connecticut, and that was back in the days when Connecticut had something called the party lever, so people could go in and just cast one vote, and it would just, you know, it could really, you know, change things in a dramatic way. So it’s a different situation.
WSHU: What is similar is that there are headwinds, to say the least, from the national level that are harming Republicans in Connecticut at this point.
MP: Now, one seat that might be vulnerable for Republicans is one of the longest-serving members of the Senate: State Senator John Kissel in Enfield. Could you just tell us a little bit about that district and why Kissel, after all these years, you know, is facing a tough time this time around?
It’s interesting. John Kissel was elected in 1992, which was an interesting time for Republicans to win that seat. It had been a Democratic seat in 1992. That was the election where Bill Clinton carried Connecticut, and it was the first Democrat in a long time to do so in a presidential race. Of course, that started a string that has continued to this day. So John Kissel, his district is northern, north-central Connecticut. His base is in Enfield. Enfield has been a very volatile town, politically speaking. It has a Democratic advantage in voter registration, but not overwhelmingly so. It’s also a place where local races have gone back and forth. Republicans ran their local government until last year. That was one of the towns that flipped for the Democrats. So there is a sense this year that, given the influence of President Trump, you know, not just in Connecticut but across the country, that there is a belief that Kissel is vulnerable, and he does seem to share that assessment. He has not conceded that he is going to lose Tuesday night. But when I saw him yesterday, campaigning with Ryan Fazio (R), the gubernatorial candidate, he said it’s been a privilege to have the seat and a good long run. And he also made a joke about not only is he like a cat with the last of his nine lives, but he is also more like the second cat’s worth of nine lives, and he’s on the last one. So we’ll see Tuesday night how much truly of a wave election this is, and you know how far it will reach?
WSHU: So how are Republicans prepared to deal with the aftermath of the election?
MP: People in both parties are already looking ahead to what the next election will be without the influence of Donald Trump. Donald Trump has been the best organizer Democrats have had in blue states, so Democrats are being pretty honest about saying his departure is going to be a challenge for them, and they’re going to have to find ways to motivate people to turn out and vote the way that Donald Trump has done for Democrats. After Trump’s election, 2016 was a big municipal year in 2017 for Democrats, followed by a big General Assembly year in 2018 for Democrats, and then, you know, the same thing happened after Trump’s return to the White House after 2024. Another big year for Democrats in the 2025 municipal races. And the question is to what extent will it happen again for the General Assembly,
WSHU: But bottom line, there’s going to be a change in the landscape, and people are trying to figure out how they’re going to deal with a post-Trump era.
MP: Yes, the Republicans will have their own internal debates about what their identity is, what issues unite them, and what issues will work in Connecticut in 2028. And then again, the Democrats. How do they motivate their people to turn out after Donald Trump isn’t on the ballot in 2028? Although who knows, I wouldn’t predict Donald Trump will disappear from the landscape just because he’s not on the ballot this time. And as he’s said over and over again, pretend I’m on the ballot. And of course, the Democrats are happier with that suggestion than the Republicans are.
WSHU: Well, thank you so much. Great having you as always, Paz.
MP: Thank you, Ebong.

text:
A sign points voters to the polling place at the Millwood High School Field House on June 16, 2026 in Oklahoma City, Oklahoma. (Photo by Courtney Bell/Oklahoma Voice)OKLAHOMA CITY – Nearly 186,500 Oklahomans voted early heading into Tuesday’s general election, about 40% more than four years ago.
In-person early voting turnout was up considerably from the nearly 132,330 who cast ballots in the 2022 midterm elections. 
This year, Republicans cast 89,799 ballots followed by 71,680 by Democrats, 24,249 independents and 780 Libertarians.
Oklahomans, who did not vote early, will go to the polls Tuesday to pick a new governor and decide the fate of a slate of legislative, congressional, judicial candidates as well as a host of people seeking statewide elective offices.
Two legislatively proposed state questions that seek to alter the Constitution will also appear on the ballot.
State Question 845 would modify the structure of the Judicial Nominating Commission, which helps select judges.
State Question 847 would slow the growth of property taxes.
But the gubernatorial race is expected to be the top draw on Oklahoman’s Nov. 3 ticket. 
It features Democrat Cyndi Munson, of Oklahoma City, Republican Mike Mazzei, of Tulsa, and independents Jerry Griffin, of Tulsa, Robert E. Brooks Sr., of Moore, and Orlando Lynn Bush, of Edmond.
Term limits prevent Republican Gov. Kevin Stitt from running for a third term.
Many other statewide elected officials are also prohibited from running again due to term limits. 
Sample ballots and polling locations can be found on the State Election Board website, which will also post the results of the races and state questions once the polls close.
Election Board Secretary Paul Ziriax encouraged voters to be kind to precinct officials and others.
“We want all voters to have a positive experience at the polls,” he said. “We ask that voters be patient as precinct officials work to process voters and help those who may need additional assistance, such as first-time voters or those with disabilities.”
Polls are open from 7 a.m. to 7 p.m. Those in line by 7 p.m. can still cast ballots.
Electioneering, or trying to influence a vote, is prohibited within 300 feet of the polling place entrance or the last person in line while an election is in progress.

name: VTDigger
title: Vermont has assigned its $195 million in federal rural health dollars. Here’s where it’s going.
description:
The largest sums of money are directed toward hospital infrastructure upgrades and funds to facilitate hospital redesign.  
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Vermont has assigned its $195 million in federal rural health dollars. Here’s where it’s going..
text:
Jill Mazza Olson, deputy director for health care reform at the Vermont Agency of Human Services, speaks before the Senate Health and Welfare Committee at the Statehouse in Montpelier on Wednesday, January 14, 2026. Photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger

Right before its deadline, Vermont has allocated all $195 million of federal Rural Health Transformation funding it received last December.
In the 10 months since receiving the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid dollars, the state has built out a team to manage the project, issued dozens of funding notices, fielded hundreds of applications and inked more than 200 individual contracts.  
Now begins implementation.
“When I look at year one, I feel really excited about how much money is directly going to the field,” said Jill Mazza Olson, the state’s Medicaid and health systems director, who is shepherding the five-year project. Other states, she said, have instead prioritized spending money on analysts and consultants. 
With the first year of funding obligated, the state now moves into the second year of the five-year program.
The work comes as Vermont’s hospitals face steep challenges to keep charges low while still meeting their bottom line. At the same time, they are preparing for Medicaid payments to drop off as changes in the same federal law that created the rural health fund take shape in 2027. In light of those dueling pressures, the state is trying to keep care available and affordable by reshaping how rural hospitals provide and share services. 
“I always say this is a tool to support the broader transformation efforts,” Mazza Olson said. The funds themselves are not, she added, a substitute for the needed redesign plans.
The Agency of Human Services divided the nearly 250 projects into four main categories. They include efforts to bolster the healthcare workforce, strengthen primary care, broaden the kind of settings where patients can receive care and invest in physical healthcare infrastructure, which the state labeled “regionalization” work.
Mazza Olson sees the categories as all in service of the state’s mission to change how rural communities reach — and afford— healthcare by regionalizing and consolidating specialty care. 
Regionalization
The state has put more than $88 million of the federal funds toward the regionalization work, making it the largest of the four priority areas. Of that, the state awarded more than $32.3 million for facility upgrades at clinics, rehab centers and nearly every hospital.
The state also put money into expanding urgent care centers for mental health and substance use disorders and toward building out mobile units to provide primary care. 
The broad funding category incorporates a wide array of support that hospitals and healthcare providers might need to meet the state’s push for rethinking how it organizes hospital care, Samantha Hefferon, the director of Rural Health Transformation for the state, said. For instance, Northwestern Medical Center in St. Albans received $2 million to facilitate its transfer of obstetrics to an independent contractor, Maitri Health Care. Brattleboro Memorial Hospital, on the other hand, has received funding under the same umbrella to develop a plan to keep birthing services in Windham County.

READ MORE

Much of the remaining funds go toward consultant work to supplement the state’s healthcare system redesign. The consulting group McKinsey received $5.1 million for “analytics and support.” McKinsey’s grant is one of the largest awards Vermont gave an individual organization.
Shared services
Efforts to better coordinate care across hospitals dovetails with the state’s efforts to regionalize.
The state awarded $34.2 million under the umbrella of shared service efforts to facilitate access to specialist care in rural areas and make care coordination smoother. 
“Really big picture, we are trying to get people to the best possible place to get the services they need,” Mazza Olson said. That’s not always the hospital, she added. Sometimes it’s a mental health urgent care or their own home, where a patient can have their vitals remotely monitored. 
The funding includes more than $10 million for providers to adopt telehealth technology and for remote patient monitoring.
The University of Vermont Health received almost $3 million to guide transfers between healthcare facilities. A collection of Vermont hospitals have received funding to work on unifying an electronic medical record platform.
Twenty-five smaller clinics and healthcare facilities have received a combined $5 million in grants to adopt AI technology to transcribe notes, which many healthcare professionals have described as radical in reducing administrative burden.
Primary care and workforce
The state is putting more than $40 million into bolstering primary care. 
That includes investments in data analytics and expanding substance use disorder recovery housing. The state funded awards meant to integrate more mental health, community support and “team-based” care. 
The state also put $26.6 million into workforce development. Though the grant did not include any payments to educational institutions, which Mazza Olson said may change next year, it did include investments in training programs, tuition assistance and mentorship projects. 
In this umbrella, $571,900 went to efforts to establish the Maple Mountain Consortium Family Medicine Residency Program that aims to train doctors in Vermont’s rural primary care settings. 
Another $8 million went to Kinney Drugs to help the pharmacy chain develop its test-to-treat work, which would allow pharmacists to test and administer treatment for certain common conditions, such as flu and strep throat. That expansion of scope was passed into law this year. 
The state now moves into the second phase of the five-year program, monitoring the obligated  funds and assigning the second year’s awards.The Agency of Human Services expected to learn of its second-year funding on Oct. 30 but has not yet received confirmation from the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services about the award, a spokesperson said Monday.

name: Rhode Island Current
title: Pre-Election Day poll predicts Democratic sweep in Rhode Island
description: Democrats look poised to sweep Rhode Island elections on Tuesday, including gubernatorial candidate Helena Buonanno Foulkes and Lt. Gov. Sabina Matos, in the first election snapshot in three weeks. The University of New Hampshire (UNH) survey of 753 likely voters puts Foulkes and Matos further ahead of their general election competitors compared with previou[...]
text:
A new University of New Hampshire poll shows Rhode Island's Democratic gubernatorial nominee Helena Buonanno Foulkes, left, and Lt. Gov. Sabina Matos, in the lead in their respective races. (Photos by Michael Salerno/Rhode Island Current)Democrats look poised to sweep Rhode Island elections on Tuesday, including gubernatorial candidate Helena Buonanno Foulkes and Lt. Gov. Sabina Matos, in the first election snapshot in three weeks.
The University of New Hampshire (UNH) survey of 753 likely voters puts Foulkes and Matos further ahead of their general election competitors compared with previous public polling, including several surveys that showed Matos in a statistical tie with her GOP opponent, John Loughlin.
Two days out from Election Day, Matos has pulled ahead with a 15-point lead over Loughlin among likely voters. 
Nearly 120,000 voters have already cast ballots as of Monday morning, the last day of early voting. 
Meanwhile, Foulkes has surpassed the 50% mark among those who participated in the Oct. 27-31 online survey, which shows Foulkes with a 21-point lead over independent gubernatorial candidate Ken Block. GOP nominee Aaron Guckian came in a distant third, with support of 8% of survey respondents. The margin of error is 3.5%.
Public polling by other outlets put Foulkes and Block much closer, with Foulkes 9 points ahead of Block as of the Oct. 13 survey by WPRI-TV 12 and Emerson College.
The contest between Foulkes and Block has set off an escalating feud in the last three weeks. Attack mailers sent by the Rhode Island Democratic Party on behalf of Foulkes depicted Block as a duck and likened his policies on wages and healthcare to President Donald Trump. Block alleges the state party spending for Foulkes’ exceeds the limit in state law, filing two complaints with the Rhode Island Board of Elections last week. 
The elections panel has not commented on the complaints or alleged violations.
In his latest TV ad, which hit airwaves one week out from the general election, Block calls Foulkes a “puppet” based on her support from state labor unions. Foulkes’ final advertising push includes more attacks on Block for his opposition to the Affordable Care Act.
The public fighting has done little to warm voters to either candidate. Nearly 4 in 10 voters viewed Foulkes unfavorably — 2 percent more than those who viewed her favorably — according to the UNH survey. The minus 2 approval rating is better than the minus 13 rating for Foulkes in UNH’s September survey.
“As we head into Election Day, the momentum and energy are clearly with Helena,” Angelika Pellegrino, a spokesperson for Foulkes’ campaign, said in a statement Monday morning. “Rhode Islanders are ready for change and she is ready to get to work making life better.”
Support for Democratic gubenatorial candidate Helena Buonanno Foulkes has increased in the six weeks since the last University of New Hampshire survey. (Courtesy of UNH Survey Center)
Block’s favorability rating dips 
Block has lost his once-positive favorability rating. He now stands at minus 1, compared with a positive 12 rating in the September survey. However, just 10% of voters were unsure or didn’t know what to think about him, compared with nearly 1 in 3 in September.
“Helena has run a misleading, one-note campaign of negativity,” Matthew Schweich, Block’s campaign manager, said in a statement Monday. “We doubt voters have responded to that.”
While Foulkes’ support includes an overwhelming majority of registered Democrats. Block carried the independent and Republican votes, with the latter backing Block over party nominee Guckian.
Nearly out of campaign cash and facing public pressure to drop out, including from his GOP primary opponent Elaine Pelino, Guckian’s support overall dropped from 17% to 8% as of the latest survey. His favorability rating also plunged, from minus 15 to minus 46, though 1 in 5 voters still didn’t know enough about him to form an opinion.
Guckian noted that a July 1 UNH survey showed him trailing Pelino by 25 points in the Republican primary. He went on to narrowly defeat Pelino.
“Polls are snapshots,” Guckian said in a statement Monday. “Elections are decided by voters.”
The gubernatorial race also includes independents Jay Gotra and C.D. Reynolds.
Democratic Lt. Gov. Sabina Matos held a 15-point lead over Republican challenger John Loughlin in a new, University of New Hampshire survey published Sunday. (Courtesy of UNH Survey Center)
Breaking the tie 
Rhode Island GOP officials have rallied behind Loughlin in the lieutenant governor’s race, seeing the former state representative as their best chance to win a state office amid polls putting Loughlin neck-and-neck with Democratic incumbent Matos.
Not anymore. 
Matos now leads Loughlin 56% to 41%, with 4% of survey respondents undecided. 
Yet even likely Matos voters don’t necessarily like the Democratic incumbent. Nearly 7 in 10 Matos supporters said they were voting for her because she was a Democrat, rather than because they liked her as an individual candidate. In contrast, more than 8 in 10 Loughlin supporters said they were choosing him as a candidate, not because he is a Republican.
Loughlin is one of few candidates on the Nov. 3 ballot who survey respondents viewed favorably, with a positive 8 approval rating compared with Matos’ negative 13. However, nearly half of survey respondents did not know or have an opinion about Loughlin, compared with 9% for Matos.
“As always, the only poll that matters is happening tomorrow,” Mark Gray, Matos’ campaign spokesperson, said in a statement. 
Gray highlighted Matos’ work addressing cost concerns, including grocery prices, through a 2026 legislative package, some of which is now law.
“Voters know that affordability isn’t a campaign buzzword for Sabina—she has lived it, and she has put forward nation-leading work on it long before the rest of the country’s politicians pivoted to it,” Gray said.
Loughlin was undeterred.
“I’m grateful for every voter who’s with us, and I’m confident that tomorrow’s results will show our campaign beating the odds —  again,” he said in a statement Monday. “We will finish strong.”  
Matos’ campaign did not immediately respond to requests for comment Monday.
Matos has also filed a campaign finance complaint against Loughlin, alleging his campaign manager siphoned taxpayer-funded campaign money from TV ad placements.
In the U.S. Senate race, Rhode Island’s senior senator Jack Reed maintained his decisive lead, with support from more than 6 in 10 voters. Another 3 in 10 backed GOP challenger Ray McKay, while 3% supported independent Michael Bahry.
Regardless of who they supported, survey respondents overwhelmingly believed the Democratic candidates — Foulkes, Matos, and Reed — would win their respective elections. Voters were also unified in their interest in the midterm elections, with more than half of survey respondents across parties saying they had paid “a lot” of attention to the general election and were “extremely interested.”
However, Democrats were more likely than independents or Republicans to discuss the midterms with friends or family.
On issues, affordability and inflation was the No. 1 concern of voters, followed by economic health or financial security. Despite state candidates’ repeated emphasis on bringing change to politics, change in leadership was a concern for just 1% of survey respondents.  
Half of survey respondents were unaffiliated, while 35% were registered Democrats and the remaining 15% were registered Republicans — on par with the split among the state’s 699,000 registered voters. Respondents represented a range of ages, education levels and geographies, and were equally divided between men and women.
Early voting continues through 4 p.m. today.

text:
A car moves through a drive-through Jefferson County Elections Center at the Kentucky Expo Center in Louisville. (Kentucky Lantern photo by McKenna Horsley)Early voting was up across Kentucky in comparison to the last midterm election in 2022.
During Kentucky’s early voting period between Thursday and Saturday, 377,269 Kentuckians cast ballots. Most of them were Democrats, 180,541. Republicans had 170,304 voters.
The combined total of absentee voters and early voters is 438,602. Republican Secretary of State Michael Adams said on X that turnout in the last midterm election year, 2022, was 337,975, so voting this year was about 30% higher. The absentee and early voting turnout out in 2023, a gubernatorial election year, was 313,009. 
Kentucky voters set the highest early voting and absentee record in 2024 with 792,476 votes ahead of the presidential election. 
The general election is Tuesday, Nov. 3. Polls across Kentucky will be open from 6 a.m. to 6 p.m. local time. The Kentucky State Board of Elections website lists addresses for all polling locations by county, along with addresses for absentee ballot drop-off locations. 
How to report suspected fraud
Republican Kentucky Attorney General Russell Coleman’s office will monitor an election fraud hotline, as it has done in previous elections. To submit tips or make reports of suspected election fraud, call (800) 328-VOTE or visit an online portal to submit information.
Ahead of midterm elections, the U.S. Department of Justice unveiled a plan to send about 1,000 federal election monitors to polling sites. Monitors are expected to be in Jefferson and Fayette counties, the largest counties in Kentucky. 
After that, Kentucky Democrats and Republicans said they are launching their own election issues hotlines. To reach the Kentucky Democratic Party’s hotline, call 833-468-6835. To contact the Republican Party of Kentucky, call (502) 557-7788 or visit protectthevote.com/report-fraud/kentucky.

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: SC grocery aid no longer covers candy, sodas, other sugary foods
description: The change took effect Sunday, after a federal court case pushed back the original start date. Some sodas and baked goods aren't part of the new limitations.
text:
Federal grocery aid will no longer buy candy and other items in South Carolina, following a change that went into effect Sunday, Nov. 1, 2026. (File photo by Carol Johnson/Stateline)COLUMBIA — Grocery assistance in South Carolina no longer covers candy, sodas and other sugary drinks after a change in the program took effect Sunday.
Last year, at the direction of Gov. Henry McMaster, the state asked for a waiver to exclude certain items considered unhealthy from the list of food and drinks people could buy using the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, commonly known as food stamps.
South Carolina was one of 23 states to receive federal approval for the change as part of the “make America healthy again” initiative, though the programs in five states are on pause as part of an ongoing lawsuit. The changes are set to last two years before officials decide whether to make them permanent.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Under the change, people can no longer use government aid to buy energy drinks, candy bars or certain sweetened beverages, including ready-made lemonade, tea, sweetened coffee and full-sugar soda.
The program already excluded alcohol, tobacco and hot, ready-to-eat meals sold in grocery stores.
Stores that accept SNAP were required to update their systems to exclude the ineligible items. If someone tries to check out with candy or sugary drinks, the system will prompt them to pay with a different method, according to the state Department of Social Services.
Still allowed are diet and zero-sugar sodas, granola bars, sports drinks, baked goods, and natural fruit and vegetable juices.
People making 130% of the federal poverty level or less, equal to $42,900 for a family of four, qualify for SNAP. Under changes included in last year’s major spending bill, childless adults without a disability must work at least 20 hours each week to receive benefits for more than three months.
Removal of sugary snacks and drinks from SC grocery benefits delayed after court order

In September, 223,375 households received SNAP benefits, according to the latest data from the Department of Social Services.
The changes were initially set to begin in August.
But the U.S. Department of Agriculture, which oversees the benefits, asked the state to push back the start date to review a ruling from a federal judge that found the program didn’t meet federal requirements.
In the lawsuit, people suing said they needed to be able to buy certain items labeled “unhealthy” for medical reasons. For instance, a woman with diabetes said she needed to buy sugary drinks to keep her blood sugar under control, and a man with insomnia and food allergies said he needed to buy low-sugar energy drinks to stay awake.
The USDA decided the ruling affected only the five states where the people who filed the lawsuit live, allowing South Carolina to remove certain items from the list starting Sunday.
The federal government has appealed the judge’s decision.
The change was meant to improve health outcomes for people who use the grocery assistance.
In his executive order directing South Carolina to participate, McMaster pointed to high rates of obesity and heart disease in the state, which can be linked to unhealthy eating.
Advocates for the poor have pushed back, saying people who use federal assistance can make their own choices about what to eat. Using government aid already comes with a stigma attached, and that only gets worse when people don’t have agency over their grocery shopping, advocates have said.
