name: Mississippi Today
title: A rare push to release Hinds County jail detainees exposes a dysfunctional system
description: Attorneys confer with Hinds County Court Judge Johnnie McDaniels, right, in court on Tuesday, Oct. 20, 2026, in Jackson.
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
Hinds County Court Judge Johnnie McDaniels’ signature was all the district attorney and public defender needed. 
It was a Friday afternoon in August when attorneys from the offices pitched the judge an unusual proposal: Release some three dozen people from the crowded Hinds County Detention Center. 
Each of the detainees faced nonviolent charges, had not been indicted and had spent at least 100 days in jail. 
But McDaniels wouldn’t agree – at least not immediately. 
Instead, the judge would issue an order days later, declaring that crowding alone did not justify a defendant’s release. He directed the attorneys to submit requests case by case.
The attorneys would comply over the next few weeks, ultimately seeking release of 19 defendants. McDaniels would grant release to 13, according to his docket.
But hearings in September did little to cut into what was then roughly 200 people jailed without indictment. Instead, they exposed deeper failures in Hinds County’s criminal justice system: defendants remaining behind bars despite being granted release and prosecutors struggling to account for cases that had languished for months, sometimes years. 
Attorneys confer with Hinds County Court Judge Johnnie McDaniels, right, in court on Tuesday, Oct. 20, 2026, in Jackson. Credit: Vickie D. King/Mississippi Today
While defendants are presumed innocent and have rights to a speedy trial, prosecutors and defense attorneys rarely invoke constitutional protections during the hearings. This is because the right has effectively been abandoned in Mississippi, one of a handful of states without a fixed deadline for obtaining an indictment after an arrest. 
The collaboration between prosecutors and public defenders represented a blip in Hinds County, where concerns about community safety have overshadowed the plight of defendants in the deadly detention center in Raymond. 
“Now, I’ve heard of this happening on the planet earth, but not in Hinds County,” said Matt Steffey, a Mississippi Christian University School of Law professor who helped write the state rules of criminal procedure. “In fact, most of my career, what I’ve heard is the opposite: the difficulty of getting the DA to agree and the judge to set reasonable bonds.” 
State Public Defender Andre de Gruy questioned why the effort was necessary. He noticed the jail population jumped last summer but did not know why: Were more people being arrested, or were prosecutors failing to move cases through the system? 
“Why are nonviolent offenders sitting in jail for months?” he asked.
McDaniels, who declined to be interviewed for this article, had similar questions. 
“That’s the giant elephant in the room, so to speak, as it relates to these matters,” he said during one of the hearings. 
A bewildering path to freedom
Another issue: Interim Hinds County District Attorney Brad McCullouch overstated the results of his office’s release efforts, according to a Mississippi Today review of records.
In a recent interview, McCullouch said his office had secured the release of 74 people jailed without indictment on nonviolent charges – far more than the 19 defendants whose release the office sought in collaboration with the public defender. 
McCullouch’s list of 74 reflects all defendants with felony charges released from jail from July 1 to Sept. 28, including 15 people facing violent charges and defendants whose release were unrelated to the DA’s efforts. 
The DA acknowledged he did not know the number of people released during the same time last year. Still, he believes his office’s efforts are paying off. 
Daniel Ray Boyd Collom poses for a portrait in Jackson on Thursday, Oct. 29, 2026. Daniel was released from the Raymond Detention Center in August, but he doesn’t know why because he never received any paperwork. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
“People have been coming in, but nobody has been getting out,” he said. 
Daniel Ray Boyd Collom calls himself one of those nobodies. 
Collom, 36, entered the Raymond Detention Center in October 2025 and faced charges of burglary and failure to appear. 
He slept on the floor. He said other detainees carried knives and set fires that left cell blocks covered in soot.
Months went by. He lost hope of ever getting out.
Then on Friday, Aug. 28 – nearly a year after he was locked up – officers loaded Collom into a van and dropped him off on a sidewalk in downtown Jackson.
He said no one told him why he got out. 
“I have no idea, no clue, not even the slightest inkling,” he said. 
To Collom, his freedom seemed as bewildering as his confinement.
A backlog of cases and a promise to act
A little over a month earlier, McCullouch stood in the federal courthouse in downtown Jackson. It was the very day the governor would appoint him district attorney after former Hinds DA Jody Owens pleaded guilty to a federal corruption charge and resigned.
Brad McCullouch, a Madison attorney appointed by Gov. Tate Reeves as Hinds County district attorney in July, discusses proposals he believes could reduce crowding at the jail. Credit: Molly Minta/Mississippi Today
McCullouch made a promise to U.S. District Court Judge Carlton Reeves: He would release people facing nonviolent charges from the jail.
Conditions at the Raymond Detention Center, which the judge oversees through a long-running consent decree, were as bad as ever. Days earlier, an 18-year-old had been stomped to death, a video of his final moments going viral. 
The jail was also crowded. The number of unindicted detainees had barely budged from October 2025, when the federally appointed jail receiver, Wendell France, had asked Owens to “expeditiously resolve” pending cases. 
About a month after appearing before Reeves, McCullouch attempted to make good on the promise. His office asked the public defender for a list of defendants facing nonviolent charges. This yielded 60 names, from which prosecutors selected 32 candidates for release. 
By the time prosecutors presented the cases to McDaniels, most of the defendants had been in jail for at least 150 days. 
Charlie King, a new prosecutor leading the release effort, told the judge some of the defendants had yet to be indicted because the DA’s office couldn’t proceed until it obtained the complete investigative file, even though prosecutors have sometimes taken cases to the grand jury without one.
“In the past,” McDaniels noted, the DA “would just kind of sit around and wait until law enforcement sent the file over.” 
King said he could not speak to Owens’ decisions. 
“The lack of file,” King said, “is unacceptable.” 
Judge presses prosecutors for answers
Hinds County Court Judge Johnnie McDaniels presides during preliminary hearings in court on Tuesday, Oct. 20, 2026, in Jackson. Credit: Vickie D. King/Mississippi Today
Once a person is arrested in Mississippi, the justice system offers few chances at freedom.
The first opportunity typically comes during an initial court appearance, when a judge decides whether to give a defendant a bond and sets an amount. If they cannot afford the amount, a defendant can ask for a lower bond after a probable cause hearing. 
If those efforts fail, defendants can find themselves in a no man’s land while waiting for a grand jury to review their charges.
The path out usually runs through one judge: Johnnie McDaniels. 
He presides over all unindicted criminal cases. His power comes from a 2023 standing order, issued by Hinds County Circuit Court Senior Judge Winston Kidd. 
In evaluating requests for release, judges in Mississippi have discretion to determine if a defendant poses a danger to the community and how likely they would be to return to court. 
In the first case the district attorney’s office presented from the public defenders’ list, McDaniels questioned why prosecutors wanted to release a man charged with possessing a firearm as a convicted felon.
King cited poor jail conditions. 
“You were in my chambers,” McDaniels, sitting behind a plexiglass barrier, told King. “I think I was pretty clear the idea of what may be happening with jail overcrowding is not going to compel this court.”
The judge asked if the DA’s office would still seek the man’s release if there weren’t an issue with jail crowding. 
“I have to hear persuasive arguments, not political arguments,” McDaniels added before granting the request. 
To reach his decisions, McDaniels considers not only the details of an offense but also a defendants’ ties to the community and their character.
“I’m not sure the facts of this matter,” the judge told the public defender, Ginny Kramer, after she asked him to release a 27-year-old father of two who had a job lined up cleaning cars at a showroom. Before his arrest, he had been working to earn a GED at a community college. 
McDaniels wanted to know what property the man was alleged to have stolen. 
In another case, McDaniels learned that a defendant who had been unindicted and in jail for nearly two years on DUI and drug charges was now in a wheelchair because he had broken his leg while incarcerated.
“He’s been through a lot while in jail,” Kramer told the judge.
McDaniels was unmoved, asserting that statistics showed people arrested for DUI had likely driven under the influence at least 40 times before being caught.
“How does the ailment,” McDaniels asked, “prevent him from driving around under the influence of alcohol?” 
Release orders don’t always mean freedom
Throughout the hearings, the judge returned to the question of why the DA’s office had yet to indict defendants they now wanted released. 
“It appears all the other parties … did their job,” McDaniels said after hearing the case of a woman charged with first-degree arson. “And at that point, nothing else happened.”
McCullouch acknowledged in an interview that his office needed to indict cases more quickly. 
The Hinds County Detention Center in Raymond, June 12, 2015.  Credit: AP Photo by Rogelio V. Solis
He hopes whoever wins Tuesday’s special election for district attorney will continue changes he made to the grand jury unit, including hiring a prosecutor focused on clearing unindicted cases.
That employee, Greta Kemp Martin, combs through jail logs every day to find cases that need to be indicted. 
The five candidates for Hinds DA agree the backlog of unindicted cases needs to be addressed, though they differ on how best to do so. 
But people keep slipping through the cracks. 
Dennis Green is among them.
He has been in jail since December 2024, accused of burglary, malicious mischief and violating parole. McDaniels had ordered him released in June 2026 and then again in September, after the DA’s office brought his case back up. 
A recently released defendant, 59-year-old Jerry Jefcoat, had been in jail since April 2026 on charges of failure to register as a sex offender. But the DA’s office said it couldn’t find the police officer who filed charges, preventing prosecutors from presenting the case to the grand jury. 
“We are still unable to ascertain who the ‘Williams’ is that is listed as the investigator,” Martin said. 
Hinds County Sheriff Tyree Jones, whose department had oversight of the jail until the federal government stripped it of control, declined to be interviewed.
The DA’s office told Mississippi Today that the judge had not denied any of its requests for release. But a review of court records showed otherwise.
McDaniels denied four motions. In three, the judge wrote the defendants had already been indicted.
Yet, court records show no indication any of the three defendants had been served with their indictments, despite remaining in county custody.
De Gruy, the state public defender, said the failure was emblematic of more breakdowns in the system. 
“Presumably, the prosecutor has a copy of the indictment,” he said. “They could hand it to the bailiff, and the bailiff could serve the person. It could happen in the courtroom. I just cannot understand how people can be indicted, in jail and the indictment not served.” 
De Gruy, who remains skeptical, said he had recently noticed the jail’s daily population counts declined, suggesting the DA’s office’s new approach might be producing results. 
“But are you going to do it again?” he asked.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: U.S. DOJ to send election monitors to New Haven Tuesday
description: New Haven is the only CT municipality the DOJ plans on sending election monitors to Tuesday, according to a Sec. of the State spokesperson.
text:
The U.S. Department of Justice plans to send election monitors to New Haven on Tuesday to observe — but not to “intrude or interfere in any way in the voting process” — on Election Day.
Mayor Justin Elicker announced that news in a Friday afternoon press release, which also included a letter sent to the DOJ on Thursday by Democratic Registrar of Voters Shannel Evans and Republican Registrar of Voters Lisa Milone.
The registrars’ letter tells the DOJ that election monitors are not allowed to enter any polling places in the city.
“We understand that the Department of Justice has a long history of conducting election monitoring in our nation,” Evans and Milone wrote. “We also recognize that there is a current climate in our nation where rhetoric and federal actions appear to be intended to cast doubt on election integrity and to intimidate voters. As such, we believe the presence of election monitors at polling places in New Haven could make our polling places feel less accessible to all. Therefore, we do not permit election monitors to enter any polling places in New Haven.”
Friday’s announcement came as the Trump administration plans to dispatch election monitors to selected polling places across the country, prompting concerns among state and local election officials that the feds may meddle with Tuesday’s results.
It also comes as the DOJ is actively suing the city in a bid to overturn New Haven’s “sanctuary policies.”
Secretary of the State spokesperson Matthew Clyburn told the Independent that, as far as his office knows, New Haven is the only municipality in Connecticut that the DOJ plans on sending election monitors to during Tuesday’s midterms.
Mayor Justin Elicker’s press release states that the city found out about the DOJ’s intention to send election monitors to New Haven in mid-October.
That information came in the form of a letter and email sent to City Clerk Michael Smart on Oct. 21 by James Thomas Tucker, a senior trial attorney with the DOJ’s Civil Rights Division.
Tucker’s email states that the DOJ intends to send election monitors to New Haven on Tuesday, Nov. 3.
“As the Civil Rights Division has done in the past, our monitors only observe,” Tucker wrote. “They do not intrude or interfere in any way in the voting process.”
Tucker asked to set up a Microsoft Teams call to discuss the matter.
He also wrote, “Generally, we are monitoring for compliance with the federal voting rights statutes that fall within the jurisdiction of the Civil Rights Division.” Those include the Voting Rights Act, the National Voter Registration Act, the Uniformed and Overseas Citizens Absentee Voting Act, the Voting Accessibility for the Elderly and Handicapped Act, the Civil Rights Act, the Help America Vote Act, and the Americans with Disabilities Act.
According to the mayor’s press release, the Secretary of the State’s office told the city that the DOJ plans to send two teams of two people, “focusing on polling locations subject to the Federal Voting Rights Act mandatory language-assistance requirement, which under federal law includes all of New Haven.” That requirement focuses on communities with a threshold of voters who speak a language other than English.
City spokesperson Lenny Speiller said that the DOJ has not advised the city which specific polling sites they intend on going to. Speiller also said that over 3,500 people have voted in New Haven so far during the early voting period.
A DOJ spokesperson did not respond to a request for comment by the publication time of this article.
“Given President Trump’s repeated attempts to undermine and cast doubt on free and fair elections across the nation and given the politicization of the Department of Justice under the Trump Administration, we believe posting federal election monitors at polling places would be counterproductive and make our polling places feel less accessible,” Elicker is quoted as saying in Friday’s press release.
“Connecticut has very clear laws and restrictions that govern poll watcher activity at voting sites. Our Registrars will be reminding and providing guidance to the city’s poll site moderators of these laws and will work to ensure they are followed.”
Also on Friday afternoon, U.S. Rep. Rosa DeLauro — a Democrat who is running for a 19th two-year term in office — sent out an email press release decrying the DOJ’s decision to send election monitors to New Haven.
“The Justice Department has a proud history of protecting the right to vote,” she said. “This is not that. This administration has spent years casting doubt on our elections. Coming from them, sending federal monitors to New Haven polling places is meant to make voters feel watched and unwelcome.”
DeLauro said that New Haven’s Democratic and Republican registrars “stand together on this, and I stand with them. Under Connecticut law, these monitors may not enter our polling places, and they have no power to arrest, detain, or search anyone. Connecticut runs free, fair and secure elections.”
DeLauro concluded: “To the people of New Haven: do not let anyone scare you away from the polls. Vote early this weekend at City Hall or Southern Connecticut State University, or vote at your polling place on Tuesday. Your vote is your voice. No one can take it from you.”
Monitors will stay 75 ft. from polls, will not be armed
On Saturday afternoon, Matthew Clyburn, a spokesperson for the Secretary of the State’s office, provided a comment from Secretary of the State Stephanie Thomas, elaborating on relevant state law and on a recent phone call with the DOJ.
“Connecticut General Statutes § 9-236 clearly defines who is permitted inside a polling place, and federal Department of Justice election monitors are not among those authorized to enter,” Thomas said. “The same rules apply to everyone, regardless of who they are or whom they represent. Like other members of the public, DOJ monitors may observe from outside the 75-foot restricted area.”
Thomas said that representatives from her office, the City of New Haven, and the Connecticut Attorney General’s office recently met with DOJ officials “to review what Connecticut law does and does not permit at polling places, including the restrictions that apply to federal election monitors.”
She said that the DOJ made clear that they plan on sending two teams of two monitors to visit New Haven polling locations “to observe compliance with federal voting rights laws, with a focus on language assistance and accessibility for voters with disabilities.”
Thomas said the DOJ assured the state and local officials that the election monitors:

Will follow all rules of the state and jurisdiction.
Will remain outside the 75-foot restricted area surrounding polling places.
Will observe without interfering with the voting process or the work of election officials.
Will not carry firearms.
Have no powers of arrest, detention, search, or seizure.
Will speak with voters only with their explicit consent, and only outside the 75-foot boundary.

She also said that the various parties agreed that:

Two teams will focus on polling locations subject to mandatory language assistance.
The monitors will focus on ensuring voters have received proper assistance with voting and that the exterior areas are accessible to those with disabilities.
The DOJ will send the names and titles of these monitors to our Office.
Monitors will not interfere with voters exercising their right to vote.
The DOJ will provide information for a point of contact and our Office will do the same.
The DOJ will send a “Do’s and Don’ts” check list for the monitors. 
Our office agreed to codify the conversation in a letter that was sent earlier today.

Thomas noted that the DOJ plans to send monitors to locations across the country, and that the rules governing their access vary by state. “Barring federal monitors from inside polling locations is not a partisan issue, but an issue of state law. Election officials in Indiana and Kentucky, among other jurisdictions, have also made clear that DOJ monitors must remain outside polling locations in accordance with their state laws.”
Thomas concluded: “I want every eligible voter in New Haven and across Connecticut to know that our polling places are ready to welcome you. Our election officials have worked hard to prepare for Election Day, and nothing about the presence of federal monitors changes your right to vote. Make your plan, cast your ballot and vote with confidence.”
This story was first published Oct. 30 and updated Oct. 31, 2026 by New Haven Independent.

name: California
title: These CA Election Day rules could block news coverage of voting
description: Some California counties are issuing guidelines restricting the press from documenting Election Day proceedings at polling places in ways that appear to violate state statutes and the First Amendment.  A coalition of media outlets, led by CalMatters, and a First Amendment advocacy group sent a letter to Kern County raising these concerns, after county electi[...]
text:
Voting booths at a polling site in California on June 7, 2022. Photo by Larry Valenzuela, CalMatters/CatchLight Local




Some California counties are issuing guidelines restricting the press from documenting Election Day proceedings at polling places in ways that appear to violate state statutes and the First Amendment. 
A coalition of media outlets, led by CalMatters, and a First Amendment advocacy group sent a letter to Kern County raising these concerns, after county elections officials issued initial media guidelines prohibiting media personnel from filming from within 100 feet of poll sites and ballot drop boxes, among other limitations. The coalition has identified other counties with similar prohibitions. 
These restrictions potentially stem from recent notices and poll worker training standards from the California secretary of state. In the guidelines, electioneering — or efforts to persuade voters to vote a certain way — is prohibited. The guidelines prohibit photographing or recording voters who are entering, inside or exiting a polling place without their permission.
But as long as outlets do not try to influence voters, these restrictions go beyond what state law limits and possibly run afoul of constitutional protections of a free press, said Ginny LaRoe the advocacy director at the First Amendment Coalition, which is part of the group raising alarm. 
Angélica Salceda, an attorney for American Civil Liberties Union Northern California, said she worries that the restrictions would also have a chilling effect on bystanders who may be discouraged from recording federal immigration activity that may occur near polling stations. 

Salceda: “We don’t want someone who might be reporting potentially unlawful federal law enforcement activity near a polling location to be told that they’re violating the law simply because of where they’re standing. Getting that clarifying guidance from county registrars, before those restrictions are misapplied, is very important.”

Barring media from capturing voters entering vote centers conflicts with a long U.S. history of reporters gathering footage outside polling stations. News organizations have previously captured long lines, voters explaining why they are casting their ballots, and politicians showing up at polls to vote.
Dedee Verdin, a spokesperson for the secretary of state’s office, emailed CalMatters Sunday night that the office is seeking more clarity from its experts and will respond when she learns more.
Read more.



Thank the CalMatters team for all their hard work on the voter guide with a donation today. Our bias-free, jargon-free and actually free guide is powered by people like you who donate to our 501(c)(3) nonprofit newsroom. Please give.

Other Stories You Should Know


Tech money in CA politics


Lobbyists and other visitors gather in the rotunda of the state Capitol in Sacramento on Sept. 12, 2025. Photo by Fred Greaves for CalMatters




A powerful force in California politics is flexing its might to influence Tuesday’s electoral outcomes: Big tech.
Homegrown tech giants such as Facebook owner Meta, Uber and Google are responsible for a fifth of all the outside campaign spending on state Senate and Assembly races, report CalMatters’ Khari Johnson and Jeremia Kimelman. 
So far outside spending from all donors has topped $128 million — well over the $74 million spent in the last midterm election in 2022. Experts say it makes sense that a powerful industry would want to attempt to protect its interests through campaign donations. Tech firms want to support moderate and pragmatic candidates who can let the industry innovate without too much regulation, one insider said. However, a state lawmaker thinks tech is trying to buy the Legislature. Others suggest tech’s donations might fuel more opposition against the sector.
Meanwhile, CalMatters’ Adam Ashton reports that the Peace Officers Research Association of California is running a much smaller-scale effort asking voters to unseat Supreme Court Justice Kelli Evans for reopening criminal cases that it believes should stay closed. The association doesn’t think it’ll succeed here, but it views the push as a warning to justices who rule on paroling inmates.



Few candidates for local school board races


Students attend class at Woodworth-Monroe K-8 Academy in Inglewood on Nov. 8, 2024. Photo by Carlin Stiehl for CalMatters




Nearly half of local school board races in California have just one candidate as more would-be stewards of taxpayer K-12 dollars opt out of running for these low-paid but crucial government jobs, writes CalMatters’ Carolyn Jones. 
Why the apprehension? 
Culture war issues in the curriculum help to steer candidates away, according to a recent report by the University of Southern California. Budget woes, strikes and school closures are also top of mind.
But races shouldn’t be unopposed, said Julie Marsh, a USC education professor and lead author of that report.

Marsh: “Otherwise it opens the door for interest groups to step in and have outsized power.” 

Read more.



And lastly: What do you want public health officials to know?


A farm manager packs freshly picked tomatoes into smaller cartons at Fiery Ginger Farm in West Sacramento on July 28, 2026. Photo by Anna Hoch-Kenney, CalMatters




Have an opinion on what health issues should be prioritized in California? CalMatters is partnering with Your Local Epidemiologist to make the real concerns and questions from Californians heard by public health officials and journalists.
Every Monday, we’ll ask about health topics affecting Californians, and it’ll only take two minutes to answer.
This week, we’re asking about how you decide what food to eat and following up on your concerns about young people and vaping. Take the survey.






California Voices
America’s affordability crisis threatens the viability of the American Dream, and things have steadily gotten worse despite political leaders promising repeatedly to make that dream possible again, writes Jennifer Mercieca, a historian of American political rhetoric.
Dolores Huerta helped build the largest farmworker movement in U.S. history — a movement that has inspired organizers and helped keep unions alive, writes Christian Paiz, an associate professor of ethnic studies at UC Berkeley.

name: North Dakota Monitor
title: 2 North Dakota counties ask voters to override property tax cap
description: At least two counties in North Dakota this week are asking voters to let them go over the state’s limit for how much local governments can increase property taxes, a crucial revenue source to funding various services. The ballot measures in Divide and Traill counties show how some local governments are struggling with the limit […]
text:
People walk into the Traill County Courthouse in Hillsboro, North Dakota, on July 13, 2026. (Photo by Jeff Beach/North Dakota Monitor)At least two counties in North Dakota this week are asking voters to let them go over the state’s limit for how much local governments can increase property taxes, a crucial revenue source to funding various services.
The ballot measures in Divide and Traill counties show how some local governments are struggling with the limit of a 3% annual increase on local property taxes set last year by the Republican-led Legislature in a bill boosting a property tax credit.
“I think it’s unrealistic,” Divide County Commission Chairman Rodney Johnson said.
[Voter Guide: 2026 General Election Voter Guide: The info you need to cast your ballot.]
A key lawmaker said he doesn’t sense any legislative support to change or abolish the 3% cap. A county government advocate said the limitation affects every county differently and some costs are out of their control.
Divide County is asking voters for an additional 2%, or roughly $37,800 annually the next four years. The additional money would help cover the county’s operations, Auditor/Treasurer Gayle Jastrzebski said. 
“With everything going up – you know, health insurance increased 10% last year. When you can only raise (property taxes) 3%, you gotta make up that difference,” she said.
The county will have to make cuts if voters don’t approve the measure, Johnson said.
“For the most part, I think they will understand, but you never know when the voters come out,” he said.
Traill County is asking voters for an additional 6.41%, or about $461,000 for each year over the next four years. The text of the ballot measure cites increases in veterans services, health insurance, cost of living and various operating expenses including roads, bridges and technology.
Traill County lies between the cities of Fargo and Grand Forks, and competition for employees is tough, she said.
“I think it’s just a matter of we’re just trying to keep up with the local economy and keep our staff,” County Auditor Heather Hovey said.
It isn’t guaranteed the county would use the full increase if voters approve it, she added.
If voters reject the increase, the county might have to consider cuts to staff and postponing road projects, Hovey said. The 3% cap is hard when the Legislature puts it on local governments but doesn’t do the same for state budgets, Hovey said.
Property taxes eliminated for 50,000 North Dakota households under new legislation

Rep. Craig Headland, who chairs the House Finance and Taxation Committee, said he’s gotten little pushback on the 3% limit, saying the counties in his area understand and abide by it. He said he doesn’t sense an appetite among lawmakers to increase or eliminate the cap. Lawmakers viewed 3% as a good, average inflationary number to use, he said.
One two-year budget cycle is not enough time to determine “if there’s any merit in what they’re saying or not,” said Headland, R-Montpelier. 
“If they can show us real hardship, then, you know, we will have to take a look,” the longtime tax legislator said.
Rising property taxes have frustrated homeowners for years. In 2024, voters rejected a ballot initiative that would have eliminated assessed-value property taxes and required the state to replace billions of dollars of revenue. Afterward, the Legislature passed property tax legislation that expanded a tax credit for homeowners and placed the cap on local property tax increases.
The North Dakota Association of Counties supports exceptions to the 3% cap for difficult costs of health insurance, elections and jail expenses, Government/Public Relations Specialist Donnell Preskey said. 
“I don’t know that we have counties out there that are just spending money to spend money,” Preskey said last week. “They’re providing the services to address the needs in their community and they know what those needs are the best.”
Roughly two-thirds of North Dakota’s 53 counties used reserves in the 2026 budget cycle, Preskey told lawmakers this year. Of those 33 counties, 13 also used the entire 3% increase. Reserves run out and are not a sustainable source for the future, she said.
Counties can also bank an unused portion of the 3% cap for future use. About two-thirds of counties did so, according to a survey by the association. 
Some counties are economic drivers and others have hardly any sources to generate revenue other than property taxes, Preskey said. The 3% cap amounts to $18,000 for Slope County, population 700, and $1.8 million for Cass County, home to one-quarter of the state’s population or more than 200,000 people, according to association data.
Property valuations might be increasing in the largest cities of Bismarck and Fargo, but they are decreasing in some areas, meaning less money for local budgets, she said.
“We really have to think about those parts of our state that are really rural and more desolate and are really trying to hang on with any kind of population they can,” Preskey told lawmakers in September.
Reach North Dakota Monitor reporter Jack Dura at jdura@northdakotamonitor.com.

title: Outside Michigan ICE detention center, activists mourn the dead and demand change
description: The day was coming to an end, and the GEO sign identifying the North Lake Processing Center in Baldwin remained covered with photographs of people who had died while in the hands of immigration enforcement. An offering of flower petals, bread, drinks and candles reflected El Día de los Muertos, or Day of the Dead, […]
text:
Protestors gather at the North Lake Processing Center in Baldwin, Michigan on Nov. 1, 2026, for a Day of the Dead ceremony to honor those who have died in ICE custody. (Photo by Erick Díaz Veliz/Michigan Advance)The day was coming to an end, and the GEO sign identifying the North Lake Processing Center in Baldwin remained covered with photographs of people who had died while in the hands of immigration enforcement. An offering of flower petals, bread, drinks and candles reflected El Día de los Muertos, or Day of the Dead, an Indigenous-rooted tradition observed Oct. 31-Nov. 2 in parts of Latin America, particularly Mexico, Ecuador, Peru and Bolivia, to honor the dead.
Organized by several Immigrant Rights advocates from Muskegon to Detroit, approximately 100 people from across the state gathered outside North Lake, the largest ICE detention center in the Midwest, to honor and remember those who have died in ICE custody, as well as those killed by ICE and Border Patrol agents this year. They were also standing in solidarity with those held inside the processing center operated by the Florida-based private contractor GEO Group.
“The purpose of this event is to amplify the names of those who have been brutally taken from their families, their loved ones, their community by ICE or CBP,” Ale Rojas with Movimiento Cosecha and No Detention Centers in Michigan, told Michigan Advance. “One of the biggest things for us right now is recognizing that we, as a community, are hurting, so we can continue to build community and remember that we can show up for each other.”
Flyers hang on the GEO Group sign at the North Lake Processing Center in Baldwin, Michigan on Nov. 1, 2026, in remembrance of individuals who have died in ICE custody or whose death were connected to immigration enforcement. (Photo by Erick Díaz Veliz/Michigan Advance)
Bringing together so many activist organizations and coalitions from across Michigan was easier than it had been a few months ago, Rojas said, noting that “the desire for action, for an actual movement, seems to be stronger now among organizations throughout the state.” 
No Detention Centers in Michigan; Movimiento Cosecha GR; West Michigan Clergy Action; the Coalition to Shut the Camps; Asamblea Popular Detroit; and Metro Detroit DSA were among the organizers.
The number of fatalities linked to immigration enforcement across the country has increased compared to previous years. Since the beginning of Donald Trump’s second administration, at least 57 deaths have been recorded in ICE custody, including the death of Nenko Gantchev, a Bulgarian citizen and Chicago resident, which occurred last December in North Lake, along with at least 11 fatal shootings involving ICE and Border Patrol agents. 
The most recent person to be fatally shot by immigration agents was Joan Sebastián Durán Guerrero, a 26-year-old Colombian national who died July 13 in Biddeford, Maine, during an ICE operation. The most recent individual to die while in custody was Guillermo Pascual Verganza, a 43-year-old Guatemalan citizen who passed away Oct. 24 at the Otay Mesa detention center in San Diego, California.
In Michigan, the most recent case of a death linked to an immigration operation involves Mario David Coronado Juárez, 35, a Guatemalan man who died Sept. 20 in a traffic accident in Grand Rapids in which ICE was involved.

(Photo by Erick Díaz Veliz/Michigan Advance)Protestors gather at the North Lake Processing Center in Baldwin, Michigan on Nov. 1, 2026, for a Day of the Dead ceremony to honor those who have died in ICE custody. (Photo by Erick Díaz Veliz/Michigan Advance)
For Nuala Richards, 24, who came to the vigil from Grand Rapids, the actions of immigration enforcement are reminiscent of what one would see in a fascist state. 
“The lobster doesn’t realize they’re being boiled until the water is boiling,” Richards said. “I don’t want this to be a continuation of what this country has been in the past. And I think if we can do anything to stop our country from being genocidal and continuing these atrocities, I think we should be doing that.”
Whitney Morton, 33, a resident of the Detroit area, hopes that elected officials and those aspiring to hold public office will understand how determined community members are to get immigrants out of detention centers. SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“We are torturing people and tormenting people,” Morton said. “And if people believe any of the things in young adult stories—in those Marvel movies you’ve watched—if you believe in that, then you hate ICE, and you’re down here demanding that our neighbors be set free.”
After leaving candles and sharing traditional breads and drinks associated with the celebration, dozens of people moved toward another gate overlooking one of the cellblocks to hold a rally, featuring chants and speeches in support of the inmates.
“Our message is clear: Immigrant lives are of value, and immigrants deserve safety, dignity, and respect. We mourn the loss of life in ICE custody, valued loved ones who deserved to return to their families alive,” said Nanci Palacios, Organizing and Membership Director at Detention Watch Network.

title: Democrats and unaffiliated voters cast about 73% of ballots in NC’s record-setting early turnout
description: Early voting in a midterm election set a record this year in North Carolina, with more than 2.7 million people voting in person by Saturday afternoon.  With mail-in ballots included, 2.8 million votes have been cast, meaning 36% of registered voters have cast ballots before Election Day, The previous high for a midterm was 2022, […]
text:
Voters in line at the Durham County South Regional Library for the last day of early voting on Oct. 31, 2026 contributed to North Carolina's record-breaking midterm early voting turnout. (Photo: Lynn Bonner/NC Newsline)Early voting in a midterm election set a record this year in North Carolina, with more than 2.7 million people voting in person by Saturday afternoon. 
With mail-in ballots included, 2.8 million votes have been cast, meaning 36% of registered voters have cast ballots before Election Day,
The previous high for a midterm was 2022, with about 2 million votes cast in person during the early voting period. 
Saturday saw the heaviest early vote turnout, with about 249,000 people showing up at the polls. 
To date, 38% of those who have voted are registered Democrats, 35% are unaffiliated and 26% are registered Republicans. 
The final days of the early voting period showed particularly strong unaffiliated voter turnout. In the last four days of early voting, unaffiliated voters outnumbered registered Democrats and registered Republicans. 
“The truly surprising dynamic to me is the rise of the early unaffiliated voter, something I and a number of colleagues have been tracking for many years now, but this year, their ‘showing up’ during early voting is pretty remarkable,” Catawba College political scientist Micheal Bitzer wrote on his Substack on Sunday.
On each day of early voting, more people voted this year than on the comparable day in 2022, Western Carolina University political scientist Chris Cooper wrote on his Substack. More people voted on a Sunday this year than they did in 2022, even though fewer counties had Sunday voting hours, Cooper wrote. 
Early voting statistics are not election forecasts. Registered Republicans typically outvote Democrats on Election Day. 
Early voting turnout so far shows enthusiasm among unaffiliated voters in NC

The early voting period is over. The last chance to vote will be on Tuesday, Election Day, when polls will be open from 6:30 am to 7:30 pm. Voters should go to their assigned polling place. 
Voters who have mail-in ballots can return them to their county board of elections office. Mail-in ballots that arrive after 7:30 p.m. on Tuesday will not be counted. The status of mail-in ballots can be checked using Ballottrax. 
People who requested mail-in ballots but haven’t returned them can vote in person. 
The U.S. Senate race is at the top of the ticket. Democrat Roy Cooper and Republican Michael Whatley are vying for the open seat.
The contest for one seat on the state Supreme Court, where incumbent Justice Anita Earls, a Democrat, faces former Republican legislator Sarah Stevens, will also be on every ballot. All voters will also be asked to fill three seats on the state Court of Appeals.
Voters will decide who will represent them in the state legislature and the U.S. House. 
Three proposed constitutional amendments are also on the ballot, two concerning taxes and one about voter ID.

name: North Dakota Monitor
title: Commentary: Cowboy Cafe’s change to a bistro a sign of a new Medora
description: MEDORA, N.D. – North Dakota’s public and private investments in Medora and Billings County are unprecedented in the region’s history. Tens of millions of dollars in taxpayer dollars, business development and philanthropic giving have been piling into this once-sleepy cow town, forever changing its character and, to some degree, its western charm. The big sta[...]
text:
The Medora sign is surrounded by autumn foliage and rolling landscapes of the Badlands, looking out from the Theodore Roosevelt Presidential Library on Oct. 5, 2026. (Photo by Jacob Orledge/North Dakota Monitor)MEDORA, N.D. – North Dakota’s public and private investments in Medora and Billings County are unprecedented in the region’s history. Tens of millions of dollars in taxpayer dollars, business development and philanthropic giving have been piling into this once-sleepy cow town, forever changing its character and, to some degree, its western charm. The big state money has meant big changes, and the long-term effects – whether for good or ill – have yet to be assessed.   
The North Dakota Legislature, for example, ponied up $50 million (to be matched by private donations) for the Theodore Roosevelt Presidential Library operations endowment. The library is having a marvelous first season. Visitations hit 100,000 in the first two months, and reviews have been overwhelmingly positive. Add to the state appropriations, millions more in public money for major road projects (a round-about in Medora!) and other transportation and bridge upgrades. Everywhere a visitor looks, construction equipment is building and digging and repairing – a few projects funded locally but mostly by combinations of state, federal and county government funding.
It’s a lot of money in a place that has not necessarily been the beneficiary of such a high level of public investment. However, the tourism growth that began decades ago with the Medora musical and has blossomed into the state’s primary summer tourist attraction has sometimes been accomplished without sufficient attention to the foundational character and genuine historical attractions of Badlands country. The magnificent and world-class TR library has accelerated the process. There are large and small indications of the pervasiveness of the change. A small one is worthy of notice.  
Any North Dakotan who has been a regular visitor to Medora knows about the Cowboy Cafe. A fixture on Fourth Street a couple of blocks from the center of town for some 40 years, the cafe was unique in every sense of that frequently misused descriptor.
“Was” is the operative word because the Cowboy Cafe is gone and its location is now occupied by the L’Amour Bistro. The western ranching and rodeo-themed cafe has been erased by an apparently sincere attempt to create a French-like ambiance that connects with the Marquis and Marquesa DeMores, who indeed were important figures in Medora’s pioneer history. The town is named after her. To that end, the bistro features two large portraits of the couple, but little else that has anything to do with the town’s cowboy and ranching history. There is nary a tip of the (cowboy) hat to the former cafe’s extraordinary display of vintage ranch and rodeo photographs, western artifacts, or the area ranch cattle brands that were burned into the scarred wooden tabletops. While some ranches faded into history, others are still active multi-generational spreads in Billings and Golden Valley counties. And of course, the cafe’s signature cowboy soup is not on the menu. Cowboy soup in a faux French bistro? Of course not!
“So what?” one might say. And for patrons of the bistro who never experienced the cafe’s down-home food and furnishings that proudly honored the region’s rodeo and ranching culture, “so what?” makes sense. They don’t know what has been lost. 
It might be that the photos, artifacts and branded tables are property that the previous family owners of the cafe wanted to keep. That is surely understandable. But that circumstance does not preclude the new owners from gathering up similar memorabilia – of which there is plenty in Billings County alone – to, at the very least, let patrons know the bistro has taken over a very special space in Medora’s western lore. Even the patrician Marquis tried his hand at ranching.
There remain really good local eateries in Medora that honor the town’s heritage. Among them is the 100-year-old Little Missouri Saloon and Dining Room, an authentic western saloon, filled with reminders of why the town is there. Boots Bar and Grill, which has been in the same location for decades on Pacific Avenue under other names, also keeps the region’s western history and hospitality with excellent unpretentious food served up in a scuffed dining room and welcoming atmosphere.
But the demise of the Cowboy Cafe and the replacement bistro are reminders of change in Medora that is altering the character of the historic town. Whether for good or ill is a matter of perspective.
That being said, the new bistro is very much worth a visit. It is a fine restaurant that adds a new and different element to the redefined charm of the town.  
But a “bistro” – a bistro, for mercy’s sake – in western, cowboy, ranching, Teddy Roosevelt’s Medora? And redecorating the old dining room so as to obliterate any trace of an historic cafe that felt like the old west just walking in the door? Say it ain’t so!
Sometimes the investment of millions of dollars in state money is beneficial. Sometimes it’s not. This time, it seems, the consequences of Medora’s accelerating development, funded by a combination of taxpayer dollars and for-profit investments, were not adequately assessed, and will not be. That horse is out of the barn. The demise of the Cowboy Cafe might seem a small matter, but it’s also a clear indication that the Medora of old is passing away.

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: Your Massachusetts midterm rundown
description: On this episode of The Codcast, we get listeners all caught up on the political landscape in Massachusetts and around the country heading into the crucial 2026 midterm elections.
text:
EPISODE INFO

HOSTS: Jordan Wolman
GUESTS: Steve Koczela, president of the MassINC Polling Group, and Chris Borick, professor of political science at Lehigh University and director of Lehigh’s Opinion Observatory








WITH ELECTION DAY upon us on Tuesday, voters here in Massachusetts and around the country are preparing to cast their ballots in the 2026 midterms.  
Nationally, much of the focus will be on whether – and at what scale – Democrats are able to translate President Trump’s unpopularity and voters’ economic angst into a congressional majority that breaks the GOP trifecta in Washington.   
In the Bay State, the stakes are a bit different. Democrats already control Beacon Hill with supermajorities, and the state’s congressional delegation is already entirely blue.  That dynamic is not expected to change after November 3. 
Still, Gov. Maura Healey and US Sen. Ed Markey are looking to secure convincing reelection victories as residents grapple with significant cost-of-living concerns. Plus, Massachusetts voters will be asked to decide a record-tying nine ballot questions on policy areas ranging from tax policy to marijuana legalization to how the state should administer elections.  
Steve Koczela, president of the MassINC Polling Group, and Chris Borick, a professor of political science at Lehigh University and director of Lehigh’s Opinion Observatory, joined CommonWealth Beacon senior reporter Jordan Wolman on The Codcast to preview the political landscape ahead of Election Day.  
“The expectations are now really high for Democrats,” Borick said. “And I understand why. A bunch of metrics point in the direction of a really special environment that they’re in politically. From a Republican perspective, I don’t think the word toxic is an overstatement.” 
On this episode, Borick and Koczela discuss whether the Democrats could really turn states like Texas and Alaska blue (2:23), how Massachusetts voters are thinking about the nine ballot questions they’ll decide (7:00), and what it will take for the state GOP to become competitive again (18:25).

name: Nevada Current
title: Metro effort to depoliticize towing contract enables conflicts, say critics
description: The Las Vegas Metropolitan Police Department’s effort to stay out of the auto towing business is exposing the department to possible legal scrutiny and potentially endangering the public, say critics who contend Metro’s towing management vendor is engaged in self-dealing.  Since 2016, Metro has outsourced its towing dispatch services to Autura, a national co[...]
text:
(Photo courtesy SNAP Towing)The Las Vegas Metropolitan Police Department’s effort to stay out of the auto towing business is exposing the department to possible legal scrutiny and potentially endangering the public, say critics who contend Metro’s towing management vendor is engaged in self-dealing. 
Since 2016, Metro has outsourced its towing dispatch services to Autura, a national company formerly known as AutoReturn. 
Metro pays nothing. Instead, Autura tacks on a $32.50 charge to customers’ bills for every law enforcement-related tow it dispatches, and the tow companies with whom it contracts reap the lucrative vehicle storage and scrap metal income. 
Tow yard storage bills can reach thousands of dollars, sometimes exceeding the value of the vehicle, which can be auctioned by the tow yard to satisfy the bill.    
In 2021, Autura removed an estimated 2,000 vehicles a month from accident scenes, DUI arrests, or for parking violations.  
Metro’s agreement with Autura allows the company to select tow companies and storage yards with little input from the police department. 
“We are no longer in the towing business,” then-Metro Sheriff Joe Lombardo, who is now governor, told the Current in 2021, shortly after the department executed its first five-year renewal with Autura. 
The arrangement was intended to eliminate the politicization of selecting vendors to be included in Metro’s towing rotation. 
“Before 2016, the department did pick the tow truck companies directly, and that is exactly what made this our most politicized contract, with every operator lobbying the sheriff and this committee,” Metro Chief Financial Officer Damon Harris told Metro’s Fiscal Affairs Committee on Thursday. “Taking that choice out of our hands is the whole point.”
But instead, the jockeying for favored status has intensified. 
SNAP Towing, which has been in Autura’s rotation for ten years, was eliminated in the recent renewal and replaced with Quality Towing, a company that was until recently owned by Autura. 
SNAP Towing owners Van Le and Danny Thompson contend that giving Autura free reign in the selection of vendors gives the intermediary too much discretion. 
Unlike government contracts, where all qualified companies are invited to bid, Autura refused to respond to SNAP’s application, Le and Thompson say. 
“The fact is they wanted Quality Towing on so they had to take a company off,” Le said via email.
 Autura’s five-year contract extension never came before the Fiscal Affairs Committee, which votes on Metro’s financial matters. Instead, it was approved in September by Clark County Sheriff Kevin McMahill, who is permitted to unilaterally sign off on some goods and services agreements.  
“There’s concern that the sheriff’s office is placing favoritism and personal/political interests over public safety, which may be a violation of the sheriff’s number one priority in this community,” says Rick McCann, who is advocating on behalf of SNAP. 
McCann contends former SNAP owner Robert Ellis, who sold the company to Le and Thompson but still owns the land, persuaded McMahill to have SNAP removed from the towing rotation, which it relies on to remain in business. Ellis, they fear, has his eye on foreclosure. 
Ellis and McMahill did not respond to requests for comment. 
SNAP Towing requested during public comment that the committee not approve a report on Metro’s contract renewal with Autura and hear it as a separate item. The committee did not act on that request. 
SNAP executives say delegating the selection of vendors to a third party is inconsistent with Metro’s commitment to transparency and public safety.  
They assert Autura is funneling business to companies in which it has a business interest. Autura is part of Vehicle Management Solutions, a company that until recently owned an interest in Quality Towing, one of the three companies servicing Autura’s contract with Metro. 
“I believe LVMPD’s contract with Autura may end up causing a great deal of embarrassment by inadvertently getting Metro involved in claims of unfair trade practices and citizen consumer-related complaints,” Christine Abbott, an Arizona paralegal and investigator who is working for SNAP Towing, told the Fiscal Affairs committee. 
Autura and its sister companies assert they’ve separated the technology and dispatch side of the business from towing operations. Abbott, who says the move is likely an attempt to ward off allegations of self-dealing, says she’s not buying it and notes the reportedly independent companies share addresses throughout the country. 
Complaints about potential conflicts prompted Metro to add a provision to its contract that requires Autura to disclose any financial or personnel ties with the tow companies, says Harris, the CFO. If Autura doesn’t disclose conflicts, Metro “may” reject a vendor or end the contract. But it’s not required to do so. 
Autura did not respond to the Current’s request for comment.   
Thompson and Le say they intend to ask state lawmakers to weigh in. They seek to “strengthen the process by which the Fiscal Affairs Committee oversees Metro,” says McCann. “There’s no question in our minds that McMahill has considerable input into awarding the dispatcher contract, as well as selecting which tow companies are added after the dispatch contract is signed.”
McCann says the lack of involvement by the Fiscal Affairs Committee, which was never asked to approve the contract with Autura, demonstrates “a critical breakdown of legitimate oversight by the committee.”
Metro did not respond to requests for comment.

name: California
title: Counties’ Election Day rules may block news coverage of voting, civil rights groups warn
description: Some of California’s most populous counties are issuing guidelines restricting the press from documenting Election Day proceedings at polling places in ways that appear to violate state statutes and the First Amendment.
text:
In summary
Some of California’s most populous counties are issuing guidelines restricting the press from documenting Election Day proceedings at polling places in ways that appear to violate state statutes and the First Amendment. 


Some of California’s most populous counties are issuing guidelines restricting the press from documenting Election Day proceedings at polling places in ways that appear to violate state statutes and the First Amendment.A coalition of media outlets, led by CalMatters, and a First Amendment advocacy group sent a letter to Kern County raising these concerns. The coalition has identified other counties with similar prohibitions. 
These restrictions potentially stem from recent notices and poll worker training standards from the California secretary of state, which sets policy on election rules. In the guidelines, electioneering — or efforts to persuade voters to vote a certain way — is prohibited. The guidelines prohibit photographing or recording voters who are entering, inside or exiting a polling place without their permission.
But as long as outlets do not try to influence voters, these restrictions go beyond what state law limits and possibly run afoul of constitutional protections of a free press, said Ginny LaRoe the advocacy director at the First Amendment Coalition, which is part of the group raising alarm. 
Dedee Verdin, a spokesperson for the secretary of state’s office, wrote in an email to CalMatters on Sunday night that she is seeking clarity from the office’s experts and will respond when she learns more.
On Oct. 27 the Kern County election office issued media guidelines that prohibited media personnel from filming from within 100 feet of poll sites and ballot drop boxes. 
Those prohibitions prompted the first of two letters from media organizations and the press rights group to the county registrar. 
Around that time, the First Amendment Coalition began looking into secretary of state materials that counties may be relying on as a potential source of the restrictions, including the anti-electioneering regulations. Research by the First Amendment Coalition identified at least nine other counties besides Kern, including large ones such as Alameda, Los Angeles and Santa Clara, that reiterate the secretary of state’s guidelines in their own rules.
LaRoe said that it’s the responsibility of counties to ensure that the restrictions they’re implementing are consistent with state law and constitutional protections.  
Angélica Salceda, an attorney for American Civil Liberties Union Northern California, said she worries that the restrictions would also have a chilling effect on bystanders who may be discouraged from recording federal immigration activity that may occur near polling stations. The ACLU of Northern California is not part of the media coalition.
“We don’t want someone who might be reporting potentially unlawful federal law enforcement activity near a polling location to be told that they’re violating the law simply because of where they’re standing,” said Salceda. 
“Getting that clarifying guidance from county registrars, before those restrictions are misapplied, is very important.”
Barring media from capturing voters entering vote centers conflicts with a long U.S. history of reporters gathering footage outside polling stations. News organizations have previously captured long lines, voters explaining why they are casting their ballots, and politicians showing up at polls to vote.
Just as “local and state officials are hard at work ensuring a free and fair vote,” journalists have their own vital role to play as watchdogs, said LaRoe of the First Amendment Coalition. “We worry that these state and local restrictions on news gathering, including photography, will impede the kind of news coverage on public accountability that serves our community.”
In the first letter to Kern County officials, CalMatters and others argued that the rules were unnecessarily restrictive and “come at an unprecedented time when the federal government is alleging election fraud and Governor (Gavin) Newsom is sending election attorneys to monitor federal poll watchers.”
After the media groups sent the letter, Kern County issued an updated guideline on Oct. 30, clarifying that outlets cannot film voters dropping off ballots if the voter “feels intimidated by being filmed.” But there is no statute that requires journalists to stop filming ballot drop-offs because a voter reports feeling intimidated, the media groups said in their second letter to county election officials. 
The updated guidelines also require the media to conduct “all interviews” at least 25 feet from the entrance of a polling site, citing a state statute. But that specific statute only relates to exit polling interviews, and does not require that every journalistic interview, such as ones discussing wait times or voting procedures, be conducted at least 25 feet, media groups’ second letter said. 
With Election Day on Tuesday, LaRoe said the media coalition is not seeking to infringe on the privacy of voters.
“But the act of going out in public and the administration of our election by public officials is inherently public,” she said. “And that’s where we have a concern with these policies, no matter how well-intended.” The coalition of media outlets and associations is made up of CalMatters, Central Valley Journalism Collaborative, First Amendment Coalition, Kern Sol News, KGET/Telemundo, KVPR/Valley Public Radio, National Press Photographers Association, SJV Water, and the Society of Professional Journalists Central California.

name: California
title: Beware the ‘red mirage’ if California Republicans have an election night lead
description: Don’t be fooled by early election returns. It can take California weeks to tally votes, leading to “red mirages” and “blue shifts.”
text:
In summary
Don’t be fooled by early election returns. It can take California weeks to tally votes, leading to “red mirages” and “blue shifts.”


It happens in close races in almost every major election. Early California returns show Republicans winning or at least faring better than expected. Then, as votes are counted over the following days, the tallies shift in Democrats’ favor.
This “blue shift” or “red mirage” isn’t a result of California Democrats “finding votes” or rigging elections, as President Donald Trump and his supporters have repeatedly claimed. 
Trump and his allies in the federal government are already laying the groundwork for questioning the election results as they embark on an unprecedented attack on California’s elections, setting up what could be a showdown over the fundamentals of American democracy. Experts urge you not to be fooled by their claims of “rigged” elections based on early returns.
The shifts in early tallies, experts say, are merely the result of when and how Democrats and Republicans tend to vote and the length of time it takes California election officials to count millions of ballots. 
Examples of the ‘blue shift’ and ‘red mirage’
The phenomenon has been described since at least 2013, but the terms gained traction around the contentious 2020 elections. 
Six years ago, election night returns showed Trump leading Joe Biden in several key states, but as counties nationwide counted ballots over the coming days, Biden ended up winning in the states that put him over the top in the Electoral College.
In the final weeks of his first term, Trump made claims, which have been repeatedly debunked, that the race was stolen from him. Thousands of his supporters stormed the U.S. Capitol in the deadly riot on Jan. 6, 2021. 
California has seen its own red mirages in congressional and local races over the years. In 2018, for instance, four Republican candidates for the U.S. House of Representatives appeared to be ahead on election night, but ended up losing to their Democratic opponents by the time all votes were counted.
In the primary this June, Spencer Pratt, a Republican former reality TV star, appeared to be beating progressive Los Angeles City Council member Nithya Raman in early returns in the race for LA mayor. Raman ended up pulling ahead and advanced to the general election to face incumbent Mayor Karen Bass.The shift led Trump to call the results “rigged” and others on the MAGA right to declare Democratic shenanigans were at work.
Experts and elections officials say you shouldn’t believe such claims.
Why vote counts shift
First, let’s state the obvious: California is the most populous state. There are 23 million registered voters in California; that’s more voters than the entire populations of the 16 least-populated states combined.Los Angeles County — the most populated in the country — alone has nearly 6 million registered voters.There are also lots of Republicans in California, even though Democrats greatly outnumber them.
Want to blow some minds at your next cocktail party? Ask your friends to name which county in the U.S. had the most Trump voters, by raw numbers, in the 2020 election. The answer: deep-blue Los Angeles County, where Biden overwhelmingly won.
So how does that translate into a red mirage?In the June LA mayor’s race, the city’s Republicans turned their ballots in earlier than Democrats did.
There was so much last-minute uncertainty over the crowded field of Democratic gubernatorial candidates who appeared on the same ballot that many liberal voters waited an especially long time to return them.  
That meant more Republican votes were reported in the first wave of election returns, a red mirage that disappeared as Democratic votes were fully tabulated.That could very well happen in the various partisan races on the ballot in California, including those that could determine which party controls Congress.
And, as usual, the rest of the country may end up waiting weeks for California’s results to get an answer.
Yes, California takes a long time to count votes
There’s no getting around it: California’s vote counting process is slow, and that gives more time for doubts about the election results to fester.“It is undermining voter confidence. It’s opening the door to election mis- and disinformation,” Kim Alexander, president of the California Voter Foundation, said in a briefing last week. “It’s leading to threats and criticism of our election staff. …. And it shortens the time required for an orderly transition of power.”
But there are reasons why California counts so slowly.
During the pandemic, California began mailing every registered voter a ballot. Mail-in ballots require far more time to process than in-person ballots. Many voters also hang on to their ballots until Election Day.
Adding to the counting delays, California gives voters a seven-day grace period for ballots postmarked by Election Day to arrive and get counted. 
California also has the longest period in the country to “cure” ballots that come in with problems such as mismatched signatures that require election officials to contact voters to fix them. This year, voters have until the day before Thanksgiving to cure their ballots, Alexander said.
The state only requires counties to count ballots for at least six hours a day, and they’re not required to count on weekends or holidays. 
Alexander said many counties go beyond that, but it’s up to each election office. The decision is often dependent on whether the county has enough election workers, can pay them over time and has space for them to work, all of which depend on local budgets. 
Recent changes to California law aim to speed up the count, and lawmakers this year provided $29 million for counties to buy more ballot-counting machines or hire more workers. Still, Alexander said some close races could remain undecided for weeks. Counties have 30 days to officially certify the results.
Ben Gips of Protect Democracy, a nonpartisan nonprofit dedicated to fighting authoritarianism, urged California voters not to be misled by those who would use such delays to sow doubt about an election that is working as intended, if slowly.“These delays really can add fuel to that strategy, and it can make it much easier to do that deception,” Gips said.

name: California
title: Why school board members aren’t running for reelection: ‘A lot of disillusionment’
description: School board members cited a slew of reasons for not running for reelection, including distress over budget cuts and labor strife, immigration raids affecting schools and youth and an overall hostile political climate.
text:
In summary
School board members cited a slew of reasons for not running for reelection, including distress over budget cuts and labor strife, immigration raids affecting schools and youth and an overall hostile political climate.


The Nov. 3 ballot is long and filled with consequential races. But one thing most voters in California won’t see: much ado about school boards.
About half of California’s school board candidates are most likely running unopposed, according to a recent USC report, leaving a dearth of public scrutiny just as enormous changes to K-12 education are underway at the state and federal levels.
“We need more people, more choices, more public debate,” said USC education professor Julie Marsh, a lead author of the report. “Otherwise it opens the door for interest groups to step in and have outsized power.”
School board members cited a slew of reasons for not running for reelection, including distress over budget cuts and labor strife, immigration raids affecting schools and youth and an overall hostile political climate. In addition, the hours are long, the pay is low, and the friends are scarce.
“A large group didn’t anticipate how emotionally draining the job can be,” Marsh said. “We saw a lot of disillusionment.”
Uncertainty and tumult
Local control has been a centerpiece of California school governance for more than a decade, since the state adopted the Local Control Funding Formula giving school districts more latitude in spending and decision-making. But the state is currently shifting more power to the governor’s office and the Trump administration is shuttering the U. S. Department of Education, leaving a tide of uncertainty and tumult for school boards.
The culture wars haven’t helped. Fights about curriculum that includes LGBTQ history, the rights of transgender students and other topics have roiled school board meetings in purple regions for the past few years. But those concerns pale compared to stress related to teacher strikes, school closures and budget woes, Marsh and her colleagues found.   
In recent years, interest groups such as labor unions and conservative political groups have sought to place their members on school boards, with some success. If they’re running unopposed, those candidates are easily elected – with little public scrutiny.
Does money help?
A few efforts to make school board jobs more attractive are underway. Assembly Bill 1390,  passed last year, allows school districts to pay board members up to $4,500 a month, depending on the size of the district. Currently, most school board members earn a small stipend, usually a few hundred dollars a month.
But even higher pay doesn’t come close to fair compensation for what’s often a 40-hour-a-week job, school board members said. And most aren’t in it for the money, anyway.
“If I run for re-election, it’s very much not for the money or personal benefit,” said Nick Caston, who won a seat on the Santa Rosa City Schools board in 2024 and became board president last year. “It’s for the long-term benefit of the students, staff and community.”
Caston, a father of three who works as a business strategy consultant, said the job has been much more stressful and time-consuming than he anticipated. The district initially thought it would have to close one elementary school to balance its budget, but that soon became six schools.
The public outcry was difficult to endure, he said.
“You feel like you’re the tangible face of things that are happening beyond your control,” Caston said. “It can be very stressful.”
Another effort to retain school board members has been improved training. The California School Boards Association provides an ever-expanding array of webinars, workshops and a 40-hour “master’s in governance” program that covers topics such as collective bargaining, community relations, the Brown Act and school finance. 
But those trainings are not mandatory. The only state requirement for incoming school board members is a two-hour ethics class. Starting next year, they’ll also have to take a four-hour finance class. In the USC report, a majority of board members said they needed more training, especially in using social media, understanding whether programs or curricula are effective, and navigating political tensions.
“Training cannot eliminate every source of stress, but it can help trustees become more confident, effective and efficient in their work,” said school boards association spokesperson Troy Flint. “Our goal is to ensure they have the tools  to succeed without having to navigate these challenges alone.”
More Latinas running 
As interest in running for a school board wanes generally, one group appears to be surging: Latinas. In 2023, Latinas represented at least 20% of California school board members in districts with large numbers of Latino students, according to a survey by Hispanas Organized for Political Equality, a Los Angeles-based nonprofit. In Los Angeles and the Central Coast, the number was closer to 30%. Oxnard School District’s board was entirely Latina.
“These are women, many of whom are first-generation, who care about their communities and want to give back,” said Helen Torres, the organization’s chief executive officer.
Torres’ group trains Latinas for civic leadership, including running for public office. In its 35-year history, the group has trained more than 2,500 people, including Maria Anguiano, chair of the UC Board of Regents; Yammilette Rodriguez, a California State University trustee; state Sen. Sasha Renée Pérez, chair of the Senate Education Committee; and state Sen. Monique Limón, president of the state Senate and former school board member. Torres also pointed to other Latinas who’ve risen to some of the state’s highest ranks in education: Daisy Gonzalez, head of the California Student Aid Commission, and Mildred García, chancellor of the Cal State system.
Latino representation is important, Torres said, because more than half of the state’s student enrollment is Latino, and Latino school board members are likely to advocate for programs benefitting immigrant and working families, such as English learner and after-school programs, she said. Marsh’s report found that in general, school board members in California tend to be white, older and wealthy.
Taking on inertia and apathy
Nabil Kherfan, a school board member for Central Unified in Fresno, is passionate about public schools and serving his community. But after just one term, he’s had enough.
It wasn’t the strife at school board meetings or agony of budget cuts that deterred him. It was the time commitment – of serving on the board as well as campaigning. 
“After putting many things in my personal life on hold for five years, I’m looking forward to advancing my career and hopefully starting a family,” Kherfan said.
Kherfan is one of California’s first elected Palestinian Americans, and at age 30, among the state’s younger school board members. He grew up in Fresno, attended schools in Central Unified and hopes to run for office again someday.
But the time commitment for someone who already works full-time can be daunting.
“We all want change, but there can be inertia against changing the status quo,” Kherfan said. “Addressing systemic inequity and apathy takes time.”

name: California
title: San Onofre’s nuclear waste is stored on the beach: Will another community agree to take it?
description: San Onofre’s nuclear waste has been stored on a beach for years. This lawmaker wants to find a community willing to take it.
text:
In summary
San Onofre’s nuclear waste has been stored on a beach for years. This lawmaker wants to find a community willing to take it.


If Rep. Mike Levin’s proposal moves forward, the spent nuclear fuel stashed on the beach at San Onofre will be stored and processed at one of several potential campuses in other states.
Levin, a Democratic congress member representing parts of San Diego and Orange County, discussed his plan from a point above the San Onofre Nuclear Generating Station last week. 
“Since I’ve been in Congress, getting this spent nuclear fuel off our coast has been one of my top priorities,” Levin said, overlooking the Pacific Ocean and the steel and concrete canisters housing nuclear fuel rods. “I have been in this fight for eight years, fighting the status quo of inaction on spent nuclear fuel.”
He’s pushing to create facilities called Nuclear Lifecycle Innovation Campuses in communities that want to recycle some of the spent fuel and store remaining waste, in exchange for economic development opportunities.
The Department of Energy said the campuses could “attract significant investment, expand domestic manufacturing, and create thousands of new high-paying jobs in their respective regions.” Utah, Tennessee, Oklahoma, Louisiana and Idaho have stepped up as potential hosts for the facilities.
Finland and Canada have embarked on similar efforts to locate nuclear waste facilities, with the consent and collaboration of local communities, according to a report by Levin’s office. Finland expects to permanently dispose of nuclear waste as soon as next year.
Levin said similar U.S. sites could begin operation by the late 2030s, and he’s pushing to make the San Onofre plant a priority for nuclear waste removal and storage.
San Onofre ceased operating in 2013, after a newly installed steam generator failed, leaving the plant inoperable. Officials began decommissioning the plant in 2020.
