Since then, 700 million tons of building material have been hauled away from the site, and the spent fuel rods were moved from cooling pools to dry storage on the beach, Levin said.
But there isn’t a permanent repository for the spent nuclear fuel, following backlash to an earlier proposal to store the waste.
“The federal government still hasn’t done what it pledged to do all the way back in 1998, and so communities like ours have been left holding the fuel,” Levin said.
The federal government previously designated the Yucca Mountain Nuclear Waste Repository in Nevada as the permanent storage site for nuclear waste. But former president Barack Obama cancelled that plan in 2010, following fierce opposition from environmentalists, local groups and tribes.
Without a permanent storage repository, spent nuclear fuel has remained on site at San Onofre, where its location on the coast, near earthquake faults and next to Camp Pendleton make the waste vulnerable to natural disaster or national security threats.
To address those risks, Levin introduced the Spent Fuel Prioritization Act with co-authors including Rep. Darrell Issa, a San Diego Republican, and Rep.Young Kim, an Orange County Republican. It would move nuclear sites with high seismic hazards, large populations and national security risk, such as San Onofre, up the list for fuel removal and storage. The bill is waiting for consideration in the House Energy and Commerce Committee, according to Levin’s 2026 report on San Onofre.
Another challenge concerns transport of spent nuclear fuel. Levin said next year a specially designed train called the Atlas Railcar System will complete testing and move the first spent fuel rods from Virginia to Idaho. The Atlas is a 12-axle railcar equipped with sensors and monitoring systems, which can transport nearly half a million pounds of spent nuclear fuel, according to the Department of Energy. It took ten years and cost $33 million dollars to build.
Levin has also introduced bills to create a nuclear waste administration, to require nuclear waste canisters to last 100 years instead of the current 40 years, and to increase public engagement and improve safety inspection at decommissioning power plants.
“I will not declare victory on this until the last canister has left San Onofre,” he said.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Jackson Lab scientists discover how pain pathways work in endometriosis
description: Using tissue samples from CT hospitals, scientists documented signaling between neurons and immune cells clustered close to the lesions.
text:
New findings by researchers at The Jackson Laboratory in Farmington show a deeper understanding of the excruciating pain women experience from endometriosis, a chronic inflammatory disease.
In patients with endometriosis, bits of the lining inside the uterus grow where they’re not supposed to — outside of it and on other organs. Jackson scientists studied tissue samples provided by Connecticut hospitals to document the signaling between neurons and immune cells that are clustered close to the endometriosis lesions.
“From that we’re able to map how they interact, and now we can target those signaling mechanisms in order to create better treatment options,” said Caroline Haney, a postdoctoral associate at Jackson, who herself suffers from endometriosis.
“We needed to kind of understand the underlying biology a little more,” she said. “The best treatment options we have right now are often hormonal medications, and that doesn’t work for a lot of people.”
Haney and her team created 3D models of sensory nerve tissue using the human stem cells to confirm their observations. They combined these models with cells taken from patient lesions. The findings, published in the journal Nature Communications, show interaction between the cells and nerves, and its relationship to the pain women experience.
The 10X Genomics – Xenium Analyzer allows the study of cells on a molecular level. Endometriosis, shown here, is researched by the EndoRISE team based at The Jackson Laboratory in Farmington. Credit: Dave Wurtzel / Connecticut Public
“What we’re really interested in is targeting the immune system,” Haney said. “Can we help the immune system calm down a little? Because it seems like the immune system is really creating this feedforward loop, where it’s also really agitated and reacting.”
A Connecticut law that went into effect in 2024 puts the state’s resources to work to better understand endometriosis. The law established EndoRISE, the only state-funded program in the U.S. that carries endometriosis samples through its biorepository. The initiative also offers education, advocacy and awareness. The tissue samples for the Jackson study were provided through EndoRISE.
About 10% or 190 million women of reproductive age worldwide are affected by endometriosis, according to the World Health Organization.
“The diagnosis is typically delayed by approximately seven years as many women and healthcare providers are not familiar with the disease,” said Dr. Hugh Taylor, chair of obstetrics, gynecology and reproductive sciences at Yale School of Medicine.
Taylor said the first symptom is often painful menstrual periods, and the pain is often dismissed as normal.
“Women are often initially told that they are simply unable to handle normal cramps,” he said. “Sometimes endometriosis is not identified until one has disabling pain. This delay leads to years of the disease progressing leading to worsening pain and potentially infertility.”
But a better understanding of pain mechanisms in endometriosis may help doctors identify it sooner, Taylor said.
“Perhaps we can distinguish normal cramps from the more severe pain induced by endometriosis,” he said. “The findings in this paper may also lead to new treatment to block endometriosis pain.”
Dr. Kate Pascucci, an OBGYN in West Hartford, pointed out that societal attitudes have long normalized menstrual discomfort in ways that may delay recognition and treatment of significant pain. Doctors, she said, will need to move away from the assumption that severe menstrual pain is simply something women must endure.
“Pain relief and quality of life deserve to be central goals of endometriosis care, alongside fertility considerations when relevant to the patient,” she said.
Research into the chronic disease is important because it brings greater attention to endometriosis-associated pain and advances our understanding of its underlying mechanisms, Pascucci said.
“A better understanding of the neural pathways and other biological processes involved in pain may help identify new therapeutic targets and ultimately lead to more effective, individualized approaches to pain management,” she said.
This story was first published Oct. 30, 2026 by Connecticut Public.

name: California
title: Need more financial aid for college? This new law will make it easier to ask for it
description: A new California law will require colleges and universities to clearly inform students how to request additional financial aid if they believe their awarded amount is not enough. Institutions must also publish how they calculate their costs of attendance, which is used to determine how much financial aid students receive.
text:
In summary
A new California law will require colleges and universities to clearly inform students how to request additional financial aid if they believe their awarded amount is not enough. Institutions must also publish how they calculate their costs of attendance, which is used to determine how much financial aid students receive.


Colleges and universities will soon have to make it easier for students to request more financial aid, as well as be more transparent about how they estimate the cost of attendance. 
A new law signed by Gov. Gavin Newsom in September requires colleges and universities to clearly display how students can request additional financial aid if they believe their awarded amount does not sufficiently cover their costs. Institutions must also publish how they calculate their costs of attendance, which is used to determine how much financial aid students receive.
Authored by Democratic Assemblymembers Celeste Rodriguez of the San Fernando Valley and Marc Berman of Menlo Park, Assembly Bill 2251 requires schools to implement the changes by the fall of 2027. 
Existing law already requires campuses to publish cost estimates, which not only include tuition and fees, but also housing, transportation, food and other likely expenses. With the new requirements, advocates say that students will now have an easier time finding what to do when their costs exceed those estimates. 
“California has a really strong record of looking at new ways to improve college affordability and AB 2251 is yet another example,” said Laura Szabo-Kubitz, senior policy advisor at The Institute of College Access and Success, an organization that advocates for college affordability. “It’s a step towards other advocacy efforts to bridge the affordability gap.”
Students can appeal their financial aid award
Junely Merwin, now a consultant for The Foster Youth Pre-College Collective, received a full-ride scholarship to attend Cal State Fullerton in 2015. But as a former foster youth and young mother, she needed additional aid to help cover childcare costs. 
“My money really went down the drain to child care and just how expensive it was,” Merwin said. “Even with the full-ride scholarship, it was not enough.”
Seeking more financial support, Merwin came across her school’s process to revise her cost of attendance. However, the website was unclear and, when she reached out to the financial aid office with questions, she was passed along to multiple staff members. 
After she was finally able to complete an appeal process, Merwin’s cost of attendance was adjusted to include her childcare expenses. This allowed her to accept more scholarship funds. Over half of colleges and universities statewide use estimates that are lower than what students actually pay to attend college, with some underestimating it by over $10,000, according to 2024 research from John Burton Advocates for Youth, the lead sponsor of the law. The California organization advocates for unhoused and foster youth.
Students cannot receive more financial aid – including loans, grants and some scholarships – than the estimated cost of attendance calculated by the campus. This can lead them to work excessive hours and take fewer classes to make up the difference, according to research from The Institute for College Access and Success. 
When students’ costs exceed those calculated by their college, they can apply for a cost of attendance adjustment. But students often don’t know that is an option.
The Financial Aid and Scholarship office at the Joyal Administration building at Fresno State in Fresno on Sept. 3, 2026. Photo by Larry Valenzuela, CalMatters
According to a March report from John Burton Advocates for Youth, almost half of colleges statewide fail to adequately inform students of the resources and options available to them when applying for aid adjustments. 
Those adjustments can be especially helpful to low-income students and former foster youth, who often receive the maximum amount of aid but still need more, said the organization’s director of education, Jessica Petrass. Because of this, students often have to turn down additional aid they would otherwise be eligible for.  
Representatives of campus programs that provide support for foster youth across the state’s three higher education systems do not find cost adjustment processes to be accessible, concluded a report by the John Burton youth advocacy organization. A majority of those surveyed said information on campus websites is insufficient and unclear. 
“That is why I see AB 2251 as both a transparency and student access issue, because it is not enough to simply have a policy in place,” Merwin said. “Information needs to be communicated clearly, consistently, in a way that students can actually understand and use.”
Colleges must clearly explain adjustment process
Colleges vary greatly in how and where they explain how to request an adjustment to the cost of attendance and financial aid limit. While some schools plainly detail costs on their websites, others lead students through a maze of weblinks and documents. 
Under the new law, campuses must publish clear details on how a student can submit an adjustment request, how long it might take and who they might need to speak to. This information will need to appear on the same page as the school’s cost of attendance details.
Student Jackie Cordero in front of the Educational Opportunity Programs office at UC Santa Cruz on Oct. 27, 2026. Photo by Jessica Parga for CalMatters
Jackie Cordero, a first-generation college student who attends UC Santa Cruz, is currently going through the process of requesting an adjustment to her cost of attendance. Cordero chose UC Santa Cruz because of the generous financial aid package she was offered. But after her father was injured and could no longer work, she was left to figure out how to pay for the  expenses her financial aid didn’t cover.
Through her own research, and by contacting the financial aid office herself, she found that requesting more financial aid was an option. But it has not been easy. Cordero said that the documents her school asked for — detailing her father’s work termination and her mother’s income — didn’t exist in physical form. She’s struggled to supplement that paperwork, and instead has had to write letters detailing her family’s finances. 
“There should probably be a little bit more help towards people who want to do a cost of attendance (adjustment),” she said. “I still am a little confused about the process and approaching (the financial aid office) can be a little difficult.”
Under federal law, students are not required to submit documentation for cost of attendance adjustments, but colleges almost always request them before granting additional awards.  
Colleges vary on cost calculation sources
Across all three public higher education systems, staff at John Burton Advocates for Youth found that 83% of campuses do not reveal the breakdown of the total cost of each expense category – such as housing and transportation – on their websites. This information allows students to have a clearer understanding of whether their expenses exceed the calculated costs and if they might be eligible for a cost of attendance adjustment.  
“At the end of the day, these budgets are an estimate … You’re doing your best guess to get the best average to represent every student’s unique circumstance,” Petrass said.
Most campuses do not cite the data sources behind their estimates. Only 17% of UCs, 26% of Cal States and 22% of community colleges explain how they come up with these estimates, according to the youth advocacy organization.Each system calculates costs differently. UC schools use a survey conducted by its Office of the President. Cal State campuses and community colleges use a mix of data, including from the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development and survey estimates from the California Student Aid Commission.
What the new law doesn’t do
While the law guarantees a new standard of transparency for financial aid, it does not provide any new financial aid funding, nor does it guarantee that any student’s cost of attendance adjustments will be approved. 
The California Student Aid Commission estimates the state may spend anywhere from $805,000 to $2.3 million more on Cal Grant awards due to adjustment applications that wouldn’t have otherwise been submitted. That assumes a 3% to 5% increase in the number of adjustments approved annually, according to the commission. 
Even if a student’s appeal for a financial aid increase is accepted, many campus financial aid websites say additional aid typically comes in the form of loans. The law will also not change the often-complicated cost adjustment process, or the way colleges estimate their cost of attendance.  
“I think there are still areas in which California could continue to change policy to better strengthen this process,” Petrass said. “I think there’s opportunities to look at reducing documentation requirements for students as well to, again, just make it a more seamless process that aligns with the minimum federal requirements.”
Mariam Farag and Max Guerra are contributors with the College Journalism Network, a collaboration between CalMatters and student journalists from across California. CalMatters higher education coverage is supported by a grant from the College Futures Foundation.

name: California
title: The ‘affordability’ crisis is also a crisis of broken trust in the American Dream
description: “Affordability” is the gap between what things cost and what you can afford to spend, yes, but it’s more than that.
text:
Guest Commentary written by

Jennifer Mercieca
Jennifer Mercieca is a historian of American political rhetoric, professor of communication and journalism at Texas A&M University, and a contributing editor at Zócalo Public Square. She is the author, most recently, of “Demagogue for President: The Rhetorical Genius of Donald Trump“. 


Affordability is the top issue in this year’s U.S. midterm election. But it’s more than that. Frustration over affordability is so severe that it threatens the viability of the American Dream — and potentially America itself.
If the American Dream was a promise made by the nation to its workers — if you work hard, you can achieve economic security — then that promise is broken. America is much less affordable than it was a few generations ago. This is true for everything from dinner at McDonald’s for a family of five — which cost the equivalent of three hours of minimum wage work in 1955, and today costs nearly an entire eight-hour work day — to buying a home — which is less than half as affordable for the average family today compared to 1960.
“Affordability” is the gap between what things cost and what you can afford to spend, yes, but it’s more than that. Affordability is a capacious political term that describes a series of shortfalls: the gap between the ultrarich and everyone else, the gap between how economists talk about the economy and people’s everyday experiences, the gap between a “poverty wage” and a “livable wage,” the gap between what politicians promise on the campaign trail and what they deliver in office, and the gap between the promise and the reality of achieving the American Dream in the 21st century.
Affordability is the political issue of our time, a crisis that isn’t going to end unless we understand and address all of those gaps. In today’s political discourse “affordability” is another (perhaps less obviously strident) way to say that for a lot of people (maybe most), capitalism feels broken. 
How did we get here? The language we use to talk about the economy offers some clues.
National economic conditions are difficult to generalize because the economy is complex, and personal economic conditions are also difficult to generalize because people do not have the exact same economic circumstances. 
That double complexity means that it’s easy to mislead with economic statistics, like the performance of stock markets, the cost of gas, or inflation or unemployment metrics. But focusing on any one of those factors — or even all of them — doesn’t tell a complete story. No one of those parts can ever stand for the whole.
Typically, that’s the kind of situation that calls for a metaphor. A metaphor is what 18th-century rhetorical scholar George Campbell called “an allegory in miniature.” Metaphors are compact little nuggets of narrative that work by comparison (comparing a known and easily recognizable thing to an unknown or difficult to describe thing). The “metaphors we live by,” explain George Lakoff and Mark Johnson, shape our very thought.
Economists represent their thinking in equations, charts and graphs that are difficult to translate into paragraphs. Translating those graphs into paragraphs is an act of metaphorical representation — in this case, using words to describe data trends. The most common metaphor used to describe today’s economy is the letter “K,” where “K” stands for the shape of a graph showing how “the rich get richer and the poor get poorer.” 
The K-shaped metaphor tells a story that resonates with a lot of Americans’ experience. “Affordability” is the word that captures that K-shaped metaphorical narrative in political discourse.  
Affordability is an interesting word because it describes a literal gap (between what things cost and what you can afford) but it also describes a rhetorical gap between the bureaucratic language of professional economists (those who speak about “national economic indicators” or “stock market gains”) and the vernacular language of people who worry about “bills” and “rent” and “interest rates” — people who know the ins and outs of “side hustles,” “GoFundMe” and “payday loans.”
There are terms that attempt to bridge the rhetorical gap: “cost of living” or “making ends meet,” perhaps, but those phrases don’t get at the real thing, which is that K-shaped gap. Affordability in America is a K-shaped story.
Affordability as a political project is about giving all Americans the power to choose how (and whether) they spend their money. The rent is too damn high, but so is everything else — and Americans have no choice but to pay now or use credit — which is to say, Americans have no choice at all. 
As a political project affordability asks: “Why don’t we have better choices in the land of the free?”
America’s affordability crisis is a violation of the bargain of the American Dream. Political leaders have promised repeatedly to make that dream possible again, but things have steadily gotten worse. America’s affordability problem has fueled outrage, instability and extremism. 
In the nation’s 250th year, the affordability crisis is existential. It isn’t just about Americans’ personal finances. It’s a national crisis of broken trust.
This commentary was adapted from an essay produced for Zócalo Public Square.

name: Pennsylvania Capital Star
title: Energy costs dominate midterms; Climate battles play out down ballot
description: In the final stretch of the 2026 midterm campaigns, the most potent climate issue in American politics arrived by delivery truck across the country.
text:
Gas and diesel prices in Indiana on Sept. 17, 2026. (Photo by Niki Kelly/Indiana Capital Chronicle)This story was originally published by Capital & Main.
In the final stretch of the 2026 midterm campaigns, the most potent climate issue in American politics arrived by delivery truck across the country.
The average price of heating oil hit $6.23 a gallon for the week of Oct. 26, up from $3.60 a year earlier, according to the Energy Information Administration. At that price, filling a 250-gallon tank cost about $1,557 — roughly $657 more than the year before. As cold weather settled over the Northeast, Democrats turned that bill into an attack on Republican candidates.
In New Hampshire, where about 43% of residents heat with oil, Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate Chris Pappas said energy costs and heating oil prices were “the beginning and end of every conversation I’m having on the campaign trail.”
That is the pattern across the closest races in this cycle. Energy is everywhere on the ballot — as heating oil, diesel, power bills and water — but almost always as a question of price. The argument over what actually powers the country — fossil fuels or renewables — surfaces mostly down-ballot, in low-profile contests for the commissions that regulate utilities and drilling.
Trailer-tractor drivers fuel up in Harrisburg on April 6, 2026. At $6/gallon, diesel prices in the commonwealth are approaching a record high. (Photo by Whitney Downard/Pennsylvania Capital-Star)
“If you talk to voters, they are upset about their energy bills and they’re upset about data centers,” Caroline Spears, executive director of Climate Cabinet, which backs climate-focused candidates in state and local races, told Capital & Main. “People want to hear from politicians about their plans on their energy bills and their plans on their data centers.”
The consequences reach far beyond any one state. Control of the Senate will determine whether Congress revisits the clean energy tax credits Republicans rolled back in last year’s budget law. And the governors and regulators elected Tuesday will approve the gas plants, transmission lines and data center deals that shape the grid for decades to come.
 The U.S. Senate
More than $191 million was spent on political ads referencing utility and energy bills in the first nine months of 2026, plus another $96.3 million from Oct. 1 to Oct. 16, according to AdImpact data analyzed by Climate Power, a Democratic-aligned advocacy group.
In Maine, heating oil defined the final weeks of the race between Republican Sen. Susan Collins and her Democrat challenger Troy Jackson. Jackson said Mainers were paying 80% more for heating oil than a year earlier. Collins countered  with an announcement: a release of 315,000 barrels from the Northeast Home Heating Oil Reserve, which she and her counterpart, Sen. Angus King, had requested of President Donald Trump. Climate itself registers here, too: In the Environmental Voter Project’s polling of eight U.S. Senate battlegrounds, Maine had the highest share of voters naming it a top-three priority at 22%.
In the farm belt, the price that matters is the cost of diesel. In Iowa, Democrat Josh Turek released a closing ad on fuel prices against Republican Rep. Ashley Hinson. Both candidates said data centers shouldn’t receive tax breaks — in a state that already gets more than 60% of its power from wind and solar. Kansas hasn’t elected a Democrat to the Senate since 1932, yet Adam Hamilton built his challenge to Republican Sen. Roger Marshall around energy and utility costs, while Marshall said Kansans were “on fire” over data centers. High fuel and fertilizer prices have strained the farm economy in a state that generates roughly 50% of its electricity from wind.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Data centers have scrambled the usual partisan lines. In Ohio, Democrat Sherrod Brown branded Republican Sen. Jon Husted “the face of data centers,” and WinSenate, the country’s main Democratic Senate super PAC, ran an ad implying corrupt dealings between Husted and an energy company, though Husted was never charged. Kelcy Warren, executive chairman of the pipeline giant Energy Transfer, gave $3,500 to Husted’s campaign in late September.
In Michigan, Democrat Abdul El-Sayed and Republican Mike Rogers agree on little except data centers: Both back moratoriums in some form. El-Sayed’s framework would bar utilities from using data center demand to weaken Michigan’s clean-energy laws, while Rogers holds up to $250,000 in a Blackstone real estate trust that backs data centers. The climate stakes are concrete: Surging data center demand could trigger a provision in the state’s climate law that lets fossil fuel plants stay online during a capacity shortage.
In Texas, where Democratic state Rep. James Talarico faces Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton for a critical U.S. Senate seat, the backdrop is Gov. Greg Abbott’s audit of every data center seeking to connect to the ERCOT grid — a review that won’t be finished until December, long after the midterm votes are cast.
In Alaska, the fossil fuel question barely registers. Both Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan and Democrat Mary Peltola support oil and gas expansion, so the fight is over who will deliver it and who is to blame for Iran war-driven fuel costs. Sullivan has made the Alaska LNG pipeline, backed by a $54 billion South Korean investment, a centerpiece of his campaign.
 The statehouses
Thirty-six states will elect governors this November, and the nonpartisan Cook Political Report considers 12 of those contests competitive — including Alaska, Iowa, Georgia, Nevada, Ohio, Florida and Texas, where Republicans now hold the office. In 39 states, utility regulators are appointed by governors or legislatures rather than elected — which means many of those governors become energy policymakers whether they campaign on it or not.
Climate surfaces more openly in Alaska’s overlooked governor’s race, where Democrat Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins has pressed the state to address climate change and said it relies too heavily on natural gas — rare talk from an Alaska politician. Republicans Dave Bronson, Treg Taylor and Bernadette Wilson are also on the ballot. Nathaniel Stinnett, founder of the Environmental Voter Project, called Kreiss-Tomkins “probably the favorite” but said the race is “extraordinarily close.” In the group’s polling, 21% of likely Alaska voters identified climate as a top-three priority, second only to Maine. “I don’t wanna pretend like this is a climate election,” Stinnett said. “But certainly thousands and perhaps tens of thousands of Alaskans are going to vote with climate change top of mind.”
A hallway in the Pennsylvania Capitol building in Harrisburg on October 14, 2025. (Photo by Jessica Kourkounis for the Pennsylvania Capital-Star)
In Nevada, the main climate focus is water. Republican Gov. Joe Lombardo sued the Trump administration over cuts to the state’s allotment of water from the Colorado River, and Arizona has since joined the suit. Nevada Conservation Voters gave Lombardo a C+ grade, crediting his support of clean energy while faulting his backing of fossil fuel projects. Because Democrats already control both chambers of the legislature, a win by his challenger, Attorney General Aaron Ford, would give the party a trifecta. Stinnett noted that Ford has talked up the clean energy transition in a state that “is kind of like the Saudi Arabia of solar energy, or it can be.”
Kansas offers Republicans their best chance to flip a Democratic-held governorship. Republican Ty Masterson is more moderate on energy than many in his party, and both he and Democrat Cindy Holscher voted for a 2025 data center tax exemption. Holscher has since said she would freeze data center development until stronger guardrails are in place.
Georgia’s open governor’s race between Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms and Republican Rick Jackson will shape the state’s energy direction too — but the most direct fight over Georgia’s power sits further down the ballot.
Legislatures may matter as much. Spears, the Climate Cabinet director, is focused on five states where Democrats could win full control — Michigan, Minnesota, Wisconsin, Arizona and Pennsylvania. “If they were a country, they’d be the world’s ninth largest climate polluter,” she said. “But 22 flipped seats stand between five trifectas and none.”
Minnesota and Michigan both passed 100% clean energy laws the last time Democrats held full control. In Pennsylvania, where Republicans control the state Senate but not the House, Spears was blunt: “The Pennsylvania State Senate is where clean energy bills go to die.”
 The regulators
This is where fossil fuels and renewables actually collide. Spears called these “weird statewides” and said that as utility bills have become a defining issue, the culture war is “getting involved in utility elections as well.”
Control of the Georgia Public Service Commission, which oversees Georgia Power, is on the ballot. Democrat Peter Hubbard, who won a special election last year, faces a rematch with Republican Fitz Johnson, while Republican Josh Tolbert and Democrat Shelia Edwards vie for an open seat. Republicans hold a 3-2 majority; if both Democrats win, Georgia would join Illinois’ commission as the nation’s only ones that are Democratic aligned. Hubbard argued the state is “oversubscribed on fossil fuels.” Johnson said data centers will pay their fair share because of protections he put in place.
In Texas, the race for the Railroad Commission — which, despite its name, regulates an oil and gas industry that supplied nearly half the country’s oil last year — tightened after Republican Bo French drew widespread condemnation for a racist post on X. The Texas Oil and Gas Association, which represents ExxonMobil and Chevron, left him off its latest endorsement list. French has been bankrolled largely through PACs funded by billionaires Tim Dunn and Farris Wilks. His opponent, Democratic state Rep. Jon Rosenthal, is a former oil-field mechanical engineer. A Democrat hasn’t held a seat on the commission since 1994.
A Cabot Oil and Gas natural gas drill is viewed at a hydraulic fracturing site on January 17, 2012 in Springville, Susquehanna County. (Photo by Spencer Platt/Getty Images)
Rosenthal traced the split to a rule backed by Jim Wright, the incumbent French ousted in the Republican primary, requiring liners for shallow oilfield waste pits so they don’t “leak noxious poison into the surrounding land and water, which I think most people think is a reasonable precaution.”
Rosenthal, who said he has taken almost no money from oil and gas operators, has proposed banning industry donations to commissioners. “If we actually had ethical campaign finance laws, you wouldn’t want these people’s campaigns to be wholly or majorly funded by the people they’re supposed to regulate,” he said. “But that’s just how it is in Texas.”
French did not respond to Capital & Main’s request for comment.
In Arizona, Republicans Kevin Thompson and Ralph Heap face Democrats Clara Pratte and Jonathon Hill for two seats on the Corporation Commission as electricity provider the Arizona Public Service seeks a roughly 14% rate increase — and the decision is not expected until after the election. Heap’s platform, endorsed by right wing group Turning Point, reportedly centers on prioritizing coal. Even if both Democrats win, Republicans keep a majority, since only two of five seats are up.
Colorado voters face the most literal version of the question. Amendment 82 would add a right to buy and sell natural gas to the state constitution and could limit state and local governments’ ability to enforce natural gas regulations. It needs 55% of the vote to pass. It is one of eight measures funded by the conservative group Advance Colorado — and the state’s own oil and gas industry opposed it, wary of upsetting its 2024 truce with Gov. Jared Polis.
The turnout
Who shows up may matter as much as what’s on the ballot. A report from the Environmental Voter Project, which works to turn out voters who prioritize climate, found that as of Oct. 26, more than 3.7 million climate voters in 21 states had already cast early ballots, including more than 400,000 voting in a midterm for the first time.
In every Senate battleground the group tracked, those voters were turning out faster than the electorate as a whole — often at twice the rate. In Georgia, 46.3% of climate voters had cast ballots by the time of the report, compared with 21.2% of all registered voters, Stinnett said. In Iowa, the figures were 22.8% and 9.5%.
Voters mark their ballots during the first day of early voting in Bismarck, North Dakota, on Oct. 22, 2026. Experts and voting rights advocates are bracing for the potential of federal influence over the results of next week’s midterm elections. (Photo by Jack Dura/North Dakota Monitor)
In Michigan and Nebraska, Stinnett said, the ratio was 2.5 to 1. “We often see that climate concerned voters are more likely to vote early than on Election Day,” he said. “But we’re not used to seeing margins like this.” His explanation: “Just because politicians aren’t talking about something doesn’t mean that voters aren’t concerned about it. Climate concerned Americans know how important these midterm elections are, and they ain’t gonna miss it come hell or high water.”
Whether they are voting over a heating oil bill or a warming planet, the result lands in the same place. The senators elected this fall will decide what Washington does about clean energy, and the regulators will decide what gets built. The harder conversation starts after Nov. 3, Spears said, when the winners realize, “Oh, now I have to actually figure out what to do.” The bills will keep arriving long after the ballots are counted.

name: Nevada Current
title: Medicare drug plans are hiking premiums while Trump claims victory on medicine prices
description: Millions of Medicare enrollees who buy stand-alone prescription drug plans will see their average monthly premiums rise by 50% in 2027, a new analysis finds. But enrollees can avoid the average increase — from $34 a month to $51 — by switching to lower-cost plans during the program’s open enrollment period, which runs through Dec. […]
text:
(Photo: Eric Harkleroad/KFF Health News)Millions of Medicare enrollees who buy stand-alone prescription drug plans will see their average monthly premiums rise by 50% in 2027, a new analysis finds.
But enrollees can avoid the average increase — from $34 a month to $51 — by switching to lower-cost plans during the program’s open enrollment period, which runs through Dec. 7.
Robert Travis Scott of Abingdon, Virginia, did just that in late October after he received a notice that his AARP-UnitedHealthcare Medicare drug plan premium would be increasing from $39.60 a month in 2026 to $121.90 in 2027. With just a little work checking prices online, Scott found a Humana plan for $19.30 with similar benefits.
“Yes, I am quite happy about that,” he said of the new plan he just found. He said he was stunned his existing plan was going up so much and worried that other seniors won’t shop for plans to save money. He estimates he saved himself about $1,000 for next year.
“With some plans increasing premiums substantially, the stakes are higher this year for people with Medicare stand-alone drug coverage if they sit on the sidelines during open enrollment,” said Juliette Cubanski, a vice president and the director of the Program on Medicare Policy at KFF, which conducted the analysis. KFF is a health information nonprofit that includes KFF Health News.
Rising drug costs are among the litany of affordability issues angering voters ahead of November’s midterm election. President Donald Trump, whose approval rating in some polls has dipped to the lowest level of his two terms in office, claims his administration has succeeded in negotiating lower prices from drug manufacturers.
“What we’re doing great with is pharmaceuticals, hundreds of billions,” Trump said at a campaign rally in Ohio on Oct. 28, ahead of the Nov. 3 midterms. “You should win just on this, everybody running. We have the lowest drug prices anywhere in the world. We went from the highest drug prices, we now have the lowest drug prices, favored nations, anywhere in the world.”
How much people actually pay for drugs varies widely, depending on what medicines individual patients need and their insurance coverage.
Medicare beneficiaries who get their drug coverage as part of private Medicare Advantage plans, which replace traditional Medicare coverage, will see much lower premium increases. The KFF analysis found these enrollees will pay an average of $9 for drugs as part of their overall monthly premium in 2027, or an increase of less than $2 per month.
More than half of Medicare beneficiaries are enrolled in Medicare Advantage health plans, which usually include a drug benefit, instead of the traditional program.
Nearly 25 million people are enrolled in Medicare stand-alone prescription drug plans, according to KFF. About 31 million get drug coverage through Medicare Advantage plans.
Premiums are just part of the higher costs Medicare enrollees are facing.
Most enrollees who buy a stand-alone drug plan or get drug benefits through Medicare Advantage plans will also have an annual deductible for drug coverage in 2027.
The average deductible in 2027 will be $643 for stand-alone plans, according to the KFF analysis, up from $540 in 2026. Drug deductibles will average $489 for those with Medicare Advantage plans, up from $360 in 2026.
In addition, most Medicare enrollees with drug coverage next year will have to pay coinsurance rather than copayments, the KFF analysis found. That can mean less predictable out-of-pocket costs because coinsurance requires paying a percentage of the cost of a drug, not a fixed amount.
One possible cause of the projected premium hikes is the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services’ decision in July to end early a three-year pilot program designed to keep down stand-alone premiums. The program paid subsidies to stand-alone plans in 2025 and 2026.
KFF said CMS’ decision to end that subsidy program after only two years could cause stand-alone premiums to rise in 2027.
CMS Administrator Mehmet Oz has called the subsidy program an insurance industry bailout.
KFF noted its analysis differs from CMS’ projection for a $1 increase in the national average premium, from $35 to $36, based on September 2026 enrollment. It said that CMS did not explain its calculation methods and that it’s possible CMS assumed people would switch to lower-cost plans.
CMS did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the KFF findings.
About 10.4 million Medicare enrollees, or 76% of enrollees in stand-alone drug plans who don’t get low-income subsidies, will pay a higher monthly premium in 2027 if they stick with the same plan, KFF found.
This includes 4.1 million enrollees who are currently in a zero-premium plan. They’ll automatically pay more in 2027, because there will be no zero-premium plans available, the KFF analysis found.
This article first appeared on KFF Health News and is republished here under a Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial-NoDerivatives 4.0 International License.

name: Nevada Current
title: Commentary: How Question 6 gives patients stronger protections
description: When a patient sits across from me in my Las Vegas practice, my job begins with listening. What symptoms are they experiencing? What medications are they taking? What worries them? What stands between them and the care they need? Sometimes, it’s a co-pay they cannot afford. Sometimes, it’s an appointment postponed because other bills cannot […]
text:
(Photo: Roberto Machado Noa/Getty Images)When a patient sits across from me in my Las Vegas practice, my job begins with listening. What symptoms are they experiencing? What medications are they taking? What worries them? What stands between them and the care they need?
Sometimes, it’s a co-pay they cannot afford. Sometimes, it’s an appointment postponed because other bills cannot wait. As a primary care physician and internist, I see how barriers to care shape my patients’ health. 
Government interference should never become another obstacle. Question 6 would establish a fundamental right to abortion in Nevada’s Constitution, protecting care provided by qualified health care practitioners until fetal viability, and afterward when needed to protect the pregnant patient’s life or health. It would give patients stronger protection to make deeply personal decisions about their pregnancies with their health care providers.
You do not have to provide abortion care to understand why this matters. In primary care, we treat the whole person. We help patients manage diabetes, high blood pressure, and other conditions that can complicate a pregnancy. We discuss medications, health risks, and plans. Those conversations require honesty and trust.
Patients should feel safe asking questions. Physicians should be able to explain medical options based on a patient’s circumstances and the best available evidence. A politician who has never met that patient cannot make medical decisions for them.
When the Supreme Court overturned Roe v. Wade four years ago, I worried about what losing federal abortion protections would mean for my patients and fellow physicians. I was grateful to practice in Nevada, where abortion care remained legal. But gratitude alone does not protect a right.
Nevada voters have understood this for decades. In 1990, we approved statutory abortion protections that cannot be amended or repealed by the Legislature alone. Those safeguards are meaningful, and voters deserve credit for establishing them. Question 6 would build on those protections by placing an explicit right to abortion in our state Constitution.
As a physician, I want patients to have confidence that their care will be guided by their medical needs and their own decisions. They deserve protections that endure beyond an election cycle.
I also know that a right can be harder to exercise when someone is already struggling financially. My patients’ experiences with prescription costs remind me how little room many families have for another obstacle. Reproductive health care belongs in that same conversation about whether people can actually obtain the care they need.
Supporting Question 6 does not require every Nevadan to hold the same personal beliefs about abortion. It requires respecting that another person’s health, family responsibilities, and circumstances may differ from our own—and that they must be able to make decisions about their own pregnancy.
In medicine, we cannot substitute assumptions for listening. We cannot treat every patient’s circumstances as interchangeable. Our laws should leave room for the individual judgment that good care requires.
In 2024, more than 64% of Nevada voters supported Question 6. But that vote was the first step. Nevada requires voter approval in two successive general elections for this kind of constitutional amendment. My responsibility as a physician is to put my patients’ health first. That means speaking up when I have an opportunity to protect their access to care.
This election, we can strengthen the freedom of Nevadans to make personal medical decisions with qualified health care professionals. We can give future patients a stronger guarantee that their health, circumstances, and choices will matter.

name: Utah News Dispatch
title: Immigration could be a solution to Utah’s ‘wicked’ demographic woes, researchers say
description: Utah is still one of the youngest states and has some of the highest fertility rates in the country. But that trend is going in the opposite direction with demographers projecting smaller household sizes and an older median age. Congress is also projecting more deaths than births come 2030. That “demographic imbalance” is a problem […]
text:
Homes in North Salt Lake are pictured on Monday, July 15, 2024. (Photo by Spenser Heaps for Utah News Dispatch)Utah is still one of the youngest states and has some of the highest fertility rates in the country. But that trend is going in the opposite direction with demographers projecting smaller household sizes and an older median age. Congress is also projecting more deaths than births come 2030.
That “demographic imbalance” is a problem that Robin Fretwell Wilson, a family and health law professor at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, said “is wicked in a way that even the culture wars are not.” And migration could help solve it, she said during a Sutherland Institute roundtable on Wednesday.
Fewer births and an older population would have substantial effects for the economy and the federal budget. According to the Congressional Budget Office, the population served by Social Security is projected to increase from 349 million people this year to 364 million in 2056. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Over the next 30 years, the rate of population growth will also slow down, dipping from an average of 0.3% a year to 0.1% from 2037 to 2056. That last year is when the total population is projected to stop growing and start to shrink.
“Net immigration (the number of people who migrate to the United States minus the number who leave) is projected to become an increasingly important source of population growth in the coming years, as declining fertility rates cause the annual number of deaths to exceed the annual number of births starting in 2030,” the Congressional Budget Office’s website says.
Olivia Whiteley, director of strategy for Reliable Refuge, said during the event that the United States has long relied on international migration to sustain its population, secure its workforce competitiveness and strengthen its care economy. However, recent immigration policy changes have shrunk the number of international admissions to the country.
Net international migration peaked at 2.7 million in 2024, according to the U.S. Census Bureau, then declined by 48% to 1.3 million in 2025, and is expected to decline even further in 2026 to about 321,000. 
Nearly 21% of Utah’s population growth was due to international migration from 2024 to 2025, Whiteley said, and both domestic and international migration is becoming a driving force behind Utah’s population growth.
With demographic dip in sight, Utah universities prepare for budget impacts 

“Not only do immigrants fund services for American retirees, they fill critical labor gaps with younger workers, often gaps caused by rates of older retiring workers. Seventy-seven percent of America’s foreign-born population is within the ages of 16 to 64, while only 60% of the U.S. born population is of working age,” Whiteley said, citing data from the American Immigration Council’s analysis of a 2023 survey.
“Labor-intensive industries with high rates of retirees — agriculture, construction, STEM, transportation — rely increasingly on immigrant labor,” she said. “Care work, an industry that will only grow in demand as America’s population ages, also depends heavily on immigrant labor.”
During 2023, immigrants were estimated to have paid about $652 billion in taxes, including $31.2 billion paid by refugees, in combined federal, state and local taxes.
For decades, Utah had built the capacity to resettle more than 1,000 refugees in the state each year, but this year only welcomed 152, Whiteley said.
“While the U.S. welcomes refugees in an effort to sustain American values, freedom, liberty, democracy, the refugee program is as much a demographic and an economic program as it is a humanitarian one; America’s return on investment in refugee resettlement is proven,” she said, citing a 2024 study by the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services that found that refugees and asylees contributed $123.8 in revenue over what they cost in expenditures by the government in a 15-year period.
“The solution is bipartisan congressional intervention, codification of a refugee floor shaped by state input, which would guarantee Utah receive a baseline number of refugee admissions each year,” she added. “Utah has already led the country in codifying the state’s administration of the refugee program. Now Utah leaders can call for an operational refugee minimum.”

name: Mississippi Today
title: Mississippians will soon be able to participate in a school-choice tax credit program. Here’s what to know
description: Proponents of school choice policies say a new federal tax credit program is a win for the state. Opponents say it undermines Mississippi voters' rejection of school choice.
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
Starting next year, Mississippi families can get a break on their taxes for donating to scholarships that will largely benefit private schools, experts say. 
The federal program, created by President Donald Trump’s 2025 “One Big Beautiful Bill Act,” will give people a break on their taxes for contributing to scholarships that can pay for education expenses at private schools, charter schools or public schools. Experts expect most of the money will flow toward private schools and families who could already afford, or were on the cusp of being able to afford, a private school education. 
Proponents of school-choice policies — which are aimed at giving families more educational options, often funding those choices with public money — say it’s a win for the state. 
But school-choice opponents argue the policies siphon money away from the public education system, which must serve every child, and force Mississippi into a program its residents have already said they don’t want. 
Republican state lawmakers, led by House Speaker Jason White, made a full-court push to expand school-choice policies in Mississippi earlier this year. However, House Bill 2, his lengthy school-choice bill, passed by a thin margin in the House and was killed by the Senate. 
Before that, in January, Gov. Tate Reeves announced that Mississippi would be participating in the federal tax credit scholarship program starting in 2027. States must opt in to that program. 
House Speaker Jason White, R-West, addresses state representatives as the House prepares to debate House Bill 2 on Thursday, Jan. 15, 2026, at the Capitol in Jackson. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
Douglas Carswell described it as an “awesome” program that allows the state to correct the Senate’s failure to expand school-choice options. He heads up the Mississippi Center for Public Policy, a conservative think tank that backs the expansion of school-choice policies.
Nancy Loome, a public school advocate and founder of The Parents’ Campaign, disagrees with Reeves’ decision. 
“Voters made it clear when House Bill 2 was debated in the 2026 legislative session that they don’t want this,” she said.
How does the federal tax credit program work?
The federal program allows taxpayers to contribute up to $1,700 each, or $3,400 for a married couple filing jointly, to an organization that awards school scholarships.
The governor designates scholarship-granting organizations, or SGOs, to award money to a school to cover costs of a child’s education. Taxpayers can’t direct their money to a particular student or school, but SGOs can focus on a particular group of students, like students who attend religious private schools. 
Reeves has not yet finalized his list of SGOs for Mississippi, according to the Mississippi Center for Public Policy, which is tracking and publishing the state’s eligible SGOs. The governor’s office did not respond to multiple requests for comment. 
Donors will get a dollar-for-dollar tax credit, a break on their taxes equal to the amount they contribute, which is about three times as much as people receive from donating to a children’s hospital or other causes. 
Families who earn up to 300% of the area’s median income qualify to participate in the scholarship program. That’s six figures in Mississippi, or about $150,000. 
The House of Representatives debate House Bill 2 on Thursday, Jan. 15, 2026, at the State Capitol in Jackson. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
Paige Shoemaker DeMio, a senior policy analyst at Center for American Progress, a progressive policy and research institute, said the people who will benefit those most from the tax credit program are wealthy and owe $1,700 or more in taxes. Research about existing state tax credit scholarship programs back that up. 
“Statistically, people who are higher income owe that much in taxes,” she said.
There’s no set amount for the scholarships. The scholarship-granting organization sets the amount. 
And across the country, school-choice scholarships and vouchers provide anywhere between $4,000 to $9,000. Nationally, private school tuition averages about $13,000. That means while federal scholarships may make it easier for families on the cusp of being able to afford private schools, that education still may be unaffordable to the neediest families.
Will federal tax credit scholarships help students from low-income families?
There’s no requirement to prioritize the scholarships for low-income students. A majority of private school vouchers across the country go to students who could already afford and were attending private schools, according to research.
Carswell recognized the reality that the scholarships may miss low-income students. 
“We need to ensure that we have SGOs that provide access to private education for low-income families, too,” he said. “That’s why we need a broad range of SGOs that offer smaller schools, and not just established ones, access to the new source of funding.”
However, the governor has little power to tailor the program to the state’s students, Shoemaker DeMio said.
The federal regulations require Reeves to approve any SGOs that meet the minimum requirements. He can’t impose additional reporting or standards.
The lack of transparency and reporting requirements is a “huge lost opportunity,” said Mike Petrilli of the Fordham Institute, a national conservative-leaning education policy think tank.
“It’s very much a light touch,” he said. “We may never know if this is making a difference for kids.”
How will tax credit scholarships for private schools affect public ones?
There’s been some movement nationally to use the program to divert money to public schools, including public charter schools, Shoemaker DeMio said, but it’s tricky to understand how that would play out. Public schools do not charge students to attend. 
And the federal guidance regulating that part of the program hasn’t been made public yet, she said. It’s also unclear how much it will cost states to administer the program, which could include monitoring fraud, reviewing audits and other duties. 
The U.S. Department of Treasury estimates the tax-credit scholarship program, which begins all over the country in 2027, will cost taxpayers $26 billion in its first three years. That would make it the federal government’s largest education expense — more than Title I, which ensures that economically disadvantaged children receive a high-quality education, and the Individuals with Disabilities Education Act, which guarantees children with disabilities receive an equitable education.
Members of the House of Representatives vote on House Bill 2, a school-choice proposal, on Thursday, Jan. 15, 2026, at the Mississippi Capitol in Jackson. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
“We’d be spending as a country more on private schools than any other (public education) program,” Shoemaker DeMio said. That could mean spending less on public education in the future, which could be especially detrimental to a state like Mississippi that heavily relies on federal funding. 
But most concerning to DeMio is that Mississippi voters have already rejected school-choice programs through legislative action. 
“Any time school choice has been on a ballot, it has failed,” she said. “This is clearly not a popular program, but people have now found a way to get around the voters and ignore what Americans want. It’s incredibly frustrating.”

name: Washington State Standard
title: These purple WA districts are trending blue. What changed?
description: This is the story of how Democrats came to win over (most of) Washington’s suburbs. Over the past decade, Democrats have amassed power in Olympia through areas further and further from their urban bases.  These are places like east King County suburbs where Republican Dino Rossi’s tenure as a state senator nearly carried him to […]
text:
The Tacoma Narrows Bridge, as seen from the east side, leads into the 26th Legislative District, where Democrats have gained momentum in recent years. (Photo by Aspen Ford/Washington State Standard)This is the story of how Democrats came to win over (most of) Washington’s suburbs.
Over the past decade, Democrats have amassed power in Olympia through areas further and further from their urban bases. 
These are places like east King County suburbs where Republican Dino Rossi’s tenure as a state senator nearly carried him to the governor’s office; northern Whatcom County, not long ago a redder shade of purple; part of the Kitsap Peninsula that has been a rare split district but may soon be represented by three Democrats; and Island County, where Democrats are gaining strength.
The shifts allow Democrats to continue expanding and strengthening a foundation for a supermajority in the Legislature, which could lead to transformational changes to state law. 
However, these new Democratic lawmakers also tend to be among the most moderate in their party, willing to buck the progressive wing of their caucuses on some of their biggest policy priorities, like this year’s income tax on high earners.
Two main factors have driven the trend. One is Donald Trump. As moderate Republicans and independent voters have soured on the president’s brash rhetoric, Democrats have provided refuge. Other Republican candidates have followed the president’s lead to some extent.
“The nonstop degrading of our neighbor, I think, is really irritating people,” said Ray Shjerven, chair of the 26th Legislative District Democrats. 
Alex Hays, a Republican campaign consultant, put it differently: “Democrats have convinced voters not to pay attention to their job performance and to instead focus on Donald Trump’s performance.”
The second reason is the suburban districts have been the recipients of new Democrat-leaning voters, driven further from urban cores by the high cost of living and the promise of hybrid or remote work. Think of Seattleites moving across the water to Port Orchard, or Tacoma residents going across the Narrows into more suburban communities for the 26th District. Urbanites have similarly been seeking refuge on Whidbey Island in the 10th District. Bellingham residents are heading north and east into the 42nd. 
“COVID really drove the crazies out of the city, and they’re bringing crazy with them where they go,”  said Tim Hazelo, a Republican candidate for state House in the 10th District.
This has helped Democrats overcome the fact that fewer voters than ever are persuadable amid intense polarization.
Republicans have also struggled to recruit strong candidates, sometimes turning to hopefuls who align more with the national party but may not be as electable in suburbia, according to Democrats and some Republicans.
“The type of person that Trump motivates to be more involved is also just not the person that is as close a fit to swing voters as a lot of people would like,” said Hays, the Republican consultant.
Dean Nielsen, a veteran Democratic consultant, said Trump “essentially traded the suburbs for a greater share of rural America.” The problem for Republicans is that rural Washington is a small piece of the state, and Latino voters are keeping some of those areas at least somewhat competitive, he added.
If Nielsen were a Republican strategist, he’d try to find business-oriented candidates who were vocally supportive of abortion and LGTBQ+ rights.
State Rep. Jim Walsh, who chairs the state Republican Party, disagrees with the premise that his allies are sputtering in these areas. He believes these are still swing districts, and politicos will be able to properly assess voting patterns in 2028. The Senate race in the 42nd and a House race in the 26th are the two most expensive campaigns for state Legislature this year.
“Trump Derangement Syndrome is intense but it has a short halflife,” Walsh wrote in a text message. “Normal people are tired of the lies and bad-faith rhetoric coming out of Olympia.”
Eastside swing
All of these examples were preceded by the 5th Legislative District in east King County. Fifteen years ago, Republicans ruled this combination of rural exurbs and affluent suburbs. Now, it’s not all that competitive as Democrats have swept all three seats, along with flipping the congressional seat that represents the area in 2018. 
Republican Dino Rossi served alongside two Republican state representatives, and even served in the Senate when Republicans had a majority. He helped write the state budget. Minority Republicans are now largely shut out of those negotiations. Rossi also came oh-so-close to the governor’s mansion.
But after rounds of redistricting, a presidential term and a half for Donald Trump and housing growth in these areas, the 5th is reliably blue. Democrats have been sailing to reelection. Rep. Zach Hall, who was appointed to the role, faces a strong challenger in longtime police leader Michelle Bennett, but she has little chance to beat him this year due to the district’s tilt.
The 5th might qualify as the first shoe to drop for Republican power in these areas, as Democratic reign has now spread far and wide.
Island breeze
The year 2022 portended a good future for Democrats in the 10th District. They’d already wrested one state House seat out of Republican hands four years earlier and took another in 2022. 
And they did so despite a damaged Democratic candidate. In the final days of the campaign, Clyde Shavers faced blockbuster allegations from his father that he’d inflated his military record. Shavers still won, unseating the Republican incumbent, but by only a couple hundred votes.
Winning in such headwinds indicated a turn toward Democrats in a district that covers Island County and parts of Skagit and Snohomish, local politicos say.  Republicans had held both House seats since the early 2000s.
Sen. Ron Muzzall, R-Oak Harbor, on the Senate floor on Wednesday, April 16, 2025. (Photo by Jacquelyn Jimenez Romero/Washington State Standard)
In two years, all eyes will be on the state Senate race, where Republican Sen. Ron Muzzall, faces a fight for another four-year term, if he runs again, given the Democratic momentum there. 
Muzzall’s 2024 run was the most expensive legislative race in the state that year, with over $1.5 million contributed to the campaigns and $2 million more spent on independent efforts to sway voters. Muzzall won by 2 percentage points, while his Democratic colleagues in the state House were reelected more comfortably. 
“We’ll do everything we can to make sure that we flip it,” said state Democratic Party Chair Shasti Conrad.
Northern expedition
To the north, Sharon Shewmake broke the ice, first by defeating a Republican incumbent to win a seat in the state House in 2018 and then four years later narrowly winning a race for state Senate after Doug Ericksen, the incumbent Republican, died. 
That solidified the Democrats’ flipping of all three legislative positions in the 42nd District, which covers the north side of Bellingham all the way to the Canadian border and the more rural east side of Whatcom County. The margins of victory for Democrats have only grown in recent years.
Republicans held the Senate seat in the 42nd for nearly 20 years before Shewmake’s victory in 2022.
The shift coincided with a buildout of housing on open land on the north side of Bellingham, said Jamie Douglass, chair of the district Democratic Party.

Shewmake isn’t running for reelection this year, but her chosen replacement, Michael Shepard, is poised to take her place after a strong primary for Democrats. Flipping the seat is among Republicans’ top priorities statewide.
The other side of the water
One year ago, 26th District Democratic state Sen. Deb Krishnadasan faced a tough race to retain her state Senate seat against longtime Republican state Rep. Michelle Valdez in an off-year election. 
Krishnadasan won by about 5 percentage points. This year, she won her primary over a lesser-known Republican by 12. 
Renee Hernandez Greenfield is now seeking to replace Valdez, who isn’t running for reelection, and deliver a Democratic triumvirate there, erasing one of the few remaining districts with split representation. Like the 42nd just a decade ago, all three seats in the 26th were held by Republicans.
State Sen. Deb Krishnadasan, D-Gig Harbor, outside the House chamber at the Washington state Capitol on Jan. 13, 2026, following Gov. Bob Ferguson’s State of the State address. (Photo by Bill Lucia/Washington State Standard)
Hernandez Greenfield faces Katy Cornell, a Republican pastor. Cornell may serve as a recent example of GOP troubles recruiting candidates. She recently found herself in hot water over resurfaced videos of sermons in which she equates abortion to murder and implies religions other than Christianity are akin to witchcraft.
The 26th covers parts of Kitsap and Pierce counties, including Port Orchard, Purdy, Gig Harbor and parts of Bremerton. Like the development in Whatcom County in recent years, the district has seen a big boost in housing since the newest Tacoma Narrows Bridge opened in 2007. 
Looking forward
Despite their successes, Democrats in these areas aren’t getting too confident.
“When I moved here, they were all Republican,” said Douglass, chair of the 42nd Legislative District Democrats. “Now all three are Democrats, and I still think, though, that it takes an incredible amount of hard work and diligence for it to stay that way.”
Next week’s elections will indicate how far Democrats have come in these areas, and how close they’ll be to supermajority power in the Legislature. 
These same factors are at play in southwest Washington, where four Democratic challengers in the August primary led Republican state House incumbents handily in areas near Vancouver and Portland. A sweep for Democrats next week would leave just Sen. Paul Harris, of the 17th, as the lone Republican remaining across those two neighboring districts. Two years ago, the GOP held all six. 
In 2022, Harris won a state House reelection bid by nearly 10 percentage points. Two years later, when he ran for Senate, that was down to just over 2 percentage points.

This creep could continue to extend, with Democrats showing electoral strength in central Washington’s 12th District, which now crosses the Cascades into exurbs like North Bend and Monroe, and the 35th District in Mason County. Rising costs in Gig Harbor and Bremerton in the 26th could force people to move into the cheaper 35th.

title: Commentary: Five questions about Missouri’s election. Some are easier to answer than others.
description:
A polling location in Jefferson City (Annelise Hanshaw/Missouri Independent).Missouri voters keep rejecting some of the GOP’s biggest ideas. Then they keep electing Republicans to run the state.
Two years ago, voters protected abortion rights and approved paid sick leave. In August, they overwhelmingly rejected proposals to overhaul the tax system and make c[...]
text:
A polling location in Jefferson City (Annelise Hanshaw/Missouri Independent).Missouri voters keep rejecting some of the GOP’s biggest ideas. Then they keep electing Republicans to run the state.
Two years ago, voters protected abortion rights and approved paid sick leave. In August, they overwhelmingly rejected proposals to overhaul the tax system and make constitutional amendments harder to pass.
Yet Republicans hold every statewide elected office, six of eight congressional seats and supermajorities in both legislative chambers.
On Tuesday, voters will revisit several of those disagreements. Here are five questions I’m watching.
 1. Didn’t we already settle the abortion question?

You’d think so.
In 2024, voters approved Amendment 3, enshrining abortion rights in the state constitution. Republican lawmakers responded by putting another amendment on the ballot.
So we’re doing this again?
Yes, but not quite the same way.
Amendment 3 would repeal those protections and restore a ban on most abortions, with limited exceptions. It would also constitutionally prohibit gender-affirming medical care for minors.
Wait, it’s also Amendment 3?
Yes. Missouri recycles amendment numbers. Political arguments, too.
This time around, a yes vote bans abortion and a no vote keeps it legal. 
What do the polls say?
An August SLU/YouGov poll found 43% in favor, 44% opposed and 13% undecided.
A small but vocal minority of anti-abortion activists oppose the amendment, arguing the proposed ban doesn’t go far enough. Meanwhile, Amendment 3’s supporters have mounted a more organized campaign than they did two years ago, particularly through churches working to mobilize voters.
The question is whether the coalition that protected abortion rights in 2024 will hold together in the face of that effort.
 2. Can Ann Wagner survive another Democratic wave?

Wagner has seen this movie before.
In 2018, Democrats gained dozens of U.S. House seats. Wagner survived, winning her suburban St. Louis district by about four points. She’s won every election since.
At some point, Democrats might wonder whether the district is actually competitive or just enjoys making them think it is.
So why is this year different?
An October Emerson College poll showed Democratic challenger Fred Wellman leading Wagner 51% to 46%. Other surveys have shown tighter margins.
Last week, Sabato’s Crystal Ball moved the district from leaning Republican to a toss-up. The result could offer a window into whether the suburban backlash against Republicans that defined 2018 is returning eight years later.
 3. Is Missouri’s redistricting fight finally over?

That depends on your definition of over.
After more than a year of Republican maneuvering and courtroom battles, the gerrymandered version of Missouri’s congressional map is finally on the ballot. The GOP-drawn map, designed to help Republicans win seven of eight U.S. House seats, won’t be used Tuesday.
But Proposition A will determine its fate in future elections.
Remind me how that works.
A yes vote approves the Republican-drawn map for future elections. A no vote rejects it.
So a no vote ends the whole thing?
Not necessarily.
Some Republicans have already floated trying again in 2027.
If voters reject Proposition A, another item on the ballot called Amendment 6 could — if it passes — make another gerrymander much, much harder. But more on that later.
 4. Will Democrats win control of the legislature?

No. No, they will not.
Democrats haven’t controlled either chamber of the Missouri legislature since 2002. And nobody is talking seriously about a Democratic takeover this year.
But they don’t need one to change how Jefferson City operates.
What does that mean?
A net gain of three House seats or two Senate seats would end the GOP’s two-thirds majority in the respective chamber.
That would mean Republicans could no longer override a governor’s veto or pass emergency clauses allowing new laws to take effect immediately without Democratic support.
And Republicans are taking the threat very seriously, spending heavily to defend districts that weren’t considered competitive just a few months ago.
Where should we look Tuesday?
The suburbs, obviously. But also rural Missouri.
Democrats haven’t won a predominantly rural House district since 2010. Whether they can expand beyond their traditional strongholds may tell us more about the party’s future than the final seat count alone.
 5. Will Missouri voters keep rejecting Republican priorities while electing Republicans?

Back where we started.
Missourians have voted for abortion rights, Medicaid expansion, a higher minimum wage and paid sick leave. Republican lawmakers have tried to reverse or limit nearly all of them.
Which brings us to Amendment 6?
Exactly.
Amendment 6 would require 80% support in both legislative chambers and another statewide vote to change laws or constitutional amendments approved by initiative, or enact laws similar to those rejected by referendum (see also: Proposition A).
But are Missouri voters turning against Republicans themselves?
Consider the auditor’s race, the only statewide office on the ballot.
Republican Scott Fitzpatrick won by nearly 22 points in 2022. He has substantially outraised Democratic challenger Quentin Wilson, and the contest has attracted relatively little attention.
Yet an August poll showed Fitzpatrick ahead by just two points, within the margin of error.
The result could be revealing even if Fitzpatrick wins. Does he approach his margin from four years ago, or is the race closer?
One result won’t establish a political realignment. But taken with the Wagner race, legislative contests and ballot measures, it could tell us whether rejecting Republican ideas is starting to translate into rejecting Republican candidates.
Or whether Missourians will keep saying no to Republican policies and yes to Republican politicians.
