name: Alabama Reflector
title: Commentary: The only certainty I have in Alabama’s elections
description:
A line of voters runs out the door and outside the building at Woodland Methodist Church in Pike Road, Alabama on Tuesday, Nov. 5, 2024. Alabama is one of a handful of states where all in-person voting takes place on Election Day. (Jemma Stephenson/Alabama Reflector)The hardest three words to say in a column are “I don’t know.”
But it’s the only honest appro[...]
text:
A line of voters runs out the door and outside the building at Woodland Methodist Church in Pike Road, Alabama on Tuesday, Nov. 5, 2024. Alabama is one of a handful of states where all in-person voting takes place on Election Day. (Jemma Stephenson/Alabama Reflector)The hardest three words to say in a column are “I don’t know.”
But it’s the only honest approach you can take in a Monday-before-Election-Day piece. Like everyone else, I see Tuesday’s results through a glass darkly. On Wednesday, we will see them face-to-face.
That’s the challenge for all political analysis. You look at past performance; you consider outside conditions, and you make a reasonable guess at what could result. That’s how good pollsters put together a sample ahead of an election.
But no one knows who will show up. No one knows the mix of Black and white voters, or Democrats and Republicans. You can’t say who will stay home and who is willing to wait hours in line to vote, or which political messages worked.
You take a guess. An informed guess, but a guess.
So that’s what follows, rooted in past experience covering Alabama politics. But to be clear: (takes a deep breath) I don’t know.
Surprises in Alabama elections are rare. (Surprises in Alabama politics are not, up to and including a governor’s love for emojis.)  From 2006 — when I covered my first state campaign — to today, I can count all the unanticipated electoral outcomes on one finger.
That’s partly because Alabama doesn’t see much regular polling. Expectations don’t get raised or lowered, rationally or otherwise.
But mostly it’s because Alabama functions as a one-party state. One party has the finances and the organization. As described in 2023’s Allen v. Milligan ruling, one party benefits from the racial polarization of a population that’s roughly two-thirds white. The other organization has places of strength, but it struggles to grow beyond those refuges. Election results aren’t preordained, but they’re generally predictable.
The only real surprise in the last 20 years was Doug Jones’ victory in the special U.S. Senate election in 2017. And that was more unexpected than shocking. Jones ran a disciplined campaign, had a major cash edge, and drew an opponent many Republicans couldn’t stand, even before allegations of sexual misconduct emerged.
Jones is once again on the ballot, this time as the Democratic gubernatorial nominee against Republican nominee Tommy Tuberville. The former senator has run a strong race, but he’s been playing from behind all year.
Still, Tuberville’s campaign has made some missteps, and Republicans are facing some major headwinds on the economy and the unpopular war in Iran. Is that enough to alter the state’s political dynamics?
Well, it depends on who shows up.
Racial polarization and straight-ticket voting have historically predicted Alabama election outcomes better than anything else. When two-thirds of all ballots go to one party or the other — and two-thirds of those go to the Republicans — census data matters more than campaigning. Arguments for or against a candidate or a policy crash onto the hard realities of Alabama’s racial divides.
So if Tuesday’s electorate is 74% white, as it was in 2024 and as two recent Republican polls of the governor’s race have predicted, it’s hard to see how Election Day results in anything but continued GOP dominance of Alabama government.
If it’s 72% white, as in Alabama Democrats’ last respectable showing in 2018, the margins could be lower, but the fundamentals in Montgomery will be unlikely to change.
If it’s lower than that, as a Democratic poll last week suggested, or if racial polarization recedes somewhat, then the results could be more unexpected.
It will be a surprise if Democrats don’t show up to vote on Tuesday. Democratic turnout jumped over 2022 levels in the May primary. The surge took place two weeks after legislative Republicans attempted to redistrict a Black congressman out of his seat, and that wasn’t a coincidence. There are signs throughout the South that Black voters, who tend to vote for Democrats, are coming out after redistricting and the U.S. Supreme Court’s attack on the Voting Rights Act.  
Unlike 2022, a catastrophic year for the party, Democrats have a strong slate of statewide candidates and a decent number of legislative candidates (though many are inexperienced first-timers).
The question is how many Republicans show up. GOP officials haven’t been shy about their concerns about apathy among the base. But on paper, at least, Alabama’s large Republican margins should give the party plenty of room for error. Nearly every Republican candidate has a cash advantage over a Democratic challenger, if they have any opponent at all.
GOP campaigns have seemed to lurch between proposals like abolishing the grocery tax that appeal to a broad swathe of voters and messaging exclusively for the hardcore followers, launching vicious but tired attacks on transgender people and throwing the word “socialism” around more than your local DSA chapter.
Will that get Republican voters out? Will national headwinds lift Democrats? We’ll know shortly. And we’ll see if this is a typical election in Alabama, or something unusual.
It will all depend on who shows up. That, I feel certain of. And if you’re looking for a particular result, you better show up, too.

Republican incumbent Andrew Sorrell, a former member of the Alabama[...]
text:
Andrew Sorrell, the Republican state auditor incumbent (left), faces Democratic nominee Violet Edwards, a Madison County commissioner,  in Tuesday's election.The two candidates vying to be Alabama state auditor are focused on a unique power of the office: its role in election administration.
Republican incumbent Andrew Sorrell, a former member of the Alabama House of Representatives, is seeking his second term as auditor. He faces Madison County Commissioner Violet Edwards, the Democratic nominee.
The Alabama state auditor is responsible for tracking and keeping inventory of property owned by the state and audits the financial records of the Alabama Department of Finance and the Treasurer’s Office.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
But both Sorrell and Edwards highlighted its appointment power. The auditor, along with the governor and the commissioner of Agriculture and Industries, appoints members to county boards of registrars, who oversee voter registration and maintain voter rolls.
Sorrell said he will appoint people to the board of registrars who believe in election integrity.
“Our current registrars are doing a fantastic job of keeping the voter rolls clean, and getting the dead people off the voter rolls, and getting people who moved to other states off the voter rolls,” he said. “When you have bloated voter rolls, you have a recipe for election fraud.”
There is no evidence of widespread voter fraud in Alabama. The Heritage Foundation surveyed the incidents of voter fraud in Alabama and found 41 convictions or findings of voter fraud since 2000. During the 2024 election, 2.2 million ballots were cast.
Sorrell said he will ensure that people he appoints to the board of registrars believe in the importance of voting. He also speaks with them to determine if they believe in election security.
“I ask them, ‘Are you serious about election integrity? Are you going to make it a point of emphasis to keep the voter rolls clean?’” Sorrell said. “I make them promise me that they will.”
Edwards said she wants to expand opportunities for people to vote. As a member of the Madison County Commission, she said she worked with her colleagues to “set a standard” for the Board of Registrars, setting a schedule for the office and outlining the skill set needed for the job. She also said she supported SB 48, sponsored by Sen. Bobby Singleton, D-Greensboro, a 2025 law that increased pay for registrars.
“It was appealing because the auditor gets 66 appointments across the state of Alabama, and I know how important those appointments are when it comes to maintaining our voter rolls, deciding who has the right to vote, or who can re-earn the right to vote when it comes to people who have been rehabilitated,” she said. “It just made sense.”
Edwards said she wants to appoint people who will follow rules, keep offices open during the same hours as other county offices, and help protect people’s right to vote.
“Everybody is not using their voice,” she said. “As auditor, I have those appointments for the Board of Registrars. I have the power to appoint people who are willing to work, and who are not just trying to get a political appointment, who will go out and register people, who will keep these rolls clean. We won’t see the massive purging.”
Sorrell initially campaigned to be Secretary of State for this cycle but changed his mind during the qualifying period and opted to seek reelection.
“The race was not shaping up the way I hoped it would for Secretary of State, and I felt like I had a greater shot of getting reelected,” he said. “I made the tough decision to change back to the State Auditor’s race. It turned out very well.”
Edwards said she was recruited by Doug Jones, the Democratic gubernatorial nominee.
“We had a discussion about purpose and progress in Alabama, where we are now, where we wanted to be in the future for our children and future generations, and then we discussed my skillset,” Edwards said. “And here I am and going for it.”

text:
On Thursday, the first day of early voting in Kentucky, people formed a line outside the Tates Creek Library in Lexington to make their choices. (Kentucky Lantern photo by Arden Barnes)This column was first published in the Northern Kentucky Tribune. 
Kentuckians are heading to the polls (no-excuse early voting was Oct. 29-31) to elect a U.S. senator, six members of the U.S. House, half the state Senate, the entire state House, many judges and local officials – and decide whether Kentucky governors should be barred from issuing pardons in the last 60 days of their terms.
That last bit on the ballot is a reminder of the state’s most unpopular governor in living memory, Republican Matt Bevin, who went wild with pardons after Andy Beshear defeated him in 2019. Bevin has played a cameo role in this election, as the supposed doppelganger of his last running mate, Ralph Alvarado, who’s running against Democrat Zach Dembo for the 6th District congressional seat being vacated by Andy Barr, the GOP nominee for the Senate seat of the retiring Mitch McConnell.
In his book, Beshear casts Bevin as “Trump lite,” aiming  his all-but-announced presidential campaign at the unpopular president. Donald Trump is not on midterm ballots but will have more influence on the national results than any other person, because he is so unpopular – even in Kentucky, which he won by an average of 30 points. Every fuel-price sign is an anti-Trump sign.
Alvarado has fled from Trump, most recently by saying the Iran War needs to end “right now” and running a TV ad saying politicians of both parties have ruined the American Dream attained by his immigrant parents. Dembo has a spot in which he says “I know you’re angry. I am, too,” and Democrats seem angrier and thus likelier to vote. 
That’s one reason the Cook Political Report sees the odds moving Dembo’s way, but a Trump-connected political action committee that’s been attacking Dembo and promoting Alvarado made a huge buy Monday for the final week, reflecting Cook’s call that the race is a tossup. It will be an early signal on election night of the size of the blue wave Democrats expect.
The Senate race has not been competitive, because 2022 Democratic nominee Charles Booker didn’t air a TV commercial until this week. However, Booker was already on paid TV, because a committee tied to Barr has been running spots attacking him in some TV markets. Barr thus follows the McConnell maxim of taking nothing for granted, and may figure that an ad with closeups of an African American man taking liberal positions as he answers questions and stares into the camera will scare some Republicans to the polls – especially in Barr’s home 6th District, which he would hate to see go Democratic.
If Booker had the sort of money Barr has, he could air one of the year’s more entertaining ads, a 60-second, A.I.-generated video that shows Barr and the senator at “McConnell’s” restaurant, a la McDonald’s, selling corporate tax breaks, corruption, Medicare and Medicaid cuts, and “lackey pie – that comes with a Barr wind-up toy that does whatever Trump tells him to do, even support a war and higher gas prices.” Barr’s most recent commercials have touted his work for constituents.
That is also the theme of the latest ad from 1st District Rep. James Comer, who’s likely thinking more about running for governor in 2027 than he is about defeating poorly funded Democrat John “Drew” Williams. Comer’s oddly drawn district and fat campaign fund allow him to legitimately run ads in the Louisville and Lexington TV markets and broaden his name recognition and favorability for next year – a legal semi-circumvention of the state law against using federal campaign money in state races.
Speaking of state and federal matters, the Trump law firm formerly known as our Department of Justice said Oct. 21 that its Civil Rights Division would send election monitors to Jefferson and Fayette counties, Kentucky’s only Democratic strongholds. Their attention might be better directed to a few counties in Comer’s district and several in southeastern Kentucky’s 5th District, where election chicanery lingers.
The 5th has been represented since 1981 by Republican Harold “Hal” Rogers, whose 89th birthday is Dec. 31 – a fact referenced by Democratic opponent Ned Pillersdorf, who said on KET Monday night that he is running because “no congressional district in the country will be hurt more by this big ugly bill,” the Trump-dubbed One Big Beautiful Bill Act that will cut Medicaid and other programs after the election. Rogers has made no joint appearances with Pillersdorf, 70.
Pillersdorf has run an ad in which former Gov. Paul Patton (who turned 89 on May 26 and says he’s “too old for Congress”) reveals that he has voted for Rogers but the congressman “sold us out to the Washington elite.” Rogers is unlikely to lose, given his decades of delivering for the district, but the voting there will be one measure of how far into the ditch Trump has driven the party he hijacked and transformed.

name: New Hampshire Bulletin
title: With property taxes on the ballot, New Hampshire’s caucus midterm turns hyperlocal
description: Activists for the progressive group Kent Street Coalition meet near Concord Hospital on a frigid October morning to urge passersby to vote no on adopting a tax cap for their school district, a question on every New Hampshire ballot Nov. 3. (Photo by Ethan DeWitt, New Hampshire Bulletin)Pam Hicks has lived in Hollis her whole life. Not all of her neighbors ha[...]
text:
Activists for the progressive group Kent Street Coalition meet near Concord Hospital on a frigid October morning to urge passersby to vote no on adopting a tax cap for their school district, a question on every New Hampshire ballot Nov. 3. (Photo by Ethan DeWitt, New Hampshire Bulletin)Pam Hicks has lived in Hollis her whole life. Not all of her neighbors have been so lucky.
The town’s rural charm, its scattered farms and orchards, and its highly ranked schools come with a price: eye-watering property taxes. Over the years, some families who moved there with kids figured that out, she says.
“We call it ‘educate and evacuate,’” she said. “They come in, the kids go through the school system, and then when their kids are graduating — their houses are for sale.” 
Hicks blames complacency on the Hollis Brookline Cooperative School Board and rising budgets. This year, she has a solution. When she votes Nov. 3, Hicks and every other Granite Stater will be asked whether they want to impose a cap on school district property taxes for the next two years. She plans to vote yes. 
“There’s no oversight for what they’re doing,” she said of the board. “So…let’s put some guardrails on.”
Not everyone is happy with that approach. 
New Hampshire’s tax cap ballot question has kicked off fierce debates and avid campaigns across the state, vaulting an issue normally reserved for spring meetings — school district budgets — into an already electric midterm election season. 
Suddenly property taxes, perhaps New Hampshire’s most animating and polarizing topic, have a dedicated space on a ballot otherwise reserved for partisan choices. In a year in which opinions on President Donald Trump’s second term have often stolen political oxygen, New Hampshire’s tax cap debate has managed to spawn mailers, signs, online advertisements, door-to-door campaigns, street corner demonstrations, and heated local meetings. 
To Democrats, who opposed adding the question to the ballot, the solution it offers is simplistic and potentially harmful to school districts. They say it subverts local control by bypassing the previous method to adopt a tax cap: at a town meeting, in the context of a budget. 
But Republicans say removing the debate from March town meetings is the point: Many residents are unhappy with rising school district budgets but too few of them attend the spring meetings to make a difference, they argue. Putting the measure on the November ballot will ensure a more representative sample of a district’s residents are heard, they say. 
The politics 
A successful “yes” vote on the ballot question would limit a school district in two ways. For two years, it would cap the total amount in local property taxes the school district could raise to the amount collected the previous year, adjusted for inflation and any new taxable property. It would also require the district to keep its School Administrative Unit spending to 6% of its overall budget for those two years. 
The measure requires the support of 60% of all voters who fill in the ballot question to pass. And whether or not the 2026 vote is successful, the law requires the question to appear on the ballot one more time, for another two-year approval period, in the 2028 presidential election. 
Once adopted, a school district’s tax cap can be overridden for a specific annual budget if at least 60% of voters at the school’s annual meeting in spring vote to do so. 
Polling suggests there is general support for the tax caps. A St. Anselm College poll conducted Oct. 19 to 20 found that 57% of likely New Hampshire voters supported the tax cap, including 83% of Republicans, 56% of undeclared voters, and 31% of Democrats. 
Yet as road signs and billboards blanket the state, it has been sometimes hard to separate the tax cap from broader politics. 
Some Republicans are hoping that not only does the ballot question lead to new school district tax caps, but that voters reward the Republican state candidates who put it on the ballot. In a midterm election environment traditionally difficult for the party in the White House, hyperlocal concerns with property tax could overpower unease with Trump, some believe. 
And some Democrats have argued Republican lawmakers passed the law specifically to drive that turnout. 
The messaging
Statewide organizations have helped drive messaging on both sides.
The Committee to Elect House Republicans helped launch a website, “NHPropertyTaxRelief.com,” advocating for voting “yes” on the tax cap, complete with a calculator claiming to show how much money a voter in a specific town with a specific home value could save.
The committee does not employ doorknockers. But after the September state primary, it did purchase nearly 10,000 yard signs urging “yes” on Question 2 and distributed them to the hundreds of Republican State House candidates it represents, said Chris Maidment, a Republican consultant who works with the committee. 
Asked Friday how many of those signs went out, Maidment ran a quick calculation. “There’s like 20 in my truck, so I guess like 9,980,” he joked. 
Because it has delegated advocacy to state legislative candidates, the committee’s “yes” campaign is necessarily entwined with Republican politics. Maidment says that’s by design.  
“The job of the Committee is to elect a Republican majority, and to win as many seats for Republicans as possible,” Maidment said. “And so, this tax cap question is more of a tool to help us do that rather than an effort to get this passed in all the various communities.”
On the other side, several organizations have mounted campaigns to oppose the ballot questions, including major teachers’ unions like the NEA-NH and AFT-NH and groups such as Engage NH and MomsRising NH.
On a frigid Wednesday morning near the Concord Hospital in late October, members of the progressive advocacy group Kent Street Coalition gathered to wave signs at passing cars urging a no vote.
Louise Spencer, a co-founder of the group, argued tax caps obfuscated the true cause of high property taxes: low state spending on education. While New Hampshire public schools collectively spend more per student than most states, the state ranks 50th in state per-pupil education aid. 
“If various spending needs to happen, and there’s this funding cap, then it’s not solving any of the problems. The real problem here is that the state is refusing to pay its fair share for public education,” Spencer said. 
The group, which organizes advocates but does not raise or spend campaign money, held other sign-waving events across the Concord area throughout the month. 
Residents on both sides of New Hampshire’s school district tax cap debate attend a meeting at the Hollis Brookline High School to voice their opinions, ahead of a Nov. 3 question on the general election ballot, Oct. 21, 2026. (Photo by Ethan DeWitt, New Hampshire Bulletin)
The local conversations
Despite the statewide campaigns, many of the liveliest conversations in recent weeks have taken place locally. In October, school boards across the state hosted information sessions, attempting to toe the line between informing constituents about the effects of a tax cap and advocating against it. And attendees of the meetings have brought plenty of opinions of their own. 
At an auditorium in the Hollis Brookline High School one Wednesday evening, the atmosphere was raw, bordering on explosive. 
Darlene Mann, the budget committee chairwoman for the Hollis Brookline Cooperative School Board, walked through a detail-laden presentation on the district’s current budget, tax rates, and the effect of the proposed tax cap to about 100 residents spread among the theater’s seats. 
The school board is already on track to propose a budget with taxation that would come under the proposed tax cap, Mann said. Additionally, the district already consistently keeps its administrative budget below 6% of the overall budget, she said. 
Still, Mann said the tax cap could force tough decisions in the event of unexpected costs from one year to the next, such as for diesel, health care, or food, all of which have risen recently. 
As they took to the microphone, some Hollis residents echoed that point.
“If we go over this tax cut, if this passes, and we go over the tax cut in our budget, what would we have to reduce?” Krista Whalan asked. 
Mann’s response: The district would have to reduce discretionary spending categories, including academic programs, technology, staff, extracurricular activities, sports, and operations, but it could not reduce its mandatory spending such as transportation, health insurance, special education services, and collective bargaining agreements. 
“I do trust the school boards, and I certainly trust our budget committees,” Whalan added. “They work extremely hard. This is not a simple process.”
But others asked why the tax cap would be so destructive if the district is already projected to obey it.
“I don’t understand why all the pushback from the school boards,” said Dave Perry. “And the point I’m coming from here is that there have been very large increases in the past, so the level of trust I have is low.”
Others took a more personal approach. Gerald Moore made his point with recent history. His tax bill in 2022 was $10,619, he said. It rose to $12,235 in 2023, to $13,069 in 2024, and to $13,981 in 2025. But the 2026 tax bill is set to be about $15,000, he said.
“I’m 82; I’m on fixed income,” he said, addressing the board. “And when you show me that everything is nice and even, and you’re doing a terrific job, and I see my taxes going up at the rate of 10% a year, when 70% plus of the budget goes to schools, I get the feeling that I’m down in Times Square watching a three-card monte game.”
One resident with kids in the school system, Mandy Hoffman, sympathized with the tax concerns. For every resident, finding the tax bill in their mailbox is an annual source of dread, she said. But she argued the tax cap would only delay the true costs of running the schools and lead to higher taxes down the line. 
“I fear that people are going to continue to open up their mailbox and not see any change and say, ‘Gosh, I voted a certain way. Why didn’t something happen?’” she said.
Like Hicks, Hoffman, who moved in six years ago, is enamored with Hollis. 
“We wanted our kids to be able to ride bikes just like we did,” she said in an interview. “We wanted our kids to be able to climb trees just like we did.” 
Hollis fit that bill. But a reduction of school services for her children is the one thing that might threaten her desire to stay, Hoffman said. 
“I don’t want my neighbors spending more,” she said. “I want my neighbors having a very smart budget with a great community and a great school system.”

title: A WKY agency is wielding eminent domain for a gas pipeline. Landowners say they’re being bullied.
description: An image showing the proposed natural gas pipeline route through Greg Davenport's family farm in Christian County. Much of the proposed route follows along Interstate 24 in Western Kentucky. (Screenshot/Court exhibit)Greg Davenport says he’s not opposed to progress. But he has serious misgivings when it comes to a proposed 16-inch natural gas pipeline that a[...]
text:
An image showing the proposed natural gas pipeline route through Greg Davenport's family farm in Christian County. Much of the proposed route follows along Interstate 24 in Western Kentucky. (Screenshot/Court exhibit)Greg Davenport says he’s not opposed to progress. But he has serious misgivings when it comes to a proposed 16-inch natural gas pipeline that a public agency wants to run through his family’s Christian County farm, property his family has owned since the 1940s. 
“Basically, they said, ‘Sign this, or we’ll take you to court. Sign this, or we’ll condemn your property,’ Davenport said. “We just don’t think that this pipeline that’s going to serve other people — it’s not going to serve us at all. I don’t think it’s even going to serve our county — that we should have to bear the blunt.” 
Davenport’s family is involved in one of more than 20 active lawsuits in Western Kentucky courts in which the Todd County-based Pennyrile Regional Energy Agency has sued landowners, citing the state’s eminent domain laws, for easements as part of a proposed 53-mile gas pipeline project across Christian County, Todd County, Trigg County, Caldwell County, and Lyon County. 
The Pennyrile Regional Energy Agency, a public agency formed by two small Todd County cities and backed by a $30 million allocation by the GOP-controlled state legislature, has said it’s secured the vast majority of easements needed to build a pipeline, something it touts as an economic development boon for the region by boosting natural gas supply. 
The agency is also still ensnared in an ongoing lawsuit with the state’s utility regulator over whether the pipeline’s construction should be subject to oversight by the regulator. Rep. Jason Petrie, R-Elkton, a powerful state lawmaker from Todd County, earlier this year sought to help the agency in that lawsuit by passing an exemption from regulation in state law. 
But some landowners being sued by the agency along the planned pipeline route say the pipeline agency has refused to negotiate in good faith over easement funding or answered questions the pipeline’s path.
Attorneys for these landowners have also asked questions and scrutinized — through depositions and testimony in one of these court cases — the future economic viability of the pipeline, the status of future customers, and whether geological formations, including sinkholes, could change the pipeline’s path. 
In late September, social media pages and a website labeled as the “Kentucky Coalition for Property Rights” were also launched lambasting the Pennyrile Regional Energy Agency over these lawsuits. When the Lantern asked who specifically was behind the social media pages and websites, it received an email in September stating the coalition was a “citizen led group” and that people “are getting lawsuits with no real negotiation, and nobody has given a straight answer about who the pipeline is for.” 
Eston Glover, the chair of the board for the Pennyrile group, told the Lantern in late October that, based on advice from his attorneys, he could not “discuss anything relative to what’s going on in the court.” 
Eston Glover, the chair of the Pennyrile Regional Energy Agency board, testifying in a March court hearing. (Screenshot/Court recording)
“There are a lot of inaccurate statements being passed around,” Glover said. “I don’t know how to correct those.” 
He declined to comment on what specifically has been inaccurate. 
Courtroom scrutiny 
The proposed gas pipeline has been years in the making, and extensive delays.
In 2022, Petrie, the powerful Todd County lawmaker who serves as chair of the Kentucky House Appropriations and Revenue Committee, and Democratic Gov. Andy Beshear hailed a $30 million appropriation that currently serves as the sole funding source for the agency, created by the Todd County cities of Guthrie and Trenton, which have a combined population of fewer than 2,000. 
The pipeline was initially proposed to provide natural gas supply to an existing Novelis aluminum recycling facility for a potential expansion, along with other “unserved and underserved areas” in the region, according to a past court filing. 
In a 2023 presentation obtained by the Lantern, the agency expected to have the pipeline operational by the end of 2025. During the Christian County court hearing, Glover cited the main reason for the delays: “Dealing with the landowners.”
The agency began to sue landowners for easements to build the pipeline starting in 2023 and has continued to file lawsuits through this year. 
The agency has also touted an agreement to supply the Fort Campbell military installation with gas supply. During a Christian County court hearing in March in one of the eminent domain lawsuits, Glover, the agency board chair, said that a Buc-ee’s gas station also expressed interest in receiving gas supply. 
During the March hearing, Dan Thomas, an attorney for William Elgin, one of the sued landowners, asked Glover whether the agency had a commitment from Novelis to expand its operations in Todd County; he questioned if Novelis’ investment to build a separate plant in Alabama meant that the Todd County expansion wasn’t happening. 
Glover responded that there was not an existing document definitively stating Novelis was “going to build” or not. 
“We are still getting information weekly on what their expectations and needs will be,” Glover said during the March hearing. Glover also said the agency was waiting to hear from Fort Campbell. 
In an email, Novelis spokesperson Fiona Bell told the Lantern the company “continues to operate our recycling center and automotive finishing plant” in Todd County and had no plans to share “regarding an expansion.”
 A history of eminent domain

As litigation has dragged on, county judges-executives along the pipeline route have fielded complaints from their own constituents about whether the pipeline agency was respecting landowners’ rights.
In a phone interview with the Lantern, Republican Trigg County Judge-Executive Stan Humphries referenced the “untethered eminent domain situation” when the federal government seized and flooded Trigg County land in the 1940s and 1960s to create Kentucky Lake and Lake Barkley, eventually becoming the Land Between the Lakes National Recreation Area. 
“There are still a lot of residents, when that word’s brought up, get really uptight about it, and rightfully so,” Humphries said, referring to eminent domain. “There’s a lot of concern, and maybe some confusion, as to what that corridor looks like and size and scope and location. So those are issues that have to be worked out for these landowners.”
Because of a new state law passed earlier this year, Humphries other county judge-executives representing counties along the pipeline route can make appointments to the pipeline agency’s board to represent their county’s interests.
Petrie, the Todd County state lawmaker, in a late October statement said the county appointments allowed through House Bill 757 were “intended primarily to increase transparency” with the agency. 
Rep. Jason Petrie, R-Elkton (LRC Public Information)
But Humphries and other elected officials question how meaningful these appointments are. 
These county representatives do not each get a vote on the board; these county representatives can only vote in a limited capacity — together as only a single vote on the board — if all county representatives agree to support or oppose a board action.
That means each county appointment, including Todd County, can essentially veto any effort by other county representatives on the board. Only Todd County has made such an appointment, and the board already is made up of Todd County residents. 
“If you’re going to run something through a county, that county should have a true voice,” said Rep. Myron Dossett, R-Pembroke, who represents a part of Christian County and is also concerned about ensuring landowners, some of them lifelong friends of his, are “treated fairly.” 
“It was a great idea, but it’s the implementation that has been horrible,” Dossett said. “I know how hard they have worked and struggled to own a piece of property, to own a home.” 
Petrie said that no “lobbyist or local official has contacted me since the original filing with general concerns about interlocal entities, or specific concerns about board appointments.” 
“I remain open to discussion about legislative action to make interlocal agreement entities better in structure and operation for all concerned,” Petrie said. 
In early September, Christian Circuit Judge Andrew Self sided with the pipeline agency in an eminent domain lawsuit against a landowner; lawyers for the landowner are seeking to vacate that order. Several of the eminent domain lawsuits remain pending and haven’t yet gone to trial. 
Humphries, the Trigg County judge-executive, said his county fiscal court still supports the idea behind the pipeline; the fiscal court passed a resolution in support of it last year. 
But he said the pipeline agency hasn’t made any additional presentations to the fiscal court since March 2025, and there are “a lot of unknowns” about the project’s status. Smith, the Lyon County judge-executive, also said she has had limited communication with the agency. 
“I think transparency, accountability, clear communication, and high respect for landowners’ rights in this process is really paramount in moving this project if it’s going to work out,” Humphries said.

name: Virginia Mercury
title: In Virginia and beyond, Democratic candidates increasingly embrace Medicare For All
description: A campaign sign outside of a polling place in Chesterfield County, Virginia reads "Medicare For All," October 2026. (Photo by Charlotte Rene Woods/Virginia Mercury)One of Chesterfield County resident John Meszaros’ sons was born with a rare metabolic syndrome, which required frequent doctor visits in his first year of life and came with hefty hospital bills [...]
text:
A campaign sign outside of a polling place in Chesterfield County, Virginia reads "Medicare For All," October 2026. (Photo by Charlotte Rene Woods/Virginia Mercury)One of Chesterfield County resident John Meszaros’ sons was born with a rare metabolic syndrome, which required frequent doctor visits in his first year of life and came with hefty hospital bills at the start of it. 
Though his son is now covered by Medicaid, Meszaros said he and his wife have had to make numerous calls with the hospital and their insurer over the past year to sort through their son’s critical early healthcare. 
“It just adds a lot of aggravation into our lives,” he said, noting that the experience highlighted his desire for universal healthcare. 
He also recalled a trip to the emergency room during a medical emergency when he was a college student, where “while I was in the gurney, they were asking me for payment — no joke.” 
“Medicare For All” was the key pillar of former 1st Congressional District Democratic hopeful Salaam Bhatti’s campaign, which clinched Meszaros’ vote in the primary. 
The concept would replace private insurance companies with government-run health insurance available to everyone. 
While living abroad in Scotland for a year, Bhatti recalled not having to pay a co-pay during a doctor visit. 
As he monitored how other countries have some form of universal healthcare he recalled thinking: “you can actually invent a policy that really helps people from a root level.”
Bhatti came in 2nd in the crowded primary and current Democratic nominee Shannon Taylor is facing off against longtime incumbent Rob Wittman, R-Westmoreland, in what’s emerged as one of Virginia’s — and the nation’s —  “toss-up” districts this year. 
Though Taylor has not spoken about universal healthcare, and did not respond to The Mercury’s inquiry about it, Meszaros is glad to know she has expressed support for undoing Medicaid changes and restoring ACA subsidies.
“Medicaid is already tricky and (Congress) made it harder,” Meszaros said of the reconciliation bill Congress passed last summer that altered it. “(Republican majorities) want to kick people off as far as I can tell.”
But beyond immediate suturing of healthcare cuts, any potential overhauling of America’s healthcare system will take time and political buy-in, U.S. Rep. Don Beyer, R- Alexandria, said. 
The six-term congressman, who is running for reelection, was among 118 co-sponsors of last year’s Medicare For All Act, a measure that didn’t advance after its introduction. 
Of the House’s 435 members, that cosponsorship represents nearly 30% of the chamber interested in universal healthcare. 
U.S. Sen. Bernie Sanders, an independent from Vermont, has long championed the concept in Congress’ other chamber. 
This year, Virginia’s own Sen. Mark Warner — a Democrat up for reelection, running against Republican Bert Mizusawa —  told The Mercury he would support universal healthcare as well. 
“We will never get to cost containment or improve quality as long as we’re arguing about who gets covered,” Warner said. 
Beyer, Warner and Bhatti all noted how even if Democrats flip the House and Senate, with President Donald Trump still in the White House for another two years, a total shift to universal healthcare may not yet be feasible.
In that time, Warner suggests Congress explore what works for other countries that have universal healthcare to help shape America’s potential version. 
“I want to start working on what a uniquely American universal coverage system can be, with the goal of building consensus and have policy ready to go,” he said. 
As a stopgap solution, Warner unveiled a bill package that would tackle the Medicaid and ACA revisions his party has sought, bolster pricing transparency for insurers and expand Medicare’s drug price negotiation program. 
 A ‘patchwork’ of policy and ideas

U.S. Sen. Mark Warner, D-Virginia, participates in a roundtable discussion in Richmond, Virginia on Oct. 22, 2026 (Photo by Charlotte Rene Woods/Virginia Mercury)
Currently, many Americans get their healthcare coverage through their employers, who contract with private insurers. 
Others purchase plans through the ACA marketplace.
Disabled and pregnant people, along with some eligible low-income people, get coverage through Medicaid — a joint state and federal program. 
A disruption is already underway for both Medicaid and ACA since Congress let subsidies for the latter expire and adopted changes that may lead to millions of Americans losing Medicaid eligibility. 
Matthew Fiedler, interim director of the Center on Health Policy at the Brookings Institute, called America’s healthcare landscape a “patchwork.” 
The difficulty in navigating it is why he surmises constituents and lawmakers alike are flirting with the single-payer system Medicare For All would represent. 
But, he said, it would mean “shifting a lot of private healthcare spending into the government’s balance sheet, it’s going to be disruptive.” 
Private insurance companies have opposed the idea, because a true single-payer system would put them out of business. 
Additionally, higher taxes could be part of that equation, he suggested, to ensure coverage for everyone. However, the government would be able to negotiate or set prices for services, prescriptions or hospital budgets. 
Like Warner, Fiedler also pointed to different pathways to universal coverage that other countries have taken that could be used as reference points.
Some countries have single-payer models while others have tightly regulated private insurers with universal coverage mandates, a contrast to how U.S. insurers don’t cover everyone. 
“Some countries have employers contribute a portion of wages for health care, like we do for Medicare now. Some countries make decisions at the national level. Others have more local governments, or a mix,” Warner said.  
Analysts stateside have also laid out blueprints for incremental steps to universal coverage. The Urban Institute, for example, suggested enhancing cost-sharing subsidies and capping provider rates, among other steps. 
The results of Tuesday’s midterm elections could have direct implications on Congress’ approach to new healthcare policy. Two-thirds of Americans support Medicare For All, according to a new KFF poll.
Amid the fallout from the Republican-controlled Congress’ healthcare actions in the past year, Democratic candidates have focused their campaigns on making care accessible and affordable for all citizens. 
As Republicans attempt to hold their majorities and Democrats attempt to flip the chambers’ control, it still may be a couple of years before universal healthcare talks become more than campaign promises. 
It can’t come too soon for people like Meszaros, or others who fear bankruptcy due to medical debt or delay care because they’re under-or-uninsured. 
“Something is not quite right here,” Meszaros said.

(Photo by Charlotte Rene Woods/Virginia Mercury)Gov. Abigail Spanberger said on Oct. 29 that she is committed to adjusting Virginia’s K-12 funding formula, after a state research group found it needs subs[...]
text:
Virginia Gov. Abigail Spanberger speaks to press on April 27, 2026 at an event in Richmond touting policy accomplished during her first 100 days in office. (Photo by Charlotte Rene Woods/Virginia Mercury)Gov. Abigail Spanberger said on Oct. 29 that she is committed to adjusting Virginia’s K-12 funding formula, after a state research group found it needs substantial changes and advanced a plan to hire an expert tasked with studying a new funding mechanism for up to 24 months. 
The existing formula is over 50 years old, does not adequately reflect the real costs of operating schools, and has forced local governments to spend far more on K-12 education than the state.
Virginia lawmakers approve plan to advance new K-12 school funding formula

While the governor did not set a firm timeline for preparing it for the next biennium’s budget in December 2027, Spanberger said in an interview with the Mercury last Thursday that she aims to complete this monumental task before the end of the current administration, which ends in 2029.
“I’d do it tomorrow if we could do it,” said Spanberger. “(However) that is not realistic, but we have to get it done before the end of our administration.”
She also argued that a modernized funding formula could help Virginia’s schools better address monetary gaps and meet student needs.
 Earlier efforts

States outside of Virginia have taken two to three years to reform their K-12 funding formulas, emphasizing the challenge such an undertaking poses for state governments.
In Virginia, lawmakers and the legislative branch have had to find alternative ways to get the necessary funds to Virginia’s schools.
One successful initiative to provide financial relief to localities for students with specific needs, such as those qualifying for free lunch, English as a second language, or special education, came during former Gov. L. Douglas Wilder’s administration 30 years ago.
In 1992, Virginia created its K–12 At-Risk Add-On funding provision and dedicated $46.9 million in the 1992-1994 biennium. 
The Governor’s Commission on Educational Opportunity for All Virginians found that educating students from low-income households costs more than the state’s basic school funding formula provides. The add-on was intended to provide additional state funding to help cover those costs.
Ultimately, the provision eventually became state law and has undergone multiple changes.
 Looking ahead

Spanberger’s administration, lawmakers and education leaders, including the Virginia Association of School Superintendents (VASS), are eager to reform the new funding formula.
Sarah Calveric, VASS president, said the association is emphasizing that it be a student-driven formula that would better address regional demographic differences and geographic needs. 
This method would also give school districts the ability to attract and retain staff through alignment with prevailing wages, and enable them to procure specialized resources such as mental health providers and literacy specialists.
“When you create a funding formula that is more student-driven, it helps keep the focus on the main thing, which is students, their specific needs, and the geographic trends that school divisions are addressing on a daily basis,” Calveric said to the Mercury.
Lawmakers will return to Richmond to discuss education legislation and other subjects starting on Jan. 13. 
During the 45-day session, which the governor could extend, the Virginia Department of Education is expected to select a consultant, who will begin work during session after publishing its formal service request and selecting a bid.
The consultant will have to include policy factors such as base funding per student, class sizes, extra weights for student needs, operating costs, transition provisions and the Local Composite Index, which determines what each locality can pay for its schools.
The process will also include input from education leaders and other key partners on shaping the new formula.
Spanberger said one challenge of such a large-scale change is the limited timeframe of a single-term governorship to complete the work in four years. 
With only three years and two months remaining, the administration is trying to be aggressive to keep the project moving forward.

title: Commentary: Survey finds fear, desire for reset in Washington. Will Trump accept the results?
description:
(Photo illustration by States Newsroom)Virginians are distressed – for their wallets and our democracy – as we approach tomorrow’s congressional elections, according to an online survey that more than 350 Virginia Mercury readers responded to.
As well they should be.
It’s not just kitchen-table issues that are animating voters and driving them to the polls i[...]
text:
(Photo illustration by States Newsroom)Virginians are distressed – for their wallets and our democracy – as we approach tomorrow’s congressional elections, according to an online survey that more than 350 Virginia Mercury readers responded to.
As well they should be.
It’s not just kitchen-table issues that are animating voters and driving them to the polls in huge numbers, at least through early voting for a midterm election. The cost of groceries, healthcare, and gasoline and diesel fuel has forced Virginians to make some tough choices about what to pay for – and what to do without.
The war of choice in Iran has contributed to the angst, too.
Virginia Mercury readers head toward midterms with rising bills and doubts about Washington

Many also fear that President Donald Trump and his administration will try to overturn accurate results in a number of states, including the U.S. Senate race in Alaska. The administration has also questioned the legitimacy of 20,000 ballots in California; state officials and legal advocates have pushed back against the federal intrusion.
“Stopping Trump,” “Threat to democracy,” and “The illegal actions of our president and non-action of Congress to stop him!” and similar comments were repeated throughout the responses by Virginia Mercury readers.
Trump is threatening actions that the United States would have condemned had they occurred elsewhere. He’s spouting falsehoods because polls show Republicans will lose their majorities in the House (definitely) and the Senate (possibly). He has lied repeatedly about the accuracy and security of our election apparatus. Trump often sounds unhinged in his pronouncements.
As of Thursday, 1.41 million voters had cast ballots early in Virginia, according to the Virginia Public Access Project. That figure already surpasses the 976,558 total for the entire early voting period in 2022, when the last midterms occurred.
Virginia had nearly 6.47 million registered voters on Oct. 1, according to the state Department of Elections.
The Mercury conducted the unscientific survey – the first of its kind for this news organization – between Sept. 22 and Oct. 17.
Participants could select one of seven options as their biggest concern heading into Tuesday’s elections or fill in their own. The choices the news site offered: shrinking healthcare access, government waste and fraud, higher food prices, rising energy costs, lack of affordable housing, data centers and climate change. 

As my colleague Markus Schmidt wrote, some respondents view this election as a chance to rein in presidential power, while others said healthcare access and costs were utmost on their minds.
“My main issue is getting universal healthcare coverage for all and neither candidate (Republican incumbent Rob Wittman or Democrat Shannon Taylor in the 1st District) speaks to that,” wrote John Meszaros of Midlothian.
That dovetails with what Amber Kostka, co-owner and chief operations officer of three restaurants in South Hampton Roads, told me last week. I learned about her through a recent article at Time.com that discussed healthcare costs and quoted the restaurateur.
Even though Kostka provides health insurance to her employees and splits the cost of premiums with them, more and more told her they can’t afford the benefit. About 35% of her eligible employees now buy the employer-sponsored health insurance, she told Time.com, down from 50% before the COVID outbreak.
“Really, it’s just like everything is getting more expensive” for her employees, Kostka, 38, told me. “Their rents are going up. Their groceries are increasing … so where can they cut?”
Kostka even took a part-time job so she could cut back on her own salary to help out her employees. 
I reached out to Eric Claville for his take on the midterms. He’s a political and legal analyst at Norfolk State University, and we’ve appeared together on PBS affiliate WHRV-FM.
“The concerns expressed by Virginia voters in the (Virginia Mercury) survey are synonymous with what voters have expressed to me and from what I’ve read in other polls,” Claville told me by email. “Virginians are concerned about affordability, the voluntary war in Iran, and democracy under this president overall.”
“Based upon voter concerns about the actions of the Trump administration, the economy and the war,” he added, “and the lack of checks and balances within Congress and the Supreme Court, voters want a change.” 
That’s why the answers to the Virginia Mercury survey are suggestive. The looming question is whether this president accepts the will of voters or instead tries to subvert the results.

name: Rhode Island Current
title: How to convince more Rhode Islanders to get health insurance? Make it cheaper.
description: Bunny Ssengooba, a navigator with the Comprehensive Community Action Plan, attends community events like a Cambodian New Year celebration to share information about HealthSource RI and help people sign up for insurance coverage. (Courtesy photo)At a time when gas prices, energy bills and groceries are all increasing, Rhode Island officials have some good new[...]
text:
Bunny Ssengooba, a navigator with the Comprehensive Community Action Plan, attends community events like a Cambodian New Year celebration to share information about HealthSource RI and help people sign up for insurance coverage. (Courtesy photo)At a time when gas prices, energy bills and groceries are all increasing, Rhode Island officials have some good news to share: your health insurance premium could be going down.
That’s the case for 30,000 people expected to sign up or reenroll in the state health exchange during the 2027 open enrollment period, which began Sunday and runs through Jan. 31.
The discounts depend on income level, age and the type of health plan. But the result is shared wallet relief that HealthSource RI Director Lindsay Lang hopes will at least preserve the existing enrollment numbers.
“The importance of having health insurance is that it can help protect against one bad turn of luck turning into lasting financial damage,” Lang said at an Oct. 21 press conference to publicize the start of open enrollment.
It’s the same message Lang preaches every fall ahead of the annual open enrollment period. 
Yet 10,000 Rhode Islanders dropped out of the state health exchange during the three-month long 2026 open enrollment period, unable to afford the surging premiums resulting from expired federal discounts. And many of the 39,000 people who did sign up for HealthSource RI opted for cheaper bronze medal plans, which have lower premiums but less comprehensive coverage and very high deductibles.
Rhode Island was not alone; more than 23.1 million people dropped coverage in Affordable Care Act-created state marketplace plans in 2026 — the sharpest decline since its 2013 creation, according to KFF. 
At least 10 states created or reconfigured their own discount programs to replace the federal tax credits for the 2026 open enrollment period, including Massachusetts and Connecticut. 
Rhode Island’s subsidy program does not begin until 2027, leaving thousands of Rhode Islanders on the lurch for 2026.
Consequences have already begun to ripple through the state’s fragile healthcare system. Commercial premiums are again poised to rise by double-digit percentages as insurers seek to recoup costs associated with covering a more limited and medically risky group of enrollees. Hospital systems, including Brown University Health, have seen a surge in debt and uncompensated care, prompting layoffs and deepening fears of future service cuts. 
“It’s probably been one of the most challenging years,” said Bunny Ssengooba, a navigator for Cranston-based social services agency Comprehensive Community Action Plan. “We had a lot of people who just kind of said, ‘we hope we don’t get sick.’”
Ssengooba has spent much of the last 10 months finding creative ways to help low-income families pay for medication and health services despite being un- or underinsured. 
Now, he is preparing to reach back out to the thousands of residents who dropped out of the health exchange to persuade them to come back. He’s making phone calls and showing up to community festivals and food pantries with information about the new and improved affordability measures.
He knows it won’t be easy.
“It’s a lot faster for people to walk away and not get enrolled,” he said. “It’s much harder to get them back.”
It’s a challenge with personal stakes for Ssengooba.
At 46, he’s had 16 surgeries in the last seven years, including a kidney transplant, because of complications from  high blood pressure that went undetected and untreated for years because he did not have health insurance.
Now healthy, insured, and married to a doctor, the East Providence resident is intent on making sure others avoid his fate.
“I tell people, ‘your life depends on it,’” he said.
Filling the gap 
One thing working in his favor: thousands of state and federal dollars that officials have leveraged to replace lost federal discounts for plan participants across a wide range of circumstances.
Gov. Dan McKee pushed for a $9.5 million carveout in his fiscal 2027 budget proposal to help offset the expired federal tax credits, which Congress chose not to renew beyond 2025. State lawmakers agreed to McKee’s proposal, adding on another $10 million earmark to carry the state funding through the 2027 calendar year.
The $19.5 million Rhode Island Marketplace Affordability Program is expected to reduce premiums for 20,000 current, former, and future HealthSource RI customers at both ends of the income spectrum.
For people whose earnings fall below 200% of the federal poverty level — $31,920 for one person or $66,000 for a family of four — the state will return average premiums to the prices people paid before federal tax credits expired, according to HealthSource RI. For enrollees whose earnings are above 400% of the federal poverty level — $63,840 for one person or $132,000 for a family of four — state funds will partially replace lost federal tax credits.
There’s money on the table for those in the middle, too. A separate state initiative born out of a March 12 executive order aims to maximize federal tax credits by manipulating the funding formula based on silver medal plan premiums, a strategy known as silver loading. At the time McKee signed the executive order, officials hoped to bring in $12 million more in federal funding to defray premium costs.
The exact funding boost will depend on enrollment, Lang said, but the formula fix already completed is expected to help another 10,000 people who fall between 200% to 400% of the federal poverty level, saving an average of $110 per person per month over current premiums.
Lang acknowledged the state’s investments and formula-maxing strategy are not a panacea for healthcare access and cost concerns.  
“This is one piece of an enormous puzzle given the shift from the federal level to the state level,” she said in an interview. “The proof will be in the pudding now as we try to connect customers to this new help.”
Initial calls to HealthSource RI’s East Providence contact center ahead of the Nov. 1 open enrollment start were tepid, though Lang expects it will pick up after Thanksgiving, as key deadlines in reenrollment or new enrollment approach
A targeted marketing campaign that includes text messages, emails and phone calls, along with online and traditional advertising, has already begun. Meanwhile, a network of 100 navigators across partner community agencies, including Ssengooba, are filling their calendars with appointments and outreach events to connect with prospective plan participants in their communities.
As of Oct. 30, Ssengooba has already booked three weeks of appointments, representing 60 to 70 potential people or households interested in learning more about — and maybe signing up for — HealthSource RI.
“I’ve kind of put everything else on hold,” Ssengooba said. “This is too important.”



Open enrollment virtual information sessions
HealthSource RI has scheduled virtual information sessions on open enrollment at 9:30 a.m. on Tuesday, Nov. 3, and 10:30 a.m. on Thursday, Nov. 5. 
To sign up, or for more information on other informational events, visit HealthSource RI’s website. Appointments with navigators or through the contact center can also be booked online. 
To shop and compare plans anonymously, visit the online enrollment portal and accompanying calculator. 
Rhode Islanders have until Dec. 23, 2026, to select and pay for coverage to begin on Jan. 1. The last day to enroll and pay is Jan. 31, with coverage beginning Feb. 1.

title: An affluent southern Vermont town considers adding housing — or keeping green space
description:
A rendering of a potential housing development on Raptor Lane in Dorset. Vermont Integrated Architecture/Courtesy of Town of Dorset

Carly Berlin covers housing and infrastructure for Vermont Public, in partnership with VTDigger. 
On Tuesday, voters in the affluent Bennington County town of Dorset will decide whether the town ought to move forward with a hou[...]
text:
A rendering of a potential housing development on Raptor Lane in Dorset. Vermont Integrated Architecture/Courtesy of Town of Dorset

Carly Berlin covers housing and infrastructure for Vermont Public, in partnership with VTDigger. 
On Tuesday, voters in the affluent Bennington County town of Dorset will decide whether the town ought to move forward with a housing project on municipal land. 
Local officials hope to encourage homebuilding at the site on Raptor Lane, citing Dorset’s need for smaller, more affordable homes for local teachers and older residents looking to downsize. But an organized opposition campaign is urging residents to vote no, arguing that the land adjacent to the town forest should be preserved as green space.
Steven Zoric moved full-time to his family’s vacation home in Dorset from New Jersey during the pandemic. He helps lead an anti-development effort called Friends of Dorset.
“Keep Dorset the way it’s always been,” Zoric said in an interview. “We want to keep this as a pristine resource that the town has.” 
The town acquired the land along Raptor Lane in 2018 in a bargain sale, said longtime town manager Rob Gaiotti. Shortly afterward, officials asked residents what they hoped to see come of the site, and identified recreation, new town offices, housing and energy generation as priorities. Then the town built out a network of mountain biking trails there, and relocated its municipal building. Last year, it turned to housing.
A recent housing market analysis solicited by the town found that a typical home price in Dorset is $709,000 – double the value before the pandemic and triple what a local teacher’s salary can afford. Most homes in town are large single-family houses, and many serve as second homes or short-term rentals. 
In response to a 2025 request for proposals for the Raptor Lane site, the Rutland-based development firm S.M. Graves proposed constructing around 120 homes at a mix of price points.
But many residents balked at the scale of that project for a town of just over 2,000 people. The town tabled the idea and went back to the drawing board, studying other possibilities and asking residents what they wanted to see built. At the same time, some residents pushed for a townwide vote.
Tuesday, voters will consider a pared-down vision for the site: up to 35 homes constructed on 30 acres, about 10% of the town-owned land. Town officials have indicated that they now hope to seek out a nonprofit homebuilder, since the smaller scale of the project makes the math for workforce housing difficult for private developers. 
The vote is a preliminary step. The ballot item asks for voter approval to convey the land for the development of homes in the future. 
Gaiotti, the town manager, said a “yes” vote gives the select board the go-ahead to start conversations with developers “a little more in earnest.” A “no” vote would make the town reconsider its direction for housing at the site altogether, he said. 
One alternative option the town could look at, Gaiotti said, would be selling off individual lots to build single-family homes. The town currently doesn’t reap any property tax revenue from the land because it’s municipally owned, he said.
The vague language of the ballot item has opened it up to criticism from naysayers like Zoric, who argue that voters should know more details about future development plans and costs.
At the heart of the issue, though, is whether residents want to see the town grow.
Ben Weiss, a retired software developer who’s lived in town for over three decades, has served on town committees studying the development potential at Raptor Lane. He sees the town’s vision for a denser housing project as a unique opportunity – and worries that if his neighbors vote it down, any developer will be wary of trying to build there. Yet he’s watched as the project’s opponents have gained momentum.
“I think that some of those groups are organized by people who, you know, were very scared of this large development going in in their backyard,” Weiss said. He’s seen some relenting, though, as the scale of the project shrinks.

text:
The United Way of Rhode Island  has increased the income limits to qualify for winter heating assistance this year. (Photo by Emma Davis/ Maine Morning Star)More Rhode Islanders will qualify for winter heating assistance this year under higher income limits that took effect Sunday for a United Way of Rhode Island program.
The statewide nonprofit’s Good Neighbor Energy Fund helps households experiencing temporary financial hardship who earn too much to qualify for federal or state assistance. 
For the 2026-27 heating season, the fund has raised its income limits by roughly $18,000 for most household sizes. A family of four can now earn up to $115,500 annually and still qualify, compared with $96,450 last year. For a family of six, the limit has increased from $129,450 to $147,450.
There’s a name for working families who are surviving but not thriving in Rhode Island: ALICE

The United Way raised income thresholds to better reflect the cost of living for working families, drawing on the findings on its recent report, “ALICE in Rhode Island: A Study of Financial Hardship”
The report published Sept. 17 found about 43% of all households in Rhode Island can’t afford basic expenses such as housing, food, transportation, healthcare and childcare. 
“The face of need in Rhode Island looks very different today than it once did. More and more working households find themselves stretched thin by the rising cost of essentials,” Cortney Nicolato, president and CEO of United Way of Rhode Island, said in a statement. “The Good Neighbor Energy Fund is there for families who do not qualify for traditional assistance but still face the choice between keeping their heat on and paying for other necessities.”
Rhode Island households in need of energy assistance due to financial struggles can call United Way’s 211 helpline or contact their local Community Action Program agency to determine eligibility for the fund.
Maximum grants vary by heating source, ranging from $600 for electricity and natural gas to $825 for oil and propane. Households using wood can receive up to $650, while those using kerosene can receive up to $600.
The United Way has distributed nearly $280,000 in energy grants to 437 households last year, according to the nonprofit.
