name: Georgia Recorder
title: Georgia helped inspire the Medicaid work rules. Its own rules could soon end.
authors: Briah Lumpkins, KFF Health News, Sam Whitehead, KFF Health News
description:
Trey Wright receives Medicaid coverage via Georgia Pathways to Coverage. The program is slated to expire at the end of the year unless it’s renewed. Photo courtesy of Trey WrightAfter years of searching for affordable health insurance, Trey Wright discovered Georgia Pathways to Coverage.
The state’s limited Medicaid expansion program allowed the 27-year-old [...]
text:
Trey Wright receives Medicaid coverage via Georgia Pathways to Coverage. The program is slated to expire at the end of the year unless it’s renewed. Photo courtesy of Trey WrightAfter years of searching for affordable health insurance, Trey Wright discovered Georgia Pathways to Coverage.
The state’s limited Medicaid expansion program allowed the 27-year-old living in the rural city of Jesup in southeastern Georgia to finally visit a primary care doctor regularly. It also covered weekly shots to manage an array of allergies, saving him more than $1,700 a year in out-of-pocket costs, he said.
Gov. Brian Kemp pursued Pathways as an alternative to full Medicaid expansion, which 40 other states and Washington, D.C., adopted as part of the Affordable Care Act to make more low-income people eligible for healthcare coverage.
Gov. Brian Kemp speaks at a Georgia Chamber event in Athens, Aug. 5, 2026. Ross Williams/Georgia Recorder
Launched in 2023, Georgia’s program currently provides health coverage through Medicaid, the federal-state insurance program, to more than 20,000 people. It requires those enrolled to prove they’re working or doing other qualifying activities such as workforce training or community service — and it served, in part, as a model for the Medicaid work requirements that will roll out across most of the country starting Jan. 1.
Now Pathways, one of Kemp’s main health policy initiatives, is slated to expire at the end of the year unless it’s renewed. That would coincide with the Republican’s term ending, leaving his successor with big decisions about the program and challenges delivering on promises for Medicaid.
It’s a tight race between Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms, a former Atlanta mayor who wants to fully expand Medicaid eligibility, and Republican Rick Jackson, a healthcare staffing executive and billionaire who has pitched “intelligent Medicaid expansion” but has provided few details.
Whoever wins the governor’s race must decide whether the state can afford to bring Pathways in line with new federal Medicaid work rules established under President Donald Trump’s signature One Big Beautiful Bill Act. The federal rules include more exemptions than Georgia’s, and state officials said that would make the program fiscally unsustainable, by expanding coverage to an estimated 100,000 more people.
Joining the states that have expanded Medicaid coverage under the ACA could open the program to an estimated 347,000 uninsured Georgians, according to the Center on Budget and Policy Priorities.
“There’s a lot of opportunity for the next governor to implement changes that are rooted in the realities of Georgians who for so long have been locked out of the ability to achieve optimal health,” said Leah Chan, director of health justice at the left-leaning Georgia Budget and Policy Institute.
Midterm elections, a looming federal decision
Georgians whose incomes are at or under the federal poverty level — $33,000 per year for a family of four in 2026 — and who complete up to 80 hours of qualifying activities a month are eligible for Pathways.
Healthcare executive Rick Jackson, a Republican candidate for governor of Georgia, talks to reporters at the state Capitol in Atlanta after qualifying to run for governor on March 6, 2026. Ross Williams/Georgia Recorder
The future of the program rests heavily with the next governor, who will have to determine whether it’s fiscally sustainable past the end of the year.
The Jackson campaign did not respond to questions from KFF Health News. His campaign website says he plans to “use better technology” to “transform healthcare.”
Bottoms would “restructure” Pathways to cut through bureaucracy until Georgia fully expands Medicaid, said TaNisha Cameron, a spokesperson for her campaign.
“As governor, she will make meaningful improvements to Georgia’s eligibility and enrollment systems to ensure people can get enrolled and prevent people from being denied simply because of paperwork barriers,” Cameron said.
Bringing the program in line with federal law requires Georgia to offer exemptions to its work rules that it doesn’t now. For example, under the new federal Medicaid work rules as outlined, those who prove they are too sick to work wouldn’t be subject to the reporting requirements. Other groups can get exemptions, too, such as people with substance use disorder or caretakers for people with disabilities.
Georgia officials want the federal government to chip in more to pay for this expanded group of people who would qualify for an exemption. The state made a similar request for additional federal funding when it applied to create Pathways, but it was denied.
Former Atlanta Mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms speaks to reporters at an early childhood education event in Atlanta Sept. 29. Ross Williams/Georgia Recorder.
A state estimate projects an additional $1.4 billion in spending for this group by mid-2028. And state officials have signaled they may let the program expire at the end of the year if they don’t get the extra cash.
“The state will have no alternative but to make decisions that imperil health policy goals around personal responsibility and healthy choices,” state Medicaid agency officials wrote in their funding request to the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services.
CMS said it doesn’t comment on pending requests.
Carter Chapman, a spokesperson for Kemp, said the governor supports the request by the Department of Community Health, Georgia’s Medicaid agency, for enhanced funding and remains “committed, as he always has been, to ensuring Georgians have access to quality healthcare while maintaining fiscal discipline for the state.”
If the federal government grants the request, it could set a precedent for other states to draw down more federal money for limited Medicaid expansions, like Georgia’s, potentially putting the federal government on the hook for additional spending.
“It’s an attractive fiscal offer for states,” said Joan Alker, a health policy researcher and executive director at the Georgetown University Center for Children and Families.
That would reduce the incentives for states to fully expand Medicaid and might even encourage some to roll theirs back, policy researchers said.
But with Georgia’s work requirements serving as a model for the nation’s work rules, the chance of full Medicaid expansion in the state isn’t so far out of reach, said Laura Colbert, executive director of the consumer advocacy group Georgians for a Healthy Future.
“It’s almost kind of silly that our lawmakers continue to hold it at arm’s length when really the federal version is shaped or has been shaped by the Georgia model,” Colbert said.
In the states that fully expanded Medicaid, to keep their coverage enrollees must show they’re working, volunteering, or attending school for 80 hours a month, starting Jan. 1. Some states, such as Nebraska, have already started enforcing the rules. The states that did not expand their Medicaid programs to cover additional low-income adults won’t have to implement the work rules.
Enrollment issues
Full Medicaid expansion would cover people with incomes of up to 138% of the federal poverty level — amounting to $45,540 a year for a family of four using the 2026 figure. But that would require support from Georgia’s legislature, where Republicans in power have held firm against such an expansion for years. If Bottoms were to win the governor’s race, the Democrat couldn’t do the expansion alone: Under a 2014 law, it would require the approval of state lawmakers.
A train advertisement in Atlanta in May 2025 promotes Georgia Pathways to Coverage, which conditions Medicaid coverage on working, studying, or volunteering. (Gabe Brison-Trezise/KFF Health News)
Full expansion would also move hundreds of thousands of Georgians from subsidized Affordable Care Act plans into Medicaid, something opponents have long warned about. Those who make too much to qualify for Georgia Pathways but still make up to 150% of the federal poverty level can qualify for federal ACA subsidies that don’t cost states anything.
But even skimpy private coverage beats being on Medicaid, said Chris Denson, director of policy and research with the right-leaning Georgia Public Policy Foundation.
“It still hopefully gives them better access to see a primary care physician and other specialists than being on Medicaid,” he said.
Jackson’s proposal to find an alternative to full expansion would probably require tinkering with some of Medicaid’s rules, which would need federal signoff. Denson said that would probably take time. Georgia submitted its application for Pathways in 2019, but a protracted legal fight kept it from launching until more than three years later.
But policy researchers worry the state simply doesn’t have the capacity to sign people up if Georgia fully expands Medicaid. They point to the low participation in Georgia Pathways, which has an enrollment process that many have found difficult to navigate. Georgia Gateway, the state’s online portal to apply for social services such as Medicaid and Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program benefits, has a documented history of glitches, errors, and slow processing times.
Combined, the state and federal government have spent more than $128 million on the Pathways program, according to state data obtained through a public records request. As of Oct. 9, more than three years into the program, 20,606 people were enrolled. The state originally projected more than 25,000 people would be signed up after just one year.
Georgia’s Department of Community Health declined to make any officials available for interviews for this report and did not respond to specific questions about Pathways.
All of this means uncertainty for Pathways enrollees like Wright. 
As a part-time worker at a law enforcement training facility, Wright would probably be able to meet the work requirements under full Medicaid expansion, but a transition might not be seamless. He was unaware that he might lose his coverage through Pathways by the end of the year. Getting taken off Medicaid “would suck,” he said. He hopes the new governor can work out some way to help him maintain coverage, he added. 
Wright said he cast an early ballot for Bottoms. 
KFF Health News is a national newsroom that produces in-depth journalism about health issues and is one of the core operating programs at KFF — the independent source for health policy research, polling, and journalism.

name: New Hampshire Bulletin
title: Water bills surge more than other costs in US homes over 10 Years, new report shows
description:
Water pumps and electronic equipment at the Concord water treatment facility. (Photo by Molly Rains, New Hampshire Bulletin)This article originally appeared on Inside Climate News, a nonprofit, non-partisan news organization that covers climate, energy and the environment. Sign up for their newsletter here.
Drinking water costs spiked faster than inflation, [...]
text:
Water pumps and electronic equipment at the Concord water treatment facility. (Photo by Molly Rains, New Hampshire Bulletin)This article originally appeared on Inside Climate News, a nonprofit, non-partisan news organization that covers climate, energy and the environment. Sign up for their newsletter here.
Drinking water costs spiked faster than inflation, grocery prices and median household income, researchers at nonprofit Food & Water Watch outlined in a first-of-its-kind report released earlier this month.
The average community water system increased household drinking water prices by 62% between 2015 and 2025 — with costs in Louisiana, Maryland and New Hampshire having particularly steep rises, according to the 17-page report. California also stood out in the data when it comes to seeing expensive water bills.
Kristin Dobbin, an assistant professor of Cooperative Extension at the University of California, Berkeley, who was not involved in the report, called the analysis “extremely important.”
The finances behind drinking water are “not something we’ve had a big picture view on across the country before,” Dobbin told Inside Climate News, noting that broad trends are much easier to review for national electricity rates.
“We need to situate the water conversation within these broader concerns about affordability,” she said. “Certainly, it’s striking that they found just how quickly water costs have risen in the decade.”
Food & Water Watch gathered and analyzed 2025 water billing data for the nation’s 500 largest community water systems, which serve more than 155 million people, or 45 percent of the country. The nonprofit compared that data to household water bills from 2015.
The new report — “Surging Water Costs amid the US Affordability Crisis” — notes that last year, the average U.S. water system charged households $531 a year for 60,000 gallons of water, an estimate of annual average water use per household.
Eleven years ago, water systems typically charged about $336 a year per household, which is about $457 in 2025 dollars when adjusted for inflation.
While water bills vary greatly nationwide, a corporate water system in San Jose, California, had the highest price for water in the report, charging $1,416 annually in 2025.
Fifty-two percent of the 25 most expensive systems reviewed by Food & Water Watch were in California, despite the state’s systems representing just 18% of the 500 systems in the dataset.
In Louisiana, Maryland and West Virginia, water bills grew about twice as fast as state median household incomes, the report found.
In New Hampshire, bills grew nearly five times faster.
Mary Grant, the water policy director at Food & Water Watch, said West Virginia jumped out in the report.
Many water utilities claim that their bills are largely still affordable for median-income households, she said.
“But in some places like West Virginia, water bills are becoming unaffordable for a typical household at the median income, and that’s really a warning sign,” Grant said. “I think that we really need to have federal action to stop this crisis before more people suffer from unaffordable water bills.”
Affordability “is a legitimate challenge for many households,” said Jenn Kocher, a spokesperson for the National Association of Water Companies, which represents regulated, private water companies, which serve nearly 40 million U.S. customers.
Due to a publication embargo, Kocher could not review Food & Water Watch’s full report.
Still, after reviewing some of the findings Kocher said any assessment of water rates should also consider system performance, including reliability, water quality compliance and long-term infrastructure conditions.
Rising water bills “reflect sector-wide cost pressures, not ownership models,” Kocher, whose group has also fought for a permanent federal water-assistance program, said Monday. “In addition, rate comparisons should account for actual household usage and customer assistance programs, rather than posted rates in isolation.”
Why are water bills so high nationwide?
Dobbin, of UC Berkeley, said factors including inflation are having a big impact on the drinking water sector, which relies on specialized materials like treatment chemicals, a supply chain that was stressed during the COVID-19 pandemic and water infrastructure that is deteriorating nationally.
The Environmental Protection Agency recently found drinking water systems across the U.S. will need $625 billion in upgrades over the next twenty years to meet existing water quality standards. The American Water Works Association placed that figure closer to $960 billion.
In Maryland, a vast majority of customers receive water from municipal water systems, with rates set by city, town, or county governments instead of the Maryland Public Service Commission, which affects affordability, said Maryland People’s Counsel David Lapp, who heads an independent state agency that represents residential and noncommercial utility customers.
“Water service is an essential public service, but small privately-owned water systems in Maryland typically lack the customer base and financial resources necessary to provide that service reliably while maintaining affordable rates: of the 22 private water companies in Maryland, most serve fewer than 1,000 customers and some serve as few as ten,” said Lapp, who could not review the full embargoed report on Monday.
“In recent years,” Lapp said, “we have seen rates for customers of some of these private water companies, mostly in rural communities including in western Maryland, increase substantially.”
Other findings from Food & Water Watch’s report:

Water bills increased at 1.6 times the overall inflation rate and more than 2 times the rate for groceries
Water bills increased 19 percent faster than the U.S. median household income
Water bills were considered unaffordable for low-income households in 93 percent of the analyzed water systems
The “worst affordability crisis” was in Puerto Rico, where low-income households were charged a “dangerous 20 percent” of their income for water, researchers said

In the report’s list of recommendations, the nonprofit said local and state governments should ban water privatization and repeal pro-privatization legislation, as well as hold polluters accountable for drinking water contamination and large corporations for emitting new contaminants.
Congress and the federal government should also “reject cuts to safe and clean water and restore federal funding to address the nation’s water affordability crisis,” report authors noted. A Congressional Research Service report from earlier this year detailed stark cuts to federal water infrastructure planned by the Trump administration.
Looking ahead, Food & Water Watch said droughts and severe weather — driven by climate change — are expected to continue to “threaten water supplies and infrastructure globally, generating expenses that will be pushed onto ratepayers.”
Data center construction and expansion, compounded by intense water-use by industries like large-scale farms, are also expected to push up water costs, Food & Water Watch said.

name: Rhode Island Current
title: Commentary: What price political influence? A lot more in Rhode Island.
description: The Rhode Island General Assembly should consider examining  whether restrictions on  political campaign contributions from lobbyists are adequate under the state’s campaign finance laws. (Getty illustration)Election Day is fast approaching, and Rhode Islanders are besieged by political advertising again. Television commercials intrude upon the evening news,[...]
text:
The Rhode Island General Assembly should consider examining  whether restrictions on  political campaign contributions from lobbyists are adequate under the state’s campaign finance laws. (Getty illustration)Election Day is fast approaching, and Rhode Islanders are besieged by political advertising again. Television commercials intrude upon the evening news, campaign literature accumulates at doorsteps, and social media feeds become an unrelenting parade of candidates’ promises. Beneath the spectacle lies a more consequential and seldom-scrutinized question: Who pays for it all, and what influence might it purchase?
Campaigns cost money. Candidates must communicate with voters and organize supporters to amplify their messages as they compete for public office. In our electoral system, political contributions are therefore a lawful, legitimate, and indeed indispensable part of democratic life. But the rules governing those contributions warrant close scrutiny, particularly when the donors are individuals whose profession centers on influencing the very officials they help elect.
A comparison between Rhode Island and neighboring Connecticut provides an instructive snapshot.
Under Rhode Island law, individuals, including registered lobbyists, may generally contribute up to $2,000 annually to a candidate. The limit doubled from $1,000 following legislation enacted in 2023. The increase permits larger donations from individuals who have a direct professional interest in decisions made at the State House.
Connecticut law generally limits registered communicator lobbyists (i.e., those who directly seek to influence government officials) to $100 in contributions to covered state candidates and political committees. The law also restricts certain fundraising and contribution-bundling activities. Moreover, Connecticut prohibits both communicator and client lobbyists from making or soliciting covered campaign contributions during legislative sessions.
Given Providence’s proximity to Hartford, the contrast merits consideration. A lobbyist who may contribute $2,000 to a Rhode Island legislative candidate would generally face a $100 limit when making contributions to a comparable Connecticut candidate, with additional restrictions during the legislative session.
The distinction raises many reasonable questions of principle. Why should two neighboring states maintain such different boundaries between lobbying and campaign fundraising? Does Connecticut’s more restrictive approach reflect a greater commitment to integrity in its political processes, or does it more so reflect a divergent conception of the relationship between money and political influence? If the answer leans toward the latter, Rhode Islanders are entitled to ask what principles inform their state’s judgment, and whether those principles adequately protect public trust.
Lobbying itself is not intrinsically suspect, nor is it incompatible with representative government per se. Labor unions, businesses, professional and trade associations, public interest groups, and community advocates all employ lobbyists to articulate their interests, though industry spending varies widely, with labor’s share of federal lobbying spending representing a remarkably paltry portion relative to corporate and business sectors. In theory, however, legislators in a pluralist polity benefit from weighing competing perspectives, especially on multiplex matters of public policy. Indeed, lobbyists and government relations professionals often have the specialized knowledge and expertise that animates the legislative process, sometimes even drafting the initial versions of consequential legislation before it heads to committee.



Quotation







Why should two neighboring states maintain such different boundaries between lobbying and campaign fundraising?


At the same time, a campaign contribution is not tantamount to quid pro quo corruption. Many donations reflect longstanding relationships, shared policy preferences, and legitimate support for a candidate’s political agenda. Under the prevailing rules of the game, assuming otherwise would be unfair.
However, the absence of demonstrable corruption does not settle the dilemma of how unequal access to political influence affects public trust. A contribution can be entirely lawful and still elicit reasonable misgivings about influence, fairness, and the specter of preferential treatment. Citizens who lack the resources to make substantial donations may reasonably wonder whether their concerns receive the same attention as those of politically connected donors.
Rhode Islanders need not resort to hypotheticals. In 2024, Rhode Island Current reported on campaign contributions from Citizens Bank’s political action committee to influential state officials as lawmakers considered a tax provision affecting the bank. The reporting did not establish that contributions determined the legislation’s outcome. It did, however, illuminate the troubling coupling of fundraising and policymaking in Rhode Island. For instance, the Providence Journal reported that lobbyists in the state collectively earned “nearly $17 million” in 2025.
Connecticut’s restrictions do not purge money from politics. Nor should one provision ever be mistaken as a panacea to the inequalities of political influence. For instance, sweeping campaign finance reform might go so far as to require a 28th constitutional amendment overturning the Supreme Court’s ruling in Citizens United v. FEC (2010). Otherwise, wealthy donors, independent political organizations, and well-financed interests still have ample alternatives for making themselves heard in electoral contests, including so-called “dark money” channels (e.g., 501(c)(4) organizations) not required to disclose the identities of their donors. With this in mind, Connecticut’s campaign finance laws show a state can distinguish between ordinary political contributions and contributions from individuals professionally engaged in influencing government decisions. Nevertheless, restrictions on contributions and their disclosure must also be evaluated against existing protections for political participation, speech, and expression.
Rhode Island already recognizes the value of transparency through its campaign-finance reporting requirements and public lobbying registry. But disclosure and restriction serve different ends. Knowing who contributed money allows citizens to examine possible conflicts. Limiting certain contributions seeks to foreclose such conflicts before they emerge.
The General Assembly should seriously examine whether Rhode Island’s campaign finance laws provide a durable foundation for public trust. This examination should include a systematic review of campaign finance laws in all state legislatures, with particular attention to Connecticut.
Asking whether money can be removed from politics altogether is certainly a worthwhile inquiry. The more targeted question, and one with a solution in sight, is where to draw the line between legitimate political participation (i.e., one which reflects the consent of the governed) and the undue influence of monied interests over lawmaking institutions.
Despite our shared border, Rhode Island and Connecticut have drawn that boundary in markedly different places.

title: Commentary: First-time voting recollections before heading to the polls
description:

So, I decided to reach out and ask the Capital Chronicle’s former interns to tell us a[...]
text:
Grab your sticker after casting your ballot. (Photo by Nuria Martinez-Keel/Oklahoma Voice)Voting is one of the most important duties you have as a citizen, but not everyone takes advantage of the opportunity. Hoosiers especially consistently rank low in turnout nationally.
So, I decided to reach out and ask the Capital Chronicle’s former interns to tell us about their first voting experience. Maybe it will remind you of your own or encourage non-voters to get out and cast a ballot. Everyone gets a say in this society, so don’t waste your opportunity.
Mia Hilkowitz
“I voted for the first time in fall 2022. Even though I was attending Indiana University Bloomington at the time, I drove the three hours home to vote in my hometown because I wanted to experience of going to the polls and voting in person. I made a whole day of it, going with my childhood best friend to vote — we went for coffee before then took photos with our “I voted” stickers. I loved going in person and getting to see everyone waiting in line, and there was a lot of excitement. What I’ve noticed from going to the polls (and now reporting on elections in the same area) is that many people are just as energized to weigh in on local issues and races as they are governor and presidential races. Every election since, I’ve voted in person and encouraged my friends and families to go vote.”
Madelyn Hanes
“When I turned 18, the thing I was most excited about wasn’t celebrating my birthday or that I was becoming a legal adult. It was voting. As someone who had always been fascinated by government and politics, I had spent years learning about elections, watching debates and talking about the things that shaped our country. But until I turned 18, voting was something I could only watch other people do or hear my family talk about.
That fall, I was taking my high school’s “We the People” government class. My teacher suggested that our class sign up to work the polls, and I immediately volunteered. I thought it would be a great way to experience an election up close, not realizing at the time just how meaningful it would feel to participate in one myself.
That Saturday, I woke up early and headed to the polling place. I was excited to spend the day helping other people vote. But there was another reason I was especially excited. When my shift was over, I would finally get to vote, too. When I walked through the doors, I quickly discovered that I was the youngest poll worker there. Naturally, that became the joke of the day. Everyone knew this wasn’t just another Saturday for me. It was going to be my first time voting.
After my shift ended, I stepped into line with everyone else. I scanned my ID, filled out the paperwork, and waited for my turn. Then, finally, I stood in front of the voting machine. For a moment, I was nervous. I had done my research. I read about the candidates. I had spent years learning about government. But standing there, with the ballot in front of me, I realized how different it was to learn about democracy and actually participate in it.
I was 18. I was still in high school. I certainly didn’t know everything, and there were races on the ballot where I found myself unsure of what I believed. But I also realized that I wasn’t expected to know everything. Voting wasn’t about having every answer. It was about taking the time to learn, making the choices I felt were right for me and allowing my voice to be counted.
So, I made my selections. And then I cast my vote.
The moment itself was surprisingly simple. There were no fireworks or dramatic announcements. But the people around me made sure I knew it was something worth celebrating. The other poll workers clapped for me, and one of them took a picture of me standing next to the voting machine. Then I did something I had been looking forward to for years.  I grabbed one of the “I Voted” stickers and stuck it on my shirt. I remember being so proud of that little sticker.”
Marissa Meador
“My first time voting was in 2020, right as I was turning 18. I was so excited  to finally be a part of the democratic process that I went around at lunch helping other high school seniors register to vote, which was probably very annoying to some of them. I always got a thrill around election season, fascinated by the idea that the future would be shaped depending on what types of people felt inspired to vote and the moment’s most salient issues. I wanted to make sure I was always a small piece of that decision. I cast my ballot early at the church across from my high school in Mooresville, Indiana, after waiting in a very quick line with a friend. And I obviously had to display my “I voted” sticker for the rest of the day. Voting has never felt quite as special, but I’ve made sure not to miss an election since. And while it can be easy to question whether your one vote really matters, all you have to do is look at some of the razor thin margins some Indiana races have had recently. You never know when a race will be close!”
Jack Forrest
“I have a hard time remembering much of anything about the first time I voted. Going early and in person during the 2024 General Election, I stood in line. I went to a booth. I filled in some bubbles. And I turned in a piece of paper. It felt pedestrian, routine even. Like I was at the dentist’s office or taking a standardized test. It was unremarkable, really.

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Top matters at stake this Indiana Election Day
description:
The City-County Building in Indianapolis on Oct. 27, 2026. (Photo by Niki Kelly/Indiana Capital Chronicle)The final ballots will be cast Tuesday for an Indiana election in which voters are deciding whether Republicans will continue their political dominance in the state.
Democrats are looking for secretary of state candidate Beau Bayh to provide a breakout v[...]
text:
The City-County Building in Indianapolis on Oct. 27, 2026. (Photo by Niki Kelly/Indiana Capital Chronicle)The final ballots will be cast Tuesday for an Indiana election in which voters are deciding whether Republicans will continue their political dominance in the state.
Democrats are looking for secretary of state candidate Beau Bayh to provide a breakout victory over Republican Max Engling, while the GOP is aiming to extend its streak of winning all statewide elections since 2014.
Signs of a negative national mood toward President Donald Trump have Democrats eyeing the potential of gaining seats in the Legislature and perhaps scoring an upset in a congressional race.
Voters will also be deciding the fate of a proposed state constitutional amendment that would give judges the power to deny bail for more defendants they believe pose a danger to the public. 
Dozens of school referendums will also be decided, and voters will see some candidates running on a partisan basis for school board for the first time.
Expensive battle for Statehouse office
Bayh benefited from connections of his father — former governor and U.S. Sen. Evan Bayh — in becoming the best-financed and best-known Democratic candidate this decade.
That’s allowed the 30-year-old attorney and Marine Corps veteran to outspend 39-year-old Engling, who was a largely unknown staffer to U.S. Sen. Jim Banks before jumping into the race in May and knocking off current Secretary of State Diego Morales for the GOP nomination.
Democratic candidate Beau Bayh smiles Thursday, Oct. 22, 2026, during a secretary of state debate against Republican candidate Max Engling at Fox59/CBS4 studios in Indianapolis. (Photo by Grace Smith/IndyStar pool)
Engling embraced the Republican mantra of election security in his campaign while attacking Bayh over his Washington-area upbringing and reliance on donors tied to his father.
Bayh, meanwhile, frequently denounced what he called corrupt spending by Morales and claimed Engling’s promise to work with the state inspector general on an internal review was an inadequate response.
Recent polls have found a tight race between Bayh and Engling, with both well ahead of Lincoln Party candidate Greg Ballard and Libertarian Lauri Shillings.
Democrats hope Bayh can boost their candidates for other state and local positions.
“It creates momentum and excitement, and you’ve got a good candidate that fits the state,” Terri Austin, a former longtime Democratic legislator from Anderson, said of Bayh’s campaign. “He has run an excellent race.”
An October poll showed 54% of Indiana voters disapproving of Trump, with 44% saying they approved of the president’s performance. Republican Gov. Mike Braun’s numbers were lower, with 48% disapproving and 38% approving.
That follows Trump winning Indiana in all three of his presidential runs by at least 16 percentage points.
“Voters, including Republicans, are souring on Trump all over the country,” said Christine Matthews, a campaign pollster for former Republican Gov. Mitch Daniels whose firm conducted the survey.
[Voter Guide: 2026 Primary Election Voter Guide: The candidates, the ballot measures, and the tools you need to cast your vote.]
Republican Indiana House Speaker Todd Huston wouldn’t speculate on what impact the secretary of state’s race will have on down-ballot races amid disgruntlement with Trump.
“When you’re the party of the president, you know that the midterm has a chance to be challenging,” Huston told the Capital Chronicle. “I feel like Max is really running a good campaign and doing everything he can. But I always tell our team we’ve got to focus on what we can control and those types of variables, they’re outside of our control.”
The secretary of state’s race drew an unusual four-candidate field with Ballard’s entry. The former Republican Indianapolis mayor’s campaign gathered more than 40,000 voter signatures to make the ballot under the Lincoln Party banner.
If Ballard receives at least 2% of the vote, the Lincoln Party’s candidates will get their names on general election ballots for the next four years in its goal to help what he called “independent-minded candidates.” If he tops 10% the new party would join Republicans and Democrats in nominating candidates through primaries.
Shillings is seeking to maintain the Libertarian Party’s ballot status that it has held since the 1994 election.
Voters will also decide the race for state treasurer between Republican incumbent Daniel Elliott and Democratic challenger Coumba Kebe, and whether Republican Elise Nieshalla will continue as state comptroller as she faces Democrat Jessica Bailey and Libertarian John Schick. 
Republicans defending legislative and congressional seats
Republicans have held two-thirds supermajority control of both state legislative chambers since the 2012 election. Democrats need to flip four seats from the current 70-30 Republican House margin to break that status and gain some more influence.
Several of the toughest races are in a cluster of Republican-held seats across the northern suburbs of Indianapolis where voters have trended more Democratic in recent years. 
Democrats even targeted Huston’s hold of his Hamilton County seat over his support of data center tax breaks and increases to the state’s gasoline tax.
Worries about data center projects and rising utility bills were a prominent part of Democratic attacks against Republicans on affordability issues 


Final days to vote
Early in-person voting for Indiana’s elections ends at noon local time Monday.
Local polling sites are open 6 a.m. to 6 p.m. local time Tuesday. Anyone determined by election officials to be waiting in line at poll closing time is allowed to vote under state law.
Any mail-in absentee ballots must be received in the county election office by 6 p.m. Tuesday in order to be counted.


A Free Press Indiana poll taken in October found 69% of likely voters surveyed opposed to new data center construction, with only 18% in favor. Similar opposition is being seen across the country.
Matthews, who has overseen frequent polls in Indiana, said Hoosiers’ attitudes have shifted rapidly to become “overwhelmingly negative” toward data center projects.
“Anyone associated with data centers is going to suffer for that,” Matthews said.
While all 100 Indiana House seats are up for election, half of the 50 Senate seats are on the ballot. 
Republicans faced turmoil in the May primary as several incumbent senators lost to Trump-backed challengers following their votes against congressional redistricting.
The fall campaign has been quieter as Republicans are virtually assured of keeping a strong Senate majority, but Democrats are hoping to chip into the chamber’s current 40-10 GOP margin.
The most competitive of Indiana’s U.S. House races is the 5th congressional district, where Republican U.S. Rep. Victoria Spartz faces Democratic state Sen. J.D. Ford.
Although Spartz won her third term by 18 percentage points two years ago, some national Democratic groups have spent heavily on attack ads against her.
Indiana’s other six Republican and two Democratic U.S. House members are also seeking new two-year terms.
Constitutional amendments and new casino question on ballots
The statewide ballot includes two public questions that, if they win approval, would amend the Indiana Constitution.
One proposal would allow judges to deny bail to any defendant if prosecutors prove that person poses a public danger if allowed out of jail.
The state constitution currently guarantees defendants the right to bail except in cases of murder or treason.
Supporters say the amendment is needed to detain defendants who repeatedly commit violent crimes while on bail, while critics worry it jeopardizes due process rights for defendants who could face months in jail without a conviction.
The second proposed amendment would allow judges of city or town courts to live outside the municipality.
Voters in three Fort Wayne-area counties also will decide whether to give permission for construction of a possible $500 million casino project.
That question is on the ballot in Allen, DeKalb and Steuben counties.
If voters in a county agree to allow a casino, prospective casino developers can submit their applications for that specific county to the Indiana Gaming Commission by Dec. 1.
Lawmakers earlier this year required a company winning that license to spend at least $500 million on the casino and related amenities within five years.

name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: Louisiana’s US Senate race no longer a ‘gimme’ for Republicans
description: National election prognosticators have downgraded the chances that Republican U.S. Rep. Julia Letlow, left, will win the U.S. Senate race in Louisiana, while Democrat Jamie Davis continues to gain ground, according to campaign analysts. (Photos by Wes Muller/Louisiana Illuminator)For months, the outcome of the U.S. Senate race in Louisiana was considered a f[...]
text:
National election prognosticators have downgraded the chances that Republican U.S. Rep. Julia Letlow, left, will win the U.S. Senate race in Louisiana, while Democrat Jamie Davis continues to gain ground, according to campaign analysts. (Photos by Wes Muller/Louisiana Illuminator)For months, the outcome of the U.S. Senate race in Louisiana was considered a foregone conclusion. Congresswoman Julia Letlow, R-Baton Rouge, was expected to easily beat Democratic candidate Jamie Davis, a farmer and one-term Tensas Parish police juror.
But on the eve of Election Day, a GOP victory appears less certain, according to election analysts as well as political advisers and elected officials from both major parties with recent experience in statewide Louisiana campaigns.
Most predict Letlow will still win the Senate seat. But nearly every person interviewed said Davis, a political unknown to most of the state until this year, could come close to victory.
“I think the race will prove to be very interesting,” said Greg Rigamer, a Metairie consultant who has conducted polls in Louisiana for decades including during this election cycle.
Two nonpartisan election prediction websites, Inside Elections and Sabato’s Crystal Ball, moved the U.S. Senate race in Louisiana from ratings of “safe Republican” and “solid Republican” to “likely Republican” last week. The change is positive development for Davis because it indicates national analysts think he has a better, if still unlikely, chance of winning the race.
Letlow’s campaign has also appeared to operate from more of a defensive position in recent days following outstanding turnout for Democrats during the early voting period. They accounted for more than 42% of all votes cast in the seven-day period, compared with 39% for Republicans.
The day after early voting closed, a super PAC supporting Letlow launched a negative attack ad against Davis, and President Donald Trump announced he would hold a virtual rally for Letlow Monday.

A win for either Letlow or Davis would be historic.
If Letlow wins, she would be the first Republican woman elected to the Senate from Louisiana and only the second from either party. If Davis wins, he would be the first Black person to hold a statewide elected office since the post-Civil War Reconstruction era 150 years ago.
“Have African Americans been this close [to winning a statewide election] in a long time? I can’t say that they have,” said former U.S. Rep. Cedric Richmond, D-New Orleans, who was also a senior adviser to President Joe Biden.
National influence
Louisiana’s political leadership has become increasingly Republican over the past decade. Only one Democrat, former Gov. John Bel Edwards, has won a statewide election since 2008.
Yet the national political climate heavily favors Democrats this year as prices for gas, food and most other consumer goods remain stubbornly high. Some policies President Donald Trump and Republicans embrace have also hit Louisiana particularly hard.
The U.S. Supreme Court decision in April that cut protections for minority political districts has spurred higher Black voter turnout, which benefits Democratic candidates. The countrywide, bipartisan backlash against data centers, which Gov. Jeff Landry and other GOP officials in Louisiana have championed, could also work in Davis’ favor, according to political experts.
In recent years, Louisiana seemed impervious to “blue wave” elections where Democrats were swept into office en masse. This year could change that narrative, however. Even if Davis doesn’t win the race but loses by a single-digit percentage margin to Letlow, it would show Republicans could be vulnerable next year when Gov. Jeff Landry and other statewide GOP officials are on the ballot, campaign consultants said.
“It definitely shows that we are capable of being part of national trends, even if we don’t change the outcomes that we have,” said Mary Patricia Wray, who ran Edwards’ successful gubernatorial campaign in 2015. She also oversaw U.S. Rep. Cleo Fields’ 2024 campaign win and Public Service Commissioner Foster Campbell’s unsuccessful U.S. Senate race in 2016.
Explosive spending, ugly ads and courtroom battles set stage for tense midterm elections

The Davis campaign maintains its candidate can win the race. It released results from a poll it paid for showing Davis and Letlow in a dead heat in the last week of the race.
The Letlow campaign responded to a request for comment about the closeness of the race by sending the same written statement it provided earlier in the week.
“Julia Letlow is going to win because she has a proven record of delivering real results for Louisiana,” it said.
Trump defines campaign
From the beginning, Letlow’s campaign has also largely been shaped by Trump’s endorsement of the congresswoman and, to a lesser extent, her link to Landry. The governor’s top political consultants are working for Letlow on the race.
But neither Trump nor Landry is particularly popular in Louisiana. The Silver Bulletin composite of several polls measuring the president’s approval rating showed him with 37% support as of Sunday. The most recent polling on Landry’s popularity was in March when the conservative Pelican Institute for Public Policy measured his approval rating at 43%.
Letlow hasn’t made many public appearances to distinguish her political views from those of the governor or president, political consultants noted. She also hasn’t participated in public debates with Davis or any other candidate since launching her campaign in January.
“I don’t think she is very well-defined, and she did not try to define herself in this general election,” said Roy Fletcher, a Republican political consultant who helped elect Mike Foster in 1995. Fletcher is not working on the Senate race but is advising candidates in U.S. House races this election cycle.
Letlow also went through a punishing party nomination process to earn the Republican spot on the Nov. 3 ballot. She eliminated the incumbent, U.S. Sen. Bill Cassidy, in the May primary and then bested state Treasurer John Fleming in the June runoff.
While Davis also went through Democratic primary and runoff elections, Letlow’s were more contentious with more attacks from better-financed candidates.
Fleming, in an interview Friday, questioned whether divisions in the Republican Party have healed since the GOP primary. He said his supporters are still concerned about the nondisclosure agreement Letlow signed related to the Meta data center project in Richland Parish.
“They are ready to stay at home rather than turn out to vote” for Letlow, Fleming said.
Louisiana Republican Party Chairman Derek Babcock said he is confident Letlow will win. While Black voter turnout was high during the early voting period — at 34%, a congressional midterm record for Louisiana —  Babcock said he isn’t worried because conservatives are more likely to vote on Election Day.
Whatever rift occurred during the Republican primary elections has healed over the past few months, he added.
“The most important vote the next senator is going to take is for Senate leadership. We can’t risk having a Democrat,” Babcock said.

title: Voters make governors, utility regulators answer for high power bills
description: A group of Maine residents protest a proposed electricity price increase ahead of an October 2025 public hearing in Freeport. Rising utility prices are increasingly drawing scrutiny from voters and state officials. (Photo by AnnMarie Hilton/Maine Morning Star)As broad affordability concerns define elections across the country, voters in several states on Tue[...]
text:
A group of Maine residents protest a proposed electricity price increase ahead of an October 2025 public hearing in Freeport. Rising utility prices are increasingly drawing scrutiny from voters and state officials. (Photo by AnnMarie Hilton/Maine Morning Star)As broad affordability concerns define elections across the country, voters in several states on Tuesday will have a say on their future utility bills.
State utility regulators, who are facing heightened levels of attention and scrutiny amid high prices, are on the ballot in nine states: Alabama, Arizona, Georgia, Louisiana, Montana, Nebraska, North Dakota, Oklahoma and South Dakota.
Most Americans are served by utilities overseen by state regulators, who approve or deny rate increase requests from providers. Public outcry over rising utility prices has pushed state regulators and lawmakers to consider rate freezes, additional energy assistance funds or new rates targeting large energy users such as data centers. And it’s brought even more attention to high prices in races for both governors and utility regulators.
“I think it’s different and it really emerged in the off-year elections,” said Ted Thomas, an energy consultant and the former Republican chair of the Arkansas Public Service Commission. “It began to emerge in 2024 as part of the overall concern on inflation, and then it seemed to have gone beyond that with a focus on energy specifically.”
Rising prices squeeze more Americans ahead of pivotal midterm elections

Utility prices played a major role in 2025 Democratic gubernatorial wins in New Jersey and Virginia. And in Georgia, Democrats last year flipped two seats on the board that regulates public utilities — the first time Democrats won statewide constitutional office there in nearly two decades.
Thomas is a senior adviser to the consumer advocacy group PowerLines, which is tracking how gubernatorial and utility regulator candidates are talking about power bills in races across the country. This cycle has so far proven bruising for incumbent utility regulators: In Alabama, two Republican incumbents were ousted during primary and runoff elections as the state faces some of the highest electricity prices in the South. Two of the three Alabama Public Service Commission seats are on the ballot Tuesday. 
Likewise, in Arizona, a Republican incumbent lost during his primary contest, leaving two Democrats and two Republicans running for two open seats this week. The Arizona Corporation Commission is currently composed of five Republicans.
“We can literally elect folks that are going to lower our electricity bills,” state Rep. Mariana Sandoval, a Democrat, said last month, according to the Arizona Mirror.
While Thomas expects an anti-incumbency wave Tuesday, he noted that there’s no guarantee for immediate relief on consumers’ bills. Though lawmakers of both parties are increasingly scrutinizing high electricity prices, state leaders say they have little ability to lower costs because of broader energy market realities.
Relief from energy bills unlikely as utilities request billions in rate hikes

While states can’t stop rising prices altogether, Thomas said they can do more to protect consumer pocketbooks and ensure residential households aren’t paying for large-scale industrial energy users.
“It’s a large, complex system that costs a lot of money, and it provides an essential service that is a good value, even at an elevated price,” he said. “But at the same time, (affordability) needs to be more of a priority. It doesn’t need to be the back burner issue.”
Utilities have requested billions of dollars in upcoming rate increases across the country.
This winter, U.S. households are projected to spend an average of $1,030 to heat their homes, an increase of $82 over last year, according to the National Energy Assistance Directors Association. That organization, which represents state employees administering federal energy assistance programs, said this winter’s predicted 8.7% increase is more than 2.5 times the rate of inflation. 
Projections are more daunting for the large share of people in Northeastern states who heat their homes with oil. The association projects a 50% spike in the average cost of heating homes with oil this winter.
The LCV Victory Fund, a political action committee associated with the League of Conservation Voters, has pledged to spend over $110 million to help elect Democrats to key House, Senate, and state races. Since summer, that organization has targeted the “energy bill voter,” which it describes as a crucial voting bloc of women, Black and Latino people, non-college-educated residents and voters who are less engaged with politics.
Data center backlash set to sway midterm elections

“This is an energy election,” Sara Schreiber, senior vice president of campaigns at LCV Victory Fund, said in an October news release. “We identified early on that Republicans were vulnerable when it came to energy costs. Voters are not simply frustrated, they’re angry at monopoly utility companies, Big Tech, and Big Oil, who are making record profits while families struggle.” 
While much of the backlash over rising costs has focused on the growing number of data centers, electricity providers say that isn’t the major driver of rising prices.
In a recent study it commissioned, the Edison Electric Institute, which represents the nation’s investor-owned electric utilities, said electric providers were working with state regulators to ensure data centers pay their fair share “and help keep electricity as affordable as possible.”
That study blamed rising prices on higher wholesale electricity prices and broader issues with regional multistate grids — components of electric bills that are not controlled by electric companies or state regulators. 
“Our focus is on protecting existing customers and communities and strengthening the grid we all rely on,” Edison Electric Institute President and CEO Drew Maloney said in a news release earlier this month.
Stateline reporter Kevin Hardy can be reached at khardy@stateline.org.

title: Opinion: A letter to the Sage of Emporia about poetry, bright red alarms and warning signs in western Kansas

text:
Kansas author Huascar Medina reads from his latest book, "Protest as Love Poem." He started his recent book tour in western Kansas. (Photo by Phillip Lee)Dear William Allen White,
It’s been some time since I last wrote you. The air is swirling across Kansas. Maddening gusts of uncertainty from east to west, and the entire nation is watching. I often call wind the prophet of change, and its message remains to be determined.
You once said of our great state, “Kansas is the Mother Shipton, the Madame Thebes, the Witch of Endor, and the low barometer of the nation. When anything is going to happen in this country, it happens first in Kansas.”
I often hark back to this quote when elucidating on the importance of Kansas. We shall see.


I‘m on a western Kansas book tour. My first stop was your hometown, where my publisher, Meadowlark Press, is based. You should know I was well received in Emporia. I left that reading fulfilled, a few books lighter and ready for what lay ahead, or so I thought.
Around midnight, at mile marker 149 on U.S. Highway 50, the blinking lights of wind turbines lay strewn across the horizon of an outstretched, overextended prairie like briar berries. They grow quickly as you enter Ford County. The blinking is synchronized, flashing like hotel alarm clocks needing a reset after a power outage.
I wonder if this is the first sign I shouldn’t be out here. Giant stoplights are an ominous sign to consider when you’re weary on the road and far from home. Out here, at this hour, I think of Marvin Bell’s “Incarnate: The Collected Dead Man Poems” and his line “On the dead man’s stopped watch, the time is always right.”
So, in my mind, I am not late. There’s no bad time to head west with all these unset alarms. I might be early.
I thought more about the first stop on my tour, just hours before, at Middle Ground Books. I sat drinking Nicaraguan coffee and breaking bread with the staff, with a large statue of a rabbit standing watch over me at the right corner of the cafe counter.
“I was born and bred in the briar patch … born and bred,” I say to myself now as I drive up Wyatt Earp Boulevard in search of a hotel parking lot.
Why would I start a book tour in western Kansas? My reply: “Why not?
 Does it seem foolish or unsafe? After all, I do consider myself a prairie fool.
There are many reasons to head west, especially right now. The recent U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement raids in the area caught my attention and infuriated me. I needed to sublimate.
Sublimation is a defense mechanism in which socially unacceptable, aggressive impulses are transformed into productive, socially acceptable, constructive behaviors. Creating art is a form of sublimation. There’s a poem in my collection titled “ICE sublimation.” You should check it out. 
Those ICE attacks were timely, coming right before election season. Officials called them “Operation Safe Community – Kansas” to gaslight the public, because masked men dressed in military tactical gear harassing hardworking Kansans is the exact opposite of safety. The optics have always been bad for the administration and, by default, the GOP. 
Those communities felt safer before the ICE raids. I know this because I was there after the fact, and people in the community told me so repeatedly. It didn’t make sense to do this now except for one reason: to intimidate the Latino and immigrant communities right before elections.
The Roger Marshall-Adam Hamilton race for U.S. Senate is extremely close. The race is a toss-up. Post-election headlines will either read: “Florida man loses bid for reelection to Kansas Senate seat” or “Local pastor too religious for Kansas conservatives.”
Trump administration officials claimed they were after “the worst of the worst” and highlighted five individuals they were targeting. A Wichita Eagle investigation later found the individuals had already been deported or were in custody. For three days, western Kansans fell under tyranny, and I didn’t hear a peep from Don’t Tread on Me enthusiasts.
I will think about that the rest of my life when I see those license plates. 
What occurred in western Kansas was an attack on the working class, the “trabajadores” who are the lifeblood of cities they live and labor in. There will probably be vitriol in response to this op-ed online, but it’s the same old tired song and dance from the alt-right, those who are fed hate daily by fake news stations drumming up nightly viewership. Soulless algorithms spread propaganda to get us to buy into the next big grift.
We don’t have much time to cover this right now, William. Just know that outside forces that don’t care about Kansans are influencing our politics like never before. I miss the days of trusted local voices who lived in the places they wrote about. Voices like you. We had a responsibility to our communities. To lie in a single line betrayed the trust to every neighborhood street and sidewalk. 
We have to walk the streets we write about. I won’t go on a tirade. The list of grievances is long. There’s already enough blame being thrown on the TV, radio and the internet. It runs back-to-back as slanderous political ads across Kansas. The fearmongering is relentless. The texts are infinite. I’ve never felt so wanted or targeted.
Independents have it the worst. We are bombarded by both sides. 
So much money is being spent on this election in Kansas. The latest figure I’ve read was $84.5 million dollars. I don’t want to hear any politician on any side say: “We don’t have money.”
What is worrying me today is what will happen next. Cults are most dangerous when they face collapse and exposure. The Branch Davidians, Jonestown, and Aum Shinrikyo all show what a cult of personality can do when the end is near.
I think about them as I finish my audiobook on my drive into Dodge City: “End Times Fascism,” by Naomi Klein and Astra Taylor. I check into my hotel via a kiosk, speaking with a virtual front-desk person from a third-party customer service provider.
Someone from another part of the world, unconcerned with what is happening here, smiles and says: “Welcome.” I walk into my hotel room. First, I check whether the alarm clock is blinking, then unplug the hotel room phone. Finally I check the weather to see what tomorrow might bring.
P.S.:
I continued my drive deeper into western Kansas. Yellow diamond-shaped road signs lined the highway. They say “Wind gusts” or “Severe side wind ahead.” All I can do is hold the steering wheel tighter. I keep trying to stay in my lane and in-between the lines, but this wind — I’ve never felt anything like it.
Here’s a poem about collective choices from my book, “Protest as Love Poem.” I hope you like it. 
Take care, my friend, 
HM
 
Found Transcript: Typewritten by the Wind on the Heads of Triticum Aestivum¹
We are bountiful, said the horizon to the skyline. We are rising,
emerging ahead, growing upright like rows of grain-filled wheat.
Every act of breaking bread begins here, in these fields—where
you and I meet. Right here, in Kansas, where souls are weighed
in bundles, not grams.
¹bread wheat
 
Huascar Medina is a poet, writer, and performer who lives in Lawrence. His latest book is Protest as Love Poem. Through its opinion section, the Kansas Reflector works to amplify the voices of people who are affected by public policies or excluded from public debate. name: Wisconsin Examiner
title: Race contrasts two approaches for the low-visibility state treasurer’s office
description: From left, Republican John Leiber and Democrat Yee Leng Xiong are running for state treasurer in Tuesday's election. Leiber is the incumbent. (Leiber, campaign photo; Xiong, Marathon County Board photo)The 2026 race for Wisconsin state treasurer is a contest between two visions for the office — a Republican incumbent who has centered his case on doing the jo[...]
text:
From left, Republican John Leiber and Democrat Yee Leng Xiong are running for state treasurer in Tuesday's election. Leiber is the incumbent. (Leiber, campaign photo; Xiong, Marathon County Board photo)The 2026 race for Wisconsin state treasurer is a contest between two visions for the office — a Republican incumbent who has centered his case on doing the job without “growing government,” and a Democratic challenger who believes the position could take a higher profile.
The campaign website for Republican incumbent John Leiber, who is seeking reelection, says that in his first term he “hasn’t added programs or built a bigger office,” but instead stuck to the list of duties assigned to the state treasurer.
Democratic challenger Yee Leng Xiong is a Marathon County Board member and treasurer of the DC Everest School Board in Weston, Wisconsin, southeast of Wausau. His campaign website says he intends to “act as an independent watchdog for Wisconsin taxpayers” advocating “transparent management and investment of public funds.”
The state treasurer’s office is among those identified in the Wisconsin Constitution. “The office was first imagined by the state’s founders as a check on the government’s financial decisions and a steward of its public lands,” the treasurer’s office website states.  
Over the years lawmakers have transferred or eliminated many of its duties, including cash and debt management, the state’s 529 education savings plan and the state local government investment pool. 
In 2018, however, Wisconsin voters rejected an amendment that would have eliminated the elected office from the constitution.
After that vote, Sarah Godlewski, who had led the campaign against the amendment, ran for state treasurer in 2018 and won, stating the agency should be a fiscal watchdog. In office, Godlewski took on public-facing roles, including working with county treasurers and promoting retirement security programs.
Godlewski didn’t seek a second term, instead joining three other Democrats seeking the party nomination to run for U.S. Senate in 2022. In early 2023 Gov. Tony Evers appointed her as Wisconsin Secretary of State when the incumbent, Doug La Follette, resigned shortly after taking office for his 12th consecutive term. Godlewski is now the Democratic candidate for lieutenant governor. 
The state treasurer’s remaining official duties include signing state checks (technically done by machine) and serving with the secretary of state and the attorney general on the state Board of Commissioners of Public Lands.
The board manages 75,000 acres of former federal land now held in trust for Wisconsin schools and also manages four trust funds. The largest, the Common School Fund, makes annual donations to school library systems. Over the last four years the Common School Fund has grown to about $1.6 billion, and the annual payments to libraries from the fund have grown each year, reaching $73.5 million in 2025-26.
Republican John Leiber
When John Leiber ran in 2022 against a Democrat who campaigned on continuing Godlewski’s approach, Leiber emphasized instead focusing on the job of treasurer as it was outlined in the state constitution and statutes. Other than Sen. Ron Johnson, Leiber was the only Republican that year to win a statewide office in Wisconsin.
Leiber has been a state legislative aide and has worked in the state Department of Revenue in the tax division. On the job since 2023, he has emphasized maintaining a lean office and focusing on his role on the Board of Commissioners of Public Lands. 
“This is the only dedicated funding for school libraries statewide and my top priority is to ensure the fund continues to thrive in the future,” Leiber said when he announced his reelection campaign a year ago.
Leiber’s campaign website states that in office, he “has not built a bureaucracy or invented new programs. He has administered the constitutional duties of the office, advocated for fiscal restraint with the Legislature, and focused on the assets he is charged to oversee.”
Democrat Yee Leng Xiong
Yee Leng Xiong has built a resume that includes election to multiple levels of state government as well as experience in running a nonprofit and membership on a state financial literacy council appointed by Gov. Tony Evers.
Xiong is a Wausau native whose parents were Hmong refugees from Southeast Asia. If elected he would be the first Hmong official elected to a Wisconsin statewide office.
Xiong says he can act as an independent watchdog over state finances.
“As Treasurer, you don’t answer to the Governor or the Legislature — you answer directly to the people,” Xiong said in January when he announced his candidacy. “I’m running to be an independent voice for taxpayers and to make sure Wisconsin’s money is managed responsibly, transparently, and in the public interest.”
On his campaign website, Xiong says that he has “experience managing budgets at every level of government” and is committed to “transparency and accountability.”
He also says he can bring his school board experience to bear in the decisions by the public lands board because he “understands firsthand how trust fund decisions impact local schools and students.”

name: Maine Morning Star
title: Collins, Jackson make their closing appeals in Maine’s pivotal US Senate race
description: Republican U.S. Sen. Susan Collins speaks to reporters outside the Winthrop Police Department on Oct. 29, 2026. (Photo by Emma Davis/ Maine Morning Star)The communications equipment for Winthrop’s emergency dispatch network had been failing almost daily, leaving the roughly 18,000 people across Kennebec County who rely on it with unreliable service. So, the [...]
text:
Republican U.S. Sen. Susan Collins speaks to reporters outside the Winthrop Police Department on Oct. 29, 2026. (Photo by Emma Davis/ Maine Morning Star)The communications equipment for Winthrop’s emergency dispatch network had been failing almost daily, leaving the roughly 18,000 people across Kennebec County who rely on it with unreliable service. So, the town manager reached out to U.S. Sen. Susan Collins. 
Collins, from the helm of the Senate Appropriations Committee, walked them through the process to secure federal earmarks, getting them a little more than $1.1 million earlier this year to purchase new equipment, including a tower that will more than double the range of wireless emergency communications. 
“It’s not a want. It’s a need,” Paul Ferland, police chief of both Monmouth and Winthrop, said after giving Collins a tour of the department on Thursday. “And for this community to take it upon themselves monetarily, it was just not feasible to get it done any time in the future.” 
This is one of several local stops Collins has made in her final days on the campaign trail before the Nov. 3 election, when she hopes to secure a sixth term. Meanwhile, her Democratic challenger, Troy Jackson, has spent his last days hosting public forums, events with high-profile national figures and press conferences highlighting Collins’ ties to President Donald Trump.  
Democrats view Collins’ seat as a key pickup opportunity in their efforts to gain more control in the U.S. Senate, and they’re hoping time has run out on the senior senator’s staying power given the Trump administration’s increasing unpopularity. 
“There are folks in the United States Congress, in the House and the Senate, that will not stand up to this president, regardless of what he decides to do,” U.S. Sen. Mark Kelly of Arizona said while stumping for Jackson in Brunswick on Wednesday. “It’s not right.”
Coupled by a late burst of ads, the last leg of the most expensive race in state history has underscored the two opposing approaches each candidates’ campaigns have centered on. 
“That’s what it boils down to,” Collins said in Winthrop. “I’ve been able to bring $1.5 billion dollars to Maine to support projects just like this one. That’s a pretty powerful argument.” 
After the event with Kelly in Brunswick, Jackson said, “People that think that Senator Collins has been doing all this, bringing in all this money, I mean, look, it’s a pittance compared to what we’re losing.” He posed the following question to voters: “Do you think the government’s working for you?” 
U.S. Senator Mark Kelly of Arizona, left, campaigns for Democratic U.S. Senate nominee Troy Jackson, right, at Flight Deck Brewing in Brunswick on Oct. 28, 2026. (By Emma Davis/ Maine Morning Star)
Final appeals
Vietnam veteran Bill Jefferson was drafted into a war he opposed. Now, the Buxton resident harbors similar resentment about the United States’ war with Iran. That’s part of why he supports Jackson, who has publicly opposed the conflict. 
During an event Jackson held with veterans at Flight Deck Brewing in Brunswick, Jefferson also said Jackson’s support of universal healthcare and eliminating U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement factor into his support. 
A lifelong Democrat, Jefferson previously worked as an immigration inspector on the Canadian border. He saw an ad for the job after 9/11 and thought he could do something positive, he said. He felt he did, but now he is reluctant to talk about his time in that role because he is appalled by how federal immigration enforcement is being run today, noting a lack of training and respect for human rights. 
“We all know right now that what’s happening in this country is completely wrong,” Jackson told the crowd of about 30 people. 
Speaking next to Kelly, who said he is considering running for president in 2028, Jackson said he wants to work with him to help “get our democracy back, get our government back, get things in place that actually helps everyday people instead of the billionaire class.”
Jackson has gotten boosts from several prominent Democrats, including Democratic U.S. Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York, independent Sen. Bernie Sanders of Vermont, and Democratic U.S. Sen. Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts. Meanwhile, former U.S. Sen. Joe Manchin of West Virginia, a Democrat turned independent, has campaigned with Collins. Trump has not visited Maine, but Vice President JD Vance praised Collins during his trip in August. 
As he has throughout the campaign,  during a press conference with the Maine Democratic Party on Friday in Portland, Jackson focused on Collins’ record of siding with the president the vast majority of the time. He also repeated his criticism of Collins voting to confirm Supreme Court Justice Brett Kavanaugh, who had a hand in overturning Roe v. Wade, during a fireside chat in Kittery with Planned Parenthood Action Fund President and CEO Alexis McGill Johnson on Thursday. 
At the same time, Collins was touting her federal earmarks in Winthrop. She pushed back on a reporter’s question about voters who said they want her to do more to stand up to Trump, listing off instances where she has clawed back funding, like the Sea Grant, and the rural healthcare fund she got put into the president’s signature spending law, which won’t offset the larger healthcare cuts in the law.   
“What I find that people are more interested in is the question, ‘Who can do more for the people of Maine?’” Collins said. “I think when I frame the question that way, the choice becomes very obvious.”  
Collins went on to say that even if Democrats win back the U.S. Senate, and she wins re-election, she’ll still have power. She’d then be vice chair of the Senate Appropriations Committee, as she was before her current role as chair. 
“Given the bad decisions that have been made in Augusta, given the fact that we’re a low-income state and that we’re also a heavily taxed state and the state with the oldest population by median age in the country, we need that help,” Collins said. “We desperately need the help.”
The senator continued to spotlight the help she’s been able to provide by way of federal earmarks in subsequent stops, which included what will soon be a new childcare building in Greenville and the ribbon cutting of a new public safety building in Milo.
Republican U.S. Sen. Susan Collins and staff in front of her campaign bus after visiting the Winthrop Police Department on Oct. 29, 2026. (Photo by Emma Davis/ Maine Morning Star)
Eleventh-hour ads
Halloween provided both candidates with opportunities to speak directly with voters. At Cross Point Church’s trunk-or-treat in Bangor, Collins displayed a trunk decorated in honor of America 250. Meanwhile, Jackson trick-or-treated with families in Portland, dressed up as a “cord of wood,” a reference to an ad Collins’ campaign aired last week that he and others have criticized as classist. 
It features retired broadcaster Bill Green, who was also in an earlier Collins ad. In the new ad, Green says, “we’re not talking about buying a cord of wood here. We’re sending someone to the U.S. Senate, and Troy doesn’t have the tools he needs to be effective.”
In response, Jackson told reporters in Brunswick on Wednesday, “Well, if taking away healthcare for people, getting us into foreign wars, and giving billionaires tax cuts are the tools, then yeah, no, I don’t have those tools.”
He added, “I’m a working class person, got into the Maine Legislature, ended up being the Senate president for six years. I know how to get shit done. She’s just scared that she’s going to lose.”
This comes after most of the negative advertising in Maine’s U.S. Senate race had come from outside groups. More than $260 million has been spent on ads, according to the ad tracking firm AdImpact, surpassing the previous state record of $200 million spent in the 2020 race between Collins and Democrat Sara Gideon.
In the final ad put out by Jackson’s campaign, the Democrat says Maine’s U.S. Senate election will decide the direction of the country, whether it’s for billionaires and Trump or everyday people.  
“It won’t be easy, but I’ve learned if your heart is in the right place, you can make things better,” Jackson says in the ad. “I owe nothing to the billionaires or Trump. I owe everything to the people of Maine.”
Democratic U.S. Senate nominee Troy Jackson speaks to veterans at Flight Deck Brewing in Brunswick on Oct. 28, 2026. (By Emma Davis/ Maine Morning Star)
