title: A procrastinator’s guide to New Hampshire’s biggest races in Tuesday’s midterms
description: On Tuesday, voters will cast ballots for governor, Congress and State House positions in a a race that could have big implications in the battles for both Congress and New Hampshire state government. (Photo by Will Steinfeld/New Hampshire Bulletin)In roughly 48 hours, voters across New Hampshire will be lining up at polls to cast ballots in a number of races[...]
text:
On Tuesday, voters will cast ballots for governor, Congress and State House positions in a a race that could have big implications in the battles for both Congress and New Hampshire state government. (Photo by Will Steinfeld/New Hampshire Bulletin)In roughly 48 hours, voters across New Hampshire will be lining up at polls to cast ballots in a number of races that could tip the balance of power in both Washington, D.C. and Concord.
Here’s a look at some of the races that will be on New Hampshire voters’ ballots Tuesday.
A nationally watched Senate race
Chris Pappas celebrates his primary election victory on Sept. 8, 2026. He defeated progressive organizer Karishma Manzur, who has never held elected office, by double digits in the primary. (Photo by Maya Mitchell/New Hampshire Bulletin)
New Hampshire’s U.S. Senate race has attracted attention from spectators across the country. Democrats are expected to make big gains in the battle for Congress, but the national Senate map is still favorable to Republicans. That means if Democrats want to take control, they’ll likely have to hold onto seats like New Hampshire’s.
The seat has been held for almost 18 years by Democratic Sen. Jeanne Shaheen, who announced she was stepping down early last year. That set up an open race.
On the Democratic side, U.S. Rep. Chris Pappas, who has been a reliably centrist voter in the House since 2018, was the first to get in the race and became the party’s nominee in September.
Republican John E. Sununu held this same seat from 2003 until 2009 when Shaheen defeated him in his first reelection bid. Now Sununu is trying to get New Hampshire to send him back to Congress. Sununu has a recognizable last name in the state. The candidate is the son and brother of two former governors and his father served as White House chief of staff to President George H.W. Bush.
Both candidates have sought to make this race about affordability, which has been a driving force across the country this election cycle.
Chris Pappas, left, and John Sununu, right, will face off in what promises to be a very expensive U.S. Senate race. (Left: Photo by Will Steinfeld/New Hampshire Bulletin; Right: Photo by William Skipworth/New Hampshire Bulletin)
Pappas blames President Donald Trump for inflation that’s been hitting Americans’ wallets, particularly his war in Iran which has driven up gas prices and tariffs which have raised costs for local businesses. Pappas has tried to tie Sununu to the president, who is suffering from very low approval ratings. To address inflation, Pappas has pitched increased funding to the Low-Income Home Energy Assistance Program (or LIHEAP) and exempting small businesses from tariffs.
John E. Sununu, brother and son of two former New Hampshire governors, files paperwork to run for U.S. Senate in the New Hampshire secretary of state’s office on June 10, 2026. Sununu has tried to distance himself from President Donald Trump, who has lost New Hampshire in three consecutive presidential elections. (Photo by William Skipworth/New Hampshire Bulletin)
Sununu has pitched old school Republican  market-based solutions to economic problems. That includes changing permitting regulations to build more energy infrastructure and reining in federal spending to address the deficit. He’s tried to distance himself from Trump and eschewed Pappas’ accusations that he’d be beholden to the president, even going so far as to say in one campaign ad, “I’ve never even met the man.”
Pappas has attacked Sununu for spearheading a plan during his time in Congress to explore privatizing Social Security. Both candidates publicly oppose cutting benefits, but Pappas argued that Sununu’s privatization plan would put the program at risk of failure. Sununu contends that the program would be in better fiscal shape today if the plan went into effect.
Sununu has argued that during Joe Biden’s presidency, Pappas supported a Democratic agenda that spurred inflation. During a WMUR debate Wednesday, the two disagreed on who contributed to inflation more: Biden or Trump.
A quieter gubernatorial race
In elections where a state has a highly contested Senate battle, the race for governor can sometimes feel overshadowed.
Gov. Kelly Ayotte is seeking reelection for the first time against a challenge from former Executive Councilor Cinde Warmington.
Ayotte was elected in 2024 (New Hampshire is one of two states with two-year gubernatorial terms) and has pushed a tough-on-crime agenda as well as a series of housing laws in her first term. Before being elected governor, Ayotte served in the U.S. Senate and as state attorney general.
Cinde Warmington, left, and Gov. Kelly Ayotte, right. (Left: Photo by William Skipworth/New Hampshire Bulletin; Right: Photo by Ethan DeWitt/New Hampshire Bulletin)
Warmington was the only democrat on the Executive Council — an elected body unique to New Hampshire that serves as a check on the governor — from 2021 to 2025. This is her second run for governor. In 2024, she was defeated in the primary by Manchester Mayor Joyce Craig, who ultimately lost to Ayotte.
Warmington was a health care attorney and lobbyist before entering elected office. Among her clients were Purdue Pharma, the drug manufacturer largely blamed for the opioid crisis, and an opioid clinic chain. Ayotte has repeatedly used her work with Purdue to attack Warmington, saying, “We can’t elect an opioid lobbyist to be our governor.”
Warmington has in turn attacked Ayotte’s record, specifically budget cuts she signed into law, the school voucher-like Education Freedom Account Program she expanded and, especially in the later days of the campaign, her opposition to marijuana legalization.
In a second term, Ayotte says she wants to implement the housing bills she signed into law and continue focusing on public safety.
Warmington has promised to reverse the budget cuts, legalize marijuana, and dismantle the Education Freedom Account Program.
Both candidates are now calling for a moratorium on new data centers amid intense public pushback.
A battle in the 1st District
Anthony DiLorenzo celebrates his primary victory as confetti flies over him in the Music Hall Lounge in Portsmouth after the Sept. 8, 2026 election for New Hampshire’s 1st Congressional District. (Photo by William Skipworth/New Hampshire Bulletin)
In the first Congressional District, which covers Manchester, Laconia and the Seacoast, Democrat Stefany Shaheen faces Republican Anthony DiLorenzo.
Shaheen is a former Portsmouth city councilor. She’s also the daughter of Sen. Jeanne Shaheen. The younger Shaheen has tried to center health care in her campaign in opposition to Trump’s biomedical research cuts and Health Secretary Robert Kennedy Jr.’s antivaccine efforts.
DiLorenzo is a Portsmouth car dealer who owns more than 20 dealerships. He’s tried to pitch himself as a pragmatic businessman who can fix problems in Washington, D.C. He’s argued he’ll bring fiscal responsibility to Congress.
Shaheen has supported a single-payer Medicare for All system, something DiLorenzo opposes. She also pitched reforming ICE, the agency behind Trump’s controversial mass deportation effort, though when she’s pressed on the issue, she has been inconsistent about whether that means she wants to “dismantle” ICE.
Left: Anthony DiLorenzo speaks to supporters in the Music Hall Lounge in Portsmouth after winning the Republican nomination for New Hampshire’s 1st Congressional District in the Sept. 8, 2026, primary. Right: Stefany Shaheen speaks to supporters at an election results watch party in Portsmouth on Sept. 8, 2026. (Photos by William Skipworth/New Hampshire Bulletin)
DiLorenzo has said he wants to keep transgender men out of women’s restrooms and sports teams and he wants to protect the 2017 tax cuts Trump signed into law during his first term. But he’s often tried to balance conservative ideals with moderate proposals in the historically purple district. For example, DiLorenzo says he opposes federal abortion legislation.
Stefany Shaheen, left, former Portsmouth City Councilor and daughter of a former governor and U.S. senator, speaks to Secretary of State David Scanlan in his office before filing paperwork her own campaign for Congress on June 11, 2026. (Photo by William Skipworth/New Hampshire Bulletin)
DiLorenzo earned the president’s endorsement but has refuted Shaheen’s accusations he’d be a “rubber stamp” for Trump’s agenda.
Democrats have accused DiLorenzo of hiding much of his wealth on his financial disclosure forms by placing many of his assets into trusts so that his net worth appears lower than it actually is. DiLorenzo has defended the move by arguing it was done to protect his businesses, the money he wants to leave to his family and the charitable causes he donates to.
Republicans, on the other hand, have accused Shaheen of nepotism. DiLorenzo has consistently said he doesn’t believe she’d be on the ballot if her last name wasn’t Shaheen. He calls her “Silver Spoon Shaheen” in campaign ads.
A rematch in the 2nd District
New Hampshire’s 2nd District covers the western half of the state, including Nashua, Concord, and West Lebanon.
Here, Democrat Maggie Goodlander is again facing Republican Lily Tang Williams. The two battled for the seat in 2024 but this time Goodlander is the incumbent.
Originally from Nashua, Goodlander is now a freshman representative who lives in Concord. She had an eventful career in Washington, D.C. before returning to her home state to run for Congress. There, she worked at the Justice Department under Biden; as a foreign policy adviser for the late U.S. Sens. John McCain and Joe Lieberman; and as a clerk to former U.S. Supreme Court Justice Stephen Breyer.
Lily Tang Williams, left, and Maggie Goodlander, right, participate in a candidate forum hosted by NHPR and the Granite State News Collaborative during their previous campaigns on Monday, Oct. 28, 2024. (Screenshot: NHPR | NHPBS | Granite State News Collaborative)
Williams was born in China but moved to Colorado in 1999. There, she had a few unsuccessful campaigns for public office as a libertarian. She then moved to New Hampshire as part of the Free State Project — a political migration movement in which a group of libertarians have attempted, with varying success depending on who is asked, to move to New Hampshire and transform the politics — though she denies involvement with the group today. Williams also ran in 2020 but did not secure the GOP nomination.
U.S. Rep. Maggie Goodlander speaks to reporters in the New Hampshire Secretary of State’s Office on June 12, 2026. The congresswoman had filed for reelection prior, but came to the State House during the filing period to meet with supporters, journalists, and the secretary of state ceremoniously. (Photo by William Skipworth/New Hampshire Bulletin)
Goodlander has touted her vote for the bipartisan 21st Century Road to Housing Act, Congress’ biggest housing legislation in decades. She has also tried to position herself as someone who will vociferously oppose the Trump administration. She’s cited her work on lawsuits against his tariff policies and opposition to the war in Iran.
Williams has tried to cast herself as more centrist this cycle. She’s pitched congressional term limits, banning stock trading by members of Congress and an amendment to the Constitution mandating a balanced budget.
In previous campaigns, she’s been criticized for being too far right. She faced allegations of antisemitism for sharing memes online that claim the Holocaust was spurred by Jews who “gave up their firearms to Hitler.” And during a 2024 debate, she declined to say that Biden defeated Trump in the 2020 election.
Lily Tang Williams files paperwork to run for the U.S. House of Representatives in New Hampshire’s 2nd Congressional District on June 4, 2026 in the secretary of state’s office. This is her third time running for the seat. (Photo by William Skipworth/New Hampshire Bulletin)
In the primary, Goodlander faced progressive attacks, particularly over her vote for the Laken Riley Act. Goodlander was one of 46 House Democrats who voted for the bill, which was pushed by Republicans following the death of a Georgia nursing student at the hands of an immigrant. Progressives and immigration advocates argued the law disregards immigrants’ due process rights, gave too much power to state attorneys general, and empowered ICE ahead of a series of aggressive crackdowns in Minneapolis, Chicago, and elsewhere. Opponents also argue crimes by immigrants are rare and that Riley’s tragic death was an outlier. Progressives have also criticized her for being noncommittal on Medicare for All, and for her past support for military aid to Israel (though her stance on the issue has changed and she voted for an unsuccessful effort to cut aid to the country and called for a “reset” on the U.S-Israel relationship).
Getting to the polls and voting
The polls will open at varying times on Tuesday morning depending on the municipality. Voters can find out where their polling location is and which races will be on their ballot on the Secretary of State’s website at https://app.sos.nh.gov/pollingplacesampleballot. New Hampshire allows same-day voter registration. To register to vote on Election Day, voters will need to provide proof of their identity (driver’s license, government-issued photo ID, or passport), age (also driver’s license, government-issued photo ID, or passport), U.S. citizenship (birth certificate, passport, naturalization papers, or other proof), and domicile (government-issued ID or documentation with an address on it).

text:
Participants in a welding program for minimum-security inmates are pictured at Southeast Technical College in Sioux Falls, South Dakota, on Oct. 7, 2024. (Photo by John Hult/South Dakota Searchlight)Inmates in the Sioux Falls area can now access Pell Grants to pay for slots in welding courses in the community and diesel mechanic courses inside prison walls.
Students can apply for federally funded Pell Grants to help them pay for post-secondary education. Since 2023, inmates in the U.S. have been allowed to apply for and receive them through a program called Second Chance Pell Grants, which can be used to pay for courses offered through institutions with approved programming for prisoners.
Southeast Technical College’s application to offer Second Chance-eligible programming was approved in the past month, according to the school’s president, Corey Clasemann.
Clasemann made the announcement during last week’s meeting of the Correctional Rehabilitation Task Force, a group that counts Clasemann as a member. The task force tentatively endorsed the use of Pell Grants for inmate skills training as part of a broader, 34-point package of rehabilitation-focused recommendations, to be compiled and voted on next month. The recommendations are a roadmap for reducing repeat offense rates in a state where half the people released from prison return within three years.
Governor commits funding to revive training program for inmates

The school’s welding program began five years ago, and tuition for the inmates who leave the prison campus in Sioux Falls for job training has thus far been paid for through grants administered by the state Department of Labor. That money ran out this fall.
Now, inmates who want to participate will need to fill out a Free Application for Federal Student Aid, Clasemann said, “just like any other student,” to determine their eligibility, although they need to use a paper form, not the online version.
The first Pell Grant-funded cohort in the welding program will begin in January, Clasemann said.
Pell Grants will also be available for students in a diesel mechanic program, which the school is setting up in the South Dakota State Penitentiary’s Jameson Annex.
Last year, Gov. Larry Rhoden gave Southeast Tech a $1.5 million grant to help fund that setup, pulling money from the Future Fund. That pool of money is built from fees collected from South Dakota employers when they remit payroll and unemployment taxes.
Southeast Tech also plans to have a satellite campus on the grounds of a $650 million men’s prison under construction in Sioux Falls. That facility will replace the oldest parts of the 144-year-old penitentiary. Jameson, the state’s only maximum-security facility, will remain in service after completion of the new prison. The first diesel training courses are scheduled to begin next August. 
Southeast Tech is the third tech school in South Dakota to be approved for Second Chance Pell Grants. Western Dakota Technical College in Rapid City offers a plumbing program for men at the state’s Rapid City minimum-security prison, and a hospitality program for inmates at the new women’s prison in that city.

Both major party candidates for Mississippi’s U.S. Senate seat in Tuesday’s midterm election have tagged their opponent with snappy, derisive nicknames.
Democratic challenger Scott Colom refers to Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith as Cindy High Prices. It is not clear whether High Prices should be hyphenated.
Hyde-Smith has labeled Colom a “Transgender Defender.”
Colom said he calls the incumbent Cindy High Prices because she has been unwilling to oppose President Donald Trump on his tariffs, his war with Iran and other issues that Colom argues have resulted in higher prices on gasoline, diesel and most retail items.
During a Trump rally last week in Corinth in northeast Mississippi, Hyde-Smith referred to Trump  as “the best president of our lifetime.”
On the flip side, why does Hyde-Smith refer to her challenger as a “Transgender Defender?” Colom, a district attorney for four counties in the Golden Triangle area, did sign a letter in 2021 stating opposition to “the criminalization of transgender people.” But he has said he opposes gender-affirming surgeries for minors, which have not occurred in Mississippi and are rarely performed nationally and then only with parental consent.
Colom told MPB in a recent interview, “Listen, I have two daughters. I believe in fairness in girls’ sports, and I don’t believe in gender-affirming surgery for children.” 
Still, fearmongering about transgender people should not be surprising. It is a tactic as old as the country for politicians to leverage people’s unease about minorities to further their own electoral goals.
Black people, gay people, immigrants and others have faced the scorn of politicians. 
In recent election cycles, the nation’s very small transgender community has been the subject of the ire of Trump and other politicians. In 2023, Mississippi Gov. Tate Reeves, facing a tough reelection campaign, accused Democratic challenger Brandon Presley of supporting transgender issues. It was in many ways the central theme of Reeves’ campaign, even though it was not an issue that affects most Mississippians’ daily lives.
In 2024, Trump used many of the same arguments against his Democratic opponent, Kamala Harris.
Now, President Trump and others are canvassing the nation before the midterm election campaigning for Republican candidates for the Senate and House and making outrageous statements about the transgender community.
At Corinth, Trump said Democrats “promote the transgender mutilization of your children,” meaning, presumably, mutilation.
A recent analysis by The Associated Press showed Republicans have spent an estimated $183 million on television ads attacking Democrats on the transgender issue.
Perhaps, the component of the issue that resonates the most with voters is what appears to be overwhelming opposition to “boys or men playing sports against girls or women.” Or, in other words, many say they are opposed to transgender athletes competing against people who were identified as female at birth.
A recent YouGov poll highlighted the opposition, with 51% strongly opposed and 11% “somewhat opposed” to transgender women competing in female sports categories, but the poll also identified many misconceptions on the issue.
For instance, despite the NCAA specifically limiting participation in female sporting events to only athletes who were female at birth, only 31% of respondents said correctly that less than 1% of NCAA female athletes were transgender.
In addition, according to the poll, 15% said they think up to 5% of the athletes competing in female events were transgender and 14% said they think up to 25% of the athletes were transgender.
It is obvious that a sizable number of politicians believe focusing on the transgender issue and attacking transgender people, regardless of the facts, can help them win elections.
It is an often-used strategy: Try to increase turnout by scaring voters.

text:
Volunteers who helped repair the Barre ice rink gather for a photo in Barre on Friday, October 30, 2026. Photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger

BARRE — On an October afternoon four days away from opening night, the Barre BOR Arena, with a coat of fresh paint and the ice bright and smooth, was quiet and still. 
It’s hard to imagine that just a week earlier, the rink was nothing but a concrete slab with more than a dozen people racing around the clock to fix the rink’s many broken pipes in time for the winter season. 
“There were 14 plumbers in this trench right here from different companies in central (Vermont),” said Trym Chouinard, one of the volunteers. “They all compete for the same jobs, get what I’m saying? But they’re all standing here together, working together for a common cause.” 
The Barre city manager first announced on October 1 that the rink might not open due to the discovery that the pipes that cool the ice had broken down. That closure meant that hockey teams, figure skaters and local enthusiasts might have to crowd into other local rinks, costing them valuable practice time and the loss of a venue where they love to skate. 
Chouinard, owner of a general contracting company, was devastated. His family donated some money to help build the rink in the 1970s. Chouinard once played hockey in this rink, and his kids now play youth travel hockey. 
“It’s a huge investment of time and money, but they love to play it,” he said. 
He’s not the only volunteer with a personal connection to the ice. Soon after the announcement, Chouinard got a call from Ed Patterson, a heating business owner whose son is a goalie for the Spaulding High School hockey team. 
“He called me in a tizzy and said, ‘This is ridiculous, and ‘We got to do something,’” Chouinard said. 
Ultimately, the effort to fix the ice pulled in more than 20 volunteers, according to Tom Baker, Barre’s facilities director. Not only did volunteers contribute roughly 160 man hours, but local businesses donated supplies and provided materials at a steep discount. 
On October 23, city manager Patrick Cushing said via press release that the issue had been completely resolved. He thanked the volunteers for making it happen. 
“Committing City cash reserves alone to another repair attempt with an uncertain outcome would have been difficult to justify,” he said in the press release. “The donated labor and  materials allowed us to make that attempt while limiting the demand on those reserves.”
Baker said the problems with the rink weren’t new, only the scale of it. 
“When you touch something that’s 50 years old, it’s an old system, and you touch it here, and then it breaks,” he said.
Earlier this month, Barre city mayor Thom Lauzon said it was only a matter of time before the rink would need a more permanent upgrade beyond the recent repairs. 
“I think we got a little complacent and figured, ‘OK, if there’s a problem, we’ll just fix it,’” Lauzon said at the time. “And it’s time to take a real hard look at replacing the system. I don’t want to go through this again.”
But repairing the rink has benefits, too. Lauzon said the arena earns the city about $130,000 in revenue each year, primarily from the cost of rink rentals. 
Chouinard pointed out that the arena is also relatively affordable compared to other local rinks. The BOR costs $220 per hour to rent, according to the city’s website. Four other arenas within a one-hour drive of Barre range from $235 to $265 per hour to rent, according to a VTDigger review of rink websites. 
Rink costs are one factor in why hockey is one of the most expensive youth sports, so anything that can keep costs down is essential. 
“You need to have this stay as a community rink,” Chouinard said.

title: Commentary: The vote that will reveal the most about Arkansas’ politics
description:

Hester’s the outgoing Republican Senate president pro tempore and Tucker’s a Democrat from Littl[...]
text:
Voters cast their ballots during the March 3, 2026 primary in Little Rock, Arkansas (Photo by Katie Adkins/Arkansas Advocate)Try as hard as you can, but you’re unlikely to find two Arkansas legislators as far apart ideologically as Bart Hester and Clarke Tucker. 
Hester’s the outgoing Republican Senate president pro tempore and Tucker’s a Democrat from Little Rock who ran for Congress eight years ago. The two state senators have been on opposite sides of issues spanning from tax policy to culture war fights. 
So it’s not a small feat that the two have paired up in an ad touting a ballot measure on economic development as something both conservatives and progressives can love.
Normally such a bipartisan front would be a sign that there’s broad enough support for this proposal that it’ll be a slam dunk on election night. 
[Voter Guide: 2026 General Election Voter Guide: The candidates, the ballot measures, and the tools you need to cast your vote.]
Instead, there’s more uncertainty surrounding the proposal — Issue 3 — than just about anything else going before Arkansas’ voters this year. It’s unlikely to gain attention outside Arkansas, especially compared to potentially competitive races for the U.S. Senate and a Little Rock-area congressional seat.
But the outcome of the vote on the proposal could reveal a great deal about the state of Arkansas’ politics, and the divides confronting legislators when they meet next year.
Referred to voters by the majority-Republican Legislature, Issue 3 would permit lawmakers to create programs, loans and grants using public money for the purpose of economic development. 
If approved, the amendment would give legislators the authority to pass laws allowing local governments to create economic development districts where incentives like tax rebates could be negotiated to attract new business to a designated area. 
Supporters of the measure say it’s a needed tool to help Arkansas compete with other states and have pointed to communities they say would benefit from such districts. It has the backing of the state’s top elected officials and the state’s business lobby.
But the proposal is going before voters during a midterm marked by a wave of anti-incumbent and anti-establishment feelings.
The uncertainty surrounding Issue 3 is underscored by recent polling from Talk Business & Politics and Hendrix College. The poll from early October showed more than one-third of those surveyed undecided about the measure, with 27% for it and 38% against. The poll had a margin of error of plus or minus 5 percentage points.
Opposition to the proposed amendment created strange bedfellows, with conservative activists and some Republicans speaking out against the measure and saying it gives the Legislature too much power on the rules for these districts.
It’s also drawn the ire of some progressives who say it’s a handout for businesses and the wrong approach for growing the state’s economy.



Let us know what you think...


 


In many ways, the objections to the proposal mirrored the bipartisan opposition to data centers in Arkansas and nationwide. Supporters say the measure isn’t intended to incentivize new data centers, but it’s running into suspicion from voters who felt burned by a lack of transparency. 
It’s also coming up for a vote as lawmakers brace for renewed discussion about the Generating Arkansas Jobs Act, which allows utilities to charge ratepayers immediately to recover construction costs for new projects. 
Hearing complaints from farmers and other ratepayers about increased bills, some lawmakers who backed the legislation last year say they regret the decision.
A defeat or even a squeaker of a vote in favor of Issue 3 could signal a difficult road ahead for the business lobby, which may be playing defense on the Generating Arkansas Jobs Act, data center regulations and other issues in next year’s session.
It may also indicate establishment lawmakers from both parties have to grapple with a populist backlash that crosses party lines.
Hester and Tucker have found an issue to agree on. The question is which bipartisan coalition will win that argument.

title: Will Vermont history repeat itself with another November nail-biter?
description:

Seen all the stories about the Vermont Republican governor facing a headline-grabbing challenge from an upstart Democrat?
Former[...]
text:
The Rutland Herald went to press around 2 a.m., on Nov. 7, 1984, with a headline deeming Vermont’s gubernatorial race “A Draw” before switching it around 4 a.m. to report Madeleine Kunin’s victory. Photo by Kevin O’Connor/VTDigger

Seen all the stories about the Vermont Republican governor facing a headline-grabbing challenge from an upstart Democrat?
Former Gov. Jim Douglas has — although he’s not talking about this fall’s contest between incumbent Phil Scott and challenger Amanda Janoo. Instead, the 75-year-old retiree is referring to his own 2004 reelection bid against then-Burlington Mayor Peter Clavelle.
“Was I concerned about the horse-race coverage?” Douglas recalled in a recent interview. “Yeah. It’s hard to ignore completely. But if I were obsessing over every story and every poll and every pundit commentary, I’d be distracted from the job to which people had elected me.”
Vermonters haven’t witnessed a close gubernatorial contest for 10 years — specifically, when Scott won his current post with 52.9% of the vote against Democrat Sue Minter in 2016. Since then, the Republican has increased his margin to 55.2% against Christine Hallquist in 2018, 68.5% against David Zuckerman in 2020, 71% against Brenda Siegel in 2022 and 73.4% against Esther Charlestin in 2024.
That momentum could shift Tuesday, when Scott faces Janoo, who the American Prospect reports “is running the most credible Democratic campaign for governor of Vermont in a decade.” If the race is a nail-biter, the Republican will be in good company: All four of his living predecessors — Madeleine Kunin, Howard Dean, Douglas and Peter Shumlin — can each tell tales of their own cliffhangers.

The Caledonian-Record of Aug. 14, 1946, reports World War II hero Ernest Gibson besting Vermont Gov. Mortimer Proctor in that year’s Republican primary. Photo by Kevin O’Connor/VTDigger

Kunin: ‘Whisker-close’
Only two Vermont governors have lost a race for reelection: Mortimer Proctor, unseated in the 1946 Republican primary by his successor, World War II hero Ernest Gibson; and F. Ray Keyser, a fellow GOP incumbent who was upset in 1962 by Philip Hoff, the first modern-day Democrat to win the state post.
Squeaker votes have been far more common. Kunin made history in 1984 with her election as Vermont’s first and so far only female governor. But the now 93-year-old Democrat had to wait until the morning after the polls closed to learn of her razor-thin victory.
Kunin, a former state legislator and lieutenant governor, and her Republican opponent, then-state Attorney General John Easton, campaigned neck and neck all fall. The late Saint Michael’s College professor Vincent Naramore, considered “the father of Vermont polling,” released what he called a “whisker-close” survey that October that showed Kunin at 43.8% and Easton at 43.2%. 
On Election Day, newspapers told the same story. The Burlington Free Press carried the headline “Too Close to Call,” while the Rutland Herald bannered the question “Who Will It Be?”
At 8:35 p.m., the first round of results found Kunin leading Easton, 54% to 45%.
By 9:40 p.m., Kunin’s margin had shrunk to 50% to 49%.
By 10:30 p.m., she was ahead by a single vote.
“The larger Democratic towns had given me a substantial early margin,” Kunin recalled in her 1994 autobiography “Living a Political Life.” “But when the rural towns started dribbling their votes in, my advantage began to erode.”
At 2 a.m., with results continuing to trickle, the Herald printed a front page with the headline “A Draw.” 
At 3 a.m., Kunin announced she was going to bed.
Around 4 a.m., the Herald stopped the press to swap “A Draw” for “Kunin” — news her opponent confirmed when he conceded the race at noon.
The final results: Kunin 116,938 (or 50%), Easton 113,264 (48.4%) — a difference of 3,674 votes.

The Rutland Herald of Nov. 8, 2000, reports that year’s presidential and gubernatorial results with the headlines “Cliffhanger” at 1 a.m., “It’s Bush, Dean,” at 2:15 a.m. and “Bush? Dean!” at 3:30 a.m. Photo by Kevin O’Connor/VTDigger

Dean: ‘Quite an uproar’
Kunin won two more terms before giving way to Republican Richard Snelling, who returned to the governorship in 1991 after serving from 1977 to 1985, only to die in office from cardiac arrest seven months later.
Enter Dean, who was juggling jobs as a physician and part-time lieutenant governor when he took over for Snelling. The now 77-year-old Democrat easily won election in 1992 (74.8%), 1994 (68.7%) and 1996 (70.5%) before besting Republican state Rep. Ruth Dwyer by a closer 55.7% to 41.2% margin in 1998.
Then in 1999, the Vermont Supreme Court ruled that same-sex couples had the legal right to marriage benefits, spurring Dean to sign a first-in-the-nation law establishing civil unions in 2000. The separate-but-equal compromise angered both voters who saw the differentiation as discriminatory (the state would move to marriage for all in 2009) and those who opposed any deal.
“It was quite an uproar,” recalled Dean, who wore a bulletproof vest on the campaign trail. “There were pretty hostile groups that would harass us, and we were getting death threats from all over the country.”
Dean went on to win 50.4% of the vote in a race that rematched him with Dwyer (who received 38%) and added Progressive candidate Anthony Pollina (who received 9.6%). But Dean’s victory wasn’t the biggest news of the night. The Herald had to stop the press and switch its headline twice to keep up with the ever-evolving presidential race between Republican George W. Bush and Democrat Al Gore.
“Cliffhanger,” the front page read at 1 a.m.
“It’s Bush, Dean,” it read at 2:15 a.m.
“Bush? Dean!” it read at 3:30 a.m. — a question that lingered until the U.S. Supreme Court ruled in the GOP candidate’s favor a month later.

The Burlington Free Press of Nov. 6, 2002, reports Jim Douglas’ first win as governor. Photo by Kevin O’Connor/VTDigger

Douglas: ‘Could go either way’
As Dean prepared to leave office in 2002 to run for president, Douglas launched a bid to replace him.
The Republican was 21 when he won election to the Vermont House in 1972, then served as secretary of state from 1981 to 1993 and state treasurer starting in 1995. He was in the latter post when he ran in a three-way-gubernatorial race against Democrat Doug Racine, then lieutenant governor, and independent Cornelius “Con” Hogan, former head of the Agency of Human Services.
The Sunday before the 2002 election, Douglas picked up the Burlington Free Press — then the state’s largest newspaper — to see a banner headline summing up its exclusive poll: “Racine takes 10-point lead.”
“I got on the phone with my pollster,” the Republican recalled, “and he said, ‘I don’t believe it. I think this is dead even. Could go either way.’ I had to get the message out to as many of my supporters as I could that we’re going to keep working as hard as we possibly can in the final 48 hours, and we did.”
Two days later, Douglas topped the tally with 44.9% of the vote, followed by Racine at 42.4% and Hogan at 9.7%. In response, his Democratic challenger quickly conceded and asked the Legislature to confirm the results (under a state provision, lawmakers have the final say on races won by less than 50% of all ballots).
Douglas was grateful to his opponent. He was less forgiving of the press and the last-minute poll, which its creator blamed on surveying voters on Halloween, “a night when fewer Republicans might have been home.”
“After this,” Douglas wrote in his 2014 autobiography “The Vermont Way,” “I became increasingly skeptical of those in the media who never left their urban offices, but made prognostications as if they knew what they were talking about.” 

The Burlington Free Press of Nov. 6, 2014, reports Gov. Peter Shumlin’s close reelection. Photo by Kevin O’Connor/VTDigger

Shumlin: ‘You have moments’
Douglas was reelected three times before Shumlin succeeded him in 2010. The now 70-year-old Democrat won a close first race against then-Republican Lt. Gov. Brian Dubie by 4,331 votes. But that was a seeming landslide compared to Shumlin’s bid for his third and final term in 2014.
His Republican opponent, Pomfret travel agent Scott Milne, was summed up in one press profile as a “reluctant candidate” who, breakfasting on oatmeal and dry wheat toast at Berlin’s Wayside Restaurant, “managed to spend an hour inside the crowded diner a month before Election Day without introducing himself to a single voter.”
Nonetheless, Shumlin reaped only 2,434 more votes than Milne on election night. The 46.5% to 45.2% margin sent the race to the Legislature, which didn’t confirm the results until January.
Politico blamed the incumbent’s numbers on “stagnant middle-class wages and high property taxes,” technical problems during the rollout of Vermont Health Connect and the candidate’s out-of-state travel as chair of the Democratic Governors Association. 
Shumlin had a different take.
“Nobody is very happy with incumbents,” he said in 2015. “I understood if I put forth a really aggressive agenda on all fronts, it wasn’t going to be a ticker-tape parade.”
Mowing the fields around his Putney home last week, Shumlin said the campaign trail was equally cutting.
“You have moments when it gets personal and less civil where you go, ‘I really want to do this job, but is this really worth it?’” he said in an interview. “That stuff really eats at you. But I loved being governor — in my view, it’s the best job in the world — so I don’t regret a minute of it.”
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Will Vermont history repeat itself with another November nail-biter?.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: CT’s most vulnerable immigrant children face new hurdles to legal status
description:

text:
Each year in Connecticut, thousands of immigrant children — some of whom arrived unaccompanied — apply for legal authorization to live in the U.S. through the federal immigration system. 
Under President Joe Biden, a growing number of those applicants petitioned for a legal status known as Special Immigrant Juvenile Status, SIJS, an option specifically designated for children and young adults under 21 who have been abused, abandoned or neglected by a parent. 
But lawyers representing SIJS applicants say the process, which starts in state court and then heads to the federal government for approval, can be expensive and emotionally taxing. Under the Trump administration, they say, the process has gotten more complicated — adding fear and anxiety for kids in especially difficult circumstances, living in a new country and processing traumatic experiences.
Applicants start in Connecticut probate court, and lawyers say children in some areas — specifically Bridgeport and Naugatuck — often face scrutiny from probate judges that’s not related to the federal application requirements. In these courts, lawyers say, children who should easily qualify are instead being interrogated about whether they speak English or how good their grades are.
The hurdles don’t stop there. The number of applicants for special status plummeted this year, partly due to fears of being deported mid-process. In immigration court proceedings, some people with the status are being told to leave the country, even though it historically allowed them to stay.
“I have had a client with this status be ordered removed from the United States,” Addie Dickens, an attorney with Connecticut Legal Services, said. “I’ve also had and know about more cases where children, because of how hostile it is right now in immigration court, have chosen to self-deport out of fear, returning to situations where they weren’t safe to begin with.”
The children and young adults applying for this status are increasingly choosing between two difficult options: sharing their traumatic story and risking deportation, or returning to the traumatic situation.
“We’re talking about cases of rape and sexual assault and violence and really horrible situations,” said Meghann LaFountain, an immigration attorney and director of legal services for the nonprofit advocacy group Building One Community. “You’ve prepared this child to have to talk about all of these things, just to be told, ‘No, I really don’t think that you should stay here.'”
A wave of applicants
Before 2021, there were only a few hundred SIJS petitions filed in Connecticut each year. But in 2021, more than 400 were filed. This number roughly doubled each of the next two years and topped 1,700 in 2024 and 2025.

This year, the number of applications filed will likely be much lower. In the first six months of 2026, only 551 petitions were filed in probate courts, less than half the number filed during the same time period in 2025.
SIJS petitions surged in early 2025 before dropping off later that year. The number of petitions filed in the first half of 2026 was half that filed during the same period in 2025. 
The influx of applicants followed a sharp increase in the annual number of unaccompanied minor-aged immigrants released by the U.S. Department of Homeland Security to sponsors in Connecticut. 
Unaccompanied minors entering the state hit a peak of 1,441 in 2021 and lingered above 1,000 each year until last year. Just 196 children entered Connecticut in 2025.
LaFountain and other lawyers attribute the decline in applicants to several factors, including an overall drop in international migration to the United States under President Donald Trump. And among immigrants already living in the U.S., there’s rising wariness that petitioning the government could lead to detention and deportation. 
“We’ve seen a lot of fear around not only the federal government but also state governments and seeking state services,” said Caroline Sennett, the chief legal program officer at the Connecticut Institute for Refugees and Immigrants. 
At each step of the process, new barriers
For those who set out to obtain Special Immigrant Juvenile Status, lawyers say there are increasing challenges and potential setbacks at every step of what’s already a complex process. 
An applicant first petitions a state court to sort out their guardianship. This may mean removing an abusive parent as their guardian and establishing another relative or foster parent in place of the parent. 
In June, the Department of Homeland Security sent a letter to state courts calling the SIJS program “rife with fraud” and urging them to “probe” applicants for specific details in their cases.
“The failure of state court judges to police the requirements of the SIJ process leads to tangible harm,” the letter reads. “It allows criminals, gang members, and even suspected terrorists to obtain lawful status, while eroding public trust and diverting court resources away from genuinely vulnerable children.”
But Connecticut lawyers say these vulnerable people are being turned away from the program because of state judges. In Connecticut, an applicant’s prospects can vary widely from one court to another. 
There are 54 regional probate courts and six regional children’s probate courts in Connecticut. State judges who take these cases look for proof that applicants cannot safely return to their home country, have been abused, abandoned or neglected by one or both parents, and that reunification with a parent is not possible. They also make decisions on guardianship based on state law and verify that applicants are unmarried and under 21, according to USCIS.
LaFountain and another lawyer who did not want to be named out of fear of retribution for their clients said Bridgeport’s probate court denies cases for reasons beyond the requirements. Presiding Judge Paul Ganim — the brother of Bridgeport Mayor Joe Ganim — frequently inquires about an applicant’s academic performance and proficiency in English, according to lawyers.
“I have had him ask questions … ‘What are your grades in school? Why do we want you here if you aren’t speaking English and your grades aren’t good?'” LaFountain said.
“When you’ve gone through trauma, it can be really hard to keep your grades up. It can be really hard to learn a new language because you have all this trauma, even just the trauma of getting to the U.S. and being in a new place and not being with your family or friends that you’re used to being around is traumatic,” LaFountain said. “So when you add on all of the extra things that have happened to someone, it can be really bad.” 
SIJS status is available to applicants up to age 21, but lawyers said Ganim isn’t inclined to approve it for applicants once they’ve turned 18. He also is hesitant to reassign guardianship if the child is getting proper medical and academic needs met under their current care, they said.
This leaves LaFountain offering clients what some may consider extreme advice: “Either move out of Bridgeport, or you have to be ready to appeal your case.”
Lea Oliveira, an immigration attorney based in Stamford, said she feels similarly about the Naugatuck probate court, which denied several of her clients’ petitions. Because of the denial rate, she doesn’t take cases out of Naugatuck anymore.
Representatives for the courts declined to make judges available to comment for this story.

The courts don’t release any information on decisions. But a count of appeals — attempts to overturn a judge’s decision on an SIJS case — shows that Bridgeport hears the most appeals yearly. Waterbury Regional Children’s Probate Court, which includes Naugatuck, heard the second-most in 2025 and 2026.
Some probate courts handle cases very differently, Oliveira said. She said she’s seen court staff hand out toys to children, for example. Often, hearings in other courts are brief, lasting just 15 minutes and ending in approvals, she said.
“I don’t see any other reason to deny SIJ cases, because they are so straightforward,” Oliveira said. “It’s black and white: If one of the parents abandoned the child, they shouldn’t give a hard time for the child to have the SIJ approved.”
Even the filing fees can vary from court to court, starting at $250 plus processing fees. In some courts, applicants must cover the cost of both the SIJ petition and the petition for change in guardianship. And some charge for other services such as printing or newspaper publishing. Some fees can be waived, but those decisions are made on a case-by-case basis.
LaFountain said she encourages clients whose probate cases have been denied to appeal. There’s a better chance of getting approved because appeals are handled in a separate court, she said. 
But they don’t always follow her advice. It can be difficult to tell and re-tell a traumatic story in a court setting, LaFountain said. And for some clients, the additional step is just not affordable.
Appeals can also become a race against the clock, since immigrants are only eligible to apply for SIJS status with USCIS until age 21.
What comes next
Once a probate court approves a case, obtaining SIJS status from U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services is relatively straightforward. 
To apply, immigrants file an I-360 form to USCIS. This form includes questions about the filer’s abuser, their immigration process and their nationality. With an approved I-360 petition, applicants officially have Special Immigrant Juvenile Status.
But the process doesn’t end there. SIJS holders must apply for a green card. There’s currently around a four-year waiting list for approval. 
While they wait, SIJS holders could be targeted for removal — adding another layer of anxiety to the process. In the past, SIJS applicants had deferred action, allowing people who did not have an immigrant visa immediately available to adjust their status to lawful permanent resident. If the U.S. opened removal proceedings against an SIJS recipient who was waiting on a green card, the case would typically be administratively closed, dismissed or terminated by an immigration court judge, allowing the applicant to wait out the green card backlog.
Under the Trump administration, that’s no longer the case. In a decision last year, the U.S. Department of Justice found that administrative closures can no longer be used in immigration court, even for SIJS recipients, and deferred action for most SIJS holders was terminated in 2025. The Board of Immigration Appeals ruled that administrative closure was intended to be a “docket management” tool, not a form of relief from removal.
In Hartford immigration court, these three outcomes — administrative closure, termination or dismissal — were most often used in removal cases dealing with young people, including some SIJS applicants. Today, they are rarely used.

The federal government has issued public statements reiterating that an approved I-360 form granting SIJS status is not a protection against deportation. 
“[DHS is] pursuing to return them to the same country where they don’t have a viable guardian and where it’s not in their best interest to return,” Dickens said. “Beyond whether it’s legal or not, it’s just morally horrifying to see what’s happening to families right now.”
Dickens said because of these changes, DHS might decide to deport a person even though an arm of that same agency, USCIS, has approved the person’s SIJS status. 
“I used to feel like, well, at least I can help someone get status and have the possibility of a better future. But now it feels like we’re unable to help people right now because of the changes in law,” Dickens said. 
A spokesperson for USCIS said the status has been abused in the past. 
“The Special Immigrant Juvenile (SIJ) program has long been used by criminal aliens, including gang members, seeking to infiltrate our country by masquerading as SIJs,” USCIS spokesperson Zach Kahler said in an emailed statement. “State court judges are the first line of defense in this process as they make determinations based on state law about dependency or custody of juveniles.”
Sennett said her organization, CIRI, is seeing more cases where the young person may qualify for SIJS status, but they’re now too afraid to go through with it — which leaves them in a vulnerable position. 
“If people are afraid to access the courthouses, if people are afraid to file any application with immigration, then they aren’t going to get to the first part of the process,” she said.

text:
Advance voting was underway Oct. 26, 2026, at the Lyon County Courthouse in Emporia. (Photo by Max McCoy/Kansas Reflector)In just 48 hours, Kansans will have a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity to shape history.
The opportunity is unexpected — and unexpectedly urgent.
I was thinking about that urgency the other day when I was part of a television panel discussion about politics at a public television station in Kansas. The set was quaint, as you might expect, and on a side table next to the host was a miniature wooden globe in a square stand. I wanted to pick up that globe, hold it to the camera and say we must meet the moment because this is what’s at stake.
I didn’t, but in my mind, I started writing this column.
This year’s midterm election has been called a “unicorn” for red America by a major political analyst. In Kansas, the surprisingly competitive U.S. Senate race has drawn the attention of the nation. For many, the race is a referendum on what may be the most corrupt administration in American history — and a repudiation of the phalanx of legislative quislings that keeps it in power.
While pundits have treated the dead-heat between incumbent Roger Marshall and challenger Adam Hamilton as a political singularity — after all, no Kansas Democrat has been elected to the U.S. Senate in nearly a century — the close race isn’t being held in a vacuum. It’s a sign of the growing resistance to authoritarianism, and not just in America.
In the past week, a student-led movement against corruption toppled 14 years of a repressive regime in Serbia. In Brazil, the beleaguered incumbent made a surprising political comeback against the far-right candidate who was expected to win. What happens in Europe or South America isn’t a prediction of what will happen here, but it is a semaphore of change.
We are witness to a historic political realignment in America. It’s difficult to see the outlines while being tossed about in the middle of it, but it appears to be on the same order that shook the nation over slavery in the 1850s or the Civil Rights movement of the mid-20th century. Every election is a throw of the dice, but even if the midterms don’t reshape the balance of legislative power — and two days out there is reason to believe it will — neither party will emerge from the fray unchanged. The cult of Trump is collapsing, leaving Republicans with empty sails and no rudder, while Democrats are learning again how to navigate by the brightest and most constant stars.
The ancient stain of slavery and the fight for equality are still problems Americans struggle with today. But if we do not put out the immediate fire in the kitchen of democracy, there may be no house left standing in which to debate anything other than the depth of our misery.
The American experiment, battered these last two years by a regime that has thrown away the hard-won lessons of two centuries and surrendered its humanity for a few crypto-coins to rub together, may yet be renewed.
We stand at the threshold of that renewal.
Kansas has oft been the wheel upon which American history has turned, beginning with its admission to the union as a free state in 1861, on the eve of the Civil War. It also produced one of our better presidents, Dwight D. Eisenhower, who was ranked fifth best by a C-SPAN survey of historians in 2021.
Eisenhower, whose hometown was Abilene, was the American general who commanded Allied forces in Europe during World War II. He oversaw the invasion of Normandy in 1944, a bloody but necessary assault that eventually broke the Nazi stranglehold on Europe.
In 1952, as the Republican nominee, Eisenhower was elected president. During his inauguration he offered a civic prayer for the nation. I’m not ordinarily a fan of public prayers, but my religion is democracy and our best hopes for the future are often supplications to a higher power within ourselves.
Eisenhower prayed for the ability to discern right from wrong, to be guided by the law of the land, and for the compassion to work for all Americans, regardless of “station, race or calling.”
When Eisenhower gave his farewell address in 1961, after two terms as president, it signaled the Sunflower State’s waning influence on national politics, Sens. Bob Dole and Nancy Kassebaum excepted.
You can scarcely read a history of Kansas without stumbling over the famous dictum by small-town newspaper editor William Allen White that, “When anything is going to happen in this country, it happens first in Kansas.” White, writing in 1922, was referring to movements including abolitionism, prohibition and populism.
“These things come popping out of Kansas like bats out of hell. Sooner or later other states take up these things,” he wrote.
The modern reader stumbles over this quote not only because it is now a century out of date, but was out of date just 20 years after White wrote it. As H. Edward Flentje points out in “Reform and Reaction: The Arc of Kansas Politics,” White wrote in his 1940s autobiography that his once-progressive Republican Party had become “chastened, weary, and disillusioned.”
By 1983, syndicated columnists Neal R. Peirce and Jerry Hagstrom had hammered a nail into the coffin of Kansas politics in their book, “The Story of America: Inside the Fifty States Today.” They described the Sunflower State as “scarcely the place where things happen ‘first.’ Indeed, nowhere on the American continent can the eclipse of a region or a state as a vital force — a focal point of creative change or exemplar of national life — be felt so strongly and poignantly as in Kansas.”
It has been a long time since any bats have popped.
This is not to say that Kansas is a hellish state. The recently released Kansas Speaks public opinion survey indicates that 77% of respondents believe the state is a good to excellent place to live. However, a deeper question about whether the state was on the right track resulted in a deep division, with 41% saying the state was on the “wrong track” compared with 37% of right trackers. The remaining 22% said they didn’t know.
The Peirce-Hagstrom obituary for Kansas influence is now 43 years old, and most Kansans weren’t even born when it was penned. The median age for the state is 37, according to the Kansas State Data Center at the University of Kansas. That means that our median-age Kansas voter has only been eligible to cast a ballot since 2007.
Their first presidential election would have been a year later, and if they voted for Democrat Barack Obama — as did 514,000 Kansans, 42% of the state total — their vote didn’t matter because of the winner-take-all Electoral College system. All of the state’s six Electoral College votes went to Republican nominee John McCain. That’s the way it has been for more than six decades, because the last time Kansas went for a Democrat for president was in 1964, with Lyndon B. Johnson.
For the U.S. Senate, the streak is even longer.
If you’ve paid even cursory attention, you’ve probably heard that when it comes to the Senate, Kansas Democrats have the longest political drought in American history. That’s one of the reasons that being a Democrat or an independent in Kansas can feel like being a small blue bubble tossed about on an ocean of red.
With state politics, it’s different.
Kansas is not averse to letting a Democrat take a turn at being governor, and three of those Democrats have been women, including the term-limited outgoing governor, Laura Kelly. It’s also historically different for the 3rd District of eastern Kansas, which encompasses much of the Kansas City metro area, where incumbent Democrat Sharice Davids is seeking her fifth term.
If you live in other parts of the state, voting for Democrats running for national office can seem futile. Among the state’s 2 million registered voters, 44% are registered Republicans and just 26% are Democrats, according to the Kansas Secretary of State.
But not all voters have declared a party, and about 29% are unaffiliated. Another 1% or so identify with small parties.
The more you look, the less red the state becomes.
Especially now.
The question that has been repeated over the last two years is this: When will Americans have had enough?
We may have found the limit.
The most distinctive feature of this satiety is anger.
There are plenty of targets at hand for this fury, from the price of a gallon of unleaded gasoline ($4.08 on Interstate 35 as I write) to the rising cost of food at the local grocery store. A roast for family dinner now costs $20. Whether you’re filling up the car or trying to put a meal on the table, these prices are being driven up by the ill-advised war with Iran, now in its eighth month. Things may get worse soon, because the Trump administration has warned Gulf States to prepare for a major U.S. offensive after the midterms. So far, the war has cost the U.S. government $47 billion, imposed death and human suffering on both sides, and wasted what remained of America’s global influence.
But voter anger is rooted in more than senseless war and rising prices.
There is a longing for the competence and decency that once guided America. If you are the aforementioned Kansan of median age, then you may remember that first vote you cast, in the 2008 presidential election. Never mind who you voted for. Think for a moment about the character of the candidates. Both Obama and McCain were motivated by a clearly articulated set of values. Even if you didn’t agree with them, you could understand them. Both men shared an essential decency, even though their backgrounds could hardly have been more different.
Remember how, a month before the election, McCain defended Obama as a “decent family man, citizen” when a voter at a political town hall in Minnesota brought up a worn conspiracy theory. Can you imagine that same kind of decency in national politics today from the Trump-addled Republican Party?
I long for the days of McCain. I think many of us do.
In 1961, Eisenhower gave his farewell address to the nation, and that speech is remembered today for his warning against establishing a “military industrial complex.” But the fullness of his thoughts bear repeating now.
Americans, Eisenhower said, expect their president and Congress “to find essential agreement on issues of great moment, the wise resolution of which will better shape the future of the nation.” The nation’s prestige depends not only on riches and military strength, but on how that power is used in the interests of world peace and humanity.
“As we peer into society’s future,” he said, “we — you and I, and our government — must avoid the impulse to live only for today, plundering, for our own ease and convenience, the precious resources of tomorrow. We cannot mortgage the material assets of our grandchildren without risking the loss also of their political and spiritual heritage. We want democracy to survive for all generations to come, not to become the insolvent phantom of tomorrow.”
Three days later, Democrat John F. Kennedy was sworn into office.
In that C-SPAN survey I mentioned earlier, Kennedy comes in eighth. The first spot is held by Abraham Lincoln. Trump is near the bottom, at No. 41, just above Pierce, Johnson and Buchanan. But you have to remember the survey was conducted just after Trump’s first term.
In 2024’s Presidential Greatness Project, a survey of presidential scholars, Trump came in dead last.
Trump came to Kansas on Oct. 19 in a panicky rescue. A second trip, a Halloween rally planned for Salina, was canceled and then rescheduled for Sunday.
In the Park City visit nearly two weeks ago, in a speech laden with racist tropes and vulgar language, Trump declared: “When you see burning steeples and raging fires in France, just remember that is what the radical Dumocrats want to ​do to America.”
It’s too bad that Eisenhower isn’t around to give Trump a history lesson about burning steeples and raging fires in France.
In February, Pete Hegseth — Trump’s secretary of defense — attempted to move the historic globe Eisenhower used during the invasion of Normandy. Hegseth wanted it for his office, but in his haste some unskilled workers dropped the globe and broke it, according to the Washington Post, smashing Antarctica and detaching it from the mounting ring that allowed it to rotate.
It is a metaphor for the Trump administration’s misuse of American power.
That Kansas is among the few states that will decide control of the U.S. Senate is reason to hope for the future, no matter the outcome of the current contest. There are signs of a return to the progressive ideals that make human freedom and dignity possible.
There may be strife to come, but that Kansas is again at the forefront of national politics is the answer to a civic prayer whispered by many conscientious and decent individuals of both parties, or of none, for the last two years.
What will the world be after Tuesday?
It’s up to us to help decide.

text:
“Hello, darkness, my old friend, I’ve come to talk with you again”

Simon & Garfunkel 1964

Yes, daylight savings time is gone again… sooner this year than normal as November 1  is the earliest date for the change allowed by law.  
They say we’ve “gained an hour,” but it sure doesn’t feel like that.  And with the shift of clocks back an hour, we’re going to see ever-earlier sunsets and darkness… as early as 4:45 p.m. this week and 4:21 p.m. by early December. 



That means our evening commutes will be in the dark, presenting new dangers.
A 2025 study in the Journal of Safety Research found fatal pedestrian and cyclist crashes rose 13 percent after the fall time change.  And researchers at Carnegie Mellon say the pedestrian death risk at 6 p.m. in November is 11 times higher than at the same hour in April.
It’s also rutting season for deer, and about three-quarters of deer crashes with cars happen outside daylight.  Connecticut had 417 such incidents from October to December 2023.  Nothing ruins a car quite like hitting 200 pounds of amorous venison.
And don’t even get me started on the “jetlag” we all feel adjusting to the clocks this week.  And that clock on your dashboard… how long will it still think it’s daylight savings time?
As for auto accidents involving other cars, reviewing University of Connecticut data from 2020 to 2024, Connecticut crashes in the 5 p.m. hour were 35% higher in November than October.  Pedestrian crashes in that hour were up 147%!
If you must walk at night, wear white.  Or better yet, a reflectorized vest so drivers can see, and hopefully, not hit you.
For senior citizens, night driving always presents problems.  It’s both biological and psychological.
By age 60, our eyes need three times as much light as they did at age 20, because pupils shrink and don’t open as wide in the dark. A 60-year-old’s eyes also take more than twice as long as a teenager’s to adjust from light to darkness.
Seniors already reluctant to drive at night are now less likely to go out for dinner or evening events if they don’t feel safe on the roads.  You may think of the “early bird special” as a dining bargain.  Seniors think of it more like a curfew.
One of the biggest problems for drivers of any age, as I wrote about last year, is the glare of oncoming headlights.  There are several reasons that headlights appear so bright. 
The first is that the headlights may not be properly aligned, aiming too high, right into your eyes.  And with more vehicles riding higher from the road (think SUVs and trucks), their headlights shine more directly into oncoming traffic.
Most problematic are the new kinds of headlights.  The older incandescent (yellowish) lightbulbs are being replaced by LED or xenon lights, which are blue-white and more glaring to your eyes.
Oncoming headlights, especially the bluish ones, cause the pupils in your eyes to constrict rapidly, temporarily blinding you until the oncoming vehicle passes and your eyes adjust.
What can you do to stay safe? 
When bright lights come at you, don’t look into the oncoming beam.  Instead, look to the right edge line of the roadway (a.k.a. the “fog line”).  Flip your rear-view mirror to its night setting, or use an auto-dimming mirror.   Most of all, slow down!  Being blinded on darkened roads, especially if they are coated with wet slippery leaves, is dangerous.
So hang in there, fellow motorists.  It’s only about 130 days (and long nights) ‘til we change the clocks again.

text:
Open enrollment for Affordable Care Act insurance plans begins Sunday through Dec. 15 for coverage that takes effect at the start of next year. For policies that take effect Feb. 1, 2027, open enrollment is available through Jan. 15. (Photo by Joe Raedle/Getty Images)Millions of Florida residents who purchase their insurance policies on healthcare.gov can begin shopping Sunday for coverage to take effect next year.
Twelve companies will offer so-called Obamacare plans on the healthcare.gov marketplace, where subsidies are available to lower the costs of monthly premiums, the Florida Office of Insurance Regulation website shows. Another three are offering Obamacare-compliant plans outside of the healthcare.gov.
The OIR data show the average 2027 monthly health insurance premiums will increase by 10.4%, a  percentage that doesn’t take into consideration the potential impact of premium subsidies.
Enrollment in healthcare.gov is open through Dec. 15 for coverage that takes effect at the start of next year. For policies that take effect Feb. 1, 2027, open enrollment is available through Jan. 15.
“Our navigators are prepared to really help people understand what might best fit their needs and to support them with making important decisions about accessing care,” Xonjenese Jacobs told the Florida Phoenix.
Jacobs is director of Florida Covering Kids and Families, which receives the federal grants to support navigation services across the state. This year’s grant is $1.379 million, which mirrors what it received last year but is a 90% reduction from 2024, when it received $13.79 million.
Florida Covering Kids and Families Director Xonjenese Jacobs (Photo via University of South Florida)
Florida Covering Kids and Families has contracted with five other navigator groups across the state to ensure they are ready to assist people in need of their services.
More than 3.85 million Floridians residents enrolled in the federal health insurance exchange and paid their first month premium to effectuate their 2026 coverage. That was a 10% dip from the 4.3 million who effectuated policies on the federal exchange in 2025.
That represents 450,000 people. Whether they became uninsured, purchased individual policies outside the exchange or enrolled in an employer sponsored health insurance policy isn’t clear yet, because 2026 uninsured rates won’t be released until next year. Florida had a 13.6% uninsured rate in 2024, before elimination of the enhanced premium tax credits that helped lower the costs of the policies.
The Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services projects that national health expenditures will exceed $6 billion in 2026 — a 6.3% jump over 2025 expenditures — and will top $6.3 billion in 2027, or $18,295 per person. Health expenditures are projected to account for 18.8% of the gross domestic product in 2027.
Jacobs maintains that people understand the importance and financial security that health insurance offers and think creatively to keep their policies, despite the rising costs.
For some people on the marketplace, that means switching from a “platinum” or “gold” plan — with higher monthly premiums but lower deductibles — to a “bronze” plan, for which premiums are lower but deductibles — amounts people must pay for care before the coverage kicks in — are higher.
Some people under 30 years old who are shopping on healthcare.gov marketplace can choose a catastrophic plan, which has the highest deductibles and the lowest monthly premiums.
“There are numerous options in the marketplace. There are many alternatives for what people have in terms of their selection,” she said. “We have grown into a culture that really understands and values the needs for access to healthcare, and I think people are willing and wanting to make a way because they simply require this.”
 Another way?

For people who cannot afford Affordable Care Act (or Obamacare) policies, Jacobs said, navigators can make referrals to federally qualified health centers and lower-cost charitable clinics.
Catalina “Cat” Jaramillo, a 43-year-old woman from Miami-Dade County who owns her home and loves her three dogs, is one of those people.
For years, she said, she went uninsured and “didn’t care.” All that changed in her late 30s, when chronic back pain drove her to a hospital, where she was diagnosed with kidney disease.
Open enrollment for Jan. 1 health insurance coverage ends Dec. 15.
She bought an Obamacare plan. 
“Thankfully, that covered my medication. I was able to see the specialist. I developed a relationship with them and I progressively got better,” she said during a Florida Voices for Health media availability last week.
But in 2026, she lost access to the enhanced tax credit that helped offset the costs of her policy. Her monthly premiums jumped from $180 a month to more than $1,000.
“The increase was just way too high. I couldn’t afford it,” she said.
Now she goes to Community Health of South Florida, a federally qualified health center where she can tap into care at a lower cost. For about $180 a month, she said, she can see her kidney disease specialists and get prescriptions to treat her ADHD and depression.
Jaramillo’s “very grateful to have this resource” but knows it’s not the same as her Obamacare plan, a health insurance policy that’s sold to qualifying individuals regardless of pre-existing medical conditions. The policies are required to cover 10 essential benefits, including emergency care, hospitalizations, maternity and newborn care, and prescription drugs. 
“The other day, I had to go to urgent care, and I’m not looking forward to that bill,” she lamented. “But you know, it’s something that was inevitable.”
 $18K in premiums annually

Dave Waalewyn is a commercial pilot who lives in Leesburg and long relied on his employer for health coverage. Waalewyn found himself without health insurance after his former employer, Spirit Airlines, ceased operations earlier this year.
For the first time, Waalewyn had to procure an individual health insurance plan and turned to a broker recommended to him by his financial adviser. They found a plan on the so-called “private” market, outside the federal healthcare exchange, that cost $800 a month. Because it doesn’t have to comply with Obamacare regulations, the policy was medically underwritten, meaning he had to answer questions about his medical history.
Waalewyn is required to pass Federal Aviation Agency screening to fly, and he has. That’s why he said disclosing the results of an abnormal stress test and a follow-up heart catheterization that showed “a trivial amount of plaque” didn’t cross his mind when he shopped for his policy.
“So, as far as I was concerned, everything was fine. So, I signed up for this $800 a month policy. About a week later, I get a letter in the mail saying, ‘Hey, what’s going on with this medical information? You know, you didn’t tell us about this,’ ” Waalewyn recalled.
Leesburg commercial airline pilot Dave Waalewyn turned to healthcare.gov for his health insurance after losing access to his employer-sponsored plan. (Screenshot Florida Voices for Health press conference Oct. 26, 2026)
Out of an abundance of caution lest the carrier deny future claims, Waalewyn said, he walked away from the non-Obamacare plan and turned to healthcare.gov. Eventually, he chose a policy that costs $1,500 a month.
“Luckily, today I start a new job and I will have medical insurance starting in December, so I don’t have to, you know, worry about that anymore until I go on Medicare at the end of the year next year in 2027,” he said.
If not for getting hired by another airline, he said, he would have paid $18,000 annually for his Obamacare policy. That doesn’t include deductibles or co-pays.
 No ACA protections

Carson Hornish is a health insurance broker in Tampa. He has clients who are enrolled in the healthcare.gov marketplace and says for those who qualify for the remaining tax subsidies (as opposed to the lapsed enhanced subsidies) that lower the costs of monthly premiums, there’s not a better plan out there.
“So, I’m never gonna push somebody away from Obamacare, especially if we’re getting a subsidy,” he said.
But he has clients who purchase what he calls “private” plans.
Carson Hornish, broker Carson Health Advising (Photo via Hornish)
Those plans are medically underwritten and not required to be issued to everyone. They aren’t required to cover mental health, substance abuse disorders, or prescription drugs. And while Obamacare plans cannot contain lifetime caps or annual limits, insurance companies can limit what they spend on policyholders’ care annually or over a lifetime. 
Those caveats have led some, including the American Lung Association, to describe them as “junk plans.” 
It’s what more of Hornish’s clients and prospective clients are looking for these days.
“I wanna say 1,000% with 100% confidence,” Hornish told the Phoenix when asked whether more people are asking him for non-ACA coverage. 
He also says that just because non-ACA-compliant plans aren’t required to meet all the requirements in the federal health care law, it doesn’t mean the plans don’t offer benefits.
“With the private marketplace, I can find whatever plan tailored for whatever person that needs coverage. So, if someone comes to me, saying, ‘Hey, I want mental health,’ well, I’m going to show them the plan that’s going to cover mental health. But it might not cover pregnancy, right?”
